11009-labor-s-martyrs-haymarket-1887-sac:
Vito Marcantonio and William Z. Foster wrote this short labour pamphlet linking two famous cases. On November 11, 1937, fifty years after Albert Parsons, August Spies, Adolph Fischer, George Engel, and Louis Lingg were executed in Chicago.

The pamphlet places Haymarket beside Sacco and Vanzetti, Tom Mooney, and the Scottsboro defendants, arguing that employers used courts to crush unions. It also credits the 1886 strike with giving the American Federation of Labor a mass base. Short and polemical, the book serves readers of labour history who want the left's own account of Haymarket, written as a memorial, not a neutral trial history.
15539-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's children's weekly for May 13, 1897 repeats the atlas offer from the week before. A Rand McNally 1897 Atlas of the World goes to any subscriber who brings in a new yearly subscription. The atlas, 160 pages of colored maps from new plates, is pitched as up to date, unlike an old atlas, which the editors compare to an old directory.

News inside turns to floods in the Mississippi Valley. A cloudburst swells a river past its banks, drowning about one hundred persons and leaving two thousand homeless, by the paper's report. Hopeful news follows: the river falls slightly in some districts, though in places it runs sixteen miles wide below New Orleans. The number mixes a sales push with sober disaster news, told plainly for young readers.
5930-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
A puppet show drives chapters twenty-six through twenty-eight of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter twenty-six continues the droll adventure of the puppet showman, as watchers hang on the interpreter's lips in silence, Tyrians and Trojans alike, until drums and trumpets sound. Chapter twenty-seven shows who Master Pedro and his ape were, and chapter twenty-eight records matters that Benengeli says readers will know by reading.

Readers get Quixote's most famous confusion of art and life, as a puppet battle moves him to draw a real sword. The chapters favor theatre, trickery, and the question of who tells a story truly. This part suits readers following volume two, since Master Pedro's show becomes a parable of Quixote's own madness and Cervantes's art.
arnald-villanova-opera-1527:
Arnald of Villanova's collected works fill this Latin Opera, in a 1527 printing. Arnald served as doctor to popes and kings across the medieval West. His writings span medicine, alchemy, theology, and sharp prophecies about the end of the present age of the world.

Few minds of the Middle Ages ranged so wide or worked so boldly. He reformed medical study, courted heresy charges, and still kept royal patients. Remedies sit beside visions in the crowded Latin pages here. The volume preserves the full mind of a versatile genius, a healer and prophet whom both church and court found hard to ignore.
arxiv-2509-00427:
Marius Băloi, working alone, presents a new approach in 2025 to constructing isogenies of elliptic curves in characteristic three. An isogeny is a structure-preserving map between elliptic curves, central to curve-based cryptography. Writing down the endomorphism ring of a curve, its ring of self-maps, amounts to solving a functional equation over rational functions, a hard task.

Instead of attacking that equation directly, Băloi first seeks formal endomorphisms, solutions in the larger field of Laurent power series. Separable formal endomorphisms match rational points of a plane cubic over that series field. A method then finds all formal separable endomorphisms in characteristic three. The detour through series may ease explicit isogeny construction.
arxiv-2509-00627:
Yuheng Zhang, with three co-authors, Miao Qiao, Zhencan Peng, and Dong Deng, addresses near-duplicate text alignment, finding all substrings in a corpus similar to a query. Older seeding methods lack accuracy guarantees and need many tuned settings, while min-hash methods ignore how important or frequent each token is.

Zhang and his co-authors propose MONO, which supports weighted Jaccard similarity, a similarity score that counts token weights, using consistent weighted sampling. They prove MONO is optimal within the hash-based framework and that its group count bound is tight. Experiments show index building up to twenty-six times faster, smaller indexes, and query times up to three times better than the prior leading method.
arxiv-2509-00927:
Masoud Bayrami, with two co-authors, studies non-minimizing critical points in cavity flow. The setting is axially symmetric cavity flow with a free boundary. Two-dimensional and axial cases have been studied qualitatively for years. Most results concern minimizers or stable solutions. Regularity of the free boundary is a focus of that work.

Much less is known about critical points that are not minimizers. Bayrami and his co-authors focus on properties of such points. They relate them to the known variational solutions. Their approach extends naturally to jet flow problems. That widens the class of free boundary flows it can address. The work fills a gap between stable solutions and the full critical set.
arxiv-2509-01127:
Magnetic particle imaging maps tiny magnetic particles inside the body, offering a way to track tracers without radiation. Asli Alpman, Mustafa Utkur, and Emine Ulku Saritas work on predicting the signals these particles give off under new test settings. Signal strength depends on the drive field, the fluid around the particles, and traits such as core size.

Their method builds a dictionary of simulated signals from a physical model of how the particles rotate. An iterative algorithm then fits weights and corrects for effects the model misses, such as the response of the measuring device. Alpman and the co-authors aim to let users forecast signals at untested settings without fresh calibration runs for each case.
arxiv-2509-01327:
Flows of complex fluids, from plastics to gels, are described at small scales by the Stokes equations, yet solving them fast and well for springy fluids is hard. Georg Rempfer, with five co-authors, presents an algorithm for an Oldroyd-B fluid, a standard model of a viscoelastic liquid. Their solver uses Fourier transforms, powered by a fast transform library.

The team validates the method on the four-roll mill, a classic flow with nearly singular stress points where fluid is stretched. Their solver captures that stress growth without the usual smoothing fix. They also characterize the power-law behavior near those points and test a criterion for when stress diverges. Future work targets active systems, moving boundaries, and microfluidic devices, where cheap accurate flow solvers are in demand.
arxiv-2509-01627:
Triangulations split a solid shape into tetrahedra, simple four-faced blocks. Geometers ask which splits can carry a true hyperbolic geometry. Ian Benway studies isolated geometric triangulations. In these, no standard small move leads to another geometric one. The moves swap two blocks for three, or three for two. Earlier work showed most key triangulations of cusped manifolds connect through those moves.

Benway shows isolation is not a quirk of small manifolds. He exhibits an endless family of once-punctured torus bundles. In each, the monodromy triangulation is isolated. Whole families of manifolds thus carry geometric triangulations stranded from their peers. The result sharpens the map of how geometric forms sit inside the wider space of triangulations.
arxiv-2509-02027:
Wenke Ren leads twenty-seven co-authors in a hunt for faint active black holes in distant star forming galaxies. Active galactic nuclei shine as gas feeds a central black hole. Broad emission lines are the telltale sign the team seeks with Webb infrared spectra. Their sample holds eighteen massive galaxies seen as they were when the universe was young.

Seven candidates emerge from dozens of aperture spectra centered on light peaks. One case is highly robust, with very broad lines, while six show narrower broad parts. Line ratio charts alone would miss them all, since they overlap normal galaxies there. Their black hole masses sit near or below the local mass relation, unlike overmassive finds elsewhere. Selection bias likely explains the contrast.
arxiv-2509-02227:
Qing Dai, Rasmus Ischebeck, Maruisz Sapinski, and Adam Grycner use large language models to mine tech docs from particle machines for skill at risk of loss. Old machines hold vast docs while staff with long skill retire, which puts know how at risk. Code based pulls can keep and pass that deep know how to new staff. Their study fits language models to this tight tech field of work.

First finds show models pull, sum up, and sort know how well from the docs. That cuts the risk of lost views as staff leave the labs in time. Caps are plain speech of the models and rare field terms, with fix plans pitched. The work casts language models as tools for care of deep field know how. Machine halls are the test bed, not the sole crowd in view.
arxiv-2509-02327:
I. Shavindra Jayasekera and five co-authors present a 2025 machine learning paper on measuring doubt in in-context learning, where a language model learns a task from examples inside the prompt. Knowing whether doubt comes from scarce examples or from noisy data guides trust.

Bayesian theory splits doubt into epistemic uncertainty, caused by missing knowledge, and aleatoric uncertainty, built into the task itself. Direct computation is intractable because the hidden parameter distribution cannot be sampled. The authors instead train probe queries that bound the aleatoric part from above, which also bounds the epistemic part from below. Tests on synthetic and real tasks show both parts behave as proper uncertainty measures should.
arxiv-2509-02627:
Jie Xiao, Mengye Lyu, and Shaojun Liu wrote a 2025 computational pathology paper on detecting mitosis, cell division, in whole-slide tissue images for the MIDOG 2025 challenge. Tumour, inflamed, and dead regions plus imaging artefacts create false alarms and missed cells.

Their two-stage design first uses an improved YOLO11x detector with attention and specialised convolutions to propose candidates at a low threshold, favouring recall. A ConvNeXt-Tiny classifier then filters the proposals, restoring precision. On a fused training set from three public sources, the pair scored clearly above the single-stage baseline, with the gain coming from precision at similar recall. The preliminary challenge score was lower, reflecting harder unseen data, and code is released openly.
arxiv-2509-02727:
Guillaume Gagné-Labelle, Vassil Atanassov, and Ioannis Havoutis present a 2025 robotics paper on teaching four-legged robots parkour-style skills: climbing, crouching, bridging gaps, and climbing stairs. Legged machines beat wheels on rough ground, but their moves need precise timing and they slip easily.

Rather than modelling every failure case, the team trains one generalist policy with reinforcement learning, where the robot learns by trial and error. The single policy rivals specialist policies trained as mixtures of experts. It also used only a quarter as many training agents. Experiments isolate which components of the generalist design matter most. The result argues that one broad policy can cover dynamic terrain skills once reserved for hand-tuned specialists.
arxiv-2509-03027:
Yu-Jan Wang and 5 co-authors reported 2025 observations of dusty, star-forming galaxies around distant quasars. The quasars sit inside enormous glowing gas clouds called ELANs, seen when the universe was at cosmic noon, its peak era of star birth. The team wanted to know whether such dense surroundings change how massive galaxies grow.

Using two radio arrays, they confirmed fifteen submillimeter galaxies as true neighbors of the quasars, all lying outside the central dark matter halos. Most showed split spectral lines, hinting at rotating disks or merging pairs. Their dust ran warm by the standards of such galaxies. Compared with field galaxies they looked much the same, though gas ran short inside the quasar halos themselves. The neighbors also seemed to trace wide, flat structures in space.
arxiv-2509-03127:
Antoni Wójcik and Jan Wójcik wrote a 2025 critique of a recent claim about light and entanglement. A team had reported breaking Bell's inequality, a limit that rules out many hidden-variable explanations of quantum effects, using photons that were not entangled. Since unentangled states are widely held to be unable to pass that limit, the claim drew sharp attention.

The authors rebuild the experiment in simplified, idealized versions. Their reading is that two steps create the appearance of a violation. One is postselection, keeping only chosen outcomes after the fact. The other is an unusual way of normalizing, or scaling, the counts. Together they yield numbers shaped like Bell correlations but without the meaning a true Bell test requires. The underlying multi-photon interference, they stress, stays valid and interesting.
arxiv-2509-03227:
Debashree Priyadarsini Das, Joy Ganguly, and Sasmita Mishra built a 2025 particle physics model linking dark matter, neutrino masses, and the cosmic matter imbalance. Their base is the scotogenic model, which adds an inert Higgs doublet and three heavy right-handed neutrinos to the Standard Model. That setup yields a dark matter candidate and explains tiny neutrino masses through a loop process.

The plain version underproduces dark matter for candidate masses in a stated middle range. The authors therefore add a dark sector and use two-sector leptogenesis, where decays in both sectors build the matter-antimatter asymmetry. A flavor symmetry disciplines the visible sector, and one shared phase drives all CP violation, the matter-antimatter distinguishing effect. Their numbers match the observed ratio of dark to ordinary matter density.
arxiv-2509-03427:
Pedro Correia and 4 co-authors brought hybrid homomorphic encryption to federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains models across devices while data stays local, but shared updates still leak information through reconstruction and membership attacks. Fully homomorphic encryption, which computes on encrypted data, protects updates at heavy cost in size and speed on small devices.

Their hybrid pairs a lightweight symmetric cipher, PASTA, with a full encryption scheme, BFV. Clients encrypt updates with PASTA and send the cipher key itself encrypted under BFV. The server then decrypts homomorphically and aggregates under BFV. A prototype on a standard federated framework kept accuracy within a small margin of plaintext on a handwritten digit task. Upload bandwidth fell by orders of magnitude, while server cost ballooned, a trade-off flagged for future work.
arxiv-2509-03527:
Bohdan M. Pavlyshenko wrote a 2025 research paper on analysing cryptocurrency news at several levels with a tuned language model. News about digital coins moves fast and carries sentiment that traders watch closely. A single summary often misses structure across many stories.

His system fine-tunes a Mistral 7B model, adjusted cheaply with a method called LoRA, and pairs it with retrieval of source material. At the first level it produces graph summaries, text summaries, sentiment scores, and structured JSON versions of each summary. Higher levels stack those outputs, merging summaries of summaries into broad reports. Representing news as a knowledge graph, a network of linked facts, is presented as a way to curb invented details. Results are described as useful qualitative and quantitative analytics.
arxiv-2509-03927:
Finitely constrained groups, a family Grigorchuk introduced that arises by closing regular branch groups, are examined in a 2025 mathematics paper by Santiago Radi. Branch groups act on rooted trees in a self-similar way, splitting into copies of themselves at every branch. 

Three properties turn out to coincide across a vast subfamily: finite generation, being just-infinite, and strong completeness. A striking consequence concerns the Hanoi towers group on three pegs, whose closure is just-infinite even though the group itself is not. An older enumeration algorithm, from Bondarenko and Samoilovych, is sharpened and used to list examples acting on the ternary tree at small depths. A sufficient condition also identifies when a Mealy automaton, a finite machine reading and writing symbols, generates a group whose closure has finite type. An isomorphism test completes the small-depth classification on binary and ternary trees.
arxiv-2509-04027:
Zeyu Gan and two co-authors' 2025 research paper explains why the length of chain-of-thought reasoning settles at an optimum. Modern language models reason better with long chains of thought, and reinforcement learning tunes how long those chains grow. Empirically the length converges instead of expanding forever, but token-level analysis cannot explain the pattern.

Their framework, CoT-Space, recasts reasoning as optimisation inside a continuous semantic space at the level of reasoning steps. The trajectory is modelled through two lenses, noise and risk, reviving classical learning theory. Convergence to an optimal chain length then falls out naturally from a fundamental tension: shorter chains underfit the problem, longer chains overfit it. Reinforcement learning elicits and verifies the predictions experimentally. The findings explain test-time scaling through reinforcement learning. Practitioners gain a foundation for shaping reasoning trajectories instead of tuning lengths by trial and error.
arxiv-2509-04127:
J G Fischer and three co-authors present newly found Arabic accounts of two historic exploding stars in a 2025 research paper. Which leftover cloud matches the supernova seen in the year 1181 is still disputed. Reports were known only from China and Japan until now. A praise poem for Saladin, written in Cairo by Ibn Sanā' al-Mulk, is re-dated here to late 1181 or early 1182. It mentions a new bright star.

Details in the poem place that star near Cassiopeia and rate it brighter than one of that group's known stars. The timing and position fit the 1181 event well. A second Cairo text, by historian al-Maqrīzī, adds an Arabic account of the supernova of 1006.
arxiv-2509-04227:
Jian Lu and two co-authors compute the size of special number sets built from two different bases in a 2025 mathematics paper. Most numbers can be written in a base system in several ways, but some have exactly one expansion. The univoque set collects those single-expansion numbers. When both bases match, earlier researchers proved the set's fractal size, its Hausdorff dimension, changes smoothly with the base. Unequal bases lacked formulas until now.

Explicit formulas for both dimension and the entropy, a disorder measure, of the underlying shift system are derived here. Both quantities vary smoothly as the two bases change. Results extend to related systems, binary shifts with a hole among them, including the doubling map and Lorenz maps.
arxiv-2509-04427:
Jordan A Bartlett and one co-author, Henry A Kobulnicky, report starlight polarized more efficiently than the usual limit allows toward a bright star in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Interstellar dust both reddens starlight and aligns its polarization, and corrections usually average over huge sky areas. The team used polarization measurements, public dust maps, and Gaia distances for twenty-five stars near the star zeta Ophiuchi. Two separate dust layers emerged, at different distances with different magnetic orientations.

Removing the nearer layer exposed the farther one's extreme efficiency, above the canonical Serkowski limit. That distant dust aligns with glowing hydrocarbon striations seen in infrared images, hinting the same grains cause both. Distance-aware foreground subtraction proves essential for reading layered dust.
arxiv-2509-05427:
Accreting neutron stars may glow in distinct gamma-ray lines, Alexander A. Mushtukov and three co-authors calculate in a 2025 astrophysics paper. In X-ray pulsars, matter falls onto a neutron star at huge speed, and nuclear reactions near the surface can emit photons at fixed energies.

The authors model how those lines are produced and how bright they should appear. Bright pulsars slow incoming matter with their own radiation, which suppresses the lines, while strong magnetic fields create electron and positron pairs whose annihilation adds another line. Their numerical framework includes light bending from gravity and magnetic absorption. The result maps where future gamma-ray missions could detect the lines and probe neutron star structure.
arxiv-2509-05727:
Structured light shaped like a skyrmion keeps its topological pattern through turbulent air, Zhenyu Guo and seven co-authors demonstrate in a 2025 optics paper. Skyrmions here are vortex-like textures of light's polarisation, and complex media usually scramble such structure, blocking uses in communication and sensing.

The team built classical and quantum optical skyrmions and sent them through experimentally simulated atmospheric turbulence. Classically the vector pattern scrambled, yet the skyrmion stayed stable through its built-in topological protection. In the quantum case entanglement faded while the topological character held. Analysis and simulation tie the shared behaviour to the states' non-separability. Noise-resistant information channels are the long-term prize.
arxiv-2509-05827:
A new way for one word to cover another is defined in a 2025 paper by Panagiotis Charalampopoulos and five co-authors. In their notion, a short word covers a longer one when its occurrences as a subsequence, letters in order but not necessarily adjacent, touch every position. They call such words subsequence covers, or s-covers for short.

Testing a candidate cover can be done in linear time for alphabets of moderate size, and a shortest cover can also be found that fast when the alphabet is fixed. Words with no proper cover of this kind are named s-primitive, and the authors bound how long such words can be; both bounds grow exponentially with alphabet size. The problem sits between classical covers and harder shuffle powers, giving string algorithms a fresh middle case.
arxiv-2509-06027:
Generating a sound that matches both a text prompt and a personal reference clip is the task DreamAudio takes on, in a 2025 paper led by Yi Yuan with seven co-authors. Ordinary text-to-audio models align with the words but cannot control the fine acoustic character of a specific sound. Users who need their particular event, not a generic one, are left short.

DreamAudio learns to extract auditory information from a few reference samples and weave those events into new audio that still follows the prompt. The team built two datasets for training and testing, plus a human-collected benchmark of real customization cases. Experiments show outputs consistent with the reference features and the text, and the system stays competitive on general text-to-audio work.
arxiv-2509-06127:
Signatures that hide the message and the signer's name at once are built from isogeny mathematics in a 2025 paper led by Soumya Bhoumik with three co-authors. Identity-based cryptography removes certificates by letting an identity act as the public key, while blind signatures let a signer sign unseen content. Their scheme, CSI-IBBS, merges both on the CSIDH framework of supersingular isogenies.

An honest zero-knowledge verifier component checks the signer's honesty without leaking extra information. Because CSIDH resists quantum attacks, the scheme targets post-quantum privacy applications. Security is analyzed in the standard model, and performance evaluation backs practical viability. The authors present the construction as a scalable step toward quantum-resistant, privacy-preserving signing.
arxiv-2509-06827:
The swirling water around a swimming alga is measured in three dimensions for the first time by Gregorius Pradipta and ten co-authors in a 2025 biophysics paper. A microorganism's flow field governs how it moves, feeds, and meets others. Capturing that field around a freely swimming cell had remained out of reach.

The subject is Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, a standard model for microbial swimming and flagellar motion. Time-resolved measurements, backed by hydrodynamic modeling, show how familiar two-dimensional features like in-plane vortices and a stagnation point arise from the full three-dimensional flow. Surprises include micron-sized vortex rings and repeating traveling vortices at very low Reynolds number, plus a structural change as the alga switches between puller and pusher styles. The three-dimensional field also sharpens estimates of the cell's energy use and its swimming and feeding efficiency.
arxiv-2509-07027:
Jisung Hwang, Jaihoon Kim, and Minhyuk Sung propose a new regularization for text-to-image models in a 2025 paper, based on Gaussianity of moments and power spectra. Their loss pushes samples toward a standard Gaussian shape. When samples follow that shape, later work in the model's latent space, where images are adjusted, becomes easier.

The method treats each entry of a high-dimensional sample as if it were a one-dimensional standard Gaussian variable. Its combined loss pairs a moment-based term, acting in the spatial domain, with a power-spectrum term in the spectral domain. The target values for both parts can be worked out in advance, so the loss rewards matching them. Inputs are shuffled at random so order does not matter. The authors also show that earlier Gaussianity methods sit inside their single unified framework.
arxiv-2509-07127:
Judging machine-drawn vector graphics the way humans do is the goal of a 2025 evaluation paper led by Leonardo Zini, with six co-authors. Generated SVG images are symbolic and resolution-free, so pixel-based metrics like FID or CLIPScore miss what makes them good or bad. A reference-based metric tuned to vectors was missing.

Their metric, SVGauge, combines two signals. Visual fidelity comes from image embeddings of a vision model, refined with principal component analysis and whitening to fit the domain. Semantic consistency compares a captioning model's description of the graphic against the original prompt, using sentence embeddings together with a term-weighting method. On a new benchmark built for the purpose, SVGauge correlated best with human judgments and reproduced the human ranking of eight zero-shot language-model generators more faithfully than existing metrics. The tool is offered for benchmarking future text-to-SVG systems.
arxiv-2509-07427:
Gravity slows time, so a light-speed trip through a dense star might beat a straight line across its surface. Shahar Hod explores that strange race in a 2025 research paper. For constant-density stars, earlier work found a critical density. Above it, a semicircular path between opposite points takes less time than the straight path through the center. Hod asks what happens for realistic stars with varied interiors.

Using analytical techniques, he proves a model-independent bound on the density parameter. Below that bound, every spherically symmetric compact object keeps the normal order: the central route is never slower. The proof holds regardless of the inner density profile. The result neatly illustrates general relativistic time dilation in strongly curved spacetime. It also pins down exactly when the surprising reversal can occur.
arxiv-2509-07827:
Paolo Ferragina and 1 co-author ask how small a piecewise linear approximation can possibly be, in a 2025 computer science paper. Such approximations summarise rising two-dimensional data with a chain of straight segments that stay within a set error. Learned data structures use them to store and search large datasets quickly.

The authors derive the first lower bounds on storage cost for these approximations, covering both compression and indexing settings. They then compare the bounds against known data structures to see which designs already sit near the limit. Knowing the floor matters: it tells engineers when a cleverer encoding can still save space and when the remaining cost is forced by the data itself.
arxiv-2509-08027:
Mars elevation maps get a machine-learning-ready training set from Rafał Osadnik and 3 co-authors in a 2025 dataset paper. Digital elevation models describe the height of the Martian surface, but building them from orbiter imagery involves complex pipelines that leave artefacts and gaps. Their dataset, MCTED, pairs high-resolution images with elevation data for direct learning.

A processing pipeline built on earlier Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX data produced nearly eighty-one thousand samples covering diverse terrain. Machines can now train to predict elevation from a single image, a shortcut around the heavy traditional processing. Reliable elevation models guide rover routes, landing site choices, and studies of Martian geology, so cheaper production has broad mission value.
arxiv-2509-08127:
Yi Wang gives a geometric test for when surgery on a knot-like space produces a left-orderable group, in a solo 2025 topology paper. Dehn filling closes a space by gluing along a chosen slope; left-orderability of the resulting fundamental group connects topology with algebra and with questions about flows on the space. Intervals of good slopes near the longitudinal slope are the prize.

The setting is a homology solid torus holding an essential free genus-one Seifert surface that is not a fibre. When the complementary piece is Seifert-fibred, or hyperbolic with a real place in its trace field, all small rational fillings on one side work. Criteria like this guide the search for orderable surgeries systematically.
arxiv-2509-08527:
Jia Choon Lee and 1 co-author generalize a spectral correspondence for parabolic Higgs bundles in a 2025 paper. Higgs bundles are geometric objects used in math and in theories of fundamental physics. The parabolic version adds marked points with extra data on a curve.

The relative moduli space, a space that lists all such bundles, is recast as a space of sheaves on a family of special surfaces. That view lets the authors describe the Hitchin map image through linear systems. They connect the geometry to the OK condition from six-dimensional field theory. Uses include proving spaces are nonempty and solving the Deligne-Simpson problem, including a stated conjecture.
arxiv-2509-08727:
Shixin Song and 6 co-authors introduce SecSep, a tool for securing cryptographic software, in a 2025 paper. Code that handles secrets must not leak them through timing. Spectre attacks, which abuse speculative execution in chips, added a new leak path in 2018.

SecSep rewrites assembly programs so secret and public data sit apart on the stack. A new typed assembly language, called Octal, recovers meaning lost during compilation and guides the rewrite. Tests on cryptographic programs allow safe speculation with low cost. The average overhead is just over one percent, far less than blocking speculation outright.
arxiv-2509-09727:
Andy Zhu and 1 co-author divide a tutoring job among specialised language model agents in a 2025 paper on financial education. Answering finance questions well demands several skills at once: stepwise arithmetic, exact terminology, and a feel for real scenarios. Single models often blur those demands, so the authors assign roles instead, letting each agent handle the part it suits best.

A base generator drafts an answer, a retriever gathers backing from six finance textbooks, and an expert reviewer critiques the draft before a final pass. On 3,532 expert-written study questions, the critique loop lifted accuracy by roughly seven to eight points over plain chain-of-thought replies. A small general model with the framework matched a finance-tuned specialist, the strongest score coming from Gemini-2.0-Flash.
arxiv-2509-09827:
Amit Kumar and 88 co-authors report optical afterglows for seven poorly located gamma-ray bursts in a 2025 astronomy paper from the GOTO survey. Wide-field space instruments often flag a burst within a huge error region, leaving its fading afterglow unfound. GOTO, a robotic telescope network with a wide view and sites in both hemispheres, races to those alerts and pins the glow down for larger instruments.

All seven long bursts were caught during 2024 after alerts from Fermi, MAXI, and other facilities. Big telescopes then measured redshifts for six, stretching from fairly near to very far, and read host galaxy fingerprints from absorption lines. Radio signals lingered for four events. Together the cases show a hard-spectrum population that quick, wide eyes can rescue from obscurity.
arxiv-2509-09927:
James Tian proves new results about random operator iterations in this solo 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is Hilbert spaces, where repeated averaging of operators is a basic tool. Tian shows that the leftover error in such random iterations shrinks at an exponential rate. This holds both on average and with near certainty. A single geometric quantity controls the rates.

From those results he builds a new object, random nonlinear fusion frames, where the building blocks arise step by step from the iteration's own residuals. These frames rebuild signals exactly and stay stable on average, with very fast sampling gains. They also cover known cases such as random projections and the randomized Kaczmarz method, tying operator theory to randomized algorithms.
arxiv-2509-10227:
Ángel Ladrón and seven co-authors build a machine learning pipeline that predicts how long aircraft parts can fly before fatigue failure in this 2025 aerospace paper. Spotting fatigue early keeps flights safe, but the standard engineering route is slow. It chains finite element simulations, load spectra, and cycle counting across several teams and tools.

Their pipeline takes the flight parameters of the missions an aircraft will fly and estimates fatigue life at different points on the wing. Tested on a realistic case, it gives accurate predictions backed by careful statistical checks and uncertainty estimates. The authors present it as a partner to traditional methods: fast learned estimates can guide decisions and cut the number of costly simulations engineers must run.
arxiv-2509-10327:
Zhejing Hu and six co-authors built MusicScaffold, a system that treats AI as a coach for teenage music makers. They describe it in this 2025 education paper. Teenagers often have strong creative urges. They have few strategies for shaping those urges, though, which leads to frustration. Ordinary AI tools remove the technical struggle. Yet they hand over finished output, teaching little.

MusicScaffold makes expressive strategies visible and learnable instead. It positions the AI as guide, coach, and partner. It also protects the student's own choices. In a study that ran four weeks, with students aged twelve to fourteen, the system had clear effects. It sharpened the precision of their musical thinking. It strengthened their self-regulation while creating. It raised their confidence in expressing themselves. The broader claim: in creative education, AI should scaffold growth rather than simply generate.
arxiv-2509-11427:
Ye Ji and 2 co-authors merge fluid simulation with design geometry in this 2025 paper. The lattice Boltzmann method is prized for parallel speed and simple boundaries, but its square grid turns curved walls into stair steps, which creates false forces near surfaces. Their isogeometric version solves the equations directly on the smooth spline shapes that engineers design with.

Working in strong form with high-order operators on exact geometry, the method keeps a uniform stream exact on curved grids. Standard tests, a lid-driven cavity, flow past a cylinder, and an airfoil, matched reference results closely on pressure and friction, with drag slightly high but shrinking under refinement. A note in the record says a corrected version of the paper will follow.
arxiv-2509-11527:
Pieter Allaart and Johannes Jaerisch settle a question about how rough a measure's spread function can be. This 2025 mathematics paper compares two forms of the pointwise Hölder exponent. The plain form gauges local growth. The sharp form first subtracts a best-fit polynomial curve.

The authors treat spread functions of Gibbs measures. The measures come from a Hölder potential on a self-conformal set. For these functions, the two exponents agree at every point. A very mild condition on the potential suffices. The sharp exponent always won before, so agreement is the news. A corollary follows. The pointwise spectrum obeys the multifractal formalism. The team applies this to conjugacy maps between expanding interval maps.
arxiv-2509-11627:
Jamal Wachira and Patrick Antolin watched rain fall on the Sun. This 2025 solar physics paper studies coronal rain. Cool plasma condenses high in the corona. It slides down magnetic loops. Three space instruments caught one full shower in November 2023. They were Solar Orbiter, the Solar Dynamics Observatory, and IRIS.

The falling clumps moved at tens of kilometers per second. Strong compressions ran ahead of them. Those were mostly isothermal. They seem to pump energy into the rain and brake it. On impact, the clumps lit up every extreme-ultraviolet channel. Hot rebound flows rose at about a million degrees. They refilled and reheated the loop. Their energy share was small next to the incoming motion. Footpoint heating matched the thermal non-equilibrium picture.
arxiv-2509-11827:
G. Harutyunyan and three co-authors watch one blazar across fifteen years of sky surveys. This 2025 astrophysics paper treats PKS 2155-304. It is a high-synchrotron-peaked blazar. Its jet points nearly at Earth. Gamma-ray, X-ray, optical, ultraviolet, and infrared monitoring spans 2008 to 2023.

The gamma-ray light curve splits into hundreds of epochs. They sort into quiescent states and four flare flavors. Each epoch's spectral energy distribution gets a synchrotron self-Compton jet model. A neural-network surrogate speeds the fitting. Tests show the jet's magnetic field shifting between states. Electron power, peak electron energy, and Doppler factor shift too. The jet's power is electron-dominated, not magnetic. Flares read as changes in acceleration efficiency and magnetization.
arxiv-2509-12427: Marek Lassak, writing alone in a 2025 geometry paper, gives three characterizations of reducedness for spherical convex polygons, shapes drawn on the surface of a sphere. A reduced body is one that does not properly contain another body of the same spherical thickness. The paper treats odd-sided polygons on the sphere, and the author notes that analogous characterizations also hold in the Euclidean and hyperbolic planes.
arxiv-2509-12827:
Ning Jia, Hamid R. Hamedi, and Jing Qian tackle a loss problem in non-linear optics in a 2025 paper. Four-wave mixing converts light from one frequency to another, but phase mismatch between the waves can severely limit how far and how efficiently that conversion proceeds. Their setting is an electromagnetically induced transparency medium, a material made transparent by applied fields.

Their optimal-control method applies fixed, linearly modulated coupling fields that induce a dark eigenmode, a state that avoids absorbing light. They globally optimize a single coupling detuning to minimize spontaneous emission loss, the main factor limiting efficiency. The approach outperformed current schemes, stayed robust against large phase-mismatch variations, and maintained efficient conversion from probe to signal. It could relax strict phase-matching requirements in tests.
arxiv-2509-13527:
Chemists hunting links between molecular structure and properties often lack large, clean datasets, a problem Yulia Pimonova and four co-authors tackle in a 2025 paper. Their method, LAMeL, is a linear meta-learning algorithm, meaning it learns from many related tasks how to start a new task well, while staying easy for humans to read.

Most tools treat each prediction task alone. LAMeL instead finds parameters shared across tasks, even when the tasks share no data, and uses that common structure as a starting point for unseen tasks. Across datasets it improves on standard ridge regression by factors from just over one to twenty-five, while keeping the plain, interpretable form of a linear model.
arxiv-2509-14327:
Hong Liu, writing alone in 2025, studies baby closed universes inside the AdS and CFT correspondence, a duality linking gravity with a quantum theory. Closed universes seem cut off from outside observers. The puzzle is how standard holography can still describe them.

Liu focuses on two cases: a cosmology from partly entangled thermal states, and the older Maldacena-Maoz example. An algebraic framing does the work. A set of operators plus a state on it encodes all physical operations inside the closed universe. In principle every observable follows from that pair, with no observer added by hand. Along the way Liu proposes an answer to a puzzle raised by Antonini and Rath about such universes.
arxiv-2509-14427:
Ilyass Moummad and three co-authors argue in 2025 that strong search hashes need no training at all in the age of pre trained models. Hashing turns images or audio into compact binary codes for fast retrieval. Standard methods train a new hasher for each scenario at high cost.

Their Hashing-Baseline freezes powerful pre trained encoders and applies classic steps only. Principal component analysis shrinks the embeddings, random projection mixes them, and thresholding turns them into bits. No fine tuning or extra learning is used. Tests across vision and audio retrieval show competitive results from that simple pipeline. A strong free baseline matters: costly trained hashers should have to beat it clearly before claiming progress.
arxiv-2509-15227:
Vasily E. Tarasov derives discrete maps with memory from fractional differential equations in a solo 2025 mathematical physics paper. Fractional derivatives encode memory naturally, because their value depends on a system's whole history. Tarasov works with Hilfer derivatives, a family that interpolates between the better-known Riemann-Liouville and Caputo forms.

Periodic kicks applied to the continuous equations convert them into step-by-step maps. The maps are obtained without approximation: each is a discrete form of the equations' exact solutions. Constructions cover arbitrary positive derivative orders, with the intervals below one and between one and two worked out as examples. Because the Hilfer family contains the other derivatives as special cases, the single derivation yields whole ranges of memory maps studied separately before.
arxiv-2509-15527:
Xiaofeng Mai leads a very large team that watched a massive core where a heavy star is forming. Heavy stars shape space around them, yet how their birth cores gather and move gas was unclear. The team viewed one core at scales from wide to fine. What they found looks like a barred spiral galaxy in miniature.

Three long arms feed gas into a central bar. The bar channels gas to a flat disk like layer, and streams carry it further in. At the center sit a spinning disk and a smaller inner disk, thought to drive a twin jet. This is the first time all these parts were seen as one linked structure. The order helps the disk gain mass and spin.
arxiv-2509-15727:
Roldán Cala leads a large team that hunts for newborn planetary nebulae. A dying Sun like star sheds its outer layers, which glow as a planetary nebula. Some young ones host masers, natural amplifiers that beam strong radio lines from water or hydroxyl gas. Few such cases are known, and in only eight has the maser spot been pinned to the nebula.

The team match maser spots from public records and their own radio telescope data against known nebulae and radio sources. They confirm one more nebula with a matching maser and list twelve candidates. They also confirm three evolved stars as water fountains, a related class. More confirmations are needed to define the group.
arxiv-2509-15927:
Zhiyu Mou leads a large team that improves auto bidding for online ads with offline learning plus safe search. Auto bidding sets ad bids to lift campaign results. A generative planner trained on past data beat classic offline learning methods. Yet it cannot explore beyond its static data, which caps its gains.

Their method, AIGB-Pearl, adds a trajectory evaluator that grades plans the generator makes. A score maximization scheme, tied down by a proven smoothness bound, then searches safely past the data. A coupling trick keeps the model regular enough for the proof to hold. Tests on mock and real ad systems reach top scores. The work blends generation with policy search.
arxiv-2509-16427:
Search tools find the papers you ask for, but chance finds may spark more joy. Devin Lange, Zach Cutler, and Maxim Lisnic built two web games that serve up random visualization papers and authors for players to guess and explore. Because picks are random, players meet research areas far from their own habits.

The games were made by visualization researchers for their own community. Playing and sharing scores can tighten community bonds, and author-centered play gives quiet exposure to scholars. The authors hope the games are simply fun, and they invite readers to try them online.
arxiv-2509-16727:
Xin Lei Lin, Soroush Mehraban, Abhishek Moturu, and Babak Taati build fake faces that show pain in a 2025 health paper. Judging pain from a face matters for patients who cannot speak. Real datasets are skewed, since gathering them faces strict ethical limits. Past face makers could not set pain levels with care.

Their system makes three-dimensional faces with set muscle moves and set pain grades. A second system reads pain from a face while keeping identity in mind. It compares the face with a calm reference shot. Together, the pair form a fairer base for training pain tools. More even data could help clinics track pain in silent patients.
arxiv-2509-16827:
Neelesh Kumar Vij and co-authors design light traps with a set far-field spread in a 2025 optics paper. Crystal cavities hold light in tiny volumes, which boosts light-matter interaction. Uses demand high quality, small volume, and strong coupling at once. The team use inverse design, where a computer shapes the cavity to meet goals.

Their cavities keep strong performance even with small build flaws. That tolerance matters, since nano-scale builds are never perfect. The frame handles several goals at once rather than one by one. It could serve low-power photonics, nonlinear optics, and quantum tools. Versatile design shortens the path from idea to device.
arxiv-2509-17427:
Hodaka Kawachi and four co-authors recover depth from a single blurred photo in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is coded-aperture imaging, where a patterned mask shapes the blur so that depth leaves a readable trace. Classic solvers lean on hand-crafted priors, while learned regressors need paired training data and lock onto one camera setup.

The team's method pairs a differentiable forward model, which enforces fit to the measured image, with a learned diffusion prior used only as a regularizer. No paired defocus and depth data are needed for training, and nothing ties the method to one camera. On rich simulations and a prototype camera, the method gave strong color-plus-depth reconstructions across noise levels. It beat both U-Net baselines and a classic coded-aperture method, with better accuracy and stability.
arxiv-2509-17527:
Giuseppe Gaetano Luciano and Andronikos Paliathanasis test an alternative dark energy model against late-time data. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies Kaniadakis holographic dark energy, a one-parameter extension of the holographic idea. In it, the horizon entropy follows Kaniadakis statistics rather than the standard rule, which reshapes the expansion equations and enriches the model's behavior.

The pair fit the model with Bayesian methods and Markov chain sampling. Their probes span Type Ia supernovae from two compilations, cosmic chronometer readings of the expansion rate, and baryon acoustic oscillation data from DESI. Judged by an information criterion, the model beats the standard model for some data mixes. Overall, though, the standard cosmological model stays slightly ahead. The authors present Kaniadakis holography as a competitive rival that also probes how generalized entropy might drive cosmic acceleration.
arxiv-2509-18527:
Referee calls in sports must follow written rules, not just pattern matching. Ziwen Chen and Zhong Wang present FERA, a decision support framework built on body pose tracking. Their 2025 paper tests it on foil fencing, where calls hinge on fast two-sided motion and right-of-way rules. The system keeps perception and rule use in separate layers.

One layer tracks the fencers and turns motion into compact tokens. A second layer judges with calibrated timing, and a small structured classifier makes the final call. The team also releases a checked benchmark with agreed labels and fixed test splits. A lifted-depth add-on strengthened the best graph-based perception model. The small classifier reached about 62 percent accuracy on the final left, right, or none call. The lesson: keep uncertainty visible and the rule boundary explicit.
arxiv-2509-18627:
Brain activity follows inner dynamics, but outside inputs keep reshaping it: sights, sounds, and stimulation. Parsa Vahidi, Omid G. Sani, and Maryam M. Shanechi present BRAID, a model that keeps those two forces apart. Their 2025 paper notes that most models treat neural populations as self-running systems. That habit can bury the very dynamics that drive behavior.

BRAID is a deep learning framework for nonlinear neural dynamics tied to behavior. It folds any measured inputs straight into a recurrent network, with a forecasting goal that separates inner dynamics from input effects. A multi-stage training scheme favors the dynamics linked to the behavior of interest. On synthetic tests, BRAID recovered the true shared dynamics. On motor cortex data from a movement task, it fit and forecast neural and behavior data better than rival methods. Adding measured sensory input was part of the gain.
arxiv-2509-18727:
Future 6G networks may locate users by mixing ground towers with low Earth orbit satellites. Yasaman Ettefagh and five co-authors study that mix under user motion in this 2025 paper. Their setup is minimal: one base station and one satellite feed a moving handset. Even that pair must yield position, clock sync, and speed.

The team derives a general signal model that accounts for motion plus clock and frequency offsets. From it they build a ladder of simpler models, ordered by computing cost. An estimation algorithm matches each rung. Careful simulations check the ladder across varied scenarios. Results show where added complexity pays and where a lean model suffices. The findings guide trade-offs for real deployments and varied uses. They target positioning and sync systems that must work while users move.
arxiv-2509-18827:
Extracting hadron properties from reaction data runs into mathematical ambiguities: several wave patterns fit the same data. Derek I. Glazier and Vincent Mathieu show how polarized light can clear the last of them in this 2025 paper. Their setting is the photoproduction of two spinless mesons. Linear polarization already removes most ambiguities.

One conjugate ambiguity survives linear light. The team extends the formalism to circular and elliptical polarization. The new observables sense the imaginary parts of amplitude products, which is exactly the missing information. With them, the ambiguity lifts and the wave solution sharpens. The over-full system then enables a trick: the reaction itself can gauge the beam's polarization. They test that idea on high-volume data for a known meson from the GlueX experiment. Future facilities, they note, can plan around this polarimeter effect.
arxiv-2509-19027:
Faruk Alpay and Hamdi Alakkad want computer systems that can be opened up and explained, like a glass box rather than a black box. They formalize that idea and build three tools for it. Their test area is branch prediction, the hardware trick that guesses which way a program will jump so chips stay busy. Performance there is fast but hard to account for.

The first tool, a transparency index, measures how much of the performance spread can be explained by internal features, with error bounds attached. The second splits throughput credit among parts using Shapley values, a fair-share method from game theory. The third gives an exact Markov model of a classic two-bit predictor, down to a closed formula for its error rate. They also prove that event rates can be recovered from combined hardware counters, with stability guarantees.
arxiv-2509-19527:
Path integrals sum over all routes a system might take, and shrinking them to fewer variables can make hard problems tractable. S. N. Storchak applies one such shrinking method to a simple mechanical system with rotational symmetry. The system lives on a product space, and the symmetry group rotates one part of it freely. A method from an earlier paper guides the reduction step by step.

Storchak computes the Jacobian factor that the shrinking introduces. He also derives the exact link between the path integrals on the full space and on the reduced space. Those integrals encode solutions of heat-like equations on each space. Clean reduction formulas matter for quantum mechanics on curved spaces, where symmetry is often the only handle. The example is simple by design, so each step can be checked in full.
arxiv-2509-19727:
A chatbot that feels warm, cautious, or bold may suit different users, but training one model per trait is wasteful. Seungjong Sun, Seo Yeon Baek, and Jang Hyun Kim carve personality into a vector. They subtract a base model's weights from a copy tuned for one trait. The leftover difference acts as a dial for that trait.

Adding the dial back at varied strength tunes the trait in a smooth range. Several dials can be merged so traits combine. The vectors also carried over to other models downstream, hinting that they capture general persona patterns. No fresh training is needed once a vector exists. Cheap trait control could help assistants match users while staying consistent. The study tests the dials across many tasks and traits.
arxiv-2509-19927:
Synthetic data can debias machine learning, if the fake records stay useful while shedding bias. Emmanouil Panagiotou and six co-authors generate fair tabular data with autoregressive decision trees, a deliberately simple tool. Deep generators dominate the area, yet trees often win on tables. Their fairness lever is soft leaf resampling: tree outputs are nudged at the leaves to cut bias while keeping predictive value.

The method assumes nothing about the data's distribution and handles mixed feature types naturally. On benchmark fairness sets it beat leading rivals, the authors report. Bias enters through hiring, lending, and policing records that models train on. Fixing the data layer helps every downstream model at once. The work argues simple methods deserve a place in fairness tooling.
arxiv-2509-20027:
Avirup Shaw wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in particle physics. It reads a recent result from the Belle II experiment through one theory of extra dimensions. Belle II measured a rare decay of B mesons that leaves a kaon plus invisible particles. The measured rate sits well above the Standard Model prediction.

Shaw tests the Non-minimal Universal Extra Dimensional model against this result. In this model, extra spatial dimensions are curled up, and each particle has heavier partners. The way those partners interact differs a lot from the simpler minimal version. The analysis pushes the lower limit on the size scale of the extra dimension to about nine hundred GeV. A check with all boundary terms set to zero gives no such limit. The contrast shows how much the details of the model matter.
arxiv-2509-20127:
Kristina Bell and four co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum computing. They study the Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm, a method for solving hard routing and planning problems. Most work encodes problems in quadratic form, which can demand many qubits as problems grow. The paper directly compares that encoding with a higher-order one on the same routing case.

The higher-order form gave better solution quality in their tests. It also scaled better in the number of qubits needed. Its cost was a larger number of two-qubit gates, which are slow and error-prone. A factoring trick then cut the gate depth of the higher-order version sharply. The team confirmed that gain on real IBM quantum hardware. The study gives practical guidance on when the richer encoding is worth its price.
arxiv-2509-20627:
Brain scans pooled across hospitals differ from site to site, and privacy rules forbid simply merging them. Yipu Zhang and seven co-authors propose a federated dictionary method for that setting in a 2025 arXiv paper. Each site learns its own dictionary of brain activity patterns locally. No raw scans ever leave the hospital.

The twist is personalization: every dictionary splits into a shared global part and a local part. Federated averaging updates the global atoms toward cross-site consistency. Local atoms refine freely to capture each site's quirks. That split respects heterogeneity instead of averaging it away. On the ABIDE autism imaging dataset, the method beat existing approaches in accuracy and robustness. The design targets multi-site neuroscience studies where data cannot move but models must.
arxiv-2509-20927:
Animated figures often move in ways no real body could, sliding through floors or defying gravity. Akihisa Watanabe and five co-authors present SimDiff in a 2025 paper on making human motion look physically real. Their model builds the rules of a physics simulator into a diffusion model for motion.

Older methods bolted a simulator check onto each step of generation, which was slow because the simulator runs one step at a time. The authors show that this check acts like guidance inside the diffusion process. SimDiff then feeds facts about the setting, such as gravity and wind, straight into the denoising steps. Real-looking motion comes out of generation itself, with no costly check loop. The work targets animation and virtual reality, where believable movement matters.
arxiv-2509-21027:
Robots that imagine the future frame by frame waste effort, since most frames barely change. Sibo Li and three co-authors present KeyWorld in a 2025 paper on robotic world models. Their framework spends heavy computation only on the frames that matter.

KeyWorld first identifies semantic key frames, the moments where meaningful transitions happen. A transformer reasons over those key frames under text conditioning. A lightweight convolutional model then fills in the intermediate frames. This split attacks two bottlenecks at once: slow inference and unphysical generated trajectories. Frame-to-frame generation ignores which transitions are important. By reasoning at the level of key events, KeyWorld aims at world models fast and believable enough for real robot planning.
arxiv-2509-21227:
Scoring whether a generated image truly matches its prompt is a central problem in text to image research. The 2025 paper is by Seyed Amir Kasaei and 6 co-authors. A prompt may name objects, traits, and links between them. A good image must match all of those parts. The field scores images with auto metrics, but those metrics are often picked by habit. The paper checks how well the metrics match human views.

The study tests many widely used metrics across varied prompt tasks. It looks past simple rank links and probes how each metric acts by task type. No single metric won across all tasks. Some metrics based on questions did not beat all others. Some based on embeddings were stronger in set cases. The work urges care in picking a metric.
arxiv-2509-21527:
Molecular dynamics codes must scale across many graphics processors on fixed size problems. Mahesh Doijade and 4 co-authors redesign a core GROMACS communication step in a 2025 paper. GROMACS is highly latency sensitive, with peak steps under a millisecond. Standard MPI routes communication through the central processor, adding latency on the critical path. Heterogeneous supercomputers make that cost worse.

Their redesign uses NVSHMEM with GPU initiated communication for halo exchange. Halo exchange shares limit data between domains. Tuned kernels fuse data packing with communication, hiding latency. Kernel fusion spans overlapped forwarding phases, and an asynchronous copy engine uses fast links. The GPU resident formulation raises communication computation overlap. Strong scaling improves as a result.
arxiv-2509-21627:
The young Sun was far more violent than today, with a bright corona and massive fast wind. Dibyendu Sur and Vladimir Airapetian simulate its effect on early Earth in a 2025 paper. Corotating interaction regions form where fast wind overtakes slow wind, driving strong shocks. Those shocks pressed the magnetospheres of early Venus, Earth, and Mars. The first six hundred million years are the setting.

A space weather modelling framework, coupled with a convection model, simulates Earth passing through such a shock. The dayside magnetopause moves much closer to the planet in the model. Joule heating deposited in the upper atmosphere also rises. Young rocky exoplanets face the same hazards, the authors note. The study links stellar activity to early planetary atmospheres.
arxiv-2509-21727:
Large deviation estimates control how often random dynamic values stray far from their means. Matthew Powell proves such estimates for quasi cyclic Gevrey cocycles in a 2025 note. Cocycles are products of matrices driven by a quasi cyclic base motion. Gevrey regularity is a smoothness class between analytic and infinitely differentiable. An approximation scheme is the main tool in the proof.

As an use, smooth change of the Lyapunov exponent in the cocycle is obtained. The Lyapunov exponent measures average exponential growth along the dynamics. Smooth change results matter because exponents can jump under small perturbations in related settings. The note is short and technical. It adds Gevrey cocycles to the list of systems with rigorous large deviation control.
arxiv-2509-21827:
Designing an experiment means choosing test settings that cover a space well, and the job gets harder when the factors are parts of a mixture. Zikang Xiong, Hong Qin, Yuning Huang, and Jianhui Ning take up that problem in this 2025 statistics paper. They study sliced designs, where one overall design splits into smaller designs that each still fill the space.

The authors give three ways to build such designs for mixture factors, using a representative-points frame and a theory of energy distance. They prove the designs settle toward the right spread as they grow. They also give step-by-step methods, both one-shot and sequential, for designs that mix mixture factors with process factors. Tests show the designs fill space better and predict better than older methods, with more freedom in the sizes of the slices.
arxiv-2509-21927:
Estimating an object's six-dimensional pose, its position and orientation, from a single photo is the goal of SingRef6D. Jiahui Wang and five co-authors present the system in this 2025 paper, accepted as a NeurIPS poster. Many current methods lean on depth sensors, which fail on clear or shiny surfaces. Photo-only methods match less reliably in dim or plain scenes, where geometry cues are thin.

SingRef6D needs just one reference photo, with no depth sensor, many views, or view-synthesis training. Its first trick fine-tunes a strong depth-prediction model with a new loss, sharpening depth even on hard surfaces. Its second trick uses that depth inside the matching step, weaving spatial relations into the comparison of image patches. On three standard data sets, including one with clear objects and one with harsh lighting, the system beat leading methods on average recall while staying lightweight.
arxiv-2509-22427:
Simon M. Dannhauer and 20 co-authors studied a glowing ring of ionized carbon in the Cygnus X star-forming region. The ring, called the Diamond Ring, spans about six parsecs and sits inside clumpy gas clouds. At its center sits a bright clump, but the data show that clump is unrelated and moves at a different speed. A hot B-type star powers the ionized region inside the ring.

Unlike normal bubbles, this one expands slowly as a flat ring, not a round shell. The team argues the bubble grew inside a flat slab of gas. Parts moving toward or away from us have faded, leaving the ring. Simulations of the bubble's growth support that flat geometry.
arxiv-2509-22527:
Andrii Litvynchuk and 4 co-authors estimate scene depth from a single camera image, fast enough for edge devices. Depth from one image aids robots, augmented reality, and self-driving cars. Prior methods often miss fine detail, break on shiny surfaces, or cost too much compute. Their model, EfficientDepth, pairs a transformer with a light convolutional decoder and a two-mode density head.

Training mixes labeled fake and real images with pseudo-labeled real ones from a strong teacher model. A staged training plan and a perceptual loss push for crisp, consistent depth maps. Results matched or beat top models while using far fewer resources. That balance suits real-time use on small hardware.
arxiv-2509-22627:
Alexandre Lopes, Roberto Souza, and Helio Pedrini estimate depth from stereo image pairs without any labeled depth data. Stereo depth matters for robots, cars, and augmented reality, yet ground truth is hard to gather across scenes. Self-supervised methods learn from unlabeled pairs instead. Their network, CCNeXt, uses a modern convolutional feature extractor tuned for this task.

A windowed cross-attention module compares the two views along the scan line where matches must lie. A redesigned decoder turns those matches into depth. On the KITTI benchmarks, the model matched top accuracy while running about ten times faster than the prior best. It led all metrics on two KITTI test sets among recent methods.
arxiv-2509-22727:
Ziqi Chen and 5 co-authors build one text-to-speech system that can speak many Chinese dialects. Dialect speech carries rich cultural diversity, but data is scarce, spellings vary, and sounds shift in complex ways. Their framework, DiaMoE-TTS, standardizes input with the International Phonetic Alphabet, which clears up letter-to-sound ambiguity. A dialect-aware mixture of experts models how dialects differ in sound.

Parameter-efficient adapters then adapt the system to new dialects with little training. The design builds on the F5-TTS architecture and uses open data rather than large proprietary resources. In tests it produced natural, expressive speech. It even handled unseen dialects and Peking Opera singing with only a few hours of training data.
arxiv-2509-22927:
Jodi Berdis and 3 co-authors publish the first near-infrared spectra of icy salt mixes tied to Europa. Their lab mixes hold water ice with epsomite and halite at deep cold. Such mixes may coat the moon Europa, so their spectra guide how flyby data get read. The team tested how well two mixing models fit the lab data.

Small ice grains shaped the key spectral band more than large grains did. For halite and epsomite, grain size marks grew hard to read once grains were large. The authors warn that surveys may favor small ice grains by bias. They also flag a likely error in published epsomite optical data.
arxiv-2509-23227:
On a sphere, spreading and clumping fight inside one free energy, and the ground states show the score. Razvan C Fetecau, Hansol Park, and Vishnu Vaidya study that diffusion-aggregation model. Entropy favors slow nonlinear diffusion, which spreads mass out. A quadratic interaction term pulls mass together. The team map how equilibria and global minimizers shift as attraction strength grows.

Distinct ranges of the diffusion exponent give distinct behavior. The energy generalizes the Onsager free energy with dipolar potential. That classic model studies phase transitions in polymer orientation. The sphere setting adds curvature to the contest. Results chart when clumps win over smooth spread.
arxiv-2509-23427:
Spam floods on open blockchains raise fees and clog service, and fee-based defenses punish honest small users too. Rowdy Chotkan and 3 co-authors built StarveSpam, a reputation protocol at the relay layer. Each node tracks local behavior, scores peers, and rate-limits abusers adaptively. No global consensus, protocol change, or trusted party is needed. Honest low-value traffic stays welcome.

Tests replay a major Ethereum NFT spam event with real data. Each node blocked over ninety-five percent of spam. Only about three percent of honest traffic was dropped. Network exposure to spam fell sharply against rule-based defenses. The team pitch it as a scalable, fairer shield.
arxiv-2509-23627:
Hurricane damage shows up on social media as fast as it hits the ground, but research data have lagged behind. Ruichen Yao and 11 co-authors built MASH, a data set of nearly sixty thousand posts about hurricane impacts. The posts come from Reddit, TikTok, and YouTube, unlike older single-platform sets. Each post is labeled jointly on its text and images, not on each part alone.

Labels cover humanitarian needs, bias, and information integrity. The team also built an online platform for exploring the data and sharing findings. They offer MASH, released openly, for work on disaster response, severity sorting, public sentiment, policy, and bias detection.
arxiv-2509-23727:
Guiding a diffusion model toward its prompt usually trades variety for obedience. Junyou Wang and 6 co-authors mix guidance signals instead of choosing one. Classifier-free guidance strengthens prompt alignment but narrows diversity. Autoguidance keeps diversity, yet on audio it has lagged behind. Their method, AudioMoG, blends diverse guidance terms, including their interactions and a deliberately weak version of the model.

At the same inference speed, the mix beat single-guidance sampling for text-to-audio work across step counts. Gains also showed in video-to-audio, text-to-music, and image generation. The approach needs no heavy retraining, which the authors stress as part of its appeal.
arxiv-2509-23827:
A vision-language model that describes a photo can leak what should stay private, and it may not know the difference. Efthymios Tsaprazlis and 4 co-authors ground the problem in law, building a multi-level Visual Privacy Taxonomy. The taxonomy spans a wide range of privacy issues and is designed to scale with future research. Legal frameworks guide what counts as a violation in context.

Several leading vision-language models were then tested against that standard. Their grasp of contextual privacy proved inconsistent, sometimes within the same kind of scene. The authors present the taxonomy as a foundation and the results as evidence that privacy-aware systems are urgently needed.
arxiv-2509-24327:
Hai Siong Tan examines a new kind of physics-informed neural network for inferring cosmological parameters from supernova and baryon acoustic oscillation data. The model estimates uncertainty for both its targets and the unknown parameters of the equations beneath the data. It blends ideas from evidential deep learning, Bayesian networks, and Gaussian processes.

Trained by standard gradient methods, it learns a posterior spread for the equation parameters. Tan applies it to current data under three cosmos models, from the standard one to variants with a changing dark energy. Posteriors from the two data sources overlapped more than classic fits suggest. Their medians for the Hubble value sat close, giving a different read on the Hubble tension.
arxiv-2510-00027:
Elhag and colleagues test a shortcut for a lab task. The task is to predict how atoms pull and push each other. Such forecasts drive models of new drugs and materials. The lab method is exact but slow. Learned stand-ins run faster. Most stand-ins build turn symmetry into their wiring. That rule keeps answers sound when a molecule turns. But it makes the models stiff and hard to scale.

Their model is TransIP. It uses a Transformer, the design behind chat tools. No symmetry rule is wired in. A training goal teaches it to match codes for turned copies. The team trained it on OMol25, a molecule set. That set spans small organics, bits of living tissue, and salt-like mixes. TransIP kept its codes aligned when molecules turned. It beat the copy-adding rival by 40 to 60 percent. Cleaner alignment tracked better accuracy.
arxiv-2510-00327:
Mark Skandera wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on immanants, a family of matrix functions between the determinant and the permanent. For matrices with positive semidefinite structure, a chain of inequalities among hook-shaped immanants was conjectured by Merris and proven by Heyfron decades ago. The chain ranks these functions neatly from permanent down to determinant. Skandera asks whether the same chain survives under a different positivity notion.

He proves the full chain of inequalities for totally nonnegative matrices as well. Such matrices have every minor, at every size, greater than or equal to zero. The result swaps a spectral assumption for a purely sign-based one. Such chains matter wherever immanants measure structured quantities in algebra and counting problems. Extending their reach to totally nonnegative matrices widens the toolbox for both fields. The proof closes a natural gap left by the older result.
arxiv-2510-01327:
Phillips and co-authors rehearse telescope observations of early galaxy motion on synthetic data to learn what can go wrong. Disk galaxies now appear surprisingly early, but proving a disk requires reading gas motion honestly. Warm gas, the kind the new telescope sees, is easily confused by outflows.

Mock integral-field observations were built from two simulated galaxies at matching resolution and noise. Lopsided disks and outflow hosts departed measurably from clean rotation when the full data cube was used. Collapsing the data into flat maps hid those differences dangerously. The lessons set practical rules for interpreting real early-galaxy spectra. Cold-gas telescopes provide the comparison tracer the study contrasts against. Standard disk criteria were stress-tested, not assumed. Full three-dimensional information proved necessary for honest classification. The SERRA suite supplied both rehearsal galaxies. Rehearsals make real observations interpretable the first time.
arxiv-2510-01627:
Liu and Wang wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a stochastic wave equation driven by random noise. The noise is white in time but linked across space through a Riesz-type pattern. The authors study a local linearization method that works with two parameters at once. Their goal is to recover the diffusion coefficient, which controls how strongly noise shakes the wave.

The authors prove that second-order increments of the true solution match those of a simpler linearized equation. That match extends earlier work, which covered only space-time white noise. They then study the quadratic variation of the solution in detail. From that variation they build an estimator for the diffusion parameter, and they show the estimator is consistent. The result gives statisticians a firmer base for measuring noise strength in wave models.
arxiv-2510-02127:
Liu and Mallada relax the rules for proving a control system safe in this 2025 paper. Safety certificates usually come from reachability analysis or control barrier functions. Both demand heavy computation: high-dimensional partial differential equations or large semidefinite programs. Their recurrent barrier functions exploit a simple property instead: trajectories come back to a safe set.

Under mild assumptions, the signed-distance function to a set satisfies the recurrent barrier condition. Function design thus collapses into identifying the right set. Strikingly, that set need not be invariant to certify safety, which widens the search. The authors add a data-driven, nonparametric way to compute such sets from trajectories. The method parallelizes massively and trades conservativeness against computational cost openly. Systems that return to safety, even without staying there, can now be certified. That shift suits robots and vehicles whose normal operation roams before recovering.
arxiv-2510-02727:
Torres, Sreenivas, and Sowers tackle a counting problem that shows up in finance and control. Their tool is the recombining trinomial tree. Each step in the tree can move up, stay flat, or move down. Such trees model option prices and other changing systems. A deep tree holds a huge number of paths. Listing them all one by one is far too slow.

The authors use two symmetries to cut the work down. Their mass-shifting method lists each distinct path just once. It also counts how many paths fall in each class. The savings grow fast as the tree gets deeper. Tests beat the old breadth-first search by a wide margin. The team also links the counts to Motzkin paths. That link may yield sharper counting rules later.
arxiv-2510-02827:
Ni and co-authors improve how language models answer questions that need several hops of facts. A single search often misses key links. Their system is called StepChain GraphRAG. It first splits a hard question into smaller sub-questions. It then pulls passages from a global index. Only those passages are turned into a knowledge graph. The graph is built on the fly, which keeps it small and focused.

A breadth-first walk then follows the graph edges for each sub-question. The walk assembles a clear chain of evidence. The model never drowns in extra context. Tests used three standard multi-hop question sets. StepChain GraphRAG set new best scores on all three. The gains were largest on the HotpotQA set. The saved evidence chains also make each answer easy to audit. That openness helps users trust the final answer.
arxiv-2510-02927:
Pankka and Pim prove a compactness result for quasiregular curves. Such curves are maps that stretch space in a bounded way. They land in manifolds that carry a special calibration form. Sequences of these curves can bubble, shedding parts as they converge. Gromov's classic theorem describes that bubbling for holomorphic maps. The authors prove a version for their wider curve class. Bounded geometry of the target is assumed.

Their main device is a bubble tree built over the starting manifold. A resolved curve on the tree captures the lost measure exactly. Approximating maps converge to it in the local uniform sense. The construction earns the name nodal resolution. A normality test for families of curves follows as a corollary. Older views of bubbling also drop out of the result. The work extends a pillar of complex analysis into metric geometry.
arxiv-2510-03127:
Li tests whether AI models truly reason or merely match patterns. Raven's Progressive Matrices pose pattern puzzles with hidden rules. Models often score well on them after training. This study withholds some rules from training on purpose. Vision models and sequence transformers both faced the test. The bench was I-RAVEN, a cleaned version of the classic task.
