Familiar rules posed little trouble for any model.

Unseen rules told a very different story. Accuracy fell sharply once a rule had been omitted. The sequence transformer beat the vision models overall. Its lead did not protect it on novel rules, though. Models often got most tokens of an answer right. Whole answers, the part that counts, failed far more often. Surface fluency can thus mask broken reasoning. Li argues the field needs symbolic structure inside neural models. Stronger built-in biases for relations are also needed.
arxiv-2510-03327:
Niraula and a large international team present a 2025 arXiv paper that computes, from first principles, how carbon dioxide molecules collide with hydrogen and helium. Such collisions blur the light signals that telescopes read from distant planets. The James Webb Space Telescope needs very exact blur values to measure planet air with confidence. Older tables drift far from the needed accuracy at high heat, which is common on warm exoplanets.

The team paired high level quantum chemistry with a scattering code named Yumi. They derived collision rates and pressure broadening across a wide span of spin states and temperatures. Their computed values met the ten percent accuracy target set for Webb exoplanet work. Fits in the style of the HITRAN database let others plug the numbers straight into their tools. The study gives exoplanet science its first full first principles base for a target molecule with more than two atoms.
arxiv-2510-03427:
Gholizadeh and Jiang present a 2025 arXiv paper on solving flow problems when two parties each hold part of a network. Neither side wants to ship all its edges to the other, so they must compute while exchanging few bits. The trivial approach needs a number of bits that grows with the square of the network size. The authors adapt an interior point method from machine optimization to this two party setting. Their protocol works for maximum flow and for the minimum cost flow problem.

The new protocol needs only about the network size raised to the three halves power in bits, an improvement. Behind it sits a result on linear programs with two sided limits and sparse rows. For sparse problems, their method matches the best one sided results while covering more cases. Cheaper computation matters for firms and agencies that must plan together without pooling sensitive network data.
arxiv-2510-03627:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper explaining how atmospheric rivers grow, decay, and move, using a vapor kinetic energy budget. Atmospheric rivers are narrow streams of water vapor that bring damaging winds, rain, and floods. The team applied two versions of the energy framework across all ocean basins. They tracked which processes add energy to a river and which drain it. The analysis asks why conversion rates differ between regions.

Across basins, rivers intensify mainly when potential energy converts into kinetic energy. Horizontal convergence of vapor kinetic energy adds a secondary push in some regions. Rivers decay through condensation and turbulent dissipation. Their eastward travel follows convergence of energy flux downstream and divergence upstream. Conversion runs stronger where baroclinic instability is high or terrain lifts the flow, notably near North America's west coast. A diagnostic that works worldwide helps forecasters and climate scientists compare storms on equal footing.
arxiv-2510-03827:
Zhou and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper questioning whether robot models that ace a popular benchmark truly understand their tasks. The benchmark, LIBERO, tests vision-language-action models that watch a scene, read instructions, and move a robot arm. Top models score above ninety percent on it. The authors suspected those scores reflect memorized routines rather than real understanding.

They built LIBERO-PRO, an extended benchmark that changes objects, starting positions, instructions, and surroundings in fair ways. Under these changes, the same models that scored above ninety percent collapsed to near zero success. Models kept grasping for objects that had been swapped for unrelated items. Their actions also stayed the same when instructions were scrambled into nonsense. The authors argue the field should drop the flawed protocol and adopt tougher tests. Honest benchmarks matter because inflated scores mislead robot builders.
arxiv-2510-04027:
Park, Choi, and Lee present this 2025 arXiv paper on teaching support vector machines to classify many classes without leaking private data. Support vector machines are classic classifiers with strong accuracy, but adding differential privacy to them is tricky. Standard multi-class schemes train many binary classifiers, and each pass over a person's data spends more of the privacy budget. With many classes, the budget drains fast and noise swamps the model.

The authors build an all-in-one multi-class SVM that reads each data sample only once. Their method, PMSVM, perturbs weights and gradients in a carefully analyzed way to guarantee differential privacy. In experiments, PMSVM beat existing private SVM methods on multi-class tasks. The single-pass structure is the key economy: privacy cost no longer grows with the number of classes. The work makes a trusted classic algorithm usable in privacy-sensitive multi-class settings.
arxiv-2510-04427:
Lisen Ding, Mingyi Wang, and Dongling Wang wrote this 2025 paper on solving a hard class of equations. The fractional Poisson equation models odd diffusion in physics, but its solutions turn rough near borders. A recent spectral Monte Carlo method solved such problems fast and with high accuracy. That method was built for one dimension only. The team extended it to round domains in many dimensions.

The extension rests on a new set of eigenfunctions for the fractional operator. New interpolation formulas connect those functions to the random walk sampling at the core of the method. The authors describe the full method and compare it with rival techniques in depth. Numerical tests confirmed that the extension works as hoped. High dimensional balls are a natural setting for physics and finance models. A fast solver there opens problems that grid methods handle poorly.
arxiv-2510-04527:
Peixue Wu and Yunkai Wang wrote this 2025 paper on boosting quantum channel capacity with privacy structure. A quantum channel carries information, and its capacity can grow when channels combine. Private states hide a secret key inside a shield system that an eavesdropper cannot read. The authors ask whether that shield can be recycled to raise capacity. Their answer builds a general test for when such amplification must occur.

The test turns on the Holevo information of an assisting channel paired with the private one. For erasure and depolarizing channels, they give explicit thresholds that depend on size and noise levels. Under a conjecture from spin alignment work, they also compute the capacity of a family of private channels in closed form. That family yields examples with zero quantum capacity but unbounded private capacity. For near private channels, they extend a superactivation proof to a wider range of settings.
arxiv-2510-04627:
Jiho Noh and three coauthors wrote this 2025 perspective paper on photonic simulators of quantum systems. Lattices of light guides or tiny pillars can mimic electrons moving in a crystal. Such platforms are clean, tunable, and easy to probe. Almost all work so far uses only the basic mode at each site. The authors survey a shift toward richer modes that carry orbital angular momentum.

Higher modes add an inner structure at each site, like extra rooms inside each atom of the fake crystal. That structure lets simulators copy topological band patterns that basic modes cannot reach. It also supports synthetic gauge fields and a field of study called orbitronics. The paper reviews recent experiments and designs across these directions. It weighs what the extra modes cost in control and loss against what they unlock. The authors argue the orbital degree of freedom is only starting to show its range.
arxiv-2510-04727:
Emanuele Mule and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on learning from group relations that have a direction. Hypergraphs link groups at once, unlike graphs that link pairs. Many group relations point one way, as when one team cites or funds another. Past models for directed hypergraphs assumed neighbors resemble each other, which fails when groups differ. The authors build networks on sheaf theory, a tool that lets each node hold richer data.

Their model, DSHN, defines a new directed sheaf Laplacian, an operator with complex values. That operator contains many graph and hypergraph Laplacians as special cases. The network uses it to pass messages that respect direction and variation. Across seven data sets, DSHN beat thirteen rival methods. Relative accuracy gains ran from two percent up to twenty percent. The wins were largest where direction and diversity matter most. A unified operator simplifies theory for the family of models.
arxiv-2510-04827:
Mohammad Tahsin Alam, Zafrin Jahan Nikita, Ying Yin Tsui, and Md Zahurul Islam wrote this 2025 paper on a laser that tunes across the near infrared. On chip photonics needs compact light sources that aim their beam in direction. Plasmonic lasers often leak light ways and spray it into stray modes. The authors build their cavity on a Tamm plasmon, a state trapped where a stack meets a metal film. A nanohole array in the metal lets the light out through transmission.

The array spacing sits below the wavelength, so diffraction orders vanish. Emission leaves in a forward beam, as a laser should. A mirror stack under the pump side blocks backward leakage near the lasing color. Forward power and efficiency rise with that addition. The design tunes across the infrared band. It does so with cheap materials rather than ones. Directional, efficient nanolasers feed sensing, communication, and devices.
arxiv-2510-04927:
Usman Akram, Yiyue Chen, and Haris Vikalo tackle radio signal recognition in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their task, automatic modulation classification, means naming how a wireless signal is encoded. Training such a classifier usually means gathering labeled signals in one place. That raises privacy costs and breaks when each site sees different signal mixes.

Their system, FedSSL-AMC, lets many clients train together without sharing raw data. Each client first learns from unlabeled signals through self-supervision, then fits a small classifier on a few labels. The authors prove the joint training converges under uneven client data. In tests on synthetic and over-the-air signals, it beat supervised federated baselines. Gains were largest where labels were scarce and skewed.
arxiv-2510-05027:
Ethan Davis proposes a standard way to judge heuristic search methods in this 2025 arXiv paper. Metaheuristics such as ant colony optimization attack hard routing and scheduling problems. They often find near-best answers quickly, but reports rarely say how reliable they are. Davis argues that success rates need honest measurement, not single lucky runs.

His framework, EEE, runs in three stages. A broad exploration scans the parameter space first. Exploitation then focuses on the best settings found. A final evaluation stage quantifies the uncertainty in the results. As a case study, he runs ant colony optimization on the berlin52 traveling salesman benchmark. One run had about a 1 in 40 chance of hitting the known optimum. Ten runs together raised that chance to about 1 in 5.
arxiv-2510-05127:
Harshit Goyal predicts cloud computing needs before they happen in this 2025 arXiv paper. Big data pipelines waste money when operators reserve too much capacity. Reserving too little degrades performance and breaks service agreements. Static rules and reactive scaling both miss the mark.

Goyal trained a Random Forest regression model on Google's Borg cluster traces. Cleaned features covered CPU, memory, and usage patterns across jobs. The model scored an R-squared near 0.99 with tiny average errors. It predicted small and medium jobs especially well, with more variance on rare huge jobs. Such forecasts could drive cost-aware autoscaling that trims waste without risking service quality.
arxiv-2510-05327:
Zahin Ibnat and six co-authors help language models write hardware code in this 2025 arXiv paper. Chips are described in Verilog at the register-transfer level. Fine-tuned models age quickly as commercial models improve. Retrieval-augmented generation instead fetches helpful examples at query time.

Their framework, DeepV, is model-agnostic and needs no hardware-specific training. It searches a large, high-quality Verilog knowledge base during generation itself. Earlier retrieval systems leaned on low-quality codebases or added costly fine-tuning. Plugged into GPT-5, DeepV raised VerilogEval performance by nearly 17 percent. The knowledge base can be updated continuously as new designs appear. The team hosts DeepV publicly on Hugging Face for chip designers and researchers.
arxiv-2510-05427:
Kübra Benli, Greg Martin, and Paul Péringuey measure how prime races in two residue classes move together in this 2025 arXiv paper. Prime counting functions for arithmetic progressions wobble around their predicted main terms. Sometimes two progressions exceed their predictions at the same time. The authors derive the logarithmic density of exactly those joint events.

Their formula comes with a method to compute the densities with rigorously bounded errors. They apply it to all residue pairs modulo 11. The results show which pairs of residues are strongly or weakly correlated. The findings illuminate the mirror image and cyclic ordering phenomena that Bays and Hudson observed. Prime races, it turns out, have a rich joint geometry beyond single-class biases.
arxiv-2510-05627:
Schlenker reviews recent progress on the geometry of three-dimensional hyperbolic manifolds. For convex co-compact manifolds, two kinds of boundary data compete to describe the interior. One records an induced metric at the boundary, the other records bending. His 2025 survey asks how far each dataset determines the hyperbolic metric.

A volume function ties the two datasets together as conjugate variables. Its first variation has a simple formula in terms of the boundary data. Depending on the manifold, the volume is ordinary or renormalized. The convex core provides the central example of a convex domain inside. Bers uniformization anchors the boundary picture for these manifolds. Some determination questions are now settled, while others remain conjectural. The Legendre transform of the volume organizes the duality cleanly. New links reach toward AdS/CFT physics and the Loewner energy from probability.
arxiv-2510-06027:
Zia and co-authors ask whether a bath of simple two-level spins can stand in for a bath of electrons, in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Their test case is a resonant-level model, where one central site exchanges particles with its surroundings. Both baths block double occupancy, so the two setups look alike at first glance.

Using exact diagonalization and a step-by-step expansion of the master equation, the team compares the dynamics of the central site. At second order in the coupling, both baths give identical behavior, since only simple two-point correlations matter. At higher orders they diverge, because electrons pick up exchange signs that spins never produce. The mismatch is largest for small to middling baths near half filling and fades for large baths. The results mark where spin baths are safe substitutes in transport simulations.
arxiv-2510-06127:
Liang and five co-authors teach a robot the tricky job of handling medical tape in a 2025 robotics paper. Chronic wounds affect more than 6.5 million patients in the United States and cost over 25 billion dollars a year. Redressing them is routine, yet it still depends entirely on trained clinicians.

The framework covers two skills: starting a tape peel and placing fresh tape securely. Force-feedback imitation learning from human teleoperation handles the delicate detachment step. On phantom skin it peeled about 18.9 millimeters per pull near 3.1 newtons of force, beating the baseline on reach and safety. A trajectory optimizer plans placement for smooth, wrinkle-free adhesion on curved anatomy. Placement tests on leg, hip, and heel models reached full coverage on the leg and strong adhesion elsewhere. An integrated pipeline ran removal, preparation, and placement in sequence.
arxiv-2510-06327:
Wong and six co-authors calibrate gravitational-wave detectors with a Bayesian null-stream method in a 2025 relativity paper. Calibration errors limit how observatories can measure cosmic signals. Earlier calibration schemes needed electromagnetic counterparts or waveform models, tying the measurement to extra assumptions.

Their method uses sky-independent null streams in closed-geometry detector networks. A null stream combines detector outputs so that a genuine gravitational wave cancels out. Whatever remains exposes calibration errors. The approach works with any gravitational-wave signal and assumes neither general relativity nor a waveform family. A proof-of-concept study demonstrates that the method is feasible. The authors discuss prospects for the Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, and LISA. Those next-generation observatories demand better calibration accuracy, especially for low-frequency science. Self-calibration from the signals themselves would remove a systematic that grows damaging as detectors become more sensitive.
arxiv-2510-06527:
Dunbar and Aaronson characterize exactly when wide random networks produce nearly independent outputs in a 2025 machine learning paper. The work targets the Alignment Research Center's computational no-coincidence conjecture. That conjecture probes interpretability limits by asking when learned features align suspiciously. A rigorous random baseline is needed to recognize genuine coincidences.

Randomly initialized wide networks supply that baseline. Their outputs are nearly independent exactly under one clean condition. The activation must be nonlinear with zero mean under the Gaussian measure. Shifted ReLU and shifted GeLU qualify. Plain ReLU and GeLU fail it, while tanh passes. The characterization is an exact if-and-only-if. Zero-mean-activation networks become a promising candidate baseline for the conjecture. The zero-mean condition is checkable for any candidate activation before experiments begin. Interpretability researchers gain a principled null model for judging surprising structure.
arxiv-2510-06927:
Yifan Yang leads a team arguing that speech synthesis has outgrown its report cards. Their 2025 position paper introduces Responsible Evaluation for text-to-speech systems. Modern systems can sound indistinguishable from humans. Yet scoring practices still focus on narrow quality numbers that saturate early and miss misuse risks.

The framework climbs three levels of responsibility. The first level demands scores that faithfully reflect true capability, with sharper objective and listening tests. The second level calls for shared benchmarks and transparent reporting, so results compare across labs. The third level confronts ethics directly, including forgery, impersonation, privacy violations, and security holes. The authors survey current practice and find gaps at every level. Similarity scores, for instance, stop improving perceptibly past a threshold. Mean opinion scores also flatten as systems get better. Their roadmap asks the field to measure what matters before synthetic voices cause wider harm.
arxiv-2510-07227:
Krishnakumar and co-authors show how to start a small language model from inside a big one. Their 2025 paper offers a cheaper path to capable small models. Instead of training from random weights, they carve a sparse subnetwork out of a trained teacher. An evolutionary search finds which pieces to keep. Knowledge from the teacher is then distilled into the small model during training. 

Their best small model matched a known rival's quality while using about nine times fewer training tokens. Search over starting pieces beat random starts under the same compute budget. Coarser search spaces worked best for the larger small models. The team released code and models for others to reuse. Cheaper pretraining could let small labs build tailored models without giant budgets. It also cuts energy costs for models built for phones and local use.
arxiv-2510-07527:
The CMS Collaboration combines its searches for pairs of Higgs bosons produced without a resonance at the Large Hadron Collider. The paper pools data from proton collisions recorded between 2016 and 2018. Higgs pairs are precious because their rate reveals how the Higgs field interacts with itself, a cornerstone quantity of the standard model. No significant excess appeared. The combined result caps pair production at about three and a half times the standard model prediction, slightly weaker than the expected sensitivity.

The self-coupling modifier is confined to a window running from modestly negative to about six times the standard strength. A second modifier, governing two vector bosons meeting two Higgs bosons, cannot be zero: that possibility is excluded at more than five standard deviations for every self-coupling value. Its allowed window brackets the standard value snugly.
arxiv-2510-07727:
Hatashita, Nathan, and Jain wrote this 2025 fluid mechanics paper on simulating two-phase flows, where liquid and gas mix and churn. Direct simulations must resolve tiny interfaces between the phases. Single-phase turbulence has clear rules for the needed grid fineness. Two-phase flows lacked comparable guidance. The authors derive scaling laws that fill that gap for both gentle and violent regimes.

Their scalings express grid points and time steps through three standard dimensionless numbers. High-fidelity simulations of churning two-phase turbulence pinned down where interface measures converge. One concrete rule says second-order schemes need a stated resolution threshold to catch sudden area bursts. The authors also coin a new number that sorts flows by which interface scale rules. Cost grows steeply with surface tension effects, and their formulas now predict that cost in advance. Simulators can plan two-phase runs with far fewer blind guesses.
arxiv-2510-07827:
Carlson, Deshpande, and coauthors wrote this 2025 electrical engineering paper on dynamic metasurface antennas for wideband wireless links. These antennas steer beams through many reconfigurable slots in a waveguide. Each slot uses a tunable element that sips power compared with phase shifters. That thrift makes the design attractive for MIMO arrays. Real devices, though, suffer waveguide loss, frequency-selective elements, and limited tuning range, and wideband signals feel all three.

The authors derive approximations for beamforming gain that include those effects. The formulas show how gain falls from the center frequency and which design knobs matter most. Narrower element spacing and wider tuning bandwidth help. They also propose a successive beamforming method that configures elements in sequence. In line-of-sight and multipath simulations, the method raised spectral efficiency over the baseline approach. The study gives antenna designers rules before they commit to hardware.
arxiv-2510-07927:
Zhang and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on benchmarking synthetic anomalies for factory inspection. Detectors need defect images, but real defects are rare and costly to label. Synthesis can fabricate defect images, yet the field judged synthesis as a helper inside detection systems. Nobody had benchmarked synthesizers themselves. ASBench is the first framework built for that job, covering twelve synthesis methods and four pipelines.

The benchmark spans five industrial datasets and four evaluation dimensions. It tests generalization, the best synthetic ratio, and whether image quality predicts detection gains. It also tests mixing complementary synthesis methods. Several lessons stood out. No single method won everywhere, and more synthetic data did not always help. Image quality metrics correlated weakly with detection performance. Hybrid synthesis, though, gave a clear boost. The results give researchers guidance for making fake defects that teach detectors.
arxiv-2510-08027:
Kohl wrote this 2025 quantum computing paper introducing unoperations, a way to run an operation backwards. Given a valid output, its unoperation produces the full set of inputs that could have produced it. He illustrates the idea with addition, building a quantum circuit performing unaddition. The same trick applied to multiplication yields an unmultiplier, a device that factors integers.

The unmultiplier's qubit count grows with the square of the input's logarithm, rivaling the best known factoring methods. Kohl shows the construction explicitly rather than only proving existence. The devices are simple enough to simulate classically for nontrivial examples. He also discusses trimming outcomes that are not factor pairs. Other trapdoor functions might be unoperated the same way. The paper offers a fresh viewpoint on reversing computations, with cryptography as the obvious stake.
arxiv-2510-08127:
Amarilli, Monet, Raphaël, and Salvati wrote this 2025 theoretical computer science paper on asking how likely a random word is to belong to a context-free language. A probabilistic word assigns each position a distribution over letters. The task computes the probability that a drawn word lands in the language. For unambiguous context-free languages it runs in polynomial time.

A broader tractable class allows a fresh unambiguous grammar per word length, covering some inherently ambiguous languages. Yet unions of two simple unambiguous languages can make the problem counting-hard. Restricted counter automata cross into hardness as well. Circuit classes from knowledge compilation unify several positive results, adding primitive words and palindrome concatenations. Most strikingly, asking whether a given grammar's problem is tractable is itself conditionally undecidable. The paper maps the border between feasible and infeasible probabilistic reasoning.
arxiv-2510-08227:
Mariana Fernández-Espinosa and a large team built ConversAR, reported in a 2025 arXiv paper, to help people practice a second language in group chats. Speaking a new language can feel stressful, and fear of mistakes keeps many learners quiet. Most practice tools offer scripted one-on-one chats, not lively group talk. ConversAR uses mixed reality, where digital items appear inside the real room around the user.

The system places AI characters in the room and reads the scene to spark fitting topics. It also creates simple 3D props on the spot to match the talk. The team first asked language experts what learners need, then tested the system with twenty-one learners. Users said they felt more engaged and more willing to speak up. They also felt safer making mistakes than in a real group setting.
arxiv-2510-08427:
Sujit Rao builds a hierarchy of certificates that lower-bound the energy gap of qubit Hamiltonians in a 2025 arXiv paper. The spectral gap, the distance between the two lowest energy levels, controls many quantum properties. Proving a Hamiltonian has a decent gap is notoriously hard in general. Semidefinite programming certificates, which a computer can check, offer a practical route.

His hierarchy applies the NPA method to constraints describing the algebra su(2^n), which governs qubit systems. Added constraints restrict which representations of the algebra may appear. The certificates have polynomial size at each fixed level, so they stay computable. Rao proves the hierarchy converges, in fact exactly at level n, the number of qubits. The proof shows allowed representations encode the sum of the two smallest eigenvalues. An example with a commuting local Hamiltonian gets a nontrivial gap bound.
arxiv-2510-08727:
Silvie Illésová and co-authors benchmark optimization algorithms for noisy variational quantum chemistry in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Variational Quantum Eigensolver estimates molecular energies by tuning circuit parameters classically. Which optimizer steers that search best on noisy hardware was unclear. They test the state-averaged orbital-optimized variant on the hydrogen molecule under several noise models.

Six optimizers compete: BFGS, SLSQP, Nelder-Mead, Powell, COBYLA, and the global method iSOMA. Noise settings span ideal, stochastic, and decoherence channels including phase damping, depolarizing, and thermal relaxation, at varied intensities. BFGS consistently reached the most accurate energies with fewest evaluations, staying robust under moderate decoherence. COBYLA suited cheap approximations, while SLSQP turned unstable in noisy regimes. Global iSOMA showed potential but cost far more compute. The findings guide optimizer choice for current noisy quantum hardware.
arxiv-2510-08827:
Al-Hossami and Bunescu define a new task for education software: finding the wrong ideas hidden in a student's code, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Beginners often form misconceptions about how a programming language works. Those false beliefs cause bugs, waste effort, and block later learning. A teacher reading one student's work can spot them, but that does not scale to large classes.

The authors name the task McMining and build a benchmark for it, pairing known misconceptions with many code samples where each one shows up. The dataset is designed to grow as new misconceptions are cataloged. They then test two miners built on large language models. Across extensive trials, the big commercial model families, Gemini, Claude, and GPT among them, proved effective at discovering the misconceptions in student code. The authors release their tools and data for others to build on.
arxiv-2510-08927:
Fu, Müller, and Sirimanna calculate how a spray of particles changes as it crosses cold nuclear matter, in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum chromodynamics. When a high-energy collision inside a nucleus births a jet, the jet's particles plow through the remaining nuclear material. The energy-energy correlator measures how the jet's energy is shared between pairs of its particles at each opening angle. It is a clean probe of what the medium does to the jet.

For electron-nucleus collisions the authors derive an exact leading-order formula for the medium's modification of that measure. The change is strongest at wide angles within the jet. Its dependence on jet energy, on the medium's transport traits, and on the path length through the nucleus is written out explicitly. They also work out the gluon-jet case for proton-nucleus collisions, comparing against early proton-lead data from the LHC.
arxiv-2510-09527:
Hossein Larki and Najmeh Rajabzadeh-Hasiri study an algebraic object tied to self-similar ultragraphs in a 2025 arXiv paper. An ultragraph generalises a directed graph by letting each edge point to a set of vertices. With a self-similar action, it generates a C-star algebra, an algebra of operators, and the authors previously built groupoid models for these algebras.

A groupoid is a generalised group where multiplication is only partly defined, and it encodes the dynamics of the system. This paper investigates when that groupoid is minimal, meaning it has no smaller invariant pieces, and when it is effective, a freeness condition on its internal symmetries. The results connect those two properties for self-similar ultragraph groupoids. As a payoff, they obtain a simplicity result for the associated algebras in a certain case, simplicity meaning no nontrivial closed ideals.
arxiv-2510-09627:
John Severn and Eric Lauga treat swimming filaments as an optimisation problem in a 2025 arXiv paper. A flexible filament that beats periodically models the flagella of sperm and algae, and also various artificial micro-swimmers. Classic studies related the internal forcing pattern to the resulting shape and swimming speed, but they explored that space case by case.

The authors instead expand the motion in eigenmodes, the natural vibration patterns of the system, and show that very few modes capture the swimming accurately. For a filament with monophasic forcing, the kind proposed for some artificial swimmers, exactly four forcing eigenmodes govern the motion, and only two of them are independent. That reduction slashes the computational cost of describing the swimmer. Building on it, they optimise such swimmers under various constraints, searching for the forcing patterns that swim best within the rules set.
arxiv-2510-10027:
Sato studies norm one tori in this 2025 arXiv paper in algebraic geometry. A norm one torus is a geometric object built from a field extension, recording elements whose norm equals one. The question is whether such a torus is p-retract rational over the base field, a weak form of being describable by independent parameters.

Sato focuses on non-Galois extensions, where the symmetry group is smaller than the degree suggests. The cases treated are those where the Galois group of the closure is the symmetric group or the alternating group, the two most common cases. For a fixed prime p, the answer decides rationality questions that feed into broader classification work on algebraic tori.
arxiv-2510-10227:
Greg Bodwin, Bernhard Haeupler, D Ellis, Hershkowitz, and Zihan Tan simplify length-constrained expander decompositions in this 2025 arXiv paper in theoretical computer science. Expander decompositions split a graph into well-connected pieces, and the length-constrained version also respects limits on path lengths inside each piece. The tool has driven several recent breakthroughs in fast graph algorithms.

The authors give simple constructions for these decompositions. Simpler proofs and constructions widen the set of problems the technique can serve, since earlier versions were intricate. Graph algorithms for routing, cuts, and distances all lean on expansion. A cleaner decomposition lowers the barrier for importing those results into new algorithmic settings.
arxiv-2510-10427:
Kim and co-authors study dark gaps in barred galaxies in this 2025 arXiv paper in astronomy. Dark gaps are dim regions along the minor axis of a galaxy's central bar. They are expected to form as the bar evolves over cosmic time, redistributing stars.

Several studies have proposed links between gap locations and dynamical resonances, places where stellar orbits sync with the bar's rotation, but results stay inconclusive. The authors test those links with galaxy data and simulations. Pinning down the connection would turn dark gaps into measuring tools for bar dynamics. Since most large galaxies host bars, a reliable gap diagnostic would read the internal clocks of a huge population.
arxiv-2510-10627:
Guy Mor-Lan, Tamir Sheafer, and Shaul R Shenhav introduce a dataset for studying how news claims earn credibility, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They define a new task, Epistemic Appeal Identification: deciding whether a factual statement is anchored in an external source, and how. Their dataset, FactAppeal, contains 3,226 manually annotated English news sentences. Unlike resources for claim detection or verification, it captures the evidence structure underneath the claims.

Annotations mark factual statements and the source mentions they rely on, at span level. They also record fine grained traits: the source type, such as expert, witness, or direct evidence; whether it is named; its role and credentials; and whether it is quoted directly or indirectly. The team modeled the task with encoder and generative models ranging from 2 to 9 billion parameters. Their best model, based on Gemma 2 9B, reached a macro-F1 score of 0.73 on the task.
arxiv-2510-10927:
Yawen Yang and four co-authors recognize medical entities whose parts are scattered through a sentence, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In biomedical text, one entity may consist of non adjacent tokens and overlap with others. Earlier methods link fragments or internal tokens, suffering error propagation and ambiguity. Their model, GapDNER, learns from the context gaps between fragments, treating each gap as an additional span type and turning the task into token pair grid tagging.

Two components model the grid. An intra span module uses a biaffine mechanism with linear attention to capture each span's internal regularity. An inter span module uses criss cross attention to capture relations among spans. At decoding time, directed edges link fragments and gaps, and a breadth first search finds valid paths through the grid. On three datasets, GapDNER set new state of the art results for this task, with clear advantages on complex entity structures.
arxiv-2510-11027:
Ganlin Yang and twenty co-authors build a robot model that reasons and acts in one system, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Vision language action models control robots end to end, but the reasoning of their vision language backbones rarely transfers cleanly into physical policy learning. Their Vlaser model is designed to integrate high level embodied reasoning with low level control. It trains on Vlaser-6M, a dataset of six million examples assembled by the team.

Vlaser reached state of the art performance across embodied reasoning benchmarks covering spatial reasoning, embodied grounding, question answering, and task planning. The team also systematically studied how different vision language initializations affect later fine tuning for robot control. Guided by those insights, their approach set state of the art results on the WidowX robot benchmark and stayed competitive on the Google Robot benchmark.
arxiv-2510-11127:
A thin film of liquid carrying solid grains spreads very differently from a clean liquid film. Alice Pelosse, Élisabeth Guazzelli, and Matthieu Roché review this problem in a 2025 arXiv fluid dynamics article. They examine granular suspensions, mixtures of solid particles in liquid, flowing as thin films over rigid solid surfaces with a free surface exposed to air.

The review develops two canonical situations: a drop spreading on a surface, and dip-coating, where an object is pulled out of a bath and carries a film with it. In drop spreading, grains pile up near the advancing contact line, which changes both the spreading rate and the shape of the surface. In dip-coating, predicting how much fluid and how many particles get entrained becomes hard once the film thickness approaches the particle size itself. Such flows matter for lava, paints, coatings, and 3D printing.
arxiv-2510-11427:
The faint glow of Lyman-alpha light from young galaxies traces cosmic structure, but much of it comes from sources too dim to detect one by one, which intensity mapping can capture statistically. Maja Lujan Niemeyer and a large collaboration present such a measurement in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. They use data from the Hobby-Eberly Telescope Dark Energy Experiment, a spectroscopic survey, and cross-correlate the diffuse Lyman-alpha intensity with catalogued emitters.

The team built the intensity map from spectra containing no individually detected emitters and modeled the measurement with lognormal mock runs including the survey's sensitivity and masking. In three redshift bins they measured the combined product of galaxy bias, intensity bias, and mean intensity. The results are consistent with hydrodynamic simulations including radiative transfer. They are much smaller than earlier quasar results, paving the way for fuller work.
arxiv-2510-12227:
Flores and colleagues map how abandoned geostationary satellites drift into chaos, in a 2025 arXiv paper in nonlinear dynamics. Satellites left near an unstable equilibrium point above the equator switch irregularly between circulating and swinging motion. These transitions are so sensitive to small disturbances that long term motion is unpredictable.

Earlier Monte Carlo studies traced many trajectories near one unstable point and found that chaos arrives in sudden episodes tied to the precession cycle, when orbital inclination is smallest. That analysis was too costly to extend beyond one starting longitude. The authors instead apply modified Lagrangian descriptors, tools that reveal dynamical structure from trajectory data at lower cost. They map behavior across all longitudes for both unstable points, at one hundred sixty five degrees east and fifteen degrees west. Chaos episodes stay linked to the inclination cycle, but their timing shifts with starting longitude.
arxiv-2510-12327:
Clavié and colleagues show that a small architectural change reliably improves ColBERT retrieval models, in a 2025 arXiv information retrieval paper. ColBERT represents documents and queries as many vectors and scores matches with a MaxSim operator. Like other multi vector methods, it shrinks each vector through a single layer linear projection, a step the authors suspected of quietly limiting performance.

They analyze how MaxSim shapes gradient flow during training and pinpoint inherent, if non critical, limits of the simple projection. They then test alternative projection blocks in a systematic sweep, including deeper nonlinear feedforward networks, gated linear unit blocks, and skip connections. Many variants beat the original projection, and the best raised average scores across retrieval benchmarks by over two ranking quality points. Ablations highlight upscaled middle projections and residual connections as the key ingredients. The effect held across random seeds, making the swap a robust drop in upgrade.
arxiv-2510-12627:
Zhang and a large team propose an interacting dark energy model that eases the Hubble tension, in a 2025 arXiv cosmology paper. The tension is the disagreement between early and late universe measurements of cosmic expansion. New data from the DESI survey prefer dynamical dark energy, which worsened the tension under standard models. Their models let dark energy interact, with a dynamical scale parameter modifying the cosmological constant.

Fitting microwave background, DESI, supernova, and local distance data, they find the scale parameter deviates from the standard value. In their preferred model the gap exceeds three standard errors. Because that parameter anti correlates with the Hubble constant, its negative value pushes the inferred expansion rate upward. With local data included, the tension drops below one standard error; even without it, microwave and DESI data alone ease the tension. The authors present the model as a viable route to reconciling the two measurements.
arxiv-2510-12827:
Tabrej and co-authors survey automatic speech recognition in this 2025 arXiv paper, reviewing how machines turn spoken language into text. Over the past decade the field moved from hybrid pipelines to fully neural systems, and the survey charts that shift for readers who need the whole landscape in one place.

The review first covers the three classic end-to-end designs, then the move to Transformer and Conformer models that use self-attention to track long-range patterns. It gives equal weight to training, tracing supervised learning, self-supervised foundation models such as wav2vec 2.0 that learn from unlabeled audio, and Whisper, trained on massive weakly labeled data. Datasets, word error rate scoring, streaming and on-device deployment, and fairness concerns round out the survey, which closes with open challenges.
arxiv-2510-13127:
Au studies precision design of cyclic peptides with AlphaFold in this 2025 arXiv paper, a solo research study. Cyclic peptides are ring-shaped short protein chains with drug potential. The target here is the HIV gp120 trimer, namely its CD4 binding site, where a blocker could interfere with viral entry. Earlier attempts generated peptides for the large trimer with high variability and many structures that could not work.

Au explored proximity-based hotspot mapping at the binding site, centroid distance penalization that pulls designs toward the target region, generative loss tuning, and custom loss functions. The enhancements produced cyclic peptides closely matching the binding conformation of the known CD4 attachment inhibitor BMS-818251. The study shows improved structural control and precision in AlphaFold-based generation, extending its use in structure-based drug discovery for difficult targets.
arxiv-2510-13227:
Singh, Mehra, Saha, and Sarkar propose ride-sharing without money in this 2025 arXiv paper. Urban commuting wastes fuel and congests roads, while profit-driven platforms optimize revenue over fairness and sustainability. Their system, Altruistic Ride-Sharing, is a decentralized peer-to-peer framework where participants alternate between driving and riding, earning altruism points instead of cash.

The design combines multi-agent reinforcement learning for dynamic ride matching, game-theoretic equilibrium guarantees for fairness, and a population model keeping the driver-rider balance sustainable over time. Tested on real New York City taxi data, the system reduced travel distance and emissions, raised vehicle utilization, and promoted more equitable participation compared with both no-sharing and optimization-based baselines. The authors present it as a scalable, community-driven alternative aligning individual behavior with collective urban sustainability, and they release code and data.
arxiv-2510-13427:
Zhang presents sparse matrix-vector multiplication as a challenge problem for software verification researchers. This 2025 arXiv paper, the first of two parts, gives plain implementations of a core scientific computing kernel. The kernel sits inside iterative solvers that tackle large sparse linear systems. Its optimized versions are intricate, which makes their correctness hard to assure.

Zhang provides a sequential version and a basic parallel version using MPI message passing. Both are written in C within the PETSc library tradition of sparse storage formats. The matrix is stored in compressed sparse row form, keeping only its nonzero entries. The code ships with a built-in correct answer, so a run flags any wrong result. A sophisticated optimized parallel version is left for the second part of the work. The simple versions still share key ingredients with that optimized one.
arxiv-2510-13627:
Centritto and co-authors design a tiny antenna that links quantum processors wirelessly inside their cryostat. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses the wiring bottleneck that blocks scaling quantum computers. Dense cables across cold stages eat space, leak heat, and add delay. A short-range wireless link inside the fridge could relieve all three pressures.

The team proposes an on-chip differential dipole antenna running at twenty-eight gigahertz. Material properties at four kelvin are built into the model from the start. Embedding the antenna in a realistic cryostat structure tests it under true conditions. It achieves a reflection coefficient of minus twenty-eight decibels in free space and minus twenty-one inside the cryostat, showing efficient impedance matching in both settings. Those numbers signal that most signal power transfers instead of bouncing back. The result supports wireless interconnects for multi-core quantum machines.
arxiv-2510-13727:
Pandya and co-authors recast AI guardrails as a control problem, so risky agent actions get corrected, not just blocked. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that safety for acting agents is sequential, not a one-shot filter. Today's guardrails classify outputs against fixed criteria and refuse when alarmed. Refusal itself can be unsafe when an agent must keep acting, as in driving.

Their framework borrows safety-critical control theory and applies it inside the model's latent world model. Predictive guardrails watch the agent's planned actions in real time. When a plan drifts toward danger, they nudge it back to a safe alternative. The wrapper is model-agnostic, so one guardrail can guard many AI systems. A training recipe based on safety-focused reinforcement learning computes them at scale. In simulated driving and shopping tests, catastrophic outcomes like crashes and bankruptcy were reliably avoided. Task performance survived the corrections intact.
arxiv-2510-13827:
Kattamuri and co-authors teach text-to-SQL models to match user intent across languages using contrastive rewards. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets systems that turn plain questions into database queries. Accuracy drops notably when users leave English, and executable queries can still miss the asker's meaning. Semantic alignment, not just runnable code, is the real goal.

Their framework trains with Group Relative Policy Optimization plus a reward based on semantic similarity. The contrastive signal pushes generated queries toward the user's true intent. On the seven-language MultiSpider dataset, fine-tuning a small Llama model lifted execution accuracy sharply. Semantic accuracy rose further still once the contrastive reward joined training. The tuned three-billion-parameter model beat a zero-shot model more than twice its size on execution. It did so with only three thousand reinforcement learning examples. Small, well-aimed training can outrun raw scale in this task.
arxiv-2510-13927:
Jishu Adhikary and Raju Maiti forecast monthly rainfall across nineteen districts of West Bengal, India, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reliable long-term rainfall forecasts matter for farming, irrigation, and water planning in the region. The authors work with a century of records, daily rainfall from 1900 to 2019 aggregated into monthly series for each district, and aim to predict nine years ahead.

Their framework works in two stages. Regression models first forecast yearly features, such as annual totals, seasonal shares, and extremes, using each district's own history plus its neighbors' history. A neural network then uses those yearly forecasts as extra inputs to predict monthly rainfall, capturing nonlinear patterns and spatial links between districts. The combined architecture produced robust long-term forecasts, which the authors present as useful for agriculture and water conservation decisions.
arxiv-2510-14127:
Pavan Chawhan and co-authors present methods for simulating neutron star merger remnants in two dimensions without the usual glitches, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Axisymmetric simulations are a cheap route compared with full three-dimensional runs, but they struggle with the singularity at the polar axis, drifts in conserved amounts, and artificial heating that corrupts evolutions.

Their flux-conservative scheme stays smooth near the axis while keeping that form of the hydrodynamics equations. It avoids the drifts in mass and angular momentum that plague other treatments. Evolving a hypermassive neutron star like a merger remnant, the scheme combined axis smoothness with conservation over timescales for viscous and neutrino-driven evolution. Because profiles stay smooth, they can remove artificial heating by tracking the entropy density. They show how heating and cooling terms follow from the basic variables. They also improve the viscosity scheme for magnetic turbulence.
arxiv-2510-14227:
Denizhan Pak examines sensorimotor contingencies, the lawful patterns linking movement to sensory change, as the foundation of a sensorimotor approach to cognition, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The topic belongs to the 4E movement in cognitive science, which treats cognition as embodied, embedded, enactive, and extended. It challenges the classic 'sandwich model', in which mental processes sit between perception and action.

Pak argues that rejecting such a long-held idea requires an accessible theory backed by firm experimental support, and that sensorimotor contingencies are the unifying thread the 4E camps share for that role. On this view, seeing is not building inner pictures. It is learning the ways sensory input changes as one moves. Cognition comes from skilled activity rather than the brain alone. The paper develops this case. It presents them as the thread around which the 4E research programs can converge.
arxiv-2510-14627:
Zhong and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a framework that teaches robots to place objects where people would expect them. Tidying a home means judging both meaning, such as cups belonging near the coffee maker, and geometry, such as avoiding collisions. Human demonstrations of good placement are scarce, which limits what a robot can learn from them directly.

Their framework, GOPLA, works in stages. A multimodal language model turns instructions and images into structured plans that state how objects relate. A spatial mapper converts the plans into three-dimensional affordance maps, and a diffusion-based planner proposes placement poses, checked against costs for collisions and for matching several plans. A separate pipeline inflates the few human demonstrations into plentiful synthetic training data. In experiments, GOPLA beat the runner-up method by 30.04 percentage points in placement success across the reported scenarios, judged on accuracy and physical plausibility.
arxiv-2510-14727:
Bartlett, Liem, and Panichella address, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how to test learning agents that will work in safety-critical settings. A test suite that finds many failures is not enough: the failures should be diverse, exposing distinct ways the agent can go wrong. The existing tool INDAGO searches for failures with a single objective, maximizing their count, so its discoveries can cluster around one error type.

The authors introduce INDAGO-Nexus, which searches with several objectives at once: failure likelihood and the diversity of the scenarios, measured with multiple metrics and Pareto front selection. They evaluated it on three agents: a humanoid walker, a self-driving car, and a parking agent. On average it found up to eighty-three percent more unique failures than INDAGO for driving and forty percent more for parking. It also cut time-to-failure by up to sixty-seven percent across all agents.
arxiv-2510-14827:
Zhu and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a smoother way for robots to learn how people move through a shared space. Maps of Dynamics summarize a site's typical motion patterns, so a robot can anticipate where walkers will be. Existing maps sample space on a discrete grid and are costly to build offline. They also leave holes where observations are sparse, and filling those holes is guesswork.

The authors replace the grid with a neural implicit function. Given coordinates in space and time, it returns the parameters of a Semi-Wrapped Gaussian Mixture Model describing motion there. Nothing needs discretization or filling-in for thinly sampled regions. On a large public dataset of long-term people tracking, the method represented motion more accurately than available baselines. Its velocity distributions were also smoother in sparse regions, and it remained computationally efficient, a practical route to modeling complex human movement.
arxiv-2510-14927:
Parc and a large collaboration report, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a look at an odd planetary system around the M dwarf TOI-756. The near-infrared spectrograph NIRPS, installed alongside HARPS in Chile, follows up planet candidates from the TESS telescope around small red stars. Its sub-Neptune program aims to learn what these worlds are made of.

Combining TESS and ground-based photometry with radial velocities from NIRPS and HARPS, the team characterized two planets. TOI-756 b transits every 1.24 days, with a radius of 2.81 Earth radii and a mass near ten Earth masses, making it a volatile-rich sub-Neptune. TOI-756 c never transits: it is a cold giant on a 149.6-day, markedly eccentric orbit, at least four times Jupiter's mass. A steady drift in the velocities hints at a third body. The pairing is the first confirmed architecture of its kind around an M dwarf.
arxiv-2510-15027:
Liu, Perea-Causin, Liu, and Bergholtz show, in a 2025 arXiv paper, that exotic fractional quantum order does not need the band structure's permission. Fractional Chern insulators, states where electrons collectively behave as fractions of themselves with quantized Hall conductance, were recently found at zero magnetic field in moiré materials. The standard expectation ties them to bands already nontrivial for single particles.

The authors project the long-range Coulomb force into a topologically trivial band of twisted multilayer graphene, a deliberately unpromising start. Ground states of this kind appear anyway, and their entanglement spectra confirm Laughlin-like character. The cause lies in the band's quantum geometry, spread very unevenly across the moiré Brillouin zone. That unevenness changes what the Coulomb force does, regardless of band topology. The same mechanism stabilizes Laughlin-like states in higher-Chern-number bands under reachable conditions.
arxiv-2510-15427:
S. O. Kara reports good news for the precision of proton physics in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. Parton distribution functions describe how a proton's momentum is shared among its inner quarks and gluons. For heavy flavors, charm and bottom quarks, rival global fits long disagreed sharply at small momentum fractions, blurring predictions for future experiments.

Kara compares the latest fits from three major groups and finds their heavy-flavor functions now converge closely. At a very small momentum fraction, the largest relative deviation between fits is about seventeen percent, nearly half the spread seen before 2013. Consistent treatments of the strong coupling and of scale choices stabilized the results. This precision halves the distribution-driven uncertainty in heavy-quark production at planned electron-proton colliders. It also steadies the theory behind searches for new particles that couple to leptons, sharpening the discovery case for those machines.
arxiv-2510-16227:
Jennifer Hu and four co-authors ask what a language model's odds on a sentence can tell us about grammar. A model's probability for a string of words is not the same as that string being grammatical, so the link needs care. Their theory starts from simple claims about how text corpora get made in the first place.

The theory makes three testable predictions, and the team checks them on two hundred eighty thousand sentence pairs in English and Chinese. First, near-twin sentences with tiny meaning gaps should get near-twin odds. Second, the gap in odds between twins should track the gap humans feel. Third, odds alone should fail to sort stray good sentences from bad ones cleanly. All three hold up, giving firmer ground for using model odds to judge what models know about sentence structure.
arxiv-2510-16327:
Nicholas J Weaver, Joshua I Faskowitz, Richard F Betzel, and Christopher W Lynn ask a pointed question. How much of the brain's activity can be guessed from a few key links? Regions of the brain rise and fall together, and those correlations fence in what patterns can occur. But which correlations matter, and how many, was unclear.

Their information-based framework ranks correlations by how much they sharpen predictions of brain states. On human cortex data, a small set of correlations explains the vast majority of the activity's variance. That makes the brain highly compressible: a sparse link network suffices to forecast large-scale activity. The pattern holds across people and mental tasks. Oddly, the most vital links are not always the strongest ones. The tools offered can hunt the key links in any brain data set.
arxiv-2510-16427:
Simran Soni and three co-authors study McKean-Vlasov equations, a class of stochastic equations where each particle feels the whole population around it. In the class they treat, both the drift and the noise terms grow faster than linearly in every variable, including the population term. Such growth breaks many standard proofs.

The team proves the equations and their particle systems are well posed, in finite and infinite time. They give two results on how the particle system approaches the population limit, one with a sharp rate. They also propose a fully explicit tamed Euler scheme for computation. Earlier schemes for this setting were semi-implicit or relied on truncation.
arxiv-2510-16527:
Shrajal Bajpai, Lakshmi Kanta Patra, and Suchandan Kayal hone life-span guesses in a 2025 paper. They guess start points for many exponential life curves. An exponential curve fits goods that run safe for a span, then start to fail. The start point is that safe span, the least life a good will show. A Linex loss scores misses in a lopsided way, to punish one side more.

They treat scale order first, then start-point order, in three cases of scale knowledge. In each case, they prove the best plain guess can be beaten. New guesses are given in closed, ready-to-use forms. Sim runs with fake data rank the new guesses by risk. Gains hold for cut-off tests, staged tests, and record data too.
arxiv-2510-16727:
Sanskar Pandey and three co-authors introduce Beacon, a benchmark that exposes sycophancy in large language models. Sycophancy is the habit of flattering or agreeing with a user instead of reasoning honestly. The authors trace it to training rewards that blur helpfulness with polite submission.

Beacon forces a choice in a single turn, with no conversation history, so the bias is measured on its own. Tests across twelve leading models split the habit into steady language and emotion-based parts, both growing with model size. The team also tries prompt-level and activation-level fixes that push the bias in opposite directions. They frame sycophancy as a measurable drift in what models treat as correct behavior.
arxiv-2510-16827:
Kangkang Deng and four co-authors review a workhorse optimization method in a 2025 paper. Optimization means finding the best solution under stated limits. Large problems in science and industry carry many such limits. The augmented Lagrangian method handles limits by folding them into the goal.

The review gathers the method's theory into one unified account. It covers smooth, rough, convex, and nonconvex problems alike. Convex here means the problem curves in a friendly, single-valley way. Newer results promise arrival at good points even without convexity. For rough problems, nearby smoothing steps keep convergence fast. The authors also cover hard whole-number problems and practical subproblem solvers. Readers get both the method's strengths and its known limits.
arxiv-2510-16927:
Egor Petrov, Nikita Kiselev, Vladislav Meshkov, and Andrey Grabovoy derive the full curvature of Transformer blocks in a 2025 paper. Curvature describes how sharply a model's error surface bends. That shape governs how training steps behave. Earlier work covered only the attention part in isolation.

The authors derive an exact formula for the complete block. Their Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, includes every block part. Layer normalization, feed-forward layers, and residual links all enter the calculation. Careful matrix calculus handles the nonlinear pieces exactly. They also bound the size of each resulting block. Computer checks against automatic differentiation matched to numerical precision. Closed-form versions also ran substantially faster. The result gives trainers a complete map of Transformer curvature.
arxiv-2510-17127:
Rongzhong Xiao proves a limit claim in ergodic theory, the study of long-run means in steady systems, in this 2025 paper. The paper looks at double means built from two maps of a system. Each map steps by a curved count that grows like a power. The power sits strictly between one and two.

For any steady system and any two bounded test maps, the limit exists. It holds at near all points of the system. The two step counts use two fixed non-zero scale factors. Such curved steps go past plain whole-step and square-step cases. The result adds a sharp case to the study of pointwise means.
arxiv-2510-17327:
Physics notation uses small labels, or tags, to keep track of which system a quantity belongs to, and Filippus S Roux gives those labels a firm mathematical base. Roux, writing alone, generalises the idea of tags and studies the tools that read them back out. From a short set of rules he defines tagged vector spaces, a new kind of space built around those labels.

Roux then applies the idea inside quantum optics to explain Dirac notation, the bracket writing physicists use daily. The swapping rules for ladder operators and the structure of a symplectic phase space both follow from the tag rules. Indexing tags by functions also lets the scheme cover position, time, and spin.
arxiv-2510-17427:
Compressed video already contains motion estimates, and Julien Zouein, Vibhoothi Vibhoothi, and Anil Kokaram ask how far those estimates can be trusted. Their subject is the AV1 video codec, widely used for streaming, compared against true optical flow, the dense motion field many vision programs need. Reusing the codec numbers could save a great deal of computing time if they prove faithful enough.

Zouein and his co-authors first measure AV1 and the older HEVC codec against known flow, and they show how encoder settings change the faithfulness. They then feed AV1 motion into a leading flow method as a head start. The warm start reached similar accuracy about four times faster, with only a small loss in precision.
arxiv-2510-17927:
N Lagarde, with twelve co-authors, maps where women stand in French professional astronomy in 2025. The survey, run by a French astronomy society commission, covers eleven institutes and about fifteen hundred staff. It includes students, postdocs, academics, and technical and support staff, a large share of the national field.

Shares of women are tracked by career stage, responsibility, job security, and pay. Set against a 2021 survey, the pattern shows the familiar leaky pipeline, with permanent posts as a main bottleneck. The report gives French astronomy a firm baseline for judging whether later reforms change anything.
arxiv-2510-19027:
P Djorwé and three co-authors propose a scheme to create three-way quantum entanglement and coherence that can survive warm surroundings. Heat usually destroys such fragile quantum resources, so finding setups that resist thermal noise is valuable for future quantum devices.

Their model couples a mechanical resonator to two light fields inside optical cavities, with a modulated photon hopping between them and saturable gain or loss in each cavity. Turning on the saturation effects greatly strengthens both entanglement and coherence compared with the plain setup, showing a practical route to hardier quantum states.
arxiv-2510-19127:
Daniel Zhao and four co-authors introduce MusicRFM, a way to steer music generation models without retraining them. Controlling what a music model produces is hard, since retraining is costly and older steering tricks can add audible flaws to the sound.

Recursive Feature Machines find interpretable directions inside a model's activations, axes that correspond to musical traits like notes or chords. Lightweight probes learn those directions inside the MusicGen model, and during generation the directions are fed back in to guide the output in real time. The result is fine-grained, understandable control over a frozen pretrained model.
arxiv-2510-19427:
M Klabunde, L Caspari, and F Lemmerich revisit a claim about robust neural networks. The claim says such networks converge to similar internal forms. A modified sameness hypothesis made that suggestion. If true, it would simplify how researchers reason about these models.

The authors confirm strong similarity in specific settings. But the pattern breaks across other datasets. Predicted behavior does not grow universal with robustness. The gap traces to the final layer. Retraining just that layer restores more uniform behavior. Sameness, they conclude, is partial. It depends on the setting.
arxiv-2510-19527:
Qing Mao and five co-authors present PoseCrafter, a method for estimating the relative camera pose between two photos that barely overlap. Pose estimation from sparse image pairs is a core problem in 3D vision, and small or zero overlap defeats most current methods. Earlier fixes synthesized in-between frames, but the frames came out blurry and frame selection was slow.

PoseCrafter couples a video interpolation model with a pose-conditioned novel view synthesis model to generate clearer intermediate frames. A selector based on feature matching then picks the frames best suited to pose estimation. On four benchmark datasets, the method clearly improved pose accuracy over leading alternatives, with the largest gains on pairs with little or no overlap.
arxiv-2510-19627:
Han Zhong and three co-authors build a superconducting quantum diode from twisted niobium diselenide and ask how much rectification a quantum circuit actually wants. In ordinary circuits, signals traveling both ways cause reflections that feed noise back into delicate qubits. A one-way superconducting element could block that, but diode efficiency has been limited.

Twisting the material by just one degree, under in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields, raised efficiency to about twenty-eight percent, well above untwisted devices. Quantum simulations then show this middling efficiency is not a flaw: it best preserves qubit anharmonicity and stable two-level behavior. Perfect one-way flow, the authors argue, is the wrong target for quantum hardware.
arxiv-2510-19727:
Stijn Cambie and Wouter van Doorn settle two conjectures of Erdős and Hall about separable numbers. The pair of theorists defined two whole numbers as interlocking when the divisors of each one alternate with the divisors of the other. They called a number separable if it takes part in such a pair. The open questions asked how common separable powers of two are.

Cambie and van Doorn prove the separable powers of two have positive lower density. In plain terms, they form a real share of all powers of two, and so do the non-separable ones. They also prove that only finitely many interlocking pairs multiply to the product of the first primes. Both conjectures are thereby resolved.
arxiv-2510-20027:
Damian Bowness and Charalambos Poullis tackle visual noise that appears when a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene is viewed from camera positions far outside its training views. In those unvisited regions the model must guess density, color, and shape, and the guesses often look unstable. Their fix works at render time rather than by retraining the scene.

The filter scores sensitivity from intermediate gradients and targets instability tied to stretched, directional splats in particular. In tests it improves visual quality, realism, and consistency more than a Neural Radiance Field method called BayesRays. Because it plugs into existing rendering pipelines in real time, users can explore freely without a costly extra step.
arxiv-2510-20127:
Nicholas M. Christopher and three co-authors show how to run one- and two-qubit gates on a protected type of superconducting qubit that stores information in quasicharge. Protected qubits aim for error rates low enough for error-corrected, large-scale quantum computers, but they need new control methods. Their gate hardware is an electronically controlled tunnel junction formed by two topological superconductors.

Both gate schemes rest on the same dynamical Josephson effect with a doubled period, so they share gate times and error behavior. Simulations in a regime with non-negligible charging energy test how robust the gates are against charge noise. The authors argue that junctions of minimal Kitaev chains of quantum dots make the plan practical.
arxiv-2510-20227:
Jinho Cha and five co-authors set out the math base for a class of update rules called Bregman Variational Learning Dynamics. The rules join Bayes updates, mirror steps, and proximal steps in one frame for worlds that shift in time. Each step is cast as a trade-off task. It joins a smooth convex loss with a Bregman gap term.

The team proves the step map is averaged and contractive in the Bregman sense. It is also stable at an exponential rate. More proofs give Fejer-type bounds, drift-aware rates, and a match with a flow form in time. In sum, the rules are well posed and come with firm bounds for use in non-steady tasks.
arxiv-2510-20327:
Fengyuan Yu and five co-authors build LEGO, a light frame to strip many private traits at once from user codes in recommender systems. Real privacy needs span more than one trait, and the needs shift in time. Past ways strip one trait at a time and adapt with poor speed. LEGO splits the work in two steps.

Step one cleans each trait from the user code on its own. Step two joins the cleaned codes in a loose, fast mix that guards all traits at once. Cast as a mutual facts cut task, the frame has a proof of joint strip skill. Tests on three real sets and three model types back the claims.
arxiv-2510-20427:
Thomas Jaffard builds volume forms from rough curves that fail the smooth tests of the classic form. He uses an integral due to Züst to make a spread law from one rough curve and the steps of some more. The Hölder rates of the curves must sit close to one, but not at it. The law shifts in a smooth way with its curves and matches the classic case when the curves are Lipschitz.

Jaffard shows these two traits fix the law in full and finds its Hölder rate. By dual means, the law then sets an integral on broad domains, and it matches the Züst build on box forms. A fresh test on the domain makes sure the integral is sound. Past edge rules come back as side cases.
arxiv-2510-20927:
Tom Reed and two co-authors audit what frontier AI model reports actually say about their chemical and biological risk evaluations, using the STREAM framework as a yardstick. Public reports are a main window into lab safety testing and a basis for outside trust and review.

Three detailed spring twenty twenty five reports, from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind flagships, are compared point by point. The audit records which method details appear and which are omitted, such as task design, scoring, and limits. Gaps found across all three show where reporting norms still fall short, giving labs and reviewers a concrete list for fuller disclosure.
arxiv-2510-21027:
Zhe Fei leads nine co-authors on customizing open source language models to extract medication attributes for opioid use disorder treatment across varied hospital record systems. Prescription details scatter across mismatched fields and free text notes, blocking unified monitoring of these medications.

Models including Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and MedGemma are tuned to pull a shared attribute set, dates, drug names, durations, quantities, and refills, from site specific formats. A standardized coverage metric is then computed for each patient record set. The practical framework aims at public health tracking that survives the messy reality of heterogeneous records.
arxiv-2510-21327:
Sebastian Brandt, Fabian Kuhn, and Zahra Parsaeian study how much randomness helps when computers in a network must solve local labeling tasks, such as coloring edges or pointing them in a direction. For most such tasks randomness gives at most a modest gain, with one puzzling fast exception that lacks a full explanation.

They focus on degree splitting tasks on regular graphs, where edges get one of two colors or an orientation. For two-color problems whose plain cost grows like the log of the network size, they pin down the randomized cost exactly. For orientation problems they partly sort which ones stay slow under randomness and which become much faster. All of the algorithms extend to general graphs with bounded degree.
arxiv-2510-21427:
Hao Liang and four co-authors teach control policies for huge networked systems, such as traffic, power, and wireless grids, that must keep working when conditions shift. Reinforcement learning struggles here twice over: the systems are enormous, and an agent trained in one setting often fails in a slightly different one.

Their framework, GSAC, pairs causal representation learning with a meta actor-critic scheme. Each agent first learns a sparse mask marking the few nearby variables that truly drive its dynamics, which provably captures a compact summary of state and setting. A shared policy then trains across several source settings while reading that summary, and at test time a handful of runs estimates the new setting's summary for instant adaptation. Guarantees cover the causal recovery, learning, and adaptation steps, and tests beat learning from scratch.
arxiv-2510-22527:
Future sky surveys will image billions of galaxies but measure detailed spectra for far fewer. Morgan Himes, with seven co-authors, builds a 2025 model that learns galaxy images and spectra together, using a large matched set from two major surveys.

Their transformer model hides most of each input and learns to rebuild the missing image and spectrum pieces. It recovers galaxy shapes, emission line peaks, and broad spectrum slopes, though fine details stay weak. Using images alone, it estimates galaxy redshift, a distance related measure, as well as or better than prior joint models, even when spectra are absent at test time.
arxiv-2510-22627:
Small edge devices running artificial intelligence need arithmetic that saves chip area and power. Mohd Faisal Khan, Mukul Lokhande, and Santosh Kumar Vishvakarma present RAMAN in 2025, an approximate posit based multiply accumulate design, where posit is a number format meant to be efficient.

Their core engine approximates part of the multiplication, then sits inside a reusable vector unit that can serve many network layers in parallel. Training that knows about the approximation helps protect final accuracy. Chip tests report large savings in lookup tables, area, and power over a baseline posit design, while handwritten digit recognition stays near ninety eight percent accurate.
arxiv-2510-22727:
Quantum particles moving through a network leave steady current patterns that might sort data into clusters. Shmuel Lorber and Yonatan Dubi introduce Qlustering in 2025, a quantum inspired unsupervised learning algorithm that uses network based quantum transport instead of ordinary distance measures.

Data become input states in a tight binding model governed by a standard open system equation. Cluster labels emerge from output currents at terminal nodes once the system settles. Stochastic updates tune the network to lower a physically motivated cost. Benchmarks on synthetic, chemical, and biological data, including molecular and flower datasets, match or beat k-means, especially on non convex or high dimensional data.
arxiv-2510-23027:
Di Zhang leads a team of nine researchers working to make reinforcement learning stable for mixture-of-experts language models. Such models route each token to a few expert sub-networks, which saves compute. Training them with reinforcement learning often turns unstable, and most prior work studied dense models instead.

The group adds a router-aware fix to importance sampling weights in off-policy learning. Rescaling guided by router scores cuts gradient variance and steadies updates. Their method targets the root cause in the router, helping large sparse models gain reasoning skill without the wild swings that blocked earlier attempts.
arxiv-2510-23427:
