Luca Melis and six co-authors present PrivacyGuard, a toolkit for checking how much private information a trained machine learning model may leak. Models are now used in sensitive areas, so teams need practical ways to measure that risk. PrivacyGuard, released in 2025, tests models in practice, rather than trusting theory alone, using the tools of differential privacy analysis.

The toolkit runs a suite of attacks that try to infer private facts from a model. These include membership inference, which guesses if a record was in the training data, plus extraction and reconstruction attacks. Users can run them as shipped or tune them for a custom study. The design is modular, so new attacks and new privacy metrics can be added with ease as research moves on. The code is released in public, so other groups can audit their models with the same tests.
arxiv-2510-23927:
Daniel Spokoyny and nine co-authors describe CHATTERBOX, a system that plays the victim in conversations with online scammers so researchers can study the scams at scale. Pig butchering frauds build trust over weeks or months of chat before striking, and losses run to tens of billions of dollars. That slow, personal style makes the operations nearly impossible to investigate one conversation at a time.

CHATTERBOX automates the engagement with a large language model. The paper covers how the team attracts scam attempts and the engineering needed to chat convincingly for the long haul. It also details the skills required to pass or dodge the milestones in a scammer's script, the staged steps that move a victim toward paying. By running many such conversations in parallel, investigators can map tactics that were previously visible only anecdotally. The system turns the scammers' own patience into an evidence-gathering tool.
arxiv-2510-24027:
Zibo Liu and seven co-authors ask which sensors a forecasting system should listen to, a choice earlier work simply assumed away. Spatio-temporal forecasting predicts values at many locations from recent readings, but budgets usually allow sensors at only a few of them. Prior methods take the instrumented locations as given; nobody had optimized the selection itself.

The proposed framework chooses variables and trains the forecaster jointly, chasing accuracy and efficiency together. Three mechanisms do the work. Masked pruning progressively drops uninformative variables and attention parameters by quantile. A replay scheme revisits low-loss past samples so the model stays stable while the input set changes. A third step spreads information from chosen variables to all others through learned spatial links. On five real-world datasets, the joint approach significantly outperforms strong baselines on both accuracy and efficiency — evidence that sensor placement deserves to be learned, not fixed.
arxiv-2510-24127:
Peter Scherbak and two co-authors simulate mass transfer between two stars when the gas can cool by radiating light. In some binary systems, one star pours mass onto a companion at a high rate, making bright outbursts and outflows around both stars. The team models a donor star of ten solar masses with a point mass companion of five.

By changing the orbital gap, they cover transfer rates across a wide range. Gas forms a disk around the companion, and at high rates much of it escapes through the outer Lagrange point in the orbital plane. At lower rates most mass is kept. The escaping gas carries a set amount of spin, and both light output and temperature rise with transfer rate.
arxiv-2510-24227:
Senuri Wijenayake and six co-authors outline a workshop aimed at joining up fragmented research on online safety. Harmful experiences online are growing, and the human computer interaction community is urged to respond. Yet safety work is split across subfields that rarely talk, which risks designs that miss user needs and policies that ignore usability.

The workshop brings together researchers from social computing, digital design, internet policy, cybersecurity, ethics, and the social sciences. Through dialogue across these fields, the organizers hope to build shared approaches to online safety. The paper describes the workshop's goals, format, and the mix of participants it seeks to attract.
arxiv-2510-24427:
Ken Gu and six co-authors present SynthWorlds, a framework that separates a language model's reasoning from its stored world knowledge during evaluation. Benchmark scores often reflect factual recall rather than true reasoning, and tricks like paraphrasing or time filtering cannot cleanly divide the two. SynthWorlds instead builds parallel corpora for two worlds with identical structure.

One world maps to real facts, where models can exploit memorized knowledge, while the other maps to a synthetic world where that knowledge is meaningless. Mirrored tasks run on both corpora, so the score gap isolates reasoning from recall. The framework offers a cleaner measure of reasoning complexity for model evaluation.
arxiv-2510-24527:
Rishi Das leads a team of four authors on flow through porous rock. The Darcy-Forchheimer equations model fast flow in such rock. Slow flow follows Darcy's law, but fast flow adds inertia effects. Mixed finite element methods split the flow into small mesh cells. The team ask if error bounds stay strong as parameters change.

They derive error bounds that hold up across parameter ranges. Those bounds are quasi-optimal, close to the best a mesh allows. They also build block preconditioners for the linearized systems. A preconditioner reshapes a hard system so solvers run fast. Theirs stay robust as permeability and inertia vary widely. Numerical tests back up the theory on several examples. The work helps engineers trust simulations of wells and aquifers.
arxiv-2510-25027:
Evan S Gawlik and Jack McKee set a bend rule for Regge metrics, a class of smooth in parts measures of space. Such measures are used when space is cut into chunks, each smooth on its own. A bend rule for them should fit both the core frame rules and the gauge rule for a change of frame.

With move frame tools, they show their bend is a spread out mass that meets both needs at once. It matches past takes on spread bend for such measures. In the flat two way case, they prove the known Gauss and Bonnet claim for these measures: total bend ties to shape type. That seals the rule in the case most used.
arxiv-2510-25327:
Runxi Huang, Mingxuan Yu, Mingyu Tsoi, and Xiaomin Ouyang propose MMEdge. Their 2025 paper speeds multimodal inference on edge devices. Edge devices have limited computing resources ready. Uses include driving, mobile health, and human effect. Prior work often ignored sensing and execution coupling. Inter-modality dependencies also complicate real-time inference greatly.

MMEdge pipelines sensing and encoding into fine-grained units. Computation starts before full sensor inputs arrive. Data are processed incrementally as they appear. A time aggregation module preserves quality across units. It captures rich changes between pipelined stages. An changing optimizer selects sensing and model settings. It works under latency limits and changing resources. A speculative skipping step bypasses slow modality units. Early confident predictions trigger that skipping safely. Tests used two public multimodal data sets. A drone based testbed showed lower latency overall.
arxiv-2510-25427:
Auguste Poiroux, Antoine Bosselut, and Viktor Kuncak introduce RLMEval. Their 2025 paper evaluates research-level neural theorem proving. Language models show impressive results on curated benchmarks. Practical impact on research mathematics remains limited, though. Formalizing proofs automatically is especially hard at research level. Real projects differ greatly from benchmark problems.

RLMEval targets theorem proving and proof autoformalization tasks. It draws on real Lean formalization projects. Lean is a formal proof assistant language. The suite contains six hundred thirteen theorems total. Those theorems come from six Lean projects. State-of-the-art models were evaluated on the suite. A significant gap appeared in their results. Benchmark progress did not translate to realistic settings. The best model achieved only about ten percent pass rate. That rate shows how challenging research theorems are. RLMEval offers a harder benchmark for automated reasoning. It should guide progress in formal mathematics tools.
arxiv-2510-25527: Valdemar Frederiksen and Henrik Bruus show how to boost resonance quality in acoustofluidic cavities. Their 2025 physics paper embeds liquid-filled cavities inside a matched elastic metamaterial. Matching the metamaterial moduli to the liquid raises the quality factor. That happens at selected resonance modes. The gain is two to three orders of magnitude. A comparable conventional cavity does far worse. The result is a compact theoretical finding for designers of small acoustic devices that hold and move fluids.
arxiv-2510-25927:
Arvin Shahbazi-Moghaddam, working alone, reviews new limits on how spacetime singularities might be resolved. A singularity is a point where gravity theory breaks down, such as inside a black hole. A theorem by Penrose and Wall constrains what can happen there, but it rests on the generalized second law, a rule that total entropy never falls. Until recently that law was proved only in an approximate way.

Shahbazi-Moghaddam highlights a non perturbative proof of that law in holographic brane world models at the species scale, where many matter fields matter. With it, a trapped surface still forces incompleteness, so any true resolution must evade the theorem conditions. He illustrates both outcomes with a BTZ black hole and a resolved null singularity.
arxiv-2510-26027:
Ali Rasekh leads four co-authors in a design that helps video language models follow action over time. Models that answer questions about video often miss detailed temporal structure, such as the order and progression of actions across frames. Their fix places stacked temporal attention modules inside the vision encoder itself, so time relations are captured before visual tokens reach the language model. Attention lets the model weigh which frames matter for each other.

Rasekh and the team report gains on video question answering, with the clearest gains in action recognition. Scores rose by up to five point five percent across three benchmarks in their tests. Strengthening the vision encoder, rather than only the language side, closes a noted gap in video understanding.
arxiv-2510-26327:
Leilei Shi, Cheng Zhang, and Da-jun Zhang review ways to write a key variable in a lattice equation and add a new route. The Nijhoff Quispel Capel equation is a general quadrilateral lattice equation, meaning it relates values at the four corners of a grid square. It is expressed through a function S of two parameters. It is viewed as the counterpart of the Q3 equation, near the top of a standard classification list.

Shi and the team survey known formulations of the variable S through the Cauchy matrix approach, the eigenfunction approach, and a spectral Wronskian, a determinant built from solutions. They then derive a new formulation from the eigenfunctions of a Lax pair for the lattice modified Korteweg de Vries equation, introducing a new Dbar problem in the derivation.
arxiv-2510-26427:
Volodymyr Sushch builds a half-discrete version of Maxwell's equations, the laws of electric and magnetic fields. Half-discrete means space is chopped into pieces while time stays smooth. His tool is discrete exterior calculus, a method that keeps the shape and structure of the original laws while moving them onto a grid.

Sushch sets out the model in both three and two dimensions and checks its main traits against the classic equations. As a test case, he works on a two-dimensional torus, a doughnut-shaped grid, where the equations become a system of first-order differential equations in time. He also derives an explicit formula for the general solution of that system. The aim is a model that stays faithful to the geometry of the field laws.
arxiv-2510-26527:
Ruilin Wang, with six co-authors, speeds up the slow step of running large language models. Their method is speculative decoding, where a small model drafts the next words and a big model checks them, which keeps output the same while saving time. Most work uses just two models in that draft-and-check loop, with little theory behind the design.

Wang and the team propose a polybasic version that can use several models at once, backed by a full theoretical analysis. They prove a basic theorem that pins down the best possible inference time for such multi-model systems. Tests across model families gave speedups of roughly three to four times, while the output distribution stayed unchanged. Code and proofs are released for others to build on.
arxiv-2510-27027:
Martin Ottens, Kai-Steffen Hielscher, and Reinhard German bridge simulation and live testing for low-orbit satellite networks. Mega-constellations promise global internet coverage, but real protocols are hard to judge inside pure simulators. The team extends the Hypatia simulator to record path traits such as delay and bandwidth between two endpoints during slow, detailed runs.

Those records are saved as trace files and replayed in real-time emulation on real systems, allowing tests with real software and human use. The method adapts easily to existing simulation models. Across several constellation scenarios, emulation tracks simulation closely, with correlation up to a high level reported by the authors. Open issues include missing feedback from emulation back to simulation and timing drift.
arxiv-2510-27527:
Yuxiang Chen, Yifan Liu, and six other co-authors push four-bit training for large language models in this 2025 paper. Training is so costly that teams want every number stored in just four bits. A new format, NVFP4, promises big savings. The catch is keeping quality near that of fuller precision.

Their method, TetraJet-v2, uses NVFP4 for activations, weights, and gradients in all linear layers. Two faults plague such training: weights that oscillate, jittering instead of settling, and outliers, rare huge values that swamp the rest. Three fixes answer: a double-block quantization scheme, OsciReset to calm the jitter, and OutControl to protect outlier accuracy. On test models, the method cut the quality gap to standard training by about half while running notably faster.
arxiv-2510-27627:
Nikos Frantzikinakis and Borys Kuca build a framework in 2025 for long-run averages along sparse step sequences in ergodic theory. Ergodic theory studies how repeated maps spread points over time. A sparse sequence grows fast, so its steps thin out. The focus is corner patterns, where two maps act in linked ways.

With the new tools, they settle a length-three case of a broad pattern theorem for linked maps. They show that key averages stay the same when steps follow sparse rules such as a power with a non-whole exponent. Results also extend known facts about common gaps in corners. The work draws on norm smoothing and special extensions of the system.
arxiv-2511-00027:
Josu Eguiluz Castaneira, Axel Brando, and Migle Laukyte argue, in a position paper, that innovation which systematically breaks basic rights should not count as innovation at all. AI now runs inside central systems and decisions where failures cause social, economic, and public harm. Analogies from flight, drug firms, and welfare systems, plus cases of synthetic false news, bias, and rogue decisions, support their case.

Thoughtful, adaptive regulation is presented as the foundation of innovation, not its brake. Policy readers get a direct challenge to the regulation-versus-innovation framing. The paper asks societies to judge new systems by the rights they respect while they spread.
arxiv-2511-00327:
A V Afanasjev, B Osei, and A Dalbah review recent progress in tuning a leading theory of atomic nuclei. The theory, covariant density functional theory, describes nuclei across the whole chart with a small set of energy functionals. Global optimization adjusts those functionals so predictions match data everywhere at once, a task that once cost too much computing time.

A newer anchor-based method changed that picture, allowing global fits at reasonable cost. It also works in very large model spaces, with a sound way to extend results toward an infinite space. That makes it possible to estimate errors from space cutoffs and from terms often left out of binding energy sums, such as electron binding. The review sums up where the field now stands.
arxiv-2511-00527:
Robab Aghazadeh-Chakherlou and five co-authors argue that benchmark scores are not enough to call a language model reliable. Accuracy over a test set says little about how a model will behave on future tasks in a real setting. Their framework, HIP-LLM, borrows from software reliability engineering: reliability is the probability of failure-free operation over a stated number of future tasks, under a stated pattern of use called an operational profile.

Domains and subdomains form a hierarchy, so evidence pools from small areas up to system-level judgments. Imprecise priors encode honest uncertainty about what is not yet known, and the output is an envelope of posterior reliability estimates rather than one brittle number. Experiments on several benchmarks show sharper, more standardized reliability pictures than existing approaches.
arxiv-2511-00627:
Jean Barré, Olga Seminck, Antoine Bourgois, and Thierry Poibeau trace the making of the detective, a literary archetype, across one hundred fifty years of French fiction. Using quantitative methods and character-level embeddings, they test whether one archetype truly unites figures from M Lecoq in 1866 to Commissaire Adamsberg in 2017. A supervised model can indeed capture that unity across the whole span.

Within the unity, the role mutates. The detective grows from a secondary figure into the central character and the reasoning machine of the classical detective story. After the Second World War, the imported American hardboiled tradition seeps into France, and the archetype darkens. The detective now navigates social violence and moral ambiguity. Computational reading makes the long arc of a cultural figure measurable.
arxiv-2511-00727:
Xuelin Yang, Licong Lin, Susan Athey, Michael Jordan, and Guido Imbens develop a way to combine randomized experiments with observational data when estimating cause and effect. Trials are trustworthy but small and costly. Observational data are larger and cheaper, yet hidden factors can bias them.

Their framework treats estimation as risk minimization, fitting one model that balances a loss from the experiment against a loss from the observational data. Cross validation across the experimental folds chooses how much weight each source receives, judged by the causal parameter itself. Tests on real and synthetic data show the method works reliably, and the authors prove non-asymptotic error bounds for the estimates.
arxiv-2511-01727:
Félix del Teso, Stefano Fronzoni, and David Gómez-Castro speed up a hard numerical task. The task is to solve for the fractional Laplacian, a diffusion operator with long-range reach. Its solutions press against the domain's edge with a weak power-law profile. Plain finite elements, built from piecewise linear parts, converge slowly for just that reason.

The fix builds the edge behavior into the basis itself. Each basis function is a piecewise linear part times a smooth stand-in for the distance to the edge, raised to the fractional power. The solution divided by that weight is smoother, and the method exploits the gain. On good meshes, the convergence order rises to two minus the fractional power. A strict error analysis gives the rates outright. Numerical tests back them.
arxiv-2511-02027:
Zeyu Yang, Clayton Souza Leite, and Yu Xiao release StrengthSense, an open dataset for tracking the activities that tax human strength. Wearable inertial sensors could monitor muscular strength, endurance, and power in daily life. But algorithm builders lacked a full dataset of strength-demanding movement. They had nothing to train and test on.

StrengthSense records eleven strength-demanding activities, such as sit-to-stand, stair climbing, and mopping, plus two non-strength activities for contrast. Twenty-nine healthy subjects wore ten inertial measurement units across limbs and torso while video recordings provided annotation references. The paper documents the collection protocol, the cleanup, and the technical validation. It includes a comparison of joint angles estimated from the sensors. Those are set against angles extracted directly from video. The match confirms the data's accuracy. The authors aim the dataset at activity recognition research and fitness and health monitoring applications.
arxiv-2511-02127:
Iago Mamede, Carlos Fiore, Gustavo Forão, Karel Proesmans, and André Vieira prove a bridge between two worlds of statistical physics. Many-body systems held between two heat baths at different temperatures settle into nonequilibrium states that are usually hard to analyse. The authors show that a large class of such systems maps exactly onto an equivalent equilibrium system, with no approximation.

The mapping hands researchers the nonequilibrium transition points directly from known equilibrium results, whatever the model, interaction pattern, or distance from equilibrium. The team checks the correspondence on the Ising, Potts, and Blume-Capel models, and examines how entropy production behaves near critical and tricritical points. They point to uses in microscopic heat engines and stochastic thermodynamics, where equilibrium knowledge is far more complete.
arxiv-2511-02327:
Yufeng Lu, a mathematician, proves that a class of nonlinear wave equations always has solutions that last for all time, even when the starting state is rough. The equations are generalised fractional Hartree equations. In them, a wave interacts with itself through a convolution potential, and the dispersion is governed by a fractional Schrödinger operator. Rough initial data, living in interpolation spaces between square-integrable functions and new spaces built from that operator's semigroup, are the hard case.

The proof adapts a splitting method developed in earlier work to modulation spaces, function spaces tuned to time-frequency analysis. It exploits how slowly the fractional semigroup grows there, at the price of some regularity. The result implies global well-posedness in modulation spaces for exponents near two, with no requirement that the starting data be small. It works in every dimension.
arxiv-2511-02827:
Mohamed Almukhtar, Anwar Ghammam, Marouane Kessentini, and Hua Ming study how single code changes lift or lower the quality of Python machine learning systems. Their 2025 study is huge: 3,340 open projects, more than 3.7 million commits, and trillions of lines of code. Prior work catalogued what changes happen, but not what they do to quality.

The team built PyQu, a tool that uses low-level software metrics to spot quality-enhancing commits with strong accuracy. With PyQu plus thematic analysis, they found sixty-one quality-improving change types, grouped into thirteen classes. About 41 percent of them were new, missed by leading change detectors. The catalogue gives builders and teachers a base for automatic quality checks in machine learning software.
arxiv-2511-02927:
Rafael Baez and five colleagues ask a hard question about fuzzing: if a long test campaign finds no bug, how risky is it to stop? Differential fuzzing hunts inputs that make two programs disagree, but it offers no guarantee about what it missed. Their 2025 paper borrows extreme value theory, the statistics of rare maxima, to estimate that leftover risk.

They applied the method to real Java libraries, hunting information leaks through side channels. Extreme value extrapolations beat simple statistical bounds in some cases and tied in most others. Where the method flagged low risk, campaigns could stop early. The team reports savings of tens of millions of bytecode executions on average from such early stops, across the libraries tested.
arxiv-2511-03027:
Paul Sutcliffe finds highly symmetric solutions of the discrete Nahm equation, a rule that steps matrices along a one-dimensional lattice. Solutions of the system correspond to SU(2) magnetic monopoles in hyperbolic space, and the number of lattice points sets the curvature of that space. Rank and symmetry conditions fix what happens at the two ends of the lattice.

Sutcliffe gets his solutions by imposing Platonic symmetry, the symmetry of the regular solids. From them he computes the spectral curves of the monopoles directly. Such curves are the standard fingerprint of a monopole, encoding its shape and charge in a single algebraic object. Symmetric cases like these are prized test beds, since they can be computed in full and often show patterns that less tidy cases hide.
arxiv-2511-03227:
Alexander Htet Kyaw and Lenin Ravindranath Sivalingam introduce a storytelling tool where a story lives as a web of linked nodes. Each node can hold text, images, sound, and video together. Creators edit single nodes by hand or by prompt, and the story can branch into side paths that run side by side.

A helper agent sends each job to the right specialist, whether the task is drafting, shaping the node web, or adding context. The authors report tests on automatic outline building and describe how editing felt in practice. They also note weak spots, such as keeping long stories steady across many nodes. Future work points toward closer human guidance inside the creative loop.
arxiv-2511-03327:
Mario Bifulco and Luca Roversi examine how chip wiring shapes what quantum annealers can solve well. Annealers attack hard optimization tasks, but each problem must first be mapped onto the fixed links between qubits. That mapping, called minor embedding, stretches each logical variable across a chain of physical qubits.

When chains grow long or uneven, answers degrade and hardware goes to waste. The study takes a hardware-aware view of those effects, comparing how different link patterns steer embedding cost. Knowing which shapes embed cheaply can guide both problem writing and future chip design. The authors frame wiring not as a fixed nuisance but as a design choice that should match the problems users bring.
arxiv-2511-03427:
Florentia Afentaki and colleagues design support vector machines that mix kernels to suit bendable electronics. Flexible circuits print cheaply and conform to curved surfaces, but their large features leave little room or power for learning hardware. Support vector machines fit that tight budget, yet single-kernel designs force a choice between cheap linear math and pricier curved kernels.

Blending kernels lets a design buy accuracy only where it pays. The team optimizes that blend for mixed-signal hardware under strict area and power caps. Near-sensor tasks, such as reading wearables or smart labels, stand to gain most. Smarter on-device sorting could cut the energy now spent streaming raw sensor data elsewhere.
arxiv-2511-03527:
Bryan L M de Oliveira and co-authors run the first systematic check of a critic-free learning method in classic control tasks. Group-relative policy optimization drops the learned critic used by its famous predecessor and grades whole trajectory groups against each other instead. That cut raises a basic question: are learned baselines needed at all?

Careful ablations isolate baselines, discounting, and group sampling across discrete and continuous tasks. Learned critics prove essential for long-horizon work, where every critic-free variant trails the classic method. Short tasks tell another story, with simple episodic grading holding its own. The findings map where the cheaper method is safe to use and where the critic earns its keep.
arxiv-2511-03927:
Nassim Athmouni, writing alone, studies the operator algebra of a rank-one boundary defect in a semi-infinite tight-binding chain. Catalog evidence carried a longer working title; the arXiv record gives the title Boundary Cochains and the Toeplitz Index on the Half-Lattice, and that record governs.

Commutators in the algebra are confined to the boundary and vanish in the bulk. Site-by-site cochains built from commutators are each coboundaries, yet the second cohomology is infinite-dimensional, carried by the bulk. On the Toeplitz algebra the summed cochain equals a symbol pairing that recovers the Fredholm index, giving a site-resolved index density. For modulated couplings the index changes only when the bulk limit crosses a threshold.
arxiv-2511-04427:
Hao He leads five authors measuring what the Cursor AI coding tool does to open-source work. Reports claim such tools multiply output, but hard evidence has been thin. The team compares projects that adopted Cursor with matched projects that did not.

Their causal design finds a large jump in development speed after adoption. The gain, though, fades over time rather than holding steady. Code quality measures move the other way, with signs of growing complexity in the code base. The study gives project leaders a grounded warning: quick early speed can carry a long-term cost that needs active management.
arxiv-2511-04527:
Amir Zur and three colleagues ask whether language models track the paths not taken. Each token choice can send reasoning down a very different route. That makes the model's true uncertainty hard to pin down.

Using hidden activations, the team predicts and steers uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. They find a clear link between token-level uncertainty and how easily steering works. Interventions bite most where alternate paths remain open, before the model commits. The results suggest models carry an internal sense of their own branching choices, a signal that could guide safer generation.
arxiv-2511-04627:
S Chockalingam and two colleagues extend phase-field fracture models with realistic strength surfaces. Classic models capture crack growth driven by toughness, but they miss how cracks start. Nucleation depends on the material's strength surface, which the older theory ignored.

Following a blueprint from Kumar and co-authors in 2020, they add a nucleation driving force. A general formula from Chockalingam in 2025 handles arbitrary strength surfaces. The team implements it in finite elements with Mohr-Coulomb, Mogi-Coulomb, and Hoek-Brown surfaces. Those surfaces span rock and soil mechanics, so the model can now predict both crack birth and spread.
arxiv-2511-04727:
Ali Faraz leads nine authors with IndicVisionBench, a benchmark rooted in the Indian subcontinent. Most vision-language tests center Western content and English text. That leaves open how models handle India's languages and cultural scenes.

The bench covers English plus ten Indian languages across three task families. Tasks include optical character recognition, multimodal translation, and visual question answering. About five thousand images carry over thirty-seven thousand question pairs. Thirteen culturally grounded topics shape the content throughout. A paired annotation corpus in ten Indic languages is released alongside, supporting fairer tests for a huge user base.
arxiv-2511-04927:
Luchang Niu and his co-author generalize the sudden freezing of entanglement in quantum systems. In one known setup, two atoms sharing a cavity field hold entanglement flat for a stretch. It stays constant, then thaws and resumes changing.

The pair extends that sharing picture to systems of any number of qubits. Methods to set both the freezing time and the frozen value are demonstrated. One regime even freezes entanglement permanently, they report. The effect appears across many setups rather than as a one-off accident. Tunable freezing could help quantum networks hold fragile links steady on demand.
arxiv-2511-05027:
Zhuoling Chen, Yi Zhong, and Martin Haenggi propose a cross-link form of the RTS/CTS handshake for millimeter-wave Wi-Fi that uses many links at once. The classic directional handshake still leaves hidden nodes, where two senders cannot hear each other but clash at a receiver.

The authors build a new point process to model who can send where under both handshake forms. They derive formulas for density, mean interference, success odds, and hidden node counts. Results show a clear trade: cross-link use lifts link quality but lowers total throughput, while the directional form does the reverse.
arxiv-2511-05227:
Alec Metsch studies whether Kantorovich potentials in Lorentzian optimal transport are semiconvex, a regularity trait known in the Riemannian case. Optimal transport moves mass at least cost; its Lorentzian form fits space-time, where cause and time twist the rules.

Metsch shows the trait does not carry over in general. Still, he proves a broad regularity result for cost-convex functions, which gives semiconvexity of the weak potentials on an open set of full measure, under set terms on the measures. That partial result is enough to prove a transport map exists and is unique.
arxiv-2511-05427:
Kelvin Wandia and co-authors set upper limits on radio emission from the K2-18 system, home to a sub-Neptune planet with claimed signs of life-linked gases in its air. Magnetic fields guard a planet's air, so the star's magnetic state is a live question there.

The team observed the system with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array to hunt for radio glow from star or planet. No claim of a detection is made; the work bounds how bright such emission can be. Those bounds weigh on how harsh the planet's magnetic home may be.
arxiv-2511-05527:
Kate Brockman and co-authors build a math model to improve treatment for neuroblastoma, a childhood cancer that is often deadly. Doctors need better ways to choose drug mixes and doses for each child. The model tracks how tumor cells interact with two kinds of immune cells that can attack cancer.

Into that system the team adds the effects of two treatments. One is interleukin-2, which boosts immune response, and the other is a chemotherapy drug. The model can simulate children at different risk levels. The authors present it as a test bed for trying treatment plans on a computer before use in care.
arxiv-2511-05727:
Kirone Mallick, Gabriel Téllez, and Frédéric van Wijland extend a classic result about the eigenvalues of large random matrices. Thirty years ago it was shown that how these eigenvalues bunch together takes a universal form, nearly independent of the random details. That was for a static snapshot in time.

Here the matrix entries themselves wander, following Dyson Brownian motion. The authors ask whether the correlations between eigenvalues at different times stay universal too. They find a large degree of universality survives in the dynamics. It is expressed through the characteristics of a partial differential equation in the complex plane. The result links random matrix theory with tools from complex analysis and statistical physics.
arxiv-2511-06027:
Susovan Pal and co-authors bring classic classification tools to the curved space of shapes. Curves, like brain surface folds or facial profiles, live in an infinite-dimensional shape space where straight-line statistics fail. Working on the flat tangent plane at a mean shape, they define means and covariances for shape-valued data.

Shape samples are encoded with a truncated Fourier basis, cutting the problem to a manageable size. Linear and quadratic discriminant rules are then built from those features, first for spaces ignoring rotation, then for the full shape space. The team shows results on synthetic data and on real curves: cortical sulci, the corpus callosum, and facial midlines from patients with fetal alcohol syndrome.
arxiv-2511-06227:
Anamul Haque Mollah, Ahmed Aljohani, and Hyunsook Do study how large language models summarize unit tests. Test code often lacks short summaries that state what a test checks, especially in generated or poorly documented projects. Because tests express intent through assertions, summarizing them differs from summarizing ordinary code.

The authors built a benchmark of ninety-one real Java test cases paired with developer-written summaries. Four code models were tried under seven prompt designs that varied which test parts were shown. Prompting with assertion meanings beat showing the full method under test while using fewer tokens. Codex and Qwen-Coder matched human summaries best in their tests.
arxiv-2511-06327:
Abdelkader Hidki and co-authors study quantum coherence inside a cavity magnomechanical system driven by squeezed magnons. Such hybrid systems link light, magnetic excitations, and mechanical motion in one device. The team tracks Gaussian coherence in each part and in the whole system while tuning phase, coupling, drive power, and heat.

Squeezing strength and phase reshape the magnon frequency and damping, letting coherence grow in one direction more than the other. Stronger drive power and photon-magnon coupling raised coherence, while thermal noise wore it down, though squeezing blunted that damage. The results present squeezed magnons as a tunable tool for steadying coherence in hybrid quantum platforms.
arxiv-2511-06527:
Navin Khoshnan, Claudia Petritsch, and Bryce-Allen Bagley make Volterra series modeling feasible for very high-dimensional nonlinear systems. Volterra series describe a system through layered kernels, but the cost explodes with input dimension. Tensor network solvers eased that burden yet still scale badly in both memory and computation.

Their Tensor Head Averaging algorithm trains an ensemble of small tensor network models, each seeing only a slice of the input space. Theory gives finite-sample error bounds against the full model and an exact split of the squared error. Correlation between included and omitted dynamics turns out to help the ensemble, pushing accuracy beyond what plain truncation of the full model would give.
arxiv-2511-06627:
Toby Sanders and colleagues rebuild magnetic particle imaging scans in full three dimensions at once. The technique tracks superparamagnetic iron oxide particles inside the body for jobs like cancer cell tracking and lymph node mapping. Conventional pipelines reconstruct multi-angle field-free-line data slice by slice, losing consistency and dynamic range.

A physics-based signal model joins tomographic operators into one three-dimensional forward model, so the whole dataset is inverted jointly. A harmonic-domain compression step shrinks memory needs by more than a hundredfold while keeping the model's structure. Phantom and animal results showed far less background haze, clearer dim regions beside bright ones, and roughly eleven-fold better iron detection sensitivity.
arxiv-2511-06927:
Shuai Feng and nineteen co-authors introduce GEHONG, a Python package that fabricates ideal data cubes for the integral field spectrograph of the Chinese Space Station Telescope. An integral field spectrograph records a spectrum at every point of an image, producing a three-dimensional cube. GEHONG builds such cubes as an ideal telescope would see them, before real instrument effects are added.

Users supply two-dimensional maps of features like surface brightness, stellar population, and line-of-sight velocity, from parametric models, real observations, or numerical simulations. From these the package generates the spectrum at each position, handling four kinds of spectra: stellar continuum, ionized gas emission lines, active galactic nuclei, and single stars. Galaxies, star clusters, and HII regions can all be mocked up for pipeline testing.
arxiv-2511-07227:
The JUNO collaboration, some six hundred thirty scientists, forecasts what the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory will learn from geoneutrinos, antineutrinos emitted by radioactive decay inside the Earth. These particles are a unique probe of the planet's composition and heat budget. JUNO, newly completed in China, should gather a sample matching the entire current world dataset in under a year, despite a heavy background from nearby power reactors.

The study folds in the site's geology, reactor fluxes, detector uncertainties, and constraints from the TAO satellite detector. Within its first years JUNO should match current flux precision, reaching about eight percent over a decade, and it will separate the uranium-238 and thorium-232 contributions with unprecedented precision. Detecting the mantle's own signal within six years is possible but demands tight knowledge of the crustal flux.
arxiv-2511-07327:
Guoxin Chen and fifteen co-authors rethink how deep-research agents work on long tasks. Current agents stuff everything into one ever-growing context window until context suffocation and noise contamination choke the reasoning. IterResearch replaces accumulation with iteration: an evolving report serves as memory. The workspace is periodically rebuilt by synthesizing what has been learned so far, keeping reasoning capacity constant across arbitrary exploration depths.

Training uses an efficiency-aware policy optimization that discounts rewards geometrically to reward efficient exploration, with adaptive downsampling for stable distributed training. The agent improved over open-source rivals by about fourteen and a half points on average across six benchmarks and kept scaling to over two thousand interactions in testing. Used purely as a prompting strategy, it also lifted frontier models greatly over ReAct on long-horizon tasks.
arxiv-2511-07427:
Phones struggle to run long language model replies because memory fills up fast. Tuowei Wang and colleagues explain that the key-value cache, which stores context during generation, grows in step with text length. Moving parts of it to flash storage helps, but fixed groupings drift out of date as decoding proceeds.

DynaKV adapts the cache layout as generation moves forward, keeping needed entries close and dropping waste. The design also respects phone limits on bandwidth, storage speed, and memory. Tests report accurate long replies with far less strain on device memory. The work targets practical on-device assistants that can sustain long conversations.
arxiv-2511-07527:
Gal Shavit and Gil Refael explore shaking quantum materials in rhythm to reveal hidden structure. Twisted moiré materials host competing ground states with collective bosonic modes, the wavelike motions of an ordered phase. Parametric driving can amplify those modes directly.

The response to driving ties closely to quantum geometry, especially how fast a ground state changes when control knobs turn. Where competing states sit close in energy, the hierarchy can be tuned and the response grows. That sensitivity turns driving into a probe of fidelity and phase competition. The theory guides experiments seeking controllable excitations in engineered quantum matter.
arxiv-2511-07627:
Kartik Singh reparametrizes the Grassmannian, the space of planes inside larger spaces, using pipe dream diagrams. Postnikov parametrized the totally nonnegative part with networks from special diagrams. Talaska and Williams covered the whole space using Deodhar pieces and Go-diagrams with their own networks.

Pipe dreams tied to those Go-diagrams now supply an alternative network construction. Images of points become easy to compute under the new parametrization. Coordinates that are simple to evaluate help algebraic geometers test positivity and cluster structures. The Grassmannian sits inside scattering amplitude and soliton research, so friendlier coordinates travel far.
arxiv-2511-08327:
T Bakx and co-authors report a warm, ultra luminous infrared galaxy seen only six hundred million years after the Big Bang. The galaxy MACS0416 Y1, at redshift eight point three, was suspected to hold unusually warm dust for such an early Lyman break galaxy. ALMA observations across several bands, including a Band 9 continuum detection, confirm dust near ninety kelvin with wide uncertainty.

Fitting the combined data gives an infrared luminosity in the ultra luminous class and a modest dust mass sitting alongside ultraviolet bright regions. JWST photometry implies less hidden star formation than ALMA sees, so dust and stars must separate on scales below two hundred parsecs. Early dust obscured growth clearly contributed strongly to building stellar mass.
arxiv-2511-08427:
Linda-Sophie Schneider and co-authors announce an updated PYRO-NN, a Python library of smooth tools for X ray CT remaking. Deep learning remaking improves when classic physics based tools sit inside neural networks, allowing end to end training. Smooth mapping and back mapping are the key building blocks for that hybrid style, across the shapes real scanners use.

The update adds fit with PyTorch and native CUDA kernels for lean mapping operations. Parallel, fan, and cone beam shapes are all supported. Extra tools simulate imaging artifacts, model arbitrary acquisition trajectories, and assemble flexible trainable pipelines through a high level Python interface. The code is publicly ready for research use.
arxiv-2511-08627:
Thomas Xiao studies how United States climate records vary over time, looking for cycles hiding inside the trends. The data come from NOAA's divisional dataset, monthly temperature, rainfall, and drought index values running from 1895 to 2024, and the tools are Fourier and wavelet decomposition.

Two rhythms dominate: the yearly seasonal cycle and a slower swing of two to seven years tied to the El Niño Southern Oscillation. Adding these harmonic terms beats plain linear trend models in most states and for most variables. Xiao reads the climate as quasi-stationary oscillation rather than a steady one-way march. Frequency-aware models, the study argues, should feed seasonal outlooks, drought monitoring, and resource planning.
arxiv-2511-08727:
Simon Hettler and Raul Arenal report a strange device that formed by accident inside an electron microscope experiment. While studying how crystal orientation affects electrical behavior in a layered compound, a nanometer gap opened at a grain boundary, and the gap turned the device into a controllable mechanical hinge.

Heating currents bend the device differentially, opening and closing the gap like a tiny accordion, and the electrical properties respond strongly. A large intrinsic voltage appears across the gap, shifting with the vacuum conditions and with the history of currents applied. The authors attribute most of this to molecules adsorbed on the interior surfaces. The lesson reaches beyond this device: inner surfaces can dominate electrical behavior even under high vacuum.
arxiv-2511-08927:
Graham Bishop writes an essay about a blind spot in machines that listen to animals. Bioacoustic systems built on transformers read other species' calls with impressive accuracy, yet they treat the animal's calls as a pattern to decode and the machine itself as a neutral window.

Drawing on Yuk Hui's ideas about recursivity and contingency, Bishop argues the listener is itself a recursive cognitive agent whose architecture and training shape what it can hear. Each side's calls grew from contingent conditions set by habitat and history, so the encounter is doubly contingent. The proposal is to recast this field as diplomacy between different forms of recursive cognition. It would not be universal pattern recognition. Model design, evaluation, and research method would all change under that framing, Bishop argues.
arxiv-2511-09027:
Zinovy Malkin tracks three decades of progress in pinning down the positions of distant radio sources, the quasars that anchor the celestial reference frame. Thirty catalogs computed between 1997 and 2025 from very-long-baseline interferometry observations are compared on the four hundred sixty-seven sources they all share.

The median position uncertainty, measured by the semi-major axis of each source's error ellipse, shrank tenfold over the period, from 0.156 to 0.015 milliarcseconds. Both that improvement and the growth in observations follow clean power laws over time. The observation count for the shared sources climbed from one point three million to fourteen point four million. Comparing the two trends, Malkin concludes the sheer number of observations, more than the number of sessions, is what bought the precision.
arxiv-2511-09427:
Georgios Pantazis and four co-authors design a scheduling system that rents out parked electric vehicle batteries as virtual energy storage. Departure times and charge limits vary unpredictably, so the parking lot manager must promise storage services cautiously. Their data-driven system uses the scenario approach to give finite-sample, distribution-free guarantees on constraint violations.

The manager can tune the balance between profit and operational safety explicitly. Added variants make the schedule robust to corrupted training samples and to Wasserstein shifts in the data, with certificates for both. Numeric studies confirm the forecast profit-risk trade-off, the authors report. Observed violation levels matched the theoretical certificates, suggesting the guarantees are honest rather than padded decoration.
arxiv-2511-09727:
Stelios Zarifis and nine co-authors raise a robot the way infants raise themselves: by touching its own body and watching its hands. Their agent, Baby Sophia, learns inside the BabyBench simulation with reinforcement learning driven purely by intrinsic, curiosity-like rewards. No external supervision tells it what self-touch or hand regard should look like.

Tactile inputs are compressed into compact representations, and rewards for novel contacts plus a curriculum push broad, balanced body coverage. For hand regard, motor babbling first teaches the agent what its hands look like. Rewards for novel hand motions then draw its gaze after them. Training progresses from one hand to two. The progression from babbling to coordinated, purposeful behavior mirrors infant development.
arxiv-2511-09927:
Chong Lin and Shijun Liao compute Stokes waves, the permanent gravity waves that travel across deep water, from tiny ripples up to the tallest possible crests. Near the limiting height, sharp crests create singularities that defeat many analytic and numerical methods. Their hybrid framework pairs the homotopy analysis method, which builds convergent series solutions, with machine learning for speed across the whole amplitude range.

One neural network, trained on only twenty representative series solutions, predicts solutions at arbitrary steepness almost instantly, matching established benchmarks. A second network maps conformal coordinates back to physical coordinates so the wave shapes can be drawn directly. The authors present the pairing as a general recipe for hard nonlinear systems.
arxiv-2511-10427:
Dieu D. Nguyen and ten co-authors test whether the coming Extremely Large Telescope can weigh supermassive black holes in distant galaxies. Today such direct mass measurements reach only nearby galaxies, within about a hundred megaparsecs. The team simulates two first-light instruments, the MICADO camera and the HARMONI spectrograph, on five bright, massive, quiet galaxies at high redshift.

They build mock images and data cubes from Hubble telescope photographs. From these they recover stellar mass models and motions, then fit them with Bayesian dynamical models. Black hole masses come back with accuracy near ten percent, and MICADO needs only about an hour per galaxy. HARMONI needs five hours or more depending on brightness, but the results show such measurements can reach back to when galaxies were young.
arxiv-2511-10627:
Edward Kim and seven co-authors build a bridge between simulated and real failures of autonomous vehicles. Failures found in simulation may be artifacts of synthetic sensor data, so engineers need to check whether the same scenario occurs in real recordings and whether the failure persists there.

The team gives a formal definition of when labeled time series sensor data matches an abstract scenario written as a scenario program in the Scenic language. Their querying algorithm then finds the matching segments of a dataset. In experiments it proved more accurate and orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art commercial vision language models used for the same task, and it scales with the length of the queried recordings. The authors frame the tool as a step toward trustworthy sim-to-real validation.
arxiv-2511-10827:
Marcin Dziubiński studies a contest where two rivals split limited forces across several fields, but one side starts with more force than the other. Each field goes to whoever puts more there, and both sides must choose without seeing the other move. He works with whole units, not fractions, and allows two or more fields.

He finds the best mix for each side and the value of the game in two wide ranges of force counts. Some cases follow from a known simpler game, but he also builds a new limited form of that game. That new form lets him solve cases the older route could not reach.
arxiv-2511-11227:
Sunil Vittal, Anthony Wilkie, and their colleagues present a recursive algorithm for preparing a family of structured quantum states called leaf-separable states. Loading a chosen state into a quantum computer is a key step for many algorithms, and general methods need a gate count that explodes with qubit number. Structured states, such as Dicke states, admit far cheaper circuits if their structure is exploited.

The method joins shallow Dicke circuits with Hamming weight encoders over a binary partition tree. Simulations on random targets with up to fifteen qubits show depth and gate counts far below general routes. Variants with and without helper qubits are compared in detail to map the trade-offs.
arxiv-2511-11527:
Thien T. Duong and Jan P. Springer compare widely used audio compression codecs on two grounds at once: how much they shrink files, and how good the result still sounds to human listeners. Perceptual quality, they argue, should count alongside raw compression numbers when anyone picks a format.

Measurements, visualizations, and PEAQ scores, a standard rating of perceived audio quality, show how each codec trades file size against fidelity. Some settings keep speech and music clear, while others introduce losses listeners can hear. For archivists, streamers, and casual users alike, the comparison gives concrete guidance on matching a codec to what the ear actually needs.
arxiv-2511-11727:
Tongda Xu shows that a popular trick for improving diffusion models carries a hidden bias. Many projects optimize the conditional input, or the data itself, by denoising score matching, assuming it stays equivalent to exact score matching. The equivalence, it turns out, breaks under that optimization.

The failure pushes solutions toward higher score norms, a systematic distortion rather than random noise. The same bias appears when a pretrained diffusion model is used to optimize a data distribution. Affected lines of work named include autoregressive generation, image compression, and text-to-3D creation. As a short workshop paper, its value is the warning: a shared assumption in several active areas does not hold.
arxiv-2511-12127:
Md Rahat Hasan, Kazi Ahmed Akbar Munim and Md. Forkan Uddin study how to share radio resources in a coordinated Wi-Fi system with several access points. Two choices must be made together: which resource units go to which users, and how coordinated spatial reuse is set. Their joint goal is to raise total throughput.

Stated as an optimization task, the problem is a nonlinear integer program, which they solve for several network cases with a standard tool. The joint design beats an uncoordinated system by a clear margin. To cut computing cost, they also give a heuristic method whose throughput stays close to the full solver.
arxiv-2511-12327:
Paul Szeptycki and Hongwei Wen study a delicate question in topology about the Sorgenfrey line, a version of the real line with a one-sided interval topology. They ask when the square of such a space, formed from a set of reals, is normal or pseudo-normal, two separation properties that govern how disjoint closed sets can be kept apart.

A known result by Przymusiński shows one direction for special Q-sets, but the converse fails in general. The authors give examples on both sides. One family of sets yields a pseudo-normal square, while under the continuum hypothesis they build a set concentrated on a countable dense part whose square is still normal.
arxiv-2511-12527:
Ronaldo F. de Lima and Giuseppe Pipoli classify special hypersurfaces inside products of two simply connected space forms, spaces with constant curvature such as spheres, Euclidean spaces and hyperbolic spaces. An isoparametric hypersurface is one whose nearby parallel surfaces share the same principal curvature behavior, a strong regularity condition.

The authors first prove a key step. Any connected isoparametric hypersurface in such a product has a constant angle function. That function measures how its normal tilts between the two factors. Using that fact, they classify both isoparametric and homogeneous hypersurfaces when the two curvatures do not have the same sign. Under extra conditions they obtain a similar grouping when the product of the curvatures is positive. The proofs are the core of the work, step by step.
arxiv-2511-12627:
Baber Jan and four co-authors present C3Net, a network for finding camouflaged objects that blend into their surroundings by color, texture and pattern. The task defeats both classic segmentation methods and modern foundation models. The authors name six linked challenges, from intrinsic similarity and broken edges to extreme scale change and confusion with salient objects.

C3Net uses a dual-pathway decoder. One pathway refines edges, using gradient-initialized modules to recover sharp boundaries from early features. The other localizes the object through an image-based context guidance mechanism that suppresses intrinsic saliency without outside models. An attentive fusion module then combines the pathways with spatial gating. The authors report state-of-the-art results on camouflaged detection benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-12827:
Ayush Chaudhary and Sisir Doppalpudi design a malware defense that a busy production system can actually afford. Adversarial defenses often slow detection by four to twenty-two times, a heavy tax on services that screen millions of files daily. Their framework pairs a trust-based raw override, letting trusted evidence overrule manipulated features, with confidence-adaptive bit-depth reduction that spends defensive effort only where confidence calls for it.

On the EMBER v2 benchmark of eight hundred thousand samples, the system kept ninety-one percent clean accuracy while cutting attack success rates sharply, with the strongest gains against optimization-based attacks. Its overhead was under twice the base cost, a large improvement over smoothing defenses, and throughput reached over a million samples per second on pre-extracted features across seventy-two production configurations. Practical robustness, they argue, means optimizing the trade-off itself.
arxiv-2511-13027:
Sadegh Mahdavi and eight co-authors scale up machines that check mathematical proofs. Language models often reach correct final answers with flawed reasoning, so progress toward rigorous mathematics depends on verifiers that can judge a proof, not just an answer. The authors first warn that evaluating on a single benchmark gives brittle conclusions, and measure both proof-based and final-answer results. They then scale two generative verification approaches, GenSelect and LLM-as-a-Judge, to millions of tokens, finding their combination the most effective for verifying and selecting answers.

Prompt choice for the judge matters a lot, though reinforcement learning can reduce that sensitivity. A sobering finding follows: reinforcement learning improved proof-level metrics without improving final-answer scores, suggesting models learn to reward stylistic or procedural correctness rather than actual validity. The paper closes with practical guidelines for building proof-verification systems that measure what math cares about.
arxiv-2511-13127:
Zonghao Ying and eight co-authors jailbreak text-to-video models with prompts that look innocent. Earlier attacks pasted adversarial noise onto obviously unsafe requests, which filters catch easily. SPARK instead writes benign-looking prompts loaded with implicit cues. Each prompt combines three parts: a neutral scene anchor that keeps the surface description plausible, a latent auditory trigger describing an innocuous sound. Like creaking or muffled noise, that exploits the model's learned links between sounds and sights, and a stylistic modulator, a cinematic direction that strengthens the effect.

Attack construction is an optimization over this prompt space, solved by guided search. Across seven text-to-video models, SPARK raised the average attack success rate on commercial systems by twenty-three percent over prior attacks.
arxiv-2511-13227:
I. Asiáin's doctoral thesis studies anomalous Higgs couplings as a probe for physics beyond the Standard Model. The work uses effective field theories, which describe known physics at low energy while leaving room for new effects. A core problem is that such theories can break unitarity at high energy, so predictions must be repaired before use.

Early chapters treat longitudinal W boson scattering at one loop and study how transverse bosons shift the mass and width of new resonances. Later chapters use unitarity and causality to bound Higgs self-interactions, even without double-Higgs data. A final part applies the same tools to gravity treated as an effective theory.
arxiv-2511-13327:
Juntao Jian and 7 co-authors propose ZeroDexGrasp, a method that plans skillful multi-finger grasps for a stated task without task-specific training data. Most grasp systems lean on costly labeled examples and struggle with new objects or new instructions. A good grasp must fit both the object's use and its physical shape.

ZeroDexGrasp uses a multimodal language model in stages to reason from task and object meaning toward a first grasp and contact points. A contact-guided optimization step then refines the pose for physical feasibility. Tests showed strong zero-shot grasps across unseen object types and complex tasks, a step toward more general robot hands.
arxiv-2511-13427:
Shivani Gupta and 3 co-authors map magnetic fields around the dark cloud core LDN 328 using polarized dust glow at submillimeter wavelengths. Polarized dust emission traces the field direction across the sky, which helps show how fields shape cloud cores as they form and change. Data come from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope with its SCUBA-2 and POL-2 tools.

The team split the nearby area into three regions, found clumps with a standard algorithm, and fit dust temperature and column density from combined telescope maps. They charted field shape, measured its spread, and estimated field strength with a modified Davis-Chandrasekhar-Fermi method. Mass-to-flux ratio and Alfvén Mach number complete the physical picture.
arxiv-2511-13527:
Ihab Asaad, Maha Shadaydeh, and Joachim Denzler expose a hidden bias in patch-wise tumor classification on large microscopy images. Labeling whole patches as tumor or not is cheaper than tracing every pixel, but patch makeup can leak the answer. Tumor patches tend to hold more tissue, while clear patches are mostly background.

The authors measure how strongly that tissue-share cue bends model predictions. They then apply the GERNE debiasing method, tuned to lift worst-group accuracy, to counter the effect. Worst-group scores rose by about seven percent over standard training at two thresholds. Gains concentrated on the hard minority cases, such as small-tissue tumor patches that models once missed.
arxiv-2511-13627:
Aristides V. Doumas and Panayiotis J. Psarrakos define and study a Redheffer-type matrix whose entries involve Fibonacci numbers. Redheffer matrices are known for ties to deep number theory, and swapping in Fibonacci entries creates a fresh object with its own determinant and spectral behavior. The authors compute those properties for the new matrix in detail.

They also treat broader Redheffer-type families and display number-theoretic examples that show the range of behavior. Several asymptotic results describe how the matrix behaves as it grows. The paper closes by presenting a new expression connected with the Riemann hypothesis, placing the Fibonacci variant inside a classic circle of ideas.
arxiv-2511-13827:
Sebastian Leontica and 4 co-authors propose a hybrid quantum-classical method that optimizes two-dimensional isometric tensor networks on quantum computers. Tensor networks approximate the ground state of flat quantum systems, but squeezing them classically hits exponential cost. Their ansatz maps naturally onto quantum circuits, so the quantum device can carry the hard contraction work directly.

Following the spirit of density matrix renormalization, they tune one tensor at a time by diagonalizing effective Hamiltonians built from a tomography-style probe of few qubits. On the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model they optimized ground states up to twenty-five qubits with modest overhead, far less than standard variational solvers. The method suits both noisy and fault-tolerant machines.
arxiv-2511-14127:
Daniel M. Kane, Anthony Ostuni, and Kewen Wu classify which symmetric probability distributions shallow circuits can produce. Each output bit of their Boolean circuit may depend on only a few input bits, fed with uniform random bits. If the resulting output distribution is close to a symmetric one, meaning it depends only on how many ones appear, strong restrictions follow.

The distribution must then be near a mixture of three families: uniform strings of even weight, uniform strings of odd weight, and biased product distributions with special bias values. The mixture weights are themselves given by low-degree, sparse polynomials over the field with two elements. The result extends an earlier classification for distributions uniform on their support.
arxiv-2511-14427:
Rickmer Krohn, Vignesh Prasad, Gabriele Tiboni, and one co-author pretrain robot policies to feel as well as see. Contact-rich manipulation needs vision, force, and body sense working together, and reinforcement learning agents struggle amid sensor noise and shifting object dynamics. Their framework, multisensory dynamic pretraining, learns joint representations before any task training begins.

A masked autoencoder transformer reconstructs full multisensory observations from only a subset of sensor embeddings, forcing cross-modal prediction and fusion. For policy learning, a critic uses cross-attention to pull dynamic, task-specific features from the frozen embeddings while the actor gets a stable pooled summary. The method learned faster and stayed robust under noise and dynamics changes in simulated and real tasks.
arxiv-2511-14627:
Mingbo Li, Junhao Cai, and Yawen Gao review recent advances in stimulus assisted nanoprecipitation for making nanoparticles. Nanoprecipitation forms particles by rapid solvent displacement. External triggers like ultrasound, electric fields, heat, light, or chemistry can now steer the process. Modern reactors from batch to microfluidic systems add further control.

The review explains how each stimulus changes supersaturation, chain motion, or droplet motion. Those changes let makers tune particle size, shape, stability, and function. Uses span drug delivery, catalysis, and solids science. Pros and cons of each stimulus and reactor pairing are compared. The synthesis helps readers choose methods for precise particle design.
arxiv-2511-14727:
Jessie de Kruijf, Giacomo Galloni, and Nicola Bartolo place the first data-driven bounds on how strongly early gravitational waves lost their quantum character. The large structures seen today began as quantum fluctuations during inflation. Contact with other fields could have blurred that quantum nature, a process called decoherence, and left a mark on the wave background.

The authors compare predicted effects with upper limits from sky maps, gravitational wave detectors, and other probes. Those limits already rule out the strongest versions of the effect. The work turns a deep conceptual question about the quantum origin of structure into numbers that data can test.
arxiv-2511-14827:
Peter Halmos and Boris Hanin look under the hood of a standard algorithm for moving probability distributions downhill in energy. The Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto scheme steps a distribution forward by trading off motion cost against energy drop, and it mimics the true flow to first order in the step size. It also enjoys stability traits that rival stepping rules lack.

The authors compute what the scheme really follows at second order in the step size. The answer is a gradient flow of a slightly shifted energy, which reveals the scheme's hidden bias. Knowing that bias helps users judge when the popular scheme quietly favors certain outcomes in sampling and optimization tasks.
arxiv-2511-15127:
Zhi-zhong Xing works out how to infer the flavor mix of high-energy neutrinos at their distant sources from the mix measured on Earth. Telescopes such as IceCube record neutrinos that have crossed the cosmos. In flight the three flavors reshuffle, following a mixing matrix with a near symmetry between the muon and tau flavors. That symmetry hides a trap in the backward calculation.

Xing derives general formulas for the source fractions and shows the muon and tau source shares can blow up, a divergence forced by the symmetry. A full set of formulas in terms of two symmetry-breaking measures follows. Applied to IceCube sky data, the method shows which source facts can and cannot be recovered.
arxiv-2511-15227:
Hiep Hong Trinh, Marjan Sirjani, and three co-authors model and verify a team of robots running on the ROS2 middleware, using a timed actor language. Multi-robot systems interact asynchronously and concurrently, so design errors hide easily until hardware is already built. Model-based development with formal checking promises to catch those errors while the system is still a blueprint.

The team uses Timed Rebeca, an actor-based language with a model checker, to capture ROS2 node graphs, repeating physical signals, and motion building blocks in timed form. The paper confronts the hard parts directly: abstracting messy detail and bridging the gap between the model and real deployment. Verified models could de-risk fleets before a single robot moves.
arxiv-2511-15427:
Andrei Zeleneev and Weisheng Zhang make a known estimator for nonlinear panel data usable in practice. Panel data follow many units over time, and interactive fixed effects capture hidden factors that affect units and periods together. An estimator for nonlinear models has existed since 2021, but it needs a hard, high-dimensional optimization that applied researchers rarely attempt.

Their two-step method first smooths the problem using a nuclear norm penalty, which favors low-complexity solutions, to get starting estimates. Gradient descent then refines those starts toward the global answer of the original problem. The estimator matches the older one in large samples, and the authors provide proven algorithms plus a ready R software package.
arxiv-2511-15627:
Chris Culliton, Amber Roberts, and six co-authors search ultraviolet spectra of quasars for gas clouds that belong to the quasar itself. Quasars are brilliant galactic centers, and absorption lines from nitrogen can reveal outflows or near gas. Using a Hubble archive, they screened hundreds of active galaxies. They kept a clean sample of Type 1 quasars split into radio-loud and radio-quiet groups.

Associated absorption systems appeared in many radio-quiet quasars but were strikingly rare in the radio-loud group. Such a deficit is very unlikely to arise by chance. Assuming both groups host such systems equally, the authors propose orientation effects. Radio-loud quasars are viewed more often along the jet, where the absorbing gas is not in the line of sight.
arxiv-2511-15927:
Vaibhav Singh and four co-authors present DiffuMamba, a diffusion language model built on a bidirectional Mamba backbone for high throughput creation. Diffusion language models rival autoregressive models, but transformer backbones impose quadratic focus or cache costs. Mamba offers linear time sequence modeling instead. A hybrid variant interleaves focus layers with Mamba blocks.

At scales up to more than a billion parameters, the models match transformer diffusion quality on downstream tasks. Throughput on long sequences rises several fold for both variants. Systematic analysis compares inference efficiency across modern diffusion designs. Cache efficient block diffusion with Mamba mixers emerges as the only linearly scaling strategy. The work charts a path to fast, long context diffusion creation.
arxiv-2511-16127:
Livia Betz develops a new way to compute shape derivatives for design problems governed by non-smooth equations. Shape optimization asks how a best shape changes when its boundary moves. Rules for a locally optimal shape guide that search. Non-smooth terms break standard calculus, so classic derivative formulas do not apply to the state system here.

Working in a functional variational frame that turns shape problems into control problems, Betz adds a sensitivity technique claimed novel even for smooth equations. No hold-all domain extension and no smoothing step are used. The method handles point observations, derivatives of the state on an observation set, and spread terms. It also clarifies how locally optimal shapes relate to control minimizers.
arxiv-2511-16827:
Bassel Abou Ali Modad, Xin Yu, Yao-Yi Chiang, and Andreas F. Molisch build a far more data-rich model of line-of-sight probability for wireless macrocells. That quantity says whether a direct path exists between tower and user, and it shapes path loss, fading, and coverage planning. Existing models rest on very limited datasets.

The authors create a framework that derives line-of-sight models from geospatial data and apply it nationally across the United States, using more than thirteen thousand real macrocell locations. Their fully parameterized model describes American macrocell deployments better than the standard 3GPP model. They further show accuracy improves when line-of-sight probability is modeled per cell with parameters treated as random variables, and simulations confirm better prediction of inter-cell interference at the cell edge.
arxiv-2511-17127:
Quentin Anthony and 20 co-authors report the first large-scale pretraining of a mixture-of-experts language model entirely on AMD hardware, using MI300X graphics processors and Pollara networking. The study tests whether AMD's full stack can rival the usual choices for frontier model training. It covers the cluster, the network, and the training software in unusual depth.

On the systems side, the team benchmarks all core communication operations across message sizes and processor counts, and profiles the MI300X's kernels and memory. From those numbers they derive sizing rules for transformer blocks and expert widths that balance training speed against inference cost. Their model, ZAYA1, matches or beats comparable open base models on reasoning, mathematics, and coding tests. The report argues AMD's stack is ready for competitive large-scale training.
arxiv-2511-17227:
Xudong Wu, Guangxu Yang, and Penghui Yao study two parties who must compute a function together while communicating as little as possible, first in classical bits and then in qubits. This hybrid model fits a near future where quantum links supplement classical ones. The authors ask how much classical pre-talk can reduce the quantum communication needed for composed functions, where an outer function combines many copies of an inner product gadget.

They prove a lifting theorem that merges two previously separate techniques, one from classical communication complexity and one from quantum lower bounds. The corollary is a firm trade-off: for read-once formulas the parties must spend either a large classical budget or a large quantum one, and classical preprocessing barely helps. The paper gives the first non-trivial trade-off of this kind for two-way hybrid communication.
arxiv-2511-17427:
Etienne Meunier, Said Ouala, Hugo Frezat, Julien Le Sommer, and Ronan Fablet present a version of the Veros ocean model that can be run through automatic differentiation. A tool that tracks how outputs change with inputs. Making an ocean code work that way takes careful changes. And the team describes what had to be altered to fit the JAX framework while keeping the numbers consistent with the original model.

Two trial uses show the point. In one, the starting state of the ocean is corrected by following the tracked changes toward better agreement with data. In the other, unknown physical values inside the model are tuned directly from observations. Both cases show how this style of coding can ease learning and tuning in ocean work, and the code is shared online.
arxiv-2511-17727:
Victor Li, Naveenraj Kamalakannan, Avinash Parnandi, Heidi Schambra, and Carlos Fernandez-Granda test vision language models on videos of stroke recovery exercises. Clinicians need clear measures of how much practice a patient does and how severe the movement problems are, and video could help if models read motion well.

In a group of healthy adults and stroke survivors, current models did poorly on exact counts and scores. Their dose guesses matched a baseline that used no images, though they could name broad actions and spot motion fairly well. The results set a sober baseline for clinical video tools.
arxiv-2511-18227:
Evangela E Shread, Trevor J Weiss, Jerome J Fang, and Cameron Law trace how galaxies stop forming stars by looking at their centres and their cold gas. The density of stars in the inner kiloparsec is a known marker of bulge growth and of quenching. The shutdown of star formation, but its link with cold gas stores was less explored. The team uses two large surveys of nearby massive galaxies with data on atomic and molecular gas.

Both gas shares fall as central density rises, and the molecular share drops more sharply past a threshold in a mass-relative version of the measure. The share of galaxies hosting active nuclei also climbs with that measure. The pattern ties central build-up, gas loss, and black hole activity together in the quenching story.
arxiv-2511-18327:
Hao Liao, Xuanqin Huang, and Ping Wang find a way to read a hard-to-measure quantum quantity from easy local data. Quantum mutual information measures how nonlocal a quantum state is, and it matters for entanglement and for out-of-equilibrium behaviour such as localisation and thermalisation. Yet measuring it directly in the lab is extremely hard, above all for states driven out of equilibrium, which are messier than ground states.

The team trains a small neural network to map local correlations, only up to second order, onto the mutual information, for states made by sudden quenches in a disordered one-dimensional model. The mapping proves broadly universal in their tests.
