Since local correlations are measurable on platforms such as superconducting qubits, the method offers labs a practical route to a quantity they could not otherwise reach.
arxiv-2511-18527: Tianyi Zhou surveys separation axioms for spaces that are not Hausdorff. These axioms grade how well open sets tell points apart, from weak T0 through T1 up to Hausdorff, where any two points have disjoint neighborhoods. Many natural spaces fail the Hausdorff test, so finer grades between the levels matter. The note reviews properties between T0 and T1 and between T1 and Hausdorff, shows how the T0 quotient changes them, and maps how they relate. It serves as an entry guide to this corner of point-set topology.
arxiv-2511-19027:
Christine Awofeso, Patrick Greaves, Oded Lachish, Amit Levi, and Felix Reidl open the study of which graph families admit one sided property tests in the random neighbor oracle model. In that model a tester samples random neighbors to judge a graph fast. A family is H-testable if, for each graph H, the trait of having no copy of H can be tested with one sided error on all its members.

Czumaj and Sohler showed any such family has a known characterization of its testable traits, a major goal of the field. Sorting the H-testable families would thus exhaust that route to characterizations. The team give a sufficient condition toward that sort. Their condition starts the map of this model.
arxiv-2511-19127:
Jin-Yang Shen and four co-authors build a holographic model of quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons, with two light flavors and one strange flavor. Holographic models map hard particle problems onto gravity-like setups that are easier to compute. The team also uses machine learning to tune the model faster.

At zero chemical potential, the model matches lattice computer results for the equation of state and the chiral transition. Varying quark masses maps how the order of the transition changes, giving a phase diagram that agrees with lattice studies. The predicted first-order region is small, and the boundary behavior shows mean-field scaling.
arxiv-2511-19427:
Jayanaka L. Dantanarayana and six co-authors add intent to a programming style where language models write behavior from code meaning. Meaning Typed Programming already builds prompts from the semantics in code, yet real applications lean on context and domain reasoning that code alone does not state. Their answer is semantic engineering.

Developers embed natural-language notes, called SemTexts, directly into program parts in the Jac language. Prompt generation then uses those enriched semantics, so the model's work reflects intent without hand-written prompts. A benchmark suite of realistic AI-integrated applications shows the enriched approach capturing developer intent more faithfully than code semantics alone.
arxiv-2511-19827:
Byeongjun Park, Byung-Hoon Kim, Hyungjin Chung, and Jong Chul Ye present ReDirector, a method for making camera-controlled retakes of videos. The system works on videos shot with moving cameras and of any length. It aims to redo a shot from a new camera path while keeping the scene intact.

ReDirector fixes a common misuse of rotary position encoding by aligning the positions of the input video and the retake in space and time. Its new rotary camera encoding adds a camera-based phase shift that links views within and across both videos. Tests show better camera control, steadier geometry, and higher video quality across many paths and lengths.
arxiv-2511-20027:
Lin Chen, Yingjian Zhu, Qi Yang, Xin Niu, Kun Ding, and Shiming Xiang present SAM-MI, a framework that pairs the Segment Anything Model with open-vocabulary segmentation. Open-vocabulary systems must segment and name any object, and SAM's universal masks could help. Two problems block the pairing: SAM tends to over-segment, and its fixed masks combine awkwardly with labels.

SAM-MI samples sparse points with a text-guided prompter instead of dense grids, which speeds mask generation. A shallow aggregation step merges partial masks to counter over-segmentation. Finally, decoupled mask injection feeds SAM's masks as guidance at low and high frequencies separately, rather than fusing them straight with labels. Benchmarks show clear gains in accuracy and speed over prior combinations.
arxiv-2511-20927:
Vitória Barin Pacela and colleagues turn a 2025 theory result into a method for disentanglement, teaching a model to represent data through underlying factors, like position, size, and colour, without labels. Recent theory showed that when factors are quantised, meaning they jump between discrete levels, the jumps create sharp edges in the factor distribution. Those edges, which the authors call cliffs, can identify the true factors.

Their method, Cliff, trains a model to produce exactly such cliffs and forces each cliff's position to stay independent of the other factors' values. On the Shapes3D benchmark, Cliff scored 80.33 on the DCI disentanglement measure, ahead of the HFS baseline at 70.64 and beta-VAE at 69.72, with near-perfect informativeness of 99.26. It also won on a balls dataset derived from dSprites, where factor distributions satisfy the assumptions. The authors report it outperformed the baselines on every benchmark tried.
arxiv-2511-21027:
Yisheng Qiu and colleagues automate in 2025 one of radio astronomy's most tedious chores: fitting molecular spectral lines. Lines from interstellar molecules reveal temperature, density, and chemistry, but fitting them has meant heavy manual work, hopeless against ALMA-scale data floods. Their Spectuner-D1 framework trains a neural network with deep reinforcement learning to map observed spectra plus molecular data straight to physical parameters like excitation temperature and column density. A local optimiser then polishes the network's estimates.

Accuracy matched global optimisation with multiple restarts, while the number of forward model runs dropped by an order of magnitude. Applied pixel by pixel to the G327.3-0.6 hot core and checked with the xclass package, the method fitted five molecules including methanol and ethyl cyanide. A 100 by 100 pixel region spanning 5 gigahertz took between 4.9 and 41.9 minutes on a 16-core desktop with one consumer GPU.
arxiv-2511-21127:
Hyeongwoo Lee and colleagues demonstrate in 2025 a microscope tip that turns shy quantum defects into bright, tunable single-photon sources. Atom-like defects in hexagonal boron nitride emit one photon at a time at room temperature and host coherent spins, but they form at random places with random colours, frustrating device builders. The team positions emitters inside tip-cavities with set plasmon resonances, controlling how strongly excitation and emission are enhanced, and the single-photon purity.

Positioning reaches sub-nanometer precision in three dimensions, so a defect can be reconfigured for brightness or purity on demand, with spectroscopy resolved in space and time. For sensing, they mounted boron nitride nanoflakes on a gold tip's apex and read single spin defects by optically detected magnetic resonance. The magnetic response reached about 116 microtesla per root hertz. The platform points toward deterministic quantum sensors built from two-dimensional materials.
arxiv-2511-21227:
Huiyu Li, Nicholas Ayache, and Hervé Delingette warn in 2025 that a trained model exported from a medical data lake can smuggle out the very images it learned from. Their attack hides image-compression codes inside a neural network's parameters, so the exported model quietly carries a compressed copy of private scans. Unlike earlier theft methods, the scheme needs no extra data smuggled during training and works with any image task.

Li and his coauthors test the attack on public CT and MR image collections and rebuild stolen scans outside the lake with high fidelity. Tricks like shrinking the model and hiding codes in unused channels cut the footprint, and with learned lossy compression the codes became 60 times smaller than a naive version. The team also probes a defense, adding Gaussian noise to parameters in the style of differential privacy, and measures how much it blunts the theft.
arxiv-2511-21327:
Darryl Biggar and Mohammad Reza Hesamzadeh work out the economics of electricity storage from first principles in 2025. Power grids leaning on variable renewables need batteries and other storage to keep supply and demand balanced, but how much storage is optimal, and what contracts should storage owners hold? The authors answer in a clean special case where each period's demand is an independent random draw from the same distribution.

Biggar and Hesamzadeh characterize the conditions for running storage optimally and for investing in the right amount of it. Their rules can be read graphically from price-duration curves, which rank prices from highest to lowest across time. In the perfectly efficient case, the buy and sell thresholds coincide at the average price. They also derive the optimal hedge contracts for storage units, showing how familiar power-market results carry over to the storage era.
arxiv-2511-21427:
Rishu Garg and Jitender Singh generalize a classical test for when a polynomial cannot be factored, in 2025. The lineage runs from Schönemann in 1846 through Eisenstein in 1850 to Dumas in 1906, who used Newton polygons, geometric diagrams of coefficient valuations, to prove far-reaching irreducibility criteria. Those results live over ordinary valued fields, where each number carries a single size ranking.

Garg and Singh prove a factorization theorem over any valued field whose valuation is a Krull valuation of arbitrary rank, a multi-level ranking of sizes. The theorem says when and how a polynomial must split over such fields. They also prove a lower bound on the degrees any factor can have. Together, the results unify several scattered irreducibility criteria in the literature and give sharp degree bounds for the irreducible factors of a given polynomial.
arxiv-2511-21627:
Yjan Gordon, Peter Ferguson, Eric Hooper, and Michael Martinez link neutrinos to flaring radio sources, in 2025. IceCube detects high-energy neutrinos from deep space, but pinpointing their sources is hard: neutrinos barely interact and arrive with fuzzy directions. Radio surveys offer a cross-check. If some neutrino sources flare in radio waves, flares and neutrino arrivals should coincide more often than chance allows.

Comparing the first two epochs of the Very Large Array Sky Survey with IceCube events, Gordon and his coauthors found an excess of associations. The excess covers neutrinos detected between the two epochs, at better than two-sigma confidence. The excess fits radio flares producing about 13 percent of IceCube's astrophysical neutrinos. Over 80 percent of the flares are invisible in gamma rays and X-rays, so radio monitoring opens a counterpart channel other wavelengths miss. The team predicts future epochs should push the signal past three sigma.
arxiv-2511-21827:
Marini and colleagues ask whether made-up clinical notes can help medical AI learn from skin lesion photographs. Multimodal systems, which combine images with text, but dermatology datasets rarely include real written notes. The team used large language models to synthesize notes for lesion images, testing different prompt designs and whether the prompts included real patient metadata.

Across skin lesion datasets, adding synthetic notes improved classification accuracy over image-only baselines, when the test data came from a different source than the training data, a challenge called domain shift. The combined system also gained an ability it was never trained for: cross-modal retrieval, finding images from text queries and vice versa. One caution stood out, because note prompts without metadata encouraged the model to invent details and weakened retrieval, while metadata-guided prompts, especially the most structured one, gave the strongest retrieval results.
arxiv-2511-22127:
Cornejo and Sankappanavar, mathematical logicians, found a new family of logics hiding inside semi-Heyting algebras. Connexive logics formalize an old idea about implication: a statement should not imply its own negation, and if A implies B then A should not imply not-B. The authors define connexive semi-Heyting logic and show it is algebraizable, with a matching new variety of algebras as its equivalent semantics, giving an effective back-and-forth translation between proofs and algebra.

They chart a small hierarchy of related varieties, proving equalities and strict inclusions among them, and show a three-valued version of the logic is deductively equivalent to three-valued intuitionistic logic. New characterizations of anti-Boolean algebras follow, plus lattice results: that variety is the unique atom here. Two new candidate connexive theses, principles future connexive logics might adopt, and several open problems on subvariety lattices and amalgamation close the paper.
arxiv-2511-22227:
Mardyban and Nesterenko, nuclear theorists, calculate excited states in the heaviest nuclei with complete spectroscopy, the even-even nobelium isotopes from mass 250 to 260. Nobelium's levels and pairing test ideas about superheavy elements. Using the quasiparticle random-phase approximation with the SLy4 Skyrme force, they examine two kinds of excitation. Collective 0+ states and the isomeric 8- states whose existence hinges on the exact arrangement of orbitals near the Fermi surface.

A deformation shell gap in the neutron spectrum of nobelium-252 and 254 sharply suppresses neutron pairing there, dragging both excitation spectra down together, a correlation the calculations make explicit. The 8- isomers come out as low-energy two-quasiparticle states in 252 through 258 but turn unobservable in 250 and 260, while the lowest 0+ states. Mixtures of pairing and beta vibrations, are predicted as the lowest non-rotational excitations throughout, matching available data reasonably.
arxiv-2511-22427:
Trakulthongchai proves two new cases of the Lonely Runner Conjecture, a number theory problem from the 1960s. Picture runners on a unit circular track, starting together, running at different constant speeds forever. A runner is lonely when all others are at least a fixed fraction of the track away, the fraction shrinking as runners are added. The conjecture says every runner eventually gets a lonely moment, whatever the speeds.

It was known for up to eight runners, the last settled by Rosenfeld with computer assistance. Trakulthongchai refines that approach with a sieve, a filter discarding speed combinations efficiently, pushing the verified cases to nine and ten runners. The proofs are computer-assisted: after reducing to whole-number speeds and one stationary runner, the sieve lets a machine check the remaining cases. Each new case strengthens a conjecture that also appears in geometry and graph colouring.
arxiv-2511-23127:
Zhang and colleagues improve camera-controlled video generation, where a user specifies a virtual camera path and a diffusion model must render a video that follows it faithfully. Existing systems condition on camera poses through per-pixel ray directions. But they must guess the scene's 3D structure implicitly. So the generated motion often drifts away from the requested trajectory.

Their model, DualCamCtrl, generates color video and a matching depth sequence together in two branches. So geometry is modeled explicitly instead of being entangled with appearance. And a fusion mechanism called SIGMA aligns the two streams using semantic guidance. The design cut camera motion errors by over 40 percent compared with prior methods in their experiments, including rotation errors specifically. Their analysis shows depth and pose signals matter at different denoising stages, early for global structure and late for local detail.
arxiv-2511-23327:
Pastine and Schvöllner introduce a new invariant of a graph that counts its flexibility. How many different graphs share its exact degree sequence and are one rewiring away. The realization graph has one vertex for every graph with the given degree sequence, with edges joining graphs related by a 2-switch. Swapping the endpoints of two edges, and the 2-switch-degree of a graph is its degree inside that meta-graph.

The paper works out which vertices of a graph are active, able to take part in a switch. And which are inactive, derives explicit formulas for computing the new degree, and evaluates it for trees and unicyclic graphs. The invariant depends on the graph and not just its degree sequence, since two unicyclic graphs with identical sequences receive different values. 11 and 10 in the worked example, so the realization graph need not be regular.
arxiv-2512-00027:
Robots that follow spoken directions through real rooms need to see, move, and talk back when orders are unclear. Nivedan Yakolli and four co-authors survey this field, called vision-and-language navigation, in a 2025 review. Their subject is how teams of robots can work with people in shared three-dimensional spaces.

The review gathers recent work on how robots read human instructions, plan routes, and coordinate with each other. It also points to open problems, such as handling vague commands and keeping communication clear when several machines act at once. Readers get a map of current methods and the directions the authors see as most promising for better teamwork.
arxiv-2512-00227:
Operator ideals called Schatten classes measure how close an operator is to being finite and small. Tamara Bottazzi and Cristian Conde investigate these ideals as semi-inner product spaces in 2025. Semi-inner products generalize the geometry of angles beyond ordinary inner product spaces.

The authors study angles and related geometry in the Schatten classes for exponents above one. Such geometry underlies quantum information, where Schatten norms measure distances between quantum states. Clarifying when these spaces behave like familiar Euclidean geometry helps analysts use them with confidence in proofs and applications. Angles in these spaces generalize the familiar geometry of Hilbert spaces. The authors work in the sense of Giles and Lumer, a standard reference point.
arxiv-2512-00527:
The fractional quantum Hall effect hosts some of the strangest states of matter known. Mytraya Gattu dresses composite fermions with artificial intelligence in 2025, using machine learning to improve their wavefunctions. Composite fermions are quasiparticles that already explain much of the effect's behavior.

Recent variational studies captured these ground states with machine learning starting from no prior physics knowledge. Gattu instead starts from Jain's composite-fermion wavefunctions, which are accurate in an idealized limit, and lets learning refine them. Combining a strong physical ansatz with flexible fitting could yield the most accurate descriptions yet of these exotic states. Composite fermions turn a strongly interacting problem into a weakly interacting one.
arxiv-2512-00627:
Sparse regression picks a few true predictors from a crowd of candidates, and priors must encode that sparsity. Chadi Bsila and co-authors develop a variational Bayes method for spike-and-slab regression in 2025, replacing the usual divergence objective with Rényi's alpha-divergence. Their setting is high-dimensional linear regression.

The method uses spike-and-slab Laplace priors within a mean-field approximation. The alpha parameter interpolates between zero-forcing and mass-covering behavior. Flexible methods matter because exact Bayesian computation is impossible at the dimensions genomics and economics now demand. Spike-and-slab priors put real probability on a coefficient being exactly zero. That honesty about exclusion is what variable selection needs. For folks who face wide data with few true clues, the gain is choice. One knob tunes how bold or how shy the fit will be as it picks its clues.
arxiv-2512-01127:
A 2025 machine learning paper proposes mode-conditioning to unlock better test-time scaling. Letting a model sample many answers in parallel should improve results, since the best of many tries often wins. In practice, gains are sharply limited by diversity collapse: the model concentrates on a few modes and repeats the same mistakes across samples.

The proposed ModC framework allocates test-time compute across reasoning modes on purpose. Modes can come from specialist models or from mode-specific prefixes that steer one model. Spreading samples across modes should surface different approaches and different errors. That makes parallel sampling worth its extra cost on hard problems.
arxiv-2512-01427:
Klara Reichard and co-authors work on finding odd objects in road scenes. Self-driving systems must spot both known and unknown things. Past methods can outline an unknown zone. They fail to say what that zone is in words.

The team adds language to the task. Their method gives a word label to each odd zone it finds. A label like debris or stray cart helps the car plan a reply. Word labels also help staff log and study near-miss events. The work pushes road vision from mere spotting toward real scene sense.
arxiv-2512-01727:
Benjamin Blakely and co-authors evaluate AI cybersecurity for nuclear infrastructure on real plant data. Advanced reactors face attackers who exploit cyber-physical links. They can twist control systems while dodging classic IT guards. Testbeds must reflect that real risk.

Their testbed uses operational data from Argonne's engineering test loop. AI methods are scored on that live-like data. Scores show which detectors catch stealthy attacks. Nuclear sites need that proof before any AI guard can be trusted near reactor controls. Operational data keeps the test honest, since lab-made attacks often miss the noise and quirks of a working test loop's traffic.
arxiv-2512-01827:
Yize Zhang and co-authors teach models to discover visual causes with CauSight. Humans grasp not just what is seen, but why it happens. Visual causal discovery asks models to infer cause and effect among scene entities. Mere detection of objects falls short of that goal.

Their learning frame targets that deeper skill. Models must state which entity drives which change. Causal reads help robots and safety systems predict what comes next. They also make model errors easier to explain and fix. Cause graphs can be graded directly, since each claimed arrow is right or wrong, unlike vague scene captions that resist scoring.
arxiv-2512-02127:
In the standard cosmology, the local mix of ordinary matter and dark matter can wobble slightly from place to place, frozen in from the early universe. Owen Jessop and five co-authors use the FLAMINGO galaxy formation model in 2025 to ask what those ripples do to galaxy formation.

In linear theory these compensated variations cancel out in total density while shifting the baryon share, with a small root-mean-square amplitude. Whether such a subtle shift leaves visible marks on galaxies was an open question for simulators. The answer affects how precisely galaxy surveys can be read as tests of the underlying cosmology.
arxiv-2512-02427:
Hossein Nekouyan and three co-authors study posted price selling, where items go to buyers at set prices. Posted prices are simple, easy to grasp, and give buyers no reason to lie about value. Sellers often raise prices over time to handle doubt about who will arrive next.

Moving prices carry costs, though: late buyers may pay more for the same goods, which feels unfair. Each price change also costs effort to run. The 2025 study weighs plans that change prices only a few times, and that stay sensitive to risk. The aim is most of the gain with far fewer moves. Fewer price shifts also mean less work for the staff who run the sale each day.
arxiv-2512-02627:
Chiara Calascibetta, Laëtitia Giraldi, and Jérémie Bec study how to steer swarms of tiny self propelled particles. Left alone in a channel, such particles pile at walls, clog passages, and form bands. That self organization fights any attempt to move the swarm in one chosen direction.

The team applies global control, a single steering signal for the whole swarm, tuned in an optimal way. The aim is directed migration despite the clogging tendencies. Lessons here could guide micro robots, drug carrying particles, and other active matter systems that must travel through tight spaces. A swarm that can be steered as one body is far more use than the same swarm left to clog.
arxiv-2512-02727:
Yifan Zhou and co-authors estimate hand poses in 3D when hands overlap and hide each other. Daily hand interactions often include severe occlusions, such as two hands crossing. Occluded joints must then be guessed from global context, not seen directly.

Their DF-Mamba model uses deformable state space modeling to link local image features with the whole scene. Local patches hint where a hidden joint sits; global shape keeps the guess plausible. Robust hand tracking underpins sign language tools, virtual reality, and robots that work safely beside human hands. Hands that cross and twist are the norm in sign and craft, so the test set leans on them hard.
arxiv-2512-02827:
Slobodan Filipovski and three co-authors settle a question about directed graphs with nearly unique short routes. A digraph is called k-geodetic when any two vertices are joined by at most one walk of length up to k. Graphs close to the limits of this property are counted by an excess value.

The title states the result plainly: there are no excess one digraphs. The proof rules out a whole borderline family that might have existed. Nonexistence results prune the search space for network designs built on unique routing. A clean no can save years: no team need hunt for a graph that math says can not be built at all.
arxiv-2512-02927:
P. Narayanan and A. Raghuram prove, rather than compute, a case of the congruence principle for L-function values. The principle links congruences between objects to congruences between special values of their L-functions. Eisenstein cohomology is their main machine for the proof.

After refining that machinery for integral cohomology, they prove the principle for ratios of critical values. The L-functions are Rankin-Selberg type, attached to pairs of holomorphic cuspforms. Proved cases anchor the principle that computations elsewhere can only suggest, advancing the Langlands program's arithmetic core. Proof locks the case in a way counts can not. Locked cases are the stones on which the next ring of this long chain of work will rest.
arxiv-2512-03227:
Galaxy motions reveal distances and cosmic growth. K. Douglass and a large team present a distance catalog from the DESI survey in this 2025 work. They use the Tully-Fisher relation, which links a spiral galaxy's spin speed to its brightness.

The team calibrated the relation with first-year DESI data. They measured spin speeds for more than ten thousand galaxies. Those speeds give distances that do not rely on redshift alone. The catalog supports maps of how matter moves in the nearby universe, which test dark energy models. Distance catalogs like this one feed maps of bulk flows across the nearby cosmos.
arxiv-2512-03427:
Drones in forests need depth vision that works among trees. Yida Lin, Bing Xue, Mengjie Zhang, Sam Schofield, and Richard Green evaluate stereo methods in this 2025 work. Autonomous forestry flights need robust depth estimates that generalize across domains.

Past evaluations focused on urban and indoor scenes, leaving vegetation untested. The team ran the first systematic zero-shot evaluation of eight stereo methods. The methods span iterative, foundation model, and adaptation styles. Results show which methods cope with dense foliage, guiding safer drone work in forests. Forest scenes punish weak stereo, since leaves repeat patterns and light shifts fast.
arxiv-2512-04827:
Wenzhang Du argues that speech and singing services should be graded by contracts, not by a single star rating. Mean opinion scores, gathered from listeners, remain the standard target for judging voice quality without a reference recording. Yet one number crushes many distinct listener hopes, ignores service-level goals, and shifts meaning between deployment setups. His 2025 arXiv paper replaces the single score with a set of plain-language experience contracts.

Each service graph is checked against every contract, yielding a satisfaction profile instead of one grade. Du shows that classic score regression is just the special case where the contract set shrinks to one degenerate promise. Contract grades stay steadier than opinion scores when results are pooled in different ways. The framework is demonstrated on speech and singing services. Providers gain a clearer way to promise, audit, and compare voice quality.
arxiv-2512-05227:
Lampros Bouranis, Petros Barmpounakis, Nikolaos Demiris, and Konstantinos Kalogeropoulos build a Bayesian framework for tracking infectious disease across groups that rise and fall together. Their tool is the multi-task Gaussian process, a flexible statistical model that learns smooth patterns over time while sharing strength between related series. A dynamic hierarchical structure keeps the model parsimonious: groups borrow a common mean process, itself modelled as a Gaussian process, so cross-dependence is captured without drowning in parameters.

The authors aim the framework at a practical need: evidence-based estimates of disease burden during outbreaks. In outbreaks, data arrive unevenly across regions or age groups, and decision-makers cannot wait for complete counts. They analyze several kinds of outbreak data from recent epidemics. The proposed models forecast better than the alternatives, suggesting that structured sharing over time is a reliable way to read an epidemic while it is still unfolding.
arxiv-2512-05627:
Hua Yan studies quantum states that cling to the border between order and chaos. Many systems have a phase space split sharply into a calm, regular region and a chaotic sea. The border is often formed by special orbits that are barely unstable, or by smooth quasi-periodic ones. Some quantum states, called eigenstates, refuse to sit cleanly on either side.

Two measures sort the states: an overlap index and an entropy based length. The part due to dynamical tunneling fades steadily as the regular region grows. The dominant share, the sticky eigenstates, hugs the border itself. Their share shrinks roughly with the square root of Planck's constant in one case, and wobbles around that pattern in the other. The findings extend known predictions about sticky states from smooth systems to sharply divided ones, and tie a clear quantum fingerprint to the classical stickiness of the border.
arxiv-2512-05727:
Michael Ruderman and Denis Efimov improve a robust control method for second order systems, the kind that govern a mass pushed by a force amid disturbances. Sliding mode controllers drive such systems to their target in finite time and shrug off perturbations. A recent design by the same authors added no overshoot and a chosen amount of damping, but left limits. Their 2025 paper modifies the nonlinear control law in three ways.

First, the control effort can now be capped by a tunable parameter across a large set of starting states. Second, the method works from anywhere in the state plane, not just a restricted region. Third, for the undisturbed case the state paths can be written down exactly. That yields a precise formula for the finishing time. For disturbed systems, two proof routes establish global stability that holds uniformly.
arxiv-2512-05927:
Zhiting Mei, Tenny Yin, Micah Baker, Ola Shorinwa, and Anirudha Majumdar teach video world models to say how unsure they are, frame by frame and patch by patch. Such generators are becoming the simulators in which robots train. Their flaw is hallucination. Today's best video models cannot express confidence, so the bad patches are invisible. The team's method, C3, trains models to be both correct and calibrated.

Three ideas carry the method. Training uses proper scoring rules, which reward honest uncertainty. Uncertainty is estimated in the model's compact latent space, avoiding the cost and instability of pixel level training. Latent uncertainty is then mapped back as heat maps, showing which frame regions to distrust. On large robot datasets, the estimates stay calibrated on familiar data and flag unfamiliar situations. A simulator that knows its blind spots beats a confident liar.
arxiv-2512-06027:
Masoumeh Khalili, Ghodratallah Fasihi-Ramandi, and Shahroud Azami introduce and explore a new class of geometric structures called second Ricci solitons. A soliton is a shape that evolves under a flow by rescaling or moving. The second Ricci soliton is exactly a steady hyperbolic Ricci soliton, studied here under a new lens. The focus falls on closed and compact examples.

Two further settings get the same treatment. Immersed submanifolds, smaller spaces sitting inside larger ones, are examined as second solitons in their own right. Warped product manifolds are tested for when the structure survives. The paper names a neighboring concept and surveys it. The results give geometers working on Ricci flow a new label with theorems attached, and clear statements about which constructions preserve the property.
arxiv-2512-06127:
Nancy Kasamala and six co-authors dismantle a planning cliché: the household without a car is not one kind of traveler. Agencies assume such households uniformly walk or ride transit. Latent class analysis of the 2022 national travel survey finds three publics, each about a third.

Shared mobility errand workers lean on transit and ridehailing for commuting and essentials. Car based shoppers reach cars informally for longer trips. Active travel shoppers walk and cycle for short local shopping. Each segment needs different policy. Differentiated planning follows naturally. Administrative categories flatten real diversity; latent analysis recovers it.
arxiv-2512-06327:
Arsen Galstyan and Alexey Tuzhilin study what happens when a growing halo around one set sweeps across a second set in a space with distances. For each radius, they take the points of the second set that fall inside the thickened first set. As the radius grows, this slice grows too, tracing a family of sets the authors treat as a curve in the world of sets.

When the second set is compact, they show this slice can jump outward but never suddenly inward, in the sense of the Hausdorff distance between sets. When both sets are convex inside a normed space, full smooth behavior holds exactly when all slices stay a finite distance apart. In flat spaces of dimension two or less that condition always holds. In dimension three and up, they build a case where that distance is endless, so smooth behavior breaks.
arxiv-2512-06427:
Andrea Combette, Antoine Venaille, and Nelly Pustelnik fix the starting settings of neural networks that use sine waves as their switches. Such networks, known as SIREN, fit signals and images by learning wavy patterns. A poor start can make gradients explode or vanish as they pass through deep stacks. It can also seed the wrong frequencies from the outset.

The authors derive a closed form recipe for the starting values. It is built from fixed points of how signals spread through the network at the start. It also uses how the output's sensitivity behaves across layers. Holding both in check keeps early activations small and gradients in a sane range. They also trace how the start shapes training through the tangent kernel view. On function fitting and image rebuilding tests, networks started their way beat the original scheme and other baselines across the board.
arxiv-2512-06727:
Sourjya Roy, Shrihari Sridharan, Surya Selvam, and Anand Raghunathan shrink the memory cache that makes large language models expensive to run. As a model writes, it stores key and value tensors for every token so far, and that cache can outgrow the model itself. Long contexts and big batches hit the memory wall first, so cutting the cache is a direct lever on cost.

Their framework, KV-CAR, attacks the cache two ways. A light autoencoder squeezes each tensor along its feature dimension before storage and restores it on demand. A second mechanism spots attention heads whose tensors barely change between neighboring layers and reuses one copy. On two models and four data sets, the cache shrank by up to nearly half, with little loss in text quality or in zero shot task scores. The method needs no change to the model's architecture, so it can ride on existing systems.
arxiv-2512-06827:
Valentin V Khoze reviews a dispute at the heart of quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force that binds quarks. A quantity known as theta controls whether that force treats matter and its mirror image the same way. Instantons, brief localized events in the theory, have long been used to work out how physical results should depend on theta. Recent claims argue instead that theta effects vanish, leaving the strong force mirror-symmetric for every value.

Khoze sets the standard instanton picture beside those claims and tests each scenario in turn. In the weak-coupling setting, instantons give a clear and nontrivial dependence on theta. Where coupling grows strong, other non-perturbative arguments take over, yet the dependence still does not disappear. The note thus defends the established view: theta matters, and the puzzle of why its observed effect is so tiny remains a real one.
arxiv-2512-07127:
Daniel A Lidar asks whether quantum supremacy, the point where a quantum device outruns any classical simulation, can be shown on hybrid machines that mix digital gates with analog evolution. His device recipe is a sandwich: a layer of single-qubit gates, one analog block mimicking a transverse-field Ising system, and a final single-qubit layer before readout. Such digital-analog-digital hardware includes today's quantum annealers.

Lidar proves the sandwich's output distribution stays within a fixed distance of an IQP circuit, a standard hard-to-simulate family. The constructions cover both fully connected machines and the bounded layouts of real trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and superconducting platforms. Given a spreading property he proves for the fully connected case. Plus a standard hardness assumption about Ising partition functions, any efficient classical sampler matching the device would collapse a cornerstone complexity hierarchy.
arxiv-2512-07227: Konstantin Storozhuk proves a small, sharp existence result in functional analysis, the study of spaces of sequences and the gauges that measure them. In a sequence space, a functional assigns each sequence a number; unbounded ones blow up somewhere. Storozhuk shows there exist unbounded functionals with a striking restraint: on any family of sequences whose supports. The positions where they are nonzero, never overlap, the functional is nonzero for at most one member of the family.
arxiv-2512-07327:
Kedarnath Buda, B V Rathish Kumar, and Anil Rathi stage a contest inside a fractional partial differential equation and ask who wins. Two controllers steer the same system, a parabolic equation with memory in time and long-range coupling in space, each pulling toward its own desired state with its own quadratic cost. That standoff is a Nash equilibrium problem: the right concept is a pair of controls where neither side gains by deviating alone.

Under convexity and coercivity assumptions on the costs, the authors prove such an equilibrium exists and is the only one. Computing it takes an iterative scheme: conjugate gradient runs applied in turn to each player's discretized problem until the pair settles. The numerical experiments agree with the theoretical estimates and show the scheme working efficiently. Fractional models describe materials and fluids whose present depends on their whole past.
arxiv-2512-07627:
Maximos Kaliakatsos-Papakostas and five co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on computer-made music. A transformer model can harmonize a melody, adding chords beneath the tune. The open problem is control: can a user force a chosen chord at an exact spot?

The user supplies the melody plus a desired chord at a set position in a set bar. The model must then weave that chord into its harmony at the right onset. Off-the-shelf generation often misses such a hard demand. The authors propose an algorithm named B-star for the task. It mixes beam search and A-star search, with backtracking when a path fails. Forcing a pretrained model this way is costly, and worst-case time grows fast. The authors present it as a first attempt that names the core difficulties. Its design leaves room for smart shortcuts that later work can add.
arxiv-2512-08427:
Kevin Park, Zoltan Haiman, Chengcheng Xin, and colleagues, astronomers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They prepare for the Legacy Survey of Space and Time at the Rubin Observatory, which will catalog tens of millions of quasars over ten years. Some of those quasars should hide pairs of supermassive black holes orbiting closely. When one hole passes before the other, its gravity briefly magnifies the light, producing a self lensing flare.

The team tests two search methods on simulated quasar light curves with flares injected. A standard period search failed: flares did not raise peaks beyond what random quasar flickering produces alone. Matched filters did far better, separating real flares from noise even at the survey expected observing rhythm. They build a three step matched filter procedure that also recovers binary properties from the light curve, cheap enough to run across millions of quasar light curves.
arxiv-2512-08527:
A G Groshev and A K Arzhnikov, physicists in Russia, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is a chiral superconducting phase on a triangular lattice. Its pairing pattern twists in a way that gives the state a topological index. They ask how heat changes that index.

Using a self consistent theory, they track the index for a two dimensional model. When the nodal points of the pairing sit well inside or outside the normal state Fermi contour, heat widens the temperature ranges where the index stays near whole values. The widening depends on the index value and on how strongly the electrons attract. As the nodes approach the Fermi contour, crossovers to new index values appear and can persist across wide temperature ranges. The authors work out how fluctuations shape those crossovers, and suggest they should show in the edge states of a finite sample.
arxiv-2512-08827:
Guilherme Guedes and Jasper Roosmale Nepveu present a method to renormalize bosonic effective field theories in general, beyond one loop. Renormalization of higher dimensional operators is essential for particle physics phenomenology and for the study of critical phenomena. A general two loop treatment, covering arbitrary gauge symmetry and scalar content, was missing.

The authors compute the renormalization group equations in such theories up to two loops and up to dimension six operators. When their general formulas are specialized to the bosonic sector of the Standard Model effective theory, simple replacement rules reproduce recent results in the literature. That check supports the correctness of the broad method. Because effective field theory is so widely used, the results can be applied to many extensions and to other theories. The data also inform scaling dimensions of composite operators in conformal field theories without fermions.
arxiv-2512-09027:
Salvador Centelles Chulia, Manfred Lindner, and Thomas Rink study how future reactor neutrino experiments could test whether the lepton mixing matrix is truly unitary. Coherent elastic neutrino nucleus scattering has been observed, and precision data could reveal new physics. Deviations from unitarity could arise from mixing with extra heavy or light fermions that carry no standard charges.

Two regimes are explored. In the seesaw limit, the new fermions are heavy and only leave effective deviations in the active sector. In the light sterile limit, they can be produced and join in propagation and scattering. The authors show how each case changes both nucleus scattering and electron scattering signals. Sensitivity projections are built by scaling up a current germanium based reactor experiment that first observed reactor scattering. Leading systematic limits for that scaling are identified. The results highlight strong potential to probe new physics at high energy scales.
arxiv-2512-09327:
Xuangeng Chu and five co-authors present UniLS, a system that generates conversational avatars which both speak and listen. Most earlier avatar systems model only the speaker. Listening is harder: a listener's face moves mostly from an inner motion habit, loosely tied to the partner's voice, so direct audio training produces stiff, frozen listeners.

UniLS learns in two stages. First it trains an audio-free motion generator that captures how faces move naturally on their own. Then it fine-tunes that generator with two audio tracks, the speaker's and the listener's, so speech can steer the learned motion. The result is the first end-to-end framework driven by dual-track audio alone, with no need for the partner's recorded motion. In evaluations it matched leading speaking accuracy and improved listening measures by a wide margin, producing livelier, more varied listener expressions suited to real-time digital humans.
arxiv-2512-09527:
Zixian Wang leads a team peering into the Milky Way's center with the MUSE spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope. The bar, bulge, and inner disk hold much of our galaxy's mass, but their stars are faint, packed, and dimmed by dust, making their history hard to read. Adaptive optics and integral-field spectroscopy let the team measure stars.

For nearly a hundred main-sequence turn-off and subgiant stars in Baade's Window, they obtained ages, abundances, and line-of-sight velocities. The age distribution has several peaks, showing star formation in the inner galaxy happened in distinct episodes, and a share of stars are younger than five billion years. Most stars are metal-rich, though the full range is broad, and the chemistry shows both alpha-rich and alpha-poor sequences. The authors argue the method opens a path for studying how the inner galaxy formed and evolved.
arxiv-2512-09727:
Junlin Xiao and colleagues improve how parallel Monte Carlo tree search combines its results when actions are continuous. Monte Carlo tree search plans by simulating many futures through a search tree, and its root-parallel variant runs searches at once to use wall-clock time well. With continuous actions, each thread tries different actions, and how to aggregate their statistics at the root was an underexplored question.

Their method uses Gaussian process regression to estimate the values of actions that were never trialed in the environment. It borrows strength across nearby actions instead of treating each thread's results in isolation. An evaluation across six domains shows the approach outperforming aggregation strategies while adding a modest increase in inference time. The paper is slated for the Reinforcement Learning Journal and presentation at the third Reinforcement Learning Conference, and it offers an upgrade for online planning in settings with action spaces.
arxiv-2512-09827:
Hamid Reza Hashempour and colleagues design an energy saving scheme for federated learning in industrial networks. In federated learning, many devices train a shared model locally and send updates to a server. Here the devices are machinery subnetworks with tight limits on delay and energy. A subnetwork can upload directly, or pass its update through a neighbor acting as a relay. Relays partly merge updates before forwarding, which cuts traffic and training time.

The authors analyze how this relay scheme converges, then split the energy problem into computing and communication parts. A grouping method sorts devices into direct and two hop senders, a relay step follows, and transmit power is tuned with an approximation method. Simulations show faster convergence, far fewer outages, and energy use cut at least in half against unaggregated cooperation, with larger savings against direct transmission.
arxiv-2512-10027:
Yassin Bahid, Eduardo Corona, and Nancy Rodriguez build a fast, exact simulator for kinetic models of social behavior. Kinetic equations, borrowed from gas theory, now model opinion change, wealth exchange, and other social phenomena. Their transition rates contain Dirac delta functions, encoding sudden jumps of state. The authors study such systems with math first, proving solutions exist and are unique globally in time. They then present a deterministic numerical scheme, the Mass Preserving Collocation Method, designed for models split into several interacting subsystems.

The solver was validated on models with up to five subsystems. It reproduces the subsystem distributions that leading stochastic agent based methods find, such as tau leaping and hybrid schemes. It does so while preserving mass exactly, a property the stochastic methods only approximate. It also runs with far less computation, and avoids their run to run variability and tuning.
arxiv-2512-10527:
I Leonov studies what doping does to a layered nickelate superconductor, a double-layer material of lanthanum, nickel, and oxygen that superconducts under pressure. Using density functional theory joined with dynamical mean-field theory, he follows how adding or removing electrons reshapes the normal-state electronic structure and the magnetic correlations between nickel atoms.

The calculations show strong, orbital-dependent renormalisation, with one set of nickel bands behaving like a bad metal while the other stays sharper. Doping changes the effective mass in a non-monotonic way, rebuilds the low-energy structure past certain levels. And hints at spin and charge stripe patterns forming. Moderate electron doping strengthens in-plane spin fluctuations, and the whole picture closely resembles the bilayer Hubbard model, suggesting stripe fluctuations help drive the pressure-induced superconductivity.
arxiv-2512-10727:
Maximilian Kotz, Veikko Geyer, and Benjamin Friedrich trace the wobble of a beating cilium back to the small numbers of its motors. Cilia are the hair-like paddles that sweep mucus and move cells. They are driven by molecular motors. The count of motors on each filament is small. It is small enough that chance fluctuations in how many are bound cannot average away. The authors ask whether that microscopic noise alone explains the messiness seen in real beats.

Their theory says yes. Fluctuations in the number of bound motors suffice to reproduce the experimentally observed beat fluctuations, including the quality factor that grades how precise the oscillation is. And the phase defects that mar the synchronisation inside a single cilium. The result constrains any theory of how motors are controlled, and it ties molecular-level shot noise directly to the non-equilibrium dynamics visible under a microscope.
arxiv-2512-10827:
Yuping Gao and co-authors tighten a bound in colouring that has stood since 1999. Colour a graph's edges so adjacent edges differ, and look at the set of colours touching a vertex. If every vertex gets a unique set, the colouring distinguishes vertices by their edges. The minimum colours for this is the vertex-distinguishing chromatic index, and a 1997 conjecture by Burris and Schelp says it is never more than one above the lower bound.

The conjecture was verified for graphs with minimum and maximum degrees, leaving the upper bound at the number of vertices plus one. Gao and colleagues prove a bound proportional to the lower bound itself, an improvement whenever that quantity is small compared with the graph's size. For regular graphs whose degree is at least the base-two logarithm of the vertex count, they do even better. At most three colours above the lower bound.
arxiv-2512-11027:
Leo Bailloeul and fellow authors study how two high intensity tests could hunt for millicharged particles, hypothetical particles carrying a tiny fraction of an electron's charge. The facilities are SpinQuest, already running, and SHiP, a planned search for hidden particles. Both use intense beams striking fixed targets, with scintillator detectors watching for faint signals.

The analysis covers three ways such tiny bits could be produced: decays of normal mesons, a process called Drell-Yan production, and protons radiating them as they brake. That last channel dominates for lighter tiny bits, a new emphasis in this update. Detailed detector model runs and background estimates yield solid reach estimates. The authors find future runs could improve sensitivity to the particle's charge by up to a hundredfold over current limits.
arxiv-2512-11127:
Kshitiz Khanal tackles the DC optimal power flow problem, the calculation that decides how generators should run to meet demand at lowest cost while respecting grid limits. Exact solvers are reliable but too slow for large systems that need frequent updates, especially with variable renewable power. Machine learning models are fast but often break constraints or miss the cheapest solution.

Khanal's two stage method first trains a graph neural network with physics informed losses that encode dispatch rules, Kirchhoff's laws, and optimality conditions, producing feasible starting points. A flow matching stage then refines those points toward optimality. On a standard thirty bus test system under varied loads, the method stayed fully feasible and landed very close to optimal cost. It offers a practical middle path between slow exact solvers and fast but unreliable networks.
arxiv-2512-11427:
Tathagata Basu and fellow authors model how outside settings change the link between two variables, using a flexible Bayesian tree ensemble. Copulas separate a joint spread's link structure from its individual margins, but letting that structure vary with background factors, such as national wealth, is hard to do well. Their conditional copula model drives the link parameter with Bayesian additive regression trees, an ensemble method known for fitting complex relationships.

To curb the overfitting trees are prone to, they use a loss based prior that penalises overly complex tree shapes. A new adaptive reversible jump sampling method explores the model space efficiently and handles awkward, non smooth likelihoods with few assumptions. Model runs show the method recovering true tree structure and tracking complicated link patterns. A case study examines how gross domestic product relates to the link between male and female life expectancy and literacy across countries.
arxiv-2512-12027:
Pei-Jun Huang and co-authors remeasure the size of the Tucana dwarf galaxy, a faint companion of the Milky Way. The half light radius marks where half the galaxy light is enclosed. Getting it right matters for comparing dwarf galaxies and testing dark matter models.

The team merges wide, deep images from the Local Volume Complete Cluster Survey with archival Hubble images. Star counts form a density profile, and after background removal a Sérsic fit gives the radius: 0.89 arcminutes, or 225.7 parsecs, with tight error bars. That is about 10 percent larger than older values, thanks to the wider field catching the galaxy faint outskirts. Small galaxies, the result hints, may often be bigger than we thought.
arxiv-2512-12227:
Muhsin Aljaf and Ilias Cholis recalculate how often primordial black holes merge in a 2025 paper. Such black holes may have formed in the early universe and may form part of dark matter. Their merger rate, seen through gravitational waves, helps test both ideas.

Older work treated each pair as alone for its whole life, merging only by wave emission. Pairs that fall into dark matter halos meet neighbors that change their orbits. The authors combine outside and inside halo paths in one numerical framework. They find the total rate at low redshift is about 50 percent higher than the older view, and they share the rates in public.
arxiv-2512-12527:
Petrus J Gerrits and four co-authors refine historical population maps of Istanbul using declassified spy satellite images in a 2025 paper. Global population grids for the 1970s to 1990s are coarse, since built-up data and census records from then are thin. Their study is the first to fold Hexagon KH-9 reconnaissance imagery into gridded population mapping, the authors say.

They segment built-up land from 1977 KH-9 images and combine it with settlement level census data for Arnavutkoy and Cekmekoy over 1975 to 1990. Standard GHSL products placed people in areas not yet developed. The Hexagon data fixed fragmented rural and peri-urban patterns. Adding local census data refined the grids further, a method that could travel worldwide.
arxiv-2512-12927:
Mai Qi and Eugenia Colafranceschi build holographic codes inside spin networks, which are graphs used in quantum gravity research. In their picture, each link between nodes can carry a set amount of entanglement. Standard work allowed only two extremes: fully linked or not linked at all.

Their enriched setup lets each link carry any amount in between, tuned by extra variables. Linking then defines a map from inner link data to outer boundary states. In a large-spin regime, they show this map acts like a code that protects information. The result gives a discrete, geometric model of holographic error correction.
arxiv-2512-13227:
Sarit Khirirat and co-authors improve momentum methods for stochastic optimization that work through a linear minimization oracle. This family includes recent high-performing methods such as Muon, Scion, and Gluon for training neural networks. Classic momentum theory, though, promises only a slow convergence rate.

The authors fold in Hessian-corrected momentum, which uses second-order information, inside the oracle framework. Their analysis works under relaxed smoothness and for arbitrary norms, not just the Euclidean one. They prove a faster convergence rate that adapts to problem geometry. Experiments training multi-layer perceptrons and LSTM networks backed up the theory.
arxiv-2512-13327:
Tsanimir Angelov and co-authors compute the shadows of rotating wormholes surrounded by plasma. A wormhole shadow is the dark outline light traces around the throat. Plasma bends and blocks light, so its presence changes what a distant observer would see.

For several wormhole solutions and plasma profiles where the ray equations separate, they derive shadow boundaries in closed form. Radial-only plasma profiles made all photon regions evolve alike, much like a Kerr black hole. Angular profiles made each wormhole look distinct. At set plasma frequencies the shadows vanish entirely, always at lower frequencies than for Kerr. Where both shadows exist, wormhole shadows are consistently smaller.
arxiv-2512-13927:
Sophia Tang writes a complete guide to spherical equivariant graph transformers for 3D molecular systems. A model must treat a turned molecule in a physically meaningful way. Such graph networks enforce that by using spherical tensors as features.

The guide builds the full foundation, from group theory and spherical harmonics to tensor products and Clebsch-Gordan splitting. It then constructs the Tensor Field Network and SE(3)-Transformer designs and explains their message passing and attention. Clear proofs and marked-up code make it self-contained. At 99 pages with 46 figures, it serves learners in chemistry, protein modeling, and making new molecules.
arxiv-2512-14527:
Shreyas Subramanian, Bala Krishnamoorthy, and Pranav Murthy propose GreedyLR, a learning-rate scheduler that watches the training loss and reacts. Most neural network training follows a preset decay curve, such as a cosine schedule, chosen before training starts. GreedyLR instead adjusts the step size as the loss changes, speeding up or easing off in response to actual progress.

Across language, vision, and large language model tasks up to seven billion parameters, it beat leading schedulers on accuracy, speed, and convergence in the authors' tests. They back the method with a convergence proof and a formula for its best scaling factor. Extra experiments checked behavior on noisy loss surfaces, where it stayed robust.
arxiv-2512-14727:
Machine learning is entering healthcare, but clinical decisions need uncertainty estimates that standard models do not reliably give. Conformal prediction is a popular fix. It wraps a model's rough scores and returns estimates with statistical guarantees.

Five authors take a critical look at the finite sample theory behind the method in medical use. Guarantees that hold only in the limit may mislead when patient samples are small, as they often are in medicine. The paper helps clinicians and model builders judge when such guarantees deserve trust, and when they call for more caution than the method's reputation suggests.
arxiv-2512-15427:
Hyakka Nakada and Shu Tanaka study random matrices in a short 2025 paper on how their eigenvalues spread out after a common scaling step. In data work, values are often rescaled so the smallest becomes zero and the largest becomes one. The authors ask what pattern the scaled eigenvalues follow in that case.

They apply a known formula for the scaled spread to derive a scaling law for the cumulative distribution. They also derive the leftover error that appears when a random matrix is split into simpler factors. Computer tests check both results. The work helps link a routine data step to the math behind it.
arxiv-2512-15727:
Tianyi Wang proves that certain supermoduli spaces are not projected in a 2025 paper, dated December 5. The supermoduli space collects super Riemann surfaces of a fixed genus with marked points of two kinds, Neveu Schwarz and Ramond punctures. Whether such a space is projected, meaning it admits a certain splitting map, affects how integrals over it can be computed.

Wang improves a result of Donagi, Witten, and Ott. The new bound says the supermoduli space with genus g, n Neveu Schwarz punctures, and 2r Ramond punctures is not projected once g is at least n plus 5r plus 3. The paper is marked as a preliminary draft.
arxiv-2512-15827:
FNU Vikas, Paul Gratz, and Daniel Jimenez present a workload characterization method for branch predictability in a 2025 paper. Processors guess the direction of conditional branches to keep execution flowing, and a wrong guess wastes work and energy. Prediction is pattern recognition over branch history, so workload traits should forecast predictor accuracy.

The authors define two measures: branch working set size and branch predictability. The working set groups the most frequent branch contexts, built from branch address plus global and local history. Analyzing 2,451 workload traces, they sort workloads into seven size and nine predictability categories. Both measures correlate strongly with miss rates of modern predictors such as TAGE and perceptron designs.
arxiv-2512-16227:
Qizhou Chen and three co-authors fix language model knowledge in a paper posted to arXiv in 2025. Models absorb errors and outdated facts, but retraining them from scratch is costly and disruptive. Editing methods patch single facts, yet fixes often fail to generalize and damage unrelated behavior.

The team grounds editing in information bottleneck theory, which compresses data down to what matters. Their editor, IBKE, squeezes a correction into a compact latent form and uses it to steer gradient updates. That keeps the edit focused: the new fact should stick, related facts should follow, and everything else should stay put. Tested across several model architectures and standard edit benchmarks, IBKE set state-of-the-art accuracy with better generality and specificity than rivals. The authors frame it as a principled path to trustworthy model maintenance.
arxiv-2512-16527:
Christopher T Hill rethinks the Higgs boson's inner life in a paper published on arXiv in 2025. In top-quark condensation models, the Higgs is not elementary but a bound state of top quarks, held like a pair in a superconductor. A recent reformulation gave that bound state an extended internal wavefunction, spread over a separation between its parts.

Hill shows the extension can be written in a manifestly Lorentz invariant way. The missing relative time between the two constituents turns out to be a gauge freedom of the bilocal field theory, not a flaw. That forces a novel, nontrivial vacuum structure for the Higgs boson, the relativistic cousin of a BCS condensate state in condensed matter physics. The paper is a formal step in an alternative account of where the Higgs and its mass come from.
arxiv-2512-16827:
Juan Sosa, Brayan Riveros, and Emma J. Camargo-Díaz map the lawmaking output of Colombia House of Representatives from 2014 to 2025, using 4,083 bills. The study asks whether party polarization shows up in who works with whom, and how bill topics shift over time.

Networks link parties to bills and members to bills, with projections that reveal co-sponsorship patterns, central actors, and influence. In parallel, semantic networks from bill blurbs, a stochastic block model, and topic models track content by party and period. A Bayesian sociability model flags terms with robust links. The blend gives a reproducible picture meant to support openness and citizen watch over the legislature.
arxiv-2512-17327:
Qi-An Su and seven co-authors proposed a sharper way to sense heat and strain by telling quantum states apart. Normal sensors hit limits set by their own hardware. Their idea builds the measuring tool in the space left over outside the main state, which makes close states easier to tell apart.

Tests with an optical microcavity reached a heat resolution of 4 times 10 to the minus 6 degrees and a strain resolution of 18 p-strain units, sensing both at once. Readers should know the record carries a withdrawal request: the note states the manuscript was not sent for a required institutional review, and the corresponding author formally asks for withdrawal. Treat the results as unreviewed and withdrawn at the author's request.
arxiv-2512-17427:
Jone Mencos and a large team give the first direct proof that a magnet with no net magnetization can still inject a spin current in a one-way, time-breaking fashion. Their injector is a film of Mn5Si3, a compensated magnet whose internal poles cancel out. In a sideways spin valve, flipping the magnet between its two time-reversed states changed the detected spin signal, the key fingerprint.

The effect showed up under both wiring setups they tried, with the same detector. Calculations tie it to the material's altermagnetic order, which sends spin-up and spin-down currents along at different strengths and angles. A magnet that looks inert from outside yet steers spin inside could shrink future memory and logic devices.
arxiv-2512-17527:
Muhammad Haris Khan of the University of Copenhagen built SafeBench-Seq, a 2025 benchmark for screening protein sequences that might be hazardous. AI models can now design new proteins, which raises biosecurity worries, yet the field lacked a simple shared test for hazard screening. His baseline runs on ordinary CPUs and uses only public data.

The classifier reads plain chemical features of a sequence, such as amino acid makeup, rather than the sequence itself, and the project shares metadata only, never risky sequences. To mimic never seen threats, similar sequences are grouped and whole groups are held out of training. Khan found that random test splits greatly overstate how robust screening is. Calibrated simple models gave the most trustworthy risk scores in his tests.
arxiv-2512-17727:
Zdzisław Brzeźniak, Enrico Priola, Jianliang Zhai, and Jiahui Zhu study a transport equation shaken by jump noise. Without noise, such an equation can fail to have a single answer. Their question is whether random jumps, of the kind called Lévy noise, can restore order.

They prove that a weak solution exists and is the only one, across the full range of jump types, even the wild regime past work could not handle. A sharp study of the flow's shape and its stretching factor carries the proof. The result extends a famous 2010 paper from smooth Brownian noise to jump noise, a first for an equation of fluid type.
arxiv-2512-18027:
Samidh Chakrabarti and five coauthors present CoPE, a small language model built to label content against a written policy. Platforms need fast, steady labeling for harmful posts, and giant models are costly for that grind. CoPE is trained to read a policy rather than memorize one fixed set of rules.

Two new tricks carry the training. One feeds the model clashing examples so it learns to weigh policy words, and the other speeds up building clear training sets. Across seven harm areas, CoPE matched or beat frontier models at about 1 percent of their size. The team released a 9 billion parameter version that runs on a single home grade graphics card.
arxiv-2512-18227:
In a second 2025 study, Deepit Sapru examines how crime gets talked about on Reddit, where city communities host constant discussion of local safety. Traditional media's role in shaping fear of crime is well studied, but social media's part is not. Sapru analyzes user submissions across Reddit communities representing 384 metropolitan areas in the United States.

Two patterns stand out. Crime discussion is more prevalent in larger metropolitan areas, and in communities with more liberal political leanings. Surprisingly, reported crime rates do not strongly influence how much or how intensely people discuss crime. Online talk about crime, in other words, tracks community size and politics more than actual offending. The findings suggest that platforms like Reddit now mediate public narratives about safety in their own right. For researchers and policymakers, perceived crime and measured crime must be treated as separate things, each needing its own evidence.
arxiv-2512-18527:
Rahul Yumlembam and five co-authors build a filter that decides when an AI image detector should distrust itself. As generated images grow photorealistic, a single confidence score is not enough. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Scientific Reports, fuses three uncertainty signals: Fisher information, Monte Carlo dropout entropy, and variance from a Gaussian process model.

Particle swarm optimization learns how to weight the signals and where to set a rejection threshold. Trained on Stable Diffusion images, the system is tested on unseen generators including Midjourney and StyleGAN3. The combined measure rejects about 70 percent of the samples the detector would get wrong, and under FGSM and PGD attacks it rejects about 61 percent of successful attacks. The cautious design accepts nearly all correct calls on natural images.
arxiv-2512-19227:
Yu Tong Liu and Myles Workman give a new measure-theoretic view of Brakke flow, a model of surfaces that move by their mean curvature. Along the flow, they track not just where the surface sits, but which tangent directions it takes over space and time. A Grassmann space collects those directions.

They prove a canonical space-time-Grassmann measure exists for any such flow on an open region. With its weight, the Brakke inequality can be stated for space-time measures directly, giving a fresh definition of the flow. Classical flows match the new form, and mean curvature, density, and tangent maps all become measurable against the weight.
arxiv-2512-19327:
Moamal Fadhil Abdul-Mahdi, Jonas Bruun Hubrechts, Thomas Martini Jørgensen, and Emil Hovad enrich a public table tennis video dataset with far finer labels. The original OpenTTGames set marks ball events such as bounces and net hits, plus ball positions and masks of players and table. Coaches and broadcasters, though, want to know the strokes themselves.

The extension adds frame-accurate shot types, split into forehand and backhand subtypes, along with body lean and leg stance for each player. Rally outcome tags close each point. A compact coding scheme and code-assisted labeling keep the process repeatable. Models can now aim at tactical questions, like which stroke sets up a winner.
arxiv-2512-19627:
Santa Claus gets the optimization treatment from Elliot Fisher and Robin Smith, who treat his Christmas Eve run as a routing problem with rolling night-time windows set by Earth's rotation. Their Travelling-Santa Ant-Colony Optimisation framework sends artificial ants along partial routes, guided by pheromone trails and a measure of allowed exploration, much like real ants foraging.

The heuristic bakes darkness feasibility straight into the pheromone signal, shrinks the sleigh's cross-section to cut aerodynamic work, and uses a cheap rogue-ant reversal to catch direction-sensitive time zones. Cruise speeds are tuned leg by leg as routes form. On tests over 15 and 30 capital cities, daylight violations vanish and total work drops by up to ten percent against a distance-only version. A 40-city stress test cuts energy use far more steeply still.
arxiv-2512-19827:
Davide Sipione, Giacomo Como, and Gustav Nilsson tackle traffic control on freeways with many classes of flow. Their problem sets ramp meters and speed limits to run a network well. The traffic model is the cell transmission model. Plain versions of the problem are non-convex. The kink is how jams form at split points in the road.

Fresh work found a tight convex relaxation for the one-class case. This study extends it to many classes. With the right demand and supply shapes, each class can get its own speed limit. The problem stays convex, so it can be solved fast. A case study uses a stretch of California freeway, fed with PeMS data. The control works there. A side test shows the gain over treating all flow as one class.
arxiv-2512-19927:
Alexey Yermakov leads a fifteen-author team giving seismology AI a shared scoreboard. Forecasting and rebuilding seismic wavefields backs quake early warning and ground-motion calls. But simulation data are huge, and real sensors are sparse. Past method comparisons have been ad hoc. Their Common Task Framework sets shared data sets, metrics, and reporting. It is modeled on frameworks that brought order to other fields.

Three wavefield data sets cover global, crustal, and local scales. The tasks span forecasting, rebuilding, and generalizing under noise and thin data. A demo study rebuilds wavefields from sparse sensors. It shows which methods suit which problem classes, with strengths and limits side by side. The long-term aim is hidden test sets. Head-to-head checks that others can rerun would become the norm.
arxiv-2512-20127:
Ruobing Chen and Sirui Yu fix a bookkeeping mismatch in superalgebra. The function algebra of the standard superspace is Koszul. But its Koszul dual is not graded commutative. So it cannot be the function algebra of the swapped superspace. The polynomial and exterior extremes show no such flaw. Their remedy is to view that algebra as living on a bigraded space.

In the bigraded sense, the dual is again an algebra of a bigraded space. The expected symmetry is restored. The differential calculus structures on the two spaces are then shown to match through the duality. The second half moves Poisson structures across the same bridge. For quadratic bigraded Poisson structures, the duality matches the calculi on both sides. With unimodularity, the match extends to the Batalin-Vilkovisky algebras.
arxiv-2512-20427:
Igor B Furtat studies how fast a nonlinear system can be forced to settle, not eventually but by a deadline. Fixed-time convergence means every solution reaches zero, or a target region, within a time bound fixed in advance. His conditions are stated through a quadratic function evaluated along the system's solutions.

A twist delivers the speed: raising the derivative of that quadratic function to a negative power during part of the evolution pushes solutions harder early on. Furtat derives conditions for convergence to zero and to a prescribed region. He applies the results to design backstepping control laws for linear plants of arbitrary order. Numerical modelling compares the new laws favourably with existing fixed-time schemes.
arxiv-2512-20727:
Lukas M Bongartz treats an organic mixed conductor, or OMC, the way the physics of gases treats a gas. OMCs are sought for bioelectronics, brain-like computing, and heat-to-power uses, and they carry both electrons and ions, with motion on many scales at once. The standard theory of semiconductors, built for very unlike stuff, fits them poorly.

Bongartz sets OMCs beside standard semiconductors from the point of view of heat and disorder. He then models their charge carriers as a lattice gas, free to fill or leave sites on a grid. The model shows a sharp, first-order change of state, much like vapour turning to liquid, with low- and high-density carrier phases side by side, as recent tests report. Stickiness near the border explains why OMC transistors remember their past. The aim: this branch of physics is the right language for such stuff.
arxiv-2512-20827:
Mohammad Taghi Dabiri and four co-authors propose city-wide clock synchronization carried by entangled photons. Precise shared timing underpins smart city networks, and quantum links promise security as well as accuracy. A central quantum hub sends one photon of each entangled pair toward a target device and keeps the partner as reference.

Targets need no active electronics: a flat array of corner reflectors simply bounces the photon back, enabling round-trip timing finer than a nanosecond. The authors model beam spread, misalignment, air turbulence, and stray light, then derive a detection probability formula. Simulations matched the model and exposed trade-offs among beam width, reflector size, and background light.
arxiv-2512-21127:
Oliver Normand, Harry Coppock, and seven co-authors ran the first real-world test of a language-model medication safety reviewer, inside actual NHS primary care records. The records cover more than two million adults in Cheshire and Merseyside. From them, the team sampled 277 patients across the spectrum of complexity and medication risk. An expert clinician graded every issue and intervention the system proposed.

Detection looked strong on headline numbers, with perfect sensitivity and specificity above eighty percent, yet the system got everything right for a patient less than half the time. The failures were mostly contextual, not pharmacological. They included overconfidence under uncertainty, and guidelines applied without adjusting to the patient. They also included misunderstanding how care is actually delivered, factual slips, and process blindness. Forty-five published vignettes document every failure pattern, a cautionary evidence base for anyone deploying clinical AI.
arxiv-2512-21427:
Sambhabi Bose, Kevin J. McGown, Ishan Panpaliya, Natalie Welling, and Laney Williams count number fields with a prescribed Galois group. A number field is an extension of the rational numbers, and its Galois group describes the symmetries of its roots. Malle's conjecture predicts how fast the count should grow as the allowed discriminant size increases.
