The group studied here is a wreath product, written C2 wr S4, acting on eight letters. Klüners had already proved Malle's conjecture for this group, with an error term that saved a modest power. Bose and her co-authors sharpen that error term substantially, showing the count equals a constant times the bound, plus a smaller remainder than before. Along the way they also obtain new bounds for four related groups, including S4 itself and GL2 over the field with three elements. Sharper error terms test whether Malle's predicted growth is exactly right.
arxiv-2512-21627:
Botao Ren, Mu Xu, and their co-authors give a navigating robot a long visual memory without a heavy object-mapping pipeline. Navigation requires remembering places across many tasks, so the agent can explore new areas and return quickly to known goals. Object-centric memories are clear but depend on detection and reconstruction steps that limit robustness.

AstraNav-Memory stores experience as images instead, compressing each view into few tokens. A vision transformer backbone with frozen DINOv3 features and small convolutional blocks encodes an image at a sixteen-fold compression rate into about thirty tokens, so hundreds of images fit in context. A Qwen2.5-VL-based policy then navigates using that compressed history. On the GOAT-Bench and HM3D-OVON benchmarks, the method performed best, improving exploration in new environments and shortening paths in known ones. Ablations show moderate compression balances efficiency and accuracy best.
arxiv-2512-21927:
Bingqiu Chen, Guangxing Li, and their co-authors dissect the largest known superbubble in the Milky Way, a vast cavity carved across the Perseus Arm by stellar feedback. Superbubbles grow when massive stars and supernovae blow gas outward, but most are shredded by the Galaxy's shear within tens of millions of years. This one has survived far longer.

Combining Gaia and LAMOST data, the team assembled young massive stars with full three-dimensional velocities and found groups at the bubble's rim. The rim expands at about six kilometers per second, with transverse motions near twenty-six. From these numbers they estimate the timescales: supernovae inject energy far faster than shear can distort the cavity, whose survival time is near two hundred fifty million years. Supernova energy and momentum suffice to sustain growth. The Giant Oval Cavity is a large, quasi-stationary superbubble.
arxiv-2512-22127:
Ala Eddine Nouali, Mohamed Sana, and Jean-Paul Jamont study cell-free MIMO networks, where many scattered access points jointly serve each phone instead of one tower cell. Serving every user from every access point will not scale, so each user gets a chosen cluster. The authors ask how the cluster and its user should treat each other: selfishly, equally, or generously.

They model cluster formation as a many-to-many social matching game where outside effects matter, then solve it with two algorithms based on deferred acceptance and early acceptance. Simulations show the chosen social attitude strongly affects both service quality and energy use. When both sides adopt the egalitarian regime, the trade-off between the two goals is best.
arxiv-2512-22427:
Amy K. Lin and four co-authors shake a battery material with terahertz light to watch its ions move faster. LLZO, a garnet-type solid electrolyte, conducts lithium ions about a hundred times better in its cubic phase than in its tetragonal one. Static structure alone may not explain conduction; lattice vibrations, or phonons, are suspected helpers. Their laser-driven ultrafast impedance spectroscopy excites phonons directly and probes ion hopping with picosecond resolution.

Exciting phonons across the terahertz range boosted the ionic conductivity of both crystal phases. The disturbance decayed with a similar time constant in each, despite their different lithium arrangements and migration routes. Together with Raman spectra and simulated vibrational densities, the results suggest low-energy optical phonons loosen the lattice in ways that help ions hop, independent of static structure.
arxiv-2512-22627:
Chen Su, Yuanhe Tian, and Yan Song answer questions about time series with a three-model team that checks its own work. Language models handle time series question answering through a unified text interface, but they stumble on complex numerical sequences. Time series have one saving grace: their reasoning steps can be verified against the original data. The proposed system, T3LLM, builds that check directly into training.

A worker model drafts step-by-step reasoning under structured prompts. A reviewer model inspects the draft, flags erroneous steps, and writes corrective comments. The corrected reasoning chains then fine-tune a student model, internalizing both multi-step reasoning and self-correction. On several real-world benchmarks, T3LLM reached state-of-the-art performance over strong language model baselines.
arxiv-2512-22727:
Sandra Robles, Walter Tangarife, and Giorgio Busoni ask what happens when very heavy dark matter particles crash into the first generation of massive stars and get captured inside them. Using stellar evolution simulations, they follow capture from a star's birth on the main sequence through its later, metal-rich stages. The capture rate depends on what the star is made of at each stage and on how the dark matter is moving through its halo.

Early on, scattering off two kinds of targets describes capture well. Later, a dense metal core forms and boosts capture so much that three target species are needed for accurate rates. For some allowed settings, captured dark matter settles, heats, and balances annihilation inside one stellar lifetime. Without annihilation it could even collapse into a small black hole that eats the star from inside.
arxiv-2512-22827:
Yue Wu and collaborators built FasterPy, a framework that uses large language models to make Python code run faster. Slow code is a common kind of performance bug, and older fixes rely on hand-written rules or on machine learning systems that need carefully built training sets. FasterPy takes a cheaper route, pairing the language model with examples of proven speed-ups.

A retrieval system searches a knowledge base of code pairs, where each pair shows code before and after a measured performance improvement, and feeds the best matches to the model. Low-rank adaptation then fine-tunes the model on the task. On the Performance-Improving Code Edits benchmark, FasterPy improved execution efficiency across multiple metrics compared with baselines. The tool and the experimental results are publicly available, and the authors present the framework as a low-cost option for automated code optimization.
arxiv-2512-22927:
Daqian Cao, Quan Yuan, and Weibang Bai present P-FABRIK, a method for computing the joint settings of parallel mechanisms, machines where several linked chains move one platform together. Classic geometric solvers exploit each machine's specific structure, which breaks down for redundant designs with extra actuators. Worse, when a target pose lies outside the workspace, those solvers return nothing and can upset the controller.

P-FABRIK adapts the FABRIK algorithm from serial robot arms and computer graphics. A new decomposition splits a parallel mechanism into serial sub-chains, adjusts each sub-chain's end target, and iterates until the chains agree on one feasible pose. Case studies cover planar, standard, and redundant parallel mechanisms, showing the same code handles all three. Simulations confirm the solver is fast, and it degrades gracefully by still returning a pose for targets outside the workspace.
arxiv-2512-23127:
Loris Di Cairano rebuilds microcanonical thermodynamics, the statistical mechanics of isolated systems, on geometry. Rather than posit an ensemble, he starts from the constant-energy surfaces in phase space and asks what structure measuring them needs. The microcanonical measure then appears as surface measure on each energy shell, and entropy becomes the log of a geometric area.

As energy changes, the shells deform, and their deformation obeys a ladder of entropy flow equations driven by curvature averages over the shell. Phase transitions, in this view, are changes of shell geometry that leave fingerprints in entropy's slopes. Two structural payoffs follow: the rebuilt thermodynamics does not depend on the description chosen, and microscopic systems sharing the same geometric content share the same thermodynamics. The approach is exercised on mean-field models, short-range lattice theories, and a long-range XY chain, recovering response functions.
arxiv-2512-23227:
Sungho Kang and co-authors improve anomaly detection for factory inspection, where defect photos are scarce and most training data show only good products. Synthetic defect images can fill the gap, but rule-based synthesis looks fake, while diffusion-generated defects cost a lot to produce. Their framework threads the needle with a pretrained text-guided translation model that creates defect images cheaply.

A retrieval model grades each generated image by similarity to normal images and discards irrelevant outputs, improving the synthetic set. Training runs in two stages: pretraining on a volume of cheap rule-based fakes, then fine-tuning on the smaller set of high-quality generated defects. That schedule cuts collection cost while lifting detection accuracy. Experiments on the standard MVTec AD benchmark demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, and the authors present the retrieval-filtered, two-stage recipe as the key to making synthetic data pay off.
arxiv-2512-23327:
Görkem Giray, Onur Demirörs, Marcos Kalinowski, and Daniel Mendez survey how software practitioners are adopting generative AI tools. Adoption is wide and deep in daily work, the study finds, especially for coding, testing, personal assistance, and maintenance. Practitioners report shorter cycle times, better quality, better support for knowledge work, and productivity gains, though few firms measure those gains.

The challenges list is equally concrete: incorrect or unreliable outputs, the craft of prompt engineering, checking overhead, security and privacy worries, and the risk of leaning on the tools too hard. Companies set rules for tool access but invest less in training and governance. Looking ahead, practitioners expect generative AI to redefine their roles rather than replace them, paired with anxiety about a contracting job market and shifting skill demands. The study grounds debates that often run on anecdote.
arxiv-2512-23727:
The COMPASS collaboration at CERN publishes an addendum updating how often certain particles are produced when muons scatter off an isoscalar target. Multiplicities of pions, kaons, and unidentified charged hadrons are basic data for understanding how quarks fragment into hadrons. The catalog entry's byline is scrambled; per the arXiv record, the author is the collaboration itself.

The update was forced by method, not by new data. A companion paper on a hydrogen target used an improved treatment of quantum electrodynamic radiative corrections, generated with the DJANGOH Monte Carlo program. This changed some corrections by up to about twelve percent in one kinematic corner. To keep the isoscalar results consistent with the proton results, the collaboration recomputed them with the same corrections. The new numbers supersede two papers published in Physics Letters B in 2017.
arxiv-2512-23927:
Lars van der Laan and Nathan Kallus work on fitted Q-iteration, a workhorse method for learning control policies from logged data in offline reinforcement learning. The method's stability is usually argued through a demanding assumption called Bellman completeness, which real function classes often fail. The authors ask whether a softened version of the method can be trusted without it.

Their key observation is local: near the best soft policy, the update behaves like ordinary policy evaluation, which shrinks errors when states are weighted by how often that policy visits them. Reweighting the fitting step by those visit ratios restores the shrinking property, and the team proves local convergence with finite data. A temperature schedule then carries the result further, starting hot, where convergence is global, and cooling step by step toward the target. Under a margin condition, a final switch to the hard method reaches the unregularized optimum.
arxiv-2512-24227:
Shuyun Wang and four colleagues edit video of driving scenes. Self-driving systems need varied training data to stay robust. Editing objects into real footage is a promising way to grow that data. Past methods struggle on two fronts at once. Visual realism is hard. So is keeping frames consistent over time.

Their model, Mirage, edits in a single diffusion step. A text-to-video prior supplies temporal consistency. Compression in the video autoencoder blurs fine detail, though. The team injects latents from a two-dimensional encoder to restore it. Inserted assets also misalign with the scene. Different objectives create a distribution mismatch between the two. A two-stage alignment strategy fixes the poses. Coarse three-dimensional alignment comes first. Fine two-dimensional refinement follows. Experiments show high realism across varied editing scenarios.
arxiv-2512-24327:
Anna Calissano and Etienne Lasalle shrink spatial graphs without flattening their shape. Spatial graphs have nodes placed in space. Transit networks, molecules, and branching structures in biology are examples. Reduction should keep the overall structure with fewer nodes. Shape matters here, because position carries meaning.

Their method collapses short edges step by step. A new filtration captures the shape features that set how far to reduce. It adapts persistent diagrams, built for point clouds, to spatial graphs. The filtration is triangle-aware. The method needs no parameters to tune. It is provably unchanged when the input is rotated, moved, or scaled. Tests used synthetic and real spatial graphs. Sizes fell a great deal under the reduction. The key shape features survived intact.
arxiv-2512-24427:
Sascha Hauck, Sandip Saha, Narsis Kiani, and Jesper Tegner model how gene networks settle into cell states. Gene networks produce stable and dynamic states in cells. Slow epigenetic feedback keeps reshaping the landscape those states live on. Maps of gene activity show rich behavior. A tractable theory linking activity, epigenetic control, and group dynamics has been missing.

The team extends dynamical mean field theory to fill the gap. Chemical marks on the genome enter as slow, feedback-driven variables. The Hopfield network and spin glass analogy guides the math. Compact stochastic equations compress the high-dimensional dynamics across timescales. Stable and oscillatory regimes both become quantifiable. The feedback visibly reshapes the effective potential, the Waddington landscape of cell fate. The frame unifies development and reprogramming questions in one theory.
arxiv-2512-24827:
Raul Steleac, Mohan Sridharan, and David Abel present a method for discovering coordinated options, meaning temporally extended joint behaviors, for teams of agents. Joint state spaces grow exponentially with team size, so earlier option methods often settle for loosely coupled or independent behaviors. Their joint-state abstraction compresses how agents relate to each other rather than listing every detail.

Relative representations between agents guide the search for options that keep coordination. Readers in multi-agent learning get a route to reusable team skills for exploration and planning. Better options could help robot or software teams act as units instead of collections of solo policies.
arxiv-2512-24927:
Yuchen Jiao, Na Li, and Changxiao Cai challenge the belief that first-order diffusion samplers are inherently slower than higher-order solvers. Higher-order ODE solvers became the standard acceleration tool, but placement of model evaluations along reverse-time dynamics also strongly affects accuracy when few evaluations are allowed. Their training-free first-order sampler exploits that placement.

A fast forward-value approach sets the leading discretization to cut error in the low-evaluation regime. Generative modeling readers get acceleration without retraining or higher-order machinery. The lesson is that where you evaluate can matter as much as the order of the solver you use.
arxiv-2512-25027:
Omar Said, Christopher Tossas-Betancourt, Mary Olive, and others model disease course in child pulmonary arterial hypertension, a worsening disease raising lung pressures and straining the right ventricle. Child cases are little studied, with limited data and few focused plans. Multi-scale, patient-certain cardiovascular models were built and tuned for four young patients.

Longitudinal MRI and catheterization data, taken about two years apart, anchor the models, which couple three-dimensional fluid-structure contact through the CRIMSON approach. Biomedical engineering readers get a template for tracking single course and testing actions in silico. Patient-certain simulation is mainly valuable where trials are hard to run.
arxiv-2601-00127:
Ana M Botti, Yikai Wu, and seven other co-authors work on detectors meant to see X-rays in space. The detectors, called skipper-CCDs, are silicon chips that can read charge with extreme precision and survive radiation well. Their weakness is light: ordinary light and near-infrared photons can flood the sensor and distort the X-ray signal. Their 2026 paper presents a thin shield against that flooding.

The team coats the chip surface with aluminum layers using a vapor process, then tests them across red and near-infrared wavelengths and with an iron X-ray source. Layers of fifty and one hundred nanometers block nearly all the light while letting the tested X-rays through. Simulations extend the results to wider energies and other thicknesses.
arxiv-2601-00327:
Naiqi Zhang leads five coauthors in uniting fine surface detail and broad meaning for spotting factory defects. Missing a tiny flaw can carry grave costs. Older methods split into two camps with clear trade offs. Structure based filters catch detail but bend under noise. Meaning based encoders stay robust but miss small marks. Their framework runs both views in parallel branches.

Image features first pass into the frequency domain. High frequency parts carry texture and edge clues. A fine structural attention module sharpens that branch. Low frequency parts carry global context and semantics. A context module guards long range consistency there. One training run covers many product classes jointly. Three benchmark sets show top tier results. Sensitivity and robustness rise together in the tests. Inspectors gain a tool that sees both the scratch and the scene.
arxiv-2601-00527:
Ravi Teja Pagidoju and Shriya Agarwal propose generating store shelf layouts, called planograms, with a cloud-based diffusion model. Drawing a complex planogram by hand takes about thirty hours on average, and each store needs its own version. Instead of rearranging an existing layout, their system learns from successful shelf arrangements across many stores and creates new ones.

Training runs in the cloud on AWS while finished models answer requests at the edge in real time, and retail constraints are built into the training objective. In simulation, design time fell by over ninety-eight percent, to about half an hour, while over ninety-four percent of constraints were satisfied. Their cost analysis estimates a break-even point of a little over four months.
arxiv-2601-00827:
Mariam Saeed and seven co-authors present, in 2026, a system that turns speech straight into pictures. Past systems first coded the speech, then fed the code to a GAN, a kind of image maker. GANs also train poorly, often collapsing to a few same-like outputs. The new system, named Speak the Art, swaps the GAN for a diffusion model, which builds images in steady steps.

Its speech coder learns under the eye of a big pre-trained model that links images and text. That watch forces the code to keep the sense of the words. Training is steadier, and the outputs vary more. The team also stretched the system to two languages, English and Arabic, as a proof of concept. On standard tests it beat the best past systems by a wide margin. The work narrows the gap between spoken and typed prompts for art tools.
arxiv-2601-00927:
Jawad Chowdhury, Rezaur Rashid, and Gabriel Terejanu measure affective polarization, the emotional dislike between opposing camps, in social media conversation. Understanding that hostility matters for judging social media's societal effects, but older studies leaned on sentiment scores or fixed classifiers that miss nuance. Their framework uses large language models to read discussions directly.

The models extract each post's stance, affective tone, and agreement patterns on divisive topics such as climate change and gun control. A rule-based scoring system, informed by domain knowledge, then converts those readings into a polarization score that works even on tiny conversations of a single exchange. Applying the method at scale, the authors find polarization patterns that shift with events, rather than staying fixed per topic.
arxiv-2601-01027:
Rafael Wampfler and five colleagues describe a platform for building digital characters that people can talk with in a story-like way. Their proof of concept is a digital Albert Einstein who chats about his life, his work, and his outlook. The team notes that a believable character needs far more than a good language model.

The system joins many parts: dialogue, a steady character and mood, memory of facts and past talk, a matched voice, animation, and links to the real world around the user. Each part has been studied on its own, but joining them smoothly is the open problem the platform attacks. The design is not tied to Einstein. It can be adapted to other figures, which points toward richer interactive stories and learning tools.
arxiv-2601-01427:
Isabella Gerrard and Christoph Federrath ask what stirs the gas between the stars in a Milky Way-like galaxy. Turbulence in that gas shapes how stars form, but several engines can drive it: supernova blasts, galactic shear, and gravity's pull. Each engine stirs in a different style, mixing squeezing motions and swirling ones in different proportions.

Using detailed simulations of a thousand-light-year patch of galactic disk over one hundred million years, the authors track a driving parameter that measures that mix. It swings over time from swirl-leaning to strongly compressive. High star formation follows about ten million years after compressive phases. Later, a certain supernova type raises the warm gas share and turbulence speed while easing the mix back. The results tie the galaxy's breathing, its cycles of stirring and star birth, into one timeline.
arxiv-2601-01527:
Fatma Zohra Bara, Slimane Zaiem, and Yazid Delenda compute how top quarks would be produced at a future electron-positron collider if space-time itself were slightly noncommutative. In such theories, coordinates fail to commute, leaving fingerprints on scattering rates. The team works inside the minimal noncommutative version of the Standard Model, using the Seiberg-Witten map to translate the theory into ordinary fields.

They carry the calculation to second order in the noncommutativity parameter and extract the total production rate, the angular patterns of the outgoing top quarks, and the forward-backward asymmetry. All three shift in characteristic ways as the noncommutativity grows. The numbers are evaluated at the energies planned for proposed linear colliders such as the ILC and CLIC. Since top quarks are the heaviest known particles, their production is a sensitive probe. The work shows collider data could indirectly test the grain of space-time itself.
arxiv-2601-01627:
Liu and 9 co-authors built JMedEthicBench, a test of medical safety for language models in Japanese. Safety tests have mostly used English and single questions, yet real care unfolds over long talks and in local language. Their benchmark rests on sixty-seven guidelines from the Japan Medical Association and holds more than fifty thousand hostile multi-turn conversations.

Seven attack styles, found automatically, probe the models, and two models score the replies. Among twenty-seven models tested, paid models stayed robust while medical-specialized ones grew more open to attack. Safety fell sharply as talks went on, and the weakness appeared in English too, pointing to training that trims safety while adding medical skill.
arxiv-2601-01727:
Paul Boisseau, Weixiao Lu, and Hang Xue set out to prove the Gan-Gross-Prasad conjecture for Fourier-Jacobi periods on unitary groups, together with a refined formula of Ichino-Ikeda type. Their paper is the second of three, and the whole series rests on comparing two relative trace formulae set up by Liu.

The task here is the comparison itself: showing that the two trace formulae, one on each side of the problem, actually match term by term. Trace formulae are bookkeeping tools that relate geometric data about orbits to spectral data about representations, and aligning them is the bridge the proof must cross. With the comparison in place, the final paper can compute the spectral sides and finish the argument.
arxiv-2601-02427:
Loïc Magne and a large team introduce NitroGen, an open foundation model for agents that play video games of many kinds. General agents need experience far beyond one title, so the team built a data set by automatically extracting player actions from public gameplay videos. The result covers forty thousand hours of play across more than one thousand games.

A unified vision action model was trained on that data by large scale behavior cloning, and a multi game benchmark measures how well agents generalize across games. NitroGen handles combat in three dimensional action games, precise control in two dimensional platformers, and exploration in procedurally generated worlds. On games it never trained on, it improved task success by up to about half over models trained from scratch. Data, tests, and model weights were released openly.
arxiv-2601-02527:
Ryan A. Rubenzahl and six co authors make Gaussian process modeling fast for astronomical measurements that are integrated over an exposure, rather than taken at an instant. Integration blurs fast variability, and once exposure times vary or overlap, the standard covariance matrix loses the structure that makes it cheap. Forcing memory and time costs that grow far too fast with data size.

Linear Gaussian state space models are known to be equivalent to Gaussian processes and can be solved in linear time with Kalman filtering and smoothing. The authors extend that equivalence to integrated measurements by adding an integral state that resets when an exposure starts and is read when it ends. The augmented model gives exactly the same posterior as the full integrated process, in linear time on a CPU and faster still in parallel on a GPU.
arxiv-2601-02627:
Nelvin Tan and five co authors improve how large language models extract evidence when checking a document for internal inconsistencies. A detector that only says a document contradicts itself is of limited use. Reviewers need the exact passages that clash, and research on extracting that evidence with language models has been thin. The authors introduce new, more complete metrics for judging evidence extraction itself.

Their framework, redact and retry with constrained filtering, masks parts of the document and retries extraction under tighter limits, which substantially improves evidence quality over other prompting methods. Strong experimental results back the approach. A new semi synthetic data set for evaluating evidence extraction is released with the work, under a record title that also adds improved metrics to the evidence extraction claim.
arxiv-2601-02827:
Xufei Zheng and five co authors design a sixth generation mobile physical layer that is AI native. With learning modules optimized together across the whole transmit and receive chain rather than one block at a time. Traditional designs separate source and channel coding, modulation, precoding, and detection, and information barriers between the blocks block end to end gains. Cooperative control agents coordinate the joint design.

On the uplink, learned joint source channel coding is fused with modulation. On the downlink, learned modulation joins precoding and the matching data detection. Several enhancement mechanisms are proposed, including a cross layer modulation method with theory behind it that widens the search for better signal constellations, and a utility oriented precoder construction. In that design the decoder of channel state feedback stops merely reconstructing the original state information and directly generates the precoder the transmitter should use.
arxiv-2601-03027:
Sindhuja Chaduvula and four co-authors target a failure mode of preference training: models rewarded for fluent, confident answers can learn to hallucinate. Their method, F-DPO, extends Direct Preference Optimization with one extra ingredient, a binary factuality label for each response. It uses those labels in two ways at once.

First, a label-flipping step repairs preference pairs so the chosen answer is never the less factual one. Second, a factuality-aware margin gives more weight to pairs with clear correctness gaps, and the method reduces to ordinary DPO when both answers share the same factuality. Across seven open-weight models, F-DPO improved factuality and cut hallucination rates, in one case reducing them fivefold while also raising factuality scores.
arxiv-2601-03627:
Jean Seo and seven co-authors introduce EPAG, a benchmark for judging how well language models handle the pre-consultation stage of medical care. Before meeting a doctor, a patient describes their history and symptoms, and a good system should follow diagnostic guidelines from that account. EPAG tests models both by comparing their interview output with guidelines and by checking final diagnoses.

One striking result: small open models fine-tuned on a well-curated, task-specific dataset beat frontier models at this job. More patient history did not always improve diagnosis, either. The language of the consultation also changed the dialogue's character. The team released the dataset and pipeline openly. For clinics, the lesson is that careful local tuning can outrank raw model size.
arxiv-2601-03927:
Vrinda Dhingra, Amita Sharma, and Anubha Goel review modeling approaches for index tracking, the passive investing strategy that copies a market index's performance as closely and cheaply as possible. The field's methods fall into three families: optimization-based models, statistical models, and machine learning approaches driven by data. The review weighs the strengths and limits of each family side by side.

An empirical study on the S and P 500 dataset compares the families head to head. An optimization model based on tracking error volatility tracked most precisely. A statistical co-integration model gave the strongest return-risk balance. A deep neural network variant performed competitively with notably low turnover and high computational efficiency, as reported. Fund designers can use the comparison to pick a modeling style that matches their priority, precision, balance, or trading cost.
arxiv-2601-04027:
Xumin Jiang and Jiongduo Xie study how area-minimising surfaces of high codimension behave far out in hyperbolic space. The question comes from a problem posed by F. H. Lin. The surfaces are described as locally rectifiable currents, a general way to handle irregular shapes.

Jiang and Xie prove boundary regularity at infinity, meaning the surfaces stay well behaved near their far boundary when viewed with the standard Euclidean metric. They also find a built-in limit: for odd-dimensional minimal surfaces, high-order smoothness can fail. Whether it fails depends on the shape of the far boundary itself. The work extends the far-field theory for such surfaces in curved space.
arxiv-2601-04127:
Leandro Stival, Ricardo da Silva Torres, and Helio Pedrini propose learning from satellite image time series one pixel at a time. Satellites pour out Earth observation data, yet most deep models read whole images or whole series at once. The team instead turns each pixel's vegetation index history into a two-dimensional recurrence plot.

Their method, PIMC, pairs those plots with the satellite imagery in a multimodal contrastive setup that needs no labels. Plots are built from three vegetation indices that track plant growth over time. Tests cover pixel-level forecasting and sorting on the PASTIS data set, plus land cover sorting on EuroSAT. The three authors report that two-dimensional forms sharpen feature extraction and that contrastive training lifts quality for both views, beating current methods on the tasks tried.
arxiv-2601-04327:
Erel Kaplan and six co-authors present ParaCodex, an autonomous coding agent built to write parallel programs that are both correct and fast, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The hard target is OpenMP GPU offload, where moving data on and off the graphics processor dominates results and unaided AI agents often produce brittle code.

ParaCodex wraps a Codex-based agent in a working engineer's routine. Find the hot spots first, plan the data movement explicitly, gate every version on correctness, then refine using real profiles from the target hardware. Translating serial processor kernels on three benchmark suites, it succeeded on every valid kernel tried but five excluded ones. Beating the reference OpenMP versions in most cases with several-fold average speedups on two suites. A second test, translating CUDA code to OpenMP, kept high compile and validation rates.
arxiv-2601-04827:
Pauli strings sit at the heart of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, but computing them on ordinary processors grows exponentially harder with each added qubit. Tran Xuan Hieu Le and 4 co-authors present PACOX in a 2026 paper, the first dedicated FPGA accelerator for Pauli string computation. An FPGA is a chip whose circuits can be rewired for one specialised job.

PACOX encodes the work in a compact binary form, using XOR steps to permute indexes and tally phases. Its parallel, pipelined processing element cluster exploits that structure for speed. Removing the Pauli string bottleneck would let hybrid algorithms scale to larger quantum systems, where classical support costs currently cap what researchers can attempt.
arxiv-2601-04927:
Wei-Yang Lai and Hong-Ying Jin calculate the masses of exotic tetraquark states in a 2026 particle physics paper. Tetraquarks bind four quarks rather than the usual two or three, and states with quantum numbers 1-+ cannot be ordinary mesons at all. The authors apply QCD sum rules at next-to-leading order, a method that connects quark-level theory to observed particle masses through carefully chosen correlation functions.

Testing compact tetraquark and molecular configurations, they exclude one candidate particle as a tetraquark and suggest it may not exist, matching recent experiments. Several predicted states near a higher mass match another candidate well. Such calculations tell experimentalists which claimed exotic particles deserve belief and where new ones should appear.
arxiv-2601-05127:
Etai Sella and 4 co-authors tackle a homely editing task with diffusion models: pasting an object into a new photograph so it belongs there in a 2026 paper. Text-guided editing gives only coarse control, so they study explicit editing without prompts, in which the user cuts and pastes an object or part of one into a chosen spot. The challenge is keeping the pasted object's identity while harmonizing it with its new surroundings.

Their method, LooseRoPE, manipulates attention inside the diffusion model in a content-aware way for semantic harmonization. Attention maps turn out to carry the information needed to blend the insert naturally. Convincing cut-and-paste editing serves designers and ordinary users alike, since most real photo fixes are placements, not fresh generations.
arxiv-2601-05227:
James Rice sets out a new frame for doubt in data that have shape and that run through time in a 2026 paper. His frame, Stochastic Latent Differential Inference, plants a rule of change with a noise term deep in a model's hidden space. The model in play is a variational autoencoder, a net that packs data down to a short code and builds it back up. Noise in that code lets the model run in smooth time, not just in stiff steps.

Both the drift and the spread of the noise are set by nets, so the doubt is learned from the data at first hand. The aim is doubt that can bend to the task yet keeps a firm math base. A frame that grades its own doubt in a true way can warn a user when a call is built on sand.
arxiv-2601-05427:
Etienne Gauthier and 2 co-authors introduce, in a 2026 paper, a way to detect when players in repeated games drift away from strategic behavior. Their test works online, without fixing the sample size in advance. It builds on e-values, a tool for inference that stays valid at any stopping time.

The method bets against a benchmark, so evidence grows whenever observed payoffs break the expected pattern. Equilibrium play serves as the benchmark, covering Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated forms in one framework. The authors analyze detection times, add procedures that limit false discoveries in large games, and extend the test to stochastic games with changing states.
arxiv-2601-05927:
Yohann Perron and 3 co-authors adapt vision transformers in 2026 to segment ultra-high-resolution images without throwing away either detail or global context. Sliding-window methods lose the big picture, while downsampling loses fine detail. Archaeology, land survey, and pathology images all suffer from that dilemma.

Their method processes each image twice in parallel: small crops at full resolution, and large crops at low resolution. A small set of learnable relay tokens aggregates and propagates features between the two branches. The design plugs into standard transformer backbones and adds under two percent more parameters. Across three ultra-high-resolution benchmarks and the conventional Cityscapes dataset, segmentation accuracy improved consistently, with relative gains up to about fifteen percent reported.
arxiv-2601-06027:
Transparent documents, where readers can hover over text to see the data behind a claim, are the focus of a 2026 paper by Alfonso Piscitelli and 8 co-authors. The authors present a language-model tool that helps writers create such interactive scholarly articles.

Built on Fluid, a programming language that tracks where data came from, the tool finds text fragments that can be computed from data. Numbers, averages, comparisons, and trend words are candidates. It then writes a query that produces the fragment and inserts it into the page, making the claim clickable. Tests on a science-table dataset showed the model often produced expressions matching the intended answers, including on hand-made counterfactual cases.
arxiv-2601-06427:
Guo-Liang Yu and 5 co-authors analyze weak decays of doubly charmed baryons in a 2026 particle physics paper. These heavy particles contain two charm quarks. In semileptonic decays, one charm quark changes through the weak force, emitting a lepton and a neutrino, and the rates depend on form factors describing the transition.

The team performs the first systematic three-point QCD sum rule analysis for transitions from spin one-half to spin three-halves states. All couplings on the particle side and all condensate contributions on the QCD side are included. Form factors computed in the space-like region are extrapolated to the physical time-like region with a fitting function. Predicted decay rates for several Xi-cc and Omega-cc channels deepen understanding of heavy baryon dynamics and inform searches for new physics.
arxiv-2601-06827:
Research by Jinhan Liu and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with PDR. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Detecting pre-training data in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for auditing data privacy and copyright compliance.

Yet it remains challenging in black-box, zero-shot settings where computational resources and training data are scarce. While existing likelihood-based methods have shown promise, they typically aggregate token-level scores using uniform weights, thereby neglecting the inherent information-theoretic dynamics of autoregressive generation. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07027:
Sergey A. Antonyan and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with characterizations of g g -ANR spaces and inverse limits. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Antonyan, Aura Lucina Kantún-Montiel, Jesús Eduardo Mata-Cano, Armando Mata-Romero. We prove that, for a compact group G G. A metrizable G G -space is a G G -ANR under the following asumptions.

If it dominates a G G -ANR space through a fine G G -homotopy equivalence. If it is G G -homotopy dense in a G G -ANR. If it contains a G G -ANR as a G G -homotopy dense subset; if. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07127:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Delong Jia(贾德龙) and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers hierarchical structure of the open cluster NGC 752 astropy ( 2 ; 1. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The structure of open clusters provides key insights into their evolution and the dynamics of the Milky Way. Using Gaia DR3 data, we applied a hierarchical clustering algorithm to the open cluster NGC 752 based.

On the kinematical information and identified four substructures corresponding to different stages of disintegration. The cluster exhibits a pronounced signature of mass segregation. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07327:
An arXiv preprint from 2026 deals with how to predict creativity ratings from written narratives. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. This tutorial paper provides a step-by-step workflow for building and analysing semantic networks from short creative texts.

The authors introduce and compare two widely used text-to-network approaches: word co-occurrence networks and textual forma mentis networks (TFMNs). We also show how they can be used in machine learning to predict human creativity ratings. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07527:
Josip Kir Hromatko and colleagues study how electric cars with several motors should share the work of driving. In straight-line driving, the motors together must meet the driver's torque demand. Many splits can meet it, but they use different amounts of battery energy. Choosing the split well saves range. Their 2026 preprint offers a new approach to that allocation problem.

The team approximates electric motor losses with higher-order polynomials that have special structure. Those polynomials are pseudoconvex, a property that makes optimization easier and more reliable. With losses modeled this way, the best torque split can be found cleanly. The paper speaks to vehicle engineers chasing efficiency through software rather than bigger batteries.
arxiv-2601-07627:
Shuzo Izumi takes up a plain-sounding question in geometry: can one solid shape rotate inside another? His 2026 preprint restricts the motion to rotation only, with no sliding. Think of turning a solid object inside a solid box. If rotation is possible at all, the center and direction of the turn may still be tightly restricted.

Naive problems like this can hide sharp mathematical structure. The space of allowed rotations depends on the exact shapes of both polytopes. Izumi studies those constraints for one polytope placed inside another. The question links geometry, motion planning, and the theory of configuration spaces. Readers who enjoy concrete problems with rigorous answers will find a careful treatment of when turning is possible and around which points.
arxiv-2601-07727:
N. K. Patra and colleagues use symbolic regression to find formulas linking neutron star traits to nuclear matter. The equation of state of dense matter inside neutron stars remains uncertain. At densities above nuclear saturation, interactions grow complex and exotic matter like hyperons may appear. Their 2026 preprint searches for the relations between matter properties and star properties. The focus is on nonlinear links and interdependencies.

Symbolic regression searches for readable formulas rather than black-box predictions. A readable formula shows which matter traits drive a star's radius or mass. That insight helps observers plan measurements and theorists test models. Neutron star data from gravitational waves and X-ray timing keep improving. The paper speaks to astrophysicists who want interpretable machine learning, not just accurate fits.
arxiv-2601-07927:
Sourav Maji and Abhishek Chowdhury count the quantum states of certain black holes with computational algebra. Their note explores algebraic geometry techniques for computing a helicity trace index. The index is the fourteenth one, for four-charge, one-eighth BPS configurations of pure D-branes. These configurations are dual to dyonic black holes built from D1, D5, momentum, and KK monopole charges. The work appears as a 2026 preprint note.

Microstate counting checks whether string theory reproduces black hole entropy. Each counted index compares a brane construction against the black hole it mirrors. Computational algebraic geometry makes counts feasible that hand calculation cannot reach. The note focuses on pure D-brane systems in type IIA superstring theory. It serves string theorists who test duality with exact numbers. Short and technical, it adds one more verified case to the counting program.
arxiv-2601-08027:
Deepak Deo, Daniel McIntosh, and five co-authors study galaxies that have just stopped forming stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at recently quenched ellipticals, a short phase between active star formation and quiet old age. What shuts star formation down in these systems is still not known.

The team studies neutral hydrogen gas and star formation across many wavelengths. Their sample holds 155 recently quenched ellipticals, plus earlier precursor and later descendant systems for comparison. By tracking gas content across these stages, readers can see how a galaxy changes as quenching begins and ends. The work helps test ideas about why star formation fades.
arxiv-2601-09427:
Sung-Soo Byun, Yeong-Gwang Jung, and Guido Mazzuca deform a classic law of random matrix theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies a q-deformed random unitary ensemble tied to the little-q Laguerre weight. The ensemble is a discrete cousin of the classical Laguerre ensemble.

In a double scaling regime, where q shrinks as the matrix size grows, the authors derive the limiting spectral distribution. The limit gives a q-deformation of the Marchenko-Pastur law, which describes eigenvalue spreads of sample covariance matrices. Deformed laws like this link random matrices to combinatorics and quantum groups. The result pins down exactly how the classic curve bends under the deformation.
arxiv-2601-09527:
Jonathan Knoop and Hendrik Holtmann write a practical guide to running language models in-house. Their 2026 arXiv paper shows how small and medium firms can do private LLM inference on consumer Blackwell graphics cards. Many firms want an alternative to cloud APIs, which raise privacy worries.

Dedicated cloud GPU rentals improve privacy but cost steadily and give limited guarantees. Professional on-premise cards such as the A100 and H100 are too pricey for most small firms. Consumer cards offer a middle path. The guide weighs cost against control for firms that must keep their data at home.
arxiv-2601-10227:
Lorenzo Campioni links split counts to semigroups of counts. A split of a count into parts can be refined if a part splits more. Some splits admit no such step with all parts distinct. Those are named unrefinable splits.

Campioni ties them to count semigroups. Those are sets of counts closed under sums, with gaps. He reads splits as Young diagrams with hook sets. That read gives new tests for when a split is unrefinable. Gaps in the semigroup map to parts that are absent. The link lets him sort splits with the most absent parts.
arxiv-2601-10327:
Suzuyo Komeda and co authors speed up a deep scan of live tissue. The scan is optical coherence tomography, or OCT. It maps tissue by light bounce in depth. A dynamic form tracks how cells move. The rig used here sweeps a full field at once.

Full field scans yield sharp maps but vast data. That bulk makes streams slow and holds back fast work. The team use a neural net to cut that load. It forms sharp dynamic maps at high speed. The aim is high throughput scans that clinics and labs can run live.
arxiv-2601-10627:
Rajdeep Mazumdar, Kalyan Malakar, and Kalyan Bhuyan test a modified theory of gravity against fresh survey data. The theory, called f(Q, L_m) gravity, changes the rules that link matter and spacetime. They use a nonlinear form of it to describe the late universe. The aim is to match how cosmic expansion speeds up today.

They check the model against baryon acoustic oscillation data from DESI DR2, a major galaxy survey release. Such data pin down the expansion history of the universe. A model that fits them stays in the race to explain cosmic acceleration. The paper shows how new survey data can sort rival gravity theories.
arxiv-2601-10827:
Simin Liu and co-authors plan robot manipulation that uses contact everywhere, not just at the fingertips. Humans lean, brace, and slide objects with whole arms. Contact-rich manipulation copies that freedom. State-of-the-art model-based planners mostly check feasibility: can a motion work at all? They rarely chase optimality, the best motion.

The authors aim for approximately optimal plans over long horizons. Their planner works on a graph of reachable sets in the plane. Contact makes dynamics rough and nonsmooth, so planning must respect geometry at each touch. Near-optimal contact plans could let robots handle clutter and heavy objects with a natural ease that fingertip-only control cannot match.
arxiv-2601-10927:
Todd Cochrane, Andrew Granville, and Junren Zheng study mixed incomplete character sums of rational functions. Character sums are sums over number-theoretic symbols that detect patterns in whole numbers. Graham and Ringrose proved strong bounds for such sums over intervals. Their result held when the modulus was squarefree and sufficiently smooth, with the interval long enough.

The new work treats mixed sums built from rational functions, with smooth moduli. Incomplete sums, cut off mid-range, are the hard and useful kind. Sharp bounds feed cryptography, where character sums guard security, and analytic number theory, where they count primes in disguise. The paper extends a classic line of estimates to a wider family of sums.
arxiv-2601-11327:
Agata Zywot, Xinyi Chen, and Maarten de Rijke test teams of small AI agents. Their 2026 report asks if such teams can beat one big model. The test bed is GAIA, a benchmark of hard general tasks. The agents are Qwen3 models with tools in hand.

Model sizes in the tests run from 4B to 32B. The team varies three things to see what counts most. One is scale, the raw size of the model used. One is explicit thinking, from none to planner-only to full. The third is tool use: search, code, and mind-maps. Tool use gave the largest and most steady gains. That finding favors smart setups over raw size alone.
arxiv-2601-11627:
Hassan Ugail, Jan Ritch-Frel, and Irina Matuzava authenticate historical drawings. Their 2026 preprint uses handcrafted features with one-class learning. Attribution of works on paper is a persistent challenge. Reference corpora are often small for a given artist.

Style in drawings lives in line and limited tonal range. The team builds a verification-based computational framework. One-class autoencoders learn from genuine works alone. Their inputs are a compact set of handcrafted features. Those features are interpretable, not black-box embeddings. The system judges if a new drawing fits the artist. Cultural heritage gains a tool for disputed sheets. Small corpora are the norm the design respects.
arxiv-2601-12027:
Raghav Bongole, Tobias J. Oechtering, and Mikael Skoglund push a classic bound in statistics to a wider case. The Fano bound limits how well any method can do. Their case is interactive, where data come from acts that change as learning runs.

Past bounds in this case deal with mean risk. Tail risk, the odds of a very bad result, was less well tracked. They swap the hard pass-fail event for a random one-bit score tied to the loss. That swap lets the bound cover tail goals for a broad class of losses.
arxiv-2601-12227:
Yuanyun Zhang, Han Zhou, Li Feng, Yilin Hong, and Shi Li learn health traits over time from records plus wearable data. Models trained on health records do well on many clinic tasks. Yet records are sparse, irregular, and driven by visits.

Wearables give dense, steady body signals, but lack labels and clinical sense. Joining the two could give traits that are both rich and grounded. Such traits could aid long-run risk and trend calls. The work builds that joint learning frame.  Joint traits could track slow shifts in health state.
arxiv-2601-12527:
Richard Liu, Itai Lang, and Rana Hanocka work on mesh deformation in computer graphics. The classic setup uses handles: a user drags a few control points and the shape follows. Classic methods give precise, fast control of the edit. The catch is that the user must know in advance where to place the handles.

The map from handle placement to final shape is often unintuitive. It is also non semantic, meaning handles do not line up with parts a user thinks about. The team propose deep feature deformation weights as a learned fix. Learned weights could spread a sparse edit in a way that respects the shape. That would let artists edit by meaning, not by trial and error.
arxiv-2601-13227:
Laura Dietz and co-authors ask a sharp test design question. Tools that write from sources are now judged by AI judges. Fact bit tests, called nugget tests, sit in both the judge seat and in the tools. That dual role can hide a leak.

The team asks how much a tool gains if it can peek at judge secrets. Such peeks would be a form of inside knowledge. If gains are large, scores may flatter tools that game the test. The study probes that risk head on. For teams that build or buy such tools, the work is a call to guard test facts as they would guard exam keys.
arxiv-2601-13327:
Po-Yu Liang, Tibo Duran, and Jun Bai design peptide binders with no need for a shape guess first. A peptide is a short chain of amino acids. Binders that grip a set target have wide use in drugs and bio chem. Many past tools first guess the 3D shape of the pair. That step adds bulk and trims the range of chains they can make.

Their tool, PepEDiff, works from the target's chain and its pocket sites alone. It spreads a protein embedding in a diffusion run to draft new binder chains. By skip of the shape step, it can roam a wider set of chains. For drug teams, a fast binder draft tool has clear worth.
arxiv-2601-13727:
Bart Jacobs works on certifying the results of a program checker called VeriFast in 2026. VeriFast checks that C and Rust code meets strict correctness claims. It runs each function on its own, guided by notes the user adds. Those notes state what must hold before and after each step, in separation logic.

Jacobs adds a path to certify VeriFast output in a foundational way. The method uses hinted mirroring to rebuild the proof in a trusted base. Users then need not trust the whole tool, just the small checker. Stronger proof chains matter for safety-critical code.
arxiv-2601-13927:
Yousef Sadegheih, Dorit Merhof, and Pratibha Kumari adapt brain lesion models to new scan types over time in 2026. Brain lesion segmentation from multi-modal MRI often assumes a fixed set of scan types. It also assumes predefined pathologies, which real cohorts break. Continual learning offers a path, but with hard limits.

Past methods impose a maximum modality configuration on the model. Or they suffer severe forgetting in buffer-free settings, with no stored old data. The team targets modality-agnostic, domain-incremental segmentation. Models that adapt without forgetting could serve hospitals with varied scanners.
arxiv-2601-14027:
Junqi Liu and a large team use a general coding agent as a formal math reasoner in 2026. Agentic systems now dominate formal theorem proving, with strong performance. They coordinate multiple models and tools to build proofs. Existing approaches often rely on task-specific pipelines and trained formal provers.

That reliance limits flexibility and reproducibility, the team argues. Their Numina-Lean-Agent is an open and general agentic reasoning system. It directly uses a general coding agent for formal mathematics in Lean. An open system lets other teams test, copy, and extend the approach.
arxiv-2601-14327:
A team at YuanLab.ai tackles a training bottleneck in this 2026 paper. Their models are Mixture-of-Experts large language models. Such models route each input to a few expert parts, so they score well with fewer active parameters. Pre-training them is still a major cost, though. Many experts sit underused, and training runs at low efficiency.

The team built LAEP, a layer-adaptive expert pruning algorithm for the pre-training stage. Pruning cuts experts that add little. Layer-adaptive means each layer is pruned by its own needs, not one global rule. The stated goal is faster, leaner pre-training without giving up the gains that make these models strong.
arxiv-2601-14627:
Tobias Schwaigert and a team of eleven co-authors strain a crystal into a new state in this 2026 paper. Epitaxial strain is a powerful means to engineer emergent phenomena in thin films and heterostructures. Their material is KTaO3, a cubic perovskite in bulk form. Grown commensurate to SrTiO3 substrates, the films feel an in-plane strain of minus two percent.

Under that strain, the team demonstrates ferroelectricity above room temperature. Ferroelectric materials hold a switchable electric polarization, useful for memory and sensors. The strained films become a highly tunable ferroelectric. Readers get a recipe for turning a non-ferroelectric bulk crystal into a working ferroelectric film.
arxiv-2601-14727:
Shuxing Fang, Ruijian Han, Yuanhang Luo, and Yiming Xu survey a classic ranking model in this 2026 paper. The Bradley-Terry model turns pairwise comparisons into ratings. It is widely used wherever items are ranked by head-to-head results, from sports to product tests. The article surveys recent progress in the model and its extensions.

The authors focus on statistical and computational aspects. They emphasize the regime in which both the number of objects and the volume of comparisons tend to infinity. That regime matches large-scale applications, where millions of comparisons feed the ratings. Readers get theory, algorithms, and applications in one review of a workhorse model.
arxiv-2601-15227:
Rafael Boto, Karim Elyaouti, and co-authors scan a two-Higgs model for signs of broken symmetry between matter and antimatter. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the complex two-Higgs-doublet model. The focus is the known 125 GeV Higgs boson and how it couples to fermions.

Large CP-violating couplings would be a major clue about the universe's matter excess. The authors explore the model's parameter space with machine learning tools. Their kit includes an evolutionary strategy algorithm and a novelty reward. Those modern tools hunt for rare corners that older scans might well miss.
arxiv-2601-15527:
Alejandro González Nevado works on Eulerian polynomials in a 2026 arXiv paper. In the classic one-variable case, these polynomials are palindromic. Their coefficients read the same forward and backward. An identity behind that fact is well known. González Nevado lifts that identity to the multivariate setting. The polynomials then depend on several variables at once.

Nice combinatorial identities follow from the generalization, he notes. They can be read off from the polynomial relation itself. The proof also uses a bijection between permutations. Such identities give exact counts for permutation patterns. Palindromicity is a strong symmetry, and it often hints at deeper structure. For combinatorics readers, the paper extends a classical result in a clean direction.
arxiv-2601-15627:
Zechun Hu, Renming Song, and Li Wang study reinforced random walks in a 2026 arXiv paper. In an edge-reinforced walk, each crossing makes an edge more likely to be crossed again. The reinforcement here is linear, with a strength parameter. The walk lives on the half-line of nonnegative integers. Edges start with weights that grow with position. For large positions, the weight follows a power of the position times a log power.

The authors study the walk's limit behavior. That means where the walk ends up spending its time as steps pile up. The work was motivated by a 2021 article they cite. Reinforced walks model memory in motion, from animal foraging to network traffic. Limit results tell us when memory traps a walker and when it still roams.
arxiv-2601-15827:
Kuntal Banerjee and three co-authors study symmetry in torus dynamics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their maps are affine automorphisms of the two-torus. Each map combines a linear part with a shift. The linear part is a matrix, and the shift is a fixed vector. All arithmetic wraps around modulo the integers. Reversibility asks whether a map can be undone by a symmetry of the system.

Strong reversibility adds stricter demands on that symmetry. The authors study both notions for these maps. Reversible systems appear in physics, where time reversal is a basic question. Torus maps are simple enough to classify yet rich enough to matter. A full account of when they are reversible gives dynamicists a clean reference case for more complex systems.
arxiv-2601-16027:
Yiran Qiao and five coauthors study risk in live streams. Their 2026 preprint notes that scams and planned bad acts can build up bit by bit. Harm can also show up again in streams that look unlinked at first. A check of one stream alone can miss that wider past. The team links proof across sessions to catch such risk.

The method pairs a large language model with search over past cases. When a new stream raises doubt, the system pulls in old proof from other streams. Past plots and tricks then help judge the new case. This past proof is the core gain of the work. It aims to help sites spot slow, spread out scams that single checks would miss.
arxiv-2601-16127:
Alphaeus Dmonte and three coauthors join tongue tuned models to cut retrain costs. Their 2026 preprint deals with large language models tuned for set tasks in many tongues. To add data or a new tongue, teams oft retrain the whole model. That full run costs much time and compute. The team tests if tuned models can be merged in place.

Merging joins the weights of models tuned for each tongue. A merged model may hold all tongues with no fresh full run. The test checks scores after merge on each tongue. Low cost merge would ease care of such models. It would also speed the add of new tongues.
arxiv-2601-16227:
Sneha Pradhan and three coauthors weigh neutron star traits in a new gravity frame. Their 2026 preprint uses NICER views of neutron stars. The frame is symmetric teleparallel gravity with a form set by a value Q. Three forms of that frame are tested side by side. They are the straight, log and growth forms of the Q term.

Bayes tools weigh which traits fit the NICER views best. Star mass and size shift with the gravity form in play. Tight fits test if the new frame can match real stars. They also bound how far the frame may stray from known gravity. The work joins sky views to gravity theory.
arxiv-2601-16727:
Julian Block, Andreas Könsgen, Jens Dede, and Anna Förster measure tiny power draws with care. Small web-linked gear must run for months on one cell. To plan that life, teams must gauge sleep-state draws. Those draws are far too small for plain tools. Their 2026 preprint tests fine gauge tricks on a real node.

Their test case is MoleNet, a net of small sense nodes. Bench tools like scopes blur at such low draws. The team weighs which tricks stay true at that scale. Sharp gauges help teams fix leaks in code and gear. Long cell life then serves farms, woods, and smart homes.
arxiv-2601-16927:
Łucja Kipczak and a large team probe how spin and lattice moves tie in a layered crystal. The crystal CrCl3 stacks in sheets that cleave with ease. Its spins line up in an anti-parallel form. Such ties shape how 2D magnets act and store. Their 2026 preprint reads the crystal's hums with split light beams.

Light reads show how hums shift with spin state. Glow and soak reads add more views of the tie. Thick flakes and bulk forms both come in view. Strong ties let fields or strain steer spin states. That steer could serve thin magnet tools in years ahead.
arxiv-2601-17127:
H. Cortés-Muñoz and a team of eight co-authors map gas clouds round far galaxies at cosmic noon. That far gas, the CGM, feeds and takes from its galaxy. Its size and flow traits stay hard to pin down. Their 2026 preprint uses pairs of quasars as twin probes. Shade lines of triply-stripped carbon mark the gas. Twin lines let the team gauge how far the gas stays in step.

Step scales tell if the gas is smooth or clumped. Clumps point to flows in or out of the galaxy. Such maps test how galaxies ate and grew then. Cosmic noon is when star birth peaked most.
arxiv-2601-17327:
Francisco J. G. de Oliveira and three co-authors study a risk where wind farms meet power lines. A turbine wake is a zone of churned air behind the blades. That churn can shake overhead conductors. Shake builds fatigue damage over time. Rules for safe gaps vary by country. In the United Kingdom, lines should stay at least three rotor widths away.

The team measures how wakes change the rate of fatigue build-up. Proof like that can firm up rules that now rest on caution. Too small a gap risks line failure. Too large a gap wastes land near farms. Their work helps planners set gaps with data in hand.
arxiv-2601-17427:
Cristopher Erazo, Santiago Acevedo, and Alessandro Ingrosso measure the Hopfield model in a new way. The Hopfield model is a spin system used in physics, learning, and brain science. The team uses Binary Intrinsic Dimension. That is a geometric measure built for binary data. It reads the true shape of data that lives in bits.

With it, they characterize the phases of the model. They also track the transitions between phases. The measure proves robust where older tools strain. A clear phase map helps all three fields that share this model. It shows where memory works and where it breaks. Neural networks with Hopfield roots gain a sharper design lens.
arxiv-2601-17527:
Yu Wang and Xiangchen Liu study how language model agents update beliefs. Models now act as economic agents in tests and tools. They read mixed signals, some personal and some aggregate. How they weigh those signals was opaque. The authors run experiments with models cast as households and firm heads. They build a Behavioral Kalman Filter frame to score the updates.

A Kalman filter is a classic tool for belief updates under noise. The behavioral form adds human-like bias. Scores show if models overreact or lag. That matters as models take real economic roles. Forecast and policy tests need agents whose belief rules are known. This work makes those rules visible.
arxiv-2601-17727:
X. C. Hu, H. Y. Yuan, and X. R. Wang study how two magnetic skyrmions interact. Skyrmions are tiny swirling spin textures. Moving many of them is key to racetrack memory and logic devices. Their mutual forces were poorly understood. The team studies skyrmion pairs in chiral magnetic films. They find the interaction has intrinsic, anisotropic traits.

Anisotropic means the force depends on direction, not just distance. Device layouts must respect that direction sense. Wrong assumptions could jam or scatter stored bits. A clear force law lets engineers space skyrmions with care. It also informs how pulses should push them. The work is basic physics with direct device stakes.
arxiv-2601-18327:
M. Y. Abd-Rabbou, Irfan Siddique, Saeed Haddadi, and Cong-Feng Qiao design a repeater chain for moving energy by quantum means over long range. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum energy teleportation. The protocol can activate local vacuum energy by spending pre-shared entanglement plus classical messages. Its practice is blocked by locality: in gapped systems, ground-state correlations fade fast with distance. That fade caps how far one step can reach. The authors propose a scalable repeater architecture for gapped systems.

Repeaters broke the same wall for quantum communication. A chain of short hops could carry the energy effect across a long span. The work extends a striking protocol toward real distances.
arxiv-2601-19327:
Boon Suan Ho generalizes a key entropy bound used in a famous sets problem. The union closed sets conjecture asks whether some element lies in at least half the sets of a union closed family. A lemma by Boppana, tying the entropy of a squared chance to the entropy itself, became a key tool in recent progress.

Ho extends that inequality past its first form. The bound involves the golden ratio, a quirk that hints at hidden structure. Stronger entropy tools may push the long open conjecture closer to a proof, or at least narrow where a counterexample could hide.
arxiv-2601-19827:
Mahdi Astaraki and Mohammad Arshi Saloot test when repeated retrieval helps a language model answer hard questions. Retrieval-augmented generation fetches evidence once, then answers. Iterative variants loop: retrieve, reason, then retrieve again with sharper queries. Scientific multi-hop questions need several linked facts, so looping sounds ideal.

The authors run a diagnostic study in scientific question answering. Surprisingly, the iterative approach can beat setups given ideal evidence. That result challenges the assumption that perfect retrieval is the ceiling. Multi-hop reasoning over sparse, mixed evidence is the stress test here. Knowing when loops pay helps builders spend compute wisely. The work also maps where static retrieval remains enough.
arxiv-2601-20527:
Arpith Kumar proposes thermodynamic consistency as a reliability test for complex Langevin simulations. The method is a promising route around the sign problem in quantum field theories with complex actions, where standard sampling fails. But it can converge to wrong results even when the run looks stable, so trustworthy checks are needed.

Existing diagnostics, like watching drift distributions, are indirect. Kumar argues that checking thermodynamic relations gives a more direct test of whether the output can be believed. A sharper test matters wherever complex Langevin results feed into claims about matter that no experiment can reach.
arxiv-2601-20727:
Victor Ojewale, Harini Suresh, and Suresh Venkatasubramanian ask how large language models can be held to account. Their 2026 paper notes that these models now sit inside big decisions. They help shape choices in health care, finance, jobs, and public services. Yet when a choice goes wrong, there is often no clear record of how it was made.

The authors propose LLM audit trails as a fix. An audit trail is a durable record of the process that others can review later. They frame it as a social and technical mechanism, not just a log file. It is meant to support continuous accountability over time. The paper gives designers and regulators a concrete way to demand a paper trail from AI systems.
arxiv-2601-20927:
Jin Ming Koh and eight co-authors entangle logical qubits without touching the physical ones. Their 2026 paper addresses a core need of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Logical entangling gates are essential for scalable machines. They are limited by the error rates and overheads of physical two-qubit gates and measurements. Every physical operation is a chance for noise to strike. A gate that needs no physical operation would dodge that risk.

The authors present a route to such gates. Logical information lives spread across many physical qubits. Manipulating that encoding cleverly can enact entanglement at the logical level. The physical layer stays idle while the logic moves. Fewer operations mean fewer errors to correct later. The work joins a broad effort to cut the cost of fault tolerance. It reframes a hardware problem as a coding opportunity.
arxiv-2601-21327:
Kael Kemp, Aman Desai, and Paul Jackson forecast how well a planned future collider could measure the Higgs boson. The machine, called FCC-ee, would smash electrons and positrons together. The team studies Higgs particles that decay into pairs of W bosons, which then decay further into light particles.

They estimate the precision on the combined rate of making a Higgs with a Z boson and seeing that decay. Clean lepton-only decays give sharp signals but few events. Knowing the reach in advance helps planners set priorities. It also shows what this decay path can teach about the Higgs itself.
arxiv-2601-21427:
Barium titanate is gaining ground as a material for chips that route light. It responds strongly both to light itself and to electric fields. Recent work has made low-loss waveguides and crisp resonators from thin films of it. Laying those films on an insulator has made the material a serious platform.

Waveguide designs decide how well such a chip can change light from one color to another. Hybrid designs mix the material with other structures to do that job better. The paper reviews and develops such designs. The goals they serve include frequency conversion and quantum photonics, two uses that need light handled with great care.
arxiv-2601-21727:
M. Ambrosch and a large team hunt hot subdwarf stars in a vast set of Gaia spectra using machine learning. Hot subdwarfs are compact, evolved stars near the extreme end of the horizontal branch. They hold clues to late stellar evolution and to the ultraviolet glow of old galaxies.

The team extends earlier work to a far larger sample of low-resolution spectra. Learning methods sort true subdwarfs and their binaries from look-alikes at scale. A bigger, cleaner catalogue sharpens the statistics on how these stars form. That feeds models of binary evolution, since many subdwarfs are thought to be shaped by a companion.
arxiv-2601-21827:
Zhi-Qiu Huang and co-authors use gamma-ray bursts to check how particles gain energy at extreme shock waves. Particle-in-cell simulations are the best tool for studying acceleration at relativistic shocks. But limited computing power constrains them, and the effect of those limits is hard to judge in advance.

The team therefore turns to observations: the late-time X-ray afterglows that bursts leave behind. Those glows carry fingerprints of the acceleration process that simulations must match. Their 2026 preprint draws out what the afterglow data imply for the simulations. This kind of cross-check matters because the same physics is invoked to explain cosmic rays and the brightest explosions in the universe.
arxiv-2601-21927:
Hong Chen and co-authors attack the memory problem that makes long conversations with language models expensive. As a chat grows, the stored key-value cache grows in a straight line, and deployment costs climb with it. Existing compression methods often ignore the structure of multi-turn dialogue.

Simple eviction rules can throw away context that later turns depend on. The team's 2026 preprint proposes SONIC, a learning-based framework that compresses past segments of a conversation into compact Nexus tokens that keep the meaning. Keeping long chats affordable matters for customer support, tutoring. And any service where a model must remember an hour of back-and-forth without renting ever more memory.
arxiv-2601-22227:
William Jarvis and co-authors study black holes hidden behind dust. Active galactic nuclei, or AGN, are luminous galactic centers, but the obscured ones are veiled by gas and dust that block direct views. The team analyzes nearly two hundred X-ray luminous AGN at modest redshifts in the GOODS survey fields.

For each object they build the spectral energy distribution. That is the light output from X-rays to the far infrared. They also classify the host galaxy's shape from its light profile. Their 2026 preprint links the hidden black holes to the galaxies that host them. Obscured growth may be the main way black holes gain mass, so catalogs like this shape the census of cosmic black hole growth.
arxiv-2601-22727:
D. Trotta and a co-author describe a wide-band amplifier built to test tiny photon sensors at picosecond scale, across a wide range of cold. Future physics runs may work silicon photomultipliers at very low heat, in harsh radiation, to time single photons sharply. Their 2026 preprint presents a trans-impedance amplifier for that characterization work.

Full maps of sensor traits across heat levels let teams pick the best trade of performance and survival. The amplifier is the enabling tool for those maps. The work is lab hardware, reported for builders. It serves the next wave of detectors.
arxiv-2601-22827:
Himal Wijekoon, Pierre Hirel, and Anna Grünebohm model, atom by atom, how defects affect switching in a key material. The material is barium titanate, a ferroelectric crystal used in sensors and memory. Its useful traits depend on tiny regions flipping their electric alignment.

One class of defects, called edge dislocations, can pin or guide that flipping. No atom-level picture of their role existed before this kind of modeling. Knowing how defects steer switching could help engineers design faster, tougher electronic parts. The study is modeled at the atomic scale, so it follows individual atoms near the dislocation rather than averaged behavior.
arxiv-2601-23127:
Sung-In Kim and three co-authors study how home-care patients keep control over their own lives. Home-based care brings medical and care services into a patient's living space. It promises care centered on the patient, yet patient agency is often weakly represented in shared planning.

Through interviews with patients, clinicians, and care workers, plus long observation, they trace how agency shows up. Information practices and relationships inside care networks shape that agency. The findings can guide tools and routines that keep patients as decision makers, not bystanders.
arxiv-2601-23227:
Jan Klíma and co-authors present SpinWaveToolkit, an open-source Python package for spin-wave physics. Spin waves are ripples in the magnetization of magnetic materials, key to future fast, low-power devices. The package models them in thin ferromagnetic films and coupled magnetic bilayers.
