It combines classic Kalinikos-Slavin theory with a semi-analytical dynamic-matrix method. Users can compute dispersion relations, group velocities, decay lengths, mode profiles, and equilibrium states. A shared toolkit lets labs compare results and design magnonic devices faster. Static equilibrium magnetization states are among the computed outputs, giving device designers the full operating picture of a film.
arxiv-2602-00127: Tong Zhu and coauthors propose ALIGN, a method that frames multi agent language model reasoning as aligned delegation. Single generation and selection pipelines often underperform on hard reasoning, and ensemble methods sample varied paths but treat candidates apart and offer no proof of gain. In ALIGN, a principal hands a task to several agents that draft solutions under designed incentives, then picks among their outputs. The design creates structured agent interaction while keeping agent and principal goals aligned, and theory shows it improves expected performance under fair comparison.
arxiv-2602-00227: Pranay Nayak and coauthors study signs of coherence in the early states used for quantum work. Standard energy measurements wipe out that coherence and change the dynamics, so they miss its effects. Using a gentle work definition that does not disturb the system, they treat a driven qubit that starts coherent while its drive stays plain. They derive a rule for how work moments evolve, capturing the coherent signature in full.
arxiv-2602-00427: Mouad El Bouchattaoui presents Topological Residual Asymmetry, a geometry based causal test in purely observational data. Many methods pick one even when data are ambiguous or near non-identifiable, where inference is fragile. The test contrasts two cross-fitted clouds after copula standardization. In truth, residuals look independent and form a two dimensional bulk, while in reverse, under low noise, the cloud hugs a one dimensional tube. A persistent homology measure gauges that bulk-tube contrast from MST edge lengths.
arxiv-2602-00927: Yihao Xue and colleagues find that under outcome-only training, out-of-distribution scores keep improving as reasoning length grows, even after in-distribution scores level off. Training models to reason longer is key to solving complex problems, via RL fine-tuning for long chain-of-thought or latent reasoning. Robustness may need a larger budget than in-distribution validation alone suggests. They explain the effect via self-loops inducing stronger built-in bias, reshaping in-distribution-optimal solutions for better transfer, and via shortcut solutions failing out-of-distribution.
arxiv-2602-01227: Zhanming Shen and co-authors push token priority as the bridge from fitting raw data to serving true human use in fine-tuning. Fine-grained token-by-token making is often taught with coarse or flat signals, a grain mismatch that caps alignment. Their position piece recasts fine-tuning as careful reshaping of data odds toward an ideal alignment shape, not plain tuning. It sorts fresh wins into positive priority for noise sifting and signed priority for toxic-mode unlearning, then maps gaps and next steps.
arxiv-2602-01327: Md. Wali Hossain backs a single-field inflation shape built on an inverse exponential curve. That curve fits combined SPA, BK, and DESI data sets well inside the one-sigma band in the tilt-versus-wave plane, giving a plain, observation-safe inflation tale. For post-inflation life and reheating, he adds a steep exponential tail that sleeps through inflation and wakes after. The full curve then dips into a trough, driving field swings and reheating the universe, with a top reheat heat of order 10 to the power 13 GeV.
arxiv-2602-01627: Haishan Ye and Luo Luo explain why adaptive zeroth order optimization works when gradients are costly or unavailable. Adaptive methods rescale gradients using the standard deviation of function values, and they perform in practice when fine tuning large language models, yet theory lagged behind. The authors show that standard deviation tracks the gradient norm with high probability. Building on that link, they analyze methods under smoothness for matrix norms. They give convergence rates and query bounds for both settings, proving faster convergence and better query efficiency than vanilla methods.
arxiv-2602-01727: Junya Koguchi and Tomoki Koriyama give the voting method for pitch a principled study, showing a robust set that lacked review. They ground its power in variance reduction for frequency, and invoke Condorcet's jury theorem for telling voiced from unvoiced sounds. To fix limits they add pre voting lining up, correcting time and frequency biases among models. A greedy method then picks a compact subset of models by error links. On speech, singing and music, the method beats top models in clean settings and keeps detection in noise.
arxiv-2602-02027: Sicheng Shen and colleagues propose light alignment for language model safety via self-review with a single neuron. Current safety alignment relies on post-training methods, which are costly and fail to transfer across models. Lightweight methods lean on prior safety boosts or the model's own powers. Their safety-aware decode method needs cheap training of an expert model and uses a single neuron as a gate, weighing inner powers with outside guidance to preserve utility. It shows gains in training cost and transfer.
arxiv-2602-02127: Zhicheng Jiang and colleagues use photoemission on single-domain Pr4Ni3O10 to untangle bands and pinpoint density-wave states. Density-wave instabilities and multi-orbital physics interplay is key to superconductivity in nickelates, yet features have long been blurred by averaging. Low-energy reconstruction is ruled by nesting between alpha and beta bands. They resolve a gap of about 44 meV on the alpha pocket. They reveal orbital-selective mass renormalization in dz2 states and resolve intrinsic trilayer beta-band splitting. These results sketch a fingerprint for nickelates.
arxiv-2602-02227: Harold Haodong Chen and others present LatentMorph, morphing latent thought into image output. Explicit paradigms decode thoughts into text at steps, with repeated decoding and re-encoding causing inefficiency, information loss, and cognitive mismatch. LatentMorph instead reasons entirely in steady latent spaces through four lightweight parts. A condenser summarizes output states, a translator converts latent thoughts into guidance, a shaper steers next token predictions, and a trained invoker decides when to reason. Experiments show gains over the base model and stated paradigms, with faster inference and lower token use.
arxiv-2602-02427:
Qihao Wen and 5 co-authors pinpoint where a language model's reasoning becomes uncertain, not just whether the final answer is shaky, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Uncertainty quantification estimates how likely an output is to be wrong. For multi-step reasoning, knowing the exact location of doubt could enable targeted fixes during generation.

The study finds that uncertain continuations tend to occur at tokens highly sensitive to small changes in the embeddings of earlier tokens. Embeddings are the model's internal numeric representations of words. Metrics built on that sensitivity located uncertain intermediate steps better than probability-based, sampling-based, and Bayesian baselines. The proposed measures are also simple and efficient to compute. The result gives practitioners a fine-grained warning light inside long reasoning chains.
arxiv-2602-02927:
Yidong Ouyang and 9 co-authors propose fixing output errors without any training in a 2026 paper. Masked diffusion models make text and images by filling masked positions in parallel. Once filled, tokens normally stay fixed, so early mistakes can accumulate through the rest of output.

The authors review earlier self-correction methods and find limits in their training needs and likelihood figures. Their training-free system uses biases already present in pretrained masked diffusion models. It changes no model settings and adds no separate evaluator. Tests cover text-to-image output and multimodal understanding. Output quality improved while using fewer sampling steps. The system also worked across other masked diffusion architectures.
arxiv-2602-03027:
Chao Wang's solo 2026 paper proves a continued fraction identity that a computer program had only conjectured. The identity concerns the constant eight divided by pi squared. It was proposed by the Ramanujan Machine, a system that hunts for math formulas. Its fractions have quartic numerators, making them harder than classic cases.

Wang's proof splits a second-order shift operator into a coupled first-order system. That maps the recurrence onto a cascaded system. The fraction then emerges as the reciprocal of a binomial series. Pincherle's theorem proves absolute convergence, since the minimal solution shrinks toward zero. The work offers a systematic method for checking automated conjectures with high-degree polynomial coefficients.
arxiv-2602-03327:
Rendering new views from very few photos is made robust by Manuel Hofer, together with 2 colleagues, by seeding the scene with a dense learned point cloud. Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting renders in real time and trains quickly, but it depends on accurate camera poses and good initial point clouds. Traditional structure-from-motion pipelines often fail when views are sparse, and learned alternatives can be sensitive to pose or depth errors in difficult scenes.

Their method uses a reference-free point cloud estimation network for dense initialization. Regularization then mitigates geometric inaccuracies through uncertainty-guided depth supervision, normal consistency, and depth warping losses. Experiments across four standard datasets, including Tanks and Temples and MipNeRF360, reached state-of-the-art performance. The approach targets practical capture settings where photographers cannot circle a scene densely.
arxiv-2602-03527:
Logic neural networks learn raw logic operations directly, which makes them fast at inference and easy to run on hardware. Lino Gerlach and 4 co-authors introduce WARP logic networks in a 2026 paper, a gradient-based framework for learning combinations of hardware-native logic blocks. Earlier logic networks were costly to train, redundant, or stuck with approximate gradients.

WARP uses a Walsh relaxation to train probabilistic logic smoothly, then returns to exact discrete behavior for inference. The authors show it yields the most parameter-efficient exact representation of Boolean functions, with several prior methods as special cases. Learnable thresholding, residual initialization, and stochastic smoothing speed convergence. Experiments show faster training and clean scaling to deeper networks and wider inputs.
arxiv-2602-03827:
When a network link fails, routers must reroute instantly using only local information. Matthias Bentert and Stefan Schmid settle when perfect resilience is achievable in a 2026 paper. Perfect resilience means every packet still reaches its target whenever source and target remain connected after the failures. A 2012 result showed perfection is not always possible, but the boundary was unknown.

The authors give a complete characterization of the perfectly resilient instances. From it they derive a linear-time test for whether an instance qualifies, and an algorithm that computes working rerouting rules whenever they exist. The rules are simple skipping rules, following an ordered priority list per incoming port and skipping failed links. Intriguingly, these simple rules prove as powerful as any general rerouting scheme here.
arxiv-2602-03927:
Ahmed Abouelkomsan and 1 co-author let a neural network decide when an exotic liquid turns to crystal. Fractional quantum Hall liquids are strange electron states in strong magnetic fields. Their 2026 paper introduces MagNet, a self-attention wavefunction trained only by minimizing energy from the underlying physics.

One architecture describes both the liquid and the electron crystal, treating them on equal footing. Across strong Landau-level mixing, the network discovered both ground states on its own. No training data or built-in physics knowledge was supplied. The result advertises first-principles AI as a tool for strongly interacting matter where intuition runs thin.
arxiv-2602-04027:
Unusual access patterns can betray an intruder inside a company network. Pratyush Uppuluri and 2 co-authors model enterprise directory access as a graph and hunt anomalies with a consensus-Bayesian method in a 2026 paper. Users act as agents and directories as topics in an opinion-dynamics simulation.

Malicious behavior enters as logical perturbations breaking the network's structural norms. Opinion variance, scaled against theory, flags the disturbance. A Bayesian score, updated over time from static and online priors, quantifies suspicion. Simulations on synthetic access graphs showed the method catches logical inconsistencies and stays robust as the network changes.
arxiv-2602-04527:
Edouard Heitzmann proposes a new way to audit a complex voting method in a 2026 paper on Meek Single Transferable Vote elections. Risk-limiting audits check reported results by recounting a small sample of ballots, but transferable vote rules depend on the order of eliminations and elections.

Heitzmann represents all possible election and elimination sequences as a graph. Before the audit, officials fix one subgraph, a chosen portion of that graph. The audit then only needs statistical evidence that the true sequence stayed inside it. This makes the check flexible and independent of chronology. The approach could bring strong audit guarantees to a voting rule that has resisted general methods.
arxiv-2602-04827:
Wu-Rong Jian and 7 co-authors mix atomistic simulation with machine learning to grasp strength in refractory alloys in a 2026 materials study. These multi-element alloys promise superb high-temperature strength, but their complex make-up hides how plastic deformation actually works.

The team computed local slip resistances for edge and screw dislocations across a dozen equal-share alloys on their main slip planes. Machine learning then linked those resistances to material traits. Raising the share of one crystal-structure family past half sharply lowered several resistance measures. Elastic anisotropy and lattice distortion also mattered. Mixing an autoencoder with a random forest model found the dominant factors. A dislocation-based model built on these insights predicted yield stress well.
arxiv-2602-05027:
Sparse autoencoders have become a loved tool for peering inside language and vision models, but audio models had been left out. Georgii Aparin and 7 co-authors fill that gap in this 2026 paper, accepted at EACL 2026. They trained the autoencoders on each encoder layer of two leading audio models, Whisper and HuBERT.

The learned features proved steady, with over half surviving retraining with varied random seeds, and rebuild quality held up. Features caught both broad sound traits and set events, from background noise to laughter and whispering. Ideas could be erased by removing only about a fifth to a quarter of the features. Steering features cut Whisper's false speech hits by 70 percent with almost no cost to transcription accuracy. Some features even tracked human brain activity while people listened to speech.
arxiv-2602-05427:
Light beams can pick up a shift called a geometric phase as they pass through optical parts, and the cause of that shift depends on the setup. Kristina Frizyuk, Evgenii Menshikov, and Mauro Spera wrote a tutorial article that sorts out these ideas for small light-shaping structures known as metaatoms. The article focuses on how structured light, such as beams that twist, interacts with such tiny structures.

Rather than report a new experiment, the authors explain the math in plain steps and compare this setting with older cases from structured-light optics. They show that phase rules that look alike can rest on quite different geometry underneath. The piece is meant as a bridge for readers who know optics but find the formal language of geometric phases hard to follow. It gives them worked, lab-relevant examples to anchor the theory.
arxiv-2602-05527:
Labeled microscopy images are scarce, so models that learn from unlabeled images first could help locate proteins in cells. Ben Isselmann, Dilara Göksu, and Andreas Weinmann test how well self-supervised vision transformers carry across microscopy domains with different stains and channel setups. They build image embeddings with three DINO backbones, pretrained on ImageNet, the Human Protein Atlas, and OpenCell itself.

A supervised classification head is trained on OpenCell labels, using each embedding set in turn. All three pretrained models transferred well to the new domain. The atlas-pretrained model, which saw microscopy data at scale, did best, slightly ahead of the OpenCell-trained model. The authors conclude that domain-relevant pretraining generalizes to related but distinct data sets. That finding matters for labs whose labeled data are too small to train deep models from scratch. The preprint has not yet been peer reviewed.
arxiv-2602-06027:
New cosmic microwave background data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, joined with Planck, sharpen the test of an inflation model with a non-zero vacuum expectation value. Dos Santos and four co-authors set fresh limits on that value's scale, finding lower values fit the higher spectral index the joint data favour. They also fold in recent BICEP/Keck polarisation data.

A lattice simulation of the inflaton over the first few e-folds finds localised, near-spherical lumps much like oscillons. These could source gravitational waves and black holes formed in the early universe. Wave amplitude sits within detector reach, but frequency lands near the gigahertz edge, far from expected bands. A reheating coupling is also estimated, with lower scale values fitting the full allowed temperature range. The paper ties fresh sky data to the universe's first moments and their possible echoes.
arxiv-2602-06127:
Pruning trims unneeded weights from large language models, but most methods cut along one axis only: depth or width. Bruno Lopes Yamamoto and 9 co-authors present MoP, short for Mixture of Pruners, which tries both at each step. One branch prunes layers, the other prunes width, and the better branch advances.

On two generations of the LLaMA model family, MoP beat rival pruning methods across many compression levels. It also beat depth-only and width-only cutting. The smaller models truly ran faster, with end-to-end delay down by a large share at strong compression. The method also improved a vision and language model, and text-only retraining restored its picture skills.
arxiv-2602-06227:
Rewards in reinforcement learning often depend on a whole history, not just the last state, which makes them hard to specify. Pierriccardo Olivieri and 3 co-authors propose writing such rewards in a rich temporal logic. Their logic lets predicates be full first-order formulas over real data, not just true-or-false flags.

That richness removes hand-coding but adds cost, so the team isolates a fragment that stays tractable while covering real tasks. On the practical side, reward machines plus a hindsight replay trick turn the logic into learnable signals and fight sparse rewards. Tests in a continuous control setting with non-linear arithmetic showed the approach allows natural wording of complex tasks.
arxiv-2602-06527:
Scaling up reasoning by sampling many solution paths helps accuracy, but only if compute splits wisely between exploring new paths and exploiting good ones. Shengxuan Qiu and 4 co-authors present HyPER, an online control policy for multi-path decoding in mixture-of-experts models. Tree search hard-codes exploration in brittle rules, while parallel sampling over-explores and picks answers weakly.

HyPER treats the problem as expand-reduce control over a pool of hypotheses. A controller shifts from exploration to exploitation as the pool evolves, a token-level refinement exploits good paths without resampling whole answers, and a length- and confidence-aware rule aggregates the final answer. Tests on four mixture-of-experts models showed the dynamic balance paid off across reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2602-06827:
Victor Dhedin and six co-authors present DynaRetarget, a pipeline that transfers human motion to humanoid robots. Raw pose-only motion paths from capture or transfer are often physically impossible for a real robot to execute. The core of the system is a sampling-based optimizer that refines those paths into motions that obey physics, advancing its planning horizon step by step so long sequences stay tractable.

The team validated the pipeline by transferring hundreds of humanoid-object demos, beating the state of the art in success rate. It also works across object masses, sizes, and shapes under a single tracking goal. That toughness opens the door to making large synthetic sets of humanoid motion paths, easing a major bottleneck in collecting real-world robot data.
arxiv-2602-06927:
Siddharth Namachivayam develops a logic for a coordination puzzle among scientists who cannot talk to each other. Each lab can run a different set of experiments, and each scientist can retract only so many times before having to stop inquiring forever. The question is how the group can guarantee they converge on the same verdict about a hypothesis, and never affirm a false one. The author calls this inductive coordinated attack.

The paper refines Lewis's account of common knowledge, where higher-order expectations hinge on shared witnesses and inductive standards, into a logic of what it calls common inductive knowledge. Its topological semantics treats each agent's information base as primitive and gives each agent a switching tolerance for learning. After proving the proof system sound, the author shows how the logic solves the coordination puzzle.
arxiv-2602-07127:
Most ways of studying exoplanet atmospheres need the planet to pass in front of its star, which rules out many worlds.  Ted M.  Johnson and one co-author present VPIE, a time-series method for combined-light spectra that recovers the planet's contribution without a transit and without a model of the star's spectrum.

VPIE builds an empirical model of the starlight at each time step from a small set of spectra, then reads the planet's signal from what remains.  Tests on simulated James Webb Space Telescope observations of TOI-519 b, GJ 876 d. Proxima Centauri b show it working across a warm giant, a warm sub-Neptune, and a temperate rocky planet, though it loses sensitivity when heat spreads very evenly around a planet.
arxiv-2602-07527:
Gear faults in aviation drivetrains must be caught early, but fault signatures hide in noisy, non-sinusoidal vibration signals. Yaakoub Berrouche presents the Local Damage Mode Extractor, a physics-grounded, unsupervised method for early fault detection.

Three layers work in sequence. Dual-path denoising preserves transient fault structure. Multiscale enhancement with a fractional-domain operator accentuates low-frequency fault signs. And fusion, where harmonics-aware signals feed an anomaly finder. The result is a set of interpretable health indicators that need no labeled fault data. Maintenance builders get an early-warning system built on physics rather than on fault cases they may not have.
arxiv-2602-07627:
Control-flow graphs of structured programs are sparse, but treewidth and pathwidth only approximate that sparsity: many low-treewidth graphs cannot arise as control-flow graphs at all.  Xuran Cai and three co-authors present series-parallel-loop breakdowns, a grammar-based method that characterizes exactly the control-flow graphs of structured programs.

The breakdown mirrors program syntax, stays compatible with current parameterized techniques, and targets precisely the graphs compilers and analyzers encounter, rather than a broader class.  Program analysis teams get an exact structural characterization where previous settings offered only an upper bound, enabling methods tuned to real control flow. The exact match matters because treewidth alone admits graphs no real program can produce.
arxiv-2602-07727:
Cyclotomic polynomials have numbers whose largest size, called the height, has long drawn number theorists. Gennady Bachman asks whether every natural number can occur as the height of some ternary cyclotomic polynomial, one built from three distinct primes.

He answers yes: for any odd prime p and any height h up to half of p plus one, he constructs large primes q and r. The polynomial for pqr then has height exactly h. The spread between largest and smallest numbers is then either 2h or 2h minus 1, based on h modulo p. The paper settles a clean existence question with plain builds.
arxiv-2602-08227:
Professional writers relate to generative AI with a mix of rivalry and collaboration, and that mix shapes how they work. Rama Adithya Varanasi and two co-authors survey 403 writing professionals across roles, finding rivalry linked mainly to relational crafting and skill maintenance. Collaboration, meanwhile, links to task crafting, productivity, and satisfaction, while eroding long-term skill.

Writers high in both orientations reconcile those differences and strengthen the positive outcomes, suggesting balance beats either stance alone. The authors draw design implications: increase productive friction to sustain rivalry and reduce over-reliance to temper collaboration. Managers and tool designers gain evidence for shaping AI relationships that protect skills while capturing productivity, aimed at the long-term success of the profession.
arxiv-2602-08327:
Waves in shallow water with friction and a steady push can settle into repeating patterns, but proving that takes care when the waves are rough. Chun Ho Lau and Taige Wang study time-periodic solutions of a forced, damped Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation on the whole line, working in low-regularity spaces where functions may be quite jagged. Their arXiv paper establishes that such repeating solutions exist and are stable.

The proof leans on energy-style estimates for the linearized problem, then treats the nonlinear convection term as a small disturbance to that linear picture. Readers get a short, focused result: even in rough settings, the forced system admits a steady periodic rhythm rather than drifting or blowing up. The paper is brief, but its claim is sharp and fully stated.
arxiv-2602-08427:
Kriging and neural networks look like strangers: one is a probabilistic spatial method, the other a black-box learner. Marius Marinescu argues they are closely related, and that seeing the link can make machine learning more interpretable, reliable, and spatially aware. His arXiv paper revisits the literature connecting Kriging, Gaussian process regression, and large neural networks.

Spatial statistics now intertwines with AI, and the paper maps where the two traditions meet and diverge. Readers get a conceptual bridge rather than a new algorithm: a way to borrow uncertainty and spatial structure from Kriging while keeping the flexibility of neural models. The piece suits readers curious about why spatial models and deep learning keep converging.
arxiv-2602-08527:
The Merton problem tells an investor how much to consume and how much to hold in a risky asset. Its answer turns on a subtle math choice: which stochastic-integral convention is used. Mario Ayala and Benjamin Vallejo Jiménez study conventions indexed by a parameter running from Itô through Stratonovich to Hänggi-Klimontovich. Their arXiv paper separates what changes from what does not.

If the drift is transformed along with the convention, the optimal policy stays put. If the drift number is held fixed, the opportunity set shifts. Under log utility, consumption is unchanged while the portfolio weight moves. For a Heston asset, that weight can even change sign across volatility states. Readers learn that the convention cannot be read off from return data alone without extra structure.
arxiv-2602-08727:
Undersampled CT scans cut time and radiation dose, but they leave artifacts that hurt diagnosis. Johannes Thalhammer and five co-authors propose a hybrid deep-learning framework that mixes 2D and 3D processing for artifact reduction. Their arXiv paper targets 3D cone-beam CT volumes acquired with sparse views.

A 2D U-Net first processes individual slices to extract feature maps. Those maps are stacked and fed to a 3D decoder, which uses context across slices to predict a clean volume. The two-stage design balances 2D speed with 3D consistency, improving inter-slice consistency in coronal and sagittal views at low overhead. Readers get a robust, efficient post-processing route for high-quality sparse-view CT.
arxiv-2602-08827:
A tiny magnetic flaw inside a superconductor creates strange trapped states called Yu-Shiba-Rusinov states. Andreas Theiler and two co-authors study what happens to electric current tunneling through such a flaw. Two odd effects show up at a quantum turning point: the current flips sign, and the local superconducting strength turns negative.

The paper shows both flips trace back to the trapped state, yet they barely affect each other. In particular, the negative local strength does not cause the current flip. Nor can the current reveal the local change, which happens over a span far shorter than the superconductor's natural length scale.
arxiv-2602-08927:
Estimating a rising-then-falling curve from data that arrives one point at a time is the problem Rohan Hore and two co-authors solve. Their setting is online monotone density estimation: each new observation must update the estimate without revisiting the past. They propose two estimators, an online version of the classic Grenander estimator and an expert-aggregation rival.

When the true density is monotone, the cumulative log-likelihood gap grows only like the cube root of the sample size. The aggregation estimator also stays close to the best offline choice made with hindsight. The same machinery yields log-optimal p-to-e calibrators for sequential testing, with experiments backing the theory.
arxiv-2602-09227:
A robot that wants to cooperate should move legibly, so observers quickly grasp its goal, but one facing adversaries should move illegibly instead. Ananya Yammanuru and three co-authors tackle the mixed case: several observers, each seeing only part of the scene, with different motives. Their Mixed-Motive Limited-Observability Legible Motion Planning problem asks for a trajectory that reads clearly to friendly observers and misleadingly to hostile ones, respecting each observer's visibility limits.

The paper maps strategies an agent can use while meeting that goal and presents DUBIOUS, a trajectory optimizer that solves the problem. Tests show DUBIOUS balances legibility against motives and limited views. Future work includes moving observers and other variations of the mixed-motive setting.
arxiv-2602-09327:
Two alkali atoms held in an optical tweezer change spin through collisions that tie their spin states to how they move relative to each other. A 2026 experiment led by Poramaporn Ruksasakchai, with five co-authors, studies what happens when that relative motion is hot, far warmer than the energies of the spins involved. The usual expectation is that heat destroys quantum entanglement, not creates it.

Here the opposite occurs: a spin state that starts out unentangled evolves into an entangled one through the coupling to thermal motion. The authors show the resulting entanglement is not a curiosity alone, since it could in principle sharpen measurements past the standard quantum limit. That prospect points toward a sturdier way of generating entanglement for future quantum devices, one that works with heat rather than fighting it.
arxiv-2602-09427:
Tire behavior shapes how autonomous vehicles handle and stay stable, yet most estimation and control methods lean on empirical fits or machine learning that need heavy calibration. Luigi Romano and three co-authors propose a model-based alternative in their 2026 paper: output-feedback lateral tracking control for all-wheel steering vehicles that fuses distributed tire dynamics with smart tire sensing. Smart tires report friction, pressure, wear, speed, and forces, grounding control in live measurements.

The controller and observer rest on combined ordinary and partial differential equation formulations, pairing rigid-body dynamics with distributed tire behavior. Two results stand out: suppression of low-speed micro-shimmy, a jittery tire phenomenon, and path-following through force control, using estimates of slip angles, vehicle kinematics, and lateral forces. The authors present it as the first rigorous control strategy joining distributed tire models with smart tire technology.
arxiv-2602-09527:
Iterative tomographic reconstruction pays twice per step: costly forward and adjoint projections for data fidelity, plus costly proximal computations often solved by inner iterations. Evangelos Papoutsellis and two co-authors study a method that cuts both bills at once in their 2026 paper. It couples randomized skipping of the proximal step with variance-reduced subset optimization of the data-fit term.

Trials on synthetic and real data show striking speedups of five to twenty times over non-skipped counterparts, the standard approach until now for efficiently solving these problems. By skipping expensive proximal work randomly while controlling variance in the data term, the method keeps accuracy while slashing compute. The authors present the work as groundwork for wider adoption of skipping methods across inverse problems.
arxiv-2602-09827:
O. Gupta and six co-authors use a rough fluid model to predict the cutoff wave number for the short-wave ion-heat-gradient mode in a Z-pinch. It depends on ion density gradient, ion heat gradient, and ion-electron heat ratio. Their 2026 paper predicts the cutoff wave number rises in line with rising ion heat gradient for enough gradient values. Direct number answers of the gyro dispersion rule from a purpose-built solver confirm the foretold scalings at large gradient values.

A weaker power-law scaling appears for middle gradient values. Joining the wave number scalings with a simple spread estimate for churned fluxes yields a forecast for ion heat gradient heat flux in churn driven by this mode. Applying the key guess additionally gives scalings for the aspect ratio of the churned eddies. Rough prediction and gyro numbers thus agree on the mode's cutoff ways.
arxiv-2602-10027:
Data warehouses split large tables into partitions and keep row-group statistics to speed searches, rather than maintaining indexes. A 2026 paper by Dominik Winecki uses those statistics for exact spatial nearest-neighbor joins, asking when whole partitions can be skipped. Existing pruning tests, he argues, are too cautious for bounds-only data because they miss directional structure.

Winecki proposes a three-bound proximity test that decides whether every point in one partition has a closer neighbor in another partition than in a third, possibly hidden one. The test lets join evaluation concentrate on a few partitions before any spatial index is built. The paper shows the algorithm is both optimal and efficient.
arxiv-2602-10227:
Waveguides with a screen pose a classic scattering problem, and the discrete version has lacked an exact treatment. A 2026 paper led by Elena Medvedeva, with two co-authors, studies waves scattering off a finite crosswise strip in a discrete square-lattice waveguide under Dirichlet rules for the strip and walls. The Wiener-Hopf setup yields an equation with a four-by-four matrix kernel, cut to two-by-two under symmetry assumptions.

Rather than pursue factoring of that kernel, the authors obtain an exact solution by pole removal. Reflection and transmission numbers for an incoming duct mode are computed to thirteen decimal places, matching continuous waveguide theory. Full reflection and zero transmission return as frequency nears the incoming mode's cut-off, and the solution checks out against a Boundary Algebraic Equations run with a tailored lattice Green's function.
arxiv-2602-10427:
Jeongmin Lee and Jisung Yoon ask which physics reaches policymakers in a 2026 study of science and policy. They link policy documents from the Overton database with publications from the American Real Society. The resulting dataset traces how physics knowledge circulates in policy debate. The question is not whether science matters, but which parts get picked up.

Their analysis finds a gap between research communities and policy writers. Policy documents draw heavily on broad, mixed-field areas of physics, while narrower specialties appear less often. The paper maps those preferences across subfields, giving a quantitative picture of selective uptake. Influence in policy follows breadth and interdisciplinarity more than depth within a single specialty.
arxiv-2602-10527:
Scott P. McGrath and four co-authors propose a system for teaching machine intelligence in medical school in a 2026 paper. AI is entering clinics quickly, but medical teaching has lagged behind the tools. Future doctors need ordered training, not brief contact to new tools.

The paper reviews the writings on AI in medical teaching, naming key skills, course plans, and build plans. Its system, AI-PACE, calls for long-run mix across the whole training span, mixed-field teamwork, and even focus to hands-on basics and clinic uses. The authors offer it as a base for teachers making courses for an AI-aided healthcare setting.
arxiv-2602-10927:
Shoham Sen and three co-authors analyze the electrostatics of dielectric crystals at two scales in a 2026 paper. Ionic crystals like solid electrolytes and complex oxides matter for energy storage, sensing, and actuation. Yet defining macroscopic tilt in a cyclic crystal is subtle. The usual unit-cell dipole moment can change qualitatively, even in sign, with the choice of cell.

Using rigorous two-scale settling, the authors examine the span limit where lattice spacing is much smaller than body sizes. The two-scale limit yields both a bulk tilt density and a surface charge density supported on the edge. The analysis resolves the cell-dependence puzzle by showing tilt emerges with edge charges as part of a single limit, giving materials modelers a principled definition.
arxiv-2602-11027:
Short-range forces between nucleons shape the links seen in collision debris. Gleb Romanenko and Francesca Bellini model the strong force with a square-well possible and solve the Schrödinger equation with Coulomb effects included. The resulting pair wave stays regular at small separations and admits many partial waves.

Applied to proton-proton femtoscopy, the model yields link curves for realistic source sizes. It shows that a common asymptotic approximation overstates the signal for small sources. Checks against numerical work with the CATS frame and the Argonne possible agree within current measurement error. The analytic form offers a handy, flexible tool for femtoscopy of nucleon and baryon pairs.
arxiv-2602-11127:
Superconducting qubits lose energy to tiny defects that are hard to pin down. Tanay Roy and seven co-authors propose a spectroscopy method for fixed-rate transmons that needs no tuning into resonance. Repeated preparation of the second excited state yields joint decay rates for adjacent transitions.

Links in those rates reveal one or more dominant two-level systems and track their rate drift over time. Strikingly, defects detuned far from the qubit transition still shape relaxation in a strong way. The method gives a practical tool for defect spectroscopy without flux tuning or Stark shifts, aiding the hunt for cleaner qubit materials.
arxiv-2602-11227:
Solar activity may answer to tides from Venus, Earth, and Jupiter. F. Stefani and three co-authors link magneto-Rossby waves in the solar tachocline to the quasi-biennial swing, recently found to hold a stable period near one and seven-tenths years. That period matches the dominant beat of spring tides from the three planets.

Analyzing dozens of ground-level enhancement events and solar flares, the authors pin the period close to that beat. Recent events, including a major storm in May 2024 and a strong flare in February 2026, align with maxima of combined tidal forcing. The paper argues tides may help synchronize both the quasi-biennial swing and the eleven-year Schwabe cycle, aiding predictability.
arxiv-2602-11827: Konstantin Kokhas and one co-author present what they describe as a correct proof of an earlier result by Chung and Tsay on the partial gossip problem. The gossip problem concerns how information spreads when people share secrets in calls. The partial version restricts which pairs may exchange information. The paper revisits that result with a proof its authors present as correct, offering readers a repaired argument for a claim in the gossip literature.
arxiv-2602-12327:
Gravitational wave event GW190814 merged objects of wildly unequal mass, a ratio near 0.1 that strains standard formation stories. Neev Shah led this work with four co-authors, linking that event to the most unequal Galactic high-mass X-ray binary, 4U 1700-37. Detailed binary models, tied to rich observations of that binary, trace its formation history.

Conservative mass transfer plus a directed natal kick prove essential to match the binary today. That system itself will likely fail to become a gravitational wave source, due to a failed common envelope phase ahead. Yet a similar path, with conservative first transfer and a large kick above 100 kilometres per second for the first-born compact object, naturally yields GW190814-like mergers at rates matching observations.
arxiv-2602-12427:
Earthquakes happen when compressed fault surfaces slip, and that slip lives in a thin layer of crushed granular rock called fault gouge. Mary Agajanian led this work with three co-authors, building a variational theory for gouge behaviour under shear, using finite kinematics. Modelling gouge is hard because of large deformations, inelasticity, rate dependence, and volume change, so researchers usually lean on standard formulas.

The team first develops a general theory for a rigid-viscoplastic, pressure-sensitive material, with plasticity following maximum dissipation. They then focus on a Cam-Clay material in a shearing, opening layer. They calibrate with convexity arguments and packing tests. They solve rate- and state-dependent shear response under constant normal stress and set shear rate. Checks with lab shear tests confirm the model and link it to standard rate-and-state friction laws.
arxiv-2602-12527:
Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes give a flexible Bayesian open-ended frame for grouped data with a shared, unbounded set of mixture parts. Naiqi Li works alone here, deriving analytic results for two exp family members within that frame: the Poisson and normal laws. Most existing uses focus on the DM paired structure, but the frame is far more general, accommodating many paired prior-fit pairs.

Direct closed-form forms are derived for the Gamma-Poisson and Normal-Gamma-Normal paired pairs under the layered build. Full proofs clarify the basic maths and show how pairing can be used step by step in layered open-ended models. The work extends HDP use beyond the DM setting, giving usable analytic results for users of layered Bayesian open-ended methods.
arxiv-2602-12627:
Double holography couples AdS3 gravity to a flat heat bath, and boundary mutual information measures shared info between two small regions on their meeting line. Yuxuan Liu led this work with two co-authors, studying that boundary mutual information, or BMI, in double holography. Entanglement entropy is caught via quantum extremal surfaces, worked out by a surface tuning method based on Surface Evolver.

Both linked and unlinked setups of the quantum entanglement wedge in the AdS3 bulk are looked at, with finite fixes to the BMI studied. Number results reveal a phase change of the BMI as gap between the two regions grows. The BMI splits naturally into two parts: a shape term from areas of the quantum extremal surfaces, and a fix term. Readers get a concrete holographic picture of how boundary info changes with gap.
arxiv-2602-12727:
Search systems that feed answers to language models live or die by the quality of their retrievers, yet training data usually mark only one right passage per question. That thin labelling creates false negatives and weak training signals. Benben Wang and four co-authors study what happens when large language models supply many positive passages instead, comparing several training objectives under one shared contrastive framework.

Their analysis shows how each objective spreads probability across the positive set, and tests on standard question-answering and retrieval benchmarks back the theory. One objective, log-sum-exp pairwise loss, proved the most robust across settings, while joint and summed likelihood versions were more sensitive to label quality. Even simple random sampling of one positive held up well as a baseline, giving practitioners a practical guide.
arxiv-2602-12827:
Caesium lead iodide in its orthorhombic phase is a perovskite of interest for optoelectronics, and its charge carriers do not follow simple parabolic bands. O. S. Sultanov and five co-authors compute electron and hole dispersion curves with density functional theory including spin-orbit coupling. Effective masses come from parabolic fits in different crystal directions, but the curves bend away from parabolas above 0.2 electron volts for electrons and 0.1 for holes.

Those energies are reachable by optical spectroscopy, so the bending is experimentally relevant rather than a high-energy curiosity. The authors propose a model in which effective masses depend quadratically on wave vector. They derive an expression that fits both electron and hole curves across all symmetric directions from zone centre to boundary. The model gives experimenters a compact way to describe carrier motion.
arxiv-2602-13227:
Sixth-generation networks are meant to be AI-native, intent-driven, and programmable in economic terms. But 5G slicing frameworks built on static policies and manual workflows cannot meet dynamic, multi-domain, service-centric demands. Eranga Bandara and eleven co-authors propose an agentic AI control plane for 6G slice orchestration, monitoring, and trading, treating orchestration as one control function spanning planning, deployment, and monitoring.

The control plane layers multiple cooperating AI agents. It adds market-aware orchestration that jointly considers slice requirements, pricing, and availability. It offers a natural-language interface through the Model Context Protocol for intent-based queries under safety and policy constraints. Fine-tuned language models in a multi-model consortium, overseen by a dedicated reasoning model, support responsible, explainable autonomy. Tests on a real testbed with multiple mobile core instances and Ericsson radio infrastructure show the combination enabling a scalable, adaptive 6G-native control plane.
arxiv-2602-13527:
Vector fields near a singular point can sometimes be put in linear form, and the Bruno ideal marks where that is possible. Given a log-type analytic vector field, the authors define a formal ideal. It comes from the locus where its semi-simple and nilpotent parts line up. Assuming the linear part's values meet the Bruno number condition, they prove that ideal is in fact analytic.

Moreover, the vector field can be put in normal form when restricted to that ideal. Its zero set is therefore an analytic variety. The leaf structure set by the restricted field can be put in linear form, tying a number condition on linear-part values to a concrete geometric result. María Martín-Vega leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-14127:
Reda Bensaid and six co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv method for few-shot adaptation of large audio-language models. Adapting big multimodal models to new tasks with few examples remains hard, and the team compares training-based and training-free routes. Their framework, MUKA, blends two views of audio: fine-grained, context-dependent features from instruction-tuned models like Pengi, and global semantic features from contrastive models like CLAP.

A product kernel aligns local similarity with global semantics, boosting representational power while keeping kernel guarantees and avoiding extra training. Across 11 diverse audio datasets, MUKA led training-free methods and even beat training-based adapters in several cases. The result offers a practical balance of adaptability and efficiency for audio tasks.
arxiv-2602-14227:
Rafael Díaz Fuentes and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv chemotaxis model with three parts. Cells move toward a pull signal and away from a push signal, while a non-local growth term caps growth. Making of the two signals follows algebraic growth laws, widening simple power-law first forms.

The paper proves global life and boundedness of classic answers under a balance rule. That balance weighs signal making exponents against non-local damping exponents. When making outruns damping, blow-up looms. When damping holds sway, answers stay bounded for all time. The result maps the edge between controlled spread and runaway growth.
arxiv-2602-14627:
Thin jets stretched by gravity break into drops, and their wobble matters for printing and fibers. Daniel Moreno-Boza builds a single one-dimensional model for weakly elastic jets under gravity. It pairs full-curvature surface tension with a Giesekus stress law.

The model first passes a Newtonian check, matching known spectra and flow shapes. Elasticity then shifts the line between steady jetting and dripping, tracked through the leading Hopf mode. At moderate elasticity, polymer tension moves both the critical Weber number and the wobble frequency. The study also breaks down where the instability energy comes from.
arxiv-2602-14727:
K. Gorska and others link a mixed Cattaneo-Vernotte law to the noisy voter model, a bridge between heat flow and crowd choice. They start from a spread law whose rate shifts with place, then join a balance law to a flow rule under varied chance readings of the spread.

Exact forms follow for the chance spread and for mean squared shift, and the plain spread limit gets a full look, with its time-mean shift worked out. From those forms, a break in ergodicity shows up: time means no longer match group means. Mixed spread thus links physics and social choice through one shared math.
arxiv-2602-14927:
Marcus Djokic and Jose L. Mendoza-Cortes present a computational study of ferrocene-functionalised covalent organic frameworks for hydrogen storage, chasing United States Department of Energy targets of 6.5 weight percent and 50 grams per litre for vehicles. Their MSUCOF-4-FeCp material, built by adding ferrocene units into IRCOF-102 under a multi-binding-sites approach, is claimed to reach 18.0 weight percent and 72.6 grams per litre at 298 kelvin and 700 bar.

Those uptakes, if realised in practice, would exceed the ultimate targets by a wide margin, and the paper details the first-principles multiscale modelling behind the claim. Hydrogen storage gains a computational candidate of striking predicted performance. Theory points to a framework worth testing in the lab.
arxiv-2602-15127:
Khodabandehlou and colleagues bring calorimetry back to life as a quantitative tool for biology. Micro-calorimetry can probe the structure and function of living systems by measuring excess heat released by cell structures as outside settings change. The paper sets out the basic framework of nonequilibrium heat study.

To show this, the team works out the heat capacity of simple models tied to ciliar motion, in the rowing model, and to molecular motor motion, in flashing ratchets. Their numbers show striking links between that value and relevant settings. Oddly, the value can even turn below zero as a result of biological activity, a signature that equilibrium heat study would miss.
arxiv-2602-15527:
Noltmann and colleagues ask whether the shape of space itself can be read off the cosmic microwave background. They also ask how that reading shifts if the early power spectrum departs from the standard near-scale-free form. They study the fully compact, orientable flat topologies E1 through E6, computing temperature correlation matrices across topologies, domain sizes, and observer spots, for both standard and altered spectra. A Kullback-Leibler measure gauges how well non-trivial and simply connected shapes can be told apart.

They also train a CatBoost classifier on harmonic-space maps to judge detection prospects in practice. Topology signals live mainly in off-diagonal correlations on the largest sky scales, and spectrum changes there can either boost those signals or push them below detectability. The upshot is that spectrum uncertainty must be handled with care in any robust search for cosmic shape.
arxiv-2602-15627:
Grebenkov and colleagues ask how fast the quickest of many searchers finds a fixed target when each searcher moves at finite speed. They study ensembles of independent searchers driven by dichotomous noise and described by the telegrapher equation, computing the mean fastest first-passage time both analytically and numerically. The contrast with Brownian searchers is stark.

For Brownian particles, the mean fastest time falls only logarithmically with searcher count, heading toward zero. For finite-speed searchers, it stays bounded below by the minimal ballistic travel time, and it converges to that bound exponentially fast as count grows. The result shows a dramatic efficiency edge for physically realistic searchers, and it warns that diffusive models can mislead about short-time behaviour. Extensions to anomalous diffusion find superdiffusive search most efficient, then normal, then subdiffusive.
arxiv-2602-15827:
Wu and colleagues present Perceptive Humanoid Parkour, or PHP, a modular framework that lets humanoid robots do long-horizon parkour alone, guided by vision, over hard obstacle courses. Agile parkour needs sturdy control, lifelike motion, long chains of skills, and sight-led choices. First, the approach uses motion matching, a nearest-neighbour search in feature space, to build long-horizon trajectories from retargeted atomic human skills.

Next, expert policies that track motion with reinforcement learning are distilled into one depth-based, multi-skill student policy, using DAgger and reinforcement learning. The robot, guided only by onboard depth sensing and a single discrete 2D velocity command, steps over, climbs onto, vaults, or rolls off obstacles of varied shapes and heights. In real tests, a Unitree G1 humanoid climbed obstacles up to 1.25 metres, 96 percent of its height, then crossed several obstacles in sequence, adapting live as they shifted.
arxiv-2602-15927:
Schlarmann and Hein present a stealthy Visual Memory Injection, or VMI, attack on multi-turn chats with large vision-language models. Security for such models in long multi-turn settings is still little studied, even as user numbers climb fast. The attack path is realistic and plain.

An attacker posts a doctored image to the web or social media. A benign user downloads it and feeds it to the model. On plain prompts the model acts normally, but on a trigger prompt it outputs a set target message to steer the user, for instance toward adversarial marketing or political persuasion. Unlike prior single-turn attacks, VMI stays potent after a long multi-turn chat. Demos on several recent open-weight models show large-scale user manipulation through doctored images is feasible, urging stronger model robustness.
arxiv-2602-16227:
J. Shi leads a very large team reporting multiwavelength observations of SN 2024abvb, the sixth Type Icn supernova found to date. It sits far from its host galaxy, about twenty-two kiloparsecs out, and ranks among the most luminous of its class. Early optical spectra show a blue continuum with narrow carbon features, consistent with wind speeds typical of a Wolf-Rayet star.

No narrow helium lines appear, supporting the Icn classification over Ibn. Unlike most Icn events, no broad features show up in late-time spectra. Light-curve modeling matches ejecta of a few solar masses interacting with circumstellar material, both larger than in other Icn cases. Local metallicity runs well below the host average. The authors favor a mid-mass star stripped by a compact companion, with enough runaway speed to reach its remote spot.
arxiv-2602-16327:
Joseph Bingham, Netanel Arussy, and Saman Zonouz take on a safety problem in CRISPR gene editing: predicting where a guide RNA will act besides its intended target. Genome sequencing and editing tools have grown easier to use, and with that growth comes a need to foresee off-target behavior before an edit is made. The authors look at the underlying biology and chemistry from a data-driven angle rather than from theory alone.

Their answer is Guide-Guard, a machine learning system that predicts how the editing system will behave for a given guide RNA, with eighty-four percent accuracy. A useful feature is that it can be trained on several genes at the same time without losing accuracy. For researchers choosing guides, the paper offers a practical predictor that covers more than one gene at once.
arxiv-2602-16627:
Mariya Trukhanova and Yuri Obukhov build a model for live effects of outside inertial and axion fields on a host of spin particles. The work asks if spin density and current density in slow quantum particle hosts could spot the axion-like dark matter thought to exist. A closed set of live laws results, covering flow, momentum, and spin density change.

Spin-rotation links and outside axion fields enter the laws in plain form. The new frame opens fresh paths for a lab hunt for dark matter axions. Physicists get a self-contained live frame tying a dark matter guess to spin and current signs that can be gauged in many-particle hosts.
arxiv-2602-16727:
Hua Yan, Heng Tan, Yingxue Zhang, and Yu Yang present MobCache, a mobility-aware cache frame for scalable language-model-based human mobility simulation. Simulating large-scale mobility aids planning, epidemic response, and transport study, but language-model agents cost too much compute to scale. MobCache uses reconstructible caches to cut that cost while keeping fidelity.

It has two parts. A reasoning part codes each reasoning step as a latent-space embedding and reuses and recombines steps via a latent-space evaluator. A decoding part uses a light decoder trained with mobility-law-constrained distillation to turn latent reasoning chains into natural language. Tests show large efficiency gains across several axes with scores comparable to state-of-the-art language-model methods, giving simulators a practical route to city-scale runs.
arxiv-2602-16927:
Jacques Carette and co-authors develop free models of quantum computing that add to classical computing just enough physical principles to represent it and no more. Quantum computing improves substantially on known classical methods for various key problems, yet the link between quantum and classical work is not yet fully understood. Free models clarify that link.

The paper builds an axiomatisation replacing standard continuous postulates with a small number of discrete equations. A free model replaces the standard linear-algebraic model with a category-theoretical one. The axioms and model rest on reversible classical computing. They isolate quantum advantage in the ability to take certain well-behaved square roots, and link to varied hardware platforms. The free model may be read as a programming language for quantum computers, with the same expressivity and universality as the standard model, plus automated verification.
arxiv-2602-17027:
Paimon Goulart and co-authors showcase transforming behavioral neuroscience discovery with in-context learning and AI-enhanced tensor methods. Scientific discovery pipelines typically involve complex, rigid, and time-consuming processes, from data prep to interpreting findings. Recent AI advances can transform such pipelines so domain experts can focus on interpreting findings, rather than debugging rigid ones or by hand annotating data.

In a collaboration between data science and AI teams and behavioral neuroscientists, the paper shows an AI-enhanced pipeline. It is built to transform and speed up how domain experts gain insights from lab data. The project studies fear generalization in mice, a key problem whose progress can advance insight into clinically major and often debilitating illness such as PTSD. In-context learning is identified as a suitable interface for domain experts to automate parts of their pipeline without knowledge of AI model training and fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-17227:
Maria Ana Pereira led an eight-author team fielding a practical quantum key distribution system for city networks. Wide adoption of quantum key distribution demands hardware that is stable, resilient, cheap, and manufacturable at scale. The paper presents a high-speed, rack-mounted system built on integrated photonics, designed for autonomous long-term stability in city settings.

The design drops chromatic dispersion compensation, which city-scale distances do not require, simplifying the build. In field tests, the system exchanged keys continuously over several kilometres of metropolitan fiber. It ran without manual intervention across more than a dozen day-night cycles. The demonstration moves quantum-secured city links from lab promise toward deployable infrastructure.
arxiv-2602-17327:
Michael Dinzinger led a six-author team releasing WebFAQ 2.0, a massive multilingual question-answer dataset for dense retrieval research. The collection holds nearly two hundred million FAQ-based natural question-answer pairs across more than a hundred languages, with bilingual aligned pairs numbering well over ten million, making it the largest FAQ-based resource. A new crawling strategy pulls web content directly, yielding greater diversity and richer context through page titles and descriptions.

Responding to community feedback, the team also releases a hard negatives dataset. It holds over a million queries across twenty languages, mined by a two-stage retrieval pipeline with cross-encoder scores for two hundred negatives per query. The resource supports two fine-tuning strategies for dense retrievers: contrastive learning and knowledge distillation. Since late 2025, structured FAQs flow regularly through the Open Web Index, keeping the resource growing, with data and scripts public.
arxiv-2602-17427:
Lorenzo Carfora led a four-author team mapping Mott-insulating phases of the Bose-Hubbard model on ladder lattices. The team computed the phase diagram for a half-filled ladder lattice, including finite on-site interactions. The rung-Mott insulator phase survives at finite interaction strength, and the paper maps its boundary with the superfluid phase in the thermodynamic limit.

The phases can still be told apart using number and parity variances, quantities a quantum-gas microscope can measure. Similar phases appear in other quasi-one-dimensional lattice shapes, with lattice connectivity shifting the phase boundaries. That pattern shows these phases come from one-dimensional structures mapped onto higher-dimensional systems, driven by reduced hopping rates along different directions. The work sharpens the picture of how ladder geometry shapes insulating behavior.
arxiv-2602-17527:
Kevin Multani led a ten-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on sensing tiny materials with millimeter-wave silicon photonic crystal cavities. Because the platform uses a dielectric rather than a superconductor, it keeps working in strong magnetic fields, where superconducting cavities fail. The team cooled one silicon cavity to cryogenic temperature and measured a quality factor above one hundred thousand.

As a proof of concept, the team placed a hexagonal boron nitride and multilayer graphene stack at a peak electric field point in the cavity and read its response at room temperature. The stack shifted the cavity resonance enough to yield a total sample conductivity. That result shows a small resonance shift can reveal the electrical response of a nanoscale sample. The authors present the device as a promising route to on-chip study of nanoscale samples at millimeter-wave frequencies.
arxiv-2602-17627:
Joseph Lakey outlines a route to direct bounds for maximal partial sums of Walsh-Fourier series, with no need for interpolation. The paper treats linearized partial sums operators tied to expansions in Walsh functions, a setting where direct estimates have proved elusive.

The main focus is the simpler case of dyadic partial sums, where the approach is laid out in full. Lakey also sketches a second approach aimed at bounds for general linearized partial sums. Readers get a clear map of two lines of attack on the problem, rather than a finished set of general theorems. The value lies in the strategy and its first concrete case.
arxiv-2602-17827:
Pedro Dall'Antonia and team propose Adaptive Complementary Exploration, or ACE, to improve exploration in Generative Flow Networks. GFlowNets are amortized samplers trained to generate discrete, compositional objects with odds proportional to a reward function. Learning stalls when training fails to reach diverse high-probability regions fast.

Recent fixes use curiosity-driven search and self-supervised random network distillation to chase unvisited, valuable states. Those methods waste samples on regions already well approximated. ACE instead trains an exploration GFlowNet to seek high-reward states in regions the canonical GFlowNet underexplores, while the canonical net learns the target distribution. Tests show ACE beats prior work on approximation accuracy to the target distribution and on discovery rate of diverse high-reward states.
arxiv-2602-18327:
Francesco Atzori and eight co-authors protect unknown quantum states from decay without knowing them in advance. Their 2026 paper starts from a core limit: environmental contact degrades quantum coherence and blocks scaling of quantum technologies. The quantum Zeno effect can freeze evolution through frequent measurement, but past versions demanded prior knowledge of the state.

The new protocol needs neither state nor dynamics knowledge. It embeds the system in a larger space and temporarily swaps its quantum information onto a decoherence-free ancillary degree of freedom. Lab tests on a quantum optical platform show that coherence and purity survive well for arbitrary polarization qubits facing decoherence. The work enables universal safeguarding of unknown states, a practical step toward scalable quantum devices.
arxiv-2602-18527:
Zhan Liu and nine co-authors give audio-visual AI models 3D perception. Their 2026 paper notes current audio-visual large language models are largely restricted to 2D via RGB video and monaural audio. That design creates a dimensionality mismatch blocking reliable source localization in complex 3D settings.

The team presents JAEGER, extending audio-visual language models to 3D space for joint spatial grounding with RGB-D observations and multi-channel ambisonics. Its core contribution is the neural intensity vector, a learned spatial audio representation encoding directional cues for direction-of-arrival estimation with overlapping sources in adverse settings. For large-scale training and evaluation, the team proposes SpatialSceneQA, a benchmark of sixty-one thousand samples from simulated environments. Experiments show the approach beats 2D baselines across spatial perception and reasoning tasks, underscoring the need for explicit 3D modeling. Code, model checkpoints, and datasets are available.
arxiv-2602-18827:
A thin film can spread, clump, or break apart, depending on competing forces. Shen Bian, writing alone in 2026, studies a higher-dimensional thin film equation. Repulsion there comes from fourth-order diffusion. Aggregation comes from backward second-order spread that degrades.

The work maps steady states for every positive diffusion exponent. It finds a key threshold for compactness and solution structure. Below that threshold, radially decreasing steady states match both inequality extremals and free-energy minimisers. A sharp threshold in a norm of the steady state then separates global survival from finite-time blow-up. Steady states thus become a pivot for a unified account of settings, energy structure, and change over time. The work is pure maths. It gives a clear map of when films settle and when they blow up.
arxiv-2602-19227:
Galaxies come in shapes set largely by two parts: a round central bulge and a flat disk of stars. Heavier galaxies tend to carry bigger bulges, with the most massive systems looking like pure ellipticals. Mergers have long been blamed for building bulges, but that story alone has not explained why the whole sequence of shapes lines up as it does. Masafumi Noguchi argues that feedback must be part of the answer.

Feedback means energy from stars and black holes pushing gas around, which changes how much material is left to form stars after a merger. In Noguchi's account, mergers supply the raw events, while feedback sets how much of each galaxy ends up in bulge versus disk. Together the two effects reproduce the observed pattern, linking a galaxy's shape to both its violent history and its internal regulation.
arxiv-2602-19427:
Standard phones can now link straight to orbit, promising coverage without ground towers. Rajan Shrestha and Hayder Al-Hraishawi note that the phone uplink is the weak link. Long distances, severe path loss, and strict phone power limits hurt reliability, especially at low elevation angles and beam edges. Their paper studies supplementary uplink technology as a fix that preserves phone power efficiency.

Using the predictable geometry of orbits, they build an elevation-aware framework. It shifts uplink work across frequency bands from elevation-based link margin estimates. The phone transmits on a primary carrier or a lower-frequency backup carrier, chosen by a switching rule with hysteresis to prevent frequent switching. Simulated trials test the design for direct phone-to-orbit service.
arxiv-2602-19627:
Neutron star mergers are nature's lab for matter at extreme density, yet the merger mess clouds readings of gravitational-wave and electromagnetic signals. Nina Kunert and seven co-authors study mock readings of gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers using next-generation detectors. They test whether those readings can pin down both nuclear physics and dark matter limits, including fermionic dark matter, non-self-interacting, inside neutron stars.

Pooling observations tightens limits on nuclear empirical parameters, though inferred values stay sensitive to modeling bias and built-in parameter trade-offs. For non-self-interacting fermionic dark matter below one percent mass fraction, decisive evidence looks unlikely from gravitational waves alone. Any bias such dark matter adds to nuclear inference should stay negligible even for next-generation detectors.
arxiv-2602-19727:
Some integers are defined by what their digits avoid: in a fixed base, certain digits never appear. A 2026 arXiv paper by Jean-François Burnol, working alone, studies the Dirichlet series built from those missing-digit integers.

It was already known in general that such series, being automatic, continue meromorphically to the whole complex plane. Burnol gives a new proof from a series representation with good convergence everywhere. He also shows that a generating function for the residues on the real axis equals one divided by the moment generating function for the related Cantor set. That makes the normalized residues a kind of generalized Bernoulli numbers.
arxiv-2602-19927:
Longitudinal electroweak gauge bosons are the most delicate ingredient of electroweak parton showers, because their gauge components do not cancel diagram by diagram. A 2026 arXiv paper by M. R. Masouminia and P. Richardson builds a gauge-invariant scheme for them inside the Herwig 7 shower.

Building on Herwig's default treatment, which defines a longitudinal current by subtraction, the authors retain the subtraction remainder as a well-defined contribution. They complete it with a Goldstone-matching term fixed by Ward identities. They derive helicity-resolved building blocks and compact splitting kernels for the relevant branchings and implement the scheme as a switchable alternative. The completion leaves the transverse sector untouched and changes only longitudinal entries. Shower studies show the two prescriptions agree at high scales and differ at lower scales exactly where symmetry breaking acts.
arxiv-2602-20427:
Planning operator order is a core challenge in software building and hardware design, and recent gradient-based methods struggle with it. Grouped choices miss the ordinal nature of time, and their tuning space scales poorly. Yaohui Cai and three co-authors propose GauS, a gradient-based method that models planning as a random relaxation with Gaussian curves, running well on graphics processors.

Writing plans as smooth Gaussian values captures the order of time and shrinks the tuning space many times over. The method freely handles varied goals and constraints, giving the first gradient-based version for complex staged scheduling. On a range of benchmarks, GauS reaches Pareto-optimal results.
arxiv-2602-20527:
Deep reinforcement learning struggles in teaching systems. It needs many samples and a well-set reward rule. Md Mirajul Islam and four co-authors turn to expert-copying learning. That method infers an expert's hidden reward rules from a few examples. It then builds rules that carry over and match best acts. Their broad method, THEMES, tracks expert student learning where many reward rules may shift over time. It builds good teaching rules.

Tested against six top rivals, THEMES ranks best. It hits high scores with an area under the curve near zero point nine and a Jaccard near zero point six five. It uses only eighteen runs from a past term to predict student teaching choices in a later term. The method gives a strong other way to build teaching rules from scarce expert data.
arxiv-2602-20627:
Monocular 3D object detection is intrinsically ill-posed, so strong models need huge labeled sets spanning scenes, objects, and poses. Zhaonian Kuang and four co-authors observe that training images entangle those three factors: specific objects always appear in particular scenes with fixed camera poses. That wastes data and invites overfitting to uniform samples. Their object-scene-camera decomposition and recomposition scheme breaks that entanglement to exploit training data better.

The scheme first splits training images into textured 3D object models and background scenes, efficiently for compute and storage. Each epoch, it rebuilds fresh training images by inserting objects into free background space and rendering them with perturbed camera poses. Refreshed data across epochs spans the full range of object, scene, and pose combinations. The scheme plugs into detectors under full and sparse supervision. Tests on five models across the KITTI and Waymo sets confirm its value.
arxiv-2602-20727:
Xindian Ma and four co-authors propose ID-LoRA, a lean way to tune large language models for new tasks. Scaling up still brings heavy trainable load, and sharply cutting rank harms multi-task scores.

ID-LoRA extracts and reuses clustered parameter groups from the trained weight matrix, forming many low-rank parts that share a single starting trainable low-rank matrix. That design cuts trainable weights while keeping model power intact. Tests on five benchmarks, math thinking, code writing, MMLU, CommonsenseQA, and safety, show it beats full tuning and current rivals. It uses up to forty-six percent fewer trainable weights than standard LoRA. In multi-task settings it beats LoRA and recent versions on code and MMLU, needing only fifty-four percent of standard LoRA's trainable weights.
arxiv-2602-21327:
Equally skilled job-seekers present on their own not alike: some self-promote while others omit crucial facts with modesty. Elbert Du, Cynthia Dwork, Lunjia Hu, Reid McIlroy-Young, Han Shao, and Linjun Zhang tackle that weighing problem in this 2026 arXiv paper with a back-and-forth AI for skill drawing out. The system finds skills right while letting people speak in their own voice.

Uses could include work linking joining or matching staff to needs during a reshuffle. A language model trained as fake humans supplies training data. Drawing out eases bias from self-reports on their own, and a strict fairness notion keeps the link between style manner and scoring error small, tackling orderly model bias too.
arxiv-2602-21827:
Alexander Lindermayr and one co-author study preemptive job ordering online over time on a single machine to cut flow time. In the old clairvoyant model, the planner learns a job's run time at arrival, and shortest remaining run time ordering wins. In the non-clairvoyant model, run time stays unknown until finish, and flow time cutting admits no constant contest ratio. The problem has thus been studied under speed boosts or predicted run times to attain constant promises.

The paper considers alpha-clairvoyant ordering, where the planner learns a job's run time once it finishes an alpha fraction. This bridges clairvoyant ordering at alpha zero and non-clairvoyant ordering at alpha one. Fusing two old methods, the authors propose an ordering rule with a contest ratio growing as alpha nears 1, shifting between known clairvoyant and non-clairvoyant bounds. A tight random lower bound rounds out the good result.
arxiv-2602-21927:
Ahmed Hussain, Asmaa Abdallah, and Abdulkadir Celik examine how the shape of a large flat antenna array affects beams that focus at close range. Future wireless systems, they note, will use big arrays at high frequencies, where beams can focus on a small region at a set depth instead of merely pointing in a direction. The 2026 arXiv paper derives the depth of focus for a general rectangular array and maps its limits.

With a fixed number of antenna elements, array shape matters a lot for focus depth, though the effect fades when the total array length is fixed instead. Long, thin arrays give a narrower focus and stretch the near-field zone, and they also yield the most spatial channels for sending parallel streams. The authors turn these findings into a new codebook for channel estimation that beat rival methods in simulation.
arxiv-2602-22027:
When a colony of still cells grows, it spreads not by crawling but by crowding: new cells shove their neighbors outward. Henri Berestycki and Antoine Mellet model this range expansion with a nonlinear, nonlocal equation for growth plus competition for space. The work is motivated by colonies of immotile cells, which show long-range shuffling when packed tight and can jam solid.

The authors first show the general evolution equation is well posed, then take a limit where spread happens only from saturated zones.
