That limit behaves like an obstacle problem with a moving free boundary marking the edge of the packed region. They prove a comparison property, track the boundary's motion, and find traveling waves with a definite asymptotic speed of spread.
arxiv-2602-22127:
L-functions encode deep arithmetic, and their average sizes, called moments, test how evenly their values spread. Sumit Kumar and two co-authors prove an upper bound for the second moment of a family of Rankin-Selberg L-functions, pairing a fixed three-dimensional form with primitive newforms of growing level. The bound matches what the Lindelöf hypothesis would predict, a gold standard for such estimates.

The result holds when the two prime levels stand in a controlled range, with the second level not much larger than the first. Within that range, the average of squared central values stays tightly bounded. Number theorists gain a sharp moment estimate for a family where direct values remain far out of reach.
arxiv-2602-22327:
Sub-Neptunes are among the most common exoplanets, yet their atmospheres remain hard to read. Nicole L. Wallack and nineteen co-authors present a mid-infrared transmission spectrum of HD 15337 c, a sub-Neptune orbiting a K-type star, observed with JWST as part of the COMPASS program. Two independent pipelines reduce the observations to consistent spectra.

The first visit's poorer precision traces to a missing pre-transit baseline, caused by an early transit arrival from previously unseen timing variations, hinting at an exterior companion. Combining timing data reveals variations over twenty minutes, showcasing JWST's timing precision. The spectrum itself is featureless, and the timing result stands as a discovery in its own right.
arxiv-2602-22427:
Retrieval-augmented generation leans on vector similarity search, but that search has a security flaw called hubness: some items appear in top results for a disproportionate share of varied queries. Idan Habler and four co-authors warn that hubs can be exploited to inject harmful content, skew rankings, bypass filters, and degrade performance. They introduce hubscan, an open-source scanner for vector indices and embeddings.

Hubscan combines four detectors: robust statistical hubness scoring, cluster-spread analysis of cross-cluster retrieval, stability testing under query perturbations, and domain- and modality-aware detection. Together they flag items whose retrieval dominance looks like poisoning rather than popularity. For teams running retrieval systems, it offers a security check before hubs become attack vectors.
arxiv-2602-23127:
James Binney constructs spread functions for spheroids. Galaxy models with several parts, including dark matter, bound by their self-made gravity field, are readily built from spread functions that are math functions of the action sums. The author shows why such models have unreal speed spreads unless the spread functions of hot parts meet certain rules as one angular momentum part tends to zero.

Spread functions for even and outward tilted round systems are built with given action dependence, as are spread functions for squashed systems with large speed gaps. Building self-made models rather than populations held by an outside pull leads to the finding that outward tilted round systems are usually wobbly under four-pole nudges. Chaos is likely key to keeping these constraints during slow disc growth.
arxiv-2602-23427:
Clara Murgui and one co-author propose a new dark matter signature: super-binomial variance in the count rate of an atom interferometer. Atom interferometers count atoms after interference, and the variance of that count usually follows binomial statistics for independent atoms. Dark matter would shift this variance, and the shift grows with N, the number of atoms per run, giving sensitivity orders of magnitude beyond an independent-atom estimate.

As an application, the authors consider dark matter interacting with electrons, protons, or neutrons through a long-range Yukawa interaction. That yields new constraints on strongly interacting dark matter that thermalizes in the overburden above conventional direct detection experiments. Searches for super-binomial variance extend and complement existing atom interferometer observables, and they suit both short- and long-ranged force searches, turning count fluctuations into a dark matter tool.
arxiv-2602-23527:
Guillaume Cébron and one co-author develop functional inequalities for Boolean entropy, building on the recently introduced notion. They define Boolean Fisher information through a de Bruijn identity and study its monotonicity in the Boolean Central Limit Theorem.

Several functional inequalities follow, including a logarithmic Sobolev inequality, alongside non-microstate counterparts with their own inequalities. The authors also introduce Stein discrepancy in the Boolean setting, leading to new Berry-Esseen type bounds in the Boolean central limit theorem. The short paper thus extends a toolkit of analytic inequalities, Fisher information, and discrepancy measures from classical probability into the Boolean domain.
arxiv-2602-23727:
Meng Li and one co-author propose direct spectral speedup of first-order methods for saddle point problems with two-linear coupling. Such problems cover limited convex tuning and more general models via a prox-friendly term in the dual goal. In steady-gain regimes, the team maps how spectral traits of the coupling matrix and goal shape set the best linear rates.

The new speedup applies to first-order primal-dual methods for two-linear-coupled saddle point problems, including affine-limited smooth strongly convex tuning and spinoffs. The final methods split goal-led and coupling-led regimes and attain best linear gains without inner loops. Random block extensions in the affine-limited case with split goals are built, with best linear rates matching the block lower bound. For fixed and random methods, matching worst-case lower bounds are given via set finite-dim hard cases.
arxiv-2602-23827:
Junkang Liu and four co-authors present FedNSAM, a federated learning method that keeps local and global flatness in step. The 2026 paper notes that standard sharpness-aware training flattens each client's loss, but under strongly varied client data that does not flatten the shared global model, so generalization suffers.

The authors define a flatness distance to explain the gap, then add global Nesterov momentum to local updates. That momentum steers each client's estimate of the global perturbation and extrapolates it, harmonizing local and global flatness. Theory gives a tighter convergence bound than the earlier FedSAM method. Tests on convolutional and transformer models show better accuracy and efficiency. The method offers a practical fix for federated training where client data differ sharply.
arxiv-2602-23927:
Laura Bocchi and three co-authors present a multiparty session type framework with asynchronous mixed choice. The 2026 paper addresses distributed protocols where participants may briefly disagree about protocol state, a reality of asynchronous messaging that stricter session types often rule out.

The core construct for mixed choice allows transient inconsistencies between participants while guaranteeing that all can always reach a mutually consistent state again. Correctness is proved through a progress property and an operational correspondence between global types and their distributed local projections. A practical toolchain built on the theory specifies and validates such protocols and programs compliant processes in Erlang's gen_statem framework. The team tests it by reimplementing part of the RabbitMQ client's AMQP handling. The end goal is a set of rules that still works when views briefly differ.
arxiv-2603-00127: Das and colleagues tackle segmentation of low-contrast XCT scans of concrete, where aggregates and mortar attenuate X-rays alike, so intensity-only tools fail. Vision transformers and convolutional networks can help but need labelled data, scarce or costly to obtain. Their self-annotation method groups similar local regions with superpixel algorithms, then ties them to global context via a convolutional model's receptive field. Against hand-labelled ground truth on unseen data, it beats greyscale thresholding on every metric, with the best sensitivity-precision balance for aggregate-phase spotting.
arxiv-2603-00327: Rodriguez and dell'Isola revisit the Principle of Virtual Work and balance laws in Paul Germain's distributional framework. They show the principle implies force and moment balance for higher-gradient continua, yet balance laws alone cannot characterize equilibrium at gradient order two or above. Re-examining Noll's theorem, they show its extra assumptions — no edge or wedge contact interactions, and bounded surface contact density — fail for general higher-gradient materials. Such curvature-dependent surface forces therefore do not contradict Noll's theorem, refuting his claim of their nonexistence.
arxiv-2603-00427: Lee offers one framework to reconcile conflicting cosmic time dilation signals from supernovae, gamma ray bursts, and quasars. Exploding stars show the classic stretch with redshift, bursts scatter widely, and quasar variability often shows none. He argues bound transient sources act as shielded geometric clocks tracing pure path dilation, while quasar disks observed at fixed wavelengths carry a selection effect that hides the signal. Splitting global coordinate time from local proper time in bound systems thus unifies the three behaviours without changing local physics.
arxiv-2603-01227: Xiong floats the Lattice Representation Hypothesis: a sign backbone grounding concept trees and logical moves in vector geometry. Linear trait ways with cutoff thresholds induce a concept lattice through half-space crossings, giving sign thought via shape meet and join moves, with a standard form when ways are free. Tests on WordNet trees show model vectors encode concept lattices and their logic, bridging smooth space and sign ideas.
arxiv-2603-02027:
Javier Lafuente Lopez proves a rigidity result for spacetimes that share the same Ricci curvature. His 2026 work defines a viable spacetime as one that admits a complete timelike geodesic. Timelike geodesics are the paths of freely falling observers, and completeness means they extend forever.

Take two causal spacetimes linked by a map that preserves causal structure and the Ricci tensor. If either spacetime is viable, that map must be a homothety, a pure rescaling of the metric. No stranger deformation can keep both causality and Ricci curvature fixed under the viability condition. Results of this kind limit how much freedom the Einstein equations leave once curvature data are pinned down. Causal order is pinned down too, a uniqueness theme at the core of relativity.
arxiv-2603-02227:
Keston Aquino-Michaels asks whether a transformer can learn which links matter in this 2026 paper. Attention links are highly focused, and a small gate can spot the key ones after training. Yet when sparse attention trains as a whole, learned gates barely beat random ones. Aquino-Michaels names this failure routing absorption and tests it on a small transformer.

Four lines of proof point the same way: the model's core weights adapt to any mask imposed. Soft gates learned or random end at near-equal quality. Hard gates get no learning signal through the mask at all. A gate copied onto adapted weights fails badly on fresh weights. Even random masks during training fail to stop the adaptation. Sparse methods with per-query gates face this pressure in full.
arxiv-2603-02327:
E Leitinger, A Miglio, J Montalbán, and colleagues question the origin of nitrogen-rich stars in this 2026 paper. Globular clusters are ancient star groups with distinct chemical patterns. Lone stars in the galaxy with those patterns are usually assumed to be cluster escapees. The team widens the search across the Kepler field, in halo and disc regions alike.

Star vibrations yield masses and ages, which are linked to chemistry and motion. Their sample holds over a hundred red giants, most with measured masses. Of twenty enriched stars, only a few are old enough to plausibly come from clusters. Most look too young, which likely reflects binary mergers or mass transfer, not true youth. Cluster origin thus fails for most of these field stars.
arxiv-2603-02427:
Ilias Triantafyllopoulos and Panos Ipeirotis detect careless survey respondents without labels in this 2026 paper. Surveys lose value when some respondents answer randomly or with low effort. Attention checks catch some, but they cost time and work inconsistently. Their framework scores each response set for coherence, using two unsupervised views.

One view rebuilds responses with an autoencoder and flags poor rebuilds. The other models dependencies between answers with a tree structure. A new loss makes the autoencoder sturdier against odd cases. Across nine real data sets, survey design mattered more than model complexity. Surveys with coherent, overlapping question batteries let even linear models separate careless respondents well. Good measurement design and easy detection, they show, go hand in hand.
arxiv-2603-02527:
Chengkang Xu determines when certain symmetry modules can be unitary in this 2026 mathematics paper. The setting is the gap-p Virasoro algebra, a family of infinite-dimensional symmetry algebras. Modules encode how the algebra acts on a space of states. A module is unitary when its action respects a positive inner product.

Xu focuses on irreducible Harish-Chandra modules, a well-behaved class with controlled weight spaces. For any such module, the paper determines the exact condition for unitarity. That condition separates the modules that admit a consistent quantum-mechanical reading from those that cannot. Representation theory of Virasoro-type algebras leans on such classifications. Knowing precisely which modules are unitary guides both pure mathematics and conformal field theory.
arxiv-2603-02627:
Praful Gagrani, Jiwei Wang, Yannick De Decker, and David Lacoste bound growth rates in chemical reaction networks in this 2026 paper. Networks of reactions underlie prebiotic chemistry and cell metabolism alike. Growth or shrinkage is usually studied through detailed kinetics with many parameters. Their approach needs only stoichiometry, the bookkeeping of what each reaction consumes and produces.

In the balanced-growth regime, they derive constraints on how fast a network can grow. A topological quantity, the maximum amplification factor, controls those bounds. It comes from an optimization over feasible reaction fluxes. Numerical tests on random network ensembles illustrate the bounds in action. The results speak to origin-of-life chemistry, where autocatalysis enables self-maintenance and growth. Synthetic network designers can also use the bounds as a structural check.
arxiv-2603-02827:
Sabine Cornelsen, Jan Kratochvíl, Miriam Münch, and colleagues ask when a graph can be drawn as strings hanging from one line. In such a drawing, each vertex is a curve below a baseline, and curves cross exactly when vertices are linked. Their 2026 paper restricts the curves to simple L-shaped bends and studies series-parallel graphs without shortcut edges.

They prove that, for these graphs, a drawing with double-bend strings exists exactly when a plain string drawing exists. A fast linear-time test decides the question. One catch remains: they build a graph that allows the double-bend form but not the stricter single L-shape. The gap between the two drawing styles is real, and now precisely located.
arxiv-2603-02927:
Tom Reichert and Iurii Karpenko separate a true signal from a shadow in collisions of atomic nuclei. Their 2026 paper concerns elliptic flow, the sideways pattern of particles flying out of heavy-ion collisions. A tidy scaling of that flow with quark count is taken as evidence for quark-gluon plasma, the hot early-universe state.

Recent STAR results show the scaling breaks at lower collision energies, but blocking by the passing spectator nuclei muddies the reading. The authors define new measures of how much flow each direction absorbs, effectively unshadowing the emitting source. A simple ballistic toy model shows how strongly shadowing distorts the scaling. Their cleanup matters for reading STAR data and for the coming CBM experiment.
arxiv-2603-03027:
Anne-Marie Aubert and Roger Plymen describe an algebra whose representation theory is shaped like a Klein bottle. Their 2026 paper works over a local field and studies a depth-zero building block for representations of the group SL8. The block is governed by a twisted Hecke algebra built from quadratic and quartic field extensions.

They write the algebra down fully, with generators and relations, and list all its simple modules, each just two-dimensional. The algebra's spectrum is an explicit variety whose compact real form is a Klein bottle, the one-sided surface, and that bottle models a family of unitary representations. Comparing with the classical untwisted setting, the two Bernstein varieties match exactly. The Klein bottle reappears, now floating inside the tempered dual of the full group.
arxiv-2603-03527:
Betul Yurdem and three colleagues measure how unsure medical vision-language models are, directly from their output scores. Such models now read pathology images beside text prompts, and clinical use demands trust. Their 2026 framework probes uncertainty at the logit level, the raw scores behind each answer, by varying the sampling temperature and tracking how much the outputs wobble.

Three models face the test, scored by similarity and divergence measures between repeated outputs. Two general medical models prove highly twitchy: their answers shift sharply, with abrupt uncertainty jumps on complex diagnostic prompts. The pathology-specific model PRISM behaves near-deterministically, barely moved by temperature at any prompt complexity. The contrast argues that logit-level uncertainty checks should gate clinical deployment, since a model's specialty training shows up clearly in its stability.
arxiv-2603-03727:
John Driscoll and five colleagues ask parents what they actually want from controls on children's chatbot use, using fake conversations to make the question concrete. A language model generated synthetic child-chatbot exchanges, four parents vetted them for realism, and twelve diverse, concerning examples were put to twenty-four parents. Their 2026 study records what worried them, what they would change, and how they wish to be told.

Three findings stand out. Parents worry about interactions that today's parental controls never flag. They want transparency and moderation at the level of the individual conversation, not blunt category switches. And they want controls that personalize, adapting to each family's strategy and each child's age. The authors aim the results squarely at designers of the next generation of family safety tools.
arxiv-2603-04027: Chen and others present test-driven tuning for auto configuration in stream processing systems. Tuning such systems for efficient cloud-native results is challenging and largely manual. Evaluation with Kafka Streams shows throughput gains up to 23% over defaults, with sampling plus early termination and annealing most effective and hill climbing adding limited benefit.
arxiv-2603-04127: Farzam and others propose a data-aware random feature kernel for models. Transformers excel, yet quadratic focus blocks scaling, and random-feature focus cuts cost to linear by estimating the softmax kernel. In pretrained models, anisotropic queries and keys cause high variance under isotropic sampling unless retrained. By data-aligning the softmax kernel, the authors obtain focus with a tractable minimal-variance proposal and better balance. Their DARKFormer learns the random-projection covariance, building an importance-sampled estimator efficiently, and narrows the gap with exact softmax focus.
arxiv-2603-04227: Li and others propose constraint-aware making re-ranking for multi-objective tuning in advertising feeds. They propose a constraint-aware making reranking method transforming constrained tuning into bounded neural decoding. Unlike earlier methods separating generator and evaluator models, their method merges sequence output and reward gauging in a single network. They further add constraint-aware reward pruning, which builds constraint satisfaction straight into decoding to efficiently produce optimal sequences.
arxiv-2603-04627: Akofor reviews completeness of spaces without induction. Completeness often rests on structures like metrics or uniformities that induce the topology. Fix instead a graded base of the topology, split into open covers, making a base space. Relaxing net convergence to approach between nets yields induction-free Cauchy nets, hence induction-free completeness. Many completeness results for uniform spaces carry over to locally symmetric base spaces, which contain uniform spaces. Carried results include existence of a completion, compactness profile, Baire's theorem, and completeness for product and function lsb-spaces.
arxiv-2603-05027: Janani Rangila and team present S5-SHB-Agent, a Society 5.0 smart home blockchain agent with resident governance. Smart home ecosystems need autonomous management of comfort, security, energy, and safety. Current methods use rigid contracts with fixed accord, a single AI model at most, and no resident governance. The method orchestrates ten agents with interchangeable language models across safety, security, comfort, energy, privacy, and health. An adaptive blockchain adjusts mining difficulty by transaction volume and emergencies, while tiered governance lets residents control automation from routine changes to immutable safety thresholds.
arxiv-2603-05327: Tai Le Quy and team offer FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based method generating synthetic financial data while mitigating bias for a protected attribute. Financial data sets often carry bias leading to unfair automated choices. Fairness constraints enter training through a classifier, ensuring synthetic data stays fair while keeping downstream predictive utility. Tested on five real-world financial data sets against current GAN-based making methods, the approach reaches superior fairness metrics without marked utility loss. It shows likely as a bias-aware making tool for financial uses.
arxiv-2603-05527: Hu brings Drifting Models into molecular conformation generation, a first for the method. The Drifting Score Identity links the drifting field's pull to a kernel-weighted average of any distribution's score, and force labels yield the Drifting Force Identity. Adding force flips across forms. Coordinate-space Force-Interpolated Drifting blends force directions with data shifts, while distance-feature-space Force-Aligned Kernel changes only kernel weights. On MD17 ethanol, both make samples in one step with over 1000 times speedup and million-fold speedup over standard molecular dynamics.
arxiv-2603-05627: Harding and Wilce define what it means for one broad chance model to explain another: a special kind of span in Prob, the group of chance models and maps. They join under a standard pullback build, even though Prob does not support any pullbacks. Every locally-finite chance model then has a standard, sharp classic explanation. This rule spreads this to every locally-finite chance theory, giving a standard, sharp classic picture, though usually non-local.
arxiv-2603-05727: El Ichi and team present a spectral splitting of vectors using the L-product for third-order tensors, tackling setting growth and repeat. Shaping tokens into spectral slices moves attention and feed-forward work into the transform domain. The Tensor Transformer splits the encoder into p spectral sub-transformers, keeping standard Transformer meaning. The L-Transformer equals p side-by-side Transformers on smaller vectors, yielding about 1/p encoder setting cut. Slice-set rate scaling improves spread. On IMDB and AG News, encoder settings fall up to 75% for p=4.
arxiv-2603-06227: Kim and his team assess the soundness and efficiency of AGN selection by mid IR variability, matching active and inactive Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxies with multi epoch NEOWISE photometry. Joining non variability deviation likelihood with W1 W2 correlation picks out AGNs well across W1 and W2 light curves over a ten year span. The method finds about 28.2 percent of light-selected AGNs, and finds AGN candidates in inactive galaxies at shares under 12 percent.
arxiv-2603-06427: Motta and colleagues examine control-affine systems with unbounded controls under impulsive extensions. Widening controls can guarantee optimal solutions yet open a gap between the infimum and the extended minimum under endpoint constraints. Since Warga's work, normality of first-order necessary conditions has been a sufficient, though far from necessary, safeguard against gaps. They prove higher-order normality, built from iterated Lie brackets of system vector fields, prevents an infimum gap. The novelty is using the L1 distance between controls, rather than the L infinity distance between trajectories, as topology.
arxiv-2603-06527: Bédel and colleagues propose a solution to an inverse problem in protrusion force microscopy, where cells exert a pressure field on their environment around the membrane. Traction force microscopy can in principle measure the pressure field. Protrusion force microscopy accesses it at high spatial resolution by measuring deformation of a thin elastic membrane with atomic force microscopy. While the pressure field is three-dimensional, the atomic-force height profile is only one-dimensional, and the authors explore the solution's regime of applicability in the experimental context.
arxiv-2603-06627: Uddagiri and team develop a mid-scale grain-envelope model for grain growth under additive manufacturing conditions, showing dendritic grains' surface through a diffuse interface. A heat-conduction model with moving heat sources and latent-heat release supplies the thermal field, while shell spread follows a tiny-melt-based kinetic law. Tested in two- and three-dimensional simulations, the model is applied to parameter effects on grain mix evolution. The authors say it offers an efficient, forward-looking approach for grain growth during multi-pass, multi-layer build-up.
arxiv-2603-06727: Feng and colleagues propose Safe Transformer, which inserts a discrete bottleneck with a readable safety flag amid the model's layers. The flag is readable as the model's safety call. It acts as a switch: one value yields helpful answers, the other yields refusals, while extra unsupervised bits carry meaning for generation. Contrastive training disentangles the safety choice from content. The design needs only light fine-tuning, and red-team tests show near-zero attack success.
arxiv-2603-06927: An and colleagues build an RGB-D system that marks safe free space for robots. Vision models often miss thin obstacles like chair legs, a safety risk. Their system pairs RGB images with 1D laser depth to capture interactions and improve detection of obstacles. Few-shot learning generalizes from few examples, cutting reliance on datasets. Older methods use only positive prototypes, risking overfitting. The team adds a contrastive branch using obstacle prototypes to refine free-space predictions, plus a two-stage attention depth module aligning depth vectors.
arxiv-2603-07027: Wang and colleagues propose resource-adaptive federated text generation with differential privacy. In cross-silo learning, sensitive text stays local under privacy rules, so retraining per task costs much bandwidth and privacy budget. A fix is private synthetic data that mimics the global mix for reuse across tasks. Yet pretrained models fail under domain shift, and uneven compute blocks weak clients from tuning, worsening skew and noise. Their framework adapts to client power: strong clients tune privately, while weak clients vote lightly to refine synthetic data.
arxiv-2603-07227: Leach and colleagues study model choice for peak value fit on changing desert heat peaks from CMIP6 output. Using annual maxima and minima of near-surface temperature, they fit generalized extreme value regression models with different time-varying parameter forms by Bayesian inference. They then compare candidates with Akaike, Bayesian, divergence, and widely-applicable information criteria. Since rule scores in peak settings are shaky, they run a model study with known ground-truth models to judge which rules best predict changes in peak levels.
arxiv-2603-07727: Jang, Carrington and Begel map social access research from 2011 to 2025, analyzing 90 papers from a 605-paper set. Their Three Praxes Framework names Artifact as making, Ecosystem as linking, and Epistemology as idea-based. Two stances and one looping cycle link the praxes. The praxes largely operate apart, risking insights that stay classroom tasks while assistive tools prop up old walls. They urge the field to build a cycle where disabled people's daily lives shape built worlds, built practice yields idea knowledge, and both transform networks of access.
arxiv-2603-08127: Lyu and colleagues present EvoScientist, a multi-agent AI scientist framework that keeps improving its research plans instead of following a fixed pipeline. Static, hand-designed AI scientist systems miss promising directions, repeat failed tests, and chase infeasible ideas because they never learn from past work. EvoScientist splits the work among three agents: a Researcher Agent generating ideas, an Engineer Agent running tests, and an Evolution Manager Agent turning lessons from prior work into reusable knowledge. Two memory modules store feasible directions and effective test methods.
arxiv-2603-08227: Wang and colleagues present SRNeRV, a scale-wise recursive framework for neural video representation. Implicit neural representations offer a promising route for video coding and compression, but current multi-scale generators stack their own processing blocks per scale, creating heavy parameter overlap. Using scale self-similarity in generation, SRNeRV replaces the stacked design with a shared architecture. Its hybrid sharing scheme splits each block into a scale-specific spatial mixer and a scale-invariant channel mixer, reusing the latter across all scales to cut model size.
arxiv-2603-08527: Alexander Fel'shtyn and Mateusz Slomiany track how Reidemeister and Nielsen counts grow when maps are repeated. For tame pairs on nilpotent groups and on compact nilmanifolds, they prove Gauss-style congruences for the count sequences. They also prove the Nielsen coincidence zeta function is rational and show the growth rate exists for the nilmanifold case.
arxiv-2603-08827: Prachi Nandi and colleagues build a low-cost smart parking system on computer vision. Fixed sensors struggle with limits and integration, while vision adapts to changing layouts and spots cars and empty bays better. Their system merges four camera views by inverse perspective mapping, extracts vacant spots, and renders a 3D plot to guide drivers.
arxiv-2603-08927: Xinqi Fan and colleagues run the 2026 micro-expression grand challenge on video question answering. Micro-expressions are brief, involuntary face movements people show while trying to hide an emotion, usually in high-stakes settings. The challenge adds two tasks, short-video and long-video question answering, and requires all entrants to post results on a public leaderboard.
arxiv-2603-09027: Thomas Schrøder and colleagues test the random barrier model against the von Schweidler law for viscous liquid dynamics. Combining particle-swap Monte Carlo with long GPU dynamics, they study a three-part Lennard-Jones glass former deep in the viscous regime. The barrier model, with no free parameters, generally fits inherent mean-squared displacement data better, predicting diffusion coefficients from short-time data more accurately.
arxiv-2603-09127: Hajime Shimao and colleagues show that committees of language models can turn tiny text changes into wholly different decisions. In a deterministic self-hosted setup, exact reruns match, yet small meaning-preserving edits still push talks apart over time and often flip the final advice. Deployed API committees also stay unstable even at temperature zero. Design choices such as role structure and feedback memory change how far runs diverge, framing stability as its own problem.
arxiv-2603-09327: Xiaofeng Wang and colleagues develop a framework for forming exotic muonic kaon atoms in semileptonic D0 decays at high-energy colliders. Combining the effective weak Hamiltonian, a helicity treatment of the leptonic current, and a bound-state projection, they compute the branching ratio. The estimate feeds a ROOT-based code projecting yields at RHIC, the LHC, and STCF. They argue these atoms probe low-momentum primordial muons and early electromagnetic radiation in unexplored phase space.
arxiv-2603-09527: Luxi Lin and colleagues introduce Efficient Draft Adaptation, a cheap way to realign draft models for speculative decoding after a target model is fine-tuned. Retraining a draft model per target is costly, and naive drafts lose acceptance speed on domain-tuned targets. Their design splits shared and private parts so only a light private piece updates, regenerates training data from the fine-tuned target, and selects high-value samples. Tests restore speculative performance with better average acceptance lengths.
arxiv-2603-09827: Kangsan Kim and colleagues define a new task: answering questions across first person videos from several embodied agents at once. Future homes and workplaces may run many such agents side by side, each seeing its own stream. Their MA-EgoQA benchmark holds questions in five areas, from social acts to time based reasoning. Current models cope poorly, while their shared memory baseline does better.
arxiv-2603-10027: Gárate and coauthors set out a rule and test frame for rule based help with first guess antibiotic choice. Such choice happens with patchy facts, where wrong cover or needless step up can harm patients and stewardship alike. Their design keeps clinic logic apart from rules that decide if advice may be given at all. Fixed conduct, clear abstention and exclusion rules make the tool open to audit and cautious by design, so high risk choice stays safe.
arxiv-2603-10427: Lucia Oliva, Qun Wang, and Xin-Nian Wang study spin correlation among the quarks inside hyperons, as seen through global spin polarization in heavy-ion collisions. Data on hyperon polarization and on spin alignment of vector mesons both constrain the phase space functions that describe spin polarization and correlation. Under some approximations, those constraints turn into inequalities. The authors argue the inequalities might offer clues that quark spin correlation is present inside hyperons at lower collision energies, where direct probes are scarce.
arxiv-2603-10627: J Chryssanthacopoulos and co-authors introduce GoBlocks, a Go package for evaluating conformal blocks quickly, built for the conformal bootstrap. Such blocks are basic pieces of theories that look the same at every scale, and in odd dimensions they have no closed form. GoBlocks uses recursive relations for rapid, parallel evaluation, with control over accuracy and speed. Benchmarks against scalar_blocks show large speed gains where moderate accuracy suffices. As a test, they ran the mixed-correlator bootstrap of the 3D Ising model.
arxiv-2603-10727: Vishva Patel analyzes energy extraction from Kerr, Reissner-Nordstrom, and Kerr-Newman spacetimes, and what it does to naked singularities over time. Rotation alone extracts little in Kerr, capped by geometry, while charge and rotation together extract most in Kerr-Newman. Equations for how mass, spin, and charge evolve show steady extraction can drive an over-extremal object toward the extremal bound. That makes such objects look unstable, and forming a horizon is the outcome that settles them.
arxiv-2603-10927: Daniel Pezzi proves sharp bounds on eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on the square torus, settling the discrete restriction conjecture with no loss for large exponents in dimensions five and up. The result improves on Bourgain and Demeter, giving the first sharp bounds of this kind since Cooke and Zygmund. The proof refines a circle method that earlier work had pushed only to subpolynomial losses. Applications include sharp bounds for spectral projectors and for the additive energy of lattice points on higher-dimensional spheres.
arxiv-2603-11127: Manik Dawar and coauthors give the first estimate of what a global quantum network built from satellite entanglement sources and ground repeaters could achieve with current and near-term technology. They fold a satellite-to-ground link model into a framework for repeater resources. It accounts for entanglement swapping and purification. They tune the end-to-end rate. Low Earth orbit constellations paired with neutral atom or vacancy-based repeaters could spread entanglement up to 20,000 kilometers, enough to connect any two points on Earth.
arxiv-2603-11827: Peretzke and co-authors build RICE-NET, a deep learning model that tells tumor recurrence apart from radiation-induced contrast changes in treated glioblastoma patients. The model joins follow-up MRI scans with radiotherapy dose maps, reading standard T1-weighted images. On 92 patients it scores an F1 of 0.92 on a held-out test set. Ablation tests show the radiation map carries most of the signal. Occlusion checks confirm the model looks at regions doctors find relevant.
arxiv-2603-11927: Zhai and co-authors present CogSearch, a multi-agent framework that turns e-commerce search into proactive decision support. Standard search just retrieves and ranks, leaving shoppers to juggle hard choices alone. Four specialist agents split the work: breaking down user intent, fusing store and outside knowledge, and shaping clear answers. Offline tests favor it on consultative and complex queries. Live A/B tests on JD.com cut decision costs by 5% and lifted overall conversion slightly. For decision-heavy queries, conversion jumped by 30%.
arxiv-2603-12027: Nguyen-Kha and co-authors tackle power use in Earth observation missions on low Earth orbit satellites. High-resolution images create huge data volumes, yet satellite power budgets stay tight and the orbit keeps shifting. Their framework pairs semantic communication with joint source-channel coding, sending meaning rather than raw pixels. A curve-fitting model links compression, signal quality, and image quality, which the hard joint problem needs. Their JCRRA algorithm then cuts total transmit power well below greedy and conventional schemes.
arxiv-2603-12227: Fumanal-Idocin, Jamalifard, and Andreu-Perez explain contrastive embeddings in set domains with fuzzy rules. Free text fills legal files and medical records, yet machines need structured input. CLIP turns text and images into shared vectors, but domain shifts weaken its output. A fuzzy rule-based classifier maps features of interest into the CLIP space. The learned rules show which features drive each class in plain form. Trials on clinical reports and film reviews, alone and mixed, reveal both the value and the limits of the route.
arxiv-2603-12327: Denney and co-authors build a traveling-wave parametric amplifier with diplexers on the chip itself. TWPAs give superconducting readout high gain at near quantum-limited noise over wide bandwidth. A strong pump tone must reach the device, usually via off-chip couplers or diplexers. Those external parts add loss, bulk, and limits on scaling to many channels. Integrated input and output diplexers route the pump on chip instead. The co-fabricated design offers a compact, scalable route for superconducting-circuit readout chains.
arxiv-2603-12427: Bhadra and Daniels speed up inference for enriched Dirichlet process mixtures with variational Bayes and truncation. Bayesian nonparametric models often demand complex MCMC runs that scale poorly. It rests on a truncation scheme built for these mixtures. It serves twice: as a leaner scheme and as warm starts for Gibbs or Pólya urn samplers. Checks come with a simple Nimble implementation. Simulations confirm the approximations, and a real dataset shows the workflow in use.
arxiv-2603-12627: Chenkai Ma and co-authors refine regret bounds for batched kernelized bandits, a black-box optimization task with noisy feedback. Queries arrive in batches, and the unknown function has bounded norm in a kernel space. They pin down the optimal batch count, constants included, and remove a batch factor from prior regret. New lower bounds cover adaptive batch sizes, which match fixed sizes in scaling. A robust variant also keeps the same regret bound under adversarial shifts.
arxiv-2603-12827: Yunsong Yang and co-authors test whether dependent types can be embedded in set theory in a feasible, mechanized way. In the types-as-sets view, they map dependent function types and universe levels into first-order logic. The target theory is Tarski-Grothendieck set theory, carried out in the Lisa proof assistant. On that base, they build a proof-producing type-checking tactic with partial subtyping support. Examples show verified automated reasoning for dependent types from set axioms alone.
arxiv-2603-12927: D Sokolovski and co-authors examine highly inaccurate measurements in both classical stochastic systems and quantum ones. A weak quantum measurement keeps coherence between the system's alternatives alive. The team shows that single-trial information about which scenario occurred is lost either way. Ensemble traits can still be read from the gathered statistics. Post-selection only reshuffles outcomes among final states, they argue. Odd meter readings thus come from reshaping a broad spread, not from rare huge values.
arxiv-2603-13027: Tianhao Fu and co-authors release SortScrews, a dataset and baseline for classifying screws from single-object images. Sorting hardware needs this skill, yet public datasets for it are scarce. The set holds 560 RGB images across six screw types plus a background class. Images come from a standard setup with mild shifts in light and camera angle. A reusable capture script helps others build like sets cheaply. Light transfer models reached strong accuracy despite the small dataset size.
arxiv-2603-13227: Helen Qu and co-authors test how well self-supervised methods learn physics-grounded representations. Most work on spatiotemporal physical systems aims at next-frame prediction, which is costly and error-prone. The team instead judges models on downstream tasks, like estimating governing physical parameters. Generic self-supervised methods sometimes beat methods built for physical modeling, they find. Methods that learn in latent space, such as JEPAs, beat pixel-level prediction methods. Parameter estimates thus offer a clear window on what a model has truly learned.
arxiv-2603-13327: Aaron Shen and Alfred Shen present DOVA, a multi-agent platform for autonomous research tasks. Single agents struggle with work that needs many sources, adversarial checks, and tailored delivery. DOVA puts deliberation first, so meta-reasoning runs before any tool is called. A persistent user model and entity-aware context guide that first step. A three-phase pipeline blends ensemble diversity, blackboard transparency, and iterative refinement. A six-level token-budget scheme cuts inference cost on simple tasks while keeping deep reasoning for hard ones.
arxiv-2603-13627: Mohammad Mostafanejad, Paul Saxe, and T. Daniel Crawford study chemical language models for molecular property prediction. Such models rival classic machine learning, but published results clash across benchmark tasks. The team runs hundreds of tightly controlled experiments on pre-training and fine-tuning. They vary dataset size, model size, and standardization, one factor at a time. Their goal is hard numbers and a clearer view of what drives model performance. Some key factors, they note, have been overlooked in the literature so far.
arxiv-2603-13827: Chandra, Paensin, and Dumke show how a Rydberg-atom sensor can measure electric fields at very low frequencies, from 0.5 Hz to 10 kHz. Normal vapor cells screen out such fields, which has blocked this range until now. Their setup pairs a paraffin-coated cell with added modulation and lock-in detection, and needs no electrodes. Reported sensitivity reaches 2 microvolts per centimeter per root hertz at 1 kHz. The method opens bands from sub-ELF up through VLF for atom-based sensing.
arxiv-2603-13927: Da Silva and co-authors tackle data augmentation for imbalanced classification tasks. Standard oversampling often makes samples that break domain rules or could never occur. Their framework, DPG-da, pulls decision rules from a trained model as plain predicates. New samples must obey those rules, so the added data stay valid and readable. On synthetic and real benchmarks, the method beats classic oversampling on accuracy. It also explains each generated sample in clear terms.
arxiv-2603-14127: Marichal, Passarella, and Randall analyze and reimplement a method that finds the pith, or growth center, in images of rough log ends. The method, by Schraml and Uhl, uses local Fourier spectrum analysis on the log face. The authors give a Python version of the algorithm. They test it on two datasets of log end images. Results on both datasets are discussed in detail.
arxiv-2603-14427: Dvořák, Kang, and Mikšaník prove a form of the Borodin-Kostochka conjecture for correspondence coloring. The 1977 guess says a graph with large maximum degree and a smaller clique number needs at most one fewer color than that degree. The authors prove the bound for the stronger correspondence chromatic number, once the maximum degree is huge. The result strengthens Reed's theorem for standard coloring. It also extends a list-coloring version by Choi, Kierstead, and Rabern.
arxiv-2603-14627: Chen, Guo and Wu prove monotonicity for a fractional semilinear equation in a half space. All positive solutions rise strictly along the x_n direction, they show. Past results asked for solutions bounded across the whole space. Here each slab alone needs a bound, a weaker ask. Only local Lipschitz control of the nonlinearity is used. A boundary Hölder estimate needs just near-boundary bounds. The moving planes proof adds a narrow region principle and two averaging effects for fractional equations.
arxiv-2603-15127: Niu and co-authors build HITS, a regional AI system for medium-range typhoon forecasts over the Asia-Pacific. Global AI models capture large-scale flow but blur the small structures that set a storm's strength and rain. HITS trains on a new 9-kilometer typhoon reanalysis dataset. It pairs regional autoregressive prediction with large-scale constraints from the ECMWF AI forecasting system. A variant adds structure-aware perceptual training for rainbands. The hybrid beat purely regional and downscaling models, and cut intensity errors by up to about 48 percent at 72 hours.
arxiv-2603-15327: Nayak and co-authors use low-frequency noise to probe hidden disorder in graphene grown by chemical vapor deposition. The 1/f noise in these films runs orders of magnitude above that in exfoliated single-crystal graphene. Grain boundaries and defect states in the polycrystalline film explain the excess. Temperature tests show the fluctuations come from thermally activated local defects. The results frame noise as a handy quality check for scalable graphene films. They also point to defect control as a lever for better large-area electronics.
arxiv-2603-15527: Tang and co-authors ask whether the dilemmas that large language models face in alignment can be fully solved. They sort the conflicts into a taxonomy, then draw the model's choices as a priority graph. Instructions and values form the nodes, and context sets the edge weights. That graph shifts across contexts and can clash with itself, which blocks any single stable alignment. They name a risk: priority hacking, where crafted contexts bend the graph past safety rules. A runtime check against external sources offers partial defense.
arxiv-2603-15727: Zhang and co-authors unveil AgentWorm, a self-spreading attack on agent ecosystems. Long-running agents with tools and messaging form dense, linked networks. One crafted message starts the whole infection cycle. The worm rewrites the victim's core configuration for persistence. It runs a payload at each reboot, then copies itself to new peers. Tests spanned five model backends, three entry paths, and three payload types. The aggregate success rate hit 63 percent. Key loop-breaking controls were off in all observed public setups.
arxiv-2603-15827: Ambrosone, Chianese, and Evoli probe slowed-down black holes with cosmic rays. Memory burden effects can choke Hawking evaporation from tiny primordial holes. Such holes then survive today and may form dark matter. The team computes proton and neutron output from burdened holes. Galactic halo and distant sources both enter the sums. Pierre Auger proton spectra set the main test bed. EeV neutron limits from the Galactic plane add a second check. For suppression k at 3 or more, bounds rival gamma-ray limits.
arxiv-2603-15927: Albi, Alla, and Calzola learn hidden interaction rules from agent swarm trajectories. Multi-agent systems hide their pairwise forces and diffusion terms from view. Only sparse trajectory data reach the analyst in their setup. The team casts kernel recovery as sparse regression tasks. Compact basis pieces span the search space. Two routes handle the unseen pairwise terms. Random-batch sampling keeps the full statistics in expectation. A mean-field route rebuilds density from data instead. Tests on benchmark swarms confirm the recovery.
arxiv-2603-16127: Yano and co-authors skip learning rate decay in pretraining to gain fine-tuning strength. Decay schedules chase the lowest pretraining loss by habit. Their Warmup-Stable-Only plan holds the rate flat after warmup. Tests span 1B and 8B parameter models in size. Decay wins right after pretraining on raw scores. After supervised fine-tuning, the flat-rate models win instead. Loss maps show decay traps models in sharper minima. Flat minima adapt better to later training stages. The pattern holds through mid-training and over-training runs.
arxiv-2603-16427: Kareinen and co-authors recognize plankton by pairing images with optical profiles. Hand labeling plankton photos is slow, so labeled sets stay small. Some instruments also record scatter and fluorescence profiles per particle. The team trains encoders for both data types together. Training needs only a yes-or-no signal: same particle or not. A small labeled gallery plus a neighbor classifier names the species. The method beat an image-only self-supervised baseline.
arxiv-2603-16627: Scholtenhuis and co-authors advance on-chip spectrometers for microwave background surveys. Studying the CMB and infrared background tests inflation and cluster history. Ground and space telescopes find full-sky detail slow and costly. On-chip superconducting units are compact and very sensitive. Recent versions still miss survey-grade needs, though. The team adds parts and fabrication tricks to close the gap. New cross-over parts and cleaner lithography help cut losses. The result is a working fourteen-spaxel integral field unit.
arxiv-2603-16727: Costa-Silva and Boschi-Filho fit light baryon spectra with anomalous holographic hard wall models. The hard wall picture reads hadron masses from a sliced AdS space. An anomalous term now shifts the operator dimensions. Its log form comes from a semiclassical look at AdS/CFT. Two variants tie the shift to angular momentum, one also to spin. A third lets the dimension grow as a power law. All three beat the plain hard wall on PDG masses. Their Regge trajectories come out near-linear.
arxiv-2603-16827: Eren and co-authors work on aligning language model outputs with the culture of a target population. Culture shapes reasoning, values, and choices, yet models often carry skewed defaults. Earlier work used survey-based metrics and hand-written culture prompts, mostly on closed models. This team re-checks those metrics on open-weight models. They then use DSPy prompt programming, treating prompts as programs tuned against a cultural-distance goal. In their tests, tuned prompts often beat hand engineering. They argue this route is more stable and transferable.
arxiv-2603-16927: Xu and co-authors design a cooperative perception system for teams of drones in low altitude networks. Drones see a scene from many views, but sending all that video is slow and costly. Their framework sends only the most informative pixels, chosen by a Top-K rule. A ground server fuses the sparse images into bird's eye view features for vehicle perception. A diffusion based learning algorithm picks which drones join and how much to sparsify. In simulations, the authors report perception gains over 5 percent with 85 percent less communication overhead.
arxiv-2603-17227: Dahal, Abdelfattah, and Rahimi ask whether the choice of anchors matters in 4D Gaussian streaming. Anchor driven methods rebuild a dynamic scene each frame from a compact set of Gaussian anchors. The default picks anchors by farthest point sampling at a fixed budget. The authors hold the pipeline fixed and swap in random, uniform, and heuristic samplers, plus a learned policy. At deployment budgets, the sampler had no measurable effect on quality. A cheap random sampler at half the budget matched the default.
arxiv-2603-17327: Sreelakshmi, Suresh, and Kattumannil develop empirical likelihood inference for two poverty measures, the Sen index and the Sen-Shorrocks-Thon index. Good confidence intervals for these indices let teams compare poverty across populations. The authors discuss empirical likelihood and its jackknife variant for both indices. For the jackknife route, they propose a new estimator of the Sen index built on U-statistics. They study the large sample traits of the ratio statistics and test finite sample performance in simulations.
arxiv-2603-17727: Akamine, Lee, and Yang prove Bernstein-type theorems for constant mean curvature graphs in the three-dimensional light cone. The graphs sit over the horosphere inside that cone. When Gaussian curvature stays bounded below, few shapes can occur. Entire such graphs must be horospheres or spheres of the cone, they show. The result echoes the classic Bernstein rigidity for minimal surfaces. Curvature control alone forces the global shape.
arxiv-2603-18227: Cech and co-authors study two phases that coexist in watched East circuit models. These ruled circuits mix chance-based steps with clean quantum steps. At any set watch strength, the records give a direct probe of which phase the system is in. The records map to states of a fake 1+1D spin chain for heat-style study. The two phases, one live and one quiet, still coexist in the quantum range as watch strength shifts.
arxiv-2603-18427: Che, Phan, and Lam present R&D, a pipeline that makes synthetic training images for semantic segmentation. Hand labels at pixel level cost much time, and plain image tweaks cannot make new shapes. Diffusion models can add shapes but often break the match with the label map. Their pipeline uses class-aware prompts and visual prior blending to keep labels true. On PASCAL VOC and BDD100K, scores rise most where real data is scarce.
arxiv-2603-18527: Wang, Jia, and Liu propose Neural Preconditioned Born Series for learning iterative neural PDE solvers. High-frequency waves in varied media challenge both classic iterative and neural solvers. A simple reference preconditioner feeds a network that predicts solution updates from preconditioned residuals. Training cuts the same preconditioned residual, giving a metric-matched objective. On heterogeneous Helmholtz problems, iteration counts fall, with larger gains at higher wavenumbers and the lowest wall-clock time in Krylov tests.
arxiv-2603-18627: Chen and co-authors add a closed feedback loop to text-to-image generation with AFS-Search. Static text encoders reason weakly about spatial relations, and open-loop sampling lets early errors grow. A vision-language model acts as critic, checking draft latents mid-run. Its spatial verdicts steer the flow field directly. Parallel rollouts explore several paths, and reward picks the best one. A Pro variant tops three benchmarks, while a Fast variant keeps most gains at higher speed. The method needs no training and builds on FLUX.1-dev.
arxiv-2603-18727: Degtyarev, Bakhurin, and Yudin design a conjugate gradient method to cancel self-interference in full-duplex radios. Sending and receiving on one band makes a device hear its own signal. Multilayer nonlinear models cancel that echo in the digital domain. Local minima and saddle points slow training, and full second-order methods cost too much. Their method borrows mixed Newton ideas without forming the full Hessian. It converges faster than first-order methods at far lower cost than classic second-order ones.
arxiv-2603-18927: Nortey and co-authors build a blended model to predict loan defaults. Their method first tunes several classifiers with a swarm search. It then blends their outputs with weights picked by a greedy rule. A small neural net acts as a meta-learner on top of the blend. Tests use Lending Club data with uneven classes and shifting borrower traits. The blend beats single models. Its best form scores 0.80 on a key ranking measure, with strong recall for defaults.
arxiv-2603-19127: Krishnan and co-authors test how spoken language models can be jailbroken through sound and text at once. They build JAMA, a joint attack that tweaks text with one method and audio with another. Tests cover four leading models and four types of audio. JAMA beats single-mode attacks by a wide margin, from 1.5 to 20 times the jailbreak rate. A faster version runs four to six times quicker. They argue that safety checks on one mode alone are not enough.
arxiv-2603-19427: Martins and co-authors ask why some tongues allow free word order while others do not. They pre-train small transformers on synthetic variants of natural languages with shuffled order. More irregular order always raises model surprise, which signals harder learning. Reversing sentences, by contrast, has only a weak effect. A blunt split into free and fixed order tongues fails to explain the gaps. The shape of the word and subword vocabulary predicts surprise far better. Word stock thus drives how learnable an order is.
arxiv-2603-19527: Flathers and co-authors study how OpenAI's Sora 2 video model depicts depression. They generated 100 videos from the single-word prompt 'Depression', half via the consumer app and half via the API. App videos showed a strong recovery bias, with 78 percent moving toward resolution, versus 14 percent for the API. App clips also brightened and moved more over time. Both routes reused a narrow set of images: hoodies, windows, and rain. Figures were mostly young adults, almost always alone.
arxiv-2603-19827: Richter-Gebert studies the twelve pentagons formed by the vertex neighborhoods of the icosahedron. He reads the pattern only through coplanarity conditions. Up to projective equivalence, the pattern has exactly two forms. Both give the vertex set of the regular icosahedron. As cell complexes they yield the great dodecahedron and the small stellated dodecahedron. The proof runs through the pentagram map. Any form forces a pentagon that maps to a scaled copy of itself. That leaves only a regular pentagon or a regular pentagram.
arxiv-2603-20027: Katsanikakis, Bekiaris-Liberis, and Bresch-Pietri design a controller for switched systems with input delay. The switching rule depends on the system's own state, which complicates prediction. Their design builds an exact predictor state from an implementable formula. That predictor feeds back to cancel the delay's effect. They prove uniform exponential stability of the closed loop. The proof uses several Lyapunov functionals and a new backstepping change of variables. A test case drawn from communication networks validates the design in simulation.
arxiv-2603-20127: Molavi, Saad, and Albarghouthi build a formal way to judge decoders for quantum error correction. A decoder reads parity checks and guesses which error struck the qubits. Its accuracy sets how large a reliable quantum computation can grow. Most teams judge decoders by Monte Carlo simulation, which needs many samples. The authors give a formal semantics for a core language matching the Stim circuit format. Their verifier then measures both decoder accuracy and robustness. Robustness covers drift in the physical error rate over time.
arxiv-2603-20527: Deng and co-authors introduce RMNP, a matrix-based optimizer that drops costly orthogonalization steps. Methods like Muon precondition updates using Newton-Schulz iteration. That iteration is effective but leaves room for speed gains. RMNP replaces it with simple row-wise L2 normalization. The swap rests on the block structure of transformer Hessians. There, normalization and orthogonalization prove asymptotically equivalent. Per-step cost falls sharply for large weight matrices. Convergence guarantees in the non-convex setting match recent results. Tests show performance stays comparable to Muon in practice.
arxiv-2603-20827: Qiu and co-authors present Swim2Real, a pipeline that tunes a robotic fish simulator from swimming videos. A vision language model compares real and simulated clips. It then proposes updates to all 16 simulator parameters at once. A backtracking line search checks each step size. This tripled the accept rate, from 14 to 42 percent. The tuned model matched real fish speeds best across motor frequencies. Policies trained in it swam 12 percent farther than BayesOpt tuned ones. Commands then ran on the real fish at 50 hertz.
arxiv-2603-20927: Vries argues that active inference gives a sound base for building physical AI agents, such as robots. Robots still lag far behind living agents in open, changing settings. He builds the case from probability theory through Bayesian learning to active inference on factor graphs. In this view, agents keep their form by minimizing variational free energy. Reactive message passing fits hard deadlines, uneven data flow, and tight power budgets. Performance then degrades gently when resources shrink. Coupled agents can also act as one higher level agent under stated conditions.
arxiv-2603-21027: Shekhar and Agrawal give a general recipe for dual forms of minimum divergence problems under integral constraints. Such problems appear in sequential inference, bandit theory, and robust optimization. Their two stage method starts with finitely supported distributions, using classic convex duality. An interchange argument then lifts the result to arbitrary distributions. They begin with mean constrained minimum relative entropy and extend it to higher dimensions. The scope widens to many f-divergences and general constraints. They build optimal procedures for testing and change detection.
arxiv-2603-21527: Miyamoto reworks dimensional analysis for cases where variables are tied by rules. The classic pi theorem cuts a problem down by grouping variables into scale-free quantities. But when definitions or laws link the variables, cutting them early gets messy. Miyamoto turns the setup into linear algebra on log scales. Rules and dimension changes become subspaces. Their overlap gives the true count of free scale-free quantities. A matrix routine then clears out the redundant ones. Examples cover falling motion, drag, and stock market gauges.
arxiv-2603-21927: Janning and co-authors study a photon condensate in a dye-filled microcavity that never reaches equilibrium. With a Lindblad master equation, they treat the condensate and its fluctuations together. The driven system parks on a long-lived plateau, held there by a ghost attractor that sits outside the physical domain. Even so, its fluctuations look thermal: they shrink with the square root of system size, as in equilibrium. A stability analysis finds exceptional points, marking several non-Hermitian phase transitions as the condensate forms and decays.
arxiv-2603-22127: Shamsabadi and co-authors plan drone flights and network links together in a satellite-assisted system. Advanced air mobility needs steady links between drones and control centers. Ground networks leave gaps and force frequent handovers. The team pairs ground networks with a geostationary satellite layer. Their deep Q-network algorithm plans each drone's path and network association jointly. The goals are lower energy use, fewer handovers, and less time disconnected. Simulations support the design inside the combined satellite-ground framework.
arxiv-2603-22327: Padarha and co-authors test whether AI agents can automate systematic literature reviews in epidemiology. Their harness, AgentSLR, covers 16,248 articles drawn from published reviews on WHO priority pathogens. Expert labels mark each review stage, so failures can be traced stage by stage. Five frontier reasoning models are tested. No model wins across all tasks, and each shows its own sub-task strengths. Structured data extraction is the weak point, with top field-level F1 under seven tenths. Costs differ by up to 96 times between models.
arxiv-2603-22427: Sarkar shows that a quantum perceptron can out-predict its classical twin under tight information limits. His model, the IMP, takes two-bit inputs and may read only one chosen bit at the node. The states passed to the node are also capped at one bit or qubit. Under that cap, the quantum version predicts better than any classical one. Sarkar shows the edge is universal, not tied to one task. For any shared task, a quantum build beats every classical build on prediction.
arxiv-2603-22527: He and co-authors teach a sidewalk robot to drive itself by imitating people. Imitation from fixed recordings tends to compound small errors on real streets. Their framework first widens the training data with corrective moves, so the robot learns to recover from its own mistakes. Sensor tweaks add more variety still. A multi-scale model then joins short-range reactions with long-range goals, using grouped trajectories and layered supervision. Street tests show clear gains in robustness across varied sidewalk scenes.
arxiv-2603-22827: Ghosh, Shrimali, and Jeong model the coupled physics of wafer-to-wafer bonding. Trapped air and wafer bending interact during bonding, shaping the bond front. The authors derive a plate equation for the wafer from three-dimensional elasticity. They couple it to a Reynolds equation for the thin air film. The combined system is solved in the FEniCSx framework with implicit time steps and a Newton solver. Simulations match reported wafer displacement histories. Studies show gap, air viscosity, and surface energy affect the bond front in nonlinear ways.
arxiv-2603-22927: Frascino and co-authors run direct numerical simulations of MILD combustion. This burning style dilutes and preheats reactants with hot products before ignition. Their setup mixes three streams: fuel, air, and hot combustion products. Four cases vary the mixing time scales between stream pairs. High dilution cases land in the MILD regime, while low dilution cases do not. Under MILD conditions, mixing with hot products mainly drives ignition. The local mode is mostly premixed autoignition there. Non-MILD cases lean more on flame-like burning, the analysis shows.
arxiv-2603-23227: Zhang and five co-authors present E3Flow, a robot policy built on SE(3)-equivariant flow. Past equivariant methods save training data but cost much compute and often use one input type. E3Flow pairs rectified flow with stable equivariant learning over mixed inputs. Spherical harmonics give it rotation symmetry. A feature module fuses point clouds and images into those features. On eight MimicGen tasks and four real trials, it gains 3.12 percent in success rate over the prior best. It also runs seven times faster.
arxiv-2603-23327: Lipman and eleven co-authors build a 3D orbital model of the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone. No single dataset can fix where the gas clouds sit along the line of sight. The team blends data across the spectrum, from dust extinction to X-ray echoes and proper motions. Each cloud gets a posterior probability map for its position. No single orbit fits all clouds well. Nested x2 orbits with axes from about 72 to 146 parsecs describe the layout better. Most clouds lie on the near side of the center.
arxiv-2603-23727: Nennouche and three co-authors model a light link from sea sensors up to a drone overhead. Underwater stations watch marine life, and drones could fetch their data cheaply. Their Monte Carlo ray tracer follows light through bubbles, a JONSWAP wave surface, and drone wobble in wind. The model folds in loss from each effect. Tests show the link holds at one megabit per second from 47 meters down. Error rates stay near one in a thousand bits in winds up to 13 meters per second.
arxiv-2603-23827: Asuke studies characteristic classes tied to deformations of foliations. These classes include the known Godbillon-Vey class and the Fuks-Lodder-Kotschick class. Asuke builds a differential graded algebra that recovers the Bott vanishing result and some formulas by Heitsch. He explores the cohomology of these algebras. Some classes there cannot be described by the two known classes, he shows. He also shows how deformable classes can give rise to further deformable classes of another kind.
arxiv-2603-23927: Sun and Li present Supermassive Blockchain, a design that scales state storage across many nodes. Sharding can spread storage, but past designs weakened safety or liveness. Their design splits state handling from execution. Erasure coding keeps state available while storage per node stays scalable. Consensus and execution layers keep the strong security of standard Byzantine fault tolerance protocols. Tests show better storage scaling than prior work, with low network overhead, they report.
arxiv-2603-24027: Mahlau and co-authors cut memory use in GPU simulations of electromagnetic fields. Time-reversible gradient computation must save field values at the domain boundary, and memory often limits inverse design work. They store those values with fewer bits and with interpolation. Accuracy stays close while memory cost drops. The method fits reduced-precision data types that GPUs and machine learning tools favor. They add it to FDTDX, an open-source differentiable solver, to support large-scale nanophotonics simulations.
arxiv-2603-24127: Guerder studies the cycle structure of random standardized permutations. These permutations come from a sequence of independent random variables. The model covers known cases such as riffle shuffles and major-index-biased permutations. Guerder first proves an exact formula for the joint counts of cycles of given lengths, using primitive words. Small cycle counts can then tend to a Poisson limit or to a sum of geometric laws. Large cycles follow the Poisson-Dirichlet process. A central limit theorem covers the total cycle count.
arxiv-2603-24827: Rodríguez and co-authors compare quantum and classical simulations of hydrogen crossing a graphdiyne membrane. Graphdiyne's sub-nanometre pores suit it to separating small gas molecules, but quantum effects may matter for light molecules. Their rigorous quantum calculations use a static membrane and improved Lennard-Jones force fields fitted to ab initio data. Classical molecular dynamics roughly reproduces how quantum permeance varies with temperature between 250 and 350 kelvin. Adding Feynman-Hibbs quantum corrections gives a lower bound on the quantum permeance.
arxiv-2603-25327: Zhang and co-authors calibrate gravity sensors in orbit for the Taiji-2 space mission. Taiji will hunt gravitational waves, and its reference sensors drift as fuel burns and parts age. Scale factors wander, and test mass centers shift against the craft. Their method turns the craft with set torque pulses, then reads star trackers and sensors together. A Kalman filter untangles the mixed signals and solves both unknowns at once. Scale error stays under 0.2 percent, and center offsets stay within 100 microns.
arxiv-2603-25527: Luo and co-authors train video models on flawed clips by picking the right moment to learn from each. Pretty clips tend to move little, and lively clips tend to look rough. That trade-off starves training of clips that shine at both. Gradient checks show a flawed clip can teach like a golden one at the right diffusion step. Their TQD method samples motion-rich clips at late steps and crisp clips at early ones. Models trained only on split flawed data beat models fed better data.
arxiv-2603-25927: Poddar and co-authors document the evidence base behind a 3GPP channel model update. The document details the measurement campaigns used by 3GPP in Release 19. It also lists the datasets behind the model in technical report TR 38.901. The update covers the 7 to 24 gigahertz frequency range. Curve fitting choices used in the validation are spelled out as well. The record is meant to show exactly which data and fits support the standard. Such channel models guide how new wireless systems are designed and tested.
arxiv-2603-26327: Andrew, Westhead, and Cutillo present MED-MAGMA, a graph-learning method for multi-axis models spoiled by multiplicative noise. Such noise is common in single-cell RNA data, where it reflects biases of the sequencing platform. Multi-axis models have a Kronecker-sum structure that the method exploits. The team tests MED-MAGMA on every public Single Cell Expression Atlas dataset under a set size limit. They report networks with better local and global structure than prior work, and release the method as a Python package.
arxiv-2603-26527: Lorenz and co-authors present CR-Eyes, a model of how players sample a screen while playing Atari games. Good user models must juggle looking and acting under time pressure, with plain pixel input. CR-Eyes learns by reinforcement under perceptual and cognitive limits, choosing both gaze and moves. It treats eye shifts as goal-driven actions inside a closed perception-action loop. The model matches human scores and broad saliency patterns well. Its scanpaths still differ from human ones in systematic ways the authors flag.
arxiv-2603-26627: Gonzalez-Conde and co-authors derive a stability test for nonlinear dissipative systems with quadratic nonlinearities. Such equations drive physics, engineering, and finance, yet exact solutions are rare and numeric ones grow costly. Turbulent behaviour can hinge on tiny changes in starting data, unless stability holds. By tracking solution norms in Sobolev spaces, the team links the linear damping, the quadratic term, and the forcing in one clear inequality. Meeting it keeps perturbations bounded for a wide set of starts, and fluid models show the test at work.
arxiv-2603-26827: Fang and co-authors present C2L-ST, a diffusion framework that creates tissue images for spatial transcriptomics. Data in this field is scarce because the experiments are costly and hard to share. A global model first learns tissue form from large image collections. Local models then adapt with a few paired image and gene spots. The synthetic images match real tissue in look and cell mix. Adding them to training improves gene expression prediction accuracy.
arxiv-2603-26927: Das and Sinha study a three-species reaction-diffusion system inside a perforated domain. The chemicals react and spread while mass flows in at the microscale boundary. The question is what the system looks like as the holes shrink away. Using two-scale convergence, the authors derive the large-scale limit. The limit stays a three-species reaction-diffusion system, but with changed diffusion coefficients. The microscale inflow survives as a global source term in the homogenized equation. Boundary effects thus persist in the effective model.
arxiv-2603-27227: Schmider and co-authors show that slit-patterned kirigami sheets can tune lift and drag in flowing air. Crossflow buckles the flat sheet into a lattice of inclined plate-like elements. That porous form generates transverse lift, not just drag. Lift appears even with the sheet held perpendicular to the flow. The structure switches between states, giving large force changes under identical conditions. Force data collapse onto a Cauchy number scaling. A continuum elastic model captures the stiffness control behind it.
arxiv-2603-28027: Su and eight co-authors adapt the Segment Anything Model to segment and classify cell nuclei in pathology images. Raw SAM misses the fine local structure that nuclei work needs, and full fine-tuning is costly. Their fix adds three parts: a multi-scale local adapter, a fusion module that keeps fine detail, and a boundary-guided mask step. Together these parts sharpen local perception and mask edges. The result is accurate nuclei segmentation at low tuning cost.
arxiv-2603-28127: Zhu and eight co-authors show that a phase defect in a Dirac material can carry its own relativistic modes. A branch cut in the complex Dirac mass traps one-dimensional waves that act like massless or massive particles. The effective mass is set by the phase jump across the cut. In acoustic metamaterials, the team demonstrates relativistic dispersion, energy-independent confinement, and Klein tunnelling. The modes even follow curved paths, such as spirals, along the defect.
arxiv-2603-29127: Minamoto studies subgraphs of the hypercubes Q6, Q7, and Q8 that avoid four-cycles. He works with odd-square edge sets that meet every four-cycle in one or three edges. He proves the largest sizes are 132, 304, and 682. Machine-checkable certificates back these values. He also sorts 19,866 known 304-edge subgraphs of Q7 into 20 types. They share one structural core and split into 180 symmetry orbits. All certified claims can be rechecked from released code and data.
arxiv-2603-29227: Dai and co-authors release Kernel-SDF, an open-source library for estimating signed distance functions in real time. Robots use these functions for planning, manipulation, and navigation. Older methods trade off resolution, training time, or uncertainty quality. Kernel-SDF learns a continuous occupancy field with kernel regression. A Gaussian process stage then refines distance estimates from surface samples. The library returns distance, gradient, uncertainty, and meshes. Tests show better accuracy than rival methods at real-time speed.
arxiv-2603-29327: Falomo and co-authors re-examine high-redshift BL Lac objects with new spectra. These objects show very weak or absent spectral lines. That makes their distances hard to measure. Distance matters for modeling their gamma-ray output. The team observed 52 objects with the GTC, a large telescope. For 16 of them, they propose new redshifts or lower limits. They confirm earlier values for 14 more. In 22 cases, the spectra stayed featureless even at high signal quality. Those objects likely lie between redshift 0.3 and redshift 1.4, based on missing host features.
