Tiered subsets serve different needs, from pretraining down to an aligned subset pairing 157,207 performances with 1,591 scores, the largest open collection of its kind. A quality classifier flags corrupted files, and an alignment pipeline fixes timing errors and missing notes. A rendering model trained on the data generalizes better to unseen pieces.
arxiv-2605-06927:
Tony Tran, Richie R. Suganda, and Bin Hu design object detectors that respect the energy budgets of edge devices. Detectors on varied hardware must balance energy, latency, and memory while staying accurate, and true energy use is device-dependent and expensive to measure directly. Their framework searches an energy-aware architecture space with a two-stage energy estimator, iterating toward one efficient base design under sparse real measurements.

Compound scaling then grows that base into the XiYOLO family for different budgets. On standard datasets the models beat YOLO baselines on the energy-accuracy trade-off, cutting energy by roughly a fifth to a half depending on device and scale. The estimator also adapts to new hardware from just a handful of samples.
arxiv-2605-07027:
Akram Mukhamedzhanov reexamines a nuclear reaction that helps set the maximum mass of black holes. When helium burns in massive stars, carbon captures a helium nucleus to form oxygen, fixing the carbon-to-oxygen balance. That balance later shapes whether stars explode in pair-instability events, leaving a gap in black hole masses.

Mukhamedzhanov argues that estimates drawn from black hole populations depend heavily on modeling assumptions, so they must respect direct nuclear evidence. Reanalyzing capture data with updated constraints favors a lower reaction rate than older evaluations. That range points to a relatively high lower edge for the black hole mass gap.
arxiv-2605-07227:
Kammampati Sai Kumar and three co-authors predict material traits from electronic charge density, the quantity that underlies a crystal's mechanical and heat response. Charge density grids are far too large to use raw. A compressor network first squeezes each grid into a compact latent form while keeping physical detail.

Fitting models then read that latent form, optionally joined with composition-based clues. Across roughly six thousand inorganic compounds, predictions were strong for stiffness measures, formation energy, and Debye temperature. The authors present charge density as a shared, physics-grounded clue that needs far less computing than full quantum calculations for each new query.
arxiv-2605-07327:
Yuan Zhang and ten co-authors distill diffusion image models down to a single generation step, using the teacher's own inner features. Sampling from pretrained diffusion models normally needs many passes, and earlier one-step methods leaned on extra networks and complex training stages. Their approach reuses the drifting objective with one loss only.

A key move replaces the separate feature extractor of the original drifting method with hidden states from the pretrained teacher itself. A light extra loss fights mode collapse and keeps output diverse. On ImageNet and a large text-to-image system, the method reached competitive quality and diversity scores while substantially simplifying distillation.
arxiv-2605-07427:
Fabio Ancona, Alessio Basti, and Fabio Camilli measure how much information numerical solutions of conservation laws really carry, using Kolmogorov entropy. Building on Lax's information-theoretic viewpoint, they prove a two-sided compactness estimate for solutions with a uniformly convex flux. The entropy scaling matches that of the exact solution set, under stated grid conditions.

The upper bound follows from a discrete one-sided Lipschitz property of the schemes, while the lower bound uses approximation over a bounded-variation class. Prototypical first-order methods thus qualify as high-resolution in Lax's sense. The authors also abstract the lower-bound mechanism into a general transfer principle for post-processing questions.
arxiv-2605-07527:
Wenxin Tai and three co-authors investigate a quirk of self-interpreting graph neural networks, whose built-in explanations can contradict themselves. When the model is reapplied to the very subgraph it named as its explanation, it may produce a different one. Why only some edges flip in this way was not understood.

The authors identify the re-explanation step itself as the cause: it perturbs the context in which edge scores are computed. Their latent signal hypothesis explains which edges are sensitive, and how conciseness training shapes that sensitivity. Since unstable edges are weak evidence, their Self-Denoising step recalibrates explanations with one extra forward pass. Across frameworks and datasets it improved explanation quality at only a few percent extra cost.
arxiv-2605-07627:
Kapil Goswami and Peter Schmelcher present a unified way to solve hard combinatorial optimization problems on a Rydberg-atom quantum annealer. Many such problems, from two-SAT to protein folding, can be written in one standard binary form, but each has usually needed its own encoding onto quantum hardware.

Their framework maps that shared form directly onto the Rydberg platform, using distance-dependent interactions and configurable local light shifts to cut resource overhead. An optimized annealing schedule then steers the system toward the target ground state. They also introduce a generalized hardness parameter that compares different problems by the structure of their optimization landscapes. The paper is a proceedings contribution to a theoretical physics workshop held in Athens.
arxiv-2605-07727:
Juil Koo and four co-authors design a robot policy that generates actions in a single step instead of integrating a differential equation. One-step generation is fast, but training such policies well is tricky. Their Drifting Field Policy frames each update as a gradient step in probability space, following a Wasserstein gradient flow toward a softer target policy.

The update splits naturally into climbing toward high-value actions and a score-matching term that keeps the policy near an anchor policy as a trust region. A tractable surrogate loss makes training practical, resembling behavior cloning on critic-selected top actions. With one-step inference the policy reached state-of-the-art results on several manipulation tasks across the Robomimic and OGBench suites, beating ODE-based policies.
arxiv-2605-07827:
Ping Chen and sixteen co-authors report optical and near-infrared observations of the supernova 2022an, a fast-declining Type Ia event of the 91bg-like family. Its light and spectra look standard for that class, except for one feature: a narrow absorption line near one micron. That line persists from about thirty to nearly ninety days after maximum light.

They attribute the feature to helium moving at very high velocity, supported by optical helium lines at earlier epochs. That speed rules out helium stripped from a companion star. It points instead to unburnt helium in the outer ejecta, the most compelling evidence yet for helium-bearing ejecta in this supernova class. Such helium is predicted by double-detonation models with a surface helium shell, and the paper notes theory has not yet modeled these late epochs.
arxiv-2605-08327:
Fei Xu Yu, Zuyuan Zhang, Mahdi Imani, Nathaniel Bastian, and coauthors train language models to produce structured outputs that auditors can check. In form filling, compliance review, and maintenance reporting, an answer must be locally right, globally consistent, and defensible against written rules, and heuristic self-debate offers no real assurance.

Their DPA-GRPO method trains a generator and a verifier as paired players. The verifier either stays silent or files a safety assurance case with a claim, an argument, and evidence; the generator then keeps or revises its output. Those paired decisions form counterfactual action groups for role-specific reinforcement updates, grounding revision in stated evidence rather than vibes.
arxiv-2605-08527:
Timothy Tin Long Yu and five coauthors present MARLaaS, a shared service for fine tuning language models with reward based learning. Training such models for tool use and multi step tasks costs so much that few groups can afford it alone. MARLaaS lets many users train at once by sharing one base model through small add on adapters.

Its split design runs rollout, environment contact, and training as separate stages that move at their own pace. With up to thirty two tasks at once, the system kept top single task quality, used hardware far better, and cut total training time sharply. Shared training could widen access greatly.
arxiv-2605-08727:
Jiaming Liang, Chi-Man Pun, Weisi Lin, and Greta Mok expose a new attack on learned image compression, the neural method that squeezes pictures into compact codes. Attackers could already distort output or shift meaning locally, but rewriting the whole meaning of a high resolution image seemed out of reach. Their analysis traces how successful attacks move regions through lazy, oscillating, and refining stages.

Standard bounded attacks fail because their step sizes cannot serve both the oscillating and refining stages. A periodic geometric decay schedule fixes that, and a minimal variant of a classic attack becomes the first to hold high resolution global manipulation steady. Compression security research gains both a threat and a theory of why it works.
arxiv-2605-09027:
Alexandre Le Mercier, Chris Develder, and Thomas Demeester warn AI agent teams not to police their own imposters. Teams can outthink lone agents, but one deceptive member can erase the edge, and detection strategy matters. In their Gambit testbed, four reasoning agents deliberate over chess moves, scored objectively by a strong engine, across hundreds of evolved imposter strategies in tens of thousands of labeled deliberations.

Warning the agents themselves backfires: decisions worsen without imposters, agents accuse themselves or scapegoat peers, costs inflate, and the imposter learns how it was caught. An outside detector that only reads deliberations adapts to new strategies from a handful of examples at a fraction of fine tuning cost. Collective AI gains a clear security rule.
arxiv-2605-09527:
Haddadi introduces the quantum capacitor, a proposed device for fast, two way energy storage through coherent quantum charge shifts. Quantum batteries have drawn wide interest as tiny storage devices that use coherence and entanglement. Yet most of that work aims to get the most work out. Classic storage, by contrast, splits into batteries and capacitors, and the capacitor side has no quantum twin. This paper supplies one, stressing stored reactive energy, coherence aided charging, and rapid release.

A spare model based on a driven two level system sets out a quantum capacitance. It tracks how stored energy reacts to outside driving. Haddadi looks at charging, coherent swings, and the harm done by outside noise. The proposal links quantum heat theory, coherence theory, and tiny scale storage design. It is theory work, giving a frame and a device idea rather than a lab demo.
arxiv-2605-09727:
He and three colleagues asked whether one transformer can generalize across reinforcement-learning domains without retraining its weights. Transformers already adapt to new tasks from context alone, but the theory behind that cross-domain reach was thin. Viewing the transformer as a functional operator that turns context into a task-specific function, the authors linked non-linear transformers to kernel-based temporal-difference learning.

The authors read the transformer as regression in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space, a space of functions with a shared kernel. They showed value functions from different domains can share one weight set when they live in the same space. Experiments across several MetaWorld robot domains backed the view, with the temporal-difference objective converging. Shared kernel structure, the paper suggests, is what lets in-context learning travel.
arxiv-2605-10427:
Emeline Decocq and four colleagues compare the two most recent comprehensive Spitzer phase-curve studies of exoplanets. Both analyze Spitzer 4.5-micron phase curves with uniform methods, but they correct instrument systematics differently and select optimal system parameters differently. Their 2026 paper asks how consistent the two studies are, at the population level and planet by planet.

Comparing constraints on planet-to-star radius ratio, eclipse depth, phase-curve amplitude, and phase-curve offset, the authors find similar population-level results, though individual planets can vary, especially in offset values. They trace whether discrepancies stem from data-reduction methods or parameter choices, and check whether chosen parameters obey Kepler's third law. One case failed that check despite all values coming from one publication. Recalculating orbital periods and comparing with the NASA Exoplanet Archive, they conclude that testing reported parameters against Kepler's law is worthwhile.
arxiv-2605-10627:
Bruno Gatti and two colleagues evaluate coreference solving by meaning, not just overlap. It is often evaluated using combined stats measures such as CoNLL-F1, which measure shape overlap between guessed and gold clusters. These measures offer limited clues, docking errors without revealing whether a system struggles with specific meaning kinds such as people, places, or events. Their 2026 paper introduces a meaning-enhanced evaluation framework.

The approach lays Concept and Named Entity Recognition onto linking outputs, giving meaning labels to nominal mentions and spreading them to entire clusters. That allows typed scores evaluating mention finding and linking capabilities split by meaning class. Across tests on OntoNotes, LitBank, and PreCo, the framework uncovers steady weaknesses obscured by combined measures. These clues can be used to design aimed, low-cost data growth strategies, gaining real out-of-domain progress.
arxiv-2605-10727:
Maria Esteban-Casadevall and colleagues give kernel-gradient drifting, a one-step generative modelling plan swapping the fixed Euclidean shift for kernel-set lines. Standard drifting trains a one-step maker, shifting samples along a kernel-set pull and push field. This gives fast top-notch making with no need to boil down a large pretrained diffusion model. Its theory is known most for Gaussian kernels, where drift lines up with smoothed score matching and is pinned down.

Their gradient-based rewrite brings this score-based shape out for plain kernels. The drift turns into the score gap between kernel-smoothed data and model spreads, giving pinned-down status for characteristic kernels and a smoothed-KL descent read of moves. Across round geospatial data, promoter DNA, and molecule making, kernel-gradient drifting hits top one-step making beyond the Euclidean set with no boil-down.
arxiv-2605-10927:
Christian Coester and Alexa Tudose close a thirty-year gap in online set chasing, the problem of serving a moving sequence of small sets in a metric space. The competitive ratio had sat between exponential lower and upper bounds, and the classic work-function algorithm was known to be suboptimal for this task.

Their deterministic algorithm reaches an optimal exponential competitive ratio, matching the best any algorithm, even randomized against adaptive adversaries, can do. They also sharpen the deterministic lower bound with a recursive sequence they conjecture to be exactly tight, proving it for sets of size three. The results tighten bounds for tree exploration and the k-taxi problem as well. Online-algorithm researchers get a settled gap and a new champion method.
arxiv-2605-11027:
Elyson De La Cruz traces software engineering's shift from code-centric production to intent-centric human-agent work. In the new mode, natural language, repository context, tools, tests, and governance shape delivery. Earlier studies cover code generation and AI pair programming. What is less clear is how open debate and journal articles together shape the near-term shift.

Through reflexive thematic analysis of a corpus spanning peer-reviewed literature, benchmarks, talks, interviews, essays, product announcements, and social-media discourse, the study finds generative AI lowering the cost of plausible code. At the same time, it raises the stakes of intent specification, context curation, architecture knowledge, verification, and security. Engineering leaders get a sourced picture of which human skills gain value as code itself gets cheaper.
arxiv-2605-11127:
Marvin Morgan and seventeen colleagues constrain a possible outer companion in the 51 Pegasi system, home of the first confirmed exoplanet around a Sun-like star. Decades of radial-velocity observations show a shallow acceleration hinting at a distant companion, and the team combines velocities, astrometry, and imaging for new limits.

Thirty-one years of radial velocities from four spectrographs, a twenty-five-year Hipparcos-Gaia astrometry span, and deep Keck and Hubble imaging show a bend in the velocities. Combined with empty imaging and astrometry searches, the data point to a super-Jupiter at roughly 15 to 100 astronomical units or a brown dwarf at roughly 20 to 170 units. The acceleration's cause stays open, but the companion's mass-distance range narrows sharply. Exoplanet teams get the tightest outer-companion limits yet for a landmark system.
arxiv-2605-11327: Xu and four colleagues introduce neural statistical functions, models that give stats directly instead of running a model again and again to sample. Old deep learning works case by case, so finding integrals, quantiles or maxima over ranges costs many runs. Their prefix statistics idea turns varied stat functions into one interval-conditional frame. An identity between prefix stats and single-case regression serves as the learning goal, and tests show up to a hundredfold fewer model runs.
arxiv-2605-11427: Li and seven colleagues introduce PD-4DGS, the first framework for progressive, on-demand transmission of four-dimensional Gaussian splatting. Current models are monolithic bitstreams that clients must download fully before any frame renders, causing black-screen waits of tens of seconds or more on mobile bandwidth. Hierarchical Deformation Decomposition splits motion into a static scaffold, one global deformation and one local refinement, so any bitstream prefix renders. On the Dycheck iPhone benchmark it cuts streamed size by over sixty percent and first-frame latency to about 1 point 7 seconds.
arxiv-2605-11527: Mahyar and three colleagues propose FERMI, a membership attack for tabular diffusion models using links between tables. Diffusion models lead tabular synthesis for sharing sensitive records, yet current attacks assume one table. FERMI adds parent-table signal to single-table features in training, though at run time the attacker sees only target-table fields. Across three diffusion designs and three real linked datasets, FERMI lifts true positive rate at 0 point 1 false positive rate by up to 53 percent white-box and 22 percent black-box.
arxiv-2605-11627: vom Dahl, De Marchi and Kanzow present near limited-memory quasi-Newton methods for nonsmooth tuning. They handle a smooth function plus a proper, lower half-steady, prox-bounded, maybe nonsmooth function, both maybe non-convex. The method builds on scaled near steps, steadied by tuning smoothing under an enough-decrease rule. They prove global settling under mild terms and full sequence settling under the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz rule. Compact forms of limited-memory updates, including a Kleinmichel rank-one formula, make subtasks fast. Tests show speedups over other methods.
arxiv-2605-12127: Leonardo Galliano and Ludovic Berthier question what truly makes ultra-stable glass stable. Past work often made stable glass by changing particle widths on the fly, and tied stability to tuned traits like even spread at large scales and neat local order. The authors tune those traits hard without touching particle widths, and the glass gains no extra stability. Tuned traits thus track stability without causing it. Rules for stable glass should target the making process itself, not the traits it tunes.
arxiv-2605-12527: Slokom and Bellogin run a live federated recommender that keeps user data on device while letting users steer the goal. In a 53-day deployment with 22 participants and 8,807 titles, users chose between personalisation and diversity-enhanced ranking. They preferred personalisation when given an explicit choice, rated control mechanisms about 3.9 out of 5, and changed settings 248 times. Users also developed a sense of how their actions shaped recommendations through immediate feedback. The study shows user control, privacy and effective personalisation can coexist in a working system.
arxiv-2605-12627: Youngblood and six colleagues revisit ultraviolet absorption toward the edge-on disk around eta Telescopii. Earlier work saw four velocity components, with the fastest near minus twenty-three kilometres per second read as a likely disk wind. Optical spectra of eta Tel and nearby stars show that component is likely between stars. The team finds three such components toward the sight line, while a fourth near minus one, seen only in oxygen, resists that account and may be circumstellar. Its carbon-to-oxygen ratio matches Earth and solar system comets.
arxiv-2605-12827: Zhao and four co-authors ask how hard it is to steal a graph neural network and whether defences can stop it. Their GraphIP-Bench evaluates twelve extraction attacks and twelve defences on shared splits, queries and budgets, plus a joint track running every attack on every defended target. Stealing proves easy at medium query budgets and most defences change little; several watermarks verify on the protected model but lose most signal on the extracted surrogate. Heterophilic graphs resist theft best.
arxiv-2605-13027: Xu and four co-authors present PRISM, a single-step diffusion framework for text image super-resolution, where tiny stroke errors can change a character and break readability. Two fixes drive it: flow-matching prior rectification, which repairs unreliable text guidance from degraded inputs. An uncertainty-aware encoder keeps trustworthy local boundary evidence while suppressing ambiguous stroke cues. On synthetic and real benchmarks it reaches state-of-the-art quality with millisecond-level inference.
arxiv-2605-13527: Kangning Zhang and ten colleagues introduce MMSkills, a framework for reusable multimodal skills for general visual agents. Each MMSkill is a compact state-conditioned package coupling a written procedure with runtime state cards plus multi-view keyframes. A generator turns public non-evaluation trajectories into reusable skills through grouping, induction, grounding and auditing. Tests across GUI and game benchmarks show MMSkills improve both frontier and smaller multimodal agents.
arxiv-2605-13727: Gergely Bodó and three colleagues prove the first result that mild answers of general random growth rules exist and are unique. The rules are driven by any tube Lévy flows in Hilbert spaces. Factors satisfy global Lipschitz rules, with no moment guesses on the driving noise. The authors build a path tuned Euler-Peano nearing scheme based on noise-tied stopping times and a fixed-point form of the mild solution tool. That gives a robust frame for scaling tube Lévy noise in endless-sized systems.
arxiv-2605-13927: Buonomo and four co-authors probe why kin colonies of the germ Pseudomonas aeruginosa shun each other in soft agar, forming sharp split lines. They pair dense counts of cells with a spare physics model. Gel squeeze, lethal attack and quorum-sensing chatter are all ruled out as causes. Split lines come instead from local food loss, driven by a loop where growth feeds motion and motion feeds growth. The tuned model fits what they see.
arxiv-2605-14327: Park and Lee propose AIM-DDI, a model-agnostic multimodal module for drug-drug interaction prediction. The hard case is unseen-drug generalization: predicting interactions for drugs absent from training. Multimodal DDI models exploit diverse drug information, but their fusion is often tied to specific architectures. AIM-DDI turns heterogeneous information into tokens in a shared latent space, with one fusion module modeling token dependencies. Tests across DDI models and DrugBank settings show consistent improvements, strongest when neither test drug was observed during training.
arxiv-2605-14427: A 2026 paper by Kopparapu tackles vocabulary size in end-to-end speech recognition, where tokens come from the training corpus rather than a fixed phone inventory. Vocabulary size is a critical hyperparameter, yet toolkits like ESPNet fix it in recipes with little documentation of the choice. Building on a cost-function framework treating tokenisation as a black box, he fits training-data curves. Calculus derivative tests then estimate the size formally. On the standard Librispeech corpus, the chosen size improves recognition performance.
arxiv-2605-14727: Fang, Chen, Chen, Sun, Liu and Cai propose CHASM, a cross-frequency harmonised axis-separable mixer for spectral token operators in vision models. Fourier-based mixers model global interactions, but existing designs either fix channel axes or mix channels per frequency without aligning directions across frequencies. CHASM shares one learned channel eigenbasis across all frequencies while keeping per-frequency positive spectral gains, then applies the operator separably along height and width. Gains over same-backbone baselines are claimed on MRI and image tasks.
arxiv-2605-14927: Elisabetta Cornacchia and Laurent Massoulié ask how clustered input features change the difficulty of learning with shallow neural networks. Real inputs like images and genomes carry correlations within the input space, not just in the target function. In their model, targets depend on few latent Boolean variables, and features cluster around those variables. Under an identifiability condition, layerwise gradient descent needs samples scaling with the hidden variables alone, independent of input size at high signal-to-noise.
arxiv-2605-15127: Laleh Nourian and five others study how students from abroad in the United States use conversational AI while adapting to a new culture. A survey of 60 students maps challenges to adoption patterns, and interviews with 14 students probe motives and limits. Students treat AI as first aid for immediate problems but want it to grow into a long-term support companion. The authors identify where AI can sustain support and where it falls short, offering advice for tailored AI-powered assistance.
arxiv-2605-15427: T. W. O. Varnish and ten others report pulsed-power reconnection experiments driving two exploding wire arrays into crashing plasma flows with anti-parallel fields near 1.2 tesla. A Helmholtz coil pair applied an outside field up to 2 tesla aligned to the rejoining electric field. With zero or weak outside field, a rejoining layer forms as before. Under a 2-tesla field, a void appears, and the team guesses the outside field freezes out of the plasma and pushes back the flows. Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations roughly support delayed layer formation.
arxiv-2605-15727: Ali Mohammadi proves a lower bound on directions set by Cartesian products in the affine plane over finite fields of squared prime order. It holds for sets sized between p to the two-thirds and p, outside any affine copy of the prime field. The proof joins a structural result of Li and Roche-Newton on product directions with a lower bound of Fancsali, Sziklai, and Takáts. A key step shows that, barring closure traits that force subfield structure, one direction makes an algebraic multiplicity parameter explicit.
arxiv-2605-15827: Philipp Schröer and six colleagues present Caesar, a deductive verifier for probabilistic programs. Its core language, HeyVL, is a quantitative intermediate verification language built on the real-valued logic HeyLo, letting users express programs, specifications and proof rules in programming-language style. Caesar translates HeyVL programs into verification conditions checked with the Z3 SMT solver, and adds a probabilistic model-checking backend for a subset of the language. The paper reports five years of development, including new proof rules and better diagnostics.
arxiv-2605-16027: Viel extends nearest-neighbour matching estimators to covariates on unbounded supports, dropping the usual compactness and density assumptions. His conditions rest instead on source and target distributions, including a measure of transferability between them. The usual convergence rates still hold, and the transferability control proves necessary for any estimator. Applied to treatment effects, the results relax the need for assignment probabilities bounded away from zero and one.
arxiv-2605-16127: Doruk, Hussein, and Ates propose WeatherOcc3D, a framework for 3D semantic occupancy prediction in bad weather. Cameras fail in low light and LiDAR suffers backscatter noise in heavy rain, so fixed fusion misjudges which sensor to trust. A CLIP-based adapter aligns weather text with sensor features, and a gate splits uncertainty into visibility and illumination. On nuScenes, the framework lifted two baseline architectures to mean IoU scores of 26.3 and 21.1, well above their original results.
arxiv-2605-16727: Castanyer and colleagues replace single-agent self-calibration with groups cross-checking each other in PopuLoRA, a population-based asymmetric self-play system for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards in language models. Teachers and students are specialist LoRA adapters sharing one frozen base; teachers set problems matched students solve under a programmatic verifier. Weight-space mutations and crossovers evolve the population at 7B scale. The population mean reportedly beats a compute-matched single-agent baseline on code and math tests. Even the weakest member also beats that baseline overall.
arxiv-2605-16827: Mushkani builds an open archive and live atlas of public-input AI projects, merging records from a trusted-AI corpus with audited cases from research and practice. The work sets a shared method for finding, vetting, merging, mapping, source tracking, and staged release. Corpus patterns show projects clustered in few countries, with input most often at problem framing, testing, and rules rather than model building or training. The atlas supports cross-case research, policy learning, and public checks through dated editions open to dispute.
arxiv-2605-16927: Feng's team reviews intervention-aware models that track how disease unfolds over time under different treatments. Static risk scores fail in clinics because care logs mix disease biology with clinician habits, treatment feedback, and uneven measurements. The review groups the field into three decision tasks, factual forecasting, counterfactual estimation, and policy evaluation, plus three data mechanisms: disease course, treatment assignment, and observation process. It maps method families to these parts and ties evaluation to claim strength, aiming to move prediction toward decision-grade clinical evidence.
arxiv-2605-17027: Mei and Zhang design a distributed optimization method that copes when a problem's smoothness changes sharply across its domain. Older methods lean on one global smoothness bound, which can be far too cautious, while raw local values can swing wildly. The pair sets out a broad regularity rule covering steady, slow-growing, and fast-growing cases. They then build a clipped tracking method with staged variance cuts that needs only local smoothness.
arxiv-2605-17327: Zhang and colleagues propose a feature-free way to start monocular visual-inertial navigation, using point clouds predicted directly by a feed-forward 3D model instead of tracked visual features. That cuts complexity and removes the usual three-to-four-second data wait. Tests on public sets give the highest success rate, past 90 percent, with startup data typically just over one second, and hold up in degraded visual settings.
arxiv-2605-17427: Florence, Hoshi and Yamasaki study rationality of norm one tori of tensor products of étale algebras and the Hasse norm principle. They prove that when factor degrees are coprime and both norm one tori are stably or retract rational, the two product tori share that rationality. For global fields the Hasse norm principle then holds for the tensor product. A new G-lattice invariant, the permutation order, links triviality to invertibility and yields large families of extensions where the principle holds.
arxiv-2605-17627: Dobosh and Yakimenko study an agent-based simulation of self-propelled particles with a speed-dependent alignment rule. The interaction is angle-weighted and acts along the line joining neighboring particles. Tuning its strength yields distinct collective regimes: disordered gas-like motion, coherent flock movement, jammed high-density phases, and densely ordered moving sets with active-crystal-like behavior. A simple local rule thus generates a broad range of group dynamics within one tiny model.
arxiv-2605-17727: Zesheng Li, Chengchang Pan, and Honggang Qi treat embedding length as a dial for meaning in frozen vision-language models. Their GraSP-VL learns one shared, near-orthogonal prefix transform so short prefixes expose coarse ideas like object identity while longer prefixes reveal finer attributes, relations, and caption-level meaning. On a 20,147-example COCO and Flickr30K pool it reaches a staircase score of 53.01 and strong hard-negative selectivity, while barely disturbing the full-dimensional space or its zero-shot accuracy.
arxiv-2605-17827: Subash Timilsina and three colleagues tackle content-style identification for models of data. Content stays constant while style varies, but proofs need content-style independence or sparse Jacobians. The team introduces content-style differential independence: shifts in content and style must push along orthogonal paths on the data manifold. That condition pins down the factors when content and style depend on each other and the Jacobian is dense. An orthogonal constraint plus a regularizer from Jacobian estimates scales training, and tests confirm gains on counterfactual generation and domain translation.
arxiv-2605-18027: A. Baksheev and three colleagues study vacuum electron-positron pair production in a uniform two-color electric field. The field mixes a strong slow part with a weak oscillating part. The team tracks helicity observables, showing assistance boosts both yield and asymmetry: right- and left-handed electrons favor their momentum half-spaces. In this range, the ratio for the two helicities depends mainly on the polar angle, and weakly on the rest. The asymmetry grows as the weak-field frequency rises, giving a signature of the dynamically assisted Schwinger effect.
arxiv-2605-18527: Huzefa Aliasger and six co-authors compare, in a 2026 paper, single-pass second-harmonic generation in BiBO and LBO crystals under a 1030 nm picosecond laser. Both crystals yield 32 watts of green output at 515 nm, a 56 percent efficiency, the highest reported green output from BiBO. Power response, stability, beam quality, pulse length, spectra, heat effects, and angular range are tested for both. The results benchmark crystal choice for high-power ultrashort-pulse frequency conversion.
arxiv-2605-18627: Jonas Gösgens and two co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, learning lifted STRIPS+ action models from traces with partial information about actions and states. Prior work learned STRIPS models from action traces alone, and STRIPS+ variants assumed fully observable states. This work relaxes both limits, giving algorithms and completeness results for three cases. The cases are: no state observability, full observability of some state predicates, and local observability of some state predicates. Given a STRIPS+ domain, the results characterize when an equivalent domain can be learned from traces.
arxiv-2605-18827: Prateek Biswas and four colleagues test whether code scaffolds help small language models on multiple-choice questions. Small models usually answer directly, yet deployed systems lean on tools, code, and repeated calls. Their Code-Guided Reasoning protocol pairs a direct solver with generated Python programs. It records direct, assisted, and generator-side answers. Across over twenty thousand retained rows, assisted accuracy reaches about sixty-six percent versus about thirty-eight percent direct, though the authors flag brittle extraction and other limits.
arxiv-2605-19127: Qiaoyuan Zheng and three colleagues introduce POLAR-Bench, a test of privacy-utility trade-offs in agents handling private user data. A trusted model with a privacy policy converses with a third-party model probing adversarially for task-relevant and protected attributes. Across ten domains and 7,852 samples, privacy and utility are scored by set membership across policies and attacks. Frontier models withhold over 99 percent of protected attributes. Smaller open-weight models score notably worse, the weakest leaking over half. The benchmark pinpoints where models' intent-following breaks down.
arxiv-2605-19327: Vasanth Iyer and S. S. Iyengar derive unified error bounds for fusing data from distributed quantum sensors under faults and decoherence. Building on classical overlap methods for faulty sensors, they give a two-parameter family set by entanglement visibility and fault share. The bound slides smoothly from the standard quantum limit with no entanglement to the Heisenberg limit at full visibility. Simulations with up to 64 sensors confirm the scaling, and tests on a 54-node lab dataset show gains of 20 to 27 decibels per cluster from entanglement.
arxiv-2605-19727: He and team present Tango3D, a model for dense correspondence and global retrieval. Existing 3D foundation models align point clouds to frozen vision-language spaces, compressing shape into a global vector, yet global-only alignment cannot establish pixel-to-point links. Tango3D encodes images into patches with a geometry-aware backbone and point clouds into 3D tokens with a 3D VAE, mapping both into one space. A three-stage training strategy stabilizes joint dense and global learning, achieving object-level pixel-to-point alignment with global retrieval.
arxiv-2605-19827: Rohe, Baumann, Ruiloba, Altmann, Stenzel and Linnhoff-Popien ask whether entangling gates help or hinder variational quantum algorithms for MaxCut. MaxCut is governed by diagonal Hamiltonians whose ground states need no entanglement in principle. The team tracks it through training with two control mechanisms and QAOA as a reference. When the optimiser can steer it indirectly, it drives it down, and a separable ansatz beats every entangled hardware efficient setup. QAOA, whose entanglement follows the problem Hamiltonian, stays entangled yet competitive. Structure, not amount, decides its value.
arxiv-2605-20027: Voskresenskaia and three co-workers examine the ComPACT galaxy cluster catalogue, built by a convolutional neural network from combined ACT and Planck maps. They confirm candidates by estimating redshifts from literature and DESI Legacy photometry, and derive masses from SZ scaling relations. About sixty percent prove to be real clusters, with redshifts from near zero to about one point seven and masses for just over half the sample. Five new massive clusters beyond redshift zero point seven expand the known population of such systems by about ten percent.
arxiv-2605-20127: Ken Nakamura and four co-workers propose recovery scores for judging model-brain alignment, since accuracy alone does not show which response-space dimensions a model recovers. From fMRI scans, they find target signals seen across splits. They predict targets from another brain or a vision model, gauging how each is found. On Natural Scenes data, early visual-cortex responses hold few stable patterns. Trained and random models reach similar prediction scores with distinct recovery patterns, showing scores alone can mask mismatches.
arxiv-2605-20427: Oliveira and two co-workers explore the conformal anomaly for a gauge vector field with an auxiliary scalar. The anomaly's form depends on regularization and renormalization schemes, and one option treats the theory as conformal away from four dimensions. An auxiliary scalar acting as compensator keeps gauge symmetry intact and avoids unitarity problems. After the 4D limit, the remnant scalar gains its own dynamics and shows further notable properties.
arxiv-2605-20727: Ningkang Peng and six colleagues propose GAMR, a geometry-aware method for learning from noisy labels. Deep networks degrade when labels are wrong, since they overfit mislabeled data, and simple filtering struggles to tell hard examples from noisy ones. GAMR instead reshapes feature-space geometry by synthesizing virtual outlier samples that build energy barriers between data manifolds. Geometric constraints promote tight within-class grouping and clear between-class separation, sharpening the line between hard and noisy samples.
arxiv-2605-20827: Yaoyao Yue and four colleagues present HyDAR-Pano3D, a hybrid design for recovering 3D craniofacial anatomy from panoramic dental radiographs. A panoramic X-ray gives only a 2D projection of complex 3D anatomy, and direct regression of cone-beam CT volumes mixes shared anatomy with patient-specific variation. Their two-stage design recasts rebuilding as disentangled anatomical recovery, avoiding over-smoothed results with blurred edges. Stage one fuses X-ray traits with SAM-derived meaning priors in a dual-encoder network.
arxiv-2605-20927: Herrero Otermin and five colleagues describe spin-polarized lasing in a 2D photonic lattice. The lattice is made from a GaAs/InGaAs semiconductor microcavity sample, with a staggered array of rounded rectangular micrometric mesas. Those mesas laterally confine and couple the optical modes. Polar-, angle-, and energy-resolved micro-photoluminescence tests reveal the shift from strong coupling to photon lasing, with wide spatial coherence across several unit cells.
arxiv-2605-21127: Lukas Twist, Helen Yannakoudakis, and Jie M. Zhang document reasoning-trace collapse, in which fine-tuning on plain instruction data strips reasoning models of valid intermediate traces while answers stay plausible. Their framework separates answer correctness from trace validity across four open-weight models, finding valid reasoning can fall sharply even as conditional performance holds. Simple loss-masking strategies, they show, substantially reduce the collapse without teacher traces.
arxiv-2605-21227: Nina Hosseini-Kivanani asks whether large language models respect community norms for word borrowing in Luxembourgish, a small contact language. Her LexNeo-Bench set holds three thousand fifty token cases drawn from Luxembourgish news, labeled as native words or French, German, or English borrowings. Without outside context, three multilingual models score only slightly above chance on borrowing type. Prompts enriched with a knowledge graph of donor language, word patterns, and analogues lift accuracy from roughly thirty percent to roughly seventy-five percent.
arxiv-2605-21627: Rohan Hore and Aaditya Ramdas study distribution-free root cause analysis in multi-stream data. When an evolving system is watched through several data streams, each may shift at unknown times, and the earliest-shifting stream points to the root cause. Their Conformal Root Cause Analysis, or CROC, builds valid confidence sets for the root-cause index under minimal assumptions: streams independent, pre- and post-change observations exchangeable within each stream. They also show any distribution-free method for root cause localization fits inside CROC, and simulations confirm localization.
arxiv-2605-21827: Daniel Tabach asks whether language models keep the rank order of strength words when words drive number actions. In an allocation setting, Claude Haiku turns prompts with one of ten degree words, from slightly to drastically, into amounts. The model shrinks ten words into five middle outputs. Starting allocation explains far more variance than word choice, with word differences gone near limits. Near the limits, weak words hedge, strong words abstain, and the strongest pushes to the ceiling. Number readings are thus squashed, state-tied, and jumpy near boundaries.
arxiv-2605-22027: Evan Luo, Julien Piet, and David Wagner present Sieve, a parser-free way to query logs with generated code. Analysts query logs to detect threats, but each source uses its own semi-structured format, so per-source parsers demand constant engineering, while raw grep queries demand effort on every format. Sieve bridges structured querying and raw immediacy by generating code that answers queries. Across 5 log types it cuts error rate over 3 times on complex temporal and cross-event queries versus manual scripting, with largest gains on multi-line correlation tasks.
arxiv-2605-22127: Yerrapati and co-authors study twisted Frobenius-Schur indicators and character degree sums in dihedral groups. For a group G, T(G) sums the degrees of its irreducible complex representations. They relate it to the count of twisted involutions for an automorphism. While T(G) equals that count for the identity automorphism in certain cases, they analyze non-identity automorphisms for groups of order p, 2p, and p squared. For dihedral groups D_n, they prove T(D_n) is at least the twisted count for every automorphism, fully classified.
arxiv-2605-22227: Kumar, Faiyaz, Sarkar and Agarwal show that an uneven electric field adds a quantum-metric term to wavepacket motion, producing oscillations even where Berry curvature vanishes. The transport response mixes an intrinsic part with one that depends on scattering time, and the latter can dominate and level off at strong fields. A tilted Dirac model illustrates the effect, though real devices would need engineered superlattices.
arxiv-2605-23527: Shao and three colleagues build LiveFigure, an agent framework that draws editable scientific figures instead of flat raster images. Real editability means structured changes to shapes, scales, attributes, and text, plus room for manual fixes, yet most generators output pixels that resist layout tweaks. LiveFigure plans blueprints from strong prior examples, writes scripts that draw through the PowerPoint interface, and refines results with visual checks. Its figures reach 80 percent publication readiness in just 17 manual edits, far above the best baseline at 24 percent, and win 60 percent of human preference votes.
arxiv-2605-24027: Saroka, Pulci, and D'Alessandro model the optical response of hydrogenated graphene superlattices, narrow strips where metal and non-metal regions swap places through hydrogenation of chosen areas. Using first-principles methods with excitonic effects, they find surface engineering can produce strong, lone absorption peaks in the far infra-red, maybe reaching terahertz range. Band-gap scaling, they add, suggests no exciton insulators form.
arxiv-2605-24127: Tregear, Aktas, and Rodriguez y Baena retrofit a custom series-elastic element to a black-box actuator, adding compliance where stiff, low-backlash designs risk damage and poor force control. A torsional element designed by finite-element analysis gives a stiffness of 2155.4 newton-metres per radian. The retrofit enables high-fidelity force measurement, lifting open-loop force-control bandwidth from 10.32 hertz to 30.32 hertz, a 2.93-fold improvement. It also beats a commercial force sensor by 7.63 percent despite costing 25 pounds, a fraction of the price.
arxiv-2605-24227: Ying and Nitzan map joint light-matter motion by two knobs: molecule and excitation count. In the Tavis-Cummings model with molecules and tiny excitation density, mean-field and single-excitation pictures agree and give linear motion. At finite excitation density, the large-molecule limit stays mean-field but bends, via a Duffing rule for cavity size with uneven Rabi rate. Cluster terms restore finite-count links beyond mean field, and local coupling reaches the same linear limit through polaron splitting and linear form.
arxiv-2605-24427: Roelands and Tiersma prove that a JB-algebra formed from a pair of its associative Jordan subalgebras is always a JC-algebra, hence special. They obtain a parallel Macdonald-style refinement for JB-algebras. They further show the free unital JB-algebra on n projections is a JC-algebra exactly when n is 1, 2, or 3. Finally, they describe the free unital JB-algebra on two projections explicitly, in the spirit of the Raeburn-Sinclair theorem for C*-algebras.
arxiv-2605-24527: Zheng Zhang and colleagues find coupled local and collective excitations in the triangular antiferromagnet NaErSe2, using neutron spectroscopy and angular-momentum models. Low-lying crystal-field doublets include a dipolar ground state with stripe order and an excited state with dipole-octupole character. Sharp spectra show magnon branches echoed on higher levels and joining the excited levels in a distinct multipolar band. A magnetic field reshapes the quantum states, polarizing the system into a multipolar ferromagnet.
arxiv-2605-25227: Rodrigo Labouriau traces ideas from de Moivre's 1733 work on the normal curve to distributional statistics. De Moivre worked out the Gaussian density first, with Stirling's constant and six-decimal tail probabilities, over seven decades ahead of Gauss. Probing probability laws with indicator functions points to the operational viewpoint behind distributional statistics. Labouriau follows four stages: coefficient extraction, generating functions, characteristic functions, and pairings of distributions and test functions. He proves a version of the De Moivre-Laplace theorem there.
arxiv-2605-25427: Udith Haputhanthri and colleagues probe why vision-language models fumble multi-object scenes humans find easy. The suspect is binding: attaching the right features to the right object, a job human vision handles by attending to one object at a time. The team tests pointing, naming objects with spatial coordinates, as a machine analogue of serial attention. Learning to point through text induces an internal visual search routine, with identifiable supporting mechanisms. Pointing transfers to new tasks after tuning, wiping out binding errors and enabling compositional generalization.
arxiv-2605-25627: Jabbari builds a functorial account of ample C*-diagonal pairs and the Weyl groupoids that go with them. His main result is a partial functoriality theorem for untwisted pairs. It starts from a diagonal-preserving homomorphism that restricts to an isomorphism. It builds a subgroupoid with an injective homomorphism and an induced homeomorphism on unit spaces. The construction extends to a contravariant functor into partial groupoid morphisms. Finally, the pair is fixed up to isomorphism by its Weyl groupoid in the principal case.
arxiv-2605-26027: Roy and Singh model protein droplet formation with a bare-bones lattice model that spells out solvent. Droplets of protein organise cell chemistry, yet their design rules are still murky. The model adds frozen disorder to stand in for crowders, idle molecules that pack the fluid. Phase maps show varied shifts, including upper-critical, closed-loop and reentrant types, as protein-solvent pull changes. Crowder pull further molds droplet shape and hold. The work points to rules for building droplets that react to cues.
arxiv-2605-26227: Ranjani Seshadri studies, in a paper published in 2026, two quantum harmonic oscillators. Their coupling, rather than their natural frequency, is driven in a repeating parametric pattern. She shows the drive can be tuned to excite any chosen normal mode selectively, leaving its partner near the ground state. Every populated state carries an even quantum number in each mode. Inside the resonance window, excitations fall off as a power law with occupation number rather than exponentially. The same scheme extends to larger oscillator systems.
arxiv-2605-26527: Ke Du and three colleagues give a formal meaning to C code with OpenMP parallelism. OpenMP turns sequential code parallel with a few annotations. Added pragmas can slip logic errors and races into correct programs. Their semantics builds on CompCert's verified C semantics plus its concurrency extension. It captures subtle links between directives and variable state that older semantics blurred. It grounds detection of bad behavior from wrong annotations: any run that succeeds ends free of data races.
arxiv-2605-26627: Chayan Banerjee and Ethan Goan name a trap that stalls reinforcement learning in safety-critical jobs like driving and medicine. Agents cannot pin down their state without knowing the dynamics, nor learn dynamics from faulty state guesses, and combined tests degrade 77 percent against a 46 percent additive guess. The pair reframe safety as an information problem, adding a coupling gauge, probing policies that seek facts, and guards that tighten as coupling grows. Passive toughness, they argue, cannot untangle coupled ignorance.
arxiv-2605-26927: Chen and four co-authors map the structure and energy of grain boundaries in self-assembled double-gyroid block copolymer networks. The energy landscape over boundary orientations holds several local minima for distinct network-switching types. The global minimum is a new asymmetric-tilt boundary beating the observed twin boundary. Unlike hard matter, where enthalpy rules, stability here is mostly entropy-driven: twist types add nodes and frustrate chain packing, while the winning type preserves connectivity.
arxiv-2605-27127: Sellati and co-authors explain large light-driven polarization rotations without invoking a real magnetization. They show a static rotation can come solely from the antisymmetric part of the third-order optical response, once Kleinman symmetry breaks down. A minimal tight-binding model on a square lattice gives a sizable response even far from dissipative resonances, and resonant coupling to phonons boosts it further. In nonmagnetic materials, this light-driven Faraday signal can far exceed the response from the inverse Faraday effect.
arxiv-2605-27227: The LIGO Scientific, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations use 236 gravitational wave sources to measure the cosmic expansion rate. They compare distances from the waves with redshifts from mass patterns and galaxy catalogs. Their estimate tightens the earlier catalog result by about a fifth, and their tests find no departure from general relativity in wave propagation.
arxiv-2605-27327: Jason Hicken shows a spectral collocation scheme gives the same answers as a discontinuous Galerkin discretization with the same quadrature. The match holds for any degree count and even when the quadrature is not strictly positive. Extra degrees of freedom sit in the operator nullspace and stay zero, though one entropy-stable splitting needs a projection fix to keep the match.
arxiv-2605-27827: Khalid Adnan Alsayed offers a set of rules for deciding when high-stakes AI is ready to ship. Most current checks only report scores or audit a system after the fact. His OADA scheme turns fairness and risk scores into grades for readiness, zones of stable behavior, and steps for raising problems. Tests on face-recognition tools show a system can pass single checks yet still be too shaky to use.
arxiv-2605-27927: Zhang and colleagues defend vision-language models against pixel-level attacks that trick them into unsafe behavior. Their lightweight SIGN defense first extracts the image's structure, then neutralizes hostile tweaks with tiny, guided changes that leave ordinary performance nearly untouched. It blocked over eighty-seven percent of attacks while altering only half a percent of pixels per image.
arxiv-2605-28127: Ke and colleagues tackle long-horizon goal-conditioned reinforcement learning from logged data alone. Their CFHRL framework refines distant goals step by step, proposing intermediate targets until each is judged locally reachable, rather than fixing hierarchy depth in advance. On OGBench it gained substantially on several long tasks, with ablations supporting its refinement and stopping rules.
arxiv-2605-28327: Günther and colleagues set insurance prices with buyer price sensitivity in view, not just fairness math. Their kernel-weighted score estimator taps nearby price structure to trim noise, feeding two price-rule methods: a plain Lasso form and a bendy neural net. In fake travel-insurance trials, neural pricing beat older methods.
arxiv-2605-28427: Alberte Heering Estad, Ignacio Peis, and Jes Frellsen ask whether diffusion models fill missing data better in a learned latent space than directly in data space. Their two-stage design first trains a robust variational autoencoder imputer on incomplete observations, then trains diffusion in the resulting latent space. Under random missingness, latent diffusion held sample quality steady up to half the data missing, while pixel-space diffusion degraded steadily. It also imputed downstream values more accurately, suggesting latent modeling curbs artifacts from zero-filled inputs.
arxiv-2605-28827: Jaber Jaber and Osama Jaber present RightNow-Arabic-Turbo, a 518M-parameter Arabic decoder model built on Qwen. The pipeline adds 27,032 Arabic tokens via mean-subtoken init, then pretrains on 504M Arabic tokens. It fine-tunes on 129,116 instruction pairs, applies preference tuning on 6,750 pairs, and merges weights across three checkpoints. On three Arabic benchmarks the merged model reaches about 36 percent mean accuracy, beating every same-class model. It ties Falcon-H1 on COPA-ar at one-third the size, and the edge build runs at 635 tokens per second on H100.
arxiv-2605-29127: Ashutosh Krishna Amaram, Aditya Koneru, and Subramanian KRS Sankaranarayanan simulate switching in Ta-HfO2-Pt memristors, where a conductive bridge was long blamed on oxygen vacancies. Molecular dynamics runs with charge transfer show metal cations also migrate, forming a hybrid filament rich in tantalum cations and poor in oxygen. Varying starting vacancy counts and layouts in the oxide changes the filament's shape and size. Switching follows field-driven formation and rupture of that filament, and the simulations match experiment, guiding designs that cut cycle and device variability.
arxiv-2605-29627: Guangyu Li and five colleagues raise rate in multi-guide pinching-antenna systems, which reshape channels by switching on beads along guides. Both travel loss and coupling effects are modeled. Their pairing method links users with nearby guides to cut path loss, placing spread users per time slot to reduce noise. A joint system tunes power and antenna spots, with spots found by search and power solved by duality and ratio math. Results show the method clearly beats random pairing, and the power method beats maximum ratio sending by far.
arxiv-2605-29727: Soowon Oh and six colleagues improve speculative decoding with block-diffusion drafters, that guess future tokens at once. Greedy single-path picks miss the target model's favoured path, since parallel guesses come from per-spot margins rather than full sequences. Their frame, BASTION, grows query-dependent trees by weighing draft quality against hardware limits, with path-confidence and latency gauges, and best-first growth that stops when checks stop paying. Training-free, it ran over six times faster than decoding and nearly forty percent ahead of diffusion rivals.
arxiv-2605-29927: Alejandra Zambrano and four colleagues ask whether plan wording changes how well a web agent performs. They build a planner-executor setup that tests plan wording apart from the agent, and sort WebArena tasks into three difficulty levels without hand grading. On hard tasks they try four plan forms — stepwise goals, story, code-like form, checklists — across agents from OpenAI, Alibaba, and Google. Two new scores track raw and steady success across runs. Both plan form and the writing model shift how tough and steady the agent proves.
arxiv-2605-30227: Wenwu Li and four co-authors unify temporal and structural credit assignment for multi-agent language-model prompt optimization. Optimization is hard because graphs are discrete and global signals sparse, so black-box optimizers cannot blame specific parts for failures. Their method splits the objective two ways: temporal credit via gates flagging key rounds, and structural credit via role policies isolating agent roles. A verbalized block descent algorithm alternates role prompts and protocols, using proxy gradients to target weak links, cutting query counts while improving results.
arxiv-2605-30727: Gurung and colleagues expose privacy risks when deep research agents combine private documents with external web retrieval. Single queries may look harmless but reveal information in aggregate, the mosaic effect. Their MosaicLeaks benchmark offers 1,001 multi-hop tasks chaining private documents and a public web corpus. An adversary model observing only external queries infers private information at three levels. Models across families and sizes frequently leak at all three levels. Their Privacy-Aware Deep Research framework combines situational rewards with a learned privacy classifier, improving accuracy and cutting leakage.
arxiv-2605-31127: Weiland and Hennig build a Bayesian simulator for nonlinear conservation laws. These are the equations behind many physical systems where flows and shocks carry uncertainty. They treat classical solvers as inference under Gaussian-process priors. They add sparse approximations that scale to large forward and inverse problems. Forward runs keep classical accuracy while reporting uncertainty in a structured way. Inverse runs recover source fields in seconds, beating neural baselines that take minutes for a poorer single estimate.
arxiv-2605-31327: Saia and colleagues tune the light system of the ICARUS neutrino detector. The 600-ton liquid-argon chamber uses 360 light-catching tubes. They feed triggers and sharpen event timing, but gain fell bit by bit during use. A test setup gauged gain from room heat down to minus 70 degrees in a cold chamber. Gain stays stable at room heat yet falls a lot, for good, when cold. That trend reveals a weak spot tied to gain. Fixes were then put in place to preserve work in deep cold.
arxiv-2605-31427: Au and colleagues propose DG-CoLearn, a joint framework for dynamic graph learning. Dynamic graph work models graphs that change, but current tools redo full snapshots each time. Links across data splits cannot be dodged, yet sharing raw shape may break privacy rules. DG-CoLearn works in small steps, touching only zones hit by updates while keeping past data. A server-run swap of vectors allows multi-hop passing without baring raw shape. Tests show up to 33.8 times faster training, lower message costs, and better node and link scores.
arxiv-2605-31527: Zhao and colleagues use charmed-meson femtoscopy in heavy-ion collisions to probe exotic hadronic states. Two-particle correlations reveal forces between emitted particles. That opens a window on charmed-meson links and possible molecular states. The team models each crash with a parton-hadron-string transport approach, and computes the pair signal with the Schrödinger equation. They find these events beat proton-proton crashes for this probe, thanks to richer charm output, lower relative momenta, and weaker early correlations.
arxiv-2606-00027:
Feier and a team at John Snow Labs stress-test medical language models with adversarial clinical scenarios in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard benchmarks miss how models behave when cases are ethically complex or rigged. Their red teaming framework, the security practice of attacking a system to find weaknesses, evaluated eleven current models on 690 clinically grounded scenarios. The scenarios spanned nine domains and over 150 subcategories, scored on a seven-dimension rubric with human validation.

Mean scores ranged widely, from about 0.79 to 0.98 across models. The top systems, including GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.1, scored above 0.97 with low variance. Yet several strong systems produced complete failures on individual safety-critical cases, showing averages can hide real clinical risk. Equity tasks were fragile: adding demographic details amplified errors by roughly 10 to 20 percent. Human reviewers also caught relevant failures that automated scoring missed entirely.
arxiv-2606-00327:
Wycik and co-authors build a tool to check group splits in data with fresh draws. Group splits seed much of the work that comes next in science. Yet splits swing with the tool, prep, and count a team picks. Claims built on shaky splits can fail to hold up.

Their tool, CARVE, tests many tools and picks at once by re-draws. It gives firm and broad marks at world, group, and case ranks. Set pick rules and joint tags round out the pack. Tests on six fake sets show it finds near-best splits where old gauges fade. On gene and protein sets, it finds fine life traits old gauges miss. It ships for both Python and R users.
arxiv-2606-00827:
Lv and co-authors extend strategic classification to peer effects in this 2026 paper. People who face a predictive model may tweak their traits to win a good call. Past fairness work in this area looks at group fairness. It also treats each agent as acting alone. Under individual fairness, near twins should get near outcomes. That link makes each agent's best move rest on what neighbors get.

Their frame, IFSC, models this peer pull head on. Agents imitate near peers who got a yes, hoping for the same. The classifier learns under the shifted data that such copying makes. Random noise in the simulation covers doubt about which peers each agent can see. On synthetic and real datasets, the authors report, IFSC lifts individual-fairness consistency. It also softens the harms that peer copying can cause. The paper speaks to any scored system where people watch and copy each other.
arxiv-2606-00927:
Ahmed fuses shape math with deep vision to sort brain tumors in this 2026 paper. MRI scans guide early diagnosis and care choices for brain tumors. Vision Transformers read such scans well, learning broad context across the image. But they can miss the deep structural patterns inside a tumor's shape.

His fusion model pairs two views of each scan. Topological Data Analysis extracts shape traits: geometry, connectivity, and form. A pretrained Vision Transformer learns high-level semantic traits in parallel. The two feature sets merge into one stronger code for the classifier. Tests use the BRISC2025 dataset, with glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and non-tumor cases. The fusion scores 99.10 percent accuracy, he reports. Precision, recall, and F1 all sit near 99 percent as well. Each view alone does worse than the pair. The work argues that tumor shape is signal, not noise, for scan readers.
arxiv-2606-01227:
Ferguson builds networks that briefly boost a signal a lot. Such boosts can reach many times the input size. The network stays stable in the long run. Hard limits on sign, sparsity, and diagonal make this tough. Past tools need slow gradient search or a change of basis. Both can break the hard limits. His DAGGER tool works in one pass with no gradients.

DAGGER starts from a stable signed sparse matrix. Its output keeps the same sign, sparsity, and diagonal. One scalar sets a budget for how much sets may shift. Peak boost grows with that budget, up to ten to the tenth power. It uses 30 to 100 times fewer eigen checks than gradient tools.
arxiv-2606-01427:
Johnson and co-authors test how well tabular foundation models gauge doubt. Foundation models generalize across tasks with no task-specific training. But key uses in mechanics need reliable uncertainty estimates too. TabPFN is the tabular model under study here. Gaussian processes serve as the classic comparison point. The team run a broad empirical study on regression tasks. Complexity, dataset size, and input dimension all vary.

TabPFN competes well on complex, high-dimensional problems with ample data. Gaussian processes often win when data are scarce. Their accuracy and uncertainty both tend to be better there. A well-chosen kernel can push GP performance far ahead. The trade-off turns on explicit versus learned priors. Code is public to reproduce the results.
arxiv-2606-01527:
Regehr, Kamath, and Lowy pin down the true cost of machine unlearning. Laws and users may demand that data leave a trained model. The right to be forgotten is one such driver. Prior work gave algorithms and error bounds for convex losses. The basic statistical cost of unlearning stayed unclear, though. Their bounds on excess risk are tight up to a condition factor. Upper and lower bounds match for mean estimation on the unit ball.

Pure unlearning shows no statistical loss versus the relaxed form. That marks a sharp split from differential privacy. The best rate is sampling error plus an unlearning penalty. For small requests, retraining from scratch is near optimal. For large requests, their method beats retraining by an exponential margin.
arxiv-2606-01627:
Dubin, Gorski, and Michelen study the shape of the giant component in random geometric graphs. Points are scattered uniformly on a Riemannian manifold. Edges join pairs whose distance stays below a radius r. Past a critical mean degree, a giant component forms in the graph. That threshold depends only on the manifold's dimension. The team ask what the giant component looks like at large scale. Equipped with graph distance, it converges to the manifold itself.

Convergence is in Gromov-Hausdorff distance, after a deterministic rescaling. The result holds even when mean degree grows slowly with n. A payoff follows for telling manifolds apart from samples. A polynomial-time algorithm distinguishes graphs on two non-isometric manifolds. First-passage percolation tools drive the proof.
arxiv-2606-01827:
Oikonomou and Loizou tune a training method that seeks flat loss valleys. Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, trains with that aim. Flat minima tend to help models on new data. But SAM is touchy about its step size. Step size is often set by costly trial runs.

The pair derive Polyak-style step rules made for SAM. The rules adapt on their own as training runs. They cover both exact and noisy training cases. For smooth losses, they prove fast rates of approach. Noisy cases settle near the best point, they show. Tests on real tasks back the design, they report. The aim is strong training with less hand tuning.
arxiv-2606-02627:
Zellmann and co-authors present Streami, a GPU library for computing field lines in fluid flows. Field lines trace flow structure for analysis. Streami targets high-performance computers. It acts as a thin layer for post-hoc or in-situ analysis. It can interface with existing MPI applications. Extensibility is a core design goal.

The paper covers the application programming interface in detail. Key design decisions behind the speed and flexibility are explained. Extensions support different fluid flow field representations. A sample application supports rapid prototyping. It also allows interactive seed point placement. Streami is released under a permissive open-source license. Flow analysts get a reusable, GPU-fast tool that plugs into current simulation stacks.
arxiv-2606-02927:
Zaied argues that deep networks do not need normalization layers to train well. Layers such as BatchNorm and LayerNorm are widely seen as essential. Zaied reports that they cause a plasticity suppression effect. Learnable activation parameters lose their adaptability when paired with normalization.

The proposed fix is SALU, a bounded learnable activation with two positive parameters. It stabilizes signals on its own, with no batch statistics or affine terms. The full design, SaluNet, swaps normalization out for SALU. It also uses two SALU variants in place of standard activations. A ResNet-18 version scored 97.35 percent on CIFAR-10 and 83.25 percent on CIFAR-100 with no normalization. At batch size one it kept most of that accuracy, where normalized designs fail. A transformer version slightly beat a LayerNorm baseline on both CIFAR sets. A larger model reached 78.67 percent top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K.
arxiv-2606-03027:
Limkonchotiwat, Ng, Nutanong, and Ngui present SEA-LION-Embedding, an open text-embedding pipeline for Southeast Asian languages. Embeddings underpin many language applications, so robustness matters. Most top models, though, rely on closed or undisclosed training data. They also remain weak for Southeast Asian languages.

SEA-LION-Embedding trains only on publicly available data, so the whole pipeline can be reproduced. The team uses it to study three design factors: data composition, training objective, and base encoder choice. The model reaches state-of-the-art results on the SEA-BED benchmark. Beyond the scores, the pipeline enables systematic analysis of what makes embeddings robust for the region. The work should interest builders of multilingual systems who need open tools. It shows that strong embeddings for under-served languages need not depend on private data. Reproducibility is treated here as a feature, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2606-03327:
Ban and co-authors supervise text-to-SQL models at the clause level. Such systems are graded by whether the final query runs right. That end signal says little about which inner choice caused success or failure. Token-level scores fit poorly too: SQL tokens do not match whole semantic choices, and can fine runs that are equal in effect.

Their method, CAPER, derives clause-level labels on its own. It intervenes on the query's syntax tree in a counterfactual way, to find which clause caused an error. The labels train CAPER-9B, a light reward model that gives feedback at clause bounds. That feedback guides policy training and checks candidate queries. On BIRD and Spider, clause-aligned supervision raised execution accuracy. It beat a top frontier model by up to about 15 percent in relative terms. On held-out failures it located the faulty clause with high accuracy.
arxiv-2606-03627:
Pham and Xue prove a sharp estimate for the spherical restriction problem over finite fields. The setting is four dimensions, over the field with p elements for an odd prime p. Spheres of nonzero radius are the objects of study. The team proves the sharp extension estimate for every such sphere. The bound holds uniformly in p and in the sphere choice.

The proof joins Hecke operator bounds with a refined fourth moment and an orthogonal decomposition. A localized version of the restriction conjecture is also stated. It predicts sharp dependence on the size of the physical support. That conjecture stays open. If true, it would yield distance estimates for almost every pin at the expected Erdős-Falconer exponent. Unconditional local estimates already give strong distance results for large sets. Two-set asymmetric versions follow as well. Harmonic analysts get a sharp endpoint result with clear next targets.
arxiv-2606-03927:
Liu and co-authors extend Forward-Forward learning from class labels to regression. The base method trains each layer with local rules, not backpropagation. That makes it cheap and more like biology. Regression is hard for it, though. A real-valued target has no clear opposite for contrast pairs. The plain score also lacks size and order clues.

Their FFR design splits neurons into groups that compete by rank. Shallow layers learn coarse rank, and deep layers refine the value. The design also gives a doubt score in one pass. On six real data sets, FFR keeps most of backpropagation's accuracy. The authors report far less training memory and faster steps. It also beats the other methods that skip backpropagation.
arxiv-2606-04127:
Erfan Nourbakhsh, Rocky Slavin, Ke Yang, and Anthony Rios test a common assumption in 2026: that retrieval always helps chatbots answer questions. Retrieval-augmented generation fetches documents to ground the answer, and it is now standard practice in medical AI.

Across five open models, ten biomedical datasets, four retrievers, and four document sets, retrieval added only small, uneven gains. Often it added none at all. The bottleneck turned out to be the model, not the retriever: models failed to use good evidence when it was handed to them. Long, noisy context hurt more than missing context helped. The authors argue that scaling retrievers alone will not fix medical question answering. Model-side use of evidence is where the work lies.
arxiv-2606-04527:
Bian and colleagues present a video generation system designed to run indefinitely in real time without forgetting its own past, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Existing methods curate memory with fixed cache schedules or heuristic compression, which loses history and compounds generation errors. Echo-Infinity instead learns its memory: a set of Memory Queries, updated by attention and gating whenever old frames leave the local window, filters and compresses any length of history at constant cost.

The queries train end-to-end with the video diffusion model, forming an evolving memory that also serves as a generation prior. A unified relative position recipe removes the finite-length constraint that normally caps video duration. Echo-Infinity reached state-of-the-art results on long and short video generation, and the authors report the first real-time rollouts lasting 24 hours, over 1.3 million frames.
arxiv-2606-04627:
Yang and colleagues teach a phone-operating AI agent to think silently instead of writing out long thoughts, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Mobile agents control apps from screenshots and language goals, but many spell their reasoning out as text, which slows interaction and raises supervision costs. MIRAGE learns continuous latent reasoning representations from visible textual thoughts, transferring explicit reasoning into compact hidden states the agent can use without decoding long rationales.

MIRAGE also aligns those latent vectors with future screenshots, so the hidden state predicts how the interface will change before the agent acts, a world-model view of the screen. On AndroidWorld, it matched explicit chain-of-thought fine-tuning in the 4B ablation at a three-to-five-fold lower decoded-token budget, and improved a comparable instruction-tuned baseline by 10.2 points. On AndroidControl, it improved action grounding while generating over 75 percent fewer tokens.
arxiv-2606-05127:
Yulin Shen and colleagues show that physics-informed distillation can build machine learning interatomic potentials at quantum-chemical accuracy with far less costly data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Non-covalent interactions, the weak forces between molecules, need errors near one wavenumber, but the coupled-cluster calculations that supply training labels are expensive. The team distills knowledge from a pretrained universal potential, then fine-tunes with coupled-cluster data.

For helium-benzene, fine-tuning with 30 percent of the coupled-cluster data beat direct training on 80 percent, cutting the compute budget by about 63 percent. A perturbation-theory-informed architecture that adapts its short-range and long-range parts lowered validation error from 0.75 to 0.49 wavenumbers.
