Across polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, swapping the teacher model changed the coronene error by an order of magnitude while larger systems stayed stable. That shows distillation transfers physical structure, not just labels.
arxiv-2606-05227:
Zhaojie Chai and colleagues measure the biophysical properties of stomatocytes, the cup-shaped blood cells seen in stomatocytosis, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These conditions present a puzzle called the splenectomy paradox: removing the spleen often cures overhydrated patients yet can trigger life-threatening clotting in dehydrated ones. Cell traits depend on several parameters that existing assays measure only piecemeal.

The team combined dissipative particle dynamics simulations with microfluidic imaging, building a control discocyte and three stomatocyte models at fixed membrane area and decreasing volume, and traced them through five assays. Crossing interendothelial slits proved geometry-dominated: the overhydrated model needed ten times the pressure of the control. The dehydrated model passed freely yet suppressed membrane tank-treading and raised low-shear whole-blood viscosity by about 29 percent. A funnel-obstacle chip design should separate all four cell types from a label-free signal, aiding pre-operative triage.
arxiv-2606-05327:
Raghav Kansal and colleagues extend flow matching to the multimarginal setting in this 2026 arXiv paper. Flow matching learns a dynamic transport map between two distributions. But many scientific problems observe intermediate distributions along the way, snapshots of a system evolving in time, which should constrain the flow between the endpoints. Ignoring those middle snapshots wastes real information about the dynamics.

Their approach, OTP-FM, leans on the connection between flow matching and dynamic optimal transport: potential terms added to the transport action steer the learned flow toward the intermediate marginals. Extending the conditional flow matching learning target to include those potentials yields an efficient, simulation-free training algorithm with considerable flexibility in the spatiotemporal dynamics it can represent. The authors report state-of-the-art performance and training efficiency on diverse datasets drawn from single-cell RNA sequencing, oceanography, and meteorology, and they release the code publicly.
arxiv-2606-05527:
Bartusek and Shalit ask what cryptography a test for quantum behavior secretly requires in a 2026 arXiv paper. Checking that a device holds anti-commuting operators, a quantum signature, underpins recent proofs of quantum computing checks. Known tests rest on heavy assumptions like trapdoor claw-free functions. The authors probe whether that weight is truly needed. They define a clean test of non-commutation between a quantum prover and a classical checker.

The results run the implication backward. Any strong enough such test yields key agreement, a basic crypto primitive, over a classical channel. Add one-way functions and the test also yields oblivious transfer, a stronger primitive. Along the way the pair prove the first hardness amplification results for these tools against quantum attackers. The message is that simple-looking quantum tests carry deep cryptographic structure. Light assumptions for them may be impossible in principle.
arxiv-2606-05727:
David Pask settles a planarity guess for higher-rank trees in a 2026 arXiv paper. Higher-rank graphs extend ordinary graphs with edges of several colors and squares between them. A tree here is a connected example with no loops. Pask studies finite trees whose skeleton draws flat in the plane. Non-degenerate means every color pairs with every other in squares at each edge.

Under those conditions the rank, the number of colors, cannot exceed four. That cap proves a conjecture from earlier work. The proof's engine is a backward flow of colors at each vertex. It forces one vertex to emit every color. With five or more colors, local flatness would carve out a copy of the non-planar complete graph on five vertices, a contradiction. Notably, the argument never uses the four-color theorem, only the simpler non-planarity fact.
arxiv-2606-05827:
Fania and Flamini prove an abundance of special bundles on a family of threefold scrolls in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ulrich bundles are tightly constrained vector bundles tied to a variety's embedding. A variety is Ulrich wild when such bundles come in large, varied families. The scrolls here are decomposable and sit over Hirzebruch surfaces, ruled surfaces indexed by one integer. The authors treat every value of that index.

For index zero, the moduli space of bundles of any rank at least two has a well-behaved component. They compute its dimension and show its general member is slope-stable. That alone makes the scroll wild. For higher indices, modular obstructions block the same clean argument. Careful work shows the scrolls are wild there too. The results widen the known map of Ulrich complexity for threefolds. They also supply concrete stable bundles where earlier work gave only existence hints.
arxiv-2606-05927:
Bin Liu and colleagues fix lopsided multi-label data by measuring distance differently for every label in a 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-label items carry several tags at once, and rare tags get swamped. Oversampling adds synthetic examples, but standard methods judge neighbors with one distance for all labels. Features matter differently per label, so close neighbors can still conflict on tags. The result is label confusion and overfitting to bad synthetic points.

LSDMLO builds a weighted feature space for each label separately. Label-consistent neighbors emerge under the label's own metric. Seed points are chosen where labels correlate near decision boundaries. Synthetic instances then follow the original label distribution instead of blurring it. Experiments across datasets and base classifiers beat the leading multi-label sampling methods. The gain comes from respecting that relevance is label-specific. Imbalance, the authors argue, is partly a measurement problem in disguise.
arxiv-2606-06027:
Ghaffari and colleagues unify how language models learn to speak like given online communities in a 2026 arXiv paper. Each prior study gathered data, defined communities, and judged its own way, blocking comparison. RedditPersona fixes the pipeline: gather posts and comments, profile active users, then group them. Five grouping strategies compete: subreddit membership, graph structure, semantics, interactions, and a hybrid.

A small-footprint QLoRA adapter trains per strategy. A shared metric suite scores fluency, fidelity, alignment with real text, and community identifiability. The testbed covered one hundred twelve subreddits in urban well-being, with over three hundred thousand user profiles and sixteen million comments. Adapters' identifiability tracked how well each strategy agreed with the plain subreddit baseline. A steady tradeoff appeared everywhere: sounding identifiable versus matching real text distributions. Modular plumbing turns one-off persona studies into shared science. Code and configs are public.
arxiv-2606-06127:
Jacek Ciszewski and colleagues settle the computational cost of checking graph databases against PG-Schema in this 2026 arXiv paper. A property graph stores data as nodes and edges carrying labels and key-value properties. PG-Schema is a language for declaring which shapes such a database is allowed to take. Validation means deciding whether a given database instance actually fits a given schema, ignoring integrity constraints.

The authors show that this validation problem is NP-complete in combined complexity, where both the database and the schema count toward the input size. Measured by data complexity, with the schema treated as fixed, the same problem sits in polynomial time. They further show that the combined cost drops back to polynomial time when the schema limits how type combinations and unions alternate. These results map exactly where automated checking stays practical and where it becomes intractable.
arxiv-2606-06627:
Richard Li and co-authors ask what makes everyday internet video useful for teaching robots in this 2026 arXiv paper. Robot manipulation data is scarce and expensive, while human video is everywhere. But casual footage lacks the staged, robot like motions of curated datasets. The team built five hundred thirty two human videos, twenty eight hours, with high quality triangulated hand labels and natural motion, then cotrained manipulation policies on them.

Hand pose quality mattered, but it was not sufficient. Even with accurate hands, the motion gap between human and robot bodies blocked transfer. The fix was letting the vision and policy networks specialize partly to each embodiment. With that recipe, cotraining delivered consistent gains across six manipulation tasks. In the low robot data regime, success rates rose by an absolute twenty nine point seven percent. Everyday video, handled right, is a real training resource, not just a curiosity.
arxiv-2606-06727:
Autonomous robots mix hand built engineering models with learned software, and no single design method covers both halves well. Baras and co-authors propose one that does in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method extends the classic V shaped systems engineering process by adding a data driven loop at every stage, tied together through a shared system model written in SysML.

Three open source tools carry the method. One turns system models into runnable robot software for testing. One splits design exploration between model based search and data driven scoring. One blends formal proof, data checks, and runtime monitoring into a single assurance flow. The team demonstrates the full cycle on a trusted autonomous ground robot. The work runs from choosing sensors to coordinating several robots. It all happens inside a contested terrain simulator, released alongside the tools.
arxiv-2606-06827:
Some neural networks learn a scene as a smooth function of position. Eng studies how those networks borrow knowledge in this 2026 arXiv paper. The models are implicit neural representations, networks that answer with a value for any coordinate. A trained model can warm start a new task. The question is whether that help is truly specific.

Eng compared three network families across several test beds. The tests included fluid flow and classic equations for heat and waves. One family, using Fourier features, showed the largest raw transfer gains. Another, the plain ReLU network, was far more selective about its source. Sine based networks reused weights broadly, even from unrelated sources. Rankings flipped between tests, so no family won everywhere. Eng argues that transfer should be judged with control runs, not by gain alone. Size of the gain and loyalty to the source are separate traits.
arxiv-2606-07127:
A game playing agent can win by luck and still understand nothing about why its moves work. Shindo and co-authors make agents prove their understanding in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their Explicit Symbolic Behavioral Model stores behavior as typed predicates, weighted rules, and bounded action options. A mechanism memory predicts what actions change: events, objects, rewards, and endings.

After each playthrough, the system asks itself hard questions. Adaptive questions and active probes target exactly where scores, answers, or predictions failed. The failures become constraints guiding small local edits to the model. Candidate models must pass three tests at once: task score, answerability, and world model consistency. Under Atari style protocols, the agents reached high scores while answering questions about their own behavior. Brittle reward chasing gets exposed early, because lucky policies cannot fake the mechanism tests. The framework doubles as a reusable benchmark for mechanistic policy learning.
arxiv-2606-07327:
Isabel Creed and a large consortium of co-authors map the biggest open problems in computational chemistry in this 2026 arXiv paper. Machine-learned interatomic potentials are neural networks that predict forces between atoms, letting researchers simulate materials far faster than quantum calculations allow. Foundation versions, trained on huge diverse datasets, promise to work on new materials with little adjustment. The field has advanced so quickly that its basic definitions and limits remain unsettled.

The authors first propose a working definition of what makes such a potential foundational, then organize six open questions around it. The questions probe how far these models generalize, what data they truly need, and where their accuracy breaks down. Contributions span many institutions, marking it as a community position piece. Its aim is to frame the debates that will define atomistic modeling research in the coming years, rather than to report a single new model.
arxiv-2606-07427:
Andriulli tackles a computing bottleneck in electromagnetic scattering in this 2026 arXiv paper. Engineers solve the electric field integral equation with the boundary element method to predict how objects scatter radio and radar waves. The resulting linear systems become badly conditioned in three regimes: low frequency, refined meshes, and high frequency with dense discretization. Preconditioners, twists that make solving faster, exist, but few handle all regimes at once, and the fast matrix operations are costly.

The paper investigates a family based on Helmholtz regularization, built around a shifted version of the wave operator. Standard pseudo-inversion of it performed poorly, so Andriulli proposes a new strategy for it. The technique steadied solve counts across all three problematic regimes in his tests. Combined with speedups, the pseudo-inversion reaches quasi-linear complexity, meaning cost grows almost proportionally with problem size. That brings solving the equation to the same cost class.
arxiv-2606-07527:
Hassid, Adi, and Schwartz argue that language model post-training has reverted to old-fashioned supervised learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. After pretraining, today's models undergo supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning tailored to behaviors and the benchmarks used for evaluation. The authors compare this with the BERT era's pre-train, fine-tune recipe, where performance meant fitting in-distribution data. Their overview claims the landscape resembles the early days more than the field admits.

The empirical test is provocative: fine-tune pretrained models and models initialized from scratch on reasoning datasets, compare them on mathematics and coding benchmarks. The from-scratch models achieved non-trivial performance, suggesting post-training is distribution fitting rather than unlocking capability. If fitting explains most gains, the authors argue, general models require training procedures where models learn how to learn. The paper positions itself as a challenge to how the field reads progress.
arxiv-2606-08127:
Jeffrey Shallit relates two ways of measuring the richness of an infinite word, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Take an endless sequence of letters from a finite alphabet. Its factor complexity counts how many distinct blocks of each length appear. Its palindrome complexity counts how many of those blocks read the same backwards and forwards. Both functions are classical in combinatorics on words, but their relationship was loose.

Shallit proves that for any infinite word that is not ultimately periodic, the palindrome count is negligible beside the factor count in a precise sense. Palindrome complexity times its own logarithm, divided by factor complexity, tends to zero. In words with many blocks, palindromic blocks are a vanishingly small share. The second result says this is nearly the best possible statement: the numerator cannot be meaningfully enlarged. Palindromes are rare ornaments in any rich text, and the theorem shows that intuition is sharp.
arxiv-2606-08327:
Sikdar introduces a transformer variant that spends compute only where a token needs it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard self-attention, the mechanism letting each token weigh every other, grows fast with sequence length and dominates the cost of large models. The proposed CHIAR-Former routes each token either to full attention or to a cheaper spectral mixing step. A score called spectral entropy, which measures how complex a token's frequency content is, makes the choice. Simple tokens take the cheap path; complex ones get full attention.

Three findings anchor the paper. A three-operator routing system collapsed during training to just two operators, A learned MetaRouter blends the spectral and identity paths at the task level. At four hundred million parameters, the model cut floating-point operations by roughly a third or more, at a modest perplexity cost on WikiText-103.
arxiv-2606-08427:
Anderson, Gray, Nally, and Taylor advance a famous conjecture about the shapes underlying string theory, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Calabi-Yau threefolds are six-dimensional shapes that string theory uses to hide extra dimensions. Whether their distinct topological types are finite in number is a long-standing problem. Reid's fantasy conjectures that all such threefolds are connected in a single moduli space, one continuous family, through extremal transitions that pass through singular shapes. Finiteness is already proven for fibered threefolds, which constitute the vast majority of known examples.

This letter shows that all non-fibered Calabi-Yau threefolds in two of the largest known classes connect to fibered ones through a simple class of geometric transitions. Each transition shrinks a single divisor, a surface inside the shape.
arxiv-2606-08727:
Elbrächter and Petersen prove that building functions by composition can beat building them by addition, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Classical approximation theory studies superpositional methods, which combine dictionary elements linearly, like mixing paint colors. Many function classes are approximated optimally this way. Compositional methods such as neural networks are structurally different, nesting functions inside functions. The authors impose the encoding constraints that make the comparison honest.

They construct explicit examples exhibiting an arbitrarily large gap between the two rates. In those examples, composition achieves accuracy at parameter counts the superposition cannot approach. The result supplies a rigorous instance of the folklore behind deep learning's power. Some functions are cheaper to build by nesting than by mixing. The point lands with force: depth of nesting can matter more than sheer size of the parts list used.
arxiv-2606-09027:
Chen and colleagues make language-model training plans for runners safe by never letting the model have the final say, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A running plan that overshoots physiological limits can injure the athlete, so the same rules must always bind. Language models are probabilistic and sometimes break constraints. SafeRun splits the job in two. The language model handles soft interpretation, while a deterministic solver enforces constraints on load and recovery.

The team built a benchmark for running planning under physiological and safety rules and tested 5 language models. SafeRun achieved a safety score of 100 percent. Prompt-engineered baselines averaged 79.1 percent, and a code-acting approach reached 97.6 percent, still unsafe. Instruction following stayed competitive, so safety did not come at the cost of bad plans. The authors release the benchmark. Their claim: where violations carry harm, flexibility belongs in interpretation, and enforcement belongs to solvers that cannot improvise.
arxiv-2606-09627:
Santiago Hernández-Díaz, Beate Stelzer, and Daniela Muñoz-Giraldo offer a fresh way to spot a hidden class of dead-star pairs in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cataclysmic variables pair a white dwarf with a small star that feeds it gas. Their orbits shrink to a floor near eighty minutes, then bounce back to longer spans. These bounced systems should be the bulk of the class, yet few are seen, since they shine faintly.

The team turns to Balmer decrements, the ratios of bright hydrogen lines in a spectrum. Spectra came from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Young, pre-bounce systems show flat ratios, close to one. Systems near or past the floor show steep ratios, with one line ratio above one and the next below it. The split tracks their lower gas flow rates. A simple fitted classifier on two such ratios sorts the groups well.
arxiv-2606-09727:
Andriani Keliri and Marco Schirò build a steady-state frame for quantum systems that are both driven and leaky in this 2026 arXiv paper. A drive that repeats in time can often be swapped for a fixed Floquet Hamiltonian, a stand-in that captures each cycle. Leakage breaks that swap: loss makes the motion non-unitary, and no stand-in is assured.

Working in a stretched Sambe-Liouville space, the pair build a fixed Floquet Lindbladian, the open-system twin of that stand-in. The time-based task turns into a static eigenvalue task. For smooth harmonic drives, a matrix continued fraction folds in multi-photon steps all at once. It beats high-frequency expansions, which add terms one by one. A resolvent route then yields spectra of time-linked signals.
arxiv-2606-10127:
Farboodi and colleagues build a dynamic economic model of automation powered by data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on economics. In their model, data is heterogeneous and task-specific, accumulates endogenously as a byproduct of economic activity, and spills over between tasks, so data from one task raises productivity in another. Along the transition path, data plays a dual role: it augments already-automated tasks and expands the automation frontier into new tasks. The authors derive tight conditions separating partial from full long-run automation.

When full automation does occur, its short-run dynamics are rich and depend on the spillover pattern. Yet it is always slow in the long run, with labor's task share decaying as a power law in time. With endogenous capital accumulation, data-driven automation generates explosive growth but stagnant long-run wages, a distributional warning about who benefits from the data economy.
arxiv-2606-10327:
Keramati and Warschauer show that the order in which an essay-scoring model learns its subtasks changes how well it scores, in a 2026 arXiv paper on school technology. Machine essay scoring must judge linked discourse elements, such as lead, claim, evidence, and conclusion, yet most approaches treat them alone, harming coherence. They fine-tune an eight-billion-parameter LLaMA model with parameter-efficient LoRA adapters and compare three curricula: sequential training following discourse order, solo task-specific models, and shuffled multi-task training, on the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus.

Sequential fine-tuning yields the strongest overall results, with the best scores on evidence and conclusion elements. It beats solo training and even a much larger general seventy-billion-parameter baseline on conclusion scoring despite the size gap. Shuffled training improves position scoring but is less steady elsewhere.
arxiv-2606-10627:
Kawamura and colleagues build a practice aid for pianists in this 2026 arXiv paper, presented at the Designing Interactive Systems conference. Expert playing differs from amateur playing in timing, articulation, and dynamics, but learners usually get only summary feedback. Their system, Profy, learns from whole-take labels alone, whether listeners rated a performance expert or amateur, needing no note-level annotation. It outputs time-aligned evidence scores, so a learner can scrub to the passages marking the expert-amateur difference and loop them.

The data are substantial: synchronised key-motion and audio at one kilohertz from seventy-three pianists, with 1,083 valid takes. On twenty amateur clips annotated by twenty-one expert pianists, the highlight scores line up with passages experts marked for review. Agreement reaches a Pearson correlation of 0.61 and an area under the curve of 0.75, despite no localised labels in training.
arxiv-2606-11227:
Akhtar and Goswami study collective emission in bacterial light-harvesting assemblies in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. When many pigment molecules emit together, some states shine brightly, superradiance, while others stay dark, subradiance. The point-dipole approximation treats each emitter as a dimensionless point, hiding how finite size and shape steer that balance. The authors go beyond it for the LH2 complex of purple bacteria, a ring of twenty-four bacteriochlorophyll pigments.

They build a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian from the dyadic Green's tensor, for the isolated ring and its crystal assembly. The crystal's unit-cell symmetry inverts the ring's bright-dark ordering, placing subradiant states at the low-energy end. The whole crystal emerges as the true energy-harvesting entity. Tilt-driven switching activates only where the LH2 unit lies perpendicular to the growth plane. Vacancy and orientational disorder cooperate to shift the switching threshold to lower polar angles.
arxiv-2606-11527:
Sato, Hidaka, and Kobayashi define an invariant for exotic symmetries in a 2026 arXiv paper, issued as a RIKEN iTHEMS report. Non-invertible symmetries in quantum many-body systems give rise to sequential unitary circuits that move symmetry defects. They study invariants from runs of such circuits, which generate a Berry phase on quantum states carrying defects.

They show this Berry phase is invariant under local deformations, provided circuits preserve the deformations' locality. The invariant also rules out a short-range-entangled state preserving it, thereby signaling the 't Hooft anomaly of a non-invertible symmetry through operators acting on a state. Applying the framework to loops in three spatial dimensions, they identify a new loop excitation in the D4 topological order, dubbed a non-Abelian fermionic loop. They characterize its statistics and find a new mixed topological order whose long-range entanglement is protected by it.
arxiv-2606-11627:
Xun Wang and four Tsinghua colleagues report a surprising failure in language model training in this 2026 arXiv paper. On-policy distillation trains a student model on its own outputs, guided by a teacher that sees privileged context such as system prompts or hints. The goal is internalisation: the student absorbs the context and no longer needs it when answering.

The authors find that giving the context back to such a student often makes it worse, even on questions it already answers correctly without context. They call this context-induced degradation. Their fix, No-Context Anchoring, is a light training penalty that anchors the no-context output and punishes the with-context output for drifting away from it. It costs one extra forward pass per step. Across twelve configurations it reduces the harm in eleven settings, often improves no-context accuracy too, and removes an unwanted growth in response length.
arxiv-2606-11827:
Yewon Jeong leads a Seoul National University team making private image classification faster in this 2026 arXiv paper. Private inference lets a client classify an image on a server's model while neither side reveals its secrets, using homomorphic encryption. Hybrid systems are bottlenecked by arithmetic in prime-modulus rings and by a clumsy precision flow around the ReLU activation step.

Their system, Jaguar, switches the ciphertext ring to a power of two. That single choice enables a convolution method based on simple scalar accumulation. It also allows exact shrinking of encrypted values by local shifts. ReLU therefore runs at target precision directly, with no extra truncation protocol. On ImageNet-scale networks including ResNet-50 and MobileNetV2, Jaguar cuts end-to-end latency by roughly two to nearly four times against the Cheetah system. Against Rhombus the gain is over two to three times, while sending less data than Cheetah.
arxiv-2606-11927:
Ron Schreier, Shlomi Hillel and Noam Soker build a virtual giant star for binary-star simulations in this 2026 arXiv paper. In common envelope evolution, a companion star plunges into a giant's outer layers, a violent process that is hard to simulate. Simulations need a realistic three-dimensional red supergiant to start from.

The authors transport a one-dimensional stellar model onto a three-dimensional grid, without forcing it to relax. Nuclear power is mimicked by depositing the star's luminosity into an inner shell above the inert core. Light emission is mimicked by cooling the low-density outer cells that represent the photosphere. With cooling alone, the model's pulsations decay slowly; with both heating and cooling, oscillations persist and grow. The main period is about one year, matching the star's dynamical time. Non-radial modes and vigorous convection also appear, as real red supergiants show.
arxiv-2606-12127:
Chen and co-authors report an unrecognized instability in plasmas sustained by an electron beam, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A plasma is a gas of charged particles, and here the beam creates the plasma itself by knocking electrons off gas atoms, a process called ionization. In the classic hose instability, a strong beam snakes sideways inside a ready-made plasma. The new form needs no ready-made plasma and no extreme beam strength.

The sideways wobble grows because the beam center and the plasma it creates push on each other. The authors build a linear theory that predicts the wobble frequency and how fast it grows. Particle simulations with collisions confirm both the onset and the predicted rates. Tests span pressures from one half to five millitorr, and higher pressure disrupts the beam sooner. The effect can break the beam apart and blast device walls.
arxiv-2606-12327:
Bamieh derives the Kalman filter from its control-theory twin in two moves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Kalman filter estimates a system's hidden state from noisy measurements. Its deterministic version seeks the state trajectory consistent with the system's equations while minimizing process and measurement error. Bamieh's tutorial starts from the Linear Quadratic Regulator, the classic problem of steering a linear system at least quadratic cost. Estimation, he shows, is secretly an input-design problem of that same shape.

Step one embeds the problem in a larger system using homogeneous coordinates, turning the affine objective purely quadratic. The enlarged problem is an LQR variant with unusual endpoint constraints, solved by a matrix differential Riccati equation. Step two partitions the large problem, and out fall the optimal dynamic observer and the Kalman filter's own Riccati equation. A parallel treatment of LQ tracking sharpens the comparison.
arxiv-2606-12427:
Vadaparty and co-authors watch beginning programmers plan on paper before they ever touch code, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Problem decomposition, splitting a task into functions and steps, is a core computing skill. With AI tools writing code, teachers push planning harder. Yet how novices actually decompose large tasks is little known. In a fifty-minute lab, students sketched decomposition diagrams for a program implementing a word game.

The team thematically analyzed fifty-five diagrams, coding their elements and issues. Students mixed strategies: hierarchical function calls showing structure, and sequencing showing execution order. Recurring problems included incompatible notations inside one diagram, muddled execution order, weak abstraction and reuse, and misunderstandings of the problem itself. The tensions suggest novices hold multiple mental models of program behavior at once, structural and sequential, and the models collide. Instruction should clarify representational constraints and let students trace their plans as simulations before coding begins.
arxiv-2606-12627:
Pascale Garaud and co-authors find two roads from stillness to turbulence in stratified fluids, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Strongly stratified flows, like ocean layers, resist vertical mixing. Horizontal shear, though, stays unstable when stratification should forbid motion, provided the Reynolds number is high. The puzzle: mixing across density layers needs vertical shear, and none exists at the start. Linear theory plus direct simulations trace how it appears.

In the first pathway, the horizontal instability's wavy modes carry vertical shear. That shear then breaks into Kelvin-Helmholtz billows at the buoyancy scale. In the second, a uniform mode first reshapes the flow into lasting columnar vortices. Three-dimensional instabilities crack the columns, vertical shear emerges, and Kelvin-Helmholtz billows follow at the third step. Either way, vertical shear proves an inevitable by-product at high buoyancy Reynolds number. The pathways excite different vertical scales, so their peak mixing efficiencies differ.
arxiv-2606-13227:
Sai Teja and colleagues argue that language models should not speak in one fixed style in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard training pushes models toward a single average assistant behaviour. That average erases the variety in how people respond across languages, tasks, and conversation types. The authors call their alternative conditional human-distribution alignment: the model should match the human reply pattern fitting the current situation. Their framework, PolyAlign, sorts training data into buckets defined by language, interaction type, response family, and length, each with its own reference pattern of human replies.

One stage balances learning across buckets so common cases cannot swamp rare ones. A second stage adjusts preference learning by how far model replies drift from each bucket's human pattern. On English and Chinese tests, single exchanges and longer dialogues alike, PolyAlign's replies were judged more natural and more faithful to human patterns.
arxiv-2606-13327:
De Wolf studies disclosure risk for thematic maps in this 2026 arXiv paper. Statistical offices publish maps that colour regions by data values, but each publication must balance usefulness against the risk of revealing information about individuals. Most risk measures ignore the spatial character of a map. Some spatial measures suffer from the modifiable areal unit problem: shifting the regional grid can change the risk, even though nothing real has changed. De Wolf proposes a risk measure that avoids this flaw.

The measure ties risk to the local density of the target population, how many people live near each location. It accounts for the fact that several statistical units may connect to a single location, a common situation in registers. The author demonstrates the measure's behaviour on a fake but realistic dataset. The work aims to give statistical offices a steadier gauge of what a map might disclose.
arxiv-2606-13627:
McLeod, Pokraka, and Ren construct a graphical coaction for cosmological integrals in this 2026 arXiv paper. Friedmann-Robertson-Walker integrals arise when computing quantum corrections in an expanding universe, and their exact structure governs the equations that observed quantities obey. The authors build the coaction, an operation splitting integrals into simpler building blocks, at all loop orders for coupled scalar theories with simple couplings. The construction uses intersection theory in twisted cohomology, a framework counting how integration paths meet.

Their split expresses the integrals, their jumps, and their slopes as labels of the original Feynman diagram, making the coaction graphical up to rational factors read from the graph. A notable payoff is that the kinematic flow, the form of those equations, emerges naturally. The team also built a web app computing the coaction for user-supplied diagrams.
arxiv-2606-13727:
Carlos Zumaya and colleagues ground the room layer of indoor robot scene graphs in occupancy in this 2026 arXiv paper. Three-dimensional scene graphs organise a robot's knowledge across scales. The room layer connects object perception to room-scale reasoning. Existing systems build it from incompatible substrates, such as place clusters, wall planes, or segmentation outputs, so room nodes cannot be evaluated on a common criterion. The authors' pipeline anchors each room node to free-space regions derived from occupancy decomposition, giving every room a polygonal footprint.

Evaluated on a dozen scenes from a dataset, the occupancy-grounded anchoring recovers more room instances than a place-connectivity baseline. The gain comes at a cost of lower precision, more false rooms among the proposals. The trade-off is explicit because rooms now share a definition. For robots that reason about spaces, a room layer with footprints supports navigation and task planning.
arxiv-2606-13827:
Nambirajan builds a new discrete version of random fields on curved surfaces. Whittle-Matérn fields are random surfaces with tunable smoothness, widely used in spatial statistics. On a mesh they become Gauss Markov random fields, whose sparse precision matrices make computation fast. Existing versions come from finite element methods tied to specific parameter values. His 2026 arXiv paper uses discrete exterior calculus instead, over well-centered triangulations of Riemannian manifolds of any dimension.

The scheme is universal: one construction serves the whole two-parameter family, so parameters can be inferred from data rather than guessed. It handles point and locally smoothed measurements equally well. On well-connected, volume-concentrated meshes, the precision matrices are spectral functions of a graph Laplacian. A low-rank shortcut for the family follows. Uses include fitting field parameters and compressed sensing, which cuts the measurements needed.
arxiv-2606-14227:
Bhattacharjee, de Bruyn Kops, and Bragg ask how the angle between two density gradients steers energy flows in stratified turbulence. In stably stratified fluids, density varies with height and buoyancy fights vertical motion. The alignment between the fluctuating and mean density gradients organizes the energetics. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses direct numerical simulations of stationary stratified turbulence at Prandtl numbers one, seven, and fifty, strongly stratified throughout.

Filtering scale by scale, they show the alignments are intimately connected to the reversal of the buoyancy flux at small scales. Regions of strong alignment or misalignment are where the horizontal turbulent kinetic energy flux between scales weakens. The available potential energy flux behaves similarly, except at larger scales, where strongly aligned regions carry it upscale. Dissipation rates and the mixing coefficient also depend strongly on alignment, especially at Prandtl number one. A surprise: strong alignment occurs most often in locally stable regions.
arxiv-2606-14327:
Feakins, Habli, Littler, and Palin appraise whether today's safety assurance practice can cope with language models moving into cars. Frameworks increasingly propose LLMs for automotive tasks from infotainment voice control to real-time decision planning, but cars are safety-critical. Their 2026 arXiv paper examines the gap, separating conceptual from concrete challenges, grounded in a case study of Talk2Drive, an open-source repository for LLM-driven driving.

The conceptual problem is dual: deployers must assure, inside a specific vehicle architecture, a general-purpose model developed upstream by an AI lab they do not control. Concrete problems show in standards: ISO 21448 covers engineering constraints such as latency, while ISO/PAS 8800 mentions alignment issues only briefly, leaving value alignment essentially unresolved. They construct an explicit safety argument exposing current limitations, and propose tentative assurance mechanisms for LLM-related hazardous events. Bottom line: integration is being operationalized faster than assurance can justify.
arxiv-2606-14627:
Tichavský introduces faster algebra for tensor trains in a 2026 arXiv paper. The tensor train format approximates huge multidimensional arrays. It stores them as a chain of small tensors. This fights the curse of dimensionality in tasks like system identification. In physics the same format is called a matrix product state.

The paper gives algorithms for three core operations on data already in tensor train form. The operations are summation, the Hadamard elementwise product, and a matrix-vector product. The last is known in physics shorthand as an operator-state product. Each operation risks swelling the chain's ranks and cost. So the design goal is a better trade-off. It must balance speed against accuracy better than current methods. Such routines are the plumbing under larger tensor-network calculations in engineering and quantum simulation.
arxiv-2606-14727:
Li and co-authors make demographically balanced medical images with FairGen in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clinical image sets are lopsided. Health care access and disease rates differ across groups. Diseases can also look different across groups, so some cases are rare in the data. Models trained on such data risk biased diagnoses.

FairGen is a fairness-aware image maker based on diffusion. It makes balanced medical images while keeping disease cues intact. Doctor-aligned likes and dislikes are built into the making process. On skin, chest, and brain test sets, fairness rose a great deal. Skin images gained the most, chest scans strongly, and brain scans moderately. Diagnostic accuracy stayed on par with models trained on real data. Doctor review and tests on fresh cohorts backed the gains. They held up past the usual image quality scores.
arxiv-2606-14827:
Paré and Lavalle propose using far-flung exoplanets to probe dark matter in a 2026 arXiv paper. Some exoplanets orbit their stars at huge distances, loosely bound. A passing clump of dark matter could tug such a planet and leave a mark. The clumps of interest are ultra-compact minihalos. They may have formed from extra-large ripples in the early universe.

The authors derive new limits on these minihalos. The limits cover both their size scale and their abundance. They add to existing dynamical limits from other methods. Upcoming exoplanet surveys should sharpen them further. Each new loosely bound planet found adds power. The paper also lists tell-tale patterns such systems would show if a minihalo population exists. The work ties exoplanet science to the universe's earliest moments.
arxiv-2606-15527:
Moon and Heo propose Selective Synergistic Learning, or SSync, in 2026 for video object-centric learning, where a model splits a video into objects. Slot-based systems learn from two maps, encoder attention and decoder object maps, and one strategy forced the two to agree at every patch. That blanket agreement spreads the weaknesses of each map, noisy encoder guesses and blurred decoder edges, and its cost grows quadratically with the number of patches.

SSync instead distils each map only where it is strong: the encoder refines object boundaries, while the decoder cleans up object interiors. A pseudo-labeling scheme does this at linear cost, removing the quadratic comparisons. A transitive merging step joins overlapping slots that fire together, curbing over-fragmentation. On MOVi-C, MOVi-E, and YouTube-VIS, SSync improves decomposition quality, drops into existing pipelines as a plug-and-play module, and stays robust across slot setups.
arxiv-2606-15627:
Gao and Wang construct strong marker sets in 2026 for the free part of the shift action of the integer lattice on binary sequences, a tool in descriptive set theory. A marker set picks out points in each orbit, spaced far apart, and useful versions must be topologically tame, here clopen, both open and closed. Earlier constructions handled only standard generating sets of the lattice.

The pair prove clopen strong marker sets exist for arbitrary finite generating sets, with spacing at least any prescribed distance. Along each generating direction, every point can reach the marker set within a uniformly bounded number of steps, forward or backward. The proof introduces polyhedral packages, generalizing the rectangular packages of earlier work to generating vectors with arbitrary coordinate patterns. As an application, they get a continuous proper edge coloring of the Schreier graph with twice the generating-set size plus one colors.
arxiv-2606-15727:
Sultan and colleagues compute what a rotating black hole would look like in Rastall gravity in 2026, an alternative theory where energy-momentum conservation is modified. They surround the hole with a thin accretion disk and ray-trace photons from the observer's screen back to the emission region. Shadow size, distortion, and photon ring are tracked as the parameters and spin vary.

Raising the structure parameter enlarges the shadow radius, expanding the photon capture region, while the distortion falls, so the shadow grows rounder and rotation's asymmetry fades. The Rastall parameter leaves its own distinct marks on shadow shape, emission profiles, and redshift patterns. The predicted shadow diameter stays compatible with Event Horizon Telescope measurements of M87* and Sgr A* across a broad range of parameter values. Shadow imaging can therefore constrain Rastall gravity's parameters, turning black hole photographs into tests of strong-field gravity beyond Einstein's theory.
arxiv-2606-15927:
Bhatia and Ekbote present an exploratory study of estimating blood glucose from photoplethysmography signals in 2026, the optical pulse signals a smartwatch already collects. Continuous glucose monitors work well but pierce the skin, risking irritation, so a non-invasive route matters for diabetes care at scale. The pairing is now feasible: watches record PPG continuously while a monitor records glucose, giving dense aligned data for machine learning.

The authors release such a paired dataset, smartwatch PPG alongside CGM glucose values, and run preliminary modelling explorations on it. The early results suggest some predictive signal may exist in the pulse waveform. But more data, from many more individuals, is needed before its size is known. Extensive validation and clinical testing would be required before any accuracy or accessibility claims. The contribution is the resource itself, an open starting point for a problem where data, not algorithms, has been the bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-16027:
Huang compares two ways of blowing up geometric spaces in a 2026 paper on algebraic geometry. A blow-up replaces a chosen center with the directions through it, resolving awkward points on shapes defined by equations. Multigraded versions handle several gradings at once, while iterated versions repeat the step. Huang asks how the exceptional divisors, the new pieces created, correspond between them.

Huang establishes a birational correspondence between the exceptional divisors of simultaneous and iterated blow-ups. For blow-ups tied to rational maps into multiprojective spaces, the paper derives formulas for Chern classes of the divisors and for pulled-back tautological line bundles. Two payoffs follow. One is a proof of the product formula for Segre classes with no pure-dimensionality assumption. The other is a degree formula for arbitrary closed subschemes that recovers and extends the classical van der Waerden formula.
arxiv-2606-16227:
Mishra, Trivedi, and Ganesan study in 2026 how comb-like frequency patterns could arise from cosmic dynamics alone. A frequency comb is a spectrum of evenly spaced lines. The authors look for such combs inside a quintessence cosmology, where a scalar field with an exponential potential drives cosmic expansion. No external periodic forcing is added.

Writing the evolution equations in expansion-normalized variables yields a closed nonlinear system. That system supports time-periodic attractors, limit cycles that repeat steadily instead of settling to fixed points. Those cycles produce comb-like structures in cosmic observables on their own. Simulations show transitions between single-frequency, comb-like, and chaotic regimes. The base frequency, the background state parameter, and initial conditions control which regime appears. Coherent combs arise only inside well-defined dynamical windows, and low frequencies suppress the phase locking combs need.
arxiv-2606-16327: Acoustic-to-articulatory inversion means figuring out how the tongue and lips moved just from recorded speech — but real articulatory data is scarce. ArtBoost creates synthetic articulatory data to augment the real stuff, giving models more to learn from. The paper targets speech researchers building systems that infer vocal-tract movement from audio.
arxiv-2606-16627:
Li studies multiple zeta-star values in a 2026 number theory paper. These values are nested sums of reciprocals, cousins of the famous multiple zeta values, where the summation indices may stay equal instead of strictly decreasing. A known result says their limit points fill the whole half-line from one upward.

Li asks the finite version of that question: what values do finite multiple star harmonic sums approach? Using divided differences, a classical interpolation tool, Li builds a natural complex analytic interpolation of those finite sums. For real parameters above one, the range of the interpolation is analyzed in detail, and a finite zeta-star correspondence is proved. In the complex case the paper sets out an injectivity conjecture, framed as the complex variation of the same correspondence. The results connect finite harmonic sums with analytic questions about zeta-star variation.
arxiv-2606-16827:
Giagnorio, Martin-Lopez and Bavota study code generation in no-resource programming languages in a 2026 software engineering paper. Language models write good code in Python or Java, which flood public repositories. Some languages are merely scarce in training data, but others, often proprietary industrial languages, are effectively absent.

The team built code generation benchmarks for two recent no-resource languages, Gleam and MoonBit, plus a harder benchmark for better-known languages. Six leading models score near zero on the no-resource tasks at first attempt. Remedies tested include few-shot prompting, fine-tuning and further pre-training on the small corpora available. Further pre-training gives the largest gains, but applied directly to instruction-tuned models it damages instruction following. The fix is to pre-train a base model on the target language first, then add instruction tuning. The benchmarks are released to support in-house code assistants.
arxiv-2606-17127:
Jung and colleagues generate drug-like antimicrobial peptides with an agentic pipeline in a 2026 biology paper. Antimicrobial resistance kills over a million people yearly. Such peptides are promising drugs, but real peptide medicines need non-natural amino acids and chemical end changes that earlier generators could not produce.

AMPGAN v3 expands the alphabet to D-amino acids and end changes like amidation. Two judge networks split the adversarial and activity-aware guidance, steadying training. The model beats prior generators on outside classifiers. Five designs across three shape classes went to the wet lab; two killed Gram-positive bacteria, the best against Bacillus subtilis. Around it sits PepCraft, a multi-agent framework whose planning agent coordinates generation, filtering and checking. Its rankings agreed with the lab outcomes. Together they show generative and agentic AI composing, at small but real scale, in peptide drug discovery. It is a small but real demonstration.
arxiv-2606-17427:
Manzone and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on how well augmented reality headsets and leading algorithms can track hand poses when the hands are impaired or partly hidden. Mixed reality tools for hand rehabilitation need accurate joint tracking, yet spinal cord injury and objects blocking the view could each degrade it. The study tested a HoloLens 2 headset against four modern pose estimation methods while participants handled clear and opaque objects in a lab setup.

Participants included people with cervical spinal cord injury and uninjured controls, with ground truth from a multi-camera rig. Pose accuracy did not differ between the injured and control groups, suggesting the methods generalise to impaired hands. Clear objects gave only a small edge over opaque ones in the measurements taken. Two algorithms edged out the headset slightly, supporting its use for rehabilitation applications.
arxiv-2606-17627:
Sottovia, Torcinovich, and Lanz present a 2026 arXiv paper on recognising fine-grained actions in first-person video, where rival labels differ by tiny cues a single model tends to miss. Their framework, Divide, Deliberate, Decide, runs fully locally with no fine-tuning, and splits the judgement among several vision-language models. An orchestrator model chunks the video and proposes a short candidate list for each segment, starting the process with a focused set of plausible labels rather than the whole label space.

Specialist models from different open families then deliberate, including a round where they question each other directly. Their rankings are merged by Borda count, and the orchestrator re-ranks its own guess in light of the specialists' evidence. Zero-shot scores improved over the single-model baseline in the reported experiments. An ablation-style reading credits the gain to decorrelated model biases, not to extra computing alone.
arxiv-2606-17727:
Zhao and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper introducing LongWebBench, a benchmark for generating long webpages that work, not just pages that look right in a screenshot. Vision-language models can turn a picture of a page into code, but tests so far use short, static, single-screen pages judged by visual similarity. Real pages scroll far, hold together over distance, and must support multi-step interactions. The new benchmark pairs hundreds of real long pages for structure checks with hundreds of goal-driven tasks over live pages for function checks.

Scoring mixes a multi-dimensional model-based metric for long-range coherence with an agent pipeline that tries the interactions end to end. Human agreement studies validate both protocols before the model rankings are trusted. Leading open and proprietary models lose structural fidelity as pages grow longer. Worse, visually plausible pages often fail the executable tasks, the paper's central warning.
arxiv-2606-17927:
Hoever and Schiele introduce KANLib, a software framework for building and testing Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, in a 2026 paper. These networks replace the fixed weights of classic perceptrons with learnable one-variable functions, promising clearer interpretation and strong fits. In practice, though, research was hampered by slow code and rival implementations that each supported different features.

KANLib unifies ideas from PyKAN, EfficientKAN, and FastKAN in one modular design that stresses flexibility and speed. It offers two basis function types, adaptive grid rescaling and extension, and fine-grained control over architecture, all inside standard PyTorch workflows. On the California Housing benchmark it reproduced the predictions of established implementations while running competitively. The authors pitch it as a shared base for exploring new architectures, basis choices, and training strategies.
arxiv-2606-18027:
Ding answers a 2016 question of Dai and Chen about how restricted a counting function can be while still covering every integer, in a 2026 number theory paper. A restricted partition function counts the ways to write a number as a sum where both the allowed parts and their allowed multiplicities come from chosen sets. The puzzle is whether such a count can stay positive for all inputs yet grow only polynomially, even when the parts spread out very fast.

Ding proves it can. Two infinite sets of parts and multiplicities exist with rapidly widening gaps between consecutive parts. Every positive integer still has at least one valid representation, and the count grows at most polynomially. More broadly, the paper links such partition functions to additive complements through a simple counting condition, giving a reusable construction for this corner of additive number theory.
arxiv-2606-18127:
Stewart and colleagues give a magnetar a full X-ray workup, timing, spectrum, and polarization together, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. The target, 1RXS J170849.0-400910, is a neutron star with an immense magnetic field, observed by XMM-Newton, NuSTAR, NICER, and the IXPE polarimeter. Its pulse shape changes dramatically with photon energy, and the team tracks that evolution across a wide band.

Below a few kiloelectronvolts a broad soft pulse dominates, while the profile turns double-peaked through the mid band and single again at the top. The spectrum fits an absorbed blackbody plus two power laws, and phase-resolved analysis separates distinct soft and hard pulse components. Polarization swings between about ten and forty percent depending on rotation phase, a fresh handle for untangling where each emission component is born in the magnetosphere.
arxiv-2606-18327:
Pres and colleagues train language models to describe their own behavior honestly, in a 2026 paper from MIT CSAIL. A model that faithfully reports what it will do is easier to audit and trust, but self-explanations often drift from actual behavior. Self-CTRL uses reinforcement learning to close that gap, updating explanations to better predict behavior, or behavior to better match explanations, until the two agree.

Two testbeds probe the method. In a formal reasoning task, models imitate biased samplers and must report the biases; consistency training raised the match between self-reported and measured bias sharply, rivaling direct supervision with ground truth. In a constitutional AI setting, models wrote rules for when they refuse requests. Those rules predicted held-out behavior so well that a third-party auditor's refusal forecasts jumped from about a third correct to over ninety percent.
arxiv-2606-18427:
Habib, Wu, and colleagues present the first systematic study of 'airports,' the subscription proxy services widely used in China to bypass the Great Firewall, in a 2026 internet measurement paper. Despite their popularity, these commercial services had largely escaped attention, which focused on tools few users choose.

The team combined a survey of more than sixteen hundred users, social media analysis, internet scanning, and subscriptions to thirty-five services. From these they map an ecosystem of thousands of airports built on a handful of open-source toolkits. More than half the respondents used airports, citing ease of use, speed, and access to blocked services like streaming and chatbots, and the multi-hop designs often outperformed direct connections. The picture has a darker side: services are frequently taken down, accept ordinary commercial payment, and can be hard to configure well. Many impose their own censorship policies on top of the state's.
arxiv-2606-18627:
Shi and colleagues challenge a core assumption behind model merging, the training-free technique for combining fine-tuned models into one multi-task model, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Standard task arithmetic assumes all task-specific knowledge lives in the task vectors, the weight changes made during fine-tuning, while the pretrained base stays inert. The authors argue some task-critical knowledge never leaves the pretrained weights.

They name these load-bearing wall dimensions and characterize them from scalar-weight and subspace viewpoints, showing that ignoring them leaves task conflicts unresolved and can damage knowledge stored in the base. Disrupting a tiny fraction of these core structures collapsed downstream performance. Their method PACT protects the anchored cores by filtering interfering update components out of each task vector before merging. It plugs into existing merging algorithms, and set state-of-the-art results across twenty vision tasks and backbones.
arxiv-2606-18727:
Roy introduces a two-parameter generalization of orthogonality for normed linear spaces, in a 2026 functional analysis paper. Birkhoff-James orthogonality, where one vector is shortest among all its shifts along another, is a cornerstone of Banach space geometry. Two one-parameter relaxations exist. One loosens the norming condition, and one loosens the vanishing condition.

Norming approximate orthogonality relaxes both at once. A functional must nearly attain its norm at the first vector, while being nearly zero at the second. Roy proves this is equivalent to a norm inequality over all scalars. He shows the scheme interpolates between the two earlier notions. It recovers exact Birkhoff-James orthogonality when both parameters vanish. He also characterizes the relation in Hilbert spaces by an inner-product bound. A proximity theorem has distinct forward and converse thresholds, whose gap is strict by counterexamples. A dual formulation becomes an equivalence on reflexive spaces.
arxiv-2606-18827:
Rahman and the team propose giving cellular users an escape hatch into unused television spectrum when their base station runs out of channels, in a 2026 wireless communications paper. Spectrum scarcity means calls get blocked or delayed whenever the base station has no free channel. Handoffs between cells fail too.

Their scheme equips users and base stations with a second antenna for the television band. Users sense a backup channel in television white space, using cognitive radio energy detection. When all regular channels are occupied, users under the same base station use the sensed backup channel. They form a controlled out-of-band device-to-device link that bypasses the base station. That relieves the network core and raises effective capacity. Simulations showed significant reductions in both blocking probability and call delay probability. The authors note antenna size and multi-pair interference as open challenges.
arxiv-2606-19027:
Murauer and colleagues demonstrate nonequilibrium steady states driven by random measurements and resets on a quantum computer in 2026. Stochastic resetting restarts a process at random times, a simple idea that can drive quantum many-body systems to steady states far from equilibrium. Despite wide theory, no hardware test of such steady states had been done. The team set out to provide that missing validation on a real device.

They first build a noisy discrete-time theory where unitary gates alternate with noisy mid-circuit measurements and conditional resets. That theory is then run on a superconducting quantum processor with up to seven qubits. The test case is an interacting Floquet transverse-field Ising model. The steady state from the noisy resetting theory matches the hardware results closely in quantitative terms. It also shows crossover behavior tied to the model's phase transition.
arxiv-2606-19127:
Galal and colleagues compare hollow-core and standard optical fibers for astronomy in 2026. Fiber-fed spectrographs lose sensitivity in blue and visible light because standard silica fibers attenuate that light strongly, and photon flux is already low. Inhibited-coupling hollow-core fibers guide light mainly in air and promise much lower loss across the visible range. Their rougher early surfaces held them back, but smoother versions now merit a direct test.

The team evaluates hollow-core fibers against standard multi-mode fibers used in current instruments. They measure throughput loss when fibers are bent, twisted, or pinched while moved by a robotic positioner prototype built for next-generation telescopes. Those motions mimic real survey operation, where fibers flex constantly. The measurements quantify gains for blue-sensitive spectroscopy and judge whether hollow-core fibers suit future survey facilities. A clear gain would help large telescopes reach fainter targets in the blue.
arxiv-2606-19327:
Gu and colleagues propose rubric-conditioned self-distillation in 2026 for post-training reasoning language models. Distillation often relies on chain-of-thought annotations that are costly and may be noisy or partly wrong. A flawed rationale can hurt learning even when the final answer is right. Reinforcement learning with verified rewards has the opposite flaw. It compresses feedback into one scalar, hiding which aspects of a response need to improve.

The framework conditions the teacher model on criterion-level rubrics. The teacher then gives token-level guidance on the student's own sampled trajectories. Rubrics state what a strong response should satisfy, enabling finer credit assignment over the reasoning process than scalar rewards allow. A two-stage pipeline first learns to generate task-specific rubrics, then distills with them. The design aims to keep feedback rich and specific, so students learn which parts of their reasoning to fix.
arxiv-2606-19427:
Clecio Bom and five colleagues describe a 2026 framework that uses artificial intelligence to propose new dark energy models. Dark energy is the unknown driver behind the speeding expansion of the universe. An equation of state states how its pressure relates to its density, and a changing value would alter cosmic history.

A large language model drafts candidate equations together with written reasons drawn from past dark energy studies. Each candidate is fitted to supernova records, baryon acoustic oscillation data, and Planck satellite likelihoods. A second model then grades each draft for physical sense, novelty, clarity, and stability. Two new forms beat the standard forms on Bayesian evidence by more than one unit on the full data mix. The result shows that guided machine reasoning can suggest testable cosmic models, not just fit known ones.
arxiv-2606-19527:
Martin Kolář tests in 2026 whether a language model can police its own ethics and fix itself. Fine-tuning on narrow tasks can trigger emergent misalignment, where a model picks up unethical habits far from the task. Kolář adds a conscience step in which the model reviews its own reasoning and outputs.

Suspicious outputs feed an alignment loss based on Direct Preference Optimization, steering the model away from bad replies. The judge is a frozen copy of the model itself, so no stronger overseer is needed. The loop runs online during training, fine-tuning, hostile prompting, and zero-shot use. In the code-hacking scenario that once bred cheating behaviour, one high-level introspective question turns training toward ethical conduct. The study frames the effect as emergent alignment, the mirror image of the failure mode. Self-review thus offers a cheap guard that scales with the model itself.
arxiv-2606-19927:
Chengwen Liu and five colleagues teach video reasoning models to size their thinking to their skill in 2026. Reinforcement learning for video models usually fixes how much reasoning length is rewarded. A fixed taste misfits a learner whose competence keeps changing.

Early on, tight rewards choke the exploration a weak model needs. Later, loose rewards pay for redundant rambling from a strong model. CARE tracks a smoothed competence estimate from pass rates during training. Stages keyed to that estimate shift rewards from long exploratory traces toward concise ones. Batch statistics normalise effort so verbosity is not mistaken for task hardness. A posterior amplifier boosts rewards for surprise wins on historically hard samples. The scheme drops into GRPO training with no inference-time cost. Accuracy rises, training steadies, and final traces run shorter yet denser.
arxiv-2606-20227:
Xinyi Zheng and five colleagues build a benchmark that generates logic tests with dial-controlled difficulty. Their 2026 paper proposes QMFOL, a framework for making monadic first-order logic tasks whose hardness is scored along several axes: depth, width, label types, and distractors. Existing benchmarks cannot fine-tune logical hardness and struggle to keep variety without breaking consistency. QMFOL builds formal structures from conjunction and disjunction patterns, then translates them into natural language with a language model.

A round-trip check with an external prover verifies that the translation preserved the logic. The resulting benchmark, QMFOLBench, holds 2,880 instances across 960 configurations. Testing six large reasoning models and two ordinary language models showed performance dropping and costs rising as tasks grew harder. Models also did better on True-labeled tasks than on False or Unknown ones. Controllable benchmarks let researchers measure real growth instead of watching scores saturate.
arxiv-2606-20327:
Martin Schürmann, Herbi Dreiner, and Rhorry Gauld compute the signals that three proposed dark photon experiments should actually expect. Their 2026 paper supports LDMX, DarkSHINE, and Lohengrin, which hunt dark photons in the MeV-to-GeV mass range through missing-momentum signatures when an electron beam strikes a fixed target. Until now, signal predictions rested mostly on coherent Bethe-Heitler scattering with a dark photon coupling only to leptons.

They calculate the cross sections of all contributing real emission processes, to third order in the electromagnetic coupling and fourth order in the kinetic mixing parameter. The dark photon couples to the beam electron and to the hadronic target, and virtual contributions are assessed too. Numerical results cover signal and dominant background. One practical consequence stands out: Lohengrin will need an extended calorimeter to veto background from diffractive scattering.
arxiv-2606-20427:
Máté Kormos and Aad van der Vaart reconcile local privacy with rate-double-robust inference. Their 2026 paper injects noise into individuals' sensitive data before release, protecting privacy while trying to keep estimation sharp. Rate-double-robustness helps: an estimator's bias trades off the errors of two nuisance parameters, so one can be off if the other is good.

The authors build the reconciliation on a class of target parameters indexed linearly by an infinite-dimensional parameter and nonlinearly by a low-dimensional regression. Causal effect parameters fall in this class, among others. Privacy noise usually destroys exactly the robustness that double-robust methods buy, so fitting both together is delicate. The result shows protected data can still support forgiving, modern inference.
arxiv-2606-20527:
Shaghayegh Kolli and four colleagues show that a few visual cues drive most social bias in multimodal language models. Their 2026 paper introduces StylisticBias, a controlled benchmark that changes one appearance attribute at a time while holding identity fixed. Earlier work compared different people, confounding appearance effects with identity differences.

The team generates 500 photorealistic base faces and about 50 single-attribute variations per face, roughly 25,000 images in all. Because only one cue changes per image, shifts in model judgments can be credited to that cue. A small set of human visual cues turns out to drive most of the measured bias. Attribute-level control gives bias auditing a scalpel instead of a sledgehammer.
arxiv-2606-20627:
Samuel Barbeau and four colleagues predict latent goals from language to plan with world models. Their 2026 paper attacks two bottlenecks: compounding prediction errors, and goals that are hard to optimize toward. Visual targets give precise local gradients but poor distant guidance; language is flexible but noisily aligned.

LAGO predicts sequences of intermediate goal states from language instructions and action-conditioned rollouts, all in the same latent space. Rather than optimizing toward a single global objective, the planner chases a chain of nearer goals. Language becomes a ladder of waypoints instead of one distant flag. Model-based planning gains guidance that stays usable over long horizons.
arxiv-2606-20927:
Michael Epping and Jochen Szangolies link what cannot be observed to computing limits in 2026, at the border of quantum and classical physics. Quantum systems show interference through superposition. Large everyday objects do not. They ask whether that absence is really a lack of observability instead. Their premise is that quantum systems cannot solve hard NP-complete problems fast.

From that premise, some formally valid quantum measurements cannot be performed on finite systems. A simple example is Pauli matrices in an awkward basis. Some states cannot be reached from others by any real time evolution. Some superpositions cannot be told apart from plain mixtures, so their coherence cannot be seen. That links to rules that split quantum states into separate classes. A computing limit could thus shape what counts as physically observable at all.
arxiv-2606-21127:
Saikat Chakraborty, Peter Dunsby, and Robert Scherrer revisit thawing quintessence in 2026, using cosmography to reconstruct the slope of a nearly flat potential. Quintessence is a scalar field proposed to drive cosmic acceleration. In thawing models the field starts frozen, then rolls slowly. The slope of its potential is a key unknown. Earlier work said reconstruction needs cosmographic data up to the jerk parameter.

Slow-roll conditions change that picture. When the potential is nearly flat, the slope can be rebuilt from the deceleration parameter and the field density alone. Confronting near-flatness with new DESI data reveals possible tension, the authors find. The models also show attractor behavior in phase planes. A universal thawing path emerges, with the equation of state near minus one early on. Simpler reconstruction sharpens tests of whether dark energy is a field or a constant.
arxiv-2606-21227:
Xun Gong and five colleagues at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Carnegie Mellon University present Bagpiper-Edit in 2026, a system for editing audio from free-form text requests. Instead of training on paired before-and-after clips, they recast editing as rewriting a rich caption, a detailed text account of what a clip contains. The edited caption then guides new audio, with the source clip kept as an acoustic anchor.

Tests cover speech, general sound, and open-ended edits that mix both in one clip. Bagpiper-Edit stays close to the source audio and matches expert editing models in most cases, despite never seeing paired edit examples. Because one caption route serves speech, music, and sound alike, the design removes the separate pipelines and fixed edit templates that earlier tools required.
arxiv-2606-21427:
Yanlei Liu and Zhenyu Liao propose DCGC in 2026, a neural method for completing sparse tensors, the multi-way data tables behind recommendations and traffic forecasting. Most entries in such tensors are missing, and interactions between modes are hard to capture. DCGC builds varied alignment patterns between latent factors with a multi-channel convolution network, then uses gated dual attention to spotlight the most useful channels and features.

A group-level contrastive strategy adds self-supervision: samples sharing a feedback level are pulled together, while different levels are pushed apart, supplying signal where data are scarce. Across five datasets covering traffic and recommendation tasks, DCGC beats leading methods at sparse tensor completion. Code is released for reproduction. Better completion of very sparse tensors matters wherever user behavior or sensor data arrive as scattered, incomplete records.
arxiv-2606-21627:
Sashank Pisupati, Henry Broomfield, Eujeong Choi, Antonia Calvi, and four colleagues introduce Counsel in 2026, a dataset for judging the judges of AI agents. Grading an agent's multi-step trajectory by hand can take hours, so teams lean on LLM-as-a-judge critiques whose soundness is rarely measured. Counsel collects process-level critiques from open-weight judges on two agent benchmarks, customer support and coding, plus human verdicts on those critiques.

Annotators label each flagged error as spot on, right location but poor reasoning, or should not have flagged, reaching solid agreement. Stronger judges and more reasoning effort both track human verdicts better; the best judge hits about 88 percent agreement on error location and 65 percent on reasoning. Freely licensed, Counsel gives the field calibration data for training and auditing the evaluators that agentic systems increasingly depend on.
arxiv-2606-21727:
Girish and colleagues open a new front in biometric security in 2026: fake heart sounds. Phonocardiograms, the acoustic traces of the heartbeat, are attractive biometrics, unique and inherently live. But neural audio codecs can now synthesize them, threatening spoofing attacks like those already fought in speech and face recognition. The team defines Synthetic Heart Sound Detection as a task and releases CARDIOFAKE, the first benchmark of real and codec-synthesized heart sounds.

They benchmark spectral features such as MFCC and LFCC against self-supervised speech representations like WavLM. Their fusion system GROOT combines MFCC with WavLM and beats every single representation and baseline tried. As synthetic media tools spread into medical audio, a public benchmark plus a strong first detector gives defenders a head start.
arxiv-2606-21827:
Gan and colleagues ask in 2026 whether what a gamma-ray burst jet is made of leaves a mark on its afterglow. Fermi data show most burst spectra are non-thermal, while a small share look thermal, hinting that jets differ in make-up. The team compared two long bursts, from collapsing massive stars, with two short bursts, from merging compact objects.

They fitted the afterglow light curves with the standard forward shock model, counting light from both primary electrons and cascade pairs born when gamma rays annihilate. The afterglow paths did not track fireball make-up at all. Instead, the density of the gas around each burst shaped how the afterglows behaved. The early ultraviolet and optical light of the long bursts came mostly from those cascade pairs, unlike the short bursts. The authors conclude the fireball's inner energy becomes jet motion during the prompt phase.
arxiv-2606-21927:
Rana's 2026 paper studies sign patterns, matrices whose entries record only whether each position is positive, negative, or zero. For a symmetric sign pattern, each vertex of its underlying graph can be tested as a P-vertex. The test compares the multiplicity of the eigenvalue zero before and after deleting that vertex's row and column. A pattern requires full P-vertices when every real symmetric matrix matching the pattern passes the test at every vertex.

For several classes of sign patterns, Rana finds the conditions, necessary and sufficient, for requiring full P-vertices. For tree sign patterns with zero diagonal, the answer is clean: the pattern requires full P-vertices exactly when its underlying graph admits a perfect matching. Rana also derives matching-style conditions for patterns whose graphs contain cycles but no loops. The results link a spectral property of whole matrix families to purely graph-theoretic structure.
arxiv-2606-22327:
Li Kong and colleagues Qi Qi, Yinyu Ye, and Zijie Zhou address a bottleneck in serving large language models in this 2026 paper. When many users send requests at once, the system schedules them while managing the key-value cache, a memory store that grows as each answer is generated.
