europmc-pmc2323727: A biology paper on modification of the Northrop-Kunitz microcataphoresis cell. The improved cell. This article preserves that laboratory technique. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2360127:
Hiyama and Hiyama reviewed telomeres and telomerase in stem cells in 2007. Telomeres are repeating DNA caps at chromosome ends that keep them stable. Each cell division trims them a little. Telomerase is an enzyme that can rebuild the caps and slow this clock.

In body cells, telomerase mostly switches off after birth, so telomeres shorten until cells stop dividing. Embryonic stem cells keep it active and stay able to divide without limit. The authors noted a surprise: most other stem cells have low or no telomerase, so their telomeres still shorten, just more slowly. A genetic disorder called dyskeratosis congenita, caused by a faulty telomerase part, shows how much human stem cells depend on cap upkeep.
europmc-pmc2363127:
Silverman and a large team studied medical history and pancreatic cancer risk in 1999. The study compared 484 patients with 2,099 healthy controls across three US areas. It asked about diabetes, gallbladder surgery, ulcers, allergies, and cancers in close relatives.

Diabetes diagnosed at least ten years before cancer carried a 50% higher risk, supporting diabetes as a true risk factor and not only a symptom. Gallbladder removal 20 or more years earlier carried a 70% higher risk, though the link was borderline. Hay fever came with a significant 40% lower risk, which the authors treated with caution. Family history stood out strongly. A close relative with pancreatic cancer tripled risk, with an odds ratio of 3.2 in the data. Ovarian cancer in the family gave an odds ratio of 5.3, the highest figure they found.
europmc-pmc2375027:
Cole and colleagues linked loneliness to gene activity in white blood cells in 2007. Loneliness here means a lasting feeling of social isolation, which earlier studies tied to higher disease risk. The team compared people scoring highest and lowest on loneliness in a long-running Chicago ageing study.

They screened 22,283 gene transcripts in circulating immune cells. In lonely people, 209 transcripts differed, covering 144 named genes, with more genes turned down than up. Closer analysis pointed to raised activity of NF-kB, a master switch for inflammation, and weaker signalling through the glucocorticoid receptor, which normally calms inflammation. Blood levels of the stress hormone cortisol stayed normal, so the change lay in how cells answered it. The authors called this the first evidence that a social factor can reshape human gene activity so broadly.
europmc-pmc2376927:
Bradburn, Clark, Love, and Altman wrote a practical guide to building survival models in 2003. Survival analysis studies how long until an event, such as death or relapse. When several factors act at once, researchers fit a model, but a badly checked model can mislead doctors.

This third part of their series covers choosing which factors belong in the model, called covariates. It then covers testing whether the model matches the survival patterns actually seen. A final section deals with checking the assumptions the maths rests on, such as steady risk ratios over time. Two real data sets run through the guide: one trial in lung cancer and one data set in ovarian cancer, both used in earlier parts. The authors aimed to promote correct use of two model families, proportional hazards and accelerated failure time models.
europmc-pmc2435427:
Dixon and colleagues, using the British Society for Rheumatology Biologics Register, asked whether arthritis drugs cut heart attacks in 2007. Rheumatoid arthritis inflames joints and also raises heart attack risk, likely through body-wide inflammation. Drugs that block the inflammatory signal TNF were suspected of helping both.

The register followed 8,670 patients on anti-TNF drugs and 2,170 on older arthritis drugs. Heart attacks occurred at 4.8 per 1,000 patient-years on anti-TNF therapy and 5.9 on older drugs, but adjustment erased the gap. The split came inside the anti-TNF group. Patients whose arthritis responded within six months had 3.5 heart attacks per 1,000 patient-years, versus 9.4 in non-responders. The adjusted rate ratio was 0.36 in the responders' favour. The authors said calming inflammation, not the drug label, seems to protect the heart.
europmc-pmc2516927:
Scattoni, Gandhy, Ricceri, and Crawley recorded the ultrasonic calls of mouse pups in this 2008 study of an autism model. The BTBR mouse strain shows social problems and repetitive behaviour resembling two signs of autism. The team asked whether its pups also communicate oddly, testing the third sign, by recording calls made when pups were separated from their mothers.

BTBR pups called more often and more loudly than the standard comparison strain. Their calls also fell into unusual types, rich in harmonics and two-syllable calls but short on chevron-shaped and brief calls. Two further strains ruled out body size as the explanation, since the odd pattern stayed unique to BTBR. Their growth milestones also ran ahead of schedule.
europmc-pmc2533327:
Lönnroth and colleagues reviewed the evidence in 2008 that heavy drinking raises the risk of tuberculosis. Doctors had long noticed the link, but drinkers differ socially from non-drinkers, so other factors might explain it. The team systematically gathered cohort and case-control studies and pooled their results by exposure level and by which other factors each study had controlled.

Across studies, people drinking more than 40 grams of alcohol a day had about 3.5 times the tuberculosis risk of others. The same held for people with an alcohol use disorder. The figure held at 2.94 after small studies were removed over bias concerns. Adjusting for social and other factors did not erase the association. The authors point to both risky social mixing and alcohol's direct effects on immunity.
europmc-pmc2535827:
Josefsen and Boyle reviewed in 2008 the light-activated drugs used in photodynamic therapy and the push to build better ones from metals. The treatment pairs a light-sensitive drug, a photosensitiser, with light of a chosen colour. The drug gathers in diseased tissue. The light then switches it on to make reactive oxygen species. These aggressive molecules wreck cells and trigger cell death.

The first approved drug, Photofrin, works against eye disease, psoriasis, and some cancers but leaves patients sensitive to light for a long time. The review surveys newer generations built on ring-shaped molecules called cyclic tetrapyrroles, with and without metal centres. It covers which candidates were tested in cells and animals, which reached clinical trials, and which are now used in patients.
europmc-pmc2546427:
Santolamazza and colleagues studied in 2008 how small jumping DNA pieces mark the splitting of Africa's main malaria mosquito into two forms. Anopheles gambiae exists as M and S molecular forms that are becoming separate species, with a few genome regions, called speciation islands, differing sharply between them. The team tracked insertions of a short element named SINE200 at 13 sites inside those islands.

Eight of the sites proved usable, and two were especially telling. One insertion on chromosome X was present in every M mosquito and absent in every S mosquito, giving the team a simple one-test way to tell the forms apart. Another site differed strongly between forms, with a differentiation measure of 0.46 that signals deep genetic separation. The markers open new ways to follow the speciation process.
europmc-pmc2572727:
Schuldiner and colleagues identified in 2008 the machinery that inserts a class of proteins into the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's shipping department. Tail-anchored proteins carry a single membrane anchor at their tail end and work throughout the cell's transport pathways. Working in yeast, the team showed a factor called Get3 grabs the anchors of these proteins that are bound for the secretory pathway.

That grab is a decision point: without it, the proteins wrongly insert into mitochondria instead. A receptor pair, Get1 and Get2, then recruits the loaded Get3 to the reticulum membrane. Cells missing the receptor let the complexes pile up and clump, crippling production of these proteins. Rebuilding the system in a test tube proved the GET complex inserts the proteins directly.
europmc-pmc2575227:
Nair-Roberts and colleagues counted the neuron types in three rat midbrain regions in this 2008 study. The substantia nigra, retrorubral field, and ventral tegmental area are famous for dopamine neurons, which drive reward and movement. But they also hold neurons using GABA, the brain's main inhibitory messenger, and some using glutamate, its main excitatory one, and those had never been counted carefully.

Using unbiased counting methods with chemical markers for each type, the team found GABA neurons were far from rare. They made up 35 percent of cells in the ventral tegmental area, 29 percent in the substantia nigra, and 58 percent in the retrorubral field. Shares varied sharply between subregions. Glutamate neurons appeared only in the ventral tegmental area, about 1,600 cells, or 2 to 3 percent of its total.
europmc-pmc2581627:
Cheung and colleagues mapped in 2008 how yeast cells keep hidden promoters inside their genes silent. Promoters are the start switches for reading DNA, and stray switches inside coding regions can launch cryptic transcripts, garbled messages that waste resources or make rogue proteins. Working in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the team asked which factors normally repress this noise across the genome.

They found a large cast of chromatin and transcription factors is needed. These factors silence cryptic promoters at at least 1,000 locations genome-wide. Some cryptic transcripts are even translated into proteins. A tested subset switches on briefly in normal cells after a change in food supply. That hints at a possible useful role. The authors conclude that clean gene expression depends on constant, genome-wide policing.
europmc-pmc2605927:
Williams, Shoo, Isaac, Hoffmann, and Langham proposed in 2008 an integrated framework for judging how vulnerable species are to climate change. Climate change threatens biodiversity worldwide, and managers must decide which species to protect first with limited resources. Existing work catalogued individual risk traits, but no unified scheme tied exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity together.

Their framework combines three things. It weighs how much climate change a species will face. It weighs how sensitive the species is, through traits like heat tolerance. And it weighs how far the species can adapt. It is meant to prioritise research and management across species, habitats, and scales. The authors argue that emission cuts alone are not enough. Conservation must rank species by how much risk each faces. The species most at risk then get help first.
europmc-pmc2652427:
Cameli and colleagues tested in 2009 whether ultrasound tracking can measure how the heart's upper left chamber stretches. This chamber, the left atrium, helps fill the main pumping chamber below it. A method called speckle tracking follows tiny marks in the heart wall on ultrasound images to gauge stretch, but normal values for the atrium were not settled.

The team scanned 60 healthy people and measured stretch across twelve wall segments. The method worked in 97 percent of segments, and repeated readings by the same or a second reader agreed closely. The average peak stretch came to about 42 percent, reached in roughly 368 milliseconds, a unit of time finer than a blink. The authors give these ranges as the reference values clinics can compare patients against.
europmc-pmc2658827:
Dillner and the Joint European Cohort Study team reported in 2008 how long a negative screening result protects women against advanced cervical cell changes. They pooled seven studies from six European countries, covering 24,295 women. Each woman had tests for the wart virus HPV, which drives cervical cancer, and standard cell checks called cytology.

Six years after a negative virus test, only about 0.27 percent of women had developed severe cell changes or cancer, a very low rate. A negative cell check gave less safety: about 0.97 percent over the same span. Women who passed the cell check but carried the virus saw their risk climb steadily, reaching 10 percent by year six. The authors conclude that virus-based screening every six years is safe, and could replace more frequent cell checks.
europmc-pmc2725827:
Sunenshine and co-authors compared in 2007 outcomes for patients with drug-resistant Acinetobacter infection. Acinetobacter is a hospital germ that lives long on surfaces and resists many drugs. Such strains had spread in hospitals and army care units. Yet their effect on patients beyond the infection itself was disputed. The team matched cases at two Baltimore hospitals by illness severity.

Patients with resistant infection stayed in hospital far longer than patients with sensitive infection. They also stayed longer in intensive care. Matched patients with no infection had shorter stays on both counts. The added stay held after accounting for severity and other disease. The authors stress control steps to stop spread between patients.
europmc-pmc2922327:
Patil and co-authors dissected in 2010 how weak chemical forces at a drug's binding site decide whether a lead compound becomes a medicine. Using computer docking, they placed a family of small molecules into two related cancer kinases, c-Src and c-Abl, and scored the fit. The forces of interest are hydrophobic contacts, where greasy surfaces huddle away from water, and hydrogen bonds, the directional attractions between polar atoms.

Three docking engines plus interaction-mapping software let them compare pose by pose. Statistical models built from the docked structures showed that tuning greasy contact area together with a few well-placed hydrogen bonds predicted binding strength and selectivity between the two kinases. The authors distill design rules: fill the hydrophobic pocket snugly first, then anchor with bonds that the wrong target cannot match.
europmc-pmc2973827:
te Velthuis and colleagues showed in 2010 that zinc can block the copying enzyme of coronaviruses and a related horse virus. Raising zinc inside cells with a carrier molecule already halted several other RNA viruses.

Low doses of zinc plus the carrier stopped both the SARS coronavirus and equine arteritis virus growing in cultured cells. Tests on isolated copying machinery showed zinc directly suppresses its RNA making. With the horse virus it blocked the very start of copying; with the SARS enzyme it slowed lengthening and weakened template grip. Removing the zinc restored activity.
europmc-pmc2993727:
Suzuki and colleagues devised REAP, a two-minute method for splitting cells into nuclear and cell-body fractions, in a 2010 article. Tracking proteins that shuttle between the two compartments is central to signalling research, but older separations take long and leak.

Their recipe uses a gentle detergent, a bench centrifuge, and ordinary tubes, finishing in about two minutes without harsh gradients. Tests on primary and transformed human cells showed clean separation of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins. Because the fractions stay faithful, measured ratios between compartments can be trusted without drugs that freeze shuttling in place.
europmc-pmc3062527:
Zwerling and colleagues introduced in 2011 the BCG World Atlas, a free website cataloging how every country uses the tuberculosis vaccine. The vaccine, called BCG, has been given since the nineteen twenties yet stays controversial, since protection varies and strains differ. Policies range from universal childhood vaccination to none at all, and they shift over time.

The atlas gathers current and past policy and practice for more than one hundred eighty countries in one searchable place. Entries cover who gets vaccinated, at what age, how many doses, and which strain. Clinicians can use it to read tuberculosis test results correctly for patients vaccinated abroad. Policy makers and vaccine designers can see which approaches the world has already tried. The authors built it as a living resource, to be updated as policies change.
europmc-pmc3195227:
Yiquan Chen and Gilles Guillemin reviewed a tryptophan breakdown route tied to many brain and immune diseases in a 2009 paper in the International Journal of Tryptophan Research. The route's first enzyme is switched on strongly by inflammatory signals, so the pathway lights up whenever immunity does. Its products both tune the immune response and act directly on nerves, some protectively, some toxically.

Imbalances along the route have been reported in Alzheimer and Huntington diseases, motor neuron disease, AIDS-related dementia, malaria, cancer, depression, and schizophrenia. The review compiles measured levels of the starting amino acid and its breakdown products in blood, spinal fluid, and brain across healthy and patient groups. It weighs how the pathway might drive each disease and where blocking or boosting steps could help.
europmc-pmc3257627:
Rong Tsao surveyed the chemistry and biochemistry of dietary polyphenols in this 2010 review in Nutrients. Polyphenols are the largest group of plant chemicals, found widely in plant-based foods, and diets rich in them have been linked to many health benefits. Tsao set out to cover the field's main advances in one place.

The review walks through how polyphenols are classified, how they are extracted from foods, and how laboratories separate and measure them. It then covers where they occur in plants and how plants build them. The second half turns to their biological activities and what they may mean for human health. Tsao also identifies the challenges the field must solve next, such as pinning down exactly which compounds do what once eaten.
europmc-pmc3299327:
Ramage, Rajendran, Sherry, and Williams reviewed why fungal infections that grow as biofilms resist treatment, in a 2012 article. A biofilm is a dense community of cells stuck to a surface, common on catheters and other medical devices. Such infections, often caused by the yeast Candida albicans, frequently survive antifungal drugs and end with surgery to remove the infected material.

The authors walk through the many defenses that make biofilms so stubborn. A slimy outer matrix slows drugs down, pump proteins throw drugs out of cells, and a few dormant cells weather attacks and regrow. Crowding, stress responses, and extra copies of drug targets add further layers. Because so many mechanisms stack together, they argue, no single fix is likely to work.
europmc-pmc3409227:
Costa and colleagues sequenced gut bacteria from horse droppings in 2012 to compare healthy horses with horses suffering colitis, an inflamed colon. The horse gut holds one of the richest microbial communities known, yet few sequencing studies had touched it. Six healthy horses and ten with unexplained colitis supplied the samples.

Healthy guts were dominated by Firmicutes bacteria, with Clostridia especially prominent, while colitis guts flipped to Bacteroidetes on top. Sick horses also carried more Fusobacteria and fewer of several healthy-associated groups. One family, Lachnospiraceae, appeared in nearly every healthy horse. The sharp split suggests colitis is a disorder of a disturbed community, not simply one germ overrunning the gut.
europmc-pmc3431227:
Quail and co-workers compared three fast DNA sequencing machines that reached buyers in 2011: the MiSeq from Illumina, the PGM from Ion Torrent, and the RS from Pacific Biosciences. Benchmarking them against the market-leading HiSeq, the team sequenced four microbial genomes spanning the full range of DNA letter mixes. Coverage, bias, and variant-calling accuracy were the yardsticks.

All three produced usable sequence, but with distinct personalities. On an extremely AT-rich malaria parasite genome, the PGM left nearly a third uncovered, a profound bias the others avoided. Ion Torrent data yielded slightly more variant calls than MiSeq but with more false alarms, while the Pacific Biosciences machine needed deeper coverage for variants. Each platform also showed its own error habits, or none. The comparison guides labs matching machines to jobs.
europmc-pmc3439727:
Nadalin, Vezzi, and Policriti presented GapFiller in 2012, a tool that stretches short DNA reads into longer, trustworthy sequences before assembly. Modern sequencers read DNA cheaply but only in short pieces, which makes rebuilding genomes from scratch hard, especially around repeated stretches. Their program starts from one read of a pair and grows it toward its partner.

The grower works by finding reliable overlaps and grouping look-alike reads, carefully stopping where evidence thins. Across twenty-four tests on simulated and real data, it extended most seeds and found their partners, with almost no false joins. The lengthened reads ran from a few hundred to several thousand letters. Cleaner, longer inputs should ease every later step of genome assembly.

Reiter and co-authors review evidence that melatonin fights cancer at every stage. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Melatonin is the body's night hormone. europmc-pmc5428827:

Those numbers describe tumor shape and texture. Baseline features already predict survival in several cancers. Nobody had tracked their change on CT during lung treatment. The team followed 107 patients. All had stage III non-small cell lung cancer. Scans came before treatment and weekly during it.

Every radiomics feature changed significantly with dose. The team built models for three outcomes. Outcomes were survival, distant spread, and local recurrence. Baseline compactness improved survival prediction. It also improved prediction of distant metastases. Baseline features said nothing about local recurrence. Texture strength at treatment's end split recurrence risk instead. High and low risk groups separated cleanly. End-of-treatment values may flag tumor response. Such flags could guide added therapy.
europmc-pmc5433227:
Lackie and co-authors review the protein-folding guards that falter in brain diseases. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Many such diseases share one feature. Misfolded proteins pile up in the brain. In Alzheimer's disease, amyloid clumps and tau tangles are the marks. Chaperone proteins form a defense line. They refold bad proteins or send them for disposal. Two families, Hsp70 and Hsp90, anchor that system.

A helper called STI1 passes clients from Hsp70 to Hsp90. Cells can also release STI1 outside. There it acts like a growth signal. It can block amyloid from binding the prion protein. That binding is one route of amyloid harm. The review weighs mixed proof on Hsp90 drugs. Blocking Hsp90 helped Alzheimer's model mice. Yet lowering it harmed a worm amyloid model. The authors chart where the network helps or hurts. Tau, ALS, Parkinson's, and Huntington's diseases all get coverage.
europmc-pmc544927:
Gougoux and co-authors scan the brains of early-blind people as they locate sounds. Their study appeared in PLoS Biology. Some people blind from early life pinpoint sounds better than sighted people do. The team asked which brain areas make that edge possible. They used PET scans and a ring of speakers in the scanner.

With one ear plugged, the best blind listeners lit up two spots in the visual cortex. Blind listeners without that edge did not show the pattern. Sighted people did not show it either. The more one spot fired, the more exact the listener's aim was. The authors conclude that the visual cortex does real hearing work in these listeners.
europmc-pmc5464927:
Shang and co-authors review how beta-catenin is regulated in cancer and where drugs might intervene. Their review appeared in Oncotarget. Beta-catenin is the core messenger of Wnt signaling. That pathway guides development and tissue upkeep. Faulty activation piles beta-catenin into the nucleus. Oncogenes like c-Myc and CyclinD-1 switch on. Colon, liver, pancreatic, lung, and ovarian cancers follow. Without Wnt, a destruction complex keeps levels low. APC and AXIN scaffold that complex. Kinases mark the protein for proteasomal disposal.

Regulation works at three hierarchical levels. Protein stability is the first level. Subcellular localization is the second. Transcriptional activity is the third. The review dissects mechanisms at each level. Cancer roles get wide coverage afterward. Initiation, progression, and dormancy all feature. Immunity and cancer stem cell maintenance follow. Recent drug efforts close the survey. Agents modulating beta-catenin activity show promise.
europmc-pmc5495127:
Ke and co-authors report an RNA study in Genes & Development on the m6A mark. This chemical mark is the most common internal edit in messenger RNA. When it is added, and what job it does, were open questions. The team tracked new RNA in cultured cells with brief labeling. They separated RNA from chromatin, nucleus, and cytoplasm for comparison.

Marks appear on exons very early, before splicing finishes, they find. Splicing itself did not need the marks to proceed. Instead, the early marks set how fast the RNA breaks down later in the cytoplasm. The work links a nuclear event to a later fate.
europmc-pmc5506427:
Biran and co-authors present a methods study in Aging Cell on counting senescent cells. Senescent cells are worn-out cells that stop dividing yet linger in tissues. They build up with age and at damage sites. Counting them inside real tissue has been hard and imprecise. A single stain alone gives false positives.

The team paired the classic senescence stain with marker stains for cell identity. An imaging flow device then read every cell one by one. The method counted senescent cells in tumors and scarred tissue, they report. Old mouse tissues could be measured the same way. Senescent cells there proved larger than their neighbors. The tool opens screening for drugs that clear such cells.
europmc-pmc5545727:
Amare and co-authors present a systematic review in Translational Psychiatry. Their question is why mood disorders and heart and metabolic diseases so often occur together. Genes shared by both groups of illness could explain part of that link. The authors search gene studies for such overlap.

They began with genes tied to diabetes, heart disease, blood pressure, and related traits. They then checked which of those genes also link to depression or bipolar disorder. The search found 24 candidate genes, among them FTO, BDNF, and APOE. Pathway analysis pointed to stress hormones, circadian rhythms, and serotonin signaling. Readers get a focused map of shared biology across body and mind.
europmc-pmc5559527:
Rasche and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications. Their subject is multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow. Doctors often judge the disease from a single biopsy site. The team asks whether that sample can miss clones growing elsewhere.

They sequenced samples from several sites in 51 patients. Sites included the hip bone and lesions found by imaging. More than 75 percent of patients showed genetic differences between sites. Key cancer genes, such as TP53, were switched off in some regions only. Larger lesions showed more local difference. The authors argue that one biopsy is not enough. Readers see a model of early spread, then regional change.
europmc-pmc5618627:
Chatterjee and Burns review heat shock proteins as cancer drug targets in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Heat shock proteins act as chaperones inside cells. They fold and guard client proteins against stress. Many of those clients are known cancer drivers.

Tumor cells lean on chaperones harder than normal cells do. Their oncoproteins are often misfolded and unstable. Extra chaperone help keeps those proteins working. That dependence opens a drug strategy. Blocking HSP90 or its kin could collapse many drivers at once. Several inhibitors showed promise in lab and clinic. The review walks through the main HSP families first. It then weighs the inhibitor record across tumor types. Combination use with standard therapy gets attention too. Readers get the logic and the evidence for chaperone-targeted treatment.
europmc-pmc5630227:
Berman and co-authors review human trial evidence on resveratrol. Their review appeared in NPJ Precision Oncology. Resveratrol is a compound found in grapes, peanuts, and berries. Lab studies suggest wide health effects. The authors ask what clinical trials actually show. They sort trials by disease area.

Most trials targeted cancer, brain disorders, and heart disease. Diabetes, fatty liver disease, and obesity also appear. The authors report good tolerance in many trials. Biomarkers improved in heart disease and diabetes trials. Results in cancer and fatty liver disease were mixed. Some outcomes were even harmful. Poor absorption in the body remains the main barrier. The review offers guidance for future trial design.
europmc-pmc5642327:
van Veldhuisen and co-authors report a randomized trial in Circulation. The trial is called EFFECT-HF. It tested intravenous ferric carboxymaltose in chronic heart failure. All patients also had iron deficiency. The treatment ran for 24 weeks against standard care. In total, 174 patients enrolled at 28 sites in nine countries. The main outcome was change in peak oxygen uptake.

Iron stores rose clearly in the treated group. Peak oxygen uptake stayed near flat with treatment. It fell in the standard care group. The gap was 1.04 units and met statistical significance. Without imputing deaths, that gap lost significance. Treated patients also reported better function and quality of life. No deaths occurred in the treated group during the study.
europmc-pmc5702627:
Bannas and co-authors review tiny antibodies as tools against cancer. Their review covers nanobodies, the binding parts of heavy-chain antibodies found in camelids. Standard antibodies are large, at 150 kilodaltons, which can slow their reach into tumors. Nanobodies weigh only 15 kilodaltons.

That small size brings high solubility, strong stability, and deep tissue entry. Nanobodies can be linked to antibody Fc parts, toxins, or other nanobodies. They can also carry drugs, radioactive tags, or light-based agents. Merged with human Fc parts, they form heavy-chain antibodies at half the standard size. The review covers recent progress and the hurdles left for tumor therapy.
europmc-pmc5757427:
The Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group pools patient data from ten trials on chemo timing. The trials compared chemo before surgery with the same chemo after surgery. They covered 4,756 women with early breast cancer. Follow-up ran a median of nine years.

Chemo before surgery shrank most tumors, the group reports. It raised the rate of breast conserving surgery from 49% to 65%. Local return of cancer was more common after early chemo, though. At 15 years it stood at 21.4% against 15.9%. Distant spread and death rates did not differ between the two paths.
europmc-pmc5802927:
Marçais and co-authors present MUMmer4, a faster genome alignment system. Alignment tools line up DNA sequences to spot matches and changes. The older MUMmer3 strained with today's huge genomes. This release rebuilds the core for scale.

A new suffix array replaces the old suffix tree. Parallel steps speed up the nucmer aligner. The size limit rises far past any real genome. As a test, human and chimp genomes align at 98 percent identity. The tool can also be called from Python, Perl, and Ruby. Readers get a guide to a versatile genomics workhorse.
europmc-pmc5811927:
Holmes and co-authors test blood fats and metabolites against heart attack and stroke. China Kadoorie Biobank holds samples from adults across China. The team measured 225 markers in each blood sample. Cases covered heart attack and two kinds of stroke.

Low-density particles raised risk for heart attack and blocked-vessel stroke. High-density particles mostly lowered heart attack risk. No lipoprotein linked to bleeding stroke at all. Triglycerides raised risk inside nearly every particle type. Sugar, ketone bodies, and an inflammation marker tied to all three diseases. Readers get a fine-grained map of which blood traits matter for which event.
europmc-pmc5817727:
Haddadi and co-authors examine PTEN and its twin gene PTENP1 in cancer. PTEN is a brake on the PI3K/Akt growth pathway. Losing that brake helps many tumors grow. PTEN levels are tuned at many steps inside the cell.

Oddly, PTEN has a near-copy gene that makes no protein. Its RNA copies still talk back to the real gene. One copy lifts PTEN levels, and another cuts them. That hidden chatter may shift cancer risk and growth. The authors weigh drugs that could exploit the pair. Readers meet a regulator regulated by its own shadow.
europmc-pmc5834427:
Liew and Mohd-Redzwan review how fungal toxins in food disturb the gut and its microbes. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. Mycotoxins ride along on moldy grain and feed worldwide. Warming climates help the fungi spread.

Five toxin families get the closest look. They damage the gut lining and tilt its microbe mix. Helpful bacteria thin out while pathogens gain ground. The traffic runs both ways, though. A balanced gut community can break toxins down and clear them. The authors link this interplay to liver cancer and to new ways of blocking poisoning.
europmc-pmc5841827:
Edwards and co-authors chart how the microbes on rice roots change as the plant grows up. Their study appeared in PLoS Biology. They sampled roots densely across three growing seasons. Two field sites, in California and Arkansas, fed the survey.

The root community churned through the young vegetative weeks. It then settled once plants reached reproduction. Microbe mixes predicted plant age well. Drought-stressed plants carried oddly youthful communities. Strains with faster development shifted their microbes sooner. The authors conclude the calendar matters less than the plant's own life stage.
europmc-pmc5861627:
Carballo and co-authors review the Sonic hedgehog signalling pathway. Their article appeared in Cell Communication and Signaling. This pathway guides growth before birth in vertebrates. It helps shape the nervous system, limbs, and other organs. When it switches on wrongly, cancers can form. Brain tumours often resist standard chemo and radiation, the authors note.

The review sets out how the pathway signals in two main modes. It also maps links with other pathways such as Wnt and Notch. New drugs that block the pathway are a major theme. The authors highlight trials that target it in brain cancer. Better knowledge of the pathway could open targeted treatments. Such treatments might also serve other cancer types.
europmc-pmc5867327:
Santana and co-authors build a framework for practising person-centred care. Their article appeared in Health Expectations. Health systems worldwide want to adopt this model of care. Many frameworks exist, but practical guidance is scarce. The team wrote theirs from a narrative review of prior work. A patient partner helped shape the synthesis. They sorted its parts with the Donabedian model of quality.

The framework divides care into structure, process, and outcome. Structure covers culture, co-designed training, and supportive settings. It also covers health technology and ways to track performance. Process stresses communication, respect, and patient engagement. Outcomes include access to care and patient-reported results. The authors offer it as a step-by-step roadmap.
europmc-pmc5879727:
Henley and co-authors compare cancer rates in rural and metro US counties. Their report appeared in MMWR Surveillance Summaries. Cancer data came from national registries and death records. Incidence was tracked from 2004 to 2013. Deaths were tracked from 2006 to 2015. Counties were split into rural, urban, and two metro classes. Rates were adjusted for age and split by cancer site.

Rural counties showed lower overall cancer incidence, they report. Yet their cancer death rates ran higher than metro areas. Death rates fell more slowly in nonmetro counties over the decade. That gap widened the rural disadvantage over time. Tobacco-linked cancers hit rural counties harder. So did cancers that screening can prevent.
europmc-pmc5913127:
Arndt and co-authors explain why aducanumab selects aggregated amyloid-beta. Their article appeared in Scientific Reports. Aducanumab is a human antibody tested for Alzheimer's disease. It binds a short stretch near the start of the amyloid peptide. Single units bind it weakly and briefly. Clusters offer many binding sites at once.

That contrast gives strong grip on harmful aggregates, they report. Rival antibodies showed clearly different binding traits. Crystal work shows the peptide sits in a shallow pocket. It adopts an extended shape unlike rival-bound forms. Weak hold on lone units may spare harmless forms. Readers get a structural case for its selectivity.
europmc-pmc5978927:
Luchetti and co-authors analyse lesion activity in progressive multiple sclerosis using a large autopsy cohort. Their study appeared in Acta Neuropathologica. The Netherlands Brain Bank cohort held 182 MS brain donors. Standard dissection yielded 7,562 lesions from 3,188 tissue blocks. Lesions were classed as active, mixed, inactive, or remyelinated. The team linked lesion traits to course, severity, and sex.

Over half of all lesions stayed active or mixed at death, they report. That was despite a mean disease length near 29 years. Worse courses came with more mixed lesions and higher load. Men held more cortical lesions than women. Remyelinated lesions were rarer in progressive disease.
europmc-pmc6002027:
Kann and co-authors report the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance results for the United States, 2017. Their report appeared in MMWR Surveillance Summaries. Risk behaviours drive much illness and death among youth. The system tracks six priority behaviour categories. They span injuries, tobacco, alcohol and drugs, and sexual behaviour. Diet and physical inactivity are also covered. Data come from national, state, and city school surveys.

This report covers 121 health-related behaviours. Results break down by sex, race, grade, and sexual identity. Trends from 1991 onward are updated as well. Such data guide and judge public health action. Obesity and asthma rates are included.
europmc-pmc6026627:
Tahamtan and co-authors review anti-inflammatory microRNAs. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that tune gene activity. Inflammation helps fight infection and repair injury. When it runs too long, it damages tissue.

Some microRNAs act as brakes on this process. They fine-tune signals so responses end on time. Current drugs often treat symptoms, not causes. They can also fail for many patients. The review covers how these molecules regulate immunity. It weighs their use as new medicines. Two drug forms are discussed: mimics and antagonists. Readers get a survey of a promising treatment path. It targets the control system behind inflammatory disease.
europmc-pmc6146527:
Willems and co-authors wrote a review in Cell Division on the Aurora kinase family. Aurora kinases are enzymes that drive cell division. The family has three members with shared structure. Each sits in a different place in the cell. Each does a different job during mitosis.

The review compares what each member does in normal and tumor cells. AurA readies the cell's poles and spindle for division. AurB and AurC guide chromosomes onto the spindle. AurC works mainly in germ cells. All three can drive cancer growth. AurA also aids tumor spread and stem-like traits. The authors weigh the family as a drug target.
europmc-pmc6155327:
Chmiela and co-authors present a methods article in Nature Communications on machine-learned force fields for molecular dynamics. Such simulations model atoms in chemistry, biology, and materials science. Their accuracy depends on the force field, the rules for forces between atoms. Classical rules often miss key quantum effects.

The team built a learning model that respects the symmetries of space and time. It constructs flexible force fields directly from high-level quantum calculations. The model matches a gold-standard quantum method in accuracy. It also allows stable simulations that treat electrons and nuclei as fully quantum. The advance points toward near-exact simulation of molecules at practical cost.
europmc-pmc6182127:
Tauschmann and co-authors report a randomized trial in The Lancet on closed-loop insulin delivery for type 1 diabetes. Keeping blood glucose in range stays hard for many patients. A hybrid closed-loop system links a sensor, a pump, and an algorithm to dose insulin day and night. The trial tested it against sensor-augmented pump therapy.

The multicentre study ran for 12 weeks in the United Kingdom and the United States. Participants were aged six and older, used insulin pumps, and had suboptimal control. Outcomes included time in the target glucose range, average glucose, and HbA1c. Time spent too low or too high and quality of life were also tracked. The trial informs how far automation can help daily diabetes care.
europmc-pmc6269627:
Short and co-authors map how to measure engagement in digital health programs. Their viewpoint appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Engagement is thought to drive whether phone and web health programs work. What counts as engagement has long been unclear. Recent models have brought the field closer to a shared definition.

Measuring engagement well is the next step. The authors gathered methods from reviews and studies they knew. Options include surveys, short in the moment reports, and app use records. Sensor data, social media traces, and body measures are also covered. Each method is judged for strengths and limits. App use alone is the most common measure, and the authors urge broader testing. Valid measures will let trials test what truly keeps users engaged.
europmc-pmc6280827:
Molinuevo and co-authors review the state of fluid biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Their review appeared in Acta Neuropathologica. The disease is complex, and no drug yet slows its course. Markers in spinal fluid or blood could sharpen trials. Each marker must be cleared for a stated use. Uses range from picking trial subjects to tracking drug response.

Three core spinal fluid markers lead the field. They cover amyloid and two forms of tau protein. Guidelines already accept them for diagnosis. Their value for other uses still needs work. Newer markers reflect other parts of the disease process. Synapse loss, inflammation, and cell stress each have candidate markers. The review weighs proof marker by marker. It sets out what each must still prove. Such markers may enable more personal care.
europmc-pmc6286427:
Inkster and co-authors evaluated Wysa, a conversational phone app for mental well-being. Their study appeared in JMIR mHealth and uHealth. Depression affects almost five percent of the world's people. Care faces staff shortages, long waits, and stigma. A chat based app offers support at any hour. It aims to supplement, not replace, professional care.

Anonymous users worldwide installed the app on their own. They chatted with the empathetic agent and rated their mood on a standard scale. Users split into high and low use groups by their activity. Symptom change was compared between the groups. Interview style data added views on engagement and experience. High users showed the pattern the team hoped to test. The study gives early real world evidence on app based support. Privacy limits are also discussed.
europmc-pmc6323927:
Mendez and co-authors describe updates to ChEMBL, an open drug discovery database. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. ChEMBL stores small molecules and their activity in the body. Curators extract data from core drug journals. Approved drugs and trial candidates are included too. Users can judge how selective a compound is. They can also judge how promising a target looks.

Recent work captures assay details more fully. A new system lets users add data sets directly. Extra data can now accompany deposits. The web interface was fully redesigned. Search and filtering grew stronger as a result. Data also flow to and from PubChem BioAssay. The base supports machine learning for target prediction. Repurposing ideas often start from its records.
europmc-pmc6327027:
Santos and co-authors measure two potent mutagens in fine airborne particles. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. The compounds are 2- and 3-nitrobenzanthrone. Both rank among the strongest mutagens found in air particles. Samples came from a bus station and an outdoor coastal site. Buses there burned a diesel and biodiesel blend.

Average levels stayed under set values at both sites. The bus station held more of both compounds. Diesel and biodiesel exhaust led the sources there. Dust resuspended from floors added a share as well. At the coastal site, traffic, sunlight-driven chemistry, and wood burning led. Cancer risk estimates stayed low at both places. The bus station risk was about two and a half times higher. The work shows how fuel and place shape air toxins.
europmc-pmc6358127:
The India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative Air Pollution Collaborators present a Global Burden of Disease study of air pollution across India. The research article appeared in The Lancet Planetary Health. It estimates exposure and health harm for every Indian state in 2017, using data gathered from many sources.

The team combined measures of fine particle pollution outdoors and smoke from solid cooking fuels used at home. They report that 1.24 million deaths in India in 2017 were linked to air pollution. Delhi and several northern states had the worst outdoor levels. Cleaner air, they estimate, would have raised average life expectancy by 1.7 years.
europmc-pmc6401027:
Wang and co-authors report a dye study in Nature Communications. Imaging inside the body works best with light in the second near-infrared window. Dyes for that window often fade when they meet water, which ruins image contrast.

Their new dyes keep glowing in water instead of quenching. Brightness rose up to about forty-four times over older forms. The dyes lit up lymph vessels in animals with sharp, stable contrast. They also change glow with acidity, letting them sense pH. The team sees uses in surgery guidance and tissue checks.
europmc-pmc6408327:
Patel and co-authors report a study in Cell Metabolism on a stress signal called GDF15. GDF15 in blood marks cell stress, and it acts on a receptor in the hindbrain. Mice without it grow fat on rich diets, hinting at a role in body weight.

The team tested how food changes GDF15 in mice, humans, and cells. Small calorie surpluses or cuts barely moved its levels. Long high-fat feeding raised it, as did an unbalanced amino acid diet. The work sets GDF15 apart from gut fullness hormones. It acts as a signal of lasting nutritional stress.
europmc-pmc6423427:
Adams and co-authors review ER stress signaling in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences. The endoplasmic reticulum folds proteins for the cell. When misfolded proteins pile up, the cell faces ER stress and must respond.

A sensor called IRE1 carries the alarm from the ER to the rest of the cell. The unfolded protein response then raises folding capacity. The review explains IRE1's structure and how it switches on. It compares a new allosteric model of that switch with older views. Faulty stress responses link to many diseases, they note.
europmc-pmc6437927:
Roberts and co-authors offer a case study in building a codebook for thematic analysis, aimed at researchers new to qualitative work. Published qualitative studies often describe their methods too thinly to judge rigor or repeat the process. This account opens up one project's coding machinery in full detail.

The parent study mixed quantitative, qualitative, and implementation phases, and the codebook grew from both prior literature and the data itself. Stages of drafting, testing, and checking agreement between coders are laid out step by step. A transparent trail like this lets readers trust the claims and lets practitioners judge whether findings transfer to their own setting.
europmc-pmc6461827:
Wu and co-authors identify a long noncoding RNA, RP11, that an m6A methylation mark switches on in colorectal cancer and that drives the cancer's spread. RP11 levels rose in tumors and climbed with stage. In culture it powered migration, invasion, and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal switch; in animals it boosted liver metastasis.

The mechanism runs through Zeb1, a master promoter of that switch. RP11, riding with the protein hnRNPA2B1, hastens destruction of the messenger RNAs for two ligases, Siah1 and Fbxo45, that would otherwise mark Zeb1 for disposal. Zeb1 protein therefore accumulates without new transcription. The authors propose RP11 as a predictive marker and drug target.
europmc-pmc6472827:
Bouckaert and co-authors describe BEAST 2.5, the latest major step for a software platform that runs Bayesian evolutionary analysis on DNA and other data. Modern questions increasingly demand joint models mixing sequences, sampling dates, fossils, radiocarbon ages, traits, and geography, which strains both statistics and code. The platform's modular rewrite, first released four years earlier, was built for exactly that.

New developments span the core engine and the model hierarchy, including population-level methods that read allele counts per species. Companion tools set up analyses, run the sampling, and summarize trees and logs afterward. The paper documents what changed so third-party developers can extend the system compatibly.
europmc-pmc6478227:
Erez and co-authors document an imported case of monkeypox in Israel in 2018. The patient was a 38-year-old resident who had worked in Port Harcourt, Nigeria, for ten years and cleared two rodent carcasses from his home days before flying back. Fever and a spreading rash followed the first lesions, and he presented in Jerusalem in early October.

Pustule swabs carried the diagnosis through several methods, electron microscopy showing brick-shaped orthopoxvirus particles, backed by PCR, tissue culture, immunofluorescence, and ELISA. The virus belonged to the West African clade behind Nigeria's outbreak of 132 confirmed cases, the largest documented there. The authors urge wider clinician awareness as travel moves such infections.
europmc-pmc6478927:
Zhang and co-authors trace an unexpected chain from cigarette smoke to pancreatic cancer growth, running through RNA methylation. Pancreatic cancer kills almost everyone it touches, with five-year survival under 5 percent, and smokers carry two to three times the risk without the usual driver-gene mutations to explain it. Smoke condensate instead over-matures a small RNA, miR-25-3p.

The condensate raises the methyltransferase METTL3 and its partner NKAP, which tag the precursor RNA with m6A and speed its processing. Mature miR-25-3p then silences PHLPP2, a brake on the AKT growth pathway. Smokers and tumor tissues showed high miR-25-3p, and high levels tracked poor prognosis, closing the mechanistic loop.
europmc-pmc6527027:
Zakhari gives an overview of how the body breaks down alcohol, writing in Alcohol Research & Health. The liver does most of the work, after a first pass through the stomach. Three enzyme systems share the task — alcohol dehydrogenase, cytochrome P450 2E1 and catalase — turning ethanol into acetaldehyde and then into acetate.

The middle product, acetaldehyde, is toxic and reactive. Along the way, the process starves liver cells of oxygen, spawns damaging oxygen molecules, and shifts the cell's chemical balance. Gene variants in these enzymes help explain why people differ in drinking habits, tissue damage and dependence. The review also covers harm to the fetus, cancer links and clashes with medicines, and lists questions still open.
europmc-pmc6537627:
Cotmore and co-authors summarize the official taxonomy of the virus family Parvoviridae, writing in the Journal of General Virology. The profile distills the report of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses. These are small, tough, non-enveloped viruses with a short single strand of DNA, just 4 to 6 thousand letters long.

Two subfamilies split the family by host. Parvovirinae infect vertebrates, with eight genera and over 55 species, several of them human. Densovirinae infect insects and other invertebrates. Most parvoviruses need dividing host cells, and some cause disease from mild to lethal. A few lean on helper viruses to copy themselves. Their tame relatives, the adeno-associated viruses, now serve as delivery vehicles in gene therapy.
europmc-pmc6546127:
Kopanos and co-authors present VarSome, a free search engine for human genetic variants, writing in Bioinformatics. Judging one variant means chasing facts across many separate databases, each with its own query rules. VarSome pulls those sources into one place, holding over 33 billion data points on more than 500 million variants from 30 databases.

Users can search by gene, location, variant ID, standard naming or a line from a VCF file, and even novel variants work. Results show the variant inside a genome browser, with frequency data, disease links, papers and an automatic rating of likely harm based on ACMG rules. Experts can add their own notes and calls on variants, building shared knowledge, and short permanent links make findings easy to cite.
europmc-pmc6547727:
Frei and co-authors present MiXeR, a statistics tool that counts how many gene variants two traits truly share, writing in Nature Communications. The usual yardstick, genetic correlation, can read zero when shared variants push in mixed directions, hiding real overlap. MiXeR works from standard genome study summaries and ignores effect direction.

It estimated about 8,300 causal variants for schizophrenia and 6,400 for bipolar disorder, with 6,200 shared between them. Schizophrenia and years of schooling shared 8,300 variants, even though their genetic correlation sits near zero, while schooling kept 2,500 more of its own. Results come as a Venn picture of shared and unique parts. The authors say the fuller count sharpens how trait families are understood.
europmc-pmc6602427:
Rodrigues, Myung, Pires, and Ascher introduce a web tool called mCSM-PPI2. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The tool predicts how a mutation changes binding between proteins. Such binding drives most core processes in the cell. Disease mutations often cluster at protein contact surfaces.

The method uses graph-based signatures drawn from protein structure. It adds evolutionary data, network metrics, and energy terms. Training drew on the SKEMPI database of measured mutation effects. The team tested the tool against 26 rival methods. It ranked first on blind CAPRI tests. The server is free for any user to run predictions online.
europmc-pmc6760227:
Hervé and co-authors explain vaccine reactogenicity, the short-term reactions that follow a shot. These include sore, red, or swollen arms, plus fever, muscle ache, and headache. Such symptoms are the visible side of the inflammation a vaccine is meant to provoke. Bad experiences can breed needle fear and lasting refusal, though.

The review covers what drives these reactions. Host traits, how the shot is given, and what the vaccine contains all play roles. Early immune cells reach the injection site within hours in animal studies. The authors aim to help vaccine teams set honest expectations. Calmer, better-informed vaccination visits should protect public confidence in vaccines.
europmc-pmc6841727:
Lloyd-Jones and co-authors present a better way to predict traits from DNA, in Nature Communications. Genome-wide studies publish summary results rather than raw data. Predicting a person's height or disease risk from those summaries is a core aim of precision medicine. Existing methods lose accuracy or demand heavy computing.

Their method, SBayesR, adapts a strong Bayesian regression model to work from summary statistics alone. They tested it on 12 real traits, using 1.1 million variants in 350,000 UK Biobank participants. It beat leading methods on accuracy while using a fraction of the computing power. Tests on height and body mass index with still larger studies confirmed the gain.
europmc-pmc6911227:
Wu and co-authors build a translation table for medical codes, in JMIR Medical Informatics. Research on health records groups billing codes into meaningful diseases called phecodes. The system was built on the older ICD-9 code set. American medicine has since moved to ICD-10, in two variants. Without a map, the large phenome-wide studies that phecodes enable would stall.

The team constructed maps from ICD-10 and ICD-10-CM codes to phecodes, drawing on official crosswalks and language resources. Most codes actually used in records found a phecode home. Phenotypes drawn through the new map matched those from the gold-standard older map closely. The authors publish the workflow so others can maintain it.
europmc-pmc6958527:
Mesin and co-authors show that booster responses draw on surprisingly few memory B cell clones. Their study appeared in Cell. A second encounter with a germ usually yields antibodies that are stronger and better fitting than the first. Memory B cells, stored after the first round, drive that improvement.

Using prime-boost experiments in mice, the team tracked which clones answered the booster. A bottleneck appeared: only a small share of the diverse memory pool reengaged. Most responding clones came from germline precursors with higher starting affinity. New germinal centers, the training sites, filled mostly with fresh cells lacking prior experience. Mutated memory cells rarely diversified further there. Beating this bottleneck, the authors argue, could help vaccines reach hard targets.
europmc-pmc7035327:
Li and co-authors chart immune-related long noncoding RNAs across cancers in Nature Communications. Long noncoding RNAs help control gene expression and play basic roles in immune regulation. The team built an algorithm called ImmLnc that finds which of these RNAs regulate immune pathways, then charted that regulation across 33 cancer types.

Cancers from similar tissues tended to share the same RNA regulators. The immune-related RNAs often showed disturbed expression in tumours and tracked closely with immune cell infiltration, which makes them candidate biomarkers. ImmLnc also split non-small cell lung cancer into three subtypes: proliferative, intermediate, and immunological. Those subtypes differ in mutation burden, immune makeup, chemotherapy response, and prognosis. The pipeline and data form a resource for hunting new immunotherapy targets.
europmc-pmc7044727:
Diaz-Aparicio and co-authors study microglia and newborn brain cells in The Journal of Neuroscience. In the adult hippocampus, new neurons keep forming, but most die soon after birth. Resident microglia quickly eat the corpses, a cleanup called phagocytosis. The standard view treats that eating as passive waste removal. The team argues it actively steers neurogenesis itself.

When microglia engulf dying cells, they release a cocktail of signals, which the authors call the phagocytosis secretome. Those secreted factors feed back on the stem cell niche and help keep production of new neurons in balance. The study traces candidate molecules in that cocktail and tests their effects on the neurogenic process. The result recasts microglia from janitors into managers of adult brain renewal, with implications for memory and for diseases where neurogenesis falters.
europmc-pmc7054527:
Peng and co-authors examine coronavirus risks in dentistry in the International Journal of Oral Science. The new beta-coronavirus, 2019-nCoV, caused severe pneumonia after emerging in Wuhan and spread quickly. It shares the human ACE2 receptor with SARS-CoV, and its genome matches a bat coronavirus at 96.2 percent, suggesting a bat origin. Spread happens through coughs, sneezes, droplets, and contact with mouth, nose, and eye surfaces, and possibly through saliva.

Dental work puts staff face to face with patients and exposes them to saliva, blood, other fluids, and sharp instruments. That makes dental clinics high-risk settings for person-to-person transmission. The authors recommend concrete infection control measures for dental practice, drawn from official Chinese guidance, to block each route. Their aim is practical: keep treatment going during an outbreak without turning the dental chair into a transmission point.
europmc-pmc7058027:
Batiuk and co-authors sort astrocytes into regional subtypes in Nature Communications. Astrocytes are a major brain cell type. They help form synapses and the blood-brain barrier, regulate blood flow, and feed other brain cells. Evidence has been building that astrocytes adapt to their region, with special forms in places such as the spinal cord and cerebellum. The team measured that diversity directly.

Using single-cell RNA sequencing in the adult mouse, they found five transcriptionally distinct astrocyte subtypes across the cortex and hippocampus. Checking the tissue in place showed the subtypes occupy distinct positions, matching groups known to differ in shape and physiology. The split exists both between regions and within a single region. The full dataset sits in an online database for other researchers. The finding recasts astrocytes from a uniform support cast into specialised local players.
europmc-pmc7082927:
Prete and co-authors review the fundamental mechanisms of thyroid cancer, in Frontiers in Endocrinology. Thyroid cancer has grown more common over four decades. It comes in distinct types, from papillary and follicular to anaplastic and medullary. Each type runs on different molecular faults.

The review covers the gene changes behind each form. Papillary cancer now splits into BRAF-like and RAS-like subtypes, with different risk levels. RET mutations drive most medullary cases. The authors also weigh the tumor's immune surroundings, better needle biopsy methods, and liquid biopsy from body fluids. These markers now guide diagnosis, risk grading, and drug targets. Readers get a full account of how far the molecular picture has come, and how much of it still has to reach daily care.
europmc-pmc7092527:
Armstrong and co-authors compare five-year death rates for diabetic foot complications with those for cancer, in the Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. Their brief report updates a 2007 summary with newer studies. They pooled mortality figures for foot ulcers, Charcot arthropathy, and leg amputations linked to diabetes.

Five-year mortality reached 29.0% for Charcot arthropathy and 30.5% for foot ulcers. Minor amputation gave 46.2% and major amputation 56.6%. Pooled five-year mortality for all reported cancers was 31.0%. Care costs also rival cancer's: diabetes care cost $237 billion in 2017 against $80 billion for cancer in 2015. The authors call prevention and remission care urgent priorities.
europmc-pmc7098027:
Yang and Shen propose targeting the cell's entry and recycling pathways as a treatment strategy for COVID-19, in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. Coronaviruses enter host cells through the endocytic pathway, and the autophagy process, in which cells digest their own parts, also shapes infection. Both pathways matter for SARS, MERS, and the new SARS-CoV-2.

Their mini-review explains how the virus uses endosomes and lysosomes to enter and copy itself. Drugs that interfere with these routes are surveyed as candidate treatments. Chloroquine, already listed in China's national COVID-19 guidelines at the time, is one example discussed. The authors argue these well-studied cell processes offer practical clues for controlling the epidemic.
europmc-pmc7154527:
Bell and co-authors set out advice for making surface-enhanced Raman scattering measures reliable and comparable between labs, in Angewandte Chemie International Edition. The method boosts faint molecular signals hugely, yet results from different labs often disagree badly. The authors are an international team of long-standing specialists in the method.

Their guidance covers three areas. First, how to check solid and liquid substrates with paired electron and optical microscopes. Second, how to measure the boost factor with suitable probe molecules. Third, general good practice in the lab. Tiny structural details dominate the boost, so casual checks mislead. The team hopes shared practice will establish the method as a dependable tool for chemical analysis.
europmc-pmc7264227:
Zheng, Liwinski and Elinav review how gut microbes and the immune system shape each other in health and disease. Their review appeared in Cell Research. Microbes living in the gut train major parts of the innate and adaptive immune system. In return, the immune system keeps the partnership with those microbes stable.

When that balance breaks in a genetically susceptible person, immune-mediated disorders can follow. The authors give molecular examples from the intestine and from organs beyond it. They also face a hard problem in the field: showing that a microbe change causes disease rather than merely tracking with it. That causal gap is the main barrier to turning microbiome findings into working treatments.
europmc-pmc7301227:
Reed and co-authors ask which patients choose a telemedicine visit over seeing their own primary care doctor in person. Their cross-sectional study appeared in JAMA Network Open. The data cover 1.1 million patients and 2.2 million primary care visits. Telemedicine here meant mostly telephone visits.

Fourteen percent of visits were scheduled as telemedicine. Patients were more likely to pick it with their personal clinician than with a stranger. Demographic traits and barriers to office visits, such as travel and wait burdens, were significantly tied to choosing remote care. The authors read the pattern as nuanced rather than a simple preference: remote visits fill gaps where reaching the office is hardest, which suggests where health systems should improve mobile access.
europmc-pmc7366427:
Pennycook and co-authors test a simple way to slow COVID-19 misinformation in Psychological Science. Across two online studies with more than 1,700 United States adults, they asked why people share false claims. Their answer is mostly inattention: people can tell true from false when asked directly, but forget accuracy when deciding what to share.

In the second study, a small nudge changed behavior. Rating one unrelated headline for accuracy at the start nearly tripled truth discernment in later sharing choices. Reflection habits and science knowledge also helped people sort claims. Because the nudge is cheap and scalable, platforms could deploy it widely. Readers get experimental evidence for fighting falsehood with attention rather than censorship.
europmc-pmc7377827:
Dong and co-authors study a form of cell death called ferroptosis in acute lung injury, in Aging. The injury model cuts blood flow to the gut and then restores it, which damages the lungs. Nrf2, a master regulator of the cell's antioxidant defenses, was their focus.

In injured lungs, markers showed the ferroptosis pattern: more lipid damage products, less glutathione, and less of the protective enzyme GPX4. Adding iron worsened the injury, while a ferroptosis blocker eased it. Silencing Nrf2 lowered two partner proteins, SLC7A11 and HO-1, and removing SLC7A11 strongly cut cell death in their models. Blocking this death route through Nrf2, they suggest, could become a treatment strategy.
europmc-pmc7402627:
Yuan and co-authors examine a shared antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 in Science. Different people often build strikingly similar antibodies against the same virus part, using the same gene segments. The team hunted for such public responses among 294 antibodies that target the spike's receptor binding domain.

One heavy-chain gene segment, IGHV3-53, was the most frequently used of all. Crystal structures of two neutralizing antibodies using it showed that mostly the inherited, germline form does the gripping, with few mutations needed. That is promising for vaccines: a near-ready antibody template exists in many people's genes, potent without long refinement. Readers get a structural explanation of a hopeful pattern in human immunity.
europmc-pmc7497427:
McNulty and co-authors pool studies on menstrual cycle phase and exercise performance in women. Hormone levels swing across the cycle, which might shift performance. Past data clashed, with no shared verdict.

The team searched four databases for experiments that tested performance in two or more cycle phases. Of 78 included studies, 51 fed the first pooled analysis. The pooled effect was trivial for both endurance and strength outcomes. Performance dipped slightly in the early follicular phase in the median result. A wider network analysis of 73 studies found the biggest gap between early and late follicular phases. Study quality varied a lot across the set. The authors give careful, evidence-based advice for training and testing across the cycle.
europmc-pmc7503727:
Galicia-Garcia and co-authors review the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes mellitus. The disease grows from two faults: poor insulin release by pancreatic beta cells, and tissues that fail to answer insulin. Both break glucose balance.

The review traces insulin making, release, sensing, and action organ by organ. It covers the paths that lead to insulin resistance in muscle, liver, and fat. Diet, activity, gut imbalance, and metabolic memory all keep the disease going. Gene and mitochondria faults add further layers of risk. The authors also link diabetes and insulin resistance to faster artery disease. Heart risk is among the gravest outcomes of the disease. The piece gives a full map from molecules to whole-body effects.
europmc-pmc7511527:
Kucharski and co-authors model how isolation, testing, tracing, and distancing cut SARS-CoV-2 spread across settings. Countries used case isolation and contact tracing early. Distancing rules joined as outbreaks grew.

The model drew on BBC Pandemic data from 40 162 UK participants, split by household, work, school, and other settings. Combined isolation and tracing beat mass testing or self-isolation alone. Self-isolation plus household quarantine with manual tracing of all contacts cut spread by 64% in the model runs. App-based tracing alone reached 47% in the same framework. With 1000 new cases a day, most tracing plans would newly quarantine 15 000 to 41 000 contacts daily. The authors weigh effect against social cost for each plan.
europmc-pmc7584927:
Wathelet and co-authors survey mental health among university students in France during COVID-19 confinement. Quarantine ran from March 17 to May 11 in France. Students faced closed campuses and life at home.

The survey covered 69,054 students who experienced quarantine. Rates of severe self-reported symptoms were high overall. Female and nonbinary students faced higher risk. Income and housing problems also raised risk. A history of psychiatric follow-up mattered as well. Symptoms matching COVID-19 linked to worse mental health. Social isolation and poor information quality played roles. The authors urge stronger prevention, watch and care access for students in such crises.
europmc-pmc7815627:
Hoffmann-Vold and co-authors track progressive lung disease in systemic sclerosis using the EUSTAR database. The database gathers patients across Europe. The team studied people whose sclerosis had scarred their lungs. They followed lung capacity over time.

The analysis included 826 patients. Over about 12 months, 219 of them, or 27%, showed progression. Moderate decline meant a 5% to 10% fall in lung capacity. Larger falls counted as significant. A group of 535 patients had repeated measures over a mean 5-year span. Each year, 23% to 27% progressed, but few did so year after year. Most progressors declined slowly, and 33% never declined at all. Male sex, worse skin score, and reflux symptoms best predicted decline.
europmc-pmc7864927:
Yang and co-authors show how galectin-9 works with PD-1 and TIM-3 to spare worn T cells. Both receptors mark exhausted T cells. Their teamwork was unclear. Galectin-9 is the binding partner for TIM-3.

PD-1 grabs galectin-9 and blunts its kill signal. That shield keeps double-marked T cells alive. Blocking galectin-9 grew killer T cells inside tumors. It also grew suppressive regulator cells, though. Pairing the block with a GITR drug cleared those regulators. The pair then attacked tumors in synergy. High galectin-9 tracks with poor outlook in many cancers. The authors name it a fresh immunotherapy target.
europmc-pmc7867227:
Galler and co-authors review how the dentine-pulp complex and nearby tissues fight inflammation. The mouth mixes soft tissue with hard tooth and bone. Teeth face hard wear, chemicals, and dense germ growth. Decay is the most common damage. Germs eat through enamel and dentine toward the pulp.

The pulp is far from helpless. Odontoblast cells line its front edge. They spot germs early and release germ-killing compounds. They also raise the alarm for immune cells. Fibroblasts, stem cells, vessels, and nerves join the fight. Without treatment, deep decay still kills the tissue. The authors map each defense step in turn.
europmc-pmc7897327:
Jiang and co-authors present a review of m6A, the most common internal mark placed on RNA in cells. The mark is a chemical edit made as RNA is built. Special proteins write it, erase it, and read it. The review gathers what is known about its roles in health and disease.

The authors name the main writer, eraser, and reader proteins. They explain how the mark shapes normal function in blood, brain, and reproductive systems. They then focus on cancer, where faulty marking can drive tumour growth. Target genes and pathways under m6A control are set out in detail. The authors propose the marking system as a source of future cancer drug targets. Readers get a structured map of a fast-growing field.
europmc-pmc7927727:
Moodie presents the first study in a series on paleopathology, the study of disease in ancient remains. The term was coined by Sir Marc Armand Ruffer in 1914. He used it for his methods of reading disease in Egyptian mummies. This paper sets out the field's scope and the evidence it can use among fossil animals.

Ruffer defined the science as the study of diseases shown in human and animal remains of ancient times. Moodie argues for a wider reach. It should take in prehistoric humans and fossil animals as well as the ancient Egyptians. The field thus draws on anthropology, paleontology, and archaeology at once. The paper surveys the kinds of traces disease leaves in bone and other remains. It lays the ground for the case studies that follow in the series.
europmc-pmc7952727:
Zhang and co-authors report a laboratory study linking a nutrient signal to a cell-death defence in cancer. The protein GPX4 uses glutathione to clean up lipid damage. That cleanup blocks ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. Making GPX4 is costly for a cell, so its supply must match nutrient levels. How the match is made was unclear.

The team found that taking up cystine does double duty. It feeds glutathione supply and switches on GPX4 production. The switch runs through a growth sensor called mTORC1. Blocking mTORC1 lowered GPX4 and left cancer cells open to ferroptosis. In mouse tumours grown from patient tissue, the two drug types together worked better than either alone. The study offers a paired treatment idea built on starving a defence.
europmc-pmc8026027:
Gadarian and co-authors ask how party loyalties shaped American responses in the first weeks of COVID-19. They fielded a survey of 3,000 American adults from March 20–23, 2020. The survey covered 38 health-related behaviors, plus policy views and worries. Party ties were gauged three ways: party identity, planned vote for president, and left-right stance. The team adjusted for many traits of the people and places involved.

Party ties explained gaps across a wide range of behaviors and views. News habits, local rules, and local deaths did not erase the gaps. In a LASSO analysis, a party indicator was the most often chosen predictor of all. The split, the authors conclude, was set from the earliest days. Health behavior in a national crisis already ran along party lines.
europmc-pmc8045927:
Ogrodnik argues that cells age long before they become senescent, and that the markers overlap. Senescence research has raced from cell culture into animal and clinical work. Its markers now judge anti-senescence treatments in trials. Yet many markers build up gradually before arrest, or appear outside senescence entirely. That blur threatens their specificity.

The review traces the internal changes of primary cells as they age. It calls this progression cellular aging, distinct from the final arrested state. Published datasets on markers in living tissue get a fresh reading. Apparent contradictions between studies, Ogrodnik argues, dissolve under this lens. Cells pass through shades of aging before fate is sealed. Broadening the paradigm this way, the author concludes, sharpens both measurement and treatment design.
europmc-pmc8125527:
Juan and co-authors revisit the chemistry of reactive oxygen species in living tissue. Every breath exposes cells to oxidants from outside and within. Controlled bursts of these species serve as signals. Uncontrolled floods scar lipids, proteins, and DNA alike. The balance between radical output and antioxidant defense decides. Much writing on the topic skips the actual reactions.

This review puts the reaction mechanisms front and center. It explains how each oxidant forms and what it attacks. Chain reactions, where one radical spawns the next, get full treatment. Damage patterns in the big molecule classes follow from the chemistry. Disease links then read as chemical consequences, not vague associations. The authors aim to arm biologists with real mechanism. Oxidative stress is a phrase too often used loosely. Here it becomes a set of writable equations. Better chemistry should mean better antidotes.
europmc-pmc8234027:
Tenório and co-authors examine N-acetylcysteine and its impacts on human health. The drug treats paracetamol overdose and loosens mucus. Its safety record is well established at normal doses.

Its power as an antioxidant rests on raising glutathione inside cells. Glutathione is the cell's chief defence against redox imbalance. The drug also calms inflammation, lowering signals such as TNF-α and IL-6. Those traits support trials in diseases driven by oxidative stress. The review weighs where the evidence is firm and where it is thin. Dose and delivery route shape both gains and harms.
europmc-pmc8333427:
He and co-authors quantify future global urban water scarcity and test solutions. City growth and climate change squeeze water supplies together. Scarcity means demand outruns what is available.
