In 2016, 933 million city dwellers faced scarcity. That was one third of the urban world. By 2050, the count may reach 1.693 to 2.373 billion. India faces the steepest growth in exposed people. More large cities will fall into scarcity too. Four scenarios frame the spread of outcomes. The authors weigh fixes that could bend the curve. Large cities face the sharpest rise in exposure counts.
europmc-pmc8430727:
Hasanuzzaman and co-authors review how plants handle reactive oxygen species under salt stress. At low levels these molecules serve as signals. At high levels they harm cell parts and membranes, and can kill the plant. Salt stress drives their overproduction.

The antioxidant defense system cleans up the excess and restores balance. Plant hormones and genes also feed into this defense. The review explains salt-driven ROS formation step by step. It then covers the oxidative damage that follows. Ways to strengthen antioxidant defense get close attention. Such gains can restore much of the growth and function that salt takes away.
europmc-pmc8522627:
Packer and co-authors analyze how empagliflozin affects worsening heart failure in patients with preserved ejection fraction. The EMPEROR-Preserved trial had shown the drug cut the combined risk of heart death or hospital stay. That gain came mostly from fewer heart failure admissions.

This analysis digs into the severity of those events. The drug cut the worst admissions, ones needing intensive care or strong support drugs. It also cut outpatient flare-ups, such as urgent visits and stepped-up diuretic use. Declines in daily function class grew less common too. Options for this patient group are few. The authors see broad gains across care settings.
europmc-pmc8604727:
Apostolidis and co-authors examine vaccine responses in people with multiple sclerosis who take anti-CD20 therapy. These drugs lower B cells, a key part of antibody defense. The team tracked antibody, B cell, and T cell responses after mRNA vaccination. They compared 20 patients with 10 healthy controls over time.

The therapy cut spike-specific antibody and memory B cell responses in most patients. Longer gaps since the last dose softened this effect. All patients still made CD4 and CD8 T cell responses to the vaccine. Helper T cell patterns shifted, with weaker follicular helper response and stronger CD8 response. The work maps what vaccine defense looks like when B cells are low.
europmc-pmc8619527:
Malesza and co-authors review how a high-fat Western diet drives body-wide inflammation through gut microbes. Gut microbes help draw energy from food and guard the gut wall. A diet high in fat can upset that balance. The review links these gut changes to long-term low-grade inflammation.

Fat intake in United States data rose from 32 percent to 45 percent of calories over the last century. High fat intake can harm the gut barrier and let bacterial products leak into the blood. The authors call this state dysbiosis. They trace the steps from diet to gut leak to inflammation. The review gathers recent work on each step in that chain.
europmc-pmc8684627:
Zenebe and co-authors pool studies on how common depression is among older adults and what drives it. Depression is a top cause of disability and is common in old age. Half of cases in elders go undiagnosed. Past studies gave widely varied rates, so a pooled estimate was needed.

The team kept 42 studies with 57,486 older people. The average rate of depression was 31.74 percent. Rates ran higher in developing countries, at 40.78 percent, than in developed ones, at 17.05 percent. The tool used to screen also changed the rate. The authors urge regular care and control steps for elders.
europmc-pmc8723827:
Dejnirattisai and co-authors show that the Omicron variant escapes much of the antibody defense raised by vaccines and past infection. Omicron carries far more spike mutations than earlier variants. The team tested blood from vaccinated people and from those who had recovered from earlier forms. Lab antibody panels were tested as well.

Blood strength against Omicron fell sharply, and some samples failed to block it at all. A third vaccine dose raised those titers to high levels. Most potent lab antibodies lost their grip on the new spike. Omicron's spike binds the ACE2 receptor tightly despite its changes. The authors describe immune escape on a wide scale.
europmc-pmc8770127:
Xiao and co-authors develop a degrader drug that targets the SWI/SNF chromatin complex in prostate cancer. This complex reshapes DNA packaging and is altered in over 20 percent of cancers. Their compound, AU-15330, destroys two of its engine subunits. Prostate cancer cells driven by hormone signals proved very sensitive to it.

Destroying the subunits quickly shut down the control sites of key cancer genes. The driver proteins were pushed off the DNA. Gene programs for growth collapsed as a result. In mouse models, the drug strongly slowed tumor growth. It paired well with a standard hormone blocker, even in resistant disease. No toxicity was seen in those tests.
europmc-pmc8812927:
Wick and Holt present Polypolish, a tool that fixes errors in bacterial genome assemblies. Long-read sequencing can build a complete bacterial genome. Small errors still remain, most often in runs of one repeated letter. Short reads can correct those errors. Most tools, though, align short reads in ways that fail in repeat regions. Errors there often survive polishing.

Polypolish instead uses all alignments for each read. The authors test it on simulated and real reads. They report that it repairs repeat-region errors other polishers miss. It also almost never adds new errors. The best results came from pairing Polypolish with other polishers. The tool is free software for genome researchers.
europmc-pmc8824427:
Almansour gives a brief review of triple-negative breast cancer, or TNBC. This cancer lacks estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors. It makes up more than 15–20% of all breast cancers. It spreads fast and answers poorly to standard drugs. No targeted treatment is specific to it. Relapse after standard therapy is common.

The review covers who gets TNBC and what raises the risk. It separates risks that can change from risks that cannot. It then maps the signaling pathways that drive the cancer. Immune-suppressing cells in the tumor surroundings get attention too. Current and experimental therapies follow, along with prognosis. A final section asks how artificial intelligence might aid diagnosis. The piece serves as a compact primer on a hard cancer.
europmc-pmc9198027:
Zhou and co-authors engineer programmable probiotics to treat inflammatory bowel disease after oral delivery. Reactive oxygen species fuel intestinal inflammation, so clearing them may curb the disease. The team modified a probiotic strain of E. coli Nissle 1917 to overproduce two antioxidant enzymes. A chitosan and alginate coating helped the bacteria survive the gut.

In mouse models of bowel inflammation, the coated bacteria relieved symptoms well. They also repaired the damaged epithelial barrier of the colon. Gut microbe communities shifted toward a healthier mix, with more of two helpful groups. The authors say the work lays groundwork for living medicines made from probiotics. Such treatments could act right where gut disease occurs.
europmc-pmc9386727:
Brandes and co-authors introduce ProteinBERT, a deep learning model built for protein sequences and functions. Language models designed for text do not fit proteins well. Proteins lack clear words, vary wildly in length, and fold distant parts together. ProteinBERT pretains on sequence filling plus a new task: predicting Gene Ontology labels.

The design mixes local and global representations for end-to-end training. On tests of structure, modifications, and physical traits, it nears or beats the state of the art. It does so with a far smaller, faster model than rivals. Code and trained weights are freely shared. The authors say the framework trains protein predictors quickly even with little labeled data. That lowers the bar for labs without big compute.
europmc-pmc9883727:
Kulmanov and Hoehndorf present DeepGOPlus, a method that predicts protein function from sequence alone. Protein function prediction aids work on disease pathways and drug targets. Many rival methods need interaction, structure, or literature data. Such data are missing for many proteins.

DeepGOPlus combines a deep convolutional neural network with predictions from similar sequences. The network scans sequences for motifs linked to known functions. On CAFA3 measures it scored Fmax values of 0.390, 0.557, and 0.614 across three ontologies. Those scores ranked near the top methods in that test. It can annotate about 40 sequences per second on common hardware. The method widens fast prediction to proteins with little added data.
europmc-pmc9913127:
Snijders and co-authors update estimates of pain prevalence in patients with cancer. Pain is one of the most common symptoms that cancer patients report. Poor relief can badly harm quality of life. New treatments and pain guidelines may have changed how often pain occurs.

The team searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane for studies from 2014 to 2021. They screened full texts and checked study quality, then pooled results. Pain prevalence and severity both fell compared with earlier research. Yet 44.5 percent of patients still reported pain. The authors stress that cancer pain needs ongoing attention. The update gives clinicians a current baseline for pain care.
europmc-pmc9916527:
Tian and co-authors detail the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway in liver cancer metabolism. Hepatocellular carcinoma is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Tumors rewire metabolism, but that rewiring stays poorly mapped in this cancer. The named pathway is often disrupted in these tumors.

The review shows how the pathway controls glucose use in cancer cells. It also covers lipid, amino acid, pyrimidine, and oxidative metabolism. Each section links pathway signals to enzymes that tumors raise. The authors then summarize trials that test pathway blockers. Such drugs aim to cut the fuel supply of tumor cells. The work frames the pathway as a target for new liver cancer therapy.
faulkner-mosquitoes-1927:
Mosquitoes, William Faulkner's second novel, came out in 1927, a year after his first. The setting is a yacht on Lake Pontchartrain near New Orleans. A wealthy patron of the arts gathers painters, poets, and hangers-on for a pleasure cruise that soon drifts off course.

For four days the guests talk, flirt, pose, and quarrel while the yacht sits stuck. Faulkner mocks the pretensions of the art world he had lately moved in. Gossip and desire drive the slight plot more than action does. The satire is lighter than his later Mississippi novels, but his ear for talk and his irony are already sharp.
frus-1861-d127:
William Dayton sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 June 1861. It is document 127 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

June opened with France still weighing its public stance on the war. Dayton's reports tracked each shade of that debate. His first of June letter adds one more careful reading from the post that watched Napoleon III most closely. France declared its neutrality in June, on terms close to those Britain had set. Terms close to Britain's made the two neutral walls a single front in law.
frus-1861-d227:
On 8 July 1861, Mr. Fogg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 227 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d27:
On 22 June 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to Henry Sanford in Brussels. The letter is document 27 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two letters in two days show a Secretary working his posts hard. The mails moved slowly, so Seward sent word whenever a point needed stress. Readers can feel the pace of a man trying to run a world wide effort from one desk in Washington. Paired days like this show Seward clearing the Brussels file in one focused sweep of the pen. One focused sweep of the pen could clear a week's Brussels business by noon.
frus-1862-d127:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 13 August 1862. It stands as Document 127 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d227:
Two Seward letters to William Stuart are dated 20 August 1862, and the first stands as Document 227 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was the acting head of the British legation in Washington.

Paired letters on a single date usually divide topics so each can be answered and filed on its own. The practice is a window into how a paper government worked: neat, numbered, and slow. Late August 1862 was anything but slow on the battlefield. And the contrast between the calm file and the moving armies is part of what makes these papers vivid. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d27:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 6 March 1862. It stands as Document 27 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d327:
William L. Dayton wrote from Paris on 17 September 1862, the day of Antietam, in a report printed as Document 327 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

The coincidence is the point: while the war's bloodiest day was fought in Maryland, the Union's man in Paris wrote in complete ignorance of it. His letter preserves the French scene as it stood before the news arrived. Few papers in the volume show the ocean's width, and diplomacy's blindness, more plainly than this one. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d427:
Horace J. Perry wrote from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 September 1862, four days after the battle of Antietam. The report is Document 427 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

News of Antietam and of Lincoln's coming emancipation order reached Europe slowly, and agents like Perry had to explain both to foreign courts. In Madrid the questions were sharp: would emancipation change Spain's view, and what would it mean for slavery in Cuba? Perry's September report fed Washington the Spanish reading of a turning point in the war. It belongs to the autumn file in which the Union's case abroad began to firm up.
frus-1862-d527:
The Washington exchange with the Netherlands minister opens on 5 June 1862, with Secretary of State William H. Seward writing to Roest van Limburg at his legation. The note is Document 527 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Van Limburg represented a government whose minister abroad, James Shepherd Pike, fills the Hague half of this same file. The first week of June 1862 brought a burst of Dutch business in Washington, with notes crossing almost daily. Seward's opening letter began that run. Resident ministers handled everything from trade complaints to questions of neutral right. The Dutch file that week shows how much formal paper a single matter could generate.
frus-1862-d627:
On 19 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Edward Joy Morris, the American minister to the Ottoman Empire. It is Document 627 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Seward wrote two days after Antietam, in the great mid-September round of orders, and even Constantinople was included. The news that followed, of emancipation declared, would reach the Bosphorus weeks later and be read there chiefly for its effect on the European powers. Morris's post stood at the edge of the war's diplomatic world, but Seward's system had no edges. Every minister got the line. He got it in the same week and in the same terms. The letter proves the system's reach.
frus-1863p1-d127:
On 24 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, and a second letter to him bears the same date. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 127 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Same-day pairs from Washington split the brief for clean use in London. Seward's late-March sheets kept Adams armed as the fight over Southern ships in British yards grew hot. This letter opens the pair of 24 March. With its mate, it shows the State Department feeding its envoy point by point, steamer by steamer, through a tense spring.
frus-1863p1-d227:
From his London post on 3 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 227 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

After the Emancipation Proclamation took effect on New Year's Day 1863, the war stood openly as a fight over slavery. That change made British support for the South harder to defend in public. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d27:
On 8 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 27 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Paired dispatches let an envoy keep topics apart: one sheet for talks with officials, one for the press or the street. Adams wrote in that habit through the war. This letter is the second of his New Year pair's follow-up, sent as London digested the freedom edict. In the run of the file, it marks how fast the legation's mail could move when the news was big.
frus-1863p1-d327:
In Washington on 2 November 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 327 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d427:
In the flow of wartime mail, Lord Lyons wrote to William H. Seward on 27 March 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d527:
The letter printed as document 527 was written on 22 May 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d627:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Mr. Smith on 8 May 1863. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d127: Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt wrote from Turkey on November 14, 1943, addressing the President, the Secretary of State, and Under Secretary Stettinius together. The dispatch is Document 127 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Turkey's stance mattered greatly that month, since the allies hoped to draw Ankara toward the war. The record names the four men and the date. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d227:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 402 aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, a proposed statement of United Nations policy for the Balkan and eastern Mediterranean region. Roosevelt had approved the text before it went to the Combined Chiefs of Staff.

The paper says the region's terrain and poor communications rule out large-scale operations, and that flashy limited ventures always eat more resources than promised. Operations there should stay small: supply Balkan guerrillas by sea and air, raid with commandos, and bomb key targets. Turkey should be pressed, with Soviet help, to join the war, but only with what she already has, and nothing may be diverted from bigger commitments elsewhere.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d27: Stalin addressed a message to Roosevelt and Churchill together on August 24, 1943, answering their joint note of the week before. It is Document 27 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A reply to both Western leaders at once was a pointed form, and the three-way exchange that month did much to fix the Tehran meeting. The record gives the date and the names. The text is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d327:
James Byrnes, director of war mobilization, sent President Roosevelt a cablegram from Washington on 26 November 1943 about landing craft. It follows his telegram of 24 November, which had set out, month by month, how far building could be raised in the first five months of 1944.

The increased program in those figures, Byrnes now warns, is possible only if a directive is issued at once giving landing craft priority over all programs of any kind. He asks Roosevelt to wire back whether he shall have Donald Nelson issue that directive. A note in the volume adds a later recollection by Byrnes. He recalled sending a second telegram that day suggesting output might run fifteen percent above the cautious figures. No copy of it has been found in official files.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d427:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt telegraphed President Roosevelt from Ankara on 2 December 1943 that Turkey's president, Ismet Inönü, had agreed to come to Cairo. Sent by military channels, the text printed here is the paraphrase prepared at the Cairo legation as delivered to the President.

Inönü's condition is quoted exactly. He comes on condition that, as between equals, he is being invited to a free discussion. He is not merely to be informed of decisions already arrived at in Tehran concerning Turkey. The British ambassador has telegraphed for authority to give that assurance. If it arrives before the morning of Friday 3 December, the party can reach Adana by train on the morning of the 4th. It can be in Cairo about one that afternoon by special planes. Some thirty people will travel in all. Steinhardt closes, all is going along well.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d527:
The British Embassy in Washington addressed a formal communication to the Department of State on December 22, 1943. Embassy-to-department notes were the standard paper of diplomacy, used when a government wanted a position stated officially. The State Department printed this one in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Formal notes lack the color of leaders' letters, but they bind governments in ways letters cannot. A British note delivered three days before Christmas, in the wake of two great conferences, formed part of the official follow-up between the allies. For readers, the document shows the alliance being administered through its proper channels while the personal correspondence ran alongside.
frus-1944-quebec-d127:
Ambassador John Winant in London forwarded three Moscow messages to Roosevelt on September 10, 1944. They came from Sir Archibald Clark Kerr, the British ambassador in Moscow, and had just reached Winant through Foreign Secretary Eden. Together they carry the Soviet government's formal answer to British appeals for help to Warsaw.

Molotov's covering letter warned that foreign aircraft over the Warsaw front might cause sad misunderstandings. The Soviet reply blamed the London Poles for launching the rising without warning, and demanded a commission to assign blame. It offered joint supply drops only under a prearranged plan. Meanwhile, Winant reported, the British chiefs had asked Eisenhower to plan an air mission to Warsaw.
frus-1944-quebec-d227:
General Marshall ordered action on Warsaw from Quebec on September 12, 1944, in a top-secret message to General Deane, his mission chief in Moscow. The condition of the Polish patriots was so critical, he wrote, that urgent action was essential. The Soviet agreement to cooperate in aid had to be turned into an operation without delay.

Deane was to confer with representatives from General Spaatz's headquarters and the Royal Air Force, prepare a plan, and secure Soviet coordination on arrangements and details. The plan had to account for the patriots' actual locations, so the maximum of supplies fell to them rather than the Germans. Risk to airmen was to be kept to a minimum while relief was achieved at the earliest possible date.
frus-1944-quebec-d27:
Prime Minister Churchill replied to Harry Hopkins on August 23, 1944, as the Quebec Conference drew near. The State Department printed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume's pre-conference correspondence.

Churchill's letters to Hopkins combined the personal and the official in a way his letters to no other American did. Late August found him preparing to cross the Atlantic for the meeting at Quebec City, where hospitality, strategy, and hard bargaining awaited. For readers, the message shows the Prime Minister in a working, friendly key, dealing with the man who would manage much of the conference from the American side.
frus-1945-50-intel-d127:
Hoover wrote to Vandenberg, the director of central intelligence, on 19 August 1946. The two chiefs addressed each other directly after weeks of writing through others. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Direct letters between rivals late in a fight often carry terms: what each will do, and what each expects. Hoover and Vandenberg had circled each other through the attorney general, the authority, and the State Department. Their August exchange brought the dispute to the level where it would actually be lived, bureau to group, station by station. Readers can close the summer's story here, with the two men whose names stand for the era's two secret services facing each other on paper.
frus-1945-50-intel-d227:
On 10 October 1947, Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter sent a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Board. It survives in print as document 227 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d27:
Forrestal wrote to Secretary of State Byrnes on 13 October 1945, the same day he wrote to Secretary Patterson. The Navy secretary was working both channels of the argument at once. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Twin letters on one day show a man managing a two-front negotiation. To Patterson, Forrestal spoke as a partner; to Byrnes, as the head of a department with claims to press. Readers who pair the two letters can watch the same mind adjust its voice to its audience, a core skill of cabinet politics. The volume's gift is that it prints both sides of such days, letting the reader sit where only the writers once sat.
frus-1945-50-intel-d327:
A letter dated 29 October 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Acting Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 327 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

The letter form mattered in this world: it was signed, it was kept, and it bound the writer's office to what it said. Read in sequence, the letters show two offices testing how far each could push the other. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d427:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 7 came out on 12 February 1948. It is document 427 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By early 1948 the first rule book was already growing. New directives filled gaps that the December 1947 set had left open. Each short order fixed one more duty, one more limit, or one more shared task. The series as a whole shows a state building its secret arm in plain, stepwise form. By February the agencies had real habits to codify, not just hopes on paper. The series can be read as a diary of the system's growth, one dated order at a time.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d127:
Seven pages, no more: Stettinius sent the President the State Department's draft on Germany's economy on 11 November 1944. His covering memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, points to Section 3 for close study. The draft answered the President's request of 20 October.

Stettinius explains why speed matters. The European Advisory Commission in London needs the American views promptly, since Germany's treatment must be coordinated with the British and Russian allies. If the draft does not match the President's views, he asks for another talk so it can be redone. The paper is the State Department's bid in the running fight with the Treasury over how harsh the occupation should be.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d227:
Stalin raised the Montreux Convention at Moscow, and Churchill reported it in this excerpt of 22 October 1944. Paragraph nine of his message number 801 to Roosevelt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The Soviet leader wanted the Straits rules changed for Russian warships.

He wished, Churchill writes, for changes giving the free passage of Russian warships. The British did not contest the point in principle. Revision is plainly needed, since Japan is a signatory and President Inönü missed his market the previous December. They left it that the detailed proposals should come from the Russian side. Stalin said those proposals would be moderate. Roosevelt's reply, noted by the editors, put Montreux on the list for the coming three-party meeting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d27: After a short pause in the letters, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on 9 December 1944. The message is document 27 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering the Malta and Yalta conferences. December brought hard fighting in Europe, and the correspondence now ran against a deadline, since the leaders expected to meet in the Crimea within about two months.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d327:
Alger Hiss took these notes in pencil, in his own hand, at Yalta on February 4, 1945. They were copied out for this volume from the longhand original. Hiss sat in as Gladwyn Jebb read a British paper on dependent peoples. The paper had been cleared through the Dominions. It was then before the War Cabinet in London.

Jebb's points, as Hiss caught them, aimed at world teamwork for the good of colonial peoples. The goals were self-government plus social and economic growth. Rather than revive the old mandates, Jebb proposed regional bodies with open reporting. The rough, broken lines show a working note, not a polished record.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d427:
Revised but still unfinished, the foreign ministers' report to the sixth plenary is dated February 9, 1945. Its first item is Poland. The ministers had debated the governmental question at length, on the basis of an American paper. The presidential committee idea was dropped, following Molotov's proposal.

For a formula on the government itself, Molotov asked for time to consult Stalin. The ministers agreed to report that they had not reached agreement. Reparations follow as the second item in the same unresolved state. Comparing this text with the earlier draft shows the report being polished while its substance stayed stuck.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d127:
Under Secretary Joseph Grew recorded President Truman's farewell meeting with the French ambassador in a memorandum dated July 6, 1945. The memo is document 127 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The meeting nearly did not happen: Truman at first refused to see Ambassador Bonnet on the eve of his departure for Berlin.

Grew persuaded the President that a refusal would do political harm, and Bonnet was kept waiting an hour before being received. Bonnet reported that General de Gaulle had accepted an invitation to visit Washington in late August. He stressed that coal was the commodity France needed most to rebuild, and that stability in Europe depended on American help. The printed extract breaks off as Bonnet turns to the main purpose of his visit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d227:
Secretary Stettinius sent the full text of his peace machinery proposal from San Francisco on June 19, 1945. The telegram is document 227 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It expands the extract printed earlier, in which he urged avoiding a formal peace conference for Europe.

A formal conference would be slow and unwieldy, Stettinius argues, and ratification of its work might be delayed for years. A small conference of a few great powers would anger the states left out. He proposes instead that the problems be handled case by case. They would be handled by a council of foreign ministers. The council would cover the United States, Britain, Russia, China, and France. Other states would be brought in when their interests are touched. The council might meet in Brussels or Vienna rather than in a capital of the powers themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d27:
Germany's fleet heads the fourth Kremlin conversation, recorded by Bohlen for May 30, 1945. Stalin said a suggestion had come from General Eisenhower: a naval commission of the four countries should consider the disposal and division of the German fleet. The American representative would be Admiral Ghormley. Stalin would name Admiral Levchenko for the Soviet side.

Eisenhower had also urged speeding the establishment of the Control Council for Germany, Stalin added. He was acting on it the next day. A meeting of heads of state and Poland fill out the subject list. The memorandum shows the Moscow talks producing machinery, not just mood.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d327:
One of the President's briefing book papers sums up policy toward Germany as Potsdam approached. It starts with the Allied declaration on Germany, issued in Berlin on June 5, 1945, and the first meeting of the Control Council that same day. The four commanders, it says, got little done beyond the declaration itself.

Marshal Zhukov had insisted the Council could not act until the armies pulled back into their set zones. Britain had wanted that pullback delayed until open questions, including the zones in Austria, were settled. Washington had partly agreed. The paper shows the control machinery for Germany stalled before the conference even opened.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d427:
Coal shipments to Europe form the third point in extracts of Stimson's letter to Grew of July 4, 1945. Grew had assumed the War Department would ship coal to northwest Europe during June, July, and August. Stimson confirms the assumption, within the limits of shipping and supply, to meet valid combined military import requirements.

That duty, he expects, will end with the August 1945 loadings. Combined British and American military authorities, he adds, are making every effort to maximize coal production in the areas of Germany they hold. The extracts go on to the allocation of German surpluses, through the Control Council once it functions, with an interim procedure meanwhile.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d527:
Displaced persons in Germany and Austria fill a memorandum by the Joint Civil Affairs Committee. Their care and repatriation, it opens, form one of the most difficult and delicate problems of military government in Germany. Nearly four million such people have been uncovered in the British and American-controlled areas. The numbers uncovered by the Russians are not known.

Approximately one and three-quarters million displaced persons, the committee reports, have already been repatriated by the British and Americans. That figure includes in excess of five hundred thousand Russians. The memorandum then lists the problems that need settlement at government level, beginning with the agreements the United States and United Kingdom each made with the Soviet Union on February 11, 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d627:
Edward Wolf wired Pauley in Moscow again on July 14, 1945, with oil figures from Ralph Davies. The secret message is document 627 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It answers Pauley's request of July 10 for tanker savings.

Davies stresses that the prime need is the oil itself, not saved shipping. Tanker savings would be a side gain, though a real one. If 15,000 barrels a day moved by rail or barge from Austria, Hungary, or Rumania, eleven class B tankers would be freed. Oil shipped from Constanta for Mediterranean ports would free seven such tankers at the same rate. Savings at other rates would run roughly in proportion. The figures armed Pauley for his Moscow talks on reparations and oil.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1027:
Molotov handed Secretary Byrnes this Soviet proposal on the Ruhr industrial district on July 30, 1945. The Ruhr, it states, remains part of Germany, but its war potential must be cut in every way. The conference is asked to place the district under joint control of the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, and France.

An Allied Council of the four powers would administer the district. Ruhr industry would serve reparations under the common plan. A provisional council should form at once, finish the groundwork within a month, and take over the district's running for the time being. The paper was not written into the Protocol.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1127:
Will Clayton wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 21 July 1945, reporting from the Potsdam side of the Atlantic. Clayton was the State Department's lead man on the money side of foreign policy. Trade, loans, and what Germany would pay all crossed his desk.

His message carried the view from inside the talks back to the home office in Washington. The two halves of the department had to stay in step while stands shifted daily. A cable of this kind is the money track of the summit in a single dispatch. It shows the expert who priced the peace keeping his chiefs informed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1227:
A second Sato report to Togo bears the date 19 July 1945. Two cables in a day from the Moscow embassy show the pace of the exchange. Tokyo wanted news; Sato had mostly warnings to send.

The envoy's problem was plain: the Soviet side gained by waiting. Each day of delay weakened Japan and strengthened Moscow's hand for the war's end. Sato's reports pressed Tokyo to face that truth and to sharpen its terms. This cable is one more turn of that screw. It is part of the secret record the Potsdam leaders read while they drafted Japan's surrender terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1327:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 17 July 1945, the summit's opening day. Grew's home office began its Potsdam circuit with this message. The circuit would run daily until the team came home.

Opening-day cables set the pattern: what Washington sent, how fast, and in what tone. The department's chief abroad needed the capital's news to bargain well. This note starts that flow in the record. It is a small, early piece of the two-ended machine that ran American foreign policy through the most crowded weeks of 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1427:
The British delegation submitted a text at Potsdam on 30 July 1945. By that date Attlee had replaced Churchill, and the British team was finishing the talks under new leadership. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

A text tabled in the summit's last days speaks to the drafting of the closing bargain. The British side, wedged between American wealth and Soviet numbers, used careful drafting as its lever. Readers can weigh this late British text against the protocol signed two days later. It shows the delegation still working its points to the end, under a prime minister who had held the job for less than a week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-127:
James Riddleberger, chief of the State Department's Division of Central European Affairs, wrote to the Secretary of State on July 29, 1945. His division handled the lands at the heart of the Potsdam agenda. Few desks in Washington knew Germany and its neighbors better. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

A division chief's letter speaks with expert weight. Riddleberger could ground advice in years of files on borders, parties, and leaders. Readers see Washington's deep knowledge reaching the conference table. The piece also shows a two-way flow: the field and the home office shaping each other's views in the final days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-27:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes covering the approval of their July 18, 1945 conclusions form an unnumbered item here. They appear in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam, out of strict sequence in the file. Three decisions are recorded in the part printed.

First, the chiefs amended two items from the 195th meeting. One now agreed in principle that part of the Southwest Pacific Area would pass to British command as soon as possible. Another now stated the rule if Russia entered the Japan war. In that event, the strategy to be pursued should be discussed among the parties concerned. Second, the chiefs approved a reply on two French colonial infantry divisions for Far Eastern operations. Third, they took up the combined staff machinery's fate after the Japan war, on the British proposal printed in volume one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d727:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 20, 1945, as document 727. Proposals were the currency of the conference. Each delegation put texts forward, and the talks tested them line by line. This American text joined the numbered papers of the second Potsdam volume.

A tabled proposal freezes a side's aim at a moment in time. Readers can measure it against the bargaining that followed. Some lines survive into final texts; others vanish. The document lets that test be run fairly. It also shows the American habit of leading with drafts. Paper, at Potsdam, was power in draft form.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d827:
Barnes reported from Bulgaria on July 30, 1945, in document 827. The representative in Sofia wrote to the Acting Secretary two days before Potsdam closed. His letters form one of the volume's most complete post records. This one entered the second Potsdam volume near the end of his run.

A closing-stage report has the air of a final entry. Barnes wrote knowing the decisions were nearly made. Readers see him placing his last facts where they would count: on the record. The document shows the dignity of the reporting craft. Influence fades; a true file endures, and his file endures.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d927:
Seymour Rubin, chief of the Division of Economic Security Controls, wrote this candid letter extract to his acting deputy on July 25, 1945. He recounts the reparations talks in Moscow and at Potsdam. Basic principles had won agreement, but the Russians held back on defining war booty and restitution.

Then the Soviet booty definition, covering nearly everything, scrapped the earlier work. A new plan let Russia pay itself and Poland from its own zone. Rubin gives the agreed shares: 56 percent Soviet, 22 percent each for Britain and America. He also reports Soviet interest in two billion dollars of Ruhr equipment, and talk of trading food and potash in exchange.
frus-1955-57v27:
Western Europe and Canada close the 1955–1957 set in Volume XXVII. European integration leads, with the Common Market and Euratom in the first blocks. NATO's strength and missile basing follow.

Britain, France, Germany, and Italy take country runs of their own. Canada closes the volume, on trade and joint defense. The papers catch Europe knitting itself together. Washington cheered the union and feared its trade walls in the same cables. The set ends where the next decade's fights were already taking shape in draft form. Defense talks with Ottawa fill the closing run here.
frus-1961-63v07-d327: An editorial note in the arms control volume traces a Joint Chiefs paper on the limited test ban. Bromley Smith's memo of a July 16, 1963, staff meeting cites the Chiefs' draft. It held that a limited ban was better than a full one, yet still harmful. High-yield Soviet leads and cheating chances are named. The Chiefs' close held that only strong non-military gains could justify the treaty. The draft, the note adds, was never sent to Secretary McNamara.
frus-1964-68v27:
Mainland Southeast Asia is the field of Volume XXVII in the 1964-1968 Foreign Relations series. Opening chapters cover the ANZUS pact and the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization. Long chapters then follow Cambodia and Thailand. The Cambodia chapters trace a break in ties with Washington in 1965, then slow efforts to restore them. The Thailand chapters weigh U.S. troops, aid, and the insurgency in the northeast.

Burma gets a short chapter of its own. In Thailand, the papers follow Thai combat troops sent to South Vietnam. In Cambodia, they track Viet Cong use of border areas and the seizure of a U.S. landing craft crew. The volume rounds out the series' Indochina coverage.
frus-1969-76v27:
Volume XXVII of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series covers Iran and Iraq from 1973 to 1976. Four chapters follow Iran by period. They deal with arms sales, oil prices, and the Shah's growing power in the Gulf. Two chapters then cover Iraq. They treat ties at a low ebb, the Kurdish war, and Baghdad's links with Moscow. An oil deal with Iran is weighed in the later papers.

Embassy cables and talk records with the Shah fill the Iran chapters. The records show Washington relying on Iran as a pillar in the Gulf. Iraq's chapters show a colder, more distant tie. The volume ends as the Ford years close.
frus-1977-80v27:
Western Europe fills Volume XXVII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1977-1980. A regional section opens the volume. Country sections follow for Canada, West Germany, France, Italy, the Nordic countries, Portugal, Spain, and the United Kingdom. Britain takes the largest country share. The papers deal with alliance burdens, Iran sanctions, and the Soviet move into Afghanistan. France's section weighs its separate line inside the alliance.

The Italy section covers the Communist vote and the Moro murder's shock. Portugal and Spain are tracked through their moves toward democracy. Summit talks among the big economies recur throughout. The volume gives the allied core of Carter policy.
frus-1981-88v04-d327: A memorandum from Secretary of State Shultz to President Reagan reports an hour-long meeting with Soviet Ambassador Dobrynin. It is document 327 in Volume IV of the 1981-1988 Foreign Relations series. The talk prepared the ground for the Geneva meeting with Gromyko. Shultz gave his planned team: Paul Nitze would join him, and the group would match the Soviet side in size. Dobrynin said Gromyko would focus on arms control. He also said Gromyko could now stay for a second session on January 8 if useful.
gao-gaoreports-b-296127:
International Marine Products protested a Navy award for ship control system work in GAO decision B-296127, dated June 13, 2005. The winner was Beach Panel Controls. The work covered checks, training, service, and urgent fixes. The firm hit its tech marks. It also claimed bias for the winner.

GAO denied the protest. A time point came first. A protest letter from the agency came on a Saturday. That day was not a work day for the firm. The clock ran from Monday, when the mail was opened. On the marks, GAO found them sound and in line with the rules. Dissent alone did not prove bias.
gao-gaoreports-b-296627:
Coastal Maritime Stevedoring protested an Army award for port work in GAO decision B-296627, dated September 22, 2005. The winner was Marine Terminal Corporation East. The site was Blount Island Terminal in Jacksonville, Florida. The work was loading ships, rail cars, and trucks. The firm was the higher rated, higher priced bidder.

GAO sustained the protest. The winner's small firm plan was marked as just fine. Yet it missed many parts the rules require. It also gave clashing facts on its small firm goals. The trade-off pick missed key edges of the firm's bid. A pick that skips key edges and backs a weak plan cannot stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-298327:
Praxair protested the terms of a NASA call for a nitrogen plant in GAO decision B-298327, dated August 24, 2006. The site was Langley Research Center in Virginia. The firm now sells liquid nitrogen to NASA. The call sought bids to build a state-owned plant run by a firm. It took no bids to keep sales from the firm or to buy its plant.

GAO denied the protest. NASA had a sound base to want its own source. That need set its least needs for the work. A call that seeks one path to meet a true need is not too strict. The firm had no right to have its own path put in the call.
gao-gaoreports-b-298527:
Technical Support Services protested a Navy award to Quantell, Inc. The contract covered administrative and training services. The buy was set aside in full for small firms. GAO decided B-298527 on October 12, 2006.

The firm's size status sat at the heart of the case. The Small Business Administration first found the firm other than small. Its appeals office later reversed that call. The firm argued that the Navy had to end Quantell's contract and award it the work. GAO disagreed. The Navy had fairly moved ahead while the first ruling stood. No rule forced it to unwind the award. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298627:
eFedBudget Corporation protested a planned sole-source award by the Department of State. The award to RGII Technologies, Inc. covered upkeep of budget and planning software. Those systems serve the agency's posts worldwide. GAO ruled in B-298627 on November 15, 2006.

Part of the case favored the agency. Key software was owned by the prior firm and closed to rivals. That fact could support a sole-source path. Yet the record showed weak advance planning by the agency. It had not taken fair steps to spur rivalry. A sole-source buy must rest on more than drift. GAO sustained the protest on that ground.
gao-gaoreports-b-299227:
L-3 Communications Corporation, BT Fuze Products Division, protested an Army award for illuminating cartridges. The contract went to SNC Technologies, Inc. through a Canadian firm. The rounds light up a field or send a signal at night. GAO decided B-299227 and B-299227.2 on March 14, 2007.

The pick rested on a trade-off of cost and technical merit. L-3 attacked the scoring, the talks, and the final call. GAO found the agency's judgment sound. The winner's approach, grasp, and depth of skill were stronger. Those gains outweighed the firm's price edge. A weighed trade-off of that kind can stand. GAO denied the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-303927:
GAO ruled on a Labor Department grant to the New York Workers' Compensation Board in B-303927. The grant aided claim work tied to the September 11, 2001 attack. The board passed $44 million on to other state bodies. GAO issued its legal ruling on June 7, 2005.

The funds law said the sum was for payment to the board for claim work. GAO held the board could not pass it to other state bodies. The Labor Department should seek the $44 million back. One path could save the spend: a plea to Congress to bless the past costs. The agency also bore a duty to watch the grant's use.
gao-gaoreports-b-311327:
Mark Whetstone saw a fresh protest thrown out in GAO decision B-311327, dated May 20, 2008. He spoke for staff at a Homeland Security site in Nebraska. The site rules on pleas for migrant gains. The agency drew work from a line in a held deal. He said the draw shifts state work to firms with no race. The law he cites sets the race rule for such shifts.

GAO dismissed the protest. The line sat in a deal made years back. The race law, by its own words, skips buys made known in public before the law took hold. Old deals sit past the new rule's reach.
gao-gaoreports-b-400127:
Two firms lost their protests. That ruling is B-400127, dated August 7, 2008. The Army killed an A-76 call for base work at White Sands Missile Range. The site sits in New Mexico. Zia Engineering and Garrison Engineering fought the kill. They said the Army lacked a fair base to end the race. The work dealt with base aid and supply runs for the range.

GAO denied the protests. The Army found its call no longer matched its needs. Work at the range will grow much in years to come. A call built on old needs can be killed with fair cause. Growth in the task is such a cause.
gao-gaoreports-b-400227:
Systems Research and Applications Corporation, known as SRA, protested a General Services Administration task order given to Science Applications International Corporation for information technology work. GAO ruled in B-400227 on July 21, 2008. SRA raised claims of conflicts of interest, unequal treatment, and flawed scoring of its bid.

GAO never reached those claims. The task order was issued before the date a new law let GAO hear task order protests. For orders from that time, the Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act of 1994 barred GAO review. The protest was dismissed for lack of power to hear it. The ruling maps that time limit in full.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-227:
Housing Finance, GAO-05-227 of March 15, 2005, studies a glitch that can halt home loan aid mid-year. Two agencies back loans: the Federal Housing Administration and the Rural Housing Service. In fiscal year 2004, they backed about $136 billion in home loans. Each holds a set cap on new loans and a set fund for long-term costs. When a cap runs out, new backing stops.

Such halts jar buyers, builders, and banks. GAO counts how often they hit in the past decade, and why. It checks how the agencies warn Congress as caps near. It lists ways to keep the aid from stalling.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-327:
Protection of Chemical and Water Infrastructure, GAO-05-327 of March 28, 2005, surveys two soft spots in the land's guard plan. Chemical plants and water works sit among 13 fields whose loss could shake the nation. The homeland chief counts about 4,000 chemical plants that hold the most feared stocks. About 53,000 town water systems face guard rules too.

GAO lists the guard rules each field must meet. It tells what the lead agencies did to spur the work. It checks what picked sites have done and if their steps track true risk. It names the blocks they hit, and Coast Guard test marks for port sites.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-427:
Military equipment and supplies stored in advance near likely conflict zones are the subject of GAO report GAO-05-427, dated September 6, 2005. The report reviews the Department of Defense prepositioning programs. It covers stocks kept at land sites and aboard ships. Congress asked GAO to judge near-term risk, the quality of oversight, and whether DOD had a joined plan for the future of these programs.

GAO found that heavy use in Iraq had left many stocks short and some gear in poor shape. The Army had drawn from nearly all of its stored stocks. The Marine Corps had used much of the gear from 5 of its 16 ships. Oversight by the department and the services was weak, and old inventory problems had been left to persist. GAO also found no coordinated plan for future programs. The report shows why stored stocks might not support a second large conflict.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-727:
Dated July 26, 2005, GAO-05-727 looks at links between airports and other ways to travel. Passenger counts were set to near 1 billion by 2015. Crowded roads to airports were a growing strain. GAO studied who builds these links, how far they have spread, and what helps or blocks them. It also weighed plans to do more.

GAO found that state and local bodies lead this work. The federal government had no set goals or fund just for airport links. Most big airports tied into local bus or rail lines. Far fewer tied into national rail or bus lines. Gains could include less road traffic and fewer short flights. High rail costs and hard funding choices were key blocks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-927:
Use of performance data by agency managers is studied in GAO-05-927, issued September 9, 2005. A 1993 law spread results-based planning across government. GAO's surveys show managers had more performance measures in 2003 than in 1997. Yet their use of the data in running programs barely moved. GAO asked how agencies can use such data to decide. It also named practices that help.

GAO identified four broad kinds of management choices the data can serve. It identified five kinds of practice that raise use of the data. Five agencies serve as worked examples in the report. Their settings differ, but the lessons can be adapted by others, GAO said. It urged wider sharing of agency experience. The report is a how-to record for managers who hold data but do not yet act on it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-27:
Prevailing wage setting for federal service contracts is studied in GAO-06-27, a report dated December 7, 2005. The Service Contract Act of 1965 sets wage and benefit floors for workers on federal service deals. The Labor Department must set local rates that match area pay. Each year its Wage and Hour Division sets rates for over 300 service jobs in 205 metro areas. The act also lets the department police contractor compliance. GAO described how the rates get built and how enforcement runs.

The rate process leans on two national wage surveys and staff judgment, GAO found. Its methods stay largely hidden from the public. GAO urged the division to publish its basic method. It also urged smarter use of past violation records to plan checks and target bad actors. Better data use could sharpen enforcement without new law. The department agreed with all of the recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-327:
A first shield against long-range missiles, fielded short of its goals, is judged in GAO-06-327, issued March 15, 2006. The defense department has spent nearly $90 billion since 1985 on ballistic missile defense. About $58 billion more is planned over six years. The Missile Defense Agency builds capability in two-year blocks. Block 2004 was to give some protection by December 2005. Its shield aimed at attacks from North Korea and the Middle East. Congress requires a yearly GAO check on the program.

An initial capability did reach the field, GAO found. It fell short of the block's original goals. GAO traced the reasons for the gaps and the fixes still owed. The agency's aim is grand: defeat missiles of any range in any flight phase. Each block is a down payment on that promise. This annual report is the receipt, marking what the money bought and what slipped.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-427:
Cleaning up decades of military and nuclear waste will cost vast sums. GAO's March 31, 2006 report, GAO-06-427, reviews the federal government's environmental liabilities. The government put the cleanup liability at $249 billion in fiscal year 2004. That made it the government's third largest reported liability. The figure was not auditable at the time.

GAO describes the nature and size of the liabilities. It checks how the Energy and Defense departments estimate and report them. Their processes are tested against federal accounting standards. GAO also lists cost uncertainties that cannot yet be estimated. Weak controls hamper long-term fiscal planning, GAO found. Readers see a huge future bill.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-627:
Oversight of the Community Services Block Grant Program is examined in GAO-06-627, a GAO report dated June 29, 2006. The program sends federal funds to states, which pass money to local groups that help low-income families. The Office of Community Services, part of the Department of Health and Human Services, runs the program. GAO reviewed how that office monitors states and supports grantees.

GAO found that the office lacked the internal controls and risk framework needed for sound monitoring. State site visits varied widely in how often they occurred. Training and aid funds did reach some grantees with problems, but data on results was thin. GAO urged the office to focus its monitoring and aid on the areas of highest risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-727:
A big anti-poverty experiment is weighed in GAO-06-727 (September 22, 2006). The Empowerment Zone and Enterprise Community program targeted poor urban and rural areas for renewal. Zones and communities won grants and tax perks across three rounds of designations. All designations were set to end by December 2009. A 2000 law told GAO to audit the results.

GAO found that first-round zones and communities used most of the $1 billion in grant funds. As of March 31, 2006, 20 percent of zone funds and 2 percent of community funds remained unspent. Conditions in the areas did improve during the program years. But GAO could not pin those gains on the program itself. Weak data left the program's true effect unclear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1127:
Smithsonian buildings are at risk from funding strain, GAO reports in GAO-07-1127, dated September 28, 2007. The Smithsonian is the world's largest museum and research complex. Most of its building funds come from federal grants. In 2005 GAO found its funds short of an estimated $2.3 billion in projects through 2013.

The board was told then to build a funding plan. GAO now tells how building state and project costs have changed since 2005. It weighs the steps taken to guard and run its property stock. It grades work on funding plans for those projects. Weak buildings and security, GAO warns, put collections in danger.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-127:
The Bureau of the Public Debt manages the Treasury securities the nation owes. GAO audited its debt schedules in GAO-07-127, a financial audit dated November 7, 2006. The audit covers fiscal years 2006 and 2005. It tests whether the schedules are reliable in all material respects. It also tests the bureau's internal control and its compliance with key laws. The debt includes securities held by the public and by federal trust funds.

GAO's opinion was clean on the schedules themselves. They present fairly, in all material respects, the debt balances for the years audited. Those balances cover September 30, 2006, 2005, and 2004. GAO also found that the bureau kept effective internal control in all material respects. The audit supports GAO's wider audit of the government's own financial statements. Federal debt is a major part of those statements.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-27:
Tax season 2006 brought better service in most areas, at a program cost in the billions. GAO graded the season in GAO-07-27, a report dated November 15, 2006. The tax agency spent about 38 percent of its $10.8 billion budget on processing and help. GAO weighed paper and electronic filing, phone help, the web site, and walk-in sites. It compared results with goals and past years. It also sought savings.

Return and refund handling improved by most measures, GAO found. Electronic filing grew, though its growth rate kept slowing. Free File rule changes cut who could use that program. A phone filing option had ended. Phone access matched the prior year's level. The agency runs 25 call sites and 400 walk-in sites. GAO saw room to merge call sites for savings. It asked the agency to report refund speed for its new processing system. The agency agreed with both points.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-627:
A global health fund's paperwork has improved, and GAO-07-627, dated May 7, 2007, still finds loose oversight of its local agents. The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria has approved about $7 billion in grants to poor nations. The United States has given $1.9 billion of that sum. Congress told GAO in 2003 to report on the fund every 2 years.

Since the June 2005 report, the fund documents its grant and renewal calls far better. Its risk model, though, has slipped its dates, and a draft risk frame is still new. The soft spot is the local fund agents. They watch grants on the ground for the fund. No set standards govern how they are judged, so quality varies unseen. GAO urged common expectations and scored reviews of the agents. The fund's board, it notes, now backs a fuller risk system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-27:
Flu vaccine supply chains are mapped in GAO report GAO-08-27 (October 31, 2007). A yearly shot is the main shield against seasonal flu. Making it is a long, rigid process that starts fresh each year. Virus strains can be hard to grow, and plant capacity is tight. Demand swings from year to year as well. All three forces set how much vaccine arrives, and when.

GAO also tracked how shots reach high-risk groups first. An expert panel widens its target list over time and narrows it in shortage years. Public messages from health officials aim to lift take-up. The report shows a system strained at every link.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-327:
Prescription drug spending by the Department of Defense (DOD) is tracked in GAO report GAO-08-327, issued April 4, 2008. The John Warner National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2007 required the study. GAO examined spending trends from fiscal years 2000 through 2006 and DOD's steps to slow growth.

Total drug spending more than tripled, from $1.6 billion in fiscal year 2000 to $6.2 billion in fiscal year 2006. Retail pharmacy spending drove the rise, climbing from $455 million to $3.9 billion, because federal pricing deals did not then apply at retail stores. DOD's uniform formulary avoided about $447 million in fiscal year 2006, by DOD's data. GAO recommended that DOD track the effect of new federal pricing at retail pharmacies and add other steps as needed. DOD agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-427:
Ship repair capacity near Guam is the subject of GAO report GAO-08-427, dated May 12, 2008. Voyage repairs are urgent fixes that a ship's crew cannot make and that cannot wait. The Navy's former repair yard on Guam is now leased to a private shipyard, and that lease may end in 2012 as a military buildup proceeds.

The Navy has not worked out what repair demand near Guam will look like in 2012 and beyond. Officials blamed unsettled force plans, yet GAO found usable inputs: past repair history, planned force shifts in the 2006 Quadrennial Defense Review, and repair capacity at sites such as Yokosuka, Japan. The Navy had named four options for providing repairs but had not weighed them or set time-critical planning tasks. GAO recommended estimating demand and picking the best option mix. The Defense Department agreed.
gide-counterfeiters-bussy-1927:
André Gide called The Counterfeiters, published in French in 1925, his only true novel. Dorothy Bussy translated it into English in 1927. Schoolboys in Paris pass counterfeit coins, and the false money mirrors false selves all through the book.

At its center stands Edouard, a novelist keeping a journal for a novel of his own. Around him, students, teachers, and rogues drift into theft, despair, and suicide. Gide weaves diary, letters, and shifting viewpoints into one design. The book asks what counts as real in art and in life. It became a landmark of the modern novel in France and beyond.
haldane-possible-worlds-1927:
Possible Worlds, published in 1927, gathers Haldane's essays on science for general readers. He writes on the size of the universe, the oddness of life, and what future ages might bring. His humor and range made him a model for later popular science writers.

One famous line holds that the universe is not only queerer than we suppose, but queerer than we can suppose. Haldane moves from stars to microbes to human society without losing his plain, lively voice. The essays show a first-rate mind enjoying hard questions in public. Each piece stands alone, so the book can be read in any order.
hales-vegetable-staticks-1727:
Stephen Hales, an English clergyman with a gift for experiment, published Vegetable Staticks in 1727. Hales measured living plants the way others measured machines. His book is often called the founding text of plant physiology.

With gauges and tubes, Hales showed how sap rises and how leaves give off water. He measured root pressure and the air plants take in and release. His methods were new: count, weigh, and test, rather than guess. Much later lab work on plant water and gases still starts from Hales. Growers and gardeners read his numbers on how fast sap can rise.
handy-polynesian-religion-1927:
Edward Smith Craighill Handy synthesized Polynesian Religion in 1927 for the Bishop Museum, the great storehouse of Pacific learning in Honolulu. Tapu, the sacred restriction, mana, the spiritual power, gods great and small, and ritual form his themes throughout. Hawaii, Tahiti, Samoa, and New Zealand supply the evidence, drawn from the museum's unmatched collections and its field reports.

Handy set scattered island traditions into one comparative frame without flattening their real differences. Priests, temples, feasts, seasons, and prayers all find their place in his calm, orderly survey of the whole region. The book remains a standard Bishop Museum synthesis of how Polynesians understood the sacred world around them.
hemingway-men-without-women-1927:
Ernest Hemingway published Men Without Women in 1927, his second book of stories, written in the wake of The Sun Also Rises. The fourteen stories circle men in worlds where women are absent, lost, or kept at the edge of the frame. It is the essential early Hemingway collection.

The Killers puts young Nick Adams in a lunchroom where two hitmen wait for their victim. Hills Like White Elephants stages a whole strained relationship in one station-bar conversation. Other tales cover bullfighting, boxing, soldiers, and an old fisherman's trade in Italy. Hemingway's dialogue does nearly all the work, with feeling buried under plain talk. Few story collections have influenced later writers more.
hesse-steppenwolf-1927:
Hermann Hesse published Steppenwolf in 1927, here in Basil Creighton's first English translation of 1929. Harry Haller's divided self and the Magic Theater make the novel Hesse's darkest work of fiction. Creighton's version was the book's English debut, two years after the German original stunned readers at home.

Harry, a writer of fifty, calls himself a wolf of the steppes, torn between bourgeois comfort and savage solitude in himself. Hermine, a dancer, tutors him in jazz, love, and laughter, and lends him Pablo and the Magic Theater's doors. In the theater, mirrors, chessmen, and a stabbed Hermine stage the selves he must learn to laugh at, not obey. Mozart's laughter closes the book's vision of humor as the soul's way out of its private hell. The novel found its mass audience forty years on, among the young of the sixties.
history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-babylonia:
Gaston Maspero opens this seventh volume with the Assyrian revival. Assur-nazir-pal, dated 885 to 860 before Christ, leads the line. Shalmaneser the Third, 860 to 825, presses the struggle for Syria. The kingdom of Urartu and its conquering princes share the stage.

Babylonian dynasties and their wars with Assyria fill the background. Later pages reach Israel, where a prophet's visions darken. Locusts, fire, a plumb-line, and summer fruit picture the doom foretold. Maspero weaves small kingdoms into the great powers' clash. Readers watch the Near East tighten toward one empire, war by war.
holmberg-finno-ugric-siberian-mythology-:
Uno Holmberg wrote this survey of the faiths of Finland, Hungary's kin groups, and Siberia for the Mythology of All Races set, and it came out in 1927. The set aimed to cover the myths of the whole world in plain English. His part deals with the far north of Europe and Asia.

The book maps gods, spirits, and the shape of the world as those peoples held it. Shamans hold a large place, as links between men and the spirit world. It served for years as the main English guide to faith in the cold north.
hortulus-hermeticus-flosculis-philosopho:
Daniel Stolcius made this Latin emblem book, the Hortulus Hermeticus, in 1627. Its title calls it a little hermetic garden of philosophers' flowers. Each flower is a copper engraving with a few short Latin verses. The book was meant as a picture storehouse for students of chymistry.

Weary laboratory workers, the title adds, may refresh themselves in its pages. Numbered emblems run past seventy in the hosted copy. Gratianus and Stephanus speak in verse on ashes, water, and mercury. The scan comes from the Wellcome collection's copy, with its marks on each leaf. The Latin is dense and playful at once.
hurston-cudjos-own-story-1927:
In 1927 Zora Neale Hurston published an account of her interviews with Cudjo Lewis in the Journal of Negro History. Lewis was the last known survivor of the Clotilda, the last slave ship to reach the United States. Hurston visited him in Alabama and recorded his memories in his own words.

Cudjo tells of his youth in Africa, his capture, and the middle passage in 1860. He recalls slavery, freedom, and the founding of Africatown by the Clotilda's survivors. His grief for his lost homeland runs through the whole account. The piece became a key source for Hurston's later book Barracoon and a rare firsthand record of the slave trade.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-27:
A fragile peace holds through Volume 27, from 1898, on the Hurons of 1645 and 1646. Between storms, the mission breathes and gathers its strength once more. Thwaites prints reports that sound, for once, almost hopeful in tone.

Baptisms continue in the towns, and new ventures westward take shape. Priests repair chapels, plant fields, and teach with fresh energy each day. Yet every calm page carries quiet dramatic weight for modern readers. They know the peace will break and the storm will return. That knowledge gives this gentle volume its deep, sad pull. Calm, here, feels more fragile than any storm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-arika-usua:
Abba Arika, usually called Rab, was a celebrated Babylonian amora and the founder of the Academy of Sura. He flourished in the third century and died at Sura in 247. His surname Arika means tall, and his height set him apart. In tradition he is known almost only as Rab, the Master.

Rab reached Babylonia in the year 219 of the common era, a date the schools took as the start of the Talmudic age. After work at Nehardea he founded his school at Sura, which became the center of Babylonian Jewish learning. His method took the Mishnah as its base and built the legal debates of the Babylonian Talmud on it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abishag-327:
Abishag was a beautiful Shunammite brought to serve the aged King David. Servants hoped her care would revive his failing strength. After Solomon became king, Adonijah asked Bathsheba to help him win Abishag as a wife.

Solomon read that request as a plot to strengthen a claim to the throne. Under old law, a king's concubines passed to his heir. Solomon therefore had Adonijah put to death. Rabbinic notes add that David never married Abishag. She still counted as part of the royal household, so asking for her was treated as treason.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-eli:
Abraham ben Eliezer ha-Levi Berukim was a cabalistic writer born before 1540. He lived long in Jerusalem and died in 1600 at an advanced age. A pupil of Moses Cordovero and Isaac Luria, he won many people to a strict religious life.

His chief aim was strict Sabbath keeping. He urged Jews to start the Sabbath before sunset, which earned him the name Berukim, sayer of benedictions. His main work, Tikkune Shabbat, gives Cabala talks on the Sabbath. Other books on the soul's travels and on creation stayed unpublished. Azulai reports that he saw the Shekinah at the Wailing Wall.
