Higher barrier scores went together with higher body weight in the survey data. Interviews named four barriers: heavy responsibilities, the child's needs themselves, parents' mental state, and poor sports facilities. Numbers alone missed some of these pressures, the authors note. Support programs need to ease time and facility problems, not just urge parents to move more.
plos-pone-0349027:
Lauren A Rutter, Prabhvir Lakhan, and Laura Germine asked in 2026 whether two personality traits change how well young adults read faces. Spotting subtle shifts between anger, fear, and happiness is a core social skill, and past findings on trait effects were mixed.

Nearly three hundred students took a test built to measure fine feeling discrimination without guessing bias, plus questionnaires on traits, mood, and stress. Women reported higher levels of both traits studied. Trait scores tracked mood symptoms closely, yet neither trait predicted face reading accuracy in the final models. The null result usefully narrows where personality does, and does not, shape social perception.
plos-pone-0349227:
Shruthi Venkataraman and colleagues interviewed thirty-one first-year medical students from Black, Hispanic, and Indigenous backgrounds across the United States about what pulls them toward or pushes them from research careers. Physician-scientists from these groups are scarce, and the first year is when intentions form. Four themes ran through the conversations.

Structured research experience before medical school proved pivotal in sparking interest. Many students framed research as a tool for social justice and community benefit. Mentorship mattered most when mentors invested genuinely and shared the student's background. Yet students also described a research arms race for residency spots that amplifies inequality and can squeeze out the very motivations that drew them in, a tension schools could relieve.
plos-pone-0349527:
Sadia Tabassum and Naushin Nower present DG-LLM, a traffic forecasting framework that borrows the pattern-finding power of large language models. Traffic data entangle daily rhythms with road-network effects across many time scales, defeating simpler predictors. Their method first decomposes the traffic signal into simpler modes, then learns a changing map of which sensors influence each other within each mode.

Those structured inputs feed a pre-trained language model, which handles the long-range time patterns. Across six real-world datasets, from city streets to highways, the framework beat leading graph-based and language-model forecasters, including at long horizons where errors usually snowball. Cities use such forecasts to time signals and pre-empt jams, so durable long-range accuracy is the prize.
plos-pone-0349627:
Jingke Wu and Fuxing Xie present this 2026 PLOS One lab study on how fast loading changes the way rock-like material breaks. They cast artificial rock cylinders from sand, cement, and gypsum in three mixes. They crushed the cylinders at varied loading rates, under two loading styles. They recorded strength and stiffness. They also tracked how absorbed energy split between stored elastic energy and energy lost to damage.

Strength and stiffness rose in a logarithmic pattern as loading sped up. The strain at failure fell. All samples failed by splitting into columns. Faster loading shattered them more fully. Force-controlled loading did more damage than displacement-controlled loading. The stored-energy share also grew with rate. The authors offer these links as a reference for support design in deep, soft rock work.
plos-pone-0349827:
Wen-Chao Zhang and colleagues mined intensive care records in 2026 for patterns in a type of white blood cell after heart attack. Earlier studies disagreed on whether eosinophil counts predict death or kidney injury in these patients.

About fifteen hundred critically ill heart attack patients were grouped by how their counts moved over time: steady low, slowly rising, or quickly rising from a middle start. The rising groups fared better than the steady low group on survival. Kidney injury partly carried the link to death. Watching the trend, not a single count, may sharpen risk judgments after a heart attack.
plos-pone-0350027:
James I Mullet, Amy Pruden, and co-authors went hunting through public genome databases for a curious kind of mobile DNA that lives a double life. These phage-plasmids can persist quietly like plasmids inside bacteria, yet also behave like viruses that infect bacteria. Little was known about where they occur or what jobs their genes do. Their 2026 search used a machine learning classifier to spot them among virus and plasmid sequences.

The search recovered more than five thousand unique elements from a striking range of settings, from human and animal hosts to soil, rivers, wastewater, and seawater. Elements from host-associated settings carried the most defense and antibiotic resistance genes, while those from open waters leaned toward making chemical compounds. Some traits, including systems that block viral defenses, appeared more often in these hybrids than in plain plasmids or viruses.
plos-pone-0350127:
Jiguang Yu and Louis Shuo Wang rebuilt the classic predator-prey model from first principles to fix a mathematical shortcut that misrepresents chance in ecology. Modelers usually sprinkle randomness onto population equations as independent noise for each species. Their 2026 derivation starts instead from the actual random events of birth, death, and predation, and proves what the true noise structure must be.

Events that couple predator and prey, like a kill that feeds a predator, force the two species' fluctuations to move against each other, something the standard shortcut cannot express. The authors also separate two modeling worlds that are often confused: one conditioned on survival, another allowing extinction. They supply a rigorous proof framework so future models can keep noise honest and boundaries sound.
plos-pone-0350727:
A J A Al-Gburi designed a very small dual band antenna for 5G phones in 2026 and checked its safety against the head. Phones at these high frequencies pack antennas near the ear, so radiation absorbed by tissue must stay well under legal limits.

The antenna works at the two main high bands planned for handsets. Three realistic head models, a full head, a skull, and a brain alone, were used to measure absorbed radiation in simulation, and a built prototype matched the simulated behaviour closely. Absorption stayed well below international limits in all three. Compact and compliant designs clear a key hurdle for high band phones.
plos-pone-0350827:
Angelo Maria Sabatini revisited a famous experiment in 2026: the mathematician Markov counting vowels and consonants in Pushkin's verse novel Eugene Onegin. Sabatini applied modern time series tools to the poem and to an Italian translation.

Letters were coded simply as vowel or consonant, and a compact chain model reproduced the poem's patterns of memory and repetition well. The Russian text lost memory gradually as it unfolded, while the translation stayed more even. Short letter patterns also tracked shifts in the story. The study shows how much structure a very simple code can reveal in a literary classic.
plos-pone-0351127:
Zhang and Chen, in a 2026 study, chart a whooping cough outbreak among children in Chengdu, China, across one year from May 2024. Whooping cough has resurged in many places despite vaccines. The team reviewed genetic test results for about nineteen thousand children at a large children's hospital, looking at season, age, sex, and where care was given.

About one in five tests came back positive. Summer dominated, with the peak month, June 2024, alone producing more than a thousand cases. School-aged children, roughly six to eleven, made up the largest share of cases and tested positive most often. Sex made no clear difference. Outpatients tested positive more than inpatients, especially in spring and summer, which may reflect who gets tested in each setting. The authors aim their findings at regional prevention, with school-age children and the summer surge as the clear targets.
plos-pone-0351327:
Jingting Zeng, Tianchi Qiu, and Linmin Shan analyse how today's readers receive a famous translation of a Chinese classic. Their 2026 study concerns Arthur Waley's 1942 Monkey, his shortened English Journey to the West. Nearly eight hundred reviews from Amazon and Goodreads were gathered. Topic modelling grouped what readers talked about. A sentiment classifier scored their feelings. A large language model helped validate the qualitative reading of themes.

The verdict leans warm. About forty-three percent of reviews were positive, against eighteen percent negative. Readers loved Waley's chatty prose. They adored Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, as a trickster hero. The book's philosophy and humour crossed cultures well. Complaints clustered elsewhere: story structures that clash with Western expectations, too little guidance on cultural background, and a poorly received British-accented audiobook. An eighty-year-old abridgement, it turns out, still wins readers, provided nobody promises them the whole epic.
plos-pone-0351627:
Irene Vianini and a large team tracked how world media covered Russia and Ukraine across more than a decade. They gathered over twenty-two million article titles from thousands of sources in nearly two hundred countries and many languages. Human reviewers worked with automated clustering to group the titles and follow story lines over time.

Coverage spiked around the Euromaidan protests, the seizure of Crimea, and the full-scale invasion of twenty twenty-two. Recurring themes included tension between Russia and the West, energy security, and false-information campaigns. Early clusters centered on gas disputes and protests, while later ones centered on the invasion and its worldwide effects. Attention kept returning to the same leaders and institutions. The dataset gives researchers a map of how a conflict's story was told globally.
plos-pone-0351727:
Yandong Song and colleagues engineered a vision model, MCCA-YOLO, to spot rice leaf diseases early, when the marks are faint and farmers' routine spraying either wastes pesticide or arrives too late. Rice feeds more than half the world, so small accuracy gains scale enormously. Their design gives the detector two feature-extracting backbones, a module that sharpens leaf texture in the frequency domain, and a feedback loop that checks its own work across scales.

The architecture targets exactly the failure mode of field photos: tiny, low-contrast lesions on cluttered leaves. Cross-scale fusion lets a pinhead spot borrow context from the whole leaf before the model commits. For extension services and drone scouts, a detector tuned for the earliest, faintest stage is the difference between spot treatment and blanket spraying, with the chemical savings and yield protection that follow.
plos-pone-0351927:
Dennis Acheampong, Kwaku Adomako, and Bismark Kyei raised three hundred broiler chickens under Ghana's humid tropical heat. Three commercial breeds took part: Hubbard, Cobb 500, and Ross 308. All birds ate the same feed and lived under the same care for six weeks. The team weighed growth, meat yield, health, and cost. A growth curve model added a second view of the same birds.

By the final weighing, the breeds were statistically tied. Weight, feed use, and cost per kilo of gain all matched. The curve model gave Cobb 500 the fastest growth path. Ross 308 died least and grew the largest gut organs, signs of toughness in heat. With headline results tied, breed choice turns on survival and local fit.
plos-pone-0352327:
Julie Agel and three colleagues borrow a chart from oncology to display young athletes' sporting lives. Their 2026 methods paper concerns sports specialisation: children dropping other sports to train year-round in one. Specialisation is suspected of raising injury risk. The data behind that debate are usually squeezed into tables that hide timing. Swimmer plots give each athlete one bar, marked with events along a timeline. The team built a dataset from recall survey patterns to demonstrate.

Two clocks were compared. One plot runs on chronological age, the other on years of participation. Each exposes different structure in the same sporting histories. Injuries appear as markers against the single-sport and multi-sport years that preceded them. Standardising a dataset matters as much as the picture. With shared variables and a visual language everyone reads at a glance, studies from different clinics could finally be compared without translation losses.
plos-pone-0352427:
Paolo Boldi and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One mathematics paper about distance-count matrices, tables recording how many nodes in a network sit at each distance from a given node. Such tables underpin measures of how central a node is, and researchers sometimes need to know whether a made-up table could come from a real network when hunting for counterexamples.

The authors prove that deciding this question is strongly NP-complete, meaning no efficient general method is likely to exist. On the brighter side, they show that many common ways of combining networks preserve the ability to compute the combined table directly from the parts. The result closes one door for counterexample hunters while opening a compositional route for structured networks.
plos-pone-0353127:
Noriko Yoshida and seven co-authors describe this 2026 PLOS One protocol for the SACLA trial. The trial is a phase II study of surgery for bleeding under the center of the retina. Such bleeding can blind patients with macular degeneration. Twenty patients will have a vitrectomy, then an injection of a clot-dissolving drug under the retina. The trial runs partly in decentralized form. Later check-ups can happen at partner sites, to spare patients travel.

As a protocol, the paper sets out the design, not results. The main measure is change in the thickness of the retina's center, one week after surgery. Vision and safety will be tracked for twelve weeks. No drug is yet approved for this use. The authors aim for the first prospective proof on whether this approach is feasible and safe.
plos-pone-0353227:
Readers should treat this entry with caution: it is a formal Expression of Concern issued by the PLOS One editors in 2026 about an earlier review article. The review in question surveyed machine and deep learning methods for classifying white blood cells from blood smear images. After publication, the editors found serious citation problems in it.

Several works the review cited had themselves been retracted, some before the review even appeared, and other citations did not support the statements attached to them or were missing entirely. The authors replied that some citations were meant only as background on model designs, but the editors state the matter is not fully resolved. The notice corrects the missing citation locations and advises interpreting the review's conclusions carefully.
plos-pone-0353527:
Ahmed and colleagues trialed a rapid on-farm culture kit for udder infection in dairy cows in a 2026 study. Usual care gives antibiotics at once, a habit that fuels drug resistance. Sixteen commercial farms assigned sick cows either to instant treatment or to treatment guided by a three-plate culture read after one day.

Culture guidance removed antibiotics entirely for nearly half the guided cases, where no growth or a certain germ class appeared. Cure rates were then compared between groups. Cutting needless doses while holding cures steady would help farms, milk safety, and resistance control at once, which is why farm-side testing draws wide interest.
plos-pone-0353827:
Maialen Zabalza-Zudaire and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for VOICE-DEP, a Spanish hospital study testing whether the voice can betray depression. Diagnosis and follow-up for major depression rest on interviews and rating scales, yet speech may carry measurable signs of severity. Past voice studies were mostly one-off snapshots, rarely in non-English speakers. This protocol sets out a standardized, repeatable way to record and analyze speech during ordinary medical interviews.

The study will follow twenty-five adults with moderate or severe depression monthly for four months, alongside fifty healthy controls recorded once. Each visit pairs the recording with the standard clinician rating scale, so voice features can be checked against accepted severity measures over time. The authors aim to learn whether speech markers move in step with recovery or relapse. If they do, voice could become a cheap, remote support for depression monitoring.
plos-pone-0354027:
Brennan-Tovey and colleagues, in a 2026 study, evaluate a peer support service for breastfeeding in Newcastle upon Tyne, in North East England. Health guidance says babies should be fed only breast milk for the first six months, yet many mothers in the United Kingdom stop within weeks. Trained volunteers who have breastfed themselves offer advice and encouragement through the service.

The team interviewed twenty-two people: mothers who used the service, plus the staff, volunteers, and health workers around it. Four themes came out, covering how the service works, the support it gives, what it achieves, and where it struggles. Mothers said the emotional support raised their confidence, and making breastfeeding seem normal mattered a great deal. Reaching mothers under twenty-five and those who speak English as a second language remained hard. The findings will guide how the service grows.
plos-pone-0354127:
An and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, teach a neural network to read the texture of asphalt roads from photographs. How rough a road surface is decides how well tires grip, and the classic field test, spreading sand and measuring the patch, is slow. Their method first builds a three-dimensional model of a pavement, then works backward to produce exact black-and-white teaching images.

A U-Net model, a design good at separating regions in images, learned to split road photos into stone and void. Its sorting quality was solid on held-out images. Texture depth computed from its output tracked the sand test closely, and a shape measure called fractal dimension tracked it too. Both links were statistically firm. The authors offer the pipeline as fast technical support for judging skid resistance from a camera instead of a sandbag.
plos-pone-0354427:
Jiarong Wang, Roxana Dev Omar Dev, and Nurhidayah Yaakop published a 2026 survey study in PLOS ONE on the mental side of stand-up paddleboarding, a balance-demanding sport. Just over one hundred seventy athletes completed three surveys covering mindfulness, coping skills such as focus under pressure, and mental toughness. They examined how the three qualities hang together, and whether coping sits between mindfulness and performance.

Athletes scored moderate to high on everything, with no meaningful gender differences Mindfulness tracked with coping skills, and both with stronger mental performance. Coping skills showed the tightest link to performance expression of all. The mediation test supported an indirect path: mindful athletes seemed to perform mentally better largely because they regulated themselves better. As a one-time survey, the authors stress these are associations, not proof of cause, but coaches get a hint that mindfulness work may pay off through coping skills.
plos-pone-0354527:
Qiu Haifei and colleagues tackled a narrow but costly problem in textile mills. The heald frame is a loom part that lifts warp threads thousands of times a minute. Their 2026 engineering study built a replacement frame as a layered sandwich. It combined carbon fiber, epoxy resin, honeycomb, and wood cores. Computer models then tuned how the carbon layers are angled and stacked.

The tuned design raised the frame's natural vibration frequencies well above the steel frame it replaces. Bench tests then confirmed less vibration, less noise, and less wear on the loom's cams. Energy use fell too. For loom builders, the work offers a tested recipe for frames that let modern machines run faster without shaking themselves apart.
plos-pone-0354727:
Jinzhi Bai, Hanlin Xia, and Lin Zhang examine an underappreciated channel through which China's central bank policy reaches the real economy, in this 2026 economics paper. Local governments there borrow heavily by issuing bonds, so their borrowing costs shape local spending and, in turn, national output. The authors first present empirical evidence that this bond channel exists, then build a multi-region economic model with layered governments to measure its strength.

In the model, monetary stimulus worked more than twice as powerfully when local governments could borrow at the risk-free rate, compared with the baseline. Spillovers between regions complicated the picture: average responses shrank, but areas facing certain bond rates responded especially strongly, and competition among local governments blunted transmission overall. The authors say the channel creates distinctly geographic effects of national policy.
plos-pone-0354827:
Kazuhiro Hayashi led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of personality and chronic low back pain in Japan. Just over a hundred clinic outpatients completed a standard personality inventory alongside scales for pain, mood, sleep, self-confidence, and quality of life. The authors traced how a neurotic tendency score flowed through these measures.

Neurotic tendency did connect with worse scores across the pain-related measures, but its effect was small next to pain intensity itself. A small share of patients also scored as prone to giving biased answers. Hayashi's takeaway is measured: personality shades how back pain feels, without driving it.
plos-pone-0354927:
Hai-jie Li and co-authors ran a three-factor greenhouse experiment to tune water and fertiliser for spring tomatoes. Greenhouse production often wastes water and nitrogen, threatening both profits and the environment. Their 2026 trial crossed two irrigation floors with two manure rates and three nitrogen top-dressing levels, including cuts of a fifth and two-fifths below convention.

The team measured leaf photosynthesis, yield, fruit quality, and how efficiently water and nitrogen were used. Combined statistical and component analyses sorted the treatment effects. The goal was a recipe that holds yield and quality while spending less water and synthetic nitrogen. Li and colleagues frame the design as a template for sustainable greenhouse practice beyond tomatoes.
plos-pone-0355727:
Wanlong Huang and co-authors analysed why drill pipe joints fail and how a redesigned joint could last longer. These threaded connections must seal and bear load deep underground, where conditions are harsh. Their 2026 study modelled single-shoulder and double-shoulder joints in three dimensions and checked the models against tests.

The double-shoulder design carried clearly lower stress than the single-shoulder one and sealed better. The team then proposed an extended thread joint that spreads stress more evenly along the thread. Contact pressure on the shoulder also spread more sensibly in the new design. Huang and colleagues present the redesign as a route to fewer joint failures during difficult drilling work.
plos-pone-0355827:
Valerie Kilders and co-authors mapped foreign farmland purchases against United States military interest points. Public and lawmaker concern about adversary-linked land near bases has surged since 2020. Their 2026 study combined social media listening with farm transaction records spanning nearly three decades.

Discussion volume spiked alongside a wave of state laws after 2022. In the records, China-linked deals, excluding one famous meat company purchase, landed in military-interest counties far more often than other foreign deals. Statistical models with state and year controls still found a small positive link. At the same time, most foreign transactions showed no such pattern. Kilders and colleagues separate measurable geography from the louder public debate.
plos-pone-0356727:
Saeed Pirmoradi and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on grading prostate cancer risk from gene activity instead of relying only on biopsy Gleason scores. Biopsy is invasive and can cause pain, infection, or worse. Their framework feeds patients' gene expression profiles and a network of gene interactions into a dual-branch graph neural network, sorting patients into low, medium, and high risk. An explanation method then shows which genes drove each call.

Distinct gene sets marked each risk tier, underlining the disease's different molecular faces. On a held-out test set, the model separated tiers well, most strongly for high risk, with accuracy around four in five patients. Pairing network-aware learning with explanations, they argue, makes predictions sharper and auditable. The main limit is plain: everything rests on one public cancer atlas, so outside cohorts must confirm the signature.
plos-pone-0357027:
Ahmed H Mohammed and seven colleagues tried to make gypsum, a cheap but weak and water-shy building binder, tougher by feeding it waste. Their 2026 study mixed nine recipes combining reactive silica, sodium silicate solution, and ground orange peel powder, then tested strength, water absorption, setting time, and internal structure under the microscope.

One blend stood clearly ahead: a tenth reactive silica, a fifth sodium silicate, and a small dose of orange peel. It reached the highest crushing and bending strengths with low water uptake, and the peel usefully slowed setting so the mix could densify. Microscopy confirmed tighter, less porous interiors. Construction gains twice here: better plaster from peels and industrial leftovers that might otherwise be dumped.
plos-pone-0357127:
Readers should treat the entry here as a formal retraction notice from the editors of PLOS One, issued in 2026. It withdraws a paper on an enhanced algorithm for balancing a circular assembly line with splittable tasks. The editors found that the work leaned too heavily on material from a technology competition run by Huawei, without clear citation or explanation of the link.

Figures, equations, a results table, and parts of the code in the paper closely matched a competition task description and another group's competition entry, the notice reports. The lead author acknowledged taking part in that competition and creating some of the shared figures. Because the overlap strikes at the work's originality, the journal removed the paper from the trusted record.
plos-pone-0357227:
Ahmad Reza Ahmadi and four colleagues test a plant compound as a shield for kidney cells against a chemotherapy drug, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cyclophosphamide cures cancers but damages kidneys at high doses. The team exposed human kidney cells in the dish to the drug, with and without protodioscin. That compound is a saponin from yam family plants, known for antioxidant effects. They measured survival signals, cell death machinery, stress proteins, and injury markers.

The compound protected the cells on several fronts at once. Death promoting signals fell, a protective protein rose, and fewer cells entered programmed death. The strained protein folding system inside the cells, a hallmark of this drug's damage, calmed down. Antioxidant defenses strengthened while injury markers eased. Cell culture protection is a long way from a patient remedy, but the multi pathway rescue makes protodioscin a candidate worth animal testing.
plos-pone-0358227:
Tang He and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE that brings natural language processing to a classic of Chinese philosophy, the Analects of Confucius. Because its many English translations differ in wording and in how they handle key concepts, He's team built a computer framework for comparing them. It lines up five English versions sentence by sentence and measures how closely they agree in meaning.

Their method cleans up concept terms and proper names first, then trains a shared sentence encoder with contrastive learning so matched sentences sit close together in the model. Tested on finding matching sentences across versions and on flagging pairs that disagree, the full model beat the alternatives they tried. Higher model scores also lined up with pairs that human judges had rated as highly consistent. They offer the tool as an aid for scholars comparing translations, not an automatic judge of quality.
plos-pone-0358327:
Tuan Anh Phan, Seohyun Nam, and Jason J Jung compare why scientists cite each other across fields, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A citation can set background, supply motivation, borrow a method, or extend a result, and fields may favor different intents. Their dataset is large: over seventeen thousand papers and more than two million citation contexts across twenty-one subject categories, each classified by intent and examined for distribution, age, and predictability.

The cultures diverge sharply. Philosophy, sociology, area studies, and history lean on background and motivation, and rarely use or extend what they cite. Artificial intelligence research inverts the pattern, dominating in uses and extensions while citing least for background. Citation ages agreed least across intents in area studies and history. Intent counts proved most predictable in biotechnology and plant science, least in the humanities and sociology. One literature, the authors show, is really twenty-one citation economies.
plos-pone-0358427:
Toshihisa Nakashima and colleagues published a 2026 drug safety analysis in PLOS ONE on tendon injuries linked to levofloxacin, a widely used antibiotic. Tendon damage is a known rare risk of this drug family, but patterns by sex, age, and how the drug is given were poorly mapped in Japan. The team mined two large spontaneous reporting databases, one American and one Japanese, covering five related antibiotics.

All five drugs showed warning signals in the American data, but only levofloxacin showed strong, consistent signals in both Japanese sources. The signal was much stronger in men, especially those aged seventy and older, and stronger for the oral form than for intravenous use. Most tendon events were reported within about two weeks of starting the drug. The authors urge Japanese clinicians to prescribe levofloxacin cautiously for older men and to watch early for tendon pain.
plos-pone-0358627:
The PLOS One Editors publish this notice in 2026 as an Expression of Concern about an earlier article on iron in wastewater irrigated soils and food crops near Sargodha. Readers are advised to interpret that article with caution. The notice centers on compliance with the journal's authorship policy, a matter that goes to who stands behind the work and its claims. Such notices are not retractions, but they are a warning attached to the record.

Alongside the warning, the editors correct a series of errors in the article's methods and results text. The corrections fix how soil and crop samples were described as collected, and restate the reported orderings and mean values for iron concentrations in water, soil, and crops across the study sites. The editors note these errors did not drive the decision to publish the notice. Anyone citing the Sargodha findings should read them through this caution.
plos-pone-0359327:
Luping Lin and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies hepatocellular carcinoma, the main type of liver cancer, in its immune-active form. Through integrated multi-omic analysis, several layers of molecular data at once, the authors characterize a continuum in the tumor's immune state.

One end of the continuum responds to interferon gamma, an immune signal; the other is myeloid-suppressive, dominated by cells that damp immunity down. Placing a tumor along this line could guide immunotherapy choices. Liver cancer researchers and oncologists are the readers for a map of how these tumors shift between immune states.
plos-pone-0359427: Wu and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on judging the quality of graduate training in mining engineering. Their method combines two tools: one maps how quality factors link to each other, the other weighs uncertain evidence in a network. Together they rate how well programs develop. Mining schools could use such ratings to find weak spots in training for a high-risk trade.
plos-pone-0359727:
Jiamin Zhang, Jiahui Zhang, Ning Lü, and Shuaiqi Chen wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on machine tools. It presents parametric finite element modeling for a machine tool with five axes, the computer-controlled cutters that shape metal parts along five directions of movement. The authors study its natural characteristics, how it vibrates on its own, as its pose changes.

A machine's vibration behavior shifts with its posture, and unwanted vibration ruins surface finish and accuracy. Parametric models let engineers test many poses quickly instead of rebuilding the model each time. Machine tool designers and precision manufacturers are the audience for pose-aware vibration knowledge.
plos-pone-0360527:
Suman Ranjitkar and colleagues followed mothers and children in 2026 to test whether a mother's selenium level during pregnancy relates to her child's mental health in early childhood. Selenium is a trace mineral needed in small amounts, and both too little and too much can disturb development. Their mother-child cohort measured the mineral in pregnancy and later assessed the children's mental health.

Cohort studies like this watch real life unfold rather than assigning treatments, and they can catch effects that only appear years after exposure. The findings speak to nutrition guidance in pregnancy, where advice must balance deficiency and excess carefully. They also add to the growing study of how a mother's body chemistry shapes a child's early mind.
pmc-1182327:
Ioannidis argues, in a widely cited essay, that most published research findings are likely to be false. Concern was already rising when he wrote in 2005. He explains that whether a claim is true depends on study size and power, on bias, and on how many teams chase the same question.

A key point is balance: when true effects are rare among the ideas tested, most positive reports will be wrong. The essay pushed journals, funders, and scientists to demand larger studies and repeat tests. It remains a sharp warning for anyone reading bold health or science headlines.
pmc-13195027:
Julia Abels is first author on a 2026 evaluation of three lab tests for detecting carbapenemase enzymes in gut bacteria. These enzymes break carbapenem antibiotics, last-line drugs, and infections with producing bacteria carry high death rates and costs. Quick, reliable detection guides treatment and infection control, but some tests give false positives in bacteria that overproduce a related enzyme.

Each variant was run on one hundred and ninety-nine isolates reflecting German hospital strains. The zinc-supplemented version performed best overall, catching every producer. A new cloxacillin-supplemented version was most accurate at ruling out non-producers, especially in the tricky related-enzyme group, though it missed a few more producers. Test choice, the authors imply, depends on the local problem.
pmc-13195627:
Carla Tamanini Ferrari Schock leads a 2026 study of body composition and quality of life in young patients treated for differentiated thyroid cancer. After total thyroid removal, patients rely on hormone replacement, which affects weight and body makeup. Fifty-one patients were assessed with body scans, questionnaires, and thyroid function tests.

Patients averaged thirty-five years old and reported quality of life scores slightly below the midpoint, alongside higher fat mass and fat percentage than expected. Greater fat measures correlated with worse self-rated general condition. Hormone levels and dose, age, and general condition predicted fat levels in the models. The authors urge multidisciplinary care that watches both body composition and quality of life during hormone therapy.
pmc-13202027:
Spotting which brain surgery patients will deteriorate could help nurses act early, and a 2026 retrospective study headed by Laiyu Xu builds three prediction models for that purpose. The research article uses records from 1,576 craniotomy patients treated at three large hospitals in Hunan Province, China, between 2018 and 2020.

The team compared logistic regression, a Bayes classifier, and a back propagation neural network, splitting patients into training and validation sets. All three models performed well, and the neural network ranked highest on the combined efficiency measure used by the authors. They recommend the neural network model as a reference tool for identifying high-risk patients on general wards.
pmc-13203027:
Influenza hides from the immune alarm by destroying its sensor, and a 2026 study headed by Ran Wei identifies the host accomplice. The research article shows how fibroblast growth factor 8 helps influenza A virus evade detection in human lung epithelial cells.

Infection raised FGF8 levels across several virus subtypes, and the factor boosted viral replication after entry by dampening interferon responses. Mechanistically, FGF8 acts as a scaffold that brings the enzyme TRIM16 to the viral sensor RIG-I, marking it for destruction at one specific lysine site. Silencing TRIM16 copied the effect of removing FGF8, so breaking this partnership is a candidate antiviral strategy.
pmc-13204627:
A sugar-tagging enzyme helps leukemia cells mature under a vitamin-based drug, and a 2026 study by Siming Zhang pins down its role. The research article studies GnT-IVa, an enzyme that branches N-glycans, during all-trans retinoic acid treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia cell models.

Enzyme levels and its branched glycan product rose sharply as NB4 and HL-60 cells differentiated under treatment. Deleting the enzyme's gene, but not its sibling gene, blocked differentiation and destabilized the surface marker CD11b that carries those branches. Public patient data showed low expression in this leukemia and better survival with higher expression in related cohorts, supporting differentiation therapy ideas.
pmc-13207927:
A seed-oil injection from traditional practice joins modern immunotherapy in a 2026 real-world analysis by Riwen Zhang for advanced lung cancer. The retrospective study reviews fifty-three patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer, lacking targetable mutations, who received Kanglaite injection alongside toripalimab and chemotherapy at one Guangdong hospital.

After four cycles, over half the patients' tumors had shrunk measurably, and disease was controlled in nearly all of them in the reported results. One-year survival figures looked encouraging, and blood levels of two tumor-related markers fell significantly with treatment. Side effects were mostly mild liver enzyme rises, though the lack of a comparison group tempers every conclusion.
pmc-13208427:
Frailty prediction tools built for the general public may misjudge people with HIV, and a 2026 protocol by Yeye Hu plans the first dedicated review of models for this group. The protocol describes a systematic review and possible meta-analysis of prognostic models that forecast frailty in people living with HIV.

Searches across major databases will feed dual independent screening, with data extracted under established prediction-model checklists. Reviewers will judge each model's bias risk and real-world applicability with a standard appraisal tool before pooling performance where justified. The protocol is registered, screening has already found five eligible studies, and analysis is scheduled for 2026.
pmc-13213127:
Timothy O. Ogunbode and colleagues test in 2026 whether well water in rural Osun State, Nigeria, meets the world goal for clean water. They took samples in 32 towns and checked them for salts, acids, and germs.

Most chemical checks passed state and world health norms, so the water showed little chemical harm. Germ checks told a worse tale. Stool germs turned up in 14 towns, and some wells scored as very poor or not fit to drink. The worst spots sat in two local areas. The team blames poor toilets and hygiene, not chemicals. They urge routine germ tests and town-led care of water points.
pmc-13215327:
Qifang Liu and colleagues review in 2026 how the Epstein-Barr virus teaches a throat cancer to hide from the immune system. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma grows in an immune-rich setting yet stays oddly tolerant, which helps explain its weak response to immunotherapy.

Viral proteins switch on two signalling routes that flood the tumour with cytokines, re-educate immune cells, and raise several checkpoint brakes at once. T cells falter, suppressive myeloid cells gather, and other cells are shut out by stromal barriers. Blocking only the famous PD-1 brake therefore disappoints. The authors survey strategies that strike viral signalling and host immunity together, aiming to reopen the tumour to immune attack.
pmc-13215427:
Daniel Madden led this 2026 animal study on African swine fever, a deadly virus disease of pigs. The team asked whether a pig protein called CD1d helps the virus enter cells, since blocking its gene in cell cultures had cut virus growth.

The researchers used gene editing to breed pigs that lack CD1d, then infected them with a strong type II strain of the virus. The edited pigs became just as sick as normal pigs, with no real difference in deaths, virus levels in blood and tissues, or organ damage. The work shows that CD1d is not required for this virus strain to cause severe disease in live pigs.
pmc-13216427:
Yamei Li and co-authors present a 2026 biomarker study of a blood protein called sTIM-3 as a window on kidney scarring. This scarring of tubules and supporting tissue drives long-term outcomes, but today it can only be graded by biopsy.

The study enrolled 256 transplant recipients with graft biopsies, 442 patients with native kidney disease, and 44 recipients followed over time. Blood sTIM-3 levels rose as kidney function worsened and climbed steadily with the severity of scarring on biopsy. In transplant patients, high levels predicted graft failure and rapid function decline, and the second prediction survived adjustment for standard measures. The authors propose sTIM-3 as a repeatable, non-invasive complement to functional tests.
pmc-13217227:
Kaplina and colleagues run a prospective study on feeding and growth in newborns with heart defects. Babies with congenital heart defects often need surgery in their first weeks. Most arrive at term with normal weight, yet many slide into malnutrition soon after, and poor nutrition raises the risks of heart surgery.

The team tracks how the makeup of breast milk relates to each baby's nutritional state over those first weeks. Fat, protein, and energy content can vary between mothers, and fragile hearts leave little margin for shortfalls. The aim is practical: spot which babies need feeding support early, before surgery, rather than after growth has already faltered.
pmc-13218527:
Ngo Cao Nghia, Phan Khanh Duy, and Bao Quoc Truong-Dinh study how hotel employees turn guests into brand promoters, in a 2026 cross-national paper. Brand evangelists do more than stay loyal: they persuade others, giving hotels free, credible promotion. The study asks whether guests spread the word for the brand's symbolic image or because they trust the relationship, and whether the answer changes across cultures.

A survey of 428 guests in Vietnam and Thailand fed a model testing how staff digital competence, proactive help, and relationship-building feed evangelism through image and trust. Both routes operated, with weights differing by country: image cues dominated in Vietnam, while relational trust won in Thailand. Loyalty programs strengthened the trust route in Thailand, and visit frequency shaped the image route in each setting. The authors offer the framework as guidance for strategies that adapt to culture rather than assuming a single mindset.
pmc-13218827:
Shun Tanaka and colleagues pilot a computer-controlled anesthetic injector for brain angiography through the wrist in a 2026 study. Cerebral angiography via the radial artery needs an anesthetic injection at the wrist, and delivery steadiness affects pain and vessel spasm. A computer-controlled device promises a smoother, reproducible injection than a syringe.

Ten adults having angiography received one milliliter of three percent mepivacaine through a needle driven by the device. Every procedure was completed with the device: no malfunction, no switch to manual injection, and first-attempt puncture succeeded in all ten patients. Pain scores stayed low, with a median of eighteen on a hundred-point scale after the anesthetic and lower still after puncture and sheath placement. Blood pressure barely moved across the procedure, and no patient developed vessel spasm or bleeding at the access site. The authors call the approach feasible and safe in this first series.
pmc-13220627:
Russell D. C. Bicknell and colleagues describe an arthropod from the late Cambrian of Quebec in a 2026 paper. The animal belongs to Corcoraniidae, a family of arthropods sitting near the base of the chelicerates, the lineage to spiders and horseshoe crabs. The family's diversity and spread are unresolved, and the late Cambrian, the Furongian, is a gap in the soft-bodied record.

The preserved specimen from the Rivière-du-Loup Formation earned a new genus and species, Magnicornaspis garwoodi. Its anatomy widens the family's range and suggests the head spines that mark the group shifted position as the lineage evolved. Finding a corcoraniid in this formation matters beyond one species: it hints that the Furongian diversity crash may be a sampling artifact rather than an extinction driven by low oxygen. The authors argue the deposit is a conservation Lagerstätte, a site of preservation, and deserves renewed excavation.
pmc-13221127:
Orson Mestanza and colleagues describe the genetics of Peru's large 2023 dengue outbreak in a 2026 report. Dengue had long been treated as a neglected disease, yet case counts surged across tropical Latin America. Peru's national health institute sequenced 245 positive samples to trace which virus types were circulating.

Three serotypes appeared, each with distinct lineages. Types 1 and 2 showed multiple introductions, rapid diversification, and wide spread across the country. Type 3 arrived in Lima in a more localized way, with links to the Caribbean. The authors call the dataset Peru's fullest genomic picture of dengue for that year, and they urge continued surveillance to guide control decisions.

pmc-13234727:

pmc-13237427:

pmc-13239027:

pmc-13239227:

pmc-13239527:

pmc-13239627:

pmc-13239827:

pmc-13241327:

pmc-13252727:

pmc-13253927:

pmc-13254427:

pmc-13255327:

pmc-13256827:

pmc-13256927:

pmc-13257027:

pmc-13257727:
Yi Chen and co-authors compare two ways to make a weak rock usable as highway fill in southern China. Argillaceous siltstone crumbles in water, so engineers mix in lime or cement to stabilize it. Their 2026 tests draw on a real expressway rebuilding project.

The authors recommend cement for heavy-duty roadbeds and caution against low lime doses.
pmc-13258127:

pmc-13258527:

pmc-13259127:
Haru Kaneko and Sozo Inoue cut false health alerts in care homes with a contrastive learning method in a 2026 paper. Daily care records plus weather data feed a model that warns of next day deterioration in older residents. Rare events make ordinary models cry wolf, which exhausts staff.

Their training loss pulls truly worsening cases together while pushing false alarms away from them. Separation is shaped directly among cases the model flags as risky. pmc-13259527:

pmc-13260027:

Early feeding meant starting tube or gut feeding within forty-eight hours, while delayed feeding followed the older practice of resting the bowel.

pmc-13260127:
Ezgi Erbasan and co-authors present a 2026 gene therapy study in diabetic rats, testing whether a hormone called GLP-1 can regrow insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. pmc-13261027:

The outcome was long-term cancer control with no subsequent hemorrhages. pmc-13261327:

pmc-13261927:

Educational meetings shaped the decision to implement by building knowledge and beliefs. Ongoing training built intention and skills through engaged practice over time. pmc-13262227:

Validation, they stress, stands between the finding and any clinical use.
pmc-13262427:
Kieffer Korvin and colleagues test large language models, AI tools that read text, for trial recruitment in a 2026 journal article. pmc-13262627:
Yi Xi and co-authors model carbon released from thawing frozen ground in a 2026 journal article. pmc-13263227:

pmc-13263327:

pmc-13263727:

pmc-13263927:

pmc-13264027:

pmc-13264127:

pmc-13264227:

pmc-13264327:

pmc-13264427:

pmc-13264627:

pmc-13264727:

pmc-13264927:

pmc-13265227:

pmc-13266227:

pmc-13267927:

pmc-13268127:

pmc-13269027:

pmc-13269427:

pmc-13270027:

pmc-13272527:

pmc-13272727:

pmc-13274127:

pmc-13275527:

pmc-13278427:

The pattern suggests a complex cause, and a finer scale may be needed, the authors say.
pmc-13278927:
Yanhua Cui and colleagues compare bio-organic fertilisers for fresh-eating corn on dry, salty Xinjiang soils in a 2026 field study. The region's drought, salt build-up, and poor soil cap the crop's yield and quality. The main local variety, Wannuo 2000, had no clear fertiliser recommendation.

Trials ran across two seasons, 2024 and 2025, with weather records kept alongside growth measures. A spell of low sunlight in late June 2024 unsettled growth and year-to-year stability. Fertiliser types steered ear development, dry matter build-up, and yield in distinct ways. One product, Tianwu Jintaiyang, scored best overall for yield and adaptability. Ear grain weight drove yield most, while bald ear tips and barren stalks limited it.
pmc-13279027:
Jun Yu and colleagues report a 2026 study of pancreatic cancer, a fast and deadly cancer of the pancreas gland. They look at a gene switch called SOX17 and ask if its level links to patient outcome after surgery to remove the tumour. They also ask how it links to immune cells inside the tumour.

Data from cell and bulk gene reads showed high SOX17 went with longer life after surgery. High levels also went with more CD8 T cells, a type of immune cell that kills sick cells. High levels went with fewer scar like support cells tied to poor outcome. The authors name SOX17 a helpful sign for outcome and a clue for new care paths.
pmc-13279327:
Juliana Helena Castro e Silva and colleagues published a 2026 study testing whether a GPR17-activating drug can rescue myelin-producing cells stalled by inflammation. In diseases such as multiple sclerosis, chronic inflammation blocks oligodendrocytes, the cells that wrap nerve fibers in myelin, from maturing. GPR17 normally rises briefly as these cells develop and then falls; under inflammation it stays switched on. The team grew oligodendrocyte cultures, exposed them to an inflammatory cocktail, and applied the activator galinex.

The exposure stunted cell shape development and lowered myelin-related markers without killing cells, while GPR17 levels climbed. Gene profiling showed wide changes in protein production, energy metabolism, and stress pathways that overlapped with signatures from inflamed mouse and human brains. Galinex partly restored features of mature cells, including performance in a synthetic fiber myelination test. The findings support GPR17 as a checkpoint worth targeting when inflammation blocks myelin repair.
pmc-13279627:
Liwen Wang and colleagues published a 2026 review of how electroacupuncture might act on long COVID through the vagus nerve's anti-inflammatory pathway. Long COVID mixes persistent inflammation, autonomic disturbance, and metabolic trouble across many organs. The cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway is a reflex in which vagus signals, acting through a nicotinic receptor, restrain immune activation. The review also follows energy-sensing pathways involving AMPK, SIRT1, and PGC-1α, which govern cell energy health.

Animal and laboratory studies indicate electroacupuncture can engage that vagal circuit and quiet inflammatory signals, while also nudging the energy pathways. Human evidence is more indirect: changes in autonomic measures, immune markers, and symptom burden. The authors sort claims by evidence level to keep direct findings separate from hypothesis-generating links. Their conclusion is measured: it is a plausible candidate for long COVID. Trials focused on patient phenotypes, with mechanistic readouts, are the way to test it.
pmc-13280627:
Santosh Chokkakula and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on viruses that are used to attack cancer. These viruses infect tumor cells and kill them, and they also wake up the immune system. The review looks past the two virus types used most often so far. It asks what newer virus types can do.

Inside, the authors explain how the viruses pick out cancer cells and spread through a tumor. They cover the first drug of this kind, which was approved for skin cancer that had spread. They also weigh weak points, such as getting the virus to the tumor before the body clears it. The review maps where the field may go next.
pmc-13281327:
Mostafa Bagherinasab and colleagues ran a small pilot trial on blood flow during heart bypass in a 2026 study. Thirty patients set for bypass graft surgery joined. All were picked because their time on the machine was likely to be long. Half got standard flow. Half got a higher flow rate plus a pulsing flow, meant to mimic a heartbeat. The team tracked waste levels in the blood, kidney markers, drug needs, and time in care.

The high-flow group showed lower levels of lactate, a waste that builds when organs lack oxygen. That gap held across the whole check period. Kidney markers ran lower too, and stays in intensive care and hospital ran shorter. Those last gaps were too small to rule out chance. The authors say the mix may guard organs during bypass. A larger trial is needed to be sure.
pmc-13281727:
Ilyas Abdullahi Khalif and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter on war, displacement, and disease in the Middle East. Wars across the region have uprooted millions into camps and informal sites. Such sites often fall far short on clean water, toilets, and shelter. The authors argue that these conditions are a recipe for outbreaks. People displaced inside their own country may fare worst, since they stay near fighting with little aid.

Studies from Gaza show lung infections in close to half of displaced people surveyed. Gut diseases struck about a quarter. Cholera, measles, and polio risks climb where shots, water systems, and disease tracking break down. Crowding speeds lung disease, and dirty water speeds gut disease. The authors urge health safeguards built into any aid response. They frame outbreak control as part of wider health security.
pmc-13282127:
Sudhanvan Iyer and co-authors report a 2026 case of a rare birth variant of the gallbladder, the small organ under the liver that stores bile. In a septated gallbladder, one or more walls of tissue divide the inside into separate chambers. Such walls can be missed or mistaken for other disease on scans. The patient was a sixty-four-year-old woman with pain in the upper right belly that spread to her right shoulder blade.

Her pain had come and gone for ten years and worsened over the past two months. Review of her earlier scans revealed the divided gallbladder. Surgeons removed it through small cuts, a method called laparoscopic surgery, and confirmed the internal walls during the operation. Her symptoms then cleared fully. The authors urge doctors and scan readers to know this variant, so symptomatic patients are not misdiagnosed and can get timely surgery.
pmc-13282427:
Niki A Konstantinides and co-authors report a 2026 study on concussion history, tinnitus, and mental health in former professional American football players. Tinnitus is ringing in the ears, a common after-effect of brain injury. The team surveyed one thousand eighty-five former players, with a mean age near fifty-eight, who had played professionally after 1960. Questionnaires covered football exposure, hearing problems, thinking, depression, and anxiety.

Players with the heaviest history of concussion signs and symptoms had nearly triple the odds of tinnitus against those with the lightest history. Tinnitus did not explain the link between concussion history and mental health scores. Still, links with perceived thinking, depression, and anxiety were stronger among players who reported tinnitus. The authors advise clinicians to ask about tinnitus when assessing long-term brain and mental health after repeated head injury.
pmc-13282927:
Goud Priyanka led a 2026 study in northern India testing a simple bedside score for sick newborns. The Modified Sick Neonatal Score uses easy checks that need no lab tests, which suits units with few resources. The team asked how well the score, taken at admission, foretold death and illness severity in a newborn intensive care unit.

Over 18 months, 190 babies aged up to 28 days were scored and followed. Babies who died had far lower scores on average than those who went home. A cut-off below ten caught most deaths while ruling out death well for higher scores. Babies who needed breathing help or blood pressure drugs also scored lower. The authors call the score a practical early warning tool.
pmc-13283327:
Live, open peer review entered a journal's workflow in a five-paper pilot Christopher I Petkov and partners describe for 2026. Peer review shapes what science gets shared and trusted. New models aim to make review more open, fast, and rewarding for reviewers.

Five draft papers went through live review sessions run by PREreview. Each session lasted 90 minutes online with a structured shared document. Authors could watch or answer questions during the live talks. Volunteers turned notes into a final review within about two weeks. Reviews were posted openly with credit and a license for reuse. One journal then used the reviews in its own decision workflow.
pmc-13283427:
Olukayode Adebola Ibitoye and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how drug resistance in bacteria is tracked in water settings. Resistant germs and their genes gather in rivers, ponds, and waste water, yet standard checks capture only part of that hidden pool. Their review weighs newer tools that pair gene sequencing with computer learning.

Methods covered include reading all genes in a sample, tracking gene activity, and sorting which germs carry which resistance genes and moving elements. Learning models help predict resistance, classify genes, and trace sources, while local data on the water setting aids reading of results. The authors call for shared, scalable pipelines so monitoring can guide risk checks and control steps.
pmc-13284427:
Jayaj Adhikari and colleagues present a 2026 case report where polycythemia made a plain head CT look like a contrast scan. Polycythemia raises red blood cell mass, so vessels can appear dense on a noncontrast scan. That dense look can mimic a contrast study or a venous sinus clot, which is also a known complication of the condition.

The patient was a 23-year-old man brought in with gasping and reduced consciousness after use of over-the-counter cough syrups. The report stresses that a dense vessel sign above a threshold value needs further imaging to sort out the cause. Spotting this mimic can prevent wrong calls and guide the right follow-up scans.
pmc-13284627:
Robin Deterding and colleagues reported longer-term safety data in 2026 for nintedanib in children and teenagers with scarring lung diseases. Fibrosing interstitial lung diseases stiffen children's lungs, and nintedanib slows scarring in adults. An earlier trial found the drug's safety acceptable in patients aged six to seventeen. This open-label extension followed those who finished the first trial, plus new patients, all taking the drug openly.

Forty-eight patients received nintedanib, with median exposure of about sixty-one weeks at the data snapshot. Diarrhoea was the most common side effect. Seven patients stopped the drug, each for a different reason, from weight loss to moving house. Lung capacity at one year changed little on average, down about one percent of predicted value in those measured, and resting oxygen saturation held steady.
pmc-13284827:
Zeinab Maloum, Soheila Rabiepoor, and Samira Barjasteh report a 2026 randomized trial of psychosexual counseling after hysterectomy. Surgery can leave lasting mental and sexual strain beyond physical healing. One hundred married women aged 18 to 49 were split evenly between four weekly group sessions based on the Schover model and routine post-surgery care.

One month after the program, the counseling group scored higher on sexual self-concept and lower on sexual distress than controls, after baseline adjustment in the authors analysis. Both gaps were large and clear in statistical terms. The authors suggest adding structured counseling to routine care could support sexual recovery after hysterectomy for benign conditions.
pmc-13285027:
Xinying Li and co-authors examine how young spring wheat plants adjust their roots when water is scarce, in a paper published in 2026. Roots decide how much water a crop can reach, yet earlier work often studied single root traits alone. The team wanted to know how deep root growth and inner root tissue work together.

Seedlings from 28 wheat types grew on a paper-based platform where a chemical simulated drought. Plants were sorted into five tolerance groups, and three tolerant cultivars were named alongside one sensitive one. Tolerant plants sent roots deeper while adjusting the share of outer tissue. The authors caution that laboratory drought differs from field conditions, so later testing is still needed.
pmc-13285327:
José A Rosario Gonzalez and co-authors describe an unusual nerve pattern found in the chest muscles, reported in 2026. Nerves to the upper arm and chest usually branch in a predictable way, and surgeons rely on that map during operations. In the case examined here, both chest muscles received extra nerve branches that skipped the usual route.

The larger chest muscle had three added branches arising directly from upper sections of the nerve bundle. The smaller muscle had two added branches, one passing through tissue meant for its neighbor. A connecting loop between nerves also took an unexpected course. Knowing such variants exist can help surgeons plan operations and avoid accidental nerve damage.
pmc-13285827:
Richard A Baylis and colleagues test cancer risk after peripheral artery disease in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Heart disease and cancer share many risk factors, yet artery disease in the legs may carry its own added danger. The team asked whether that risk stands apart from other forms of heart and vessel disease.

Claims data from 2013 to 2023 sorted adults into three groups, led by close to ninety thousand people with leg artery disease and millions with no vessel disease at all. Weighted models that counted shared risks still found higher cancer risk in the leg artery group than in either comparison group. Checks on the 20 most common cancers tied the leg condition to several specific types. The result hints that clogged leg arteries signal more than heart trouble ahead.
pmc-13285927:
Tien Zubaidah questions a foodborne disease surveillance report from Shengsi County, China, in a letter to the editor from 2026. The study under review had claimed a sharp surge in Salmonella findings during 2024 in the coastal county. The letter argues that the claim runs ahead of what the small data set can bear.

Only 11 positive samples out of 118 tested sat behind the reported jump, with no error ranges or significance tests offered. A stiff case rule that required frequent diarrhea may also have missed patients whose illness showed as fever and vomiting instead. Fever cases peaked the same year, yet the report never checked whether those patients were the Salmonella cases. Claims about tourism and new strains lack gene data, the letter notes, and future reports should add such checks.
pmc-13286327:
Andrew J Barnhart and colleagues warn that a new health chatbot feature could deepen US care gaps in a 2026 commentary. ChatGPT Health, launched in January 2026, merges personal medical records with consumer app data inside a chatbot. Its makers pitch the tool as a guide through a broken system of costly insurance, care deserts, and staff shortages.

The authors argue the tool risks widening what they call a solidarity gap instead. It may bless risky self-rationing, mistriage emergencies, and lock in first impressions that skew later care, hitting hardest the people already shut out. Their remedies split into rebuilding the shared foundations of access upstream and fencing the tools with accountable safeguards downstream. Framed as a stand, the piece urges that such tools support human care rather than quietly stand in for it.
pmc-13286527:
Vanessa Cunha Brito and a ten-author team map a sex-shaping hormone inside unborn calves in a 2026 anatomy study. Anti-Mullerian hormone, made by Sertoli cells, erases the female duct system in male embryos, while egg follicle cells make a matching supply. In testes, staining filled Sertoli cells inside the developing sperm cords at every age, sparing seed cells and the tissue between cords. Ovaries showed faint staining in follicle helper cells but intense staining inside the egg itself, from the earliest follicles to the most mature. pmc-13286927:

Bee survival, foraging, colony growth, and honey output looked unaffected, and risk to other hive organisms rated low. The authors place the tool inside integrated pest management rather than as a stand-alone cure.
pmc-13287027:
Jian Sun and colleagues pool cohort studies on whether a combined index of triglycerides, glucose, and body mass predicts diabetes that arises during pregnancy. The index condenses insulin resistance and body size into one number from routine tests.

Women with higher index values faced roughly double the odds of gestational diabetes overall, though results varied widely between studies. The association held firmly in prospective cohorts, in younger women, and in large studies, and looked weaker in smaller or retrospective work. Sensitivity checks kept the finding stable. The authors call the analysis exploratory and stress the heavy variation between studies.
pmc-13287127:
Yinan Huang and Sandeep K Agarwal scope natural language processing in rheumatoid arthritis research in a 2026 scoping review. Billing codes and structured records miss the disease activity, lab values, and reasoning buried in doctors' free-text notes, and language tools promise to mine that residue. Notes from health records supplied most of the raw text. pmc-13287227:
Vinícius Cordeiro Rocha and colleagues combined microscopy and gene activity profiling in 2026 to describe the heart and its helper cells in two stick insect species. One species supplied the anatomy work, while the other supplied matching tissue for sequencing.

Blood cells gathered nearby and carried most immune-related gene activity, including dark pigment defences. The authors conclude that the organ does more than pump fluid: with its surrounding cells it also cleans the blood and supports immune defence in these insects.
pmc-13287827:
Md Rakibul Islam and co-authors checked in 2026 whether common worming drugs still work against gut worms on ten sheep and goat farms near Mymensingh in Bangladesh. pmc-13288327:

The authors replied, yet the journal judged the evidence still short of what the claims required.

pmc-13288627:

Sex, home area, and illness length also counted. Blood sugar control played a part as well. Early checks and treatment may help, they say. Proof from fresh studies is still wanted.
pmc-13288727:

Two proteins climbed in blood as well.
pmc-13289027:
Shangkun Si and colleagues track dirty air harm in BRICS nations in 2026. Their study spans 1990 to 2023. BRICS means Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. Data came from the Global Burden of Disease study. Fine dust in air is the risk at hand.

India bore the heaviest load and it grew. China stayed high but leveled off. Brazil and Russia cut their loads a lot. Aging drove much of the rise in China.
pmc-13289227:

pmc-13289327:

pmc-13289427:

pmc-13289827:

pmc-13289927:

pmc-13290227:

pmc-13290427:

Zheng and colleagues weigh the remaining challenges and sketch where targeted delivery for reversing fibrosis should head next.
pmc-13290927:
Short parent questionnaires catch real developmental gaps in two-year-olds born very preterm, Anna Markkula and colleagues show in a cross-sectional study from 2026. pmc-13291127:

Larvae favored proteins that support movement, adults leaned on stable scaffolds, and early aggregates shifted toward transport plus targeted protein breakdown at cell contacts. Chemical marks on proteins changed in step with rebuilding, offering a map of how simple animals reprogram their inner structure.
pmc-13291227:
Yuyu Liu and colleagues write a 2026 letter on a hard type of acute leukemia. The blood cancer carries a gene change called FLT3-ITD. Standard strong drug treatment often fails to clear it fully. A newer drug, venetoclax, may help when added.

Three drug mixes were used across the group. Of 61 patients who could be judged, nearly all responded to treatment. The letter supports wider testing of this pairing for this gene group.
pmc-13291327:

pmc-13292327:

pmc-13292427:
Barbaros Hayrettin Unlu and co-authors hunt a 2026 early warning sign for retinal damage from tamoxifen, a breast cancer drug, before doctors can see anything wrong. They measured light reflectivity of three outer retinal layers and a choroid blood index in 45 eyes of treated women and 50 eyes of matched healthy controls. Scans sampled the fovea and rings around it.

The ellipsoid zone, a photoreceptor layer, already looked dimmer at the central fovea and temporal perifovea in tamoxifen users. The other two layers and the choroidal index stayed level between groups. Longer treatment weakly tracked with brighter readings in the membrane above the ellipsoid zone, and age pulled ellipsoid brightness down in one region. The authors suggest ellipsoid dimming may flag patients needing closer eye monitoring, pending longitudinal proof.
pmc-13293127:

Low estrogen in this condition, called functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, has been tied to blood vessel problems, yet direct evidence of artery disease was missing. The group compared five sets of women, including exercisers with the condition, women with polycystic ovary syndrome, and healthy controls.

Only the exercising women with amenorrhea showed thicker artery walls than non-exercising controls, a difference that held after accounting for body mass index. Their cholesterol and insulin measures looked favorable by contrast, which makes the artery finding more striking. The authors urge earlier heart screening in this group.
pmc-13293727:
Nigel Flower and Liina Pylkkänen use brain magnetic recordings, in a 2026 study, to ask whether words, phrases, and sentences pass through the same processing stages when seen all at once. Readers can grasp sentence structure in a flash, faster than older models allow.

All three forms gave highly alike waveform shapes, with early activity for raw form, then activity in left temporal and frontal areas tied to combining parts. One left frontal-temporal area tracked how common two-word pairs are, hinting at step-by-step probing after a first global snapshot. The authors propose a model where the brain first takes the whole shape, then tests how parts combine.
pmc-13294127:
