pmc-13294327:
Magda M Awad, Yehia A Osman, and Mohamed Abdelmoteleb compare RNA-binding proteins across staph genomes in a 2026 bioinformatics study. Staphylococcus aureus adapts well to hosts, and proteins that grip RNA steer gene activity after copying, yet bacterial roles stay murky. Genomes and proteomes of 51 pathogenic strains were sorted into drug-resistant and drug-sensitive groups and family trees were built from single-letter variants.

Eight conserved RNA-binding proteins emerged. Cold shock proteins A and B plus S1 domain proteins differed in family pattern, binding parts, and simulated motion between resistant and sensitive strains. Such splits hint that RNA control helps drive toughness and could offer drug targets.
pmc-13294427:
Keqi Zhao and colleagues review glowing carbon dots made from biomass waste in a 2026 article on imaging materials. Dots brewed from plants, algae, farm leftovers, and microbes promise cheap, gentle production versus classic routes. Glow can span visible to near-infrared light with tuned recipes, suiting single-photon, multi-photon, and sound-based imaging mixes.

Three gaps block clinic use: glow mechanisms still lack one agreed theory, brightness often sits below 30% yield with shaky batch consistency, and body fate plus long-term toxicity data are sparse. Surface tailoring and controlled cooking are mapped as fixes. Green origin alone does not guarantee medical readiness.
pmc-13295027:
Shin-Yong Yeoh and co-authors try to rebuild mayonnaise without the egg, in a 2026 food science study. Egg yolk gives mayonnaise its body and stability, but it carries salmonella risk, cholesterol, and cost concerns. The candidates here are refined palm oil, Malaysia's abundant cooking fat, and sunflower lecithin, a plant emulsifier. Each was tested alone and in blends across a range of doses for texture, droplet structure, and resistance to going rancid in storage.

Palm oil firmed the sauce but made it less cohesive, while lecithin thickened it and kept oil droplets small and even. Too much palm oil made droplets clump, yet lecithin blends oxidized more slowly, showing lower rancidity markers over time. One formula, five percent palm oil with three percent lecithin, matched the structure and stability of the egg standard most closely. The pair, the authors conclude, can credibly stand in for yolk.
pmc-13295327:
Lucia H. Rhode and co-authors train deep learning to spot a blinding emergency on eye scans, in a 2026 study. Infected corneas can melt through and perforate, and catching that moment early decides whether sight survives. The team gathered front-of-eye optical scans from 150 patients with confirmed microbial keratitis, using their healthy other eyes as extra controls, and had two masked specialists agree on which eyes had perforated. A ResNet-34 network read six slices per eye and voted on the whole eye.

Four training variants all discriminated strongly. The best model, trained without healthy eyes or image masking tricks, reached near-excellent accuracy with good sensitivity and specificity at its chosen threshold. Adding healthy eyes did not help, and masking the lower image helped one setup while hurting another. The authors see automated scan reading as decision support for a complication no clinician wants to miss.
pmc-13295427:
Wenyi Xie, Jialin Liu, and Siru Liu examine patient-facing health language models in a 2026 viewpoint. Unlike one-off chatbots, personal health models build running stories from symptoms, wearable readings, and records that patients choose to link. Patients may trust and bring those stories into visits before any clinician review.

The shift turns the old two-way doctor-patient balance into a three-way negotiation with an algorithmic voice. Benefits include tidier symptom records, better health understanding, and stronger self-care between visits. Risks span wrong or biased advice, clashes with clinical judgement, privacy gaps, and blurred blame when harm follows, prompting calls for clear governance.
pmc-13296327:
Xuanyu Jin and colleagues review immunotherapy for advanced clear cell kidney cancer in a 2026 article. This subtype accounts for most renal cell carcinoma cases, and many patients already have spread at diagnosis. The review organises current treatments around the cancer-immunity cycle, the steps the immune system needs to attack a tumour.

Four stages receive close attention: antigen presentation, T cell activation, reversing T cell exhaustion, and tumour immune evasion. Combinations of checkpoint inhibitors with tyrosine kinase inhibitors now lead first-line care. Vaccines and cytokines alone, by contrast, have shown limited benefit in advanced disease. The authors close with future directions, including treatment tailored to each patient and markers that might predict response.
pmc-13296727:
Nadine Matthie, Melinda Higgins and Coretta Jenerette run, in 2026, a pilot trial of home headset therapy for chronic pain in sickle cell disease. Adults were assigned to daily headset sessions or to matched audio content for eight weeks, keeping pain diaries and joining interviews.

Headset users averaged more daily minutes and reported less pain, better coping with pain and better sleep than at the start. Motion sickness symptoms actually eased after sessions. Interviewees found both options acceptable and helpful, with some practical barriers noted. The authors call for a larger trial of virtual reality as self-care.
pmc-13297127:
Scott F. Huntington and colleagues compare first treatments for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia in older Medicare patients in a 2026 real-world study. Trial results may not carry over to everyday older patients, who often carry other illnesses. United States Medicare records were used to compare venetoclax-based therapy, BTK-inhibitor therapy, and other regimens.

Patients starting venetoclax-based treatment lived longer than those in the other groups. They were also less likely to need a further treatment later. Targeted oral drugs have largely replaced older chemotherapy for this disease, yet head-to-head everyday evidence has been scarce. The findings give doctors and researchers practical information for choosing first therapy in older adults.
pmc-13297227:
Lan Lin and colleagues present a lightweight neural network that estimates brain age from scans across the whole lifespan in a 2026 paper. Brain age gaps flag brains ageing faster than expected. Their design pairs local-detail modules with a transformer that reads global patterns, plus a small quantum-inspired component in the middle.

Training used more than twenty-two thousand people from seventeen data sources, spanning infancy to age ninety-six. Average prediction error came in under three years. Repeated scans of the same person gave highly consistent answers, and accuracy held across sites. The authors offer the tool for large-scale brain-health monitoring and tracking of development or decline.
pmc-13297727:
Shuo Liang, Kun Zhang, and Hong Zhang present a sixty-six-year-old woman whose left heart artery sprang from the wrong vessel, in a 2026 case report. The fault, present from birth, rarely lets patients reach old age, since the artery draws low-pressure blood meant for the lungs. She had suffered chest and upper back pain for three months.

Detailed computed tomography scans traced the artery from the lung trunk along its usual groove, with the partner artery swollen and winding from years of extra work. A film-style three-dimensional rendering made the layout vivid for the care team and for counselling. Given her age and rich backup circulation, doctors chose watchful management over surgery.
pmc-13299827:
Qin Zhang and others review a chemical RNA modification called m7G in colorectal cancer, in a 2026 survey. This common mark helps regulate RNA stability, processing, and translation, and its disruption tracks with poor clinical outcomes in this cancer. Key proteins, including a methyltransferase pair and a protein-making factor, receive full coverage.

The review organises evidence on how the mark shapes cancer growth, worsening, outlook, diagnosis, and therapy. Drug failure, return, and spread remain major problems in colorectal care despite screening and treatment gains. The authors place m7G regulators as candidate markers and drug targets for precision strategies, while the field works toward bedside proof.
pmc-13300227:
Chelsea Zimmer and colleagues describe a 2026 workflow built to help surveillance laboratories turn viral sequencing into variant reports with modest computing skill. Their open-source pipeline, written in Workflow Description Language, takes sequence and quality files from an Ion Torrent S5 instrument, assigns clades and variants, and merges results with patient metadata. REDCap, a research data platform, stores run records and results as the central backbone.

On top of that storage layer, the team built an interactive dashboard for real-time monitoring and visual summaries. Laboratories can also generate a consolidated variant report from the same data. The design keeps a local repository inside each institution, so smaller molecular labs can adapt the system to their own reporting needs. Although built around SARS-CoV-2, the framework is presented as adjustable for other emerging pathogens.
pmc-13300627:
Osama Alkouri and co-authors measure metabolic syndrome among Middle Eastern patients who already have atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, in a 2026 analysis. Data combined a prospective Jordanian cohort from nine centers with pooled records from six regional registries, grouping 1,016 patients by how many standard modifiable risk factors they carried. The team then looked for independent predictors of the syndrome.

Metabolic syndrome was present in about forty-three percent of the cohort. Its frequency climbed steeply with risk factor count, from barely two percent in patients with none to sixty-two percent in those carrying three or four. Older age, diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, heart failure, higher body mass index, and higher triglycerides each predicted the syndrome, while higher protective cholesterol and smoking ran in the opposite direction. The authors press for region-specific prevention aimed at the whole risk cluster rather than single factors.
pmc-13301027:
Manapat Praditaukrit and co-authors compare outcomes for preterm babies born small for their gestational age in a 2026 matched cohort study. Drawing on a database collected from 2014 to 2025, the team matched 298 small babies with 298 appropriately grown preterm peers. They also ran a separate look at the very preterm subgroup, where 190 babies qualified.

Small babies carried nearly double the adjusted risk of the combined outcome of death or major complications. Their mortality risk alone ran about three and a half times higher, and the risk of death or serious lung disease roughly doubled. The very preterm subgroup echoed every one of those patterns and added a higher risk tied to treated eye disease. The authors urge focused management of small preterm infants, especially where resources are limited and the margin for rescue is thin.
pmc-13301427:
K Lomper and K Kempfert check whether newer blood thinners win patients over in a 2026 single center study. One hundred people with atrial fibrillation averaged seventy-three years old and about three years on treatment. They split between drug types. The older vitamin K antagonists demand blood test monitoring. The newer direct agents do not. Adherence and satisfaction were measured with questionnaires.

Neither measure separated the groups. Adherence scores averaged about twenty-two for the older drugs and twenty-three for the newer ones. The gap missed significance, and satisfaction landed close. No feature, from rhythm type to pill burden, predicted adherence. What did travel together was satisfaction and adherence within both groups: happier patients took their medicine more reliably, with a moderate correlation. The authors conclude the newer drugs' convenience does not convert into better taking, so clinics should work on how patients feel about therapy itself.
pmc-13302127:
A cornea that gives too easily under air pressure may be heading toward keratoconus, Se Hoon Choi and colleagues test in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Two hundred seventeen participants had corneal shape mapped by Pentacam and stiffness probed with the Corvis ST device. Normal eyes were compared with eyes suspected of early keratoconus, a bulging disorder that distorts sight.

Suspect eyes showed smaller surface radii front and back, plus higher elevation readings against the enhanced reference sphere. Of all measures, the speed at which the cornea first flattened under the air puff separated the groups most accurately. Softer, more deformable tissue, the authors conclude, marks suspect eyes before shape alone betrays them.
pmc-13302327:
Patients feel recovered long before their calf agrees, Firat Dogruoz and colleagues show in a 2026 study of Achilles tendon repair. Seventy-six men who had open surgery for acute rupture between 2015 and 2023, followed for at least a year, completed two standard outcome questionnaires. A single-leg heel-rise test supplied the hard measure, scored as symmetry against the uninjured side.

Median questionnaire scores looked superb, at 97 and 98 points. Median heel-rise symmetry, though, reached only 87.5 percent, and just 40.8 percent of men cleared the ninety percent bar. Scores and symmetry barely correlated. Clinicians, the authors argue, should pair what patients report with what the leg can actually do.
pmc-13302727:
V Portero and co-authors demonstrate, in a 2026 study, a wearable closed-loop device that can stop atrial fibrillation without any electric shock. The system pairs microelectronics with optogenetics, using light-sensitive proteins to control heart rhythm on detection. Wearables usually only monitor; this one also treats.

Freely moving rats wore the system while eating, sleeping, and walking, and episodes were terminated as they occurred. The team also confirmed light-based rhythm control in human atrial tissue and in models built at true human atrial scale. The full system operated successfully inside the human body in translational tests. The authors present the work as a step toward on-demand personal heart therapy.
pmc-13303327:
A wing that snaps between stable lengths could let small aircraft reshape themselves mid-flight, Ruixin Wang and Bin Niu design in a 2026 engineering study. Their section hides a multistable honeycomb core whose curved beams click between states, holding each span without continuous power. A nonlinear force model, finite-element checks, fluid-structure simulations, and a physical prototype all test the concept.

The prototype achieved 35.6 percent span change with reversible transitions in both directions. Simulations showed lift responding to span as intended while the structure carried typical aerodynamic loads. The authors present the honeycomb approach as a lightweight route past the motors and rails that burden conventional morphing wings.
pmc-13304127:
Erkan Topkan, Duriye Ozturk, and Ugur Selek compare two health-based scores for outlook in advanced lung cancer in a 2026 study. Both scores blend inflammation, nutrition, and weight loss measures, but head-to-head proof was missing.

Records covered 795 patients with stage IIIC non-small cell lung cancer treated with combined chemo and radiation between 2010 and 2020. Both scores split patients into three groups with clearly different survival spans. The CARWL score separated groups a bit more widely on every measure and kept its value beside the rival score. Simpler bedside scoring may sharpen counseling for this group.
pmc-13304227:
Laith Glissa and Latifa Berrezouga share first case reports in 2026 of a dental implant joined to a custom zirconia shield for damaged tooth sockets. Normally an implant needs a drilled hole and firm grip in bone, which broken sockets cannot offer.

Digital planning shaped a one-piece zirconia membrane fitted to each defect, with an inner extension linking it to the implant. Two patients received the joined unit right after tooth removal, fixed to hard bone with screws and no drilling. Scans two years later showed good bone bonding in both cases. A fuller study is planned to test the idea properly.
pmc-13304927:
Eun-Seop Lee, Chae-Min Kim, and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, whether a Korean brown seaweed can yield antibacterial compounds for the resistance era. Kelp samples from two coasts were extracted at three ethanol strengths, and the extracts were tested in the lab alongside computer docking and drug-property predictions.

The mid-strength extract carried the most phenolics and the strongest antioxidant activity in radical-scavenging tests. Antibacterial action was selective: growth of Staphylococcus aureus fell in a dose-dependent way, while Escherichia coli was barely affected. Docking pointed to two seaweed sterols, fucosterol and 24-methylene cholesterol, binding tightly to several bacterial enzymes at once. Predicted drug properties looked favorable apart from high fat solubility and a possible heart-channel flag, so the authors propose optimization work.
pmc-13305627:
M Wise, M Allen, and co-authors report, in a 2026 survey abstract, how well a carbapenem combo drug performs against resistant Gram-negative bacteria collected across the United Kingdom. Imipenem paired with relebactam, which blocks two beta-lactamase classes, was tested against more than four thousand clinical isolates gathered between 2020 and 2024 under a global monitoring program.

Over ninety-nine percent of the main enteric group could be killed by the drug, including every isolate carrying the KPC resistance enzyme. Against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the success rate reached about ninety-six percent overall. The pairing kept working against most strains resistant to standard beta-lactams and against roughly seven in ten multi-drug Pseudomonas strains, edging out a rival pairing. The authors conclude it offers an important option for difficult UK hospital infections.
pmc-13305727:
Johanna Eggeling followed blood immune patterns during tuberculosis treatment in a 2026 prospective study. Samples came from 51 patients and 34 healthy controls, taken before therapy, after 14 days, and when treatment ended.

Flow testing measured 386 cell populations, and machine learning built two short scores from five populations each. Both scores separated patients from controls well and tracked change across treatment in the reported accuracy figures, though one score moved opposite to disease severity. Two cell types carrying PD-L1 appeared in both scores, marking them as leads for diagnosis and monitoring research. Such scores could one day help doctors track how well treatment is working.
pmc-13306027:
Enrique A. Nieves reviewed soft, highly flexible drug carriers called transferosomes in a 2026 critical survey. Built from fat layers softened by edge-activating agents, the vesicles aim to cross skin and other tight barriers without injections.

Uses span skin, eye, nose, mouth and other mucosal routes, yet progress is slowed by mixed naming, varied recipes and unstandardised bending tests in the authors' account. Attention centres on fat mix, softener choice, particle traits, drug release and body performance. The review calls for shared quality measures and clearer proof of how carriers cross barriers before clinical use widens.
pmc-13306527:
Fatemeh Azadegan-Dehkordi tested plant acids loaded into chitosan particles against bowel inflammation in rats in a 2026 study. Eighty male Wistar rats were split into ten groups of eight, and colitis was triggered with acetic acid placed in the rectum.

Seven days of treatment followed, covering loaded particles, single acids, plain particles and a standard drug for comparison. Disease raised IL-32 protein and gene activity for IL-33, IL-34 and NF-κB in reported measures, while every treatment arm lowered those signals. The authors link benefit to calming a specific cytokine axis.
pmc-13306727:
Łukasz Rybak adapted a geometric splitting algorithm to sort mixed radar pulses in a 2026 review and test study. Crowded signal environments blend pulses from many emitters, and separating them is a core step before any source can be named.

A history of the Hypergeometrical Divide method and recent sorting work sets up trials on real, anonymised pulse records. Checks measure how well clusters match true emitter types and support later pulse analysis. The authors present the adapted method as a candidate for reliable sorting in dense modern signal scenes. The work adds a clean test case for pulse work in mixed signal scenes.
pmc-13306927:
Norbert Nickel and colleagues measure in 2026 how hydrogen binds inside large-area graphene grown by chemical vapour deposition. Deuterium labelling let them track the light atoms cleanly during heating experiments. Samples sat on silicon with oxide layers of differing thickness, which let substrate effects show.

Effusion spectra revealed a sharp peak in the hydrogen binding distribution at a defined energy value. Oxide thickness influenced that peak, pointing to interaction between graphene and its support. Their model explains the data through breaking of carbon-hydrogen bonds. Questions about pure graphene storing hydrogen motivated the work, since many storage claims rely on metal decoration. Knowing where growth leaves hydrogen behind matters for electronic devices and isotope work alike. The study supplies binding energies where direct measurements were scarce.
pmc-13307127:
Sizhen Wang engineered fat particles that deliver an immune-activating gene message for pancreatic cancer in a 2026 study. Such tumours stay cold to immunity, and messenger RNA often traps inside cell entry sacs before it can work.

A pH-sensitive coating sheds in acid sacs, exposing charged groups that fuse membranes and free the message, while a second coating targets dendritic cells. The cargo encodes a STING variant, R283S, meant to lift pathway suppression inside tumours. The combined design aims to wake immune attack in a hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13307227:
Jacob Waldron and co-authors detail in 2026 an all-keyhole operation that rebuilds both the hip labrum and the front capsule in a patient with repeated instability after earlier arthroscopy. A worn labrum breaks the joint's suction seal, while a weak capsule removes its static restraint. Open surgery would add heavy morbidity before later bone correction.

The labrum was rebuilt with a tendon graft taken from a donor, and donor skin tissue restored the deficient capsule, fixed with knotless anchors. Restoring both structures together steadies the joint before a planned pelvic bone operation. Sequencing soft tissue first, then bone, spreads the surgical burden. The authors present the approach as reproducible and less invasive. For young, active patients, they argue, it may slow joint degeneration while definitive correction waits its turn.
pmc-13307827:
Maria Júlia Cadrieskt-Ribeiro and co-authors sequence in 2026 a vaccinia virus strain spreading into rural northeastern Brazil, where it causes pustular disease in dairy cows and their milkers. Outbreaks in two states supplied twelve positive samples, and five genomes were fully read. No full genome from the northeast had been described before.

The new genomes cluster with recent isolates from Brazil's midwest and southeast, while differing from older southeastern strains. Two isolates carried extra variation and signs of genetic mixing with a midwestern strain. Some animals also carried a second poxvirus at the same time. The pattern suggests several separate introductions rather than one wave. The authors warn against drinking raw milk from affected herds and stress the economic hit when milking must stop for weeks.
pmc-13308927:
Farhan Mohiuddin and co-authors describe a 2026 case of a pyloric gland adenoma in the gallbladder stub of a man aged 67 years, spotted by scope guided biopsy. The man had lost part of his gallbladder eight months before, when dense scar tissue blocked a full removal at surgery.

Scans of the stub showed a mass that looked like cancer, which raised hard choices for the care team. Scope ultrasound found a mass that measured 28.4 by 14 millimetres inside the lumen, and a needle sample named the benign growth with low grade change. A firm call before surgery helps plan the cut and weighs bile leak risk with care.
pmc-13309427:
Jhon Eric Alves Fernandes and co-authors report a 2026 hunt for hidden viruses inside public gene databases. Computer clouds now let researchers scan huge stored samples for viral traces at low cost. The team focused on one virus order that infects plants and fungi.

A cloud pipeline screened stored samples and hand checks confirmed 111 likely viral genomes. Most fell into one family that split into three distinct branches, with dozens of likely new species. The split was large enough that the authors propose two new family names. The work shows how much viral variety still sits unnoticed in data that were gathered for other reasons.
pmc-13309527:
Ankoji Parvathala offers a 2026 commentary on materials that glow when pressed or rubbed, focused on a simple oxide spiked with chromium. Recent work on that oxide points to glow centered on the added chromium atoms, driven by charge movement under stress. Older accounts spread the process across the whole material instead.

Centering the glow on the added atoms could let designers tune brightness by choosing dopants with care. One gap remains: what first splits the charges that the chromium centers need. Fields at internal boundaries may play that role, but proof is still thin. The author urges targeted tests so design rules rest on a settled mechanism, not on rival stories.
pmc-13309827:
Seema Bibi Qureshi, Ambreen Usmani, and Junaid Tariq measure emotional intelligence in 2026 among 172 medical students in rural Sindh, Pakistan, and test its link with grades. A validated trait questionnaire scored global emotional intelligence plus well-being, self-control, and sociability facets. Students were in their second to fourth years.

Global scores landed at a moderate level, with well-being the strongest facet and self-control the weakest. Men and women did not differ significantly on any measure, which the authors note against mixed earlier findings. Grades showed no real connection with emotional intelligence overall. Only sociability correlated weakly with grade average, a small effect they treat cautiously. Medical training stresses students heavily, so the null result matters for curriculum claims. Emotional skills may aid resilience, they conclude, without functioning as a grade lever.
pmc-13309927:
Zirui Chen and colleagues steer a robot swarm in 2026 using fear signals read from a mouse brain through an implanted interface. Neural patterns from the amygdala region, home of the fear response, were decoded in real time. When a cueing sound predicted an aversive stimulus, the decoding flagged rising fear and the swarm switched behaviour.

In normal mode the ground robots explored their surroundings to learn the terrain. Under fear signalling they tightened into a defensive formation with higher alert posture. The fearful brain state scaled down swarm speed and reshaped the swarm's overall motion. The work fuses swarm intelligence with direct brain input, a step beyond single-robot brain control. Applications the authors imagine include hazard response where an operator's threat sense redirects machines instantly.
pmc-13310427:
Dilip D Hinge, Abhijeet Shelke, Ramesh Kawade, and Satish Patil map the genetics of atrial fibrillation in 2026, the commonest sustained heart rhythm disorder. Family studies suggest genes account for a large share of risk, especially in early-onset cases. The review organises disease genes into four functional groups and weighs variant prevalence and penetrance for each.

One group covers faulty ion channels that govern the heart's electrical signals. A second covers structural proteins of the muscle and its scaffolding. Transcription factors that shape heart development form the third group, and calcium-handling proteins the fourth. Despite differing jobs, these defects converge on shared electrical and structural weaknesses in the atria. Understanding which module a patient's variant sits in could guide targeted therapy. The authors frame genetics as the route from blanket treatment toward precision cardiology.
pmc-13310727:
Nils Kurzen and colleagues propose a staged plan for long term inflammation in a 2026 concept paper. Unlike brief inflammation, chronic inflammation locks in through repeated signals, stored immune memory in tissue, and loops that resist shutoff. Standard dose choices alone may fail to break those loops.

Their CURE plan has three steps in plain terms. First, strong early treatment aims to push inflammation below a key threshold. Next, a guided step down holds gains while natural calming paths recover. Last, light ongoing care guards against relapse. The name does not promise a cure, but a path to stable control. Proof from trials is still needed.
pmc-13310827:
Jan Abel Olsen and colleagues track what drives gaps in life quality in Norway in a 2026 long term study. Past work often paired one health sign with one social sign and missed daily habits. The team followed adults over two decades to weigh social roots against habits like smoking, activity, and weight.

Data came from the Tromsø Study, with 11,313 adults aged 25 to 54 years at the start and 21 years of follow up. Habits explained most of the explained gaps in all three health scores, well above social factors. Curbing childhood hardship still matters, but gains from healthier habits look large for cutting adult gaps.
pmc-13311127:
Maria Rizzo and co-authors review surgery results for severe elbow breaks with no pulse in children in a 2026 study. Supracondylar arm breaks are the most common child elbow injury, and the worst type risks nerve and vessel harm. Care must judge blood flow, not pulse alone, to pick who needs vessel surgery.

Twelve children treated from 2023 to 2025 had bone fixing within 12 hours of injury. Ten with true low flow had vessel checks, while two with warm pink hands were watched closely. Overall results were fair, yet half had angle deformities and only half scored excellent on a standard scale. Flow guided care is backed.
pmc-13311327:
Arnab Ghosh and co-authors in 2026 detail a study on how nitric oxide tunes airway muscle in asthma through an enzyme called G6PD. The enzyme helps ready a partner protein, sGC, to respond to nitric oxide.

Airway cells from donors with and without asthma were treated with low-dose nitric oxide plus a drug that stimulates sGC. Most asthma cells showed low G6PD and a poor antioxidant balance, a pattern also seen in mouse asthma lungs. Adding G6PD back raised the sGC pair's readiness, while removing it blocked that gain. Mouse strains with too little or extra G6PD matched the cell results.
pmc-13312027:
Hester Elizabeth Lacey, Yi Min Khoong, and Keith Altman present a 2026 systematic review of virtual surgical planning for bone work in facial feminization surgery. Reshaping the facial skeleton demands precision, and digital planning promises better accuracy than conventional freehand methods. Searching seven databases and grey literature in April 2025, the reviewers gathered studies of adult transgender women whose operations used virtual planning to guide bone cuts, then pooled what could be pooled.

Seven studies qualified. Operations using virtual planning ran significantly shorter, with a pooled effect of minus 0.72 standard units in the meta-analysis, and one comparison reported accuracy of 95.25 percent against 78.25 percent without planning. Complication rates stayed low, between 0 and 1.77 percent across studies, and patient satisfaction ran consistently high. Planning time, however, varied wildly between reports. The authors see a growing role for planning and augmented reality navigation, while asking for prospective studies with standard outcome measures.
pmc-13312127:
Ding Yang Hsu reports a 2026 pilot study on customizing CPAP nasal mask cushions using three-dimensional scans of patients' faces. Continuous positive airway pressure is the standard treatment for obstructive sleep apnea, but poor mask fit, discomfort, and air leaks lead many patients to quit, with roughly 70 percent blaming mask problems.

Hsu pairs facial data analysis with a replaceable rapid mold design, so a cushion shaped to one person's face can be produced efficiently. The customized cushions lowered pressure on the face, reduced the strap tension needed, and cut air leakage compared with standard fits. Patients said they preferred the personalized cushions for long-term use. The author presents the approach as a practical route to better comfort and steadier treatment adherence.
pmc-13314427:
Guanlin Chen and colleagues track how shifts in borderline blood sugar shape later heart, kidney, and metabolic disease in a 2026 study. The question was whether the path of impaired fasting glucose over time matters, not just a single reading.

From the Kailuan Study, 43,073 adults free of heart disease, diabetes, and kidney disease were checked in 2006 and 2010 and classed as steady normal, worsening, recovered, or stuck high. Over a median follow-up of 11.0 years, per the report, 1795 people gained at least two of the three diseases. Against the steady normal group, risk ratios came out at 1.93 for the worsening group, 1.69 for the recovered group, and 3.10 for the stuck-high group, all kept mid-sentence as reported. Even recovery left extra risk, which argues for early action.
pmc-13314627:
Jianxin Xu and co-workers assemble the full mitochondrial genome of a showy Himalayan plant in a 2026 report. Holmskioldia sanguinea is prized for its hat-shaped flower cups and slope-healing roots, yet its place in the Lamiales order was disputed for lack of gene proof.

Its chloroplast genome was known, but the mitochondrial one was not. The team sequenced and built the circle of DNA, which runs to 405,461 base pairs with a GC share of 46.00 percent as stated in the report. It holds 36 protein-coding genes, three ribosomal RNAs, and 33 transfer RNAs by their count. Repeats abound, with 550 spread repeats found in the genome as reported. The map gives breeders and taxonomists a firm base for placing this plant.
pmc-13315427:
Alessandro Marchese and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 imaging study, whether colour-coded fundus autofluorescence can catch vitreoretinal lymphoma. The cancer masquerades as inflammation and resists diagnosis. The team reviewed twenty eyes from ten patients, reading the colour-coded images from the EIDON system alongside blue and green autofluorescence and retinal scans. They scored how each method performed on the disease's lesions.

Reader agreement on the colour-coded images was excellent. The method found retinitis-like lesions, two of two eyes, and lymphomatous pigment detachments, four of four, where both methods missed most of them. The conventional methods detected none of the first type and one of four detachments. The granular pattern showed equally on all three. Green imaging still read the central macula best, while colour-coding exposed fluorophores, atrophic patches, deposits, and vessel infiltrates. The authors propose it as a tool that widens what clinicians can see.
pmc-13316227:
Adeniyi Adeleye and co-authors show in 2026 that heart muscle cells reprogrammed by two factors release exosomes that protect other heart cells from death. Delivering modified RNA for STEMIN, a tuned serum response factor, plus YAP5SA, an always-on YAP variant, reshaped chromatin and gene activity in rat and human heart cells.

Cell cycle, DNA copying, and survival pathways switched on, and a strong set of microRNAs tied to death resistance was induced. Those microRNAs were selectively packed into exosomes that target caspases and TP53-linked death routes. Functional tests showed less cell death in dishes and in animals.
pmc-13316427:
Haozhe Wang and co-authors introduce, in 2026, a computer framework named VeloRM for tracking chemical marks on RNA inside single cells. Such marks control how RNA works and how long it lasts. How they change over the RNA life cycle and as cells switch type has been hard to follow.

VeloRM separates marks present before splicing from those present after splicing, a distinction no earlier tool made. It models the speed of change in those marks, predicts future states and rebuilds cell trajectories from the mark data alone. Tests on m6A methylation and A-to-I editing recovered known patterns for the cell cycle and differentiation. The tool also found m6A sites heavily marked on unspliced RNA near splice junctions.
pmc-13316627:
Moritz Kühlein and colleagues, reporting in 2026, examine leaky tricuspid valves that persist after a catheter repair of the mitral valve. Such leakage is common and linked to poor outcomes. Its meaning may depend on whether the tricuspid valve can still be treated by a later catheter procedure.

Two centres reviewed 905 patients treated between 2015 and 2025 for severe mitral leakage. Among those with follow-up imaging, severe tricuspid leakage persisted in a minority at three months. Patients judged ineligible for later tricuspid treatment had much lower two-year survival, while eligible patients fared much like those without persistent leakage. Advanced right heart remodelling and worse starting leakage predicted persistence, and women were affected more often.
pmc-13318227:
Céline Mamie and a large team apply, in 2026, multiple molecular methods to perianal fistulas, painful tunnels near the anus with few good treatments. Fistulas arise either from infected glands or alongside Crohn's disease. Earlier work linked one tissue-changing process to Crohn's fistulas, but detailed mechanisms remained unclear.

Samples came from 23 Crohn's patients and 17 patients with gland-origin fistulas, including rectal biopsies, swabs, fistula scrapings and blood. Gene activity differed sharply between rectal lining and fistula tracts, yet the two fistula types looked remarkably similar. Genes for tissue transition, inflammation and a key signalling pathway stood out in both. Microbe communities inside tracts also overlapped, while rectal communities differed. A small gene set may help tell the two types apart.
pmc-13318627:
Jeetendra Eswaraka and colleagues test, in 2026, whether continuous cage monitoring with machine learning catches illness in laboratory mice earlier than human checks. Daily visual inspection happens while mice sleep and lasts only moments, so subtle signs are missed. Reduced movement was proposed as an early warning signal.

Movement data gathered by the same sensor system at three institutions were analysed retrospectively. Learning models generated alerts that were checked against clinical records. The models flagged animals in distress three to six days before signs were noticed or death occurred, with accuracy rising the earlier the alert was judged. The authors argue that pairing visual checks with automated monitoring improves welfare, sharpens study endpoints and makes research more reproducible, while also saving staff time.
pmc-13318927:
Zheping Zhou and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of walking problems in older adults with type 2 diabetes. Wearable sensors measured gait in 41 patients and 55 matched controls. Brain scans rated shrinkage of the medial temporal region. Thinking tests and grip strength completed the comparison of brain versus body factors.

Patients walked markedly worse than controls. Their gait speed was about 35 percent lower in the reported comparison. Brain factors explained most of the speed difference in the models. Grip strength added little and did not predict speed independently. Step rhythm, by contrast, drew on both brain and peripheral factors. The authors suggest future treatment research should target the brain more. They caution that one-time data cannot prove cause.
pmc-13319027:
Julia Siebielec and Filip Raciborski offer a 2026 assessment of vaccine information accuracy across four large language models. ChatGPT, Copilot, DeepSeek, and Gemini each answered ninety multiple-choice questions drawn from a government vaccine website. Data were collected in March 2026. Two open questions probed sources and the pros and cons of universal vaccination.

Gemini scored highest, with a correct share of 0.98 across the test set. ChatGPT scored lowest at 0.86 in the same test. Results differed significantly between models. On open questions, all named suitable information sources. All cited herd immunity as an advantage and adverse reactions as a disadvantage. Answers were correct but thin. The authors judge the models a limited information source on their own.
pmc-13319127:
Marina Klimovich, Jean-François Rouet, and Tobias Richter report a 2026 set of four studies on mind wandering while reading in a first versus a foreign language. Each study paired different languages, mixing German, English, and French readers. Participants reported wandering frequency, felt difficulty, and comprehension. Later studies also separated deliberate from accidental drifting.

Readers with weaker foreign-language vocabulary wandered more in that language than in their first. Readers with matched vocabulary showed no such gap. When weak vocabulary hurt deeper comprehension, drifting was mostly unintentional. When basic understanding held, drifting turned deliberate, and felt difficulty carried the vocabulary effect. The authors read this as a resource story: overloaded minds drift by accident, while coping minds choose to disengage.
pmc-13320027:
Tigist Batu, Chu Thu and Lara K Mahal map, in 2026, how small RNA molecules regulate an enzyme that attaches fucose sugars to cell surfaces. That enzyme, FUT1, helps set blood type, shapes gut microbes and influences cancer behaviour. MicroRNAs usually switch genes down, so finding they can also switch this one up was notable.

High-throughput screening across cell lines confirmed both directions of control on the enzyme and its sugar product. Blocking natural microRNAs changed enzyme and sugar levels, proving biological weight. Binding sites for the up-regulating and down-regulating microRNAs all sat in unusual positions. The up-regulating molecules are scarce in several cancers, matching the loss of this sugar pattern seen in oesophageal cancer, melanoma and spread of disease.
pmc-13320327:
Anaïs Deglos and her team review, in 2026, the endocannabinoid system in skeletal muscle and the possible role of cannabidiol in muscle disease. The system uses signalling lipids made in the body, their enzymes and two main receptors, and it shapes insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial energy work, protein balance and muscle growth. Upset of the system accompanies obesity, diabetes and wasting conditions.

Cannabidiol, a cannabis compound with no mind-altering effects, is drawing interest as a treatment candidate. The review explains how one receptor in particular shapes muscle growth and function, then gathers early evidence on cannabidiol in settings such as age-related muscle loss, cachexia and muscular dystrophies. The authors present the field as hopeful but still emerging, with mechanisms only partly mapped.
pmc-13320427:
Luis A Moncayo-Martínez presents a data set of solved stock placement puzzles for thirty eight real supply chains in a 2026 data article. Placing spare stock to promise a set delivery time can slash holding costs across a chain with many tiers. Past papers gave chain shapes but not full best answers, so solver builders lacked a hard test bed.

Each chain is profiled by depth, branch width, and stage type, from parts and making to shipping and shops. Best spare stock levels were found with a cut based solver in trade software under bell curve demand. Files give best costs, solve times, and all values for each case, with the largest case holding thousands of choices and near nineteen thousand limits. Four cases still carry a wide best gap for challengers.
pmc-13321027:
Brandon Baer and co-authors study lung surfactant loss in a 2026 mouse model of acute lung injury. Surfactant keeps air sacs open, and its key fat, phosphatidylglycerol, drops sharply in severe lung failure in patients. An enzyme that cuts fats, secretory phospholipase A2, rises at the same time, hinting at a linked process.

Injury was triggered in mice and tracked over 240 hours as harm peaked and then cleared. At peak injury, enzyme driven breakdown of the fat rose and fat levels fell, alongside worse surfactant function; all changes vanished after recovery. A blocking drug given at peak injury cut enzyme activity and raised surfactant fat levels.
pmc-13321827:
Chunye Qi and co-authors model dosing for an antibiotic against urinary infection in a 2026 laboratory study. Nemonoxacin is approved for pneumonia, but its value for uncomplicated urinary tract infection from E. coli was unsure. The team built an in vitro model that mimics drug levels in urine over 24 hours.

Twelve clinical E. coli samples were tested in both standard broth and synthetic human urine. Drug levels needed for effect were higher in urine, and exposure over time divided by sensitivity best predicted killing. A 500 milligram once daily dose hit targets for most samples by broth based goals, though urine based goals were stricter. Clinical trials are still needed.
pmc-13323227:
Junrey Amas and co-authors review genomic progress in neglected Brassicaceae crops and their wild relatives, in a 2026 article. These orphan species hold traits such as stress tolerance, pest resistance, better oil quality and useful bioactive compounds, yet receive far less breeding investment than major Brassica crops.

Chromosome-level genomes, pan-genomes and transcript maps now span many of these species, revealing genome evolution and gene families behind key traits. Breeding tools include marker-assisted selection, genome-wide association, genomic selection and gene editing. Close kinship within the family lets knowledge and useful alleles move into cultivated crops. Joining genomic and other omics layers should speed that transfer for hardier and more nutritious harvests.
pmc-13323327:
Lou Liu and colleagues describe a lung cancer case where HER2-targeted drugs controlled disease in sequence, in a 2026 case report. The patient first had stage IA2 lung squamous cell carcinoma removed, then developed metastatic recurrence in the lungs.

Gene testing of the removed tumour found an ERBB2 exon 20 change, MET amplification and losses in several other genes. After platinum therapy failed, trastuzumab deruxtecan gave meaningful control but stopped over suspected lung inflammation with infection. Pyrotinib then held disease despite gut side effects, and a lower dose of the first drug later won about seven more months of control. Heart and lung problems complicated the final course.
pmc-13323627:
Yue Gu and co-authors report two cases where deep infiltrating endometriosis turned malignant, in a 2026 case report with a literature review. Both women had long-standing deep disease with kidney swelling from ureter pressure, a rare and hard-to-spot transformation.

The first patient, aged 44 years, had radical surgery with ureter reimplantation, and pathology showed well-differentiated endometrioid adenocarcinoma. She stayed disease-free after chemotherapy and targeted therapy. The second, aged 47 years with eighteen years of painful periods, had the same cancer type and stayed clear after chemotherapy including an antibody-drug conjugate. A review found 57 further cases, most often in bowel, vagina or ureter.
pmc-13324127:
Rachid Aguennouz and co-authors issue a 2026 correction to their study of growth-promoting actinobacteria from Anacyclus pyrethrum, a Moroccan medicinal plant. Four references in the published article were wrong and have been removed, with correct sources put in their place.

Each swap is spelled out in full, giving the faulty citation, its replacement and the sentence it supports. One replacement backs a discussion point that Bennett medium recovered more actinobacteria than ISP2 medium, on page 11 of the article. Another supports background on endophytic actinobacteria in the introduction, on page 2, while a further swap touches a discussion passage on page 12 about sustainable cropping.
pmc-13325227:
Elena Streck and team report the open surgical treatment of a chronic artery-vein fistula of the lateral plantar artery after coil embolization failed. Their 2026 case paper explains that trauma-induced plantar fistulas are very rare, and that growing shunt flow can over time cause venous overload and backup. Closing the fistula is essential to restore normal venous flow, and endovascular blocking is usually the first, least invasive choice.

In this case, coil blocking proved not enough, with lasting symptoms and partial thrombosis on angiography. Surgeons excised the fistula through an extensive medial approach under bloodless conditions. They fully resected the large venous aneurysm, removed all prior coil material, and closed the arterial connection from within with a simple suture. The authors present surgery as a reliable and promising alternative when vessel treatment cannot finish the job.
pmc-13326227:
Tommaso Bini and team report the first known hole in the descending aorta during transseptal puncture for left atrial pouch closure. Their 2026 case paper follows a 57-year-old woman in whom radiofrequency-powered puncture with a 15-French steerable sheath tore that aorta without knowing. Aortic root injury during septal puncture is rare but known; injury to that aorta in this setting had not earlier been seen.

Repeat echocardiograms showed no pericardial effusion and initial blood measures stayed stable, yet the patient later grew a mediastinal hematoma and bilateral pleural fluid. Management required emergency percutaneous thoracic endovascular aortic repair, followed by surgical evacuation of the clot. The authors blame excessive tenting during that puncture, related to septal aneurysm and atypical echocardiographic windows, and warn that extracardiac injury should be suspected even without heart-sac fluid after puncture.
pmc-13326527:
Sara Beatriz Mendes and team gauged how much we really know about neglected seed spreaders in Europe. Their 2026 study confronts research splitting: work splits by spreader guild, mainly birds, slowing understanding of each group's own share and risking wrong calls about ecosystem bounce-back. The team tested how information on more than 11,000 links among 1,902 plant and 455 animal species built up over 400 years, gauging completeness by guild, plant type, and dispersal mechanism.

Sample coverage for plants dispersed by each animal group ranged from 27% to 79%, with birds of prey, ants, and rodents most ignored at 27%, 28%, and 31%. Research favored fleshy-fruited plants and internal spread, while scientists' perceptions of the most ignored guilds did not match the count estimates. The authors urge join-up studies across guilds, mechanisms, and plant types to predict nature responses to global change and guide conservation.
pmc-13327527:
Lara Calegari and team report an ampullary adenoma first flagged only by itching. Their 2026 case paper trails a 64-year-old woman with body-wide itching, right upper belly ache, and a bile-blocked liver injury pattern. She was later found to have an ampullary growth blocking bile flow. Ampullary adenomas are rare growths with cancer potential that often show vague signs, making spotting hard.

First scope checks and biopsy hinted at low-grade cell change, and bile drain brought brief relief. Lingering signs led to a repeat scope removal of the papilla. Final lab work showed high-grade cell change with positive edges, raising worry that a cancer hid from the first biopsy. The team flags the shifting face of ampullary adenomas and the limits of shallow sampling, urging full lab checks and close watch for suspect growths.
pmc-13327627:
Hui Li and colleagues review microbe-based ways to break down hydrocarbon plastics in a 2026 article. Standard recycling handles these plastics poorly, even though they form the largest share of plastic waste. The authors survey a fast-moving field built on living degradation.

They cover finding new microbes and enzymes that attack major polymers. They also weigh mixed microbe teams that beat single strains, and natural breakdown studies that show what speeds or slows the process. Lab tools and computer methods for screening and engineering are highlighted as well. The goal is to fold living degradation into waste systems so stubborn plastics become feedstock for reuse rather than lasting trash.
pmc-13328027:
Yan Wang and co-authors frame an immune salt-sensing pathway in kidney injury in a 2026 article. Salt-sensitive hypertension is usually blamed on kidney sodium handling and vessel faults, yet immune cells also taste excess salt. The authors argue that the SGK1 kinase and the ENaC sodium channel form an axis that turns salt into inflammation.

In antigen-presenting cells, high salt switches on SGK1, raises channel numbers, and sparks oxidative stress, inflammasome firing, and cytokine release, while in T cells the same kinase backs harmful effector responses. Rather than a side effect of high pressure, immune salt sensing may actively sustain kidney inflammation and harmful remodeling. Pinpointing where the axis runs could open targeted treatments.
pmc-13328327:
Avik Kumar Dhar and co-authors spin biodegradable filter webs from plant-based plastics in a 2026 study. Most melt-blown filter media use polypropylene that never breaks down, so the team blended polylactic acid with polyhydroxyalkanoate and tuned air pressure, melt heat, and blend share. The webs target fine particle filtration for respiratory protection.

Fibers measured 3 to 7 micrometers wide, and adding PHA thickened them while lowering the softening point from 62.9 °C for pure PLA to 58.3 °C at a 90/10 blend in their thermal tests. After electric charging, webs removed over 96 percent of PM0.3 particles with low breathing resistance, and strength rose by about 14.1 percent in peak force. Compostable masks come a step closer.
pmc-13329727:
Alexander Manevich and colleagues set out a 2026 study plan on how doctors spot prolonged grief in older adults. Grief that stays intense can harm health and raise death risk, and older adults face many losses. Since the diagnosis is new in manuals, many doctors may miss it or confuse it with other distress.

The plan has two aims: map what geriatric, psychiatry, and family doctors know and do now, then test a short training video. Doctors will answer an online survey with case stories, then be split at random to watch either the grief training video or a matched control video on bereavement. Blinded scoring will judge whether training improves recognition and use of criteria.
pmc-13330527:
Norni Mualip questions the assumed edge of science-stream schooling in early nursing study in a 2026 report. Data came from 108 first-semester nursing students taking a course on human structure and function at a public institute in Malaysia. Course scores came from official records, while drive, study habits, and felt support came from a questionnaire.

No clear score gap appeared between science-stream and other students in the reported tests. Drive, habits, and support also showed no clear links to scores. The full model explained almost none of the score spread. Mualip argues that teaching design and learning setting may matter more than past stream. Active, meaningful teaching should take priority, the author concludes.
pmc-13330627:
Jordan E Sealey and colleagues trace the source of drug-resistant gut bacteria on Welsh shop meat in a 2026 study. Beef mince and lamb cuts came from independent butchers across Wales, 50 selling beef and 46 selling lamb. Gene family trees compared meat bacteria with farm dung samples and with bacteria from human infections nearby.

Resistance to common drugs appeared in a fair share of samples, while resistance to top-tier drugs stayed rare in the reported rates. Lamb meat bacteria matched sheep-area dung far more than cattle dung, pointing to contamination at or around slaughter. No close matches linked meat bacteria to human infection strains. Wider risk to people looks small, the authors conclude, pending fresher surveys.
pmc-13331227:
Rajat Gupta, Nityanand Pandey, and Basanti Mazumdar report a rare two-sided case of Hirayama disease in a 2026 article. A 23-year-old man had six years of growing weakness and wasting in both lower arms, starting on the right. The pattern spared one forearm muscle, a classic clue, and nerve tests showed chronic lower neck nerve loss with intact feeling.

Standard scans showed a thinned lower neck cord. Bending scans then showed backward cord squeeze with a glowing crescent space behind the cord, matching Hirayama disease. Two-sided even disease is rare and can mimic motor neuron disease. Back-of-neck stabilisation halted progress and improved function in this case.
pmc-13331427:
Shaofei Ni and a large team compare scope methods for deep brain bleed surgery in a 2026 study. Basal ganglia bleeding is a severe stroke type where surgery cuts clot bulk and pressure. Records covered 335 patients treated between January 2021 and May 2024 at 8 Suzhou centres, split into microscope, standard scope, and contact scope groups.

Both scope groups had shorter operations, less blood loss, and shorter intensive care stays than the microscope group in the reported comparisons. Infection rates also ran lower with scopes. Clot removal shares and function scores at 3 months did not differ clearly by method. Age, blood pressure, and clot size predicted poor outcome, not technique.
pmc-13332227:
Tariq Ullah and colleagues study 2026 how small inlet fins affect turbocharger compressor stability and output. Compressors can suffer local and global instability when run off their design point, narrowing the safe working range. The paper tests whether fins at the inlet can curb backflow at the entry and widen the surge-free range. Both bench tests on a small turbocharger and high-fidelity flow simulations were used, with the simulation method validated and checked for mesh independence.

The fins curbed upstream backflow and pre-swirl and steered flow more evenly into the spinning impeller. Under stable, high-flow running, the fins had a neutral to modest effect on peak performance. The value lies in stability: a wider surge margin lets the compressor run safely across more conditions. Designers gain a simple inlet change, backed by both test and simulation, for steadier turbocharger behavior.
pmc-13332427:
Zhao and colleagues compared bedside judgment with lab-confirmed diagnosis in 2026 for pneumonia in critically ill patients on ventilators. Clinicians decide on suspicion, yet how often it matches a verdict built on lung washings, called bronchoalveolar lavage, was undefined. In a single-center study from 2018 to 2022, clinicians rated their suspicion the same day as each washing, and an independent panel adjudicated the true diagnosis.

Among 659 patients, 84 percent were adjudicated to have pneumonia. Clinicians had rated one in five of those patients as low suspicion, while three in ten patients judged free of pneumonia had been rated high suspicion. Vital signs and lab values did not separate the missed group from the caught group. The authors urge humility about clinical gestalt in this setting.
pmc-13333327:
Eduardo Solís García and colleagues frame a 2026 challenge in interventional pulmonology: landing safely on peripheral lung nodules for diagnosis. The essay opens with a space-age metaphor: humanity dreamed of landing on the moon in the twentieth century, while pulmonologists now dream of reaching lung nodules safely and efficiently. Recent advances make that goal increasingly achievable in interventional units, moving from empirical navigation toward real-time precision guidance.

Flexible bronchoscopy has long been used to evaluate peripheral nodules. Baaklini and colleagues reported an overall diagnostic yield of sixty percent, lower for benign lesions and falling with distance from the hilum. Nodule size drove performance, with yields of twenty-three percent for lesions up to two centimetres, dropping to fourteen percent when also peripheral. Complementary techniques such as radial endobronchial ultrasound, detailed in the full paper, aim to lift that modest yield.
pmc-13333427:
Guanglong Wang and Suo Zhang review what triggers pelvic inflammatory disease and what damage it can leave behind, in a 2026 review. The infection of the upper genital tract burdens women's reproductive health worldwide, with half a million to a million new cases a year.

Searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for 2010 to 2025 evidence, the authors sort causes into groups. These include sexually transmitted infections, imbalance of the cervicovaginal bacteria, and medical procedures such as device insertion and fertility treatment. They also include anatomical quirks, other gynecological conditions, habits of daily life, and exposures in the environment, with weight on the vaginal microbiome's role in cases with no clear source. Beyond the fallout of blocked tubes, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, they gather links to ovarian and colorectal cancer, heart and metabolic disease, bowel obstruction, and mental health problems. Early diagnosis, antibiotics, and risk sorting are their prescriptions.
pmc-13333727:
Chakema Carmack and co-authors explored how community research advisory boards experience engagement with academic teams, in a 2026 qualitative study set in urban neighborhoods. Such boards are meant to build trust and ethical practice, but little work has asked board members how engagement feels from their side.

Seven members of the advisory board for the HEALTH Research Center at the University of Houston joined two virtual focus groups held between November 2024 and February 2025. Reflexive thematic analysis produced four themes. Members wanted feedback and lasting engagement, described feeling ignored or used by researchers at times, and asked for advocacy and resources rather than problem descriptions alone. The study spells out what respectful partnership requires from academic teams.
pmc-13334127:
Lei Zhang and co-authors mined the FDA's adverse event database for drug-related muscle toxicity in a 2026 disproportionality analysis. Statins are the famous culprit, but the team wanted a wider map of implicated medicines, with special attention to rhabdomyolysis.

Reports spanning 2004 through 2024 yielded 49,289 muscle toxicity reports covering 47,241 cases and 220 drugs. Three signal-detection methods were applied, with checks by sex, age, and reporter type, plus validation against the WHO VigiAccess database. Nervous system drugs formed the largest share at 27.3 percent, ahead of anti-infectives and cardiovascular drugs. Atorvastatin, simvastatin, and rosuvastatin topped the counts. Some flagged drugs carry no prominent muscle warning in their labeling, which the authors flag for follow-up.
pmc-13334327:
Timothy P W Jones and co-authors tracked outcomes of surgical site infection after cranial surgery at a UK tertiary center in a 2026 retrospective study. Evidence on managing these infections, including how long drug courses should run, is thin.

The Oxford team studied 94 patients who needed repeat surgery for infection after craniotomy, craniectomy, or cranioplasty between January 2019 and April 2022, tracking outcomes to 24 months. Infections stayed superficial in 40 percent of cases, reached the extradural space in 33 percent, and the subdural space in 27 percent. Staphylococcus aureus and Cutibacterium acnes were the most common germs. Repeat surgery rates were similar for superficial and deep infections. Steroid use and long antibiotic courses were each tied to worse outcomes in the analysis, a caution against simply extending treatment.
pmc-13334427:
Ahmet Sami Konca and Hüseyin Ateş built a conceptual model of scientific agency in preschool STEM in a 2026 theoretical article. Early STEM is usually defended by future test scores or described by materials used, neither of which explains how playful exploration turns into inquiry a child actually directs.

Their Play-Based STEM Agency Model treats agency as a young child's situated capacity to shape how a phenomenon gets questioned, interpreted, investigated, and revisited with others. The pathway runs in a loop: play creates accessible uncertainty, uncertainty sparks curiosity, hands-on investigation tests ideas against material feedback, and meaning-making ties experience to comparison and explanation. Agency appears when children's contributions steer the inquiry and teachers and peers recognize them. The model yields testable hypotheses for classroom research.
pmc-13335327:
Ahmed Ibrahim Atalla and co-authors measured upper molar movement during clear aligner treatment in a 2026 prospective imaging series. Sequential distalization with aligners is a popular way to fix Class II bites, but how much of the movement is true translation versus tipping is debated.

Ten maxillary quadrants from seven adults were treated with a standard aligner protocol using vertical attachments, without Class II elastics or skeletal anchorage. Cone-beam CT scans before and after distalization were superimposed in three dimensions. First and second molar crowns moved back by 1.24 and 1.02 millimeters at the cusp tips on average, while root tips barely moved, showing crown-led tipping rather than bodily movement. Front teeth also shifted forward at their edges, a side effect planners should anticipate.
pmc-13336427:
Ying Zhao and co-authors put forward a general recipe for growing metal-organic frameworks on covalent organic frameworks in a 2026 synthesis study. These COF@MOF hybrids tune pores and electronics beautifully, but growing them in a controlled way has lacked a universal method.

Their metal pre-fixation strategy uses carboxylate groups on a pyrene-based COF to anchor metal ions first, guiding later MOF growth across shapes and particle sizes. Mixing experiments with density functional calculations, the team explained the control through ion spread guidance, a crystal-facet shielding hypothesis, and aperture synergy effects. The hybrids separated methane from heavier hydrocarbons better and kept activating hydrogen peroxide efficiently. The strategy turns a bespoke art into adjustable craft for layered porous materials.
pmc-13337827:
Huong Dinh Nguyen and colleagues measure skull base anatomy in Vietnamese cadavers in a 2026 study. The Kawase approach reaches deep areas near the clivus through the petrous bone. Detailed two-sided measurements for Southeast Asian anatomy were lacking.

Dissections followed the standard outer route in 21 formalin-fixed heads, giving 42 sides. Key nerves, the cochlea, ear canal, and petrous artery were found in every case as reported. Average nerve length was 10.66 mm, with set distances between bony openings also recorded in the study. Surgeons can use these figures to judge safe drilling limits before operating on similar patients.
pmc-13338827:
Serhat Al reviews fermented animal foods as a One Health tool against foodborne disease in a 2026 article. Animal foods nourish people but also carry germs that cause illness. Standard safety work targets contamination in food plants, often missing host defenses in the gut.

They also strengthen the gut wall, tune inflammation signals, and support helpful microbes that resist invaders. Pathways involving Toll-like receptors and NF-kB receive special attention. The review argues food safety should pair plant hygiene with diet steps that harden the gut itself.
pmc-13339027:
Maryam Kookhaee and colleagues model protective fluoride layers on a solid battery electrolyte in a 2026 theory study. LATP conducts lithium well but reacts with lithium metal, breaking down at contact. A lithium fluoride coat may block electrons while guarding the surface.

Three crystal faces of the coating on LATP were compared with density theory and motion simulations. Energy, charge flow, and electric field measures judged each layout. The (100) face gave the cleanest blocking response, with no strong trapped states and less charge shift in the reported analysis. Crystal direction therefore matters as much as coating choice for stable solid-state batteries.
pmc-13340727:
Kenneth Mlay and colleagues reported bilateral tension pneumothorax in 2026 in a 3 year old boy four hours after tonsil removal. The child arrived with sudden swelling of face, neck, and chest plus breathing difficulty.

Chest X ray before treatment showed bilateral tension pneumothorax with both lungs collapsed. Urgent needle decompression with a 16 gauge cannula was followed by bilateral chest tubes and decompression of subcutaneous emphysema. By day ten the boy recovered and went home. The case stresses early recognition of this rare, life threatening complication.
pmc-13341427:
Tiny vesicles shed by neutrophils and platelets are hunted in children's arthritic joints by Lillemor Berntson's team in a 2026 pilot study. The exploratory work compared seven children with active, untreated juvenile idiopathic arthritis against ten healthy controls, sampling blood and joint fluid.

Flow cytometry found these vesicles in both blood and synovial fluid of every patient. Two plasma vesicle types ran significantly higher than in controls, and markers of neutrophil nets appeared in both compartments. Activated platelet vesicles stayed mostly in blood. No ties to disease activity scores emerged. The authors present this as a first map of these signals in the disease.
pmc-13341527:
A rare streptococcus causing heart valve infection with brain complications is reported by Hong Zheng's team in their 2026 case report and review. The 68-year-old Chinese man arrived with fever, loss of speech, joint pain, and right-sided weakness from cerebral infarction with bleeding.

Early ultrasound missed the valve growths, which showed only after his brain settled. Culture named Streptococcus sinensis, and antibiotics were adjusted again and again by sensitivity results. Four weeks of linezolid plus cefazolin stabilized him; he declined valve surgery and continued oral therapy for 4 more weeks at home. The case stresses early pathogen identification in endocarditis.
pmc-13345127:
Xiaodong Lin and Alexandru Vlad wrote in 2026 about a single-crystal organic cathode that could lift solid-state batteries. They comment on work by Dincă and co-authors. Solid-state batteries promise safer storage and lithium metal anodes. Yet they often lose power where solid cathode bits meet solid electrolyte.

The featured cathode joins a layered, ordered crystal with its own electric flow and careful electrode design. This eases poor contact, incomplete use of active stuff, and decay at the join that hold the field back. Molecular design and device build are joined in one substance, not kept apart. The comment argues that this mix shows a workable path to high-power batteries that are safe and can be made at scale.
pmc-13345727:
Gustavo Monsalve-Morales and colleagues mapped in 2026 how clinicians and ethicists handle medical futility at the end of life. Following established scoping review methods, the team gathered 36 published studies, mostly retrospective observations and qualitative work. They sorted the clinical, ethical, and prognostic criteria that shape choices about stopping or withholding therapy in adults with limited life expectancy. The synthesis offers teams a clearer shared language for honest talks with patients and families when further treatment would burden without benefit.
pmc-13346027:
Aryan Shah and co-authors systematically review chest infection after heart surgery in 2026.
