Deaths ranged from 1.5 percent with early care to 60 percent in delayed fungal cases. Staphylococci led the germ list, and diabetes, obesity, kidney disease, and long bypass runs raised risk. Timed antibiotics, sugar control, and negative-pressure dressings anchor prevention bundles.
pmc-13346227:
Kuei-Hao Li and Chia-Kai Chang report a 16-week classroom trial, issued in 2026, of an artificial intelligence system that acted as both lecturer and teaching assistant for English learners in Taiwan. The platform, Uedu.tw, taught 120 students at B1 level, split evenly between an artificial intelligence group and a control group with the same teacher and syllabus.

The supported group gained more in learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, and inner motivation, while outer goal orientation did not shift in the same way. Logs of 6,235 assistant queries showed most learners moving from asking for answers toward asking about their own thinking. Interviews added context, though gains after support ends remain untested.
pmc-13348027:
Sean Coyne and co-authors characterise gut bacterial enzymes that alter cortisol and steroid drugs, in a study from 2026. Three enzymes from named gut species trim the same carbon site on cortisol, two giving the beta form and one the alpha form. Kinetics, acidity tests, and docking models compared their reach across related steroid medicines.

All three strongly favoured cortisol yet kept real activity on prednisone and prednisolone. Speed values spanned a wide range in the reported measures. The beta pair also touched triamcinolone. Acidity could choke the beta enzymes at high doses, a quirk docking tied to a single good fit inside the active pocket, raising drug-response questions.
pmc-13349827:
Chunyan Liang and colleagues searched for gene markers of kidney ischemia-reperfusion injury linked to cuproptosis, a copper-driven form of cell death, in a 2026 analysis. They mined public gene datasets, using one cohort for discovery, another for validation, and a third for single-cell work.

From the cuproptosis-related genes that changed in injured kidneys, they built a machine learning diagnostic model and checked it with a nomogram. Pathway and immune analyses showed which signals and immune cells tracked with the marker genes, and patient samples fell into distinct molecular subtypes. Gene changes were then confirmed in a mouse model of the injury. Such markers could speed diagnosis of a common cause of acute kidney injury.
pmc-13349927:
Paola Triggianese and colleagues measured frailty in older people with a rare swelling disease in a 2026 study in Rome. The disease, hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor shortage, causes lifelong attacks. Patients from a specialist centre were compared with healthy controls of similar age.

Everyone had a full check of memory, mood, daily tasks, and balance. Disease activity and quality of life scores captured the burden of the attacks. Other illnesses were also counted. Long years of attacks plus other health problems can shrink independence and social life. Grading frailty directly shows clinicians what older patients need beyond attack control.
pmc-13350027:
Zishan Liang and colleagues reviewed gene editing tools for four workhorse Gram-positive bacteria in 2026. These species serve industry as fermenters, probiotics, and synthetic biology platforms, but their thick walls and varied genetics make editing uneven.

Coverage runs from older recombination methods to CRISPR-Cas9, base editors, and tools that insert large DNA stretches, traced species by species. The four are Lactobacillus plantarum, Lactococcus lactis, the spore former Bacillus subtilis, and Corynebacterium glutamicum. Shared hurdles include each host's repair habits and whether editors function inside it. The authors close with practical advice on picking a tool for a given job, aiming to save other labs trial and error.
pmc-13350527:
Lukasz Przybylski and Gregory Kroliczak scanned brains in 2026 to map how people process what objects afford, the actions things invite. Sixty-two participants, over half of them not right-handed, viewed 12 tools and 12 control objects during three tasks: recognising tools, planning a functional grip, and miming tool use.

Grip planning and miming leaned on the left brain, while simple tool viewing did not, depending on the region. Three processing streams contributed differently by task and complexity, and side preferences correlated between some task pairs and with handedness for two tasks. The results refine how perception and action systems share the work of skilled tool use.
pmc-13351427:
Daniel Perin and Rodrigo Leal Alves wrote a 2026 editorial arguing that training and judgement, not gadgets, remain the core technology of airway management. Anaesthetists now have video scopes, better breathing tubes, ultrasound, and cheap printed devices, vastly widening the toolkit over two decades.

Discussing three studies in the same journal issue, including a low-cost 3D-printed video laryngoscope, they stress that tools fail without structured education and practised decision making. Success still rests on knowledge, preparation, and experience when a patient's airway turns difficult. Their message to the specialty is to invest in people as heavily as in equipment.
pmc-13352427:
Jasmine Hernández and co-authors study brain patterns tied to the value of helping family during adolescence in 2026. Supporting family matters deeply to many teens across cultures, and teen years bring growth in value-based choices. A total of 266 adolescents, in groups aged 9 to 15 and 19 to 20 years, did a giving task during brain scanning.

In the task, teens could give money to caregivers, friends, or strangers at a cost to themselves. Stronger family duty values predicted weaker coupling between the ventral striatum and social and control networks in older teens during family giving. Younger teens showed a weaker or reversed pattern. Results suggest social brain areas tune how strongly duty shapes reward signals.
pmc-13352627:
Ji Hyeon Kim leads a 2026 drug study that turns a weak kinase blocker scaffold into a targeted protein degrader for CDK6. Breaker drugs built from blockers usually keep blocking action, and type II CDK blockers are notoriously weak in cells. Starting from regorafenib, the team built a small library of bifunctional molecules that recruit the CRL4-CRBN disposal machinery.

Protein-wide mass checks unexpectedly flagged CDK5 and CDK6 as disposal targets, though the parent drug does not block them. Tuning gave JHK-02-108-2, a selective CDK6 degrader with no hook effect at high doses. It destroys CDK6 strongly despite weak binding and almost no blocking, showing degradation can reach targets that inhibition alone cannot.
pmc-13353027:
Shanshan Xu led a 2026 network study of academic involution and anxiety among Chinese undergraduates. Involution describes escalating effort that yields little academic return, a pattern now common in Chinese higher education. Earlier work linked involution to anxiety overall, but the symptom-to-symptom connections stayed unclear.

A snapshot survey of 1,403 undergraduates in Shandong Province checked involution with a twenty-four-item scale and anxiety with the twenty-item Zung scale. A regularised partial correlation network mapped links between single symptoms. The study reveals which involution pressures connect most closely to which anxiety symptoms, pointing support services toward the most damaging links.
pmc-13353527:
Yuhei Kasai and co-authors describe a shoulder lift trick that salvaged a heart lead extraction in 2026. A woman aged 50 years with cardiac sarcoidosis, ventricular fibrillation, and complete heart block had a defibrillator placed 5 years earlier. Her ventricular lead misread signals and blocked pacing in a pacing-dependent patient, causing repeated near-faints, so extraction and replacement were planned.

A tandem approach with snare capture still failed to align the extraction sheath with the lead. Laser and mechanical sheaths from Cook Medical and Philips also stalled. Lifting the shoulder shifted the lead path and let a Byrd sheath advance to finish the job. The healthy atrial lead was left in place throughout.
pmc-13355027:
Hong Xu and co-authors used light-based brain scans in 2026 to spot how ischemic stroke changes brain function. They recorded 115 stroke patients and 45 healthy adults at rest, during a word task, and during a hand grip task. Computer models, from simple classifiers to a deep learning model, then tried to tell the groups apart.

Stroke patients showed weaker links between movement and sense areas at rest and odd blood flow in speech and planning areas during tasks. The deep learning model did best, reaching 86 percent correct on the grip task. The authors say pairing these scans with smart models could aid stroke checks and rehab planning without surgery or radiation.
pmc-13355227:
Giulio Gualdi and others told of a new inside-out operation for localised hidradenitis suppurativa, in 2026. This chronic swelling disease of hair follicles causes painful nodules, abscesses, tunnels, and scarring in skin folds. Drugs control swelling, but lasting tunnelled lesions often need surgery, and standard deroofing or excision works from the surface inward.

The broad reverse approach, called BRASH, instead tackles the lesion from inside out, aiming for thorough tunnel clearance while keeping surrounding tissue. The paper sets out the challenge, the method, and its rationale for selected localised cases. Surgeons gain an other approach for lesions where surface-first surgery leaves disease behind.
pmc-13355527:
Philippe Le Moal and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 39-year-old man who suffered severe kidney failure after taking traditional Sri Lankan medicine for neck pain for about two weeks. He developed gut upset, a wide rash, and kidney failure that needed dialysis and intensive care. A kidney biopsy showed an inflamed pattern with granulomas, which hinted at a drug cause.

Steroid treatment let dialysis stop and his kidneys fully recovered. The team then tested the traditional products with a precise chemical method and found many hidden compounds known to harm kidneys and trigger allergy, among them pain drugs of the NSAID type. The case warns that unknown mixes can hide risky drugs.
pmc-13355727:
Neha R Tandon and others tested the repeatability of a new photopic microperimetry approach in geographic atrophy, in 2026. Geographic atrophy damages central vision, and a test that targets the central one millimetre of the fovea could track function more sensitively than broader tests. Before such a test can serve trials, its repeatability must be proven.

Twelve people with non-subfoveal atrophy, seventeen eyes in total, performed focal photopic tests on a forty-five-point grid, twice up to four weeks apart, with other visual function assessments. Repeatability and links to lesion area were studied. Teams gain evidence on whether this focused test is stable enough to detect real change over time.
pmc-13356727:
Kazumasa Takayama and Hiromu Ito compared two shoulder operations in 2026 for patients with rotator cuff tears too large to repair directly. One option replaces the joint with a reverse implant, and the other rebuilds the top capsule with a thigh tissue graft. Twenty and twenty-two patients were followed for at least two years, with strength and movement measured.

The implant group recovered more lifting strength, at 67 percent of the healthy side versus 52 percent. The graft group recovered full inward rotation strength and moved the shoulder further in several directions. Outward rotation strength did not differ. The authors say the strength-versus-motion split can guide surgical choice.
pmc-13358827:
Tao Lin and co-authors build a simple forecast for lung cancer spread in a 2026 study. Whether lung adenocarcinoma has reached nearby lymph nodes drives staging and treatment. The team wanted a tool any clinic could use before surgery, built from facts already on hand: tumor size and a blood marker called CEA.

They studied 6,406 patients whose cancer was removed, splitting them by date into building and testing groups. Only tumor size and the blood marker proved to be independent predictors of node spread. Their chart, a nomogram, turns those two facts into a risk estimate. A simple, honest tool like this can guide how widely surgeons should sample nodes.
pmc-13359527:
Bojie Chen and co-authors study a hidden cost of antibiotics in cancer care in a 2026 paper. Patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a cancer behind the nose, are treated mainly with chemotherapy plus radiation. Antibiotics are often added to fight infections during that treatment. The team found that patients who received them had worse cancer-specific survival.

The likely culprit is the gut: antibiotics disturb gut microbes, which dulls the immune response the treatment depends on. The authors urge doctors to weigh infection control against this risk and to time antibiotic use with care. More study is needed to build precise rules that protect both aims.
pmc-13360827:
İlknur Keskin and co-authors tested a heart drug as a possible colon cancer aid in rats in a 2026 study. The drug, hydroquinidine, is used for abnormal heart rhythms, and reusing known drugs is a fast route to new cancer options. First the team checked safety, dosing rats daily for 90 days under standard rules. The drug was tolerated up to a mid dose, while the top dose caused liver strain signs without deaths.

They then gave safe doses to rats with chemically triggered colon cancer, comparing them with a standard chemo drug. Tissue checks and marker tests covered inflammation, cell death, and pathways that help cancer spread. Early animal work like this shows whether a reused drug deserves deeper study, and where its safe dose range lies.
pmc-13361527:
Huaxin Cai and co-authors built a nanoparticle bait against the red imported fire ant in a 2026 study. This invasive ant damages farms, wildlife, and people, while standard poisons pollute and lose power as ants resist them. The team made silver nanoparticles with help from pyrethrins, a plant insecticide, through a green process. They tested the particles on worker ants in bait feeding tests.

The bait proved highly toxic: at a mid dose, all worker ants died within nine days of feeding. The particles stayed effective after time in the open, showing good staying power. A deep chemical scan of treated ants revealed how their metabolism was disrupted. The work points to a greener weapon against a pest that spreads across warm regions worldwide.
pmc-13362427:
Leonardo Jacobsen and co-authors set out a 2026 hypothesis paper on hard-to-treat endometriosis, a painful condition where womb-like tissue grows outside the womb. They suggest that low levels of gut hormones called incretins in the belly fluid may help keep the disease going. From that idea, they argue the diabetes drug tirzepatide, which boosts those hormones, might ease the disease on several fronts at once.

The paper maps how the drug could, in theory, curb cell fuel misuse, calm immune cells, slow scar-like tissue growth, and blunt pain signals. The authors are clear that no direct test in endometriosis exists yet. The piece is a plan for future lab and clinic work, not proof that the drug helps.
pmc-13362727:
Qiwen Qiu and Denvid Lau report a 2026 methods study on how salt chloride creeps into cement mortar under coastal style cycles of salt fog and drying. Chloride rusts the steel inside concrete, so measuring its slow entry matters for bridges and sea walls. The pair built a new test rig with an outer tank and four inner chambers, then watched chloride profiles form over months of cycling.

A steady flow state emerged, with straight-line chloride slopes in two zones, and the team fit a two-segment line model to match. Their derived spread rates line up with field data for concrete in salty air. Water mix and fog heat shifted the rates somewhat, and the authors give upgrade advice for coarser mixes.
pmc-13363427:
Sergi Casanova-Crespo and colleagues present a 2026 rat study on a diet rich in fermentable fiber and polyphenols, the plant compounds in fruit, tea, and cocoa. Healthy female rats ate either a standard diet or the enriched diet for nine weeks. The team then read immune markers in blood and gut tissue, the cecal microbe mix, and the fatty acids those microbes produce.

The enriched group carried more of the main antibody type in blood and more of one subtype in gut tissue, with no change to gut shape or blood fats. Their microbes were more even in mix and made more acetate and propionate, helpful fermentation products. The authors say plant-rich eating can tune gut and immune balance in health.
pmc-13364427:
Ke Ma and co-workers test in 2026 how two forms of silicon help rice young plants bear cold snaps. One form is plain dissolved silicon. The other is silicon in tiny grains. Cold cut growth, green tint, and leaf gas work in the test plants.

Both forms eased the cold harm, but the tiny grain form did more. It kept plant height, root reach, and dry weight high, and it lifted leaf gas work and sugar flow. It also cut cell harm marks. The work backs grain silicon as a shield for rice in cold spells.
pmc-13365127:
Gizem Örnek and co-workers test in 2026 two web fed ways to teach new teachers. One is flipped class, where first reads move home and class time turns to group work. The next is plain web lessons. They track 74 third year teacher trainees for six weeks of class in a life science course.

Flipped class beat web lessons on views toward group learn. Both beat old class style on learn plan skills by a clear gap. The team backs flipped class as a strong pick for teacher schools that want team skills and smart learn habits built in, not just facts taught.
pmc-13366427:
Abbigail McCune and co-workers find in 2026 a feed loop that locks young blood cells into the myeloid line, the white cell arm that eats germs. A growth cue and a stat signal path work as a pair. The team uses fish with switch genes, cell sorts, and gene maps to trace the loop.

The stat path turns the cue gene on, and the cue boosts the stat path in turn. The loop runs in ripe blood growth, not the first wave. Set blood cells from this loop heal flesh more well. A human blood ill line needs the cue too, a drug lead.
pmc-13369527: Breen and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their qualitative study of the DEPPLOY project. That project explored a primary care effort in England to help older adults living with frailty stop unneeded medicines safely. Author Daisy Halligan has been removed from the author group, and the corrected author list is given in the notice. A key table of implementation framework domains also had its construct and description columns out of line, and the realigned table replaces the original in the journal record.
pmc-13370727:
van Helden and colleagues argue that the inflammation triggered by snake venom is not just side damage but part of how venom spreads, in 2026 toxinology research. Envenomation switches on defenses through factors that raise blood vessel permeability, opening large pores in the smallest vessels, which the authors call inflammation-activated pores. Plasma then leaks into tissues. Their experiments show the same pores let large molecules, including venom toxins, flood directly from tissue into the bloodstream, against the outward plasma flow.

The team measured the pore radius at 21 nanometers, with a confidence interval from 18 to 24 nanometers in tracer tests. Dextran test molecules confirmed this absorption route works alongside the lymphatic drainage route, clearing molecules from tissue spaces. They name the process inflammation-facilitated macromolecular absorption. van Helden suggests venom evolved to exploit the body's inflammatory plumbing, a reframing that could matter for designing antivenoms and first aid that limit toxin uptake.
pmc-13370827:
David Evans and co-workers weigh in 2026 block chain tech as a fix for kidney data woes: split sets, share risk, and dim source trails. Chain logs can not be re writ, join cross sys, and run set rules by code. Those traits could guard care data and prove its path.

Like gains could track drug lots, bio banks, and gear care logs. Yet clash with wipe rights in EU law, slow speed, and cost cloud the worth. The team holds the tech as a may be, to test where its traits pay more than its drag.
pmc-13374227:
Andre Matthias Müller and colleagues measure empathy in newly enrolled health students in Singapore in a 2026 study. Empathy can be nurtured, yet starting predispositions predict success in training and practice. New students in dentistry, medicine, nursing, and pharmacy at the National University of Singapore completed the Jefferson empathy scale and a custom empathic care intentions measure.

Of 646 participants, a 37 percent response rate, median empathy was 109 out of 140. Medicine students scored higher than other disciplines, and dentistry students scored higher than nursing students, with similar patterns for care intentions. The findings can inform admissions and curricula, helping schools build on existing empathy rather than assuming all entrants start from the same place.
pmc-13374627:
Pratik Rathi and co-authors share a hard brain ill case in a 2026 report. A woman aged 23 grew odd in acts and clouded in mind. She was first thought to have a mind ill alone. Then tests found immune marks in her spinal fluid and a cold sore virus in the same fluid.

The virus can spark a grave immune attack on the brain weeks on. She got virus drugs plus a stack of immune calmers, from steroids to blood wash and a B cell drug. A long intensive stay brought lung fail, shock, and kidney harm. The case shows why both germ and immune checks count in such turns.
pmc-13375427:
Grace Gorecki and co-authors chart two decades of a grave protein ill in a 2026 study. The ill lays stray protein in the heart and nerves and was long a death call. A new immune drug has joined care in late years, but real-world trends were not mapped.

A world health web gave 43,878 adults from 2006 to 2025, once kin ills were barred. Life odds rose in the last decade next to the first, with a risk cut of one fourth. Mid-stage heart cases gained the most. The worst heart stage gained none. The split tells teams where new care has yet to reach.
pmc-13377827:
Saloua Lemrabett and colleagues study parental views on HPV vaccination in northern Morocco in a 2026 mixed-methods paper. Morocco launched national HPV vaccination in 2022 to prevent cervical cancer, yet coverage remains very low, likely due to parental hesitancy. Parents of young girls in the north were surveyed face to face between 2024 and 2025, with a focus group adding depth.

Of 300 parents, mean age near 38, only 10 percent knew persistent HPV causes cervical cancer, and only 8.7 percent knew about the national programme. Overall, 60 percent reported good acceptability of vaccination. Older age and formal education were linked to greater hesitancy. Qualitative findings suggested excellent acceptability in principle, with low uptake driven mainly by lack of awareness rather than opposition.
pmc-13380127:
Priyal Mehta and colleagues present a 2026 case of a fast-growing lymphoma that hid behind two seemingly separate problems. Their patient, a 76-year-old man, kept developing fluid around the lungs and bleeding from the gut. Such a cancer usually shows as a rapidly growing lump, so the picture was misleading.

Tests eventually found the lymphoma in several places outside the lymph nodes: the stomach, liver, and the lining around the lungs. The team also reviews published cases of unusual presentations. Because treatment started early gives the best chance, they urge doctors to consider this cancer when fluid and bleeding recur without a clear cause. It accounts for about a third of adult lymphomas of its broad type.
pmc-13380327:
David A Febre-Alemañy and co-authors describe a 2026 case of Rapunzel syndrome, where swallowed hair forms a mass that blocks the gut. Their patient was a 17-year-old girl with autism who had three weeks of belly pain, nausea, and vomiting. Her guardian reported no hair pulling or eating of non-food items, which made the cause less obvious.

Scans showed a continuous large mass filling the stomach and the next section of bowel. A camera test confirmed a hair mass blocking the stomach outlet. Surgeons opened the abdomen and removed two masses, one from the stomach and one further along. The report highlights the diagnostic challenge when the usual history is absent.
pmc-13380727:
Kaisa T Oja and a very large team present a 2026 study widening the picture of a developmental disorder linked to a gene called ABCA2. Faults in both copies of the gene were already tied to intellectual disability. The team asked what happens when only one copy is faulty, and how wide the range of effects is.

Clinical details were gathered through questionnaires and published reports. The team also modelled the protein, tested blood chemistry broadly, and used a cell model to study how gene variants affect drug sensitivity. Combining those strands builds a fuller picture of the condition. A clearer spectrum helps doctors recognise the disorder and counsel families about what to expect.
pmc-13383127:
Yuke Cui's team tested whether heart rate predicts in-hospital trouble after ST-elevation heart attack, in a 2026 study. The team followed 309 consecutive patients who received primary percutaneous coronary intervention at Ruijin Hospital between September 2018 and December 2020. Rates at first medical contact, at admission, and at 24 hours were each tested.

Admission and 24-hour rates both predicted in-hospital cardiovascular events, driven mainly by acute heart failure. Each 5-beat rise in admission rate raised event risk by 18.6 percent, and each 5-beat rise at 24 hours raised it by 19.8 percent. First-contact rate carried little predictive value, so ward teams should weight later rates more heavily.
pmc-13383927:
Mark Kodsy's team describes a donor-graft rebuild technique for unstable kneecaps, in a 2026 surgical paper. Kneecap instability strikes adolescents and young athletes after medial patellofemoral ligament injury, and graft tension and fixation problems persist. The team presents a method emphasizing stepwise tightening of medial knee layers, anatomic femoral tunnel placement, and all-suture kneecap fixation.

The approach restores both the static hold of the graft and the dynamic steadying effect of medial soft tissues, creating a bumper effect akin to shoulder stabilization. It works alone or alongside bony or cartilage procedures. The technique offers surgeons a durable, thoughtful option for recurrent kneecap instability.
pmc-13385727:
Stanton and colleagues discover that having two X chromosomes protects embryonic stem cells against chromosome errors, in 2026 stem cell genetics research. Aneuploidy, gaining or losing chromosomes, plagues stem cell cultures and mirrors cancer biology. Mining RNA and protein data from lines derived from 170 Diversity Outbred mice, the team detected aneuploid subpopulations in 62 lines. They also found originally female XX lines that had lost one X, becoming XO during culture.

A lower proportion of XX lines were aneuploid than XY or XO lines. Single-cell data showed XY aneuploid lines expressed X-linked genes at less, and a culture study confirmed XY cells accumulate chromosome errors faster than XX cells. Protective mechanisms are proposed: XX lines keep two-cell-like cells, a genome-guarding state, and express more X-linked tumor suppressor genes, and they outcompete abnormal neighbors in mixed culture. Stanton links chromosome X dosage directly to genomic integrity.
pmc-13385827:
Wei Jia's team quantified how crowding plus poor ventilation drives respiratory infection risk, in a 2026 study. Crowded indoor spaces drive outbreaks and superspreading, yet the interplay of crowding, room size, and ventilation was underexplored. The team built a framework using effective clean flow rate, combining clean airflow with volume-time air clearance and intake fraction time.

Outbreak data from jails, earthquake shelters, and dormitories showed modest spaciousness of 16 to 32 cubic meters per person raised effective clean flow by 8.7 to 17.6 liters per second per person in low-ventilation settings. Current ASHRAE 62.1-2022 standards fall short in crowded spaces, the authors warn, heightening infection risk where people pack tightest.
pmc-13386027:
Harneet Kaur Bhullar and co-authors disable two calcium transport routes in mice to test whether they back each other up. One route passes calcium through cells via the channel TRPV6; the other slips it between cells through the junction protein claudin-2. Their 2026 study crosses mice lacking each route to make double knockouts.

Single mutants mostly compensated: claudin-2 knockouts wasted calcium in urine but kept normal blood calcium and bone density. The double knockouts could not compensate. They developed low blood calcium, raised active vitamin D, and reduced bone density, and their kidneys wasted even more calcium than claudin-2 knockouts alone, despite unchanged calcium loss in faeces. Gene activity rose in the colon and kidney, showing partial rescue attempts by other segments. The authors conclude the two pathways jointly guard calcium balance, and that TRPV6 also matters in the kidney's later segments.
pmc-13386827:
Laura Andrea Charola-Ramos's team built a TaqMan real-time PCR test for psittacine adenovirus 1, in a 2026 paper. Psittacine adenoviruses can kill parrots or infect them silently, and silent carriers entering the bird trade can spread virus widely, so sensitive, specific diagnosis matters. The team compared the new TaqMan assay with standard PCR and SYBR Green PCR on serial dilutions and clinical samples, using a parrot-specific control assay to check DNA extraction quality.

All three methods showed comparable sensitivity on liver samples. The TaqMan assay detected virus better in cloacal swabs than standard PCR, while keeping high specificity and showing no cross-reaction with other avian pathogens. The test offers a rapid, sensitive, specific tool for routine diagnosis and surveillance of psittacine adenovirus, especially in asymptomatic birds.
pmc-13386927:
Larry He's team linked socioeconomic factors to chlamydia and gonorrhea positivity in the United States from 2022 to 2024, in a 2026 study. Prior work tied area-level poverty and eviction rates to STI rates, but patient-level evidence was thin. The team drew urogenital test records for patients aged 15 to 44 from the Truveta electronic health record dataset, stratifying positive rates by demographics, recent eviction, and educational achievement.

Among about 1.8 million chlamydia tests and about 1.8 million gonorrhea tests, overall positive rates ran about 5 percent for chlamydia and about 2 percent for gonorrhea. Patients with no college education on record tested positive more often than those with four-year degrees, for both infections. Recent eviction also tracked with higher positive rates for both infections. The findings argue for targeted, cross-sector efforts on housing and education to improve STI prevention and care.
pmc-13388227:
Lina Ataya and colleagues report a giant liver growth that masked a separate chest infection in a 2026 case report. A 41-year-old man arrived with fever, chest pain, and a large fluid collection around his right lung after a lung biopsy. Scans also showed a large liver lesion with atypical features that suggested cancer or spread infection.

Liver biopsy instead proved a benign cavernous hemangioma, a common slow-growing vessel tangle. The chest fluid proved to be empyema, most likely seeded by the recent biopsy procedure itself. The authors use the case to warn against anchoring on one dramatic finding when two diseases coexist.
pmc-13388727:
Ece Ozkan presents, in 2026, a new electrochemical sensor built to detect a blood marker linked to acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. This cancer accounts for most leukaemia cases in children, yet diagnosis still relies on blood counts and bone marrow sampling, which can be slow and invasive.

The sensor uses a plastic film moulded to recognise phosphoenolpyruvate, a compound tied to the disease, fixed onto a carbon electrode. Tests showed very high sensitivity, with detection limits far below levels found by standard methods. Readers in medical diagnostics gain a proof-of-concept device that points toward faster and simpler early testing, while the report details the film recipe and the checks used to confirm selective detection.
pmc-13390027: Zhang writes a letter questioning whether the prognostic nutritional index, an albumin-and-lymphocyte score, merits any role in cancer care, in 2026 correspondence with Li and colleagues. Zhang argues the index duplicates standard variables such as stage and performance status, and that reviews rarely test whether it adds discrimination or reclassifies patients. Raising albumin or lymphocytes through nutrition has not been shown to reverse the inflammation driving cancer progression. The index remains a descriptive marker of reserve, not a directive tool for decisions.
pmc-13391727:
Catia Nicodemo, Cheti Nicoletti, and Joaquim Vidiella-Martin investigate, in 2026, why the youngest children in a school year are more often treated with ADHD medication. The pattern is usually blamed on comparison with older classmates, but the mechanisms behind it remain debated.

Using English administrative data and the sharp first of September entry cutoff, the team compared children born just before and after the line. Early starters were far more likely to be treated by age fifteen, and the gap was driven entirely by first prescriptions between ages five and eight. Education and health policymakers gain a decomposition showing that early mislabelling, not later catch-up prescribing, creates the lasting gap.
pmc-13392627:
Zahra Torabi Mirabadi, Fariba Khalili, and Elmira Ziya Motalebipour tested whether treating beet microgreens before and after harvest could slow their rapid fading in storage. These tiny greens are prized for colour and health compounds but spoil within days. Plants were sprayed daily with calcium chloride for two weeks before cutting, then given ultraviolet light or a vitamin B12 compound after harvest.

Calcium spray lifted pigment levels, looks, antioxidant strength, and sugar content, with the strongest dose performing best. Ultraviolet treatment after harvest further protected colour and health compounds, and those greens decayed slowest over four cold days. The vitamin compound at low dose hurt every measure instead. The pairing of calcium before harvest with ultraviolet after it gave the best keeping quality in this trial.
pmc-13392827:
Taslim Uddin leads a seventeen-author review of reactive oxygen species, the corrosive oxygen by-products that cancer cells both exploit and fear. Tumours live under constant oxidative pressure from faulty energy systems and stress. They use moderate levels of these molecules as growth signals. At the same time they build strong defences, centred on glutathione, thioredoxin, and the Nrf2 control switch, to keep levels survivable. Some cancers grow dependent on that defence wiring.

Therapies that push oxidation higher have repeatedly stumbled in the clinic, squeezed by side effects, poor tumour targeting, and tumours rewiring their shields. Large trials of antioxidant pills even raised cancer risk in places. The review highlights ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death from fat oxidation, as a weak spot in heavily defended tumours when key guard systems fail. Matching treatment to each tumour's redox state is presented as the way forward.
pmc-13393727: Yasutaka Kaihara and seven colleagues issue a correction to their study of incompetent lip seal, mouth breathing, and stress in Japanese young adults. Its factors span nose disease, lip seal and mouth breathing, teeth and gum condition, bad breath, and lip dryness. Every intercorrelation in the corrected matrix is statistically real. pmc-13430827:

pmc-13431427:

pmc-13434127:

pmc-13435427:

pmc-13435627:

pmc-13435727:

pmc-13435827:

pmc-13445527:

Precision treatment that modifies disease course over the long term is the stated goal. The lining moves to centre stage as both driver and drug target.
pmc-13448827:
Zhe Wang and coauthors review a 2026 roundup of anti-death BCL-2 family proteins, the living factors that guard the powerhouse outer membrane against inner cell death. The review traces many-layer control spanning gene-reading factors, splicing and micro-RNAs, and protein-level tweaks that set protein steadiness and function.

Venetoclax set BCL-2 aiming as strong therapy in chronic lymph blood cancer and acute myeloid blood cancer, yet fight-back through MCL-1 boost, BCL-2 gene change, and energy rewire persists. BCL-XL blockade causes clotting-cell poison risk. MCL-1 blockers carry heart risk, so the authors survey aimed breakers, defense pairs, next-new blockers, and marker-guided picking.
pmc-13449027:
Collins and colleagues test whether a blood marker can show when an Alzheimer's drug has cleared amyloid from the brain in this 2026 trial analysis. The drug, donanemab, removes amyloid plaques, and doctors normally confirm clearance with PET brain scans. The candidate substitute is plasma p-tau217, a blood form of the tau protein, measured in participants of the phase 3 TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 trial with early symptomatic disease.

P-tau217 levels fell during donanemab treatment. Still, the marker identified scan-confirmed clearance only weakly. Its discrimination score was about 0.61 at 52 weeks, a value the authors report for the 830 treated participants assessed. That performance is barely better than chance for individual decisions. The authors conclude the blood test cannot currently replace imaging for judging whether amyloid clearance has been achieved.
pmc-13449327:
Cristiane Pontes de Barros Leal and Flávia Martão Flório surveyed Brazilian dental schools in 2026 about teaching on sleep-disordered breathing. The condition ranges from simple snoring to obstructive sleep apnea, which carries heart, metabolic, and brain risks. Dentists are well placed to spot it early, yet earlier studies in other countries found thin coverage in dental courses.

The team sent questionnaires to coordinators and orthodontics teachers at the 238 schools that took part in Brazil's 2019 national student exam, collecting replies from March to October 2022. About half of coordinators and most professors responded, and the answers map what is taught, how much time it gets, and what blocks wider teaching. Curriculum planners can see where training lags and what support faculty say they need.
pmc-13450027:
Myungjin Jung and colleagues ask in 2026 whether the brain benefits of aerobic exercise arrive at the same ages for all. They followed 107 adults, fifty-five to eighty, through a six-month program, split between moderate-to-vigorous intensity and a light-intensity comparison. Tests of executive function and processing speed, plus brain scans, bracketed the program. A time-varying statistical method let the links between brain network change and cognitive change bend with age.

The stronger program paid off in set windows. Processing speed improved at ages fifty-eight to sixty-five, and connectivity in the dorsal attention network rose at sixty-seven to sixty-nine. Across the mid-sixties to mid-seventies, gains in connectivity inside control, default mode, and salience networks tracked better scores in the harder-training group. The authors say intensity and timing both matter. Programs should aim the vigorous dose at these receptive years.
pmc-13450527:
Yuhua Wen and colleagues pool world data in 2026 on how often two long-term lung diseases sit alongside bronchiectasis, a lasting widening of the airways. They searched three large databases for studies of adults whose airway damage was confirmed by chest scans. The COPD pool held 52 studies, and the asthma pool held 47.

About 18 percent of patients with bronchiectasis also had COPD, while about 16 percent also had asthma. Rates shifted by region, study design, and age, and the share of women in a study weakly tracked its asthma rate. The authors urge clinics to screen for both extra diseases, since overlap shapes symptoms and care.
pmc-13452327:
Mohamed Ellabbad and co-authors test in 2026 whether repeat reads of a heart strain protein beat one read for adults born with heart defects. Past work in this group was small with short follow-up. The team drew 3,674 adults with two-chamber hearts and a left main pump, each with at least two reads of the protein between 2003 and 2023.

Two thirds of patients saw the protein climb over time. Both the first level and the climb tied to death risk in every subgroup, and repeat reads out-forecast single reads plus standard clinic scores. About an eighth of the group died in follow-up. The authors tout the cheap blood test for long-term watch.
pmc-13454027:
Michela Rossi, Marta Gomarasca, and Ettore Luzi open a journal collection on non coding RNA networks in bone health and disease with this 2026 editorial. These RNAs do not build proteins; they tune which genes speak, and they have reshaped how scientists read bone growth, aging, and decay. The editorial frames the collection around three RNA classes: micro, long non coding, and circular forms.

The pieces gathered cover how these RNAs steer bone building and bone eating cells, vessel growth, and joint swelling signals. One review maps micro RNA control in osteoporosis, including RNA cargo shipped between cells in tiny vesicles. The editors stress the RNAs' double promise as blood markers of bone disease and as drug targets in their own right. Aging, cell senescence, and immune cross talk run through the collection as shared threads.
pmc-13454327:
Pei Wen and others tied TLCD1 to liver cancer growth in 2026, through ERK signal firing. Liver cancer spreads fast and kills with a poor outlook, and finding driver genes is key to good cures. TLCD1, a membrane-traffic and fat-handling gene, ran high in tumours by computer hints, but lab proof was missing.

Gene-read and stain data showed TLCD1 high in liver tumours, with high levels tied to short whole and disease-free survival. Cell models with TLCD1 raised or cut showed it spurred growth and spread, while a cut held them back. Lab work tied TLCD1 to ERK cascade firing. Cancer doctors gain a driver gene and path for liver cancer cures.
pmc-13454427:
Héloïse Bizière-Maco leads a fourteen-author study, from 2026, of chemical chatter among Rhodococcus bacteria. Bacteria use quorum sensing, releasing signal molecules to coordinate group behavior. In Streptomyces, such signals are gamma-butyrolactones, small ring-shaped chemicals that control spore formation and useful compound making. Whether cousin genera share the system was poorly known.

Gene comparisons showed the signal-making and signal-reading genes are widespread and clustered in Rhodococcus. Protein models matched the Streptomyces versions closely. Chemical tests then confirmed that the strain R. erythropolis R138 releases active signal-like molecules. Without its signal gene, a Streptomyces partner failed to form spores nearby, and adding the Rhodococcus strain restored that step. Two regulators appear to fine-tune signal output. The authors say the system could be harnessed for biocontrol and natural product work.
pmc-13454927:
Zach G. Walters, Marie Deliaval, Aimee Long, and Neil K. Garg report, in a 2026 chemistry study, palladium-driven reactions of a molecule long deemed too unstable to use. Anti-Bredt olefins carry a double bond at a bridgehead spot that small rings cannot comfortably hold. The team generated one such fleeting species, built on a tight bicyclic frame, inside the reaction flask.

Palladium catalysis caught the short-lived molecule and joined it with indole-based partners, yielding unusual ring-fused products. The trick works because two scarce, temporary species meet productively at low concentration. Calculations suggest the metal steadies the wild olefin by forming a ring-shaped intermediate. The authors mapped which partners react well. They expect the approach to widen the chemistry of strained, short-lived building blocks that textbooks once wrote off as unusable.
pmc-13455327:
Wenting Pan and colleagues design a drinkable gel for bowel inflammation in a 2026 animal study. Standard colitis drugs often miss the colon, cause whole-body side effects and leave excess oxidants and immune imbalance untouched, while vitamin B2, riboflavin, is absorbed too early to help the colon. The team built a food-grade alginate liquid that turns into a sticky gel in the mildly acid colon, carrying riboflavin inside acid-sensitive platinum particles.

Once the gel settled, acid broke the particles open, releasing riboflavin and platinum ions together at the sore site. In a mouse colitis model the gel stayed longer and cleared harmful oxygen species. It calmed one inflammatory immune cell type, rebalanced two others, strengthened the gut lining and shifted gut microbes toward a healthier mix. A 14-day repeat-dose safety check is noted, but human trials must still show whether it works and stays safe in people.
pmc-13455427:
Aimé Nun and colleagues pilot crisis training built for French public health residents in a 2026 feasibility study. Public health residents manage crises from offices and agencies, not bedsides, yet most crisis training was designed for clinical teams. The pilot, named ISP25, paired a French health administration session with a high-fidelity crisis-room simulation for six residents in Île-de-France, using newly French-adapted rating tools.

All six residents valued the prebriefing and debriefing. Self-rated leadership and communication trended upward, while problem-solving scores stalled or fell for some. The authors read that pattern as humbled self-judgement after immersion. With only six participants, effectiveness cannot be judged, but the study shows the format is feasible and accepted, and it leaves French tools ready for larger, controlled trials.
pmc-13455727:
Dongxu Du and five colleagues set out, in a 2026 methods study, to weight the parts of a motor health score for preschool children. Judging young children's movement health takes many indicators, and how much each should count is contested. The team blended two logics: expert judgment through a Delphi panel, and data-driven entropy weights drawn from the spread of real scores.

The system holds six main indicators and 26 sub-indicators. Combined weights for the main six summed to one, ranging from about 0.11 to 0.21. At the top level, the blended weights agreed with neither parent method on its own, a sign the blend truly mixed the two views. At the sub-indicator level, agreement with both parents ran strong. The authors present the scheme as a fairer basis for grading preschool motor health than expert opinion or data alone.
pmc-13457027:
Bo Tang, Mingyue Hou, and Rui Yang test, in a 2026 trial, whether training with light weights strapped to the legs sharpens soccer players in season. Thirty highly trained male college players were split by lot into two groups of fifteen. One group wore garments loaded with two percent of body mass on the lower limbs, three sessions a week for eight weeks, inside normal team training. The other wore look-alike unloaded gear.

The loaded group improved more on short sprints over ten and thirty meters. Jump height rose by about eleven percent, and a change-of-direction drill quickened. The rate at which the thigh muscle built force jumped by about eight percent. Top strength, muscle electrical activity, and muscle size did not shift apart between groups. Effort ratings matched, so the gains came without feeling harder. The authors credit neural sharpening, not bigger muscles.
pmc-13457227:
Laura Zengerle and co-authors test whether neck discs can be made to herniate in the laboratory under loads resembling daily life. Herniated cervical discs are a common source of neck pain and disability, yet the exact failure process is hard to observe in patients. The 2026 laboratory study loaded six motion segments from four human donors aged 19 to 58, with mild to moderate degeneration, through 3,000 cycles of combined motion.

Intact specimens never herniated, even under exaggerated long-term loading. Only after a 1-millimeter cut in the posterior longitudinal ligament, the band behind the discs, did one prolapse and one protrusion appear, both in younger, less degenerated specimens. Fully cutting the ligament added no further herniations. Microscopy showed torn fibers in the rear disc wall with nucleus material pushing through. The authors conclude the ligament is the disc's main guard, and younger, healthier discs may paradoxically carry the higher herniation risk.
pmc-13457927:
Buse Fatma Çapkınoğlu and colleagues revisit under-the-muscle breast reconstruction, refining a mesh-free total subpectoral technique for patients unsuited to the fashionable above-muscle approach. Classic subpectoral work suffers animation deformity, where the implant jumps when the chest muscle flexes, and a pinched lower pole. Their 2026 retrospective series covers 119 patients and 181 breasts reconstructed immediately after mastectomy with the method.

The technique preserves the inframammary ligament, the serratus fascia, and intercostal blood vessels, using controlled fascial releases and limited upward dissection to seat the implant and free the lower pole. Over a mean follow-up of 28.1 months, minor complications affected 28.6 percent of cases and major ones 6.7 percent, the low end of published ranges. Revisions were needed in 7.6 percent, mostly for contour, and all were fixed in one stage. The 100 patients who completed BREAST-Q surveys averaged 76.6, supporting the method as a stable, reproducible, cheaper alternative.
pmc-13458727:
Caixia Li and colleagues predict immune therapy benefit in advanced liver cancer from exosome metabolites plus PD-1 and PD-L1 in a 2026 study. Only 20 to 30 percent of advanced liver cancer patients respond to checkpoint inhibitors, yet early prediction could spare others toxicity and cost. The team studied 824 treated patients, split 7:3 into training and test sets, screening clinical, sac chemical and PD-1/PD-L1 factors with single-factor and adjusted stats models.

Child-Pugh class, distant spread, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, sphingosine-1-phosphate, glutamine and PD-L1 level flagged response on their own. A random forest fusion model performed best, with areas under the curve of 0.757 in training and 0.751 in testing. The single-centre model offers an early reference for spotting who will gain, pending multi-site outside checks before medical use.
pmc-13459227:
Katherine Krishna and co-authors catalogued combined MD/MBA programs across the United States, where doctors earn a medical degree and a business degree together. Such programs have grown fivefold in twenty years, but most take five years with a dedicated business year, while a minority compress both degrees into four. Their 2026 cross-sectional study identified 93 programs in January 2025 from national databases and compared their admissions rules, credit loads, and teaching formats against a 2022 analysis.

The total barely changed from 92 programs in 2022, yet the details shifted significantly. Programs demanding the full MBA credit load jumped from 9 percent to 37 percent, while GMAT requirements fell from 34 percent to 15 percent of programs. Only twelve programs, 13 percent, offered the four-year track. Those tracks offered far more MBA specializations and lighter credit loads, and 42 percent delivered business coursework mostly online.
pmc-13459427:
Mohammad Abdalbaset T. Al-Bitar and colleagues review whether tiny cuts speed front-tooth lining up in brace work in a 2026 meta-analysis. Shorter treatment is prized by adult patients, and tiny cuts, a low-key surgery method, promise faster tooth movement, yet its value in pulling versus no-pulling cases was unclear. Nine studies with 246 patients comparing tiny-cut-assisted therapy with usual treatment were pooled.

Lining-up time fell by 56.31 days overall, but the benefit was focused in pulling cases, saving 79.8 days with high trust, while no-pulling cases showed no clear gain. Overall treatment time fell by 262.68 days across three studies, though evidence was low trust and highly mixed, and pain evidence was scarce. Teeth doctors gain support for tiny cuts mainly in pulling treatment, pending higher-quality trials.
pmc-13460227:
Fan Tang and Zhihong Tang pooled in 2026 seven studies to test whether two nutrition-based scores predict death after surgery for aortic dissection, a torn aorta. Both scores blend blood proteins and immune cell counts into a single number. The combined data covered 2,967 operated patients, of whom about sixteen percent died. Searches ran across three databases into February 2026.

A lower prognostic nutritional index clearly meant higher death risk in type A dissection, and the index separated survivors from non-survivors with useful sensitivity and specificity. The geriatric nutritional risk index also tracked mortality, with lower scores carrying higher risk. The authors argue that a cheap preoperative nutrition check could flag fragile patients who need extra support around a dangerous operation.
pmc-13461427:
Sofia Rubi and colleagues describe in 2026 how Ohio communities in a large federal study deployed mobile medical units. The units deliver naloxone, the overdose reversal drug, and link people to medications for opioid use disorder. Cost, distance, and scarce clinics keep many high-risk people from both tools. Within the HEALing Communities Study, some counties chose vans as their delivery platform, and facilitators in each county reported what helped and what blocked the work.

Their accounts cover practical terrain: where units parked, how staffing and supply chains held up, and which partnerships opened doors in wary neighborhoods. Barriers and facilitators are organized so other regions can copy what worked rather than rediscover it. The authors present the case study as an implementation field guide, with the parent trial registered publicly.
pmc-13461727:
Shalini Mann, Harsh Raj, and Anjan Trivedi describe, in a 2026 case report from eastern Uttar Pradesh, India, how a routine stool test uncovered a worm infection. The parasite, Strongyloides stercoralis, lives in soil and enters through bare skin, often where sanitation is poor. The patient was a 71-year-old farmer near Gorakhpur. He had watery diarrhea for two years.

He was admitted with fever of unknown cause. Recent weeks brought a painful urge to empty the bowel. Under the microscope, moving young worms in his stool showed the parasite's clear body features. Blood tests showed mild anemia and raised levels of a white cell type linked to worm infection. No other parasites were found. He received ivermectin for two days and improved. The authors stress a stool check still matters for older rural patients with gut complaints, since missed infection can turn severe in weak patients.
pmc-13461927:
Manasawee Tanariyakul and co-authors asked whether erasing splicing factor mutations from the blood predicts better outcomes in myeloid blood cancers, or merely reflects treatment received. These gene changes drive myelodysplastic syndromes and some leukemias but rarely act alone. In their 2026 review, ninety five adults treated at a referral center from 2016 to 2025 were tracked for clearance, remission, transplantation, and survival. Fifty seven had acute myeloid leukemia.

The changes became undetectable in twenty two leukemia patients and eight in the MDS group after treatment. In leukemia, clearance tracked with receiving a stem cell transplant but not with remission or survival. In MDS, clearance tracked with remission but again not with survival or transplant receipt. Median survival actually ran numerically longer for the persistent group in MDS, 23.7 against 16.7 months in the comparison reported. Clearance is a weak leftover disease marker here.
pmc-13462027:
Gao ran a 2026 survey study of family support and online English learning among Chinese university students. Learning English online demands self-management in loosely watched online settings, and family backing may quietly shape that effort. The study traced paths from family support through self-regulation and positive emotions to how well students felt they learned.

Four hundred and thirty students with university online English experience filled in the cross-sectional survey Gao designed. Path modelling with five thousand resamples tested the indirect paths between the measures. Family support linked with higher self-regulation, positive emotions, and reported learning effectiveness alike. The path through self-regulation alone was clear, as was the chained path through self-regulation and then feelings. The path through emotions alone did not hold up, while a direct link from family support also stayed.
pmc-13463527:
Stein and co-authors built an online training module in 2026 for internal medicine residents at the University of Toronto. The module teaches ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, a full day of readings taken during normal life. Guidelines treat those reports as a reference standard for diagnosing high blood pressure. A survey first confirmed how large the training gap was.

Of 62 residents surveyed at the start, more than half had no prior exposure to reading these reports. Fewer than one in four felt comfortable doing so. The case-based module is built around a five-step reading framework. After finishing it, 22 of 26 residents felt comfortable interpreting reports. And 24 felt ready to diagnose high blood pressure in clinic. More than nine in ten rated the module valuable and easy to use.
pmc-13463927:
Wissmann and colleagues tested in 2026 whether spreading the same total balance training across different schedules changes how much adolescents improve. Balance training is known to boost postural control in youth, but the role of scheduling was unclear. Twenty-five teenagers, about 16 years old, were assigned by chance to train three times a week for four weeks or twice a week for six weeks, with total volume kept equal.

Wissmann measured balance with a timed one-legged stance test and a reach test in several directions. Both groups improved on every stance measure and every reach measure from start to finish. Only one outcome differed between schedules: the backward-sideways reach improved more in the group that trained more often over fewer weeks. The authors conclude that how training is spread matters little for most gains, with a small edge for packed practice on one measure.
pmc-13464827:
Wang and co-workers in China set in 2026 two ways to brew Fu tea, a dark tea shaped by a gold bloom fungus. They read how the end drinks split in hue and stuff. One way ferments the tea in tanks of liquid. The trade way grows the fungus on damp leaves, then draws the goods out with hot water. Hue tools and a wide chemical scan read both drinks.

The tank brew poured darker, a deep red brown, and ran rich in two hue goods the leaf brew lacked. The scan split all three drinks clean apart. Free food building blocks, the amino acids, sank low in the leaf brew. The tank brew kept the fullest pool and the most leaf goods. The route, not just the fungus, writes the cup.
pmc-13465527:
Feng and co-authors combined two risk measures into one index in 2026 and tested it against future disease in China. The parts are a blood-fat-based atherogenic index and a frailty index counting health deficits. Multiplied together, they form the AIPFI. Data came from a national aging study with 7,995 participants at baseline. A subgroup of 4,483 had repeat measures three years apart.

Over a median follow-up of nine years, 747 participants, about nine percent, developed cardiometabolic multimorbidity. That means multiple heart and metabolic diseases together. Risk climbed steadily across quarters of the index. The top quarter carried about two and a half times the risk of the bottom quarter after adjustment. People whose index stayed high and rose fared worse too, with about half again the risk. Hypertension, heart disease, and the index itself were the strongest signals in the prediction model.
pmc-13465627:
Ayla Arslaner and Özlem Yılmaz compared four salts in Erzincan Tulum cheese, a Turkish cheese with protected origin status, in a 2026 food study. Cheeses made with Kemah spring salt served as the control against Sivas spring salt, Çankırı rock salt, and a half-potassium low-sodium blend. All batches ripened for 120 days just below freezing.

Salt choice changed the mineral mix clearly, with the low-sodium batch carrying more potassium and less sodium than the rest. Protein breakdown ran highest in that same blend, while the rock salt batch held the most free fatty acids among the groups. Tasters scored the rock salt cheese highest overall and the Sivas version lowest, and fifty aroma compounds were detected across the cheeses.
pmc-13465727:
Mehmet Tatlı and co-authors survey Turkish ambulance and emergency workers who faced violence at work, linking trauma symptoms to a quiet withdrawal from effort on the job, in a 2026 study. Of 327 people who answered the online survey, 305 had faced workplace violence in the prior six months and formed the analysis group. Four short scales measured trauma symptoms, felt job stress, emotional exhaustion, and quiet quitting.

Trauma symptoms tied directly to quiet quitting at first pass. Once stress and exhaustion entered the model, that direct link faded, pointing to a chain that runs through strain and burnout instead. The authors checked the pattern again while accounting for age and gender, with similar results.
pmc-13465827:
Xifeng Tang and colleagues studied severe Epstein-Barr virus infection in 2026 among children at Shanghai Children's Hospital. Most children get glandular fever and recover, but some develop organ damage and severe disease. Records from 144 children admitted from January 2019 to March 2024 were split into severe cases and ordinary glandular fever cases.

Severe cases showed more gut symptoms, neck gland swelling, liver enlargement, and gallbladder involvement, plus higher viral DNA copies. Haemoglobin, D-dimer, and interferon-gamma emerged as independent risk markers, with D-dimer predicting best at an area of 0.93 and a cut point of 2.4 milligrams per litre. Early checks of these three markers may flag children heading for severe illness.
pmc-13465927:
Giusy Elia and a large team test the drug cabozantinib against anaplastic thyroid cancer cells in the lab, reporting in 2026. This cancer grows fast and resists most treatments, and the drug already holds approval for a slower thyroid cancer type. No earlier study had checked its combined cancer-fighting and immune effects in this setting.

Cultures came from two sources: long-kept cell lines and fresh cells taken directly from five patients, which keep more of the original tumor's character. The drug showed clear activity against tumor growth in both kinds of culture. It also shifted immune-related behavior in the cells, a dual effect the authors say could support more personal treatment choices.
pmc-13466027:
Gonzalo Pérez and a large team built an automatic way to mine word-finding tests for early signs of mild cognitive impairment, reporting in 2026. Ninety-six people took part, 53 with the impairment and 43 without, listing words under time pressure in two standard fluency tasks. Traditional scoring counts only correct answers, which leaves much of the speech signal unused.

Software pulled out word traits such as frequency and length, plus timing traits such as pauses, and machine learning used them to separate the groups well. The measures also stood comparison against standard thinking tests. Beyond sorting people, the speech features predicted brain patterns and blood levels of a tau marker tied to Alzheimer disease.
pmc-13466327:
Wang surveyed young university teachers in China in 2026 on how clashes between work and family life shape their identity as professionals. Four standard questionnaires measured work-family conflict, mindful teaching, professional identity, and workplace support. Of 528 questionnaires sent, 505 valid replies came back from married faculty aged 28 to 40. The sample split almost evenly between men and women across 13 institutions.

Conflict clearly eroded professional identity. Mindful teaching carried part of that harm, acting as a bridge between strain and self-image. Workplace and family support softened the damage. Where support ran high, conflict hurt mindfulness and identity less. The pathways differed by gender. For men, the bridge ran through mindfulness toward others. For women, it ran through inner mindfulness, and support cushioned them more strongly. The author suggests mindfulness training and support-building as practical responses, with different emphases for men and women.
pmc-13466427:
Serdar Bozlak and colleagues report a patient with arterial tortuosity syndrome whose gene fault also involved the brain's blood vessels. The syndrome twists and narrows arteries body-wide and stems from faults in SLC2A10, a gene for a sugar transporter called GLUT10.

Clinically, the patient combined severe artery twisting, heart defects from birth, hernias, and loose connective tissue. The patient's copy of the gene carried the same stop fault on both sides, found by whole-exome sequencing. Modelling showed the fault chops the transporter down from twelve membrane spans to five, gutting its shape. Nine test compounds bound the mutant more weakly than the normal protein, and simulations showed the mutant complex far less stable. Gene activity levels, though, matched carriers and controls, Bozlak notes, so the harm is structural, not a quantity problem.
pmc-13467327:
Areti Batzikosta and colleagues report a 2026 follow-up study on sleep, thinking skills, and social understanding in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. The study separated memory-led impairment from other forms and added a healthy comparison group. Sleep was measured with wrist devices rather than self-reports, and thinking was tested three times over roughly 16 to 20 months.

The full group held 179 people: 46 healthy controls, 75 with the memory-led form, and 58 with other forms of impairment. Tasks covered mental control, such as planning and switching, plus theory of mind, the ability to grasp what others think or mean beyond literal words. The design lets the team ask whether sleep measured earlier predicts later change in each skill, and whether that link differs by impairment type.
pmc-13467527:
Noor and co-authors test how 3D-printed stainless steel wears under sliding friction. Their 2026 paper examines plates of 316L steel built by wire arc additive manufacturing, a welding-based printing method whose industrial adoption lags over reliability concerns. Pin-on-disk tests slid a tungsten carbide ball across the plates under dry conditions at two loads and a range of speeds.

Friction stayed reassuringly steady, with a coefficient around 0.6 across conditions, though it fluctuated more at some speeds. Counterintuitively, wear volume generally fell as sliding speed rose, a shift the authors attribute to a change in wear mechanism. Lighter loads wore less, while the wear factor barely responded to load. Microscopy showed a two-phase ferrite-austenite microstructure with residual delta-ferrite, a fingerprint of the printing thermal history, governing the behaviour. The authors conclude the printed steel suits applications needing stable friction.
pmc-13467627:
Hanyu Zhao and colleagues investigate in 2026 a soybean gene that may restrain the root nodules where bacteria turn air nitrogen into plant food. Soybean yields in China are limited by nitrogen supply, and better biological fixation would cut fertilizer needs. Comparing gene activity in two soybean types with contrasting fixation performance, the team singled out a member of the GmRD22 gene family for testing.

Functional tests showed the gene acts as a negative regulator of nodulation, changing the activity of genes that build nodules and thereby lowering nitrogenase performance. Family pattern analysis also hinted that the gene region shifted during soybean domestication. Knowing a brake on fixation is as useful as knowing an accelerator: breeders could select against the brake to raise the crop natural nitrogen supply.
pmc-13468427:
Gaetano Pacinella and colleagues review in 2026 how diet steers the metabolism of the heart. The heart burns huge amounts of energy and must switch fuels flexibly as meals, hormones, and demand change. The review analyzes the molecular machinery of that flexibility. It covers how fatty acids, glucose, ketone bodies, and branched-chain amino acids are chosen, transported, and burned. It also covers how chronic eating patterns reprogram the heart over time.

Nutrient-sensing networks, including the carnitine shuttle, insulin signaling, AMPK, mTOR, and the PPARα-PGC-1α axis, coordinate the heart mitochondrial power plants. Long-term diet also writes itself into gene regulation and epigenetic marks, shifting the heart energetic character for better or worse. By connecting plate-level choices to molecular switches, the authors give cardiology a framework for thinking of food as a metabolic drug the heart takes every day.
pmc-13469027:
Luo and co-authors charted six decades of research on extrachromosomal DNA in cancer in 2026, using bibliometrics, the statistical study of publication patterns. These DNA circles float free of chromosomes and can multiply cancer genes fast. The team pulled 3,328 publications from two major databases, spanning 1965 to 2025. Software mapped who publishes, where, and on what themes. Keyword bursts revealed when topics surged.

Two countries dominate the field. The United States produced about 38 percent of the papers and China about 26 percent. Original research made up roughly 82 percent, with reviews near 10 percent. The field's language tells its story. Early work spoke of gene amplification, treating the circles as a counting curiosity. Recent hot terms are circular DNA, chromatin topology, and drug resistance. The shift marks a move from describing copies to explaining structure and treatment failure. The authors close with challenges blocking clinical use, and routes around them.
pmc-13469727:
Noda and co-authors present a 2026 case report. It concerns a hidden genetic cause of Muir-Torre syndrome. That condition pairs skin tumors with internal cancers. Their patient, a 47-year-old man, developed a sebaceous carcinoma near the armpit and a colon cancer at the same time. Standard gene panel testing found no inherited cause, which would normally leave the case classed as Lynch-like syndrome.

Staining of both tumors showed the same two repair proteins, MSH2 and MSH6, missing in each, a pattern pointing to an inherited defect rather than chance. Whole-genome sequencing then uncovered a change deep inside a non-coding part of the MSH2 gene that panels miss. Follow-up RNA testing confirmed the change inserted 11 extra letters into the gene's message, disrupting how the protein is built.
pmc-13469827:
Ittup and colleagues described in 2026 a trial protocol testing cultural competence training for nurses in India. Culturally competent care means respecting patients' values, communication styles, and beliefs. Migration within India and medical tourism have raised the need for such care.

In the trial phase, 110 nurses were randomised evenly to the training module or to routine practice. The module runs as five one-hour sessions plus booster sessions. The main outcome is nurses' cultural competence score after training, with patient satisfaction and ninety-day retention as further measures. Data collection passed seventy percent completion, and patient enrolment reached 92 of the planned 120. Full analysis is expected by mid-2026. The authors say the trial will show whether the module beats routine care and can scale with India's shifting population.
pmc-13470127:
Tadashi Inuzuka and colleagues separated true hepatitis B reactivation in 2026 from fleeting viral blips in patients with resolved infection on immune suppression. pmc-13470727:

His approach replaces fitting with direct comparison. A library of ready-made data sets is the reference. The sets span plausible energy ranges and heat levels. Tests showed the two key parameters could be estimated well. The error margin was usually small. Only basic data tools were needed. pmc-13471527:
Moghadari Koosha and colleagues interviewed family members caring for stroke survivors at home in Iran about what wears them down and what keeps them going. Against that erosion stood culturally grounded meaning-making, kinship help, growing know-how, and occasional healthcare support. The authors portray adaptation as a moving balance rather than a finish line, and suggest support policies built around that reality.
pmc-13471627:
Lau and colleagues audited whether humanitarian organizations running surgery in war zones build services that survive after they leave. Escalating violence permanently closed 13.0% of programs and interrupted 9.3%, and only six organizations had public policies at all.
pmc-13472727:

Code and documentation are publicly available.
pmc-13472927:
Matthias Michael Walter and colleagues review in 2026 the measurement quality of tools that grade the clinical learning environment for health professions students. pmc-13473027:

pmc-13473227:

pmc-13473827:

Some hormone-based treatments are already proven, such as SGLT2 inhibitors, while others aim at scarred tissue itself. The authors propose matching antifibrotic care to each patient's hormone profile.
pmc-13475827:
Chakraborty and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare overlap of two heart conditions in a thirty-seven-year-old man. They stress that recognising the overlap takes high suspicion, combined imaging, and gene testing.
pmc-13476327:
Chang Xu and co-authors study in 2026 whether age and first treatment shape deaths unrelated to lymphoma in early follicular lymphoma. Registry data held 6,030 adults diagnosed from 2000 to 2020. pmc-13477127:

Fourteen patients received the staged approach against seven historical patients operated on in one stage. Staged patients had no operative deaths against 43 percent historically, needed far fewer transfusions, and survived significantly better, with median survival of 28.1 months. Half recurred, mostly with distant spread. The staged strategy offers safer management in experienced multidisciplinary centres.
pmc-13477227:

The toxin, cuprizone, is a stand in for diseases like multiple sclerosis, where the wrap around nerve wires is lost. Past work looked at late harm. A harm type mark did not move at either span. The authors read a quick swap: as wrap makers die, guard astrocytes wake first, long before the wrap itself is gone.
pmc-13477327:

The measure, called the stress hyperglycemia ratio, compares blood sugar during illness with a person's usual level. Patients with moderate to severe valve leakage were split into four groups by this ratio.

The registry held 531 patients with an average age near 71 years, followed for a median of about six years. The highest ratio group had roughly double the risk of death from any cause and from heart causes compared with the lowest group. Adding the ratio to standard risk factors improved prediction slightly. The authors propose it as a simple tool for judging which valve patients need closest attention.
pmc-13478327:

pmc-13478527:

pmc-13479427:

Treatment ideas aimed at restoring flow include growth factor approaches such as VEGF-C therapy. The authors frame lymphatic repair as a fresh therapeutic direction beside the usual focus on plaques themselves.
pmc-13479727:

At the third month, one group showed a significant advantage on the reported measures, detailed in the results. pmc-13479927:
Chiara Molinari and coauthors present a 2026 cross-sectional study from Italy asking whether standard heart risk calculators spot silent artery disease in adults with type 1 diabetes. Heart disease is the top killer in this group, yet risk tools were built to predict events in the general population, not hidden plaque in diabetes. Several published risk models were scored for each person and checked against the imaging truth. pmc-13480127:
Daniel Inácio Cazeiro and co-authors present a 2026 case that weighs whether to close a hole in the heart when lung pressures run high. pmc-13480227:

pmc-13481327:

pmc-13483527:

pmc-13483627:

pmc-13483827:

pmc-13486027:

pmc-13486827:

pmc-13488227:

pmc-13489627:

pmc-13489727:

pmc-13490027:

pmc-13490327:

pmc-13490427:

pmc-13490627:

pmc-13490727:

pmc-13492027:

pmc-13493827:

pmc-13493927:

pmc-13494027:

pmc-13495327:

pmc-13495427:

Both groups improved on every module and reached plateaus, the residents starting higher and leveling sooner. The two raters agreed excellently, which backs the scoring sheet. The machine's sight and touch feedback stayed consistent enough to build early skill. pmc-13495527:

pmc-13501627:

pmc-13501827:
Chao Ma leads a seventeen-author team reporting a 2026 study of cell aggregates that speed bone defect healing in mice. The aggregates mimic the clumping of cells during embryonic development. The team focused on one skeletal progenitor subset marked by Gli1, cells known to maintain bone. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed the Gli1-high cells expressed genes for bone building, blood vessel growth, and matrix production. Inside bone these cells clustered near the growth region, hugging the bone master switch RUNX2 and the type H blood vessels that couple vessels to bone growth.

The team sorted the Gli1-positive cells and formed them into aggregates. In dishes the aggregates coaxed endothelial cells into tubes through secreted signals. Implanted into mouse thigh-bone defects, they regenerated bone faster than unsorted or Gli1-negative aggregates, by summoning type H vessels. The authors pitch precision-sorted aggregates as a regenerative strategy.
pmc-13502627:
Eun Gyu Lee leads a seven-author team with a 2026 chemistry study where electricity, not chemistry, calls polymers into existence. Their building block joins perylene diimide, a stacking-prone dye, to the amino acid histidine. Left alone it stalls in small trapped dimers held by internal hydrogen bonds. Adding sodium dithionite, a chemical reducing agent, rapidly converts those dimers into favoured helical nanofibers, and the fibers can serve as seeds of tunable length.

Applying a voltage achieved the same reorganization on electrode surfaces, with tighter pi stacking that carried current better. Seeded growth then grew fibers to predictable lengths from seeds made by either route, chemical or electrical. The dual approach treats pathway selection as a variable users can set: trap, release, and regrow on command. The authors aim the platform at adaptive materials for electronics, sensing, and catalysis, where assembly timing and electron transport must be controlled together.
pmc-13503627:
