Christopher Mendias and Tariq M Awan describe a 2026 case series on lasting pain in the scrotal contents. The pain has many possible causes, from nerve and muscle problems to blood flow and mental health factors. Their clinic tested a four-week plan that mixed several forms of physical therapy.

Twenty-eight men finished the plan, which used laser treatment, dry needling, magnetic field therapy, hands-on work, and graded exercise, plus a daily drug. Pain scores fell from 8.0 to 0.8 on a ten-point scale by the last visit. Scores for body and mental health also rose. Months later, most men who were reached had no return of pain, though the study had no control group.
pmc-13503927:
Yuxin Shi leads a team that gave carbon dots a twist, letting them emit twisted light for display screens, in a 2026 paper. Twisted, or circularly polarized, light serves 3D displays and quantum tools. Carbon dots are safe and stable, but their twist is usually far too weak to use.

The team coated fluorinated carbon dots with a helical helper compound. Strong electric and hydrogen bonds guided the dots into ordered spiral stacks. The stacks soaked up twisted light with a dissymmetry score far above past carbon dot values. Built into light-emitting diodes, the stacks shone brightly and kept a clear twist in their output. The work marks the first such devices from carbon dots and a step toward metal-free twisted-light tech.
pmc-13504027:
Rupali Saini leads a team reviewing how computer screening can find plant compounds against lung cancer, in a 2026 paper. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, and many patients are found late. Plant chemicals offer a wide pool of candidate drugs, yet testing each one in the lab is slow.

The review covers tools that model how compounds fit cancer targets, how the body would handle them, and how they sit in wider cell networks. Four targets drew most work: EGFR, KRAS, ALK, and PD-L1. Compounds like quercetin, curcumin, and luteolin bound several targets at once and showed fair drug-like traits on paper. The authors frame computer screening as a cheap first filter that links folk plant care with precision cancer care.
pmc-13505027:
Xiaodie Mu and three colleagues compare six simple insulin resistance indexes as kidney risk flags in people with diabetes, in a 2026 cohort study. Insulin resistance helps drive chronic kidney disease, yet the gold-standard test is impractical for routine care. Surrogate indexes built from routine labs offer a cheap stand-in.

Data came from a national aging study in China, with more than three thousand diabetic participants. Kidney risk rose with most indexes as they climbed. One index, an estimated glucose disposal rate, pointed the other way: higher values meant lower risk, and its top quarter cut risk by about a third. That index also forecast best on accuracy checks, though all indexes were modest alone.
pmc-13505127:
Christina B. Del Azodi and others launch two Bioconductor kits for multi-state counted trait locus analysis. In 2026, the software paper presents QTLExperiment, a holder for storing and handling QTL summary numbers with labels, and multistateQTL, tools for number analysis, sharing counting, link sorting, charts, and model. Modern QTL studies span tissues, cell types, growth stages, and settings.

The kits follow Bioconductor rules for a steady, noted workflow, letting team compare gene control across states and find links unique to subsets of states. Such disease-fitting signals can be masked in bulk studies. Both kits are open-source and free to get, giving gene team handy tools for many-sided multi-state data.
pmc-13506327:
Hagop Kantarjian leads the group reporting five-year results in 2026 from OPTIC, a phase 2 trial of ponatinib for chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia. The trial enrolled 283 people whose disease had resisted earlier kinase drugs or carried the T315I change. Patients started at 45, 30, or 15 mg daily, with dose cuts after a good response.

After about six years of follow-up, deep responses were most common in the 45 mg group, and survival passed 80 percent in every group. Blood vessel blockage events stayed in a low range across doses. The results support response-based dosing, with the clearest gain in patients who carried T315I.
pmc-13507227:
Erin R Claussen, Miles D Woodcock-Girard, Samantha N Fischer, and Kevin Drew present DirectContacts2 in 2026 work, a learning model that tells direct protein contacts apart from indirect ones. Proteins work inside complexes where some partners touch and others merely co-occur. Checking all roughly 200 million human pairs with structure prediction is far too costly, so a filter must come first.

Training drew on more than 25,000 mass spectrometry experiments, a method that weighs molecules from digested samples. Applied to about 25 million pairs, the model beat earlier resources and enriched for accurate structural models, including some 2500 from AlphaFold3. Disease complexes, such as one tied to a developmental syndrome, gain clearer mutation interpretation. Cell wiring maps become practical guides for targeted screening.
pmc-13507327:
Wenda Zhao presents, in 2026 work, a combined AI framework that generates ceramic surface designs and scores their visual quality. Traditional ceramic design leans on artisan intuition, which is slow and hard to scale, while generic image generators miss tradition-specific style. The pipeline reads briefs or reference images with a vision-language model backed by a ceramic knowledge graph.

A diffusion generator then paints vessel decorations under fine style control. A separate scorer grades composition, color harmony, texture, and style consistency against expert judgment, reaching strong rank agreement with human panels. Tests used over 21,000 annotated images from five traditions centered on Chinese porcelain and stoneware. The author cautions that scores judge flat imagery only, not clay, glaze, or firing.
pmc-13508427:
Wen-Qi Li and five co-authors study a gene fault's role in womb cancer, with an eye to young patients hoping to keep fertility, in 2026 work. The team read tumor genes and tissue stains in patient groups, then compared cancers with and without faults in the CTNNB1 gene. Treatment responses in young patients on hormone therapy were also tracked.

Most fault-carrying cancers sat in a group with no clear molecular label, and one hot spot change led the list. These cancers were more often the common glandular type and at earlier stages. A tissue stain for the partner protein could hint at the fault, though imperfectly. Worryingly, patients with the fault answered hormone treatment poorly, a pattern the authors link to lower levels of a related signal protein. Testing for the fault could steer young patients toward or away from womb-sparing care.
pmc-13509827:
Pranvera Breznica Selmani, Arlinda Daka Grapci, Blerina Koshi, Zana Sllamniku Dalipi, and Rozafa Koliqi pool animal studies of tiny drug carriers for lung cancer chemotherapy, in a 2026 review. The group searched the literature through February 2025 and graded study quality with a standard tool for animal research. Thirty studies with 47 experiments in mice met the entry rules.

Carrier-based treatment shrank tumors far more than the same drugs given free, on average. Targeted carriers that home in on cancer cells showed the largest average gains, though plain carriers also helped. Results varied a great deal between studies, and differences in formulas and study design cloud direct comparison. The authors stress that the findings concern lab models only, support better standardized animal work, and do not prove benefit in patients.
pmc-13510927:
Sungsu Jung and colleagues report a birth cohort study, published in 2026. They write for the PSKC Study Group. The study asks whether childhood allergies travel with unexplained physical complaints. These are complaints with no clear medical cause. The team studied 1,577 seven-year-old Korean children. They related eczema, food allergy, and respiratory allergies to behaviour checklist scores.

Eczema was linked to more somatic problems. Food allergy was linked to more as well. Somatic problems are bodily complaints such as aches. Children with both conditions had markedly higher odds. Their odds exceeded those with either condition alone. Hay fever accounted for part of the eczema link. A direct link still remained. This supports screening allergic children for such complaints.
pmc-13512827:
Grzegorz Ulacha and Mirosław Łazoryszczak propose a new image compression method that works in lossless and near-lossless modes, in 2026 work. Their Multi-ctx2 encoder predicts each pixel from its neighborhood using a generalized multi-context scheme. Five simple rules assign a context number that picks a tailored linear predictor and also corrects running prediction error. Errors are then coded in two stages, first with an adaptive Golomb code and then with binary arithmetic coding.

Compression and decompression both run fast, and the design suits hardware because it uses fixed-point math and never needs the whole image in memory to tune itself. Across two test sets, the method beat the standard JPEG-LS by roughly seven percent in lossless mode and by about ten percent in near-lossless mode. The authors pitch it as a practical balance of ratio, speed, and energy cost.
pmc-13513327:
Murat Karamanlıoğlu and Pınar Akın Kabalak test whether combined blood indices can flag right heart strain in patients with acute pulmonary embolism, a lung artery blockage, in 2026 work. Strain on the right side of the heart drives bad outcomes in this emergency. Records covered 270 patients at a referral center from January 2024 to March 2026, sorted by imaging proof of right ventricular dysfunction.

About forty-four percent of patients showed the dysfunction. Those patients carried heavier clot loads, worse imaging findings, and poorer clinical courses. Eight composite indices were built from admission labs, blending sugar-fat balance, inflammation, clotting products, and nutrition markers such as albumin ratios. Statistical checks weighed each index against the imaging verdict and against each other. The authors say cheap lab composites could help sort risk early where advanced imaging is delayed, pending fuller results in the complete report.
pmc-13514527:
Büşragül Yılmaz heads a thirteen-author team testing a disarmingly simple screening trick in a 2026 study of older adults with chronic kidney disease. In the finger-ring test, a person wraps thumb and forefinger around the opposite calf; a loose ring hints at low muscle mass. The team assessed 113 patients aged sixty-five and older with body-composition scans and broad geriatric measures.

Low muscle mass appeared in about half of those whose ring sat loose, compared with about a quarter of those whose fingers could not meet. The test tracked calf size and body mass index closely, yet its accuracy for low muscle mass alone stayed modest, catching roughly seven in ten cases. Yılmaz's group recommends the test only as a quick extra clue that prompts proper measurement, never as a stand-alone verdict.
pmc-13514627:
Fenna Brunken and five colleagues compare three detector technologies for mobile C-arm X-ray machines used during orthopaedic surgery in a 2026 study. Surgeons rely on these live images to check fracture repair and implant placement, and detectors built on amorphous silicon, CMOS, or IGZO electronics differ in noise and sharpness. The team imaged four human specimens at four body sites, at two pulse rates and two dose levels, then had observers rate quality and make forced choices between matched images.

The CMOS and IGZO systems beat the amorphous silicon system in roughly nine of ten head-to-head comparisons, with clearly higher ratings for overall quality and perceived noise. Between CMOS and IGZO, no consistent preference or quality gap appeared. Brunken's team concludes that either newer technology gives surgeons a visibly better picture than the long-standard silicon panels.
pmc-13515227:
Asseghaf Bintang Ramadhani leads a twelve-author team tuning water-filter membranes in a 2026 study of activated carbon set inside a polyethersulfone plastic. The team varied two levers: how hard the blocks were pressed, and whether vapour exposure preceded the setting bath. The goal was balancing flow speed against how well the membrane holds back unwanted protein.

Gentle pressing with no vapour step left large internal voids, giving the highest porosity and the fastest gravity-driven flow. A ten-minute vapour step instead built a sponge-like network that slowed the water and exposed it longer to carbon sites, yielding the best rejection of a test protein. Hard pressing of vapour-treated blocks sealed the carbon too tightly and cut performance, though it maximised strength. The authors frame the settings as dials that makers can turn toward flow, cleaning power, or toughness.
pmc-13515327:
Yikun Yang leads a twelve-author review, published in 2026, of Talbot cavities for laser diode arrays. Rows of semiconductor lasers can deliver great power, yet keeping their beams in step, tidy, and stable is hard. A Talbot cavity exploits a self-imaging effect to couple every emitter to the whole array, locking their phases without active control. The authors explain the principle and compare three layouts: the classic cavity, a V-shaped Littrow variant, and a version built into the chip itself.

Experimental highlights span near-infrared, blue, terahertz, and mid-infrared devices, with arrays from a few emitters to thousands. Reported results include far-field patterns with visibility up to ninety-nine percent and blue arrays with very narrow spectral lines at high power. Simulation work on stability and tuning receives its own treatment.
pmc-13516327:
Ahmed I Anwar leads a sixteen-author review of pridopidine, a candidate drug for neurodegenerative disease, published in 2026. Huntington's disease and ALS now get treatments that ease symptoms without slowing the underlying decay. Pridopidine crosses into the brain and switches on the sigma-1 receptor, a helper protein sitting where the cell's internal store meets its power plants. That switch steadies calcium signals, supports mitochondria, and raises anti-death activity inside neurons.

The review gathers the mechanism evidence and the clinical record so far. Dopamine pathways, which swing too high or too low across these diseases, form part of the picture, yet the drug barely touches the classic dopamine receptor. Available evidence suggests better motor outcomes and slower decline in Huntington's disease and ALS. Anwar's team presents sigma-1 activation as a plausible disease-modifying strategy, while the proof base continues to build.
pmc-13518227:
Sarah F Tyson and Russell Fleming, both living with ME themselves, co-produce a clinical needs checklist for the condition in a 2026 study. People with myalgic encephalomyelitis often find services measure the wrong things. Working with patients and NHS clinicians at every stage, the pair drafted the CNAME questionnaire from research and lived experience. They piloted it with cognitive interviews before four hundred patients completed it online.

Understanding proved excellent, with over ninety-seven percent of items answered. A few questions hit their ceiling and were cut, and eight overlapping ones were merged. Patients judged the final tool relevant, complete, and easy to finish. Because answers are yes-or-no snapshots rather than scores, the authors skip the usual repeat-testing statistics as beside the point. They present CNAME as a valid, workable way for clinics to ask what patients actually need.
pmc-13518827:
Minjia Yan and six colleagues design a single-atom copper catalyst in 2026 that switches on under light for photo-Fenton cleanup of polluted water. Fenton chemistry uses hydrogen peroxide to make hydroxyl radicals that destroy pollutants, though tuning single metal atoms for the job is delicate. Their copper sites sit in an uneven nitrogen-sulfur pocket, written Cu-N2S.

Calculations showed strong orbital mixing raised the site's energy level and reshaped how it grips hydrogen peroxide. Dark sites stayed quiet, while light flipped them active, sustaining radical output. The system removed 98.9 percent of the antibiotic sulfamethoxazole, worked across pH 3 to 11, tolerated messy water, and lasted through long runs.
pmc-13518927:
Yubo Yuan and five colleagues present a 2026 deep learning method for spotting chest lesions on X-rays across many sizes and shapes. Lesions vary wildly in scale and outline, and small ones are easily missed inside complex anatomy. Their system first enriches features with both whole-chest context and local lesion detail.

An adaptive focusing stage then pools features at several scales to catch small lesions, while a shape-aware training rule using a normalized distance measure steadies box placement for irregular shapes. On the VinDr-CXR dataset the method gained 6.3 percent in average precision and 8.6 percent in recall over leading rivals. Gains on ChestX-ray8 confirmed the approach travels across datasets.
pmc-13520427:
Andrew R Coggins and colleagues observe in 2026 teamwork, stress and surroundings during emergency department cases of extracorporeal resuscitation, where a machine takes over heart and lung work during cardiac arrest. Such cases are rare, urgent and team-heavy, so human factors may shape success as much as technique.

Six real cases across two hospitals involved detailed observation of eighteen providers in key roles. Heart-rate tracking, saliva stress hormone sampling, teamwork scoring, noise readings and headcounts were combined. Fixed roles, crowd control and leader summaries appeared consistently. Small numbers limit firm conclusions, yet the field notes offer rare direct evidence from live resuscitation work.
pmc-13521527:
Karunakaran and colleagues tested in 2026 whether an extract of Nigella sativa, known as black seed, improves a dental repair material called mineral trioxide aggregate. Working in the lab, they mixed the extract into the material at 30 and 50 percent levels and checked cell safety, setting time, and mineral formation on bone-like cells.

The extract raised cell viability as its share grew, with the 50 percent mix giving the highest values. Both extract mixes set faster, at the start and at final hardening, than the plain material. Mineral deposits also increased, again most strongly at the higher level. The authors suggest the black seed extract could be a useful additive for root-end dental treatments, pending further testing.
pmc-13521927:
Zhenchao Xu, Xiyang Wang, Guanghui Zhu and Zheng Liu build in 2026 layered microspheres that release two antibiotics in sequence to treat infected bone defects, where body-wide dosing reaches poorly. Vancomycin and rifampin were loaded in opposite core-shell orders for comparison.

Spray-formed spheres were uniform and smooth, with the vancomycin-shell version showing better matched release timing. Bone-forming cells tolerated both versions well, keeping growth and differentiation intact. Killing of free Staphylococcus aureus exceeded 95 percent, while biofilm formation was prevented. In infected rats, spheres sped wound healing, cut bacterial load and eased inflammation near the implant site.
pmc-13523227:
Natalia Savychuk and colleagues report a mismatch between jaw positions in chronic jaw joint disorder in a 2026 case report. A thirty-year-old woman had seven years of night-time clenching and persistent clicking on the right side, unrelieved by earlier orthodontics and a night guard. Magnetic resonance imaging was performed in several jaw positions to compare disc location with how the jaw bone seated.

The right joint showed advanced degeneration and a disc displaced forward without returning on opening, while the left disc displaced but returned. In the splint-guided therapeutic position, the left disc was partly recaptured, yet the jaw still did not reach the reference centric position. Night wear of a repositioning splint over three months reduced clicking and improved function. The authors recommend imaging in multiple positions before committing to long-term treatment.
pmc-13523427:
Baoluhe Zhang and a large team hunt for personalized neoantigens in bile duct cancer in a 2026 multiomics study. Neoantigens are altered protein fragments unique to a tumor that can train the immune system. Paired tumor and normal samples from thirty-three patients underwent DNA and RNA sequencing to map mutations and candidate neoantigens, and selected peptides were synthesized and tested for immune activation.

The familiar cancer gene TP53 was the most frequently mutated, and higher mutation counts tracked higher neoantigen loads. Nearly eight hundred neoantigens were identified across twenty-two samples. Sixteen peptides from three patients triggered strong T cell responses in laboratory tests, with the most potent coming from three named genes. Predicted receptor sequences for those responses were also reported. The authors frame the work as proof of concept for personalized immunotherapy in this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13525727:
Izadian Bidgoli and co-authors present a diagnostic trap in this 2026 case report of a 40-year-old man with relapsed mixed phenotype acute leukemia, a rare cancer carrying features of two leukemia types. Midway through prolonged leukemia therapy, he developed one-sided swelling and pain around the eye, and scans suggested orbital cellulitis, a serious infection of the eye socket.

Broad-spectrum antimicrobials should have helped, but serial CT and MRI scans showed stubborn thickening of the upper orbital tissues without clinical improvement. An eye biopsy finally revealed the truth: moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva, already invading small vessels, rather than infection or leukemic spread, which blood tests excluded. The authors stress two points. Profound immune suppression from leukemia treatment can hide a second cancer behind an infection's disguise. And any orbital inflammation failing to respond deserves early biopsy rather than more antibiotics.
pmc-13526727:
Bérénice Chavanel and colleagues examine, in a 2026 rat study, how alcohol and its main breakdown product reshape mutation patterns across organs. Alcohol is a major cancer risk factor, especially for head and neck sites, and acetaldehyde is blamed for oral cancers, yet the mutational evidence was indirect. Rats were chronically exposed to ethanol or acetaldehyde.

Whole-genome analysis covered head-and-neck tumors plus forestomach and liver tumors. A signature called SBS17 appeared early in about thirty-eight percent of head-and-neck tumors, pointing to inflammation and oxidative damage as mediators. Tumors with driver-like changes in Tp53 all carried that signature, echoing a pattern in human esophageal cancers. Other mutation classes showed no exposure-specific pattern, and classic human alcohol signatures were absent. The authors infer mostly non-mutational carcinogenic routes.
pmc-13526827:
Wenchuan Zhang and colleagues built a deep learning model to predict breast cancer chemotherapy response from needle biopsy images. Published in 2026, the Mamba-based model, called MCEN, drew on 1,646 patients across five tertiary hospitals. Samples from one hospital trained and validated the model, while the other four hospitals served as outside test sets.

The model scored strongly on training data and held up well on validation and outside tests, with accuracy measures ranging from roughly three quarters to four fifths externally. Adding clinical and pathology details lifted scores further across all sets. The authors present MCEN as a decision aid for tailoring chemotherapy before treatment, sparing nonresponders futile therapy and delay. Readers get a multi-hospital validated predictor, still needing prospective trials.
pmc-13528327:
Yongkai Liu and ten colleagues build a reasoning language model to forecast recovery after stroke in a 2026 study. The tool, named COPE, reads discharge notes rather than neat data tables. Records covered 464 patients with ninety-day function scores. Two open-source models work in sequence. The first drafts clinical reasoning. The second turns it into a score prediction.

COPE matched the commercial GPT-4.1 closely on every metric. It also matched a strong model fed hand-built variables. Simpler text models and a one-step version fell behind. Errors grew for older patients and those with clot removal or long notes. Results held steady across sex and age groups. The authors stress privacy: open models can run inside hospitals. No retraining or manual feature work was needed.
pmc-13528427:
Bahar Yilmaz and Berna Erdal tested whether fluids from probiotic bacteria can kill colon cancer cells. Published in 2026, the study used cell-free supernatants from two Lactobacillus strains, which carry bioactive compounds released during bacterial growth, against two colon cancer cell lines and one healthy colon cell line. Colon cancer treatment failures drive interest in such postbiotic compounds.

The supernatants killed cancer cells markedly, with fluorescent staining confirming more programmed cell death. Treated cells piled up in the resting phase of the cell cycle while synthesis-phase cells fell, and death-promoting genes rose as a protective gene fell. Both live and inactivated preparations showed targeted effects. The authors propose these fluids as a future biotherapy option, pending animal and clinical studies.
pmc-13530127:
Tri Dung Dang and Hoang-Kha Nguyen rank ten Southeast Asian economies in 2026 on energy efficiency joined with climate resilience. Rising demand and worsening climate risk press the region from both sides at once. Earlier work usually treated saving energy and weathering climate harm as separate questions.

Their framework weights each factor by a data-driven method, then ranks countries against an ideal benchmark. The Philippines placed first. Myanmar and Singapore came next, with Brunei, Malaysia, and Laos furthest from the ideal mark. Climate risk, policy readiness, clean energy shift, and efficiency spending separated the field most. Alternate ranking methods gave similar orders.
pmc-13531927:
Merve Geylani and Şeyma Göral survey in 2026 whether psychological resilience predicts disaster readiness among psychiatric nurses. A total of 140 nurses completed scales for resilience and psychological preparedness for disaster threats, plus personal background forms. Disaster work demands mental toughness beside technical skill in this specialty.

Resilience did predict preparedness, though it explained under seven percent of the differences. Nurses with formal disaster training scored clearly higher, as did those with five or more years of experience. Night-only staff scored lowest, from a very small subgroup. Training access for every shift is the practical message.
pmc-13534627:
Luo Lv and colleagues study in 2026 whether a combined cholesterol, HDL, and glucose index, joined with obesity measures, predicts heart disease in early cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome. Single markers miss the linked nature of these conditions. Data came from a Chinese ageing cohort with 6,705 people followed for a median of seven years.

Risk rose step by step across index quartiles, and each standard rise in the combined scores linked to higher heart disease rates. Combined scores sorted risk slightly better than the base index alone, with the waist-to-height version generally strongest. Clinical value still needs outside confirmation.
pmc-13534727:
Low and colleagues report a 2026 study of gut bacteria in people who carry a harmful E. coli strain, ST131, in Southeast Asia. This strain can live in the gut silently and spread within households. The team used shotgun DNA reading of stool samples to compare persistent carriers, intermittent carriers, non-carriers, and their household contacts.

Carriage shifted the gut community's mix without lowering its overall diversity. Samples with ST131 had fewer helpful commensal species and less of one sugar-breakdown pathway. Persistent carriers showed the most disturbed communities, rich in pathobionts, meaning microbes that can turn harmful, and in pathways for iron capture and cell-wall building. Household comparisons flagged vitamin and sugar pathways that may sway who gets colonized. Knowing what gut states favor this strain could guide ways to clear it before it causes infection.
pmc-13536627:
Yuang Hao and colleagues ask in 2026 whether hip muscle size before surgery predicts two-year outcomes after hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement. Records covered 74 patients treated in 2021 and 2022, with scans measuring area and width of three hip muscle groups. Outcome scores were collected two years after surgery.

Larger glute and hip flexor measures linked modestly to better scores and acceptable symptom states. One glute measure stayed a clear predictor in adjusted models, and male sex also helped one score. Muscle size may aid expectations, though the predictive strength stayed limited overall.
pmc-13538527:
Xianjie Yuan and colleagues simulate powder densification during high-velocity compaction of an aluminum alloy in a 2026 modeling study. Fast hammer strikes can pack alloy powders tightly for aerospace parts, yet packing workings stay murky. A three-dimensional multi-particle model varied friction, impact energy per mass, hammer mass, and strike speed. Displacement maps traced particle shuffling and squashing, with bench tests checking the simulated trend.

Higher friction choked energy transfer and lowered final density. Raising impact energy lifted density sharply to the best value seen. Matched hammer mass and speed pairings best promoted rearrangement and plastic squashing. Bench results followed the simulated trend, running slightly higher than predictions. The authors judge the model fit for trend guidance and particle-level insight.
pmc-13539927:
Göksal Sezen and Selim Doblan report a 2026 field study on feeding safflower plants with algae preparations instead of relying on synthetic fertiliser. Safflower is an oilseed crop, and chemical inputs raise concerns for soil, water, and health.

Two algae, a spiral blue-green species and a filamentous green one, were sprayed alone or mixed at several strengths across three growth stages. Every treatment beat the untreated control on height, weight, seed yield, and leaf pigments. One mixed dose more than tripled seed yield per plant against the control, while another pairing lifted fresh weight sharply. The authors favour algae mixes as a greener support for safflower growing.
pmc-13540327:
Malak Munir and colleagues mine a United States safety database in a 2026 study. They hunted heart and circulation harms linked to bispecific antibodies. These lab-made proteins pull immune T cells onto blood cancer cells. Such harms had never been mapped across all the approved drugs.

Reports naming these drugs as the prime suspect numbered 7,647. The reports spanned December 2014 to September 2025. About eighteen percent involved a heart or vessel event. Signals stood out for a clotting disorder called DIC. Low blood pressure and fatal events also stood out. Heart events arrived earlier than other side effects.
pmc-13542127:
Xingchen He and colleagues built a one-step light-signal fix that slashes the cost of long-distance fiber cleanup. Published in 2026, the physics-informed neural method keeps the side-by-side shape of a Volterra-series transfer model that learns its fixes from data. Fiber signal warping caps reach and capacity, and standard digital back-tracking rebuilds signals step by step at high cost.

On a 1,125-km link, the method matched the best back-tracking scores at 19 percent of the work and one twenty-fifth the delay. On a 12,057-km link, costs fell to about 6.6 percent with one one-hundred-seventy-sixth the delay, an overall gain above 2,600-fold. The design suits hardware and keeps performance while cutting the performance-cost-delay trade-off. Readers get a path to usable signal-warp cleanup in next-gen optical networks.
pmc-13542427:
Gabriella Harb, Samuel Rowe, and Ruth Zadoks published a 2026 laboratory study on whether treating dairy bedding can slow the growth of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium behind environmental mastitis in cows. Sand and wood shavings were each treated with a commercial bedding conditioner or a disinfectant, then deliberately seeded with the bacterium under controlled conditions. Growth in the two bedding materials and under each treatment was compared.

The results indicate that both the bedding material itself and the treatment chosen shape how well the bacterium multiplies. Because the work was done in the laboratory rather than in working barns, the authors are careful to present it as an early step. Farm trials are still needed before any product can be recommended for routine use. Even so, the study gives dairy managers a reason to treat bedding choice and bedding treatment as part of mastitis control, not an afterthought.
pmc-13543427:
In 2026, Jichang Guo and colleagues published a study sorting Chinese adolescents into mental health profiles that combine distress with life satisfaction, rather than judging either alone. The dual-factor idea holds that a teenager can be symptom-free yet dissatisfied, or struggling yet content. A total of 1,682 adolescents, average age about fourteen, completed a depression scale and a life satisfaction scale, and latent profile analysis looked for natural groupings, separately by gender.

Three profiles emerged overall: a healthy group holding about sixty-two percent, a troubled-arousal group near thirty percent with moderate subclinical distress, and a severe distress group of seven percent. Boys reproduced the same threefold pattern, while girls were best described by two profiles, and girls clustered more heavily in distressed groups with worse symptoms at the severe end. Screening that counts only symptoms, the authors imply, will miss dissatisfied but quiet teenagers.
pmc-13546727:
Zeynep Çelik Kenar and co-authors examined in 2026 how the gut parasite Giardia duodenalis damages the small intestine of naturally infected lambs, at both the tissue and gene level. Twenty-four lambs were grouped by damage severity after microscopic review, ranging from uninfected controls to severe cases. Tissue sections were scored for villus shape, surface integrity, inflammation, and blood vessel congestion, while five gut-related genes were measured.

Damage deepened step by step with severity: villi shrank, surfaces broke down, and immune cells crowded the tissue. Two genes tied to repair rose early in mild and moderate cases, while a detoxifying gene fell in worse cases, suggesting fading protection. A sealing gene rose in all infected groups, as if the gut were trying to patch its barrier.
pmc-13546927:
Bansal and a large team tracked what drug resistance costs in lives and cash in Indian hospitals. Their 2026 study used a national watch network of twenty large hospitals. It drew on case records from April 2022 to April 2025. The team found more than twenty-six thousand infections from gram-negative germs, a broad group of bacteria. It then matched deaths and drug costs for germs that resist key drugs with those that do not.

Death risk was higher for resistant infections for each of the four main germs in the study. The worst deaths came from resistant germs in the blood, where close to half of patients died. Drug costs ran up to twice as high for resistant cases as for plain cases. The team calls for tighter checks to stop infections and fair access to drugs that still work. It also backs strict rules on antibiotic use.
pmc-13547227:
Amare Aleminew and Tessema Miliket ran a 2026 field trial in Ethiopia's Banja District. They sought the best pairing of blended fertilizer and seed rate for bread wheat, a staple whose yields lag far behind world averages. During the 2024 main season they tested five rates of an NPSB blend, which supplies nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, and boron, against four seeding rates in replicated plots.

Fertilizer and seed rate worked together rather than separately for most measures. Tall plants and heavy straw came from the top two fertilizer rates, yet grain yield and harvest share peaked at the middle pairing: 150 kilograms per hectare of each. That pairing also returned the highest profit with a very large marginal return, and the authors recommend it for the district.
pmc-13547327:
Caterina Mancarella and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a protein shed into blood, IGF2BP3, can flag which young patients with Ewing sarcoma face the highest risk. Ewing sarcoma is the second most common bone tumor of childhood, and its course varies widely. The team measured the protein in blood samples from 60 patients treated at one Italian institute, comparing diagnosis samples, samples after initial chemotherapy, and healthy controls.

Levels ran higher in patients than in healthy donors, and in just over two fifths they reached notable concentrations, mirroring levels inside the tumor. Among patients whose disease had not spread, high blood levels marked much worse survival prospects. Levels that stayed up after chemotherapy also predicted poor outcomes. The authors propose the simple blood test for early risk sorting.
pmc-13548527:
Gillian Mwale and colleagues test eye protection for newborns receiving light therapy at a large hospital in Malawi, in a 2026 bench study. Babies treated for jaundice need their eyes shielded from intense blue light, yet the hospital lacked standard shields, so nurses improvised with gauze, plaster, and face masks. The team built a reusable cotton shield and measured how much light passed through each material.

Light meter readings were taken at four distances from the lamp, with twenty samples of each shield type. Face masks blocked the least light, and gauze varied with thickness. The new cotton shield and the reference shield let no measurable light through at any distance. For wards without commercial shields, the authors offer the washable cotton design as a workable substitute.
pmc-13548627:
Ran Gao and colleagues ask whether chewing betel nut blunts the effect of pre-surgery drug treatment for mouth cancer, in a 2026 retrospective study. Betel nut is a widespread habit and cancer risk across South and Southeast Asia. The team reviewed 192 patients who received combined immunotherapy and chemotherapy before surgery, comparing the forty-two chewers with the rest on how completely the tumor vanished or shrank in the removed tissue.

Complete disappearance of tumor was about half as common in chewers, and major shrinkage was also clearly less frequent. Chewers showed lower scan response rates, less downstaging, and more unfavorable tissue features, with the worst picture in better-differentiated tumors. Survival free of disease over three years, however, did not differ significantly. The authors suggest chewing history could help doctors stratify patients and set expectations before combined treatment.
pmc-13550427:
Lenz and colleagues tested in 2026 how reliable short heart rate variability measures are in patients with atrial fibrillation that comes and goes. This measure, the beat-to-beat change in heart timing, reflects the body's automatic control system and is lower before attacks, but strict lab rules limit its clinic use. Fifty patients wore 48-hour heart monitors, and the team compared standard clinic readings with day and night segments picked by hand.

Lenz found wide disagreement between repeat readings: the spread for the standard measures ran from well under half to nearly three times the first value. Night-time segments taken during presumed sleep agreed better with each other than daytime ones, but absolute agreement stayed poor there too. The authors blame both the loose real-world measurement process and natural swings in the body. They warn the readings cannot support decisions about single patients in this workflow.
pmc-13551527:
Afschin Gandjour examines in this 2026 article whether Germany's healthcare system spends its money efficiently, judging value from the view of its public health insurance funds. Germany spends a large share of national income on care, yet its health outcomes sit near the European average.

Gandjour compared system-wide costs per year of life gained, using national data from 2011 to 2014, against the cost-effectiveness reported for newly approved cancer drugs. Surprisingly, the whole system looked broadly as cost-effective as those new drugs. Changing assumptions about how much of the mortality decline came from healthcare barely moved the result. He argues the inefficiency may be spread thinly across many sectors rather than concentrated in one fixable area.
pmc-13551727:
Hui-Hui Shao, Dong-Yu Bao, and Yun Yang published a 2026 cross-sectional survey of oral care knowledge and behavior among older residents of Nanjing, China. Online questionnaires went to adults aged 60 and above by convenience sampling, and 294 valid replies came back from 314 distributed. The team asked what residents knew about oral health and how that knowledge related to daily practices.

Only about one in nine respondents showed adequate oral health knowledge in the reported scoring, with cosmetic dentistry topics especially weak. Adjusted analysis tied behavior to income, education, brushing frequency, toothbrush replacement, rinsing after meals, and several specific knowledge items. The authors call knowledge a changeable lever and urge targeted promotion for lower-income, less-educated older adults.
pmc-13554127:
Paulina Nowicka-Krawczyk leads a six-author team probing how green algae slowly eat away at brick and plaster in a 2026 study. Algae films dull building fronts and can weaken the materials over time. Five kinds of algae grew on brick and plaster for a year, in the lab and outdoors. The team mapped their small-molecule output with fine chemical tools.

Each kind showed its own chemical pattern, shaped by the surface it grew on. Plaster pushed algae toward stress-linked chemistry, while brick favoured steady growth patterns. Small organic acids turned up again and again, acids able to sour the surface and loosen metals. The team ranked the five kinds by likely harm, giving conservators an early warning list.
pmc-13555927:
Mahnaz Arshad and three colleagues test how print angle affects temporary three-tooth bridges from a light-based printer in a 2026 study. Bridges were printed at several tilt angles along two axes, twelve per group. A profilometer measured surface roughness, and a universal machine broke samples to find fracture load. Both printing directions shaped the results clearly.

The smoothest surfaces came from one tilt paired with a steep sideways angle. The strongest bridges shared that same tilt but paired it with no sideways angle. Where on the bridge the roughness was measured made no clear difference. The best angle thus depends on the goal: smoothness for comfort and looks, zero sideways tilt for strength. Clinics can tune printing to the case.
pmc-13558627:
Elloïse Fangel-Lloyd and five colleagues simulated in 2026 whether lightning can spark in the atmosphere of K2-18b, a much-debated exoplanet observed by the James Webb telescope. Weather on such worlds is speculation until physics constrains it. The team fed photochemical model atmospheres built from the telescope data into a validated plasma code. That code simulates streamers, the branching discharges that precede lightning bolts.

Breakdown in this atmosphere needs only about half the electric field required on Earth, marking it as more lightning prone. Streamers ignited in all three atmospheric recipes tested. Water vapour content changed how often inception occurred, tying the planet's debated composition to its electrical weather. The authors present the work as the first streamer simulation for an exoplanet atmosphere, a step toward forecasting alien storms.
pmc-13560427:
Wanwen Jia and Yitian Shao grade China's national medical resource allocation policies with a quantitative text-evaluation model. Their 2026 study screens out sixteen national-level policy documents, mines their keywords into a co-occurrence network, then scores each text with the PMC-index approach. Quality grades and time periods are compared for structural patterns.

The average index came to 6.67, which the authors read as relatively high overall quality. Weaknesses clustered in predictable places: thin forward-looking and predictive content, little medium- and long-term planning, and too few high-level policy instruments. Scores rose from an exploration stage into a deepening stage, then dipped modestly in the recent focus stage. The authors recommend strengthening the policy hierarchy, lengthening planning horizons, and refining implementation mechanisms. Their aim is a steadier, more systematic allocation framework for a system under reform pressure.
pmc-13562527:
Tahereh Mohammadi and five colleagues study a cell-death pathway that may let stray womb tissue survive in endometriosis. In that condition, lining-like tissue grows outside the womb, and weak self-destruction of cells may be part of the cause. The pathway rests on two partner proteins, Fas and its ligand, which together trigger a cell to die. The 2026 team grew stromal cells from misplaced tissue, normal-position tissue, and healthy controls, then measured both proteins in cells, blood, and fluid from the abdomen.

Misplaced and normal-position cells from patients carried less Fas protein than control cells. The misplaced cells carried more of the ligand, and they released more of its soluble form into their surroundings. Gene activity in fluid and blood cells shifted in opposite directions too. The authors read this as a survival trick: weak death signals at home, strong ones aimed outward.
pmc-13563727:
Rose Hosking and five colleagues take a portable handwashing gadget into three Fijian communities and ask, carefully, whether people actually like it. The Spatap is a silicone tap that screws onto a bottle, giving households a handwashing point without plumbing. The 2026 team handed out the devices, surveyed 207 people within a week, and scored acceptance with a seven-question method grounded in an established framework. Five months later they returned for focus groups with 22 participants.

Scores ran from 18 to 35 with a median of 29, signalling broad approval. Ease of use, water saving, and convenience won people over, and children found the taps simple. Effort and refill time scored worst; big households tired of refilling, some could not afford larger bottles, and minor leaks appeared. Background factors barely mattered. The authors judge the device welcome where portability counts, while urging cost checks against cheaper options before any wide rollout.
pmc-13569327:
Marion C. Lanteri leads a 2026 multicenter study checking whether delayed processing and long storage distort antibody tests for the virus that causes COVID-19. The question matters for nationwide blood donor surveys run by the two largest United States collectors. Paired blood samples were tested fresh, then after days of refrigeration or months of freezing.

Antibody readings stayed stable across delays and storage conditions for both spike and nucleocapsid targets, with only minor average shifts in some comparisons. Wide agreement ranges in one storage arm argue for care with individual samples. Overall, survey teams can trust results from samples that waited days before separation or sat frozen for months, supporting large pandemic tracking programs.
pmc-13570527:
Adèle Rohée-Traoré and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether facial photographs can flag Stickler syndrome, a rare collagen disorder whose eye complications can blind children before the condition is recognized. Machine learning models trained on two- and three-dimensional face photos learned to separate patients from healthy controls.

Full-face photos gave about ninety-two percent accuracy in both formats. Narrowing the three-dimensional view to the eye and nose region raised accuracy to about ninety-six percent. A camera-based screen could shorten the long diagnostic delays that make this syndrome dangerous, offering clinics a cheap, non-invasive first check while genetic confirmation follows.
pmc-13572327:
Liuqing Zhao and colleagues survey, in a 2026 nationwide multicenter study, problems outside the gut in 2,252 Chinese inpatients with inflammatory bowel disease across ten centers. Such extra-intestinal problems, from joint pain to eye and skin inflammation, add heavy burden, yet large Chinese data were scarce.

About seventeen percent reported at least one such problem, more in Crohn's disease than in ulcerative colitis. Joint complaints and mouth ulcers led the list, and mouth ulcers clustered strongly in Crohn's disease. Problems often traveled together, with joint disease tied strikingly to eye and skin conditions. In about a fifth of timed cases, the outside problem arrived before bowel symptoms, a warning for doctors chasing unexplained joint or eye inflammation.
pmc-13572527:
Jianqiang Tang, with nine colleagues, reports a 2026 research note on a gene that shapes how chickens respond to a gut parasite. The parasite, Eimeria tenella, causes coccidiosis, a costly disease of poultry that infects the cecum. A past gene scan had flagged three candidate genes in yellow-feathered broilers, and this note rechecked them in a commercial flock.

Gene tests on cecal tissue after infection showed raised levels of IL-6, an inflammatory signal, among the shifts tracked. The team then focused on one gene, SGK1, in cell tests. There, SGK1 shaped the levels of inflammatory cytokines, the share of cells the parasite's first stage entered, and rates of cell death by apoptosis. The other two candidates, FABP1 and BMP3, serve as comparison points from the first scan. The note offers SGK1 as a marker for breeding birds that resist the disease.
pmc-13573327:
Junyu Ma, with four colleagues, reports on a 2026 study of a heart measure that flags leftover high lung pressure after surgery for chronic clots. The surgery, endarterectomy, clears hardened clots from lung arteries, yet pressure stays high in some patients and recovery suffers. A simple ratio from an ultrasound scan may warn ahead of time.

The team reviewed 183 patients treated at a high-volume centre from 2017 to 2025. Leftover high pressure, set as a mean lung pressure above 30, hit 48 patients, just over a quarter. Those patients started with a lower ratio and higher vessel resistance. Both measures held up as solo predictors in the joint model. The paired model sorted risk a bit better and fit the data well, with steady results on repeat sampling. The authors back the pair for pre-surgery risk talks.
pmc-13573427:
Asma Ashfaq, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 field study of heavy metals in citrus groves in Sargodha, Pakistan. The district is famed for top citrus fruit. More groves now water with household wastewater, which can load soil and fruit with hazardous metals and put eaters at risk.

The team sampled irrigation water, soil, and fruit from groves watered by canal and by wastewater, then compared metal build-up between the two. That side-by-side design ties any gap in fruit metal levels to the water source rather than to chance. Health and ecological risk scores turn the lab numbers into plain terms for farmers and officials. The stakes are high on both sides: wastewater saves fresh water in a dry land, yet metals in food can harm over years. The authors aim to show where the trade-off tips.
pmc-13574727:
Lane H McCoy, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 case of a fungal bone infection in a child that looked like cancer. Coccidioidomycosis is a lung infection from a soil fungus of dry regions, and spread beyond the lung strikes under one percent of cases. Bone spread in children is rarer still.

The patient was a healthy 12-year-old with six weeks of growing pain in the left pelvis, night sweats, and weight loss, with no lung complaints. Scans showed a bone-eating lesion in the pelvis with a soft tissue mass, a picture that raised cancer fears. A biopsy instead found fungal forms with a giant cell reaction, and culture confirmed Coccidioides. Strong antifungal drugs, first by vein then by mouth, cleared the pain. At six months the child was fully active with pelvic function intact. The authors urge the fungus onto the suspect list.
pmc-13576027:
Adrian Hernandez Lopez leads a 2026 study of mildly low platelet counts at delivery and the risk of heavy bleeding afterwards. Postpartum haemorrhage is a leading cause of severe harm to mothers. Whether a mild dip in platelets, the blood cells that aid clotting, raises that risk was not well studied.

Records covered 305,794 pregnancies in a large health maintenance organisation from 2008 to 2020. Transfusion after birth occurred in 1.2 percent of the mild low-platelet group against 0.9 percent with normal counts, a small but clear gap. Rates of heavy bleeding, stronger transfusion need, extra procedures, and medicines to contract the womb were also higher. Every gap held after adjustment for other factors. The authors frame the risk rise as real yet modest.
pmc-13576327:
Noa Gueron-Sela and four colleagues ask whether a mother's depression risk after birth affects her baby's development differently across cultures, in a 2026 Israeli cohort study. Records covered 401,942 children born between 2014 and 2020 and followed at mother-child clinics to age two. Depression risk was scored with a standard postnatal questionnaire.

Higher maternal risk linked to more developmental delay in each of the first two years of life, by every measure used: recorded interventions, nurse judgement, and milestone scales. Yet the size of that link ran significantly smaller among Muslim-Arab families than among Jewish families, for every measure and both years. The authors read this as support for a cultural buffering idea, where strong family and community ties soften the blow. They urge services to build on those strengths.
pmc-13578227:
Ying Wang and colleagues measured how a warm ocean eddy reshapes tiny grazers that eat bacteria in the South China Sea. Eddies, swirling water masses, rearrange nutrients and food webs, but their depth-by-depth effects on nanoflagellate grazing were unclear. Using fluorescent-bead feeding tests inside a warm-core anticyclonic eddy, their 2026 study tracked two grazer groups at the surface, at the deep chlorophyll peak, and down to 500 metres.

Surface mixotrophic plankton, cells that both photosynthesise and eat bacteria, rose 2.8-fold and shifted to larger cells, raising bacterial turnover. Heterotrophic grazers also ate more, and dominated in the deep zone, rising 2.7-fold at 500 metres. The authors describe a depth-split response linking large-scale ocean motion to microbial carbon processing.
pmc-13578427:
Ronak Majid and a large team of co-authors dissect what makes a wheat stem strong enough to stay upright, in a 2026 study. Lodging, where stems bend or break near harvest, steals yield across wheat regions. The team measured stem traits along the first three segments of many wheat types, from wall thickness to fiber makeup, and hunted gene markers tied to strength.

The second segment from the base carried the day. Types that resist lodging packed that segment with thicker walls, more weight, more fiber, and more of the stiffening compound lignin. Weak types stretched the segment longer and thinner instead. Two gene markers each explained close to a quarter of the strength gap, giving breeders handles for tougher wheat.
pmc-13578727:
Samuel Akpasam Assam, Jonah Chukwuemeka Agunwamba, and Moses Udo Akpabio test ash from periwinkle shells as a strength booster for clay soil under roads, in a 2026 study from Uyo, Nigeria. Shells pile up at markets and eateries, and careless dumping harms the area. Clay dug near the town was mixed with varied shares of burnt, ground shell ash, then put through standard strength and density tests.

A dose near five and a half percent gave the best results. Crushing strength rose by about a sixth, and load bearing scores nearly doubled for dry samples, with soaked samples gaining as well. The mix also packed denser and drank a bit more water. Microscope and crystal checks showed new calcite forming in the treated clay, which helps explain the gain.
pmc-13579827:
Chan Zhang and colleagues map how brain networks miswire in teenagers with a first bout of major depression, in a 2026 study. Twenty nine adolescents who had never taken treatment were matched with twenty nine healthy peers of like age and sex. Resting brain scans were split into four big networks, and links were read both as steady averages and as shifting states over time.

Depressed teens showed weaker links inside and between three networks, covering self focus, salience, and control. A fourth link, between attention and salience systems, trended the other way, toward excess. Their brains also lingered longer in highly linked states and switched states less often. Weaker links tracked worse depression scores, while longer stays in the overlinked state tracked worse scores too.
pmc-13579927:
Kyle R Embry and colleagues pit a fully powered prosthetic leg against the microprocessor knees people already wear, in a 2026 crossover study. Twelve adults with thigh level limb loss took part. Each trained on a powered knee and ankle prototype for about ten sessions. Each then ran a full battery of walking, energy, and balance tests on both devices. A two month gap between rounds washed out learning effects.

The powered leg, far heavier, still cost no extra body energy to walk on, hinting its push made up for the weight. Yet walkers moved a touch slower on it, and step timing symmetry slipped a bit. Endurance and balance matched the standard knees. The authors say the prototype holds its own on effort but has yet to beat the incumbent, and they call for sharper shared test routines.
pmc-13582227:
Kaiqi Wei and colleagues wire up robot surgery console surgeons to catch the body's stress signals as they work, in a 2026 field study. Seven senior urologists wore brain, muscle, and heart sensors through one live operation each. To avoid breaking focus, each surgeon later watched the console video and marked when stress had spiked, giving one hundred fifty one rated windows to match against the traces.

High stress windows came with a higher ratio of fast to slow brain waves at the crown sensor. Shoulder muscle tension rose in the same windows. Heartbeats also crowded closer together and varied less, two classic strain marks. Many other signals showed nothing. The authors see paired video review and light monitoring as a workable way to flag the hardest moments of an operation for coaching.
pmc-13586327:
Zhiming Sun and colleagues find a disposal route that can make brain tumors answer to chemotherapy again. Glioblastoma is a fierce brain cancer treated with a drug called temozolomide, which damages tumor DNA. Tumors lacking the usual repair protein MGMT should be sensitive, yet many still resist, pointing to a backup repair path centered on a protein named ALKBH2.

Their 2026 study shows an enzyme called LMO7 grabs ALKBH2 and tags it for shredding, and cell stress strengthens that tagging. A single change in ALKBH2's code blocked the tagging and weakened the drug-sensitizing effect. Removing ALKBH2 made MGMT-free tumor cells die more readily under the drug, while putting it back restored toughness. Patient data tied high ALKBH2 and low LMO7 each to shorter survival, which frames the pair as a treatment lever.
pmc-13587427:
Markos Christidis and colleagues examine the support tissue around thyroid tumors for signs of how the cancer will behave. Tumors grow in a bed of tissue called stroma, and fibroblasts roused by the cancer, known as cancer-associated fibroblasts, can feed its spread. Their 2026 study stained tissue from 85 thyroid cancer cases for two fibroblast markers and for the scar-like growth called desmoplasia, then matched the patterns to tumor features.

One marker, alpha-SMA, ran higher in men's samples, in tumors over a centimeter wide, and in tumors with aggressive traits. The second marker, FAP, tracked with the amount of desmoplasia present. That scar tissue itself, oddly, ran lower in the larger tumors. The authors read the fibroblast signs as companions of progression in thyroid cancer and as possible handles for sorting patients by risk.
pmc-13587827:
Tsagkari and colleagues explore in 2026 whether the fluid that seeps from the gum margin can reveal how a young patient's teeth and skeleton are maturing. Such biomarkers could help orthodontists time treatment to growth.

The team collected gingival crevicular fluid from 54 young patients and profiled its small molecules with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, an untargeted method that catalogs whatever chemistry is present. Dental development was scored from X-rays by the Demirjian method and skeletal maturity from neck vertebrae shape. Of 63 compounds found, two stood out for dental age: cadaverine and the amino acid valine. Both rose during tooth development and fell in late stages, while two acids declined as dental age advanced. Cadaverine plus two other amino-acid relatives tracked skeletal maturation strongly. The authors call for broader profiling to confirm the signals.
pmc-13589927:
Mei Yang and ten colleagues review, in 2026, tiny drug carriers taken by mouth for bowel disease and bowel cancer. A swallowed drug must cross four walls in the gut: acids and enzymes, gut microbes, mucus and gut lining cells, and local immune tissue. Small and very small particles can linger at a sore spot and hold more drug there, which suits local care.

Yang and the team sort recent designs by the wall each one aims to cross or calm. They weigh gains in drug build up and stay time against open problems. Safe use in people, large scale making, and proof of gain in real patients still need work, the review concludes.
pmc-13590927:
Timothy Lawn and four colleagues probe a snag in a brain imaging method that links scan data to maps of chemical receptors in the brain. Those receptor maps overlap a lot in space, a problem called collinearity. The team tested all pairings across 19 receptor and transporter maps. Overlap grew fast as more receptors were modeled at once, they found, and stayed much the same at each map scale.

Using repeat scan data, Lawn and the team show that joint models lose trustworthiness as receptors are added, while modeling one receptor at a time stays stable. In a study of LSD versus placebo, the single receptor route more clearly found the known serotonin target. They advise the simpler route as the default.
pmc-13591927:
Yiting Wu and three colleagues trial, in 2026, an okra based eyelid patch against standard drops for meibomian gland dysfunction, a common cause of dry eye. The glands rim the lids and oil the tear film; when they fail, tears dry fast. Forty patients were split at random between the patch and drops pairing an artificial tear with an antibiotic. Eyes were checked over 28 days of care.

By the final visit the patch group scored better on symptoms, signs, tear film stability, and surface damage marks. The oil layer on their tears also thickened more. One patch user reported lid redness, with no real gap in side effects between groups. Wu and the team offer the patch as a fresh option for dry eye care.
pmc-13592327:
Andrés López-García and eight colleagues coax, in 2026, tiny metal particles out of a cerium oxide support to crack ammonia into hydrogen. Particles grown from inside the support sit socketed and resist clumping at heat, yet ceria normally refuses to dissolve the needed metals. Adding gadolinium into the ceria lattice changed that, letting ruthenium and rhodium dissolve and later emerge as specks near three nanometers wide, some as mixed alloys.

The ruthenium version cracked ammonia steadily for 260 hours, beating a surface coated rival and ranking among the best at moderate heat. López-García and the team credit the dopant for widening which metals can be exsolved. They see the trick spreading to other catalyst families that need stable, fine particles.
pmc-13593627:
Hatice Turgut and colleagues named risk factors for drug toughness and death in newborn blood cases in a Turkish critical-care unit. Gram-negative sepsis kills many babies, and multi-drug toughness tangles treatment. Their look-back cohort study read 197 babies with hospital-linked gram-negative blood cases found between 2010 and 2025.

Multi-drug toughness hit fifty-seven point nine percent, led by Klebsiella at fifty-one point three percent of samples. Wide enzyme output reached sixty-eight point six percent, and carbapenem toughness hit thirty-nine point one percent. Acinetobacter showed the highest drug toughness and multi-drug rates. Older age at onset, breathing machines, and prior drug use flagged toughness, while right early therapy shielded against it. Overall forty-two point one percent died within 28 days, driven by sickness rather than toughness itself. The authors stress right first-guess therapy.
pmc-13593927:
Juan Darío Ortigoza-Escobar and colleagues describe a new variant in KCNA1, the gene for the Kv1.1 potassium channel, found in a sixteen-year-old with autism spectrum disorder, borderline intellectual ability, and tremor. Changes in this gene usually cause episodic ataxia or epilepsy, neither of which this patient had, so the team tested the variant's effect in laboratory cells.

The altered channel passed far less current and switched off faster than normal, both losses of function. Yet it also began opening at lower voltages than it should, a gain of function mixed into the same variant. Mixed defects like these are rare in this gene family. The authors say the case widens what doctors should expect from KCNA1 changes, adding autism and tremor to a list that already spans many movement and seizure disorders.
pmc-13597527:
Sun Young Lee leads a twelve-author team mapping Parkinson's disease chemistry in place, layering metabolite imaging and protein measurement over the two brain regions the disease hits hardest. Their 2026 study used a toxin model of Parkinson's in rodents, imaging small molecules where they sit and sorting cells by laser to read their proteins in the substantia nigra and striatum.

Each region carried a distinct molecular signature in both layers, as expected at the lesion sites. Less expected were wide off-target changes rippling through connected circuits far from the damage, showing the model's footprint is anything but local. The authors argue that even a simple toxin model involves broad network reorganization, not just dopamine cell death. They present the spatial multi-omics approach as a foundation. It can be used to follow how that reorganization unfolds over time and across the brain.
pmc-13598027:
Enver Kerem Dirican reviews the state of automation in the IVF laboratory in 2026. He sorts the field into four domains. They cover embryo selection, freezing and thawing, and sperm injection. The fourth is the new frontier of fully integrated end-to-end laboratory automation. That frontier produced its first peer-reviewed clinical findings this year.

The research base is strikingly uneven. Deep learning embryo grading beats individual embryologists in retrospective tests, and large trials anchor the freezing domain, while other domains still sit at proof of concept. Clinician-side automation in the same treatment cycle, by contrast, rests on an older and broader literature, and Dirican argues the two sides must advance in parallel before system-level gains can appear. One pointed observation closes the review: the lab task where operator skill most directly moves outcomes, genetic testing biopsy, is precisely the one automation has skipped.
pmc-13612427:
Jingyi Zhang leads a seven-author team reading frailty off a pendant sensor in 2026. Frailty and fear of falling feed each other in older adults, yet both are usually measured by questionnaires needing a professional in the room. The team recorded forty-eight hours of chest acceleration from 146 participants and converted the activity streams into barcode-like patterns. Complexity metrics plus a bidirectional LSTM network fed a multi-task model that predicts both conditions at once.

The joint model scored F1 values of 93.12 percent for physical frailty and 86.27 percent for concern about falling. Because the two outcomes were learned together, the model could exploit their known interplay. The authors claim the first joint prediction of frailty and fall concern from real-world wearable data. Their pitch is practical: a cheap pendant worn for two days could flag elders before the spiral of fear, inactivity, and decline takes hold.
pmc-13613827:
Katalin Bodor and Zsolt Bodor report a 2026 analysis of the nutritional value of 60 bread products sold by wholesalers on the Romanian market. Bread is a daily staple, so its makeup matters for public health. On average the loaves held 1,026 kilojoules of energy per 100 grams, from 44.46 grams of carbohydrate, 9 grams of protein, and 2.52 grams of fat, plus 9 grams of fibre and 1.25 grams of salt.

Sorting the breads by type with cluster methods showed wide swings in energy, fibre, fat, and salt between recipes. Potato bread came out lowest in energy among the types checked. Shoppers get a clear comparison of what common loaves actually deliver, while bakers can see where salt and fat could be trimmed without guessing. The study treats a humble food with the care usually kept for more complex products.
pmc-13616127:
Shilin Zhong leads a team studying in 2026 which ultrasound findings during pregnancy point to a baby infected in the womb with cytomegalovirus, a common virus that can harm development. The team looked back at records from three medical centres from 2015 to 2024, covering 1,174 pregnant women whose amniotic fluid was tested for the virus after suspicious scan findings. Only 45, or 3.83 percent, tested positive.

Some findings carried infection rates above 50 percent, including bright spots in the brain, sticking inside the brain's chambers, an enlarged liver and spleen, and a thickened placenta. Babies with several findings were infected far more often, at 10.42 percent, than those with one finding alone, at 2.14 percent. The ranking helps doctors decide which mothers should be offered the fluid test and closer monitoring.
pmc-13619727:
Jéssica C S Alves, Christian E Schaerer, and Cláudia P Ferreira built a mathematical model for releasing mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia bacteria. Such releases can suppress the Aedes aegypti mosquitoes that spread dengue and other viruses, because infected insects pass the bacteria to offspring and block breeding with wild ones. Heat waves, though, can temporarily clear the infection and threaten the whole strategy.

Their model uses equations with sudden release pulses, matching how programs actually drop batches of mosquitoes at intervals. Analysis produced an explicit release threshold needed for the infected insects to establish themselves and persist despite heat-driven loss. Simulations checked the math and compared three Wolbachia strains with different fitness costs and heat tolerance. Extra runs tested cases where mothers passed the bacteria to only some offspring. The authors offer the framework as a design tool for planning release schedules under a warming climate.
pmc-13620127:
Agnes Andreason and nine colleagues studied which patients with asthma or chronic obstructive lung disease keep suffering symptoms long after COVID-19. Their cross-sectional study drew on a Swedish cohort surveyed in 2022, covering adults diagnosed in primary and secondary care. Among 494 patients with confirmed infection, fifty-nine percent reported lingering post-COVID symptoms.

Severe initial infection stood out as the strongest risk factor by far. Older age, female sex, and obesity each raised the odds, as did anxiety or depression and chronic pain. Asthma and COPD patients showed a higher symptom burden than reported in many general-population studies. The authors say these flags can help clinics spot, early on, which lung patients deserve closer follow-up after infection, rather than treating every case as equally likely to recover on its own.
pmc-13620827:
Kalliopi Straka, Eleni Christakou, and Baisakhi Banerjee report a three-year-old boy whose hidden birth defect nearly killed him, and propose an emergency routine. His stomach had slipped through a hole in his diaphragm and swollen inside his chest, crushing his lung and shifting his heart's housing, a crisis called tension gastrothorax. It first looked like a collapsed lung under pressure.

An X-ray showed a large air-and-fluid level filling the left chest, which gave the diagnosis away. A nose tube failed to drain the stomach because its entry had twisted, so the team used an emergency needle and drain straight into the trapped stomach, with instant relief. Scans then confirmed the hernia held stomach, spleen, bowel, and colon. Surgeons repaired it the same day. Lung injury and sepsis followed, yet he recovered fully. The authors urge teams to hold this rare mimic in mind.
pmc-13621227:
Alvin Turay and five colleagues review the Kush drug epidemic gripping Sierra Leone and spreading across its neighbors. Kush is a smoked mix built on plant material laced with synthetic cannabinoids and powerful nitazene opioids, and its recipe shifts from batch to batch. The reviewers searched medical databases from 2016 to 2025 plus government, aid agency, and media sources.

Use has been tied to sudden psychosis, thinking damage, severe illness, and rising deaths, though weak surveillance almost surely undercounts the toll. Drivers sit deep in the economy: youth joblessness, poverty, fast city growth, war's long trauma, and scarce schooling and mental care. Sierra Leone declared a public health emergency in 2024, yet the response still leans on policing while treatment and prevention starve. The authors call for a health-led, regionally coordinated strategy.
pmc-13623127:
Victoria A Rastrygina leads a team mapping how two protein families talk to each other inside the body. One family, the tumour necrosis factor superfamily, sends signals that control cell survival and immunity, and its members are already drug targets. The other, the small S100 proteins, bind calcium and were recently found to latch onto some of those signals and mute them.

Using a light-based method that watches proteins bind in real time, the team tested thirteen signal proteins against twenty-one S100 proteins. They found twenty-seven pairings, all needing calcium to hold, with strengths ranging from very tight to weak. Computer modelling pointed to shared binding sites on both sides. Changing one spot on an S100 protein, its hinge region, broke several pairings, which supports the map. The authors say this network could guide new drugs for diseases where these signals run wild.
pmc-13623827:
Kelsey I Gasior published a 2026 methods study comparing ways to judge which settings matter most in a mathematical model of a living system. Such models contain many rate values drawn from experiments, and sensitivity analysis shows which ones drive the results. The most detailed method is accurate but slow, so cheaper screening steps are often run first.

Gasior tests two cheap partners for the detailed Sobol' method: a ranking method based on partial correlation, and the Morris screening method, which flags important settings and interactions. The test case is a model of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a cell change involved in development and cancer spread. The two pairings sometimes gave diverging answers about which rates matter, which makes conclusions hard to draw. The author suggests the methods disagree because they probe different things, and recommends running all three together for a fuller picture.
pmc-13624227:
Mohammed Alrehili models the flow of a Maxwell nanofluid, a stretchy, particle-laden liquid, across a stretching sheet inside a porous material. Such flows sit inside polymer processing and cooling systems, and most earlier models switched on only a few real effects at a time. Alrehili's version runs many effects together, including heat generated inside the fluid, electrical heating, and properties that shift with temperature.

Equations were converted into a simpler form and solved numerically, with benchmark checks confirming the method. One factor stood out: when density falls as the fluid heats, the layer runs hotter while flow speed and particle spread drop, and heat and mass transfer at the surface climb. Making the medium more porous raised surface transfer rates, at the cost of higher drag. The author offers the results as design guidance for heat exchangers and nanofluid cooling, with the drag trade-off kept in view.
pmc-13624327:
Huiting Liu and colleagues re-examine the deposits behind an itchy inherited skin disease, primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis, and find fat tangled with the protein everyone blamed. The deposits sit in the upper skin, and the standard story held them pure degenerated protein. Mutations in a receptor gene, OSMR, cause the family form of the disease, but how they produce deposits was unclear.

Staining and chemical profiling of patient tissue showed the deposits carry loads of both protein clumps and lipids. In engineered skin cells and mice, losing the receptor's function drove both accumulations, and adding unsaturated fatty acids was enough to make proteins clump. The chain ran through a dampened signal switch and a raised enzyme that scrambles fat handling. Blocking that axis reversed both problems. The authors recast the disease as a fat-processing disorder as much as a protein one, with new targets to match.
pmc-13624727:
Bo Yu and five colleagues build a search system that designs brain-wave networks for warning of epileptic seizures before they strike. Reading scalp electrical signals, called EEG, is slow by hand, and network design by hand eats time and computing power. Their framework, CMS-NAS, mixes three network styles, convolutional, Mamba, and spiking, and lets an evolution-style search breed candidate designs.

The search scores each candidate on both accuracy and small size, keeping designs light enough for real use. Tests ran on two public data sets and one private set, and the found networks performed on par with strong hand-built rivals. Automatic mixing of network styles, the authors argue, can shorten the path from raw brain signals to a working seizure alarm.
pmc-13626027:
Annabell Coors, Yaakov Stern, and Christian Habeck, publishing in 2026, test whether the flicker of the resting brain helps explain cognitive reserve. The term names a puzzle: some people's thinking stays sharp despite an aging brain. The team used resting brain scans from 470 adults aged twenty to eighty. They measured how much each region's signal varied over time. From those measures they derived variability patterns tied to age and to four thinking skills.
