Patterns tied to memory, fluid reasoning, and vocabulary explained extra thinking performance beyond brain structure, age, sex, and schooling. The share ran between about a tenth and a fifth of the differences between people. In some regions the reserve patterns ran opposite to the age patterns. Flexible signal, the authors argue, is one way brains keep working well.
pmc-13628527:
İlknur Özkan and Seçil Taylan mapped nearly four decades of research on caring behaviours in nursing, the everyday actions through which nurses show care. Their bibliometric analysis covered 351 documents from 158 sources indexed between 1987 and 2025, charting who publishes, where, and on what themes.

Output grew steadily and sped up after 2016, led by the United States, Iran, China, and Turkey, though cross-border co-authorship stayed rare. Early work centred on patient satisfaction, while recent themes turn toward nursing education, empathy, emotional intelligence, and compassion fatigue. The authors describe a maturing field anchored by classic caring theorists and measurement studies, and they urge more international collaboration and cross-cultural testing of its tools.
pmc-13631127:
Ann-Cathrine Froitzheim and five colleagues compared real-world hospital costs for two intensive treatments in Germany. Both treat diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. One is engineered CAR T-cell therapy. The other is the patient's own stem cell transplant. Drug prices usually dominate this debate. So the authors left out the CAR T product's purchase price. They compared everything else using insurance billing and national inpatient data.

Initial care cost modestly more for CAR T patients. Follow-up costs ran far lower. Average inpatient bills came in at less than half the transplant figure. Hospital stays were nearly identical, at about twenty-seven days. Side effect profiles differed. Low blood counts were common to both. The authors say payment debates miss much of the true cost picture.
pmc-13632327:
Austen El-Osta and five colleagues analyzed loneliness and social capital in a huge volunteer survey across England. More than one hundred thirty-five thousand community-dwelling adults answered questions, making the dataset one of the largest of its kind in the United Kingdom. Loneliness was measured with two established scales. Social capital was scored from neighborhood trust, cohesion, and how much people help each other.

Younger adults, especially those aged sixteen to twenty-five, reported more loneliness, as did single, unemployed, and disabled respondents. People with nine or more friends had far lower odds of loneliness on both scales. Education pointed in opposite directions on the two measures, which shows that wording matters. Older, married, and retired respondents reported stronger social capital, while long-term illness and disability reduced it. Because volunteers chose to join, the authors treat the results as leads for later representative studies.
pmc-13638727:
Christian M. Frausto-Avila and four colleagues describe a 2026 method for sorting heart rhythm recordings with a small neural network instead of deep learning. Deep learning systems can read electrocardiograms well but need heavy computing power and large labeled datasets.

Their network uses seventeen features drawn from each heartbeat signal by math and signal-processing steps. It sorted five rhythm types, including normal rhythm and atrial fibrillation, with accuracy near ninety-six percent on two public databases. Because the model is compact and runs fast on a normal processor, the authors suggest it could suit low-cost devices.
pmc-13641927:
Fulai Yu and nine colleagues present a 2026 study of the genes of a healing plant rich in a valued compound called verbascoside. How the plant builds this compound, and why some plants hold more of it, was largely unknown.

The team built a full gene map of the plant and checked which genes were active in each tissue. That work laid out the whole path the plant uses to make the compound. Ninety-five plants grown side by side for three years pointed to one region of Hainan as the source of the richest stock. One gene sat under strong selection, and its active form tracked with richer plants.
pmc-13645727:
Ning Guo and six colleagues describe, in a 2026 paper, an ultrasound system that doctors can run by voice with help from large language models. Super-resolution ultrasound can show tiny blood vessels beyond normal imaging limits, yet its settings are complex and reporting is slow. The team's platform pairs custom imaging hardware with two AI models, one for language and one for image reading. Spoken commands are turned into imaging settings automatically.

The system then rebuilds the sharp images, measures vessel features, and drafts structured reports in about four minutes. Fourteen clinicians judged the reports well formed and consistent in wording. A built-in score adjusts filtering of the microbubbles used for contrast. The authors say the setup could bring this demanding imaging method closer to everyday hospital use in brain, cancer, and heart care.
pmc-13646727:
Jiawei He and three colleagues review how macrophages, versatile immune cells, rewire their energy use and how that rewiring steers their behavior in cancer and other diseases. Changes in sugar burning, mitochondrial power, fat handling, and amino acid use shape whether macrophages inflame, present targets, or calm down. Inside tumors, low oxygen, scarce nutrients, and tumor waste push these cells toward states that help the cancer hide, grow blood vessels, and resist therapy.

The review gives close attention to lactate buildup, cholesterol reshaping, and amino acid dependencies that starve T cells of what they need. A form of cell death tied to iron and fat damage, called ferroptosis, links metabolism with immune outcomes as well. Drug ideas follow from each metabolic node the authors map. They also warn that mouse and human macrophages differ, which can distort translation to patients.
pmc-13647327:
Ahmad Majed and eight colleagues report a fast, scalable way to make layered metal carbosulfides that mix titanium and niobium in any proportion. These sheet-like materials pair metallic layers with sulfur bonds, a recipe of interest for electronics and energy research. The team mapped how the mixed crystals behave as the metal ratio slides from pure niobium to pure titanium. Heat stability, lattice size, stiffness, and magnetism were all measured.

The titanium end member proved more heat-stable and stiffer, while the niobium end expanded more with heat and fell apart in hot air into a sulfur-bearing oxide. Lattice dimensions shrank in a straight line as titanium rose. High-niobium samples showed a magnetic shielding hint of superconductivity, which the team traces to trace impurities rather than the bulk material. Their synthesis route gives materials scientists a full, quickly made palette of this family.
pmc-13647427:
Marcus Vinícius F. Rodrigues and three colleagues simulate, atom by atom, whether noble metal nanoparticles dissolved in an amine liquid can help capture carbon dioxide. Rising CO2 from human activity drives climate disruption, and capture technology needs better materials. Their virtual systems paired platinum or palladium particles with the amine DETA, water, and CO2. Quantum calculations set up the molecules, and molecular dynamics then watched them interact, with a battery of stability and attraction measures.

The platinum system won on nearly every measure: it held its shape longest, showed the deepest interaction energy, and kept CO2 close with strong, stable contacts. The palladium version trailed in the same analyses. Because the whole study is computational, the authors present the ranking as a design lead rather than a proven device. Their next-step suggestion is a practical capture structure built around platinum particles in this amine.
pmc-13648127:
Park and colleagues link how often Korean adults eat delivered food with levels of bisphenols, chemicals that disrupt hormones, in their urine, in 2026 public health research. Delivery meals arrive in plastic containers, a likely exposure route. The team measured bisphenol A and its substitutes, bisphenol S and bisphenol F. They then tested whether delivery frequency predicted each chemical with social factors held equal and plastic-related habits such as receipt handling.

Each step up in delivery-food frequency came with a 1.54 percent increase in urinary bisphenol S after adjustment, a strong statistical link. Neither bisphenol A nor bisphenol F showed a real link, with their estimates near zero in the same models. Because Korean delivery containers are usually bisphenol-free, Park reads the bisphenol S signal as a marker of the delivery routine, including thermal receipts and labels. The authors call for tracing which delivery items carry the chemical.
pmc-13648227:
Garrett McKay and seven colleagues separate natural organic matter from the Suwannee River into fractions and compare their light-related behaviour. Dissolved organic matter shapes how sunlight drives chemistry in rivers, and separating it by charge-to-size ratio offers a different lens than the usual size-based methods.

The least mobile fraction proved lightest, least aromatic, and yet the most efficient at producing fluorescence and reactive oxygen species under light. The most mobile fractions were dominated by a tannin-derived phenol rather than lignin, contrary to common expectations. The authors argue that charge and structure, not just aromatic content, drive how this material interacts with sunlight.
pmc-13648827:
Vincent Dang and Nathan Grant Smith survey 633 undergraduates on bias toward bisexual men, called binegativity. Such bias rests on false tales, such as claims that bi men are loose or pass HIV to women. The team asked if HIV facts, stigma toward HIV shield drugs, and knowing bi people shift that bias.

Students filled forms on their HIV facts, their contact with bi people, and their views of bi men. More HIV facts and more contact each tied to less bias. Stigma toward the shield drugs tied to more bias. Contact did not change how the other links ran. The authors urge frank, gay-inclusive sex health teaching with true facts on HIV and its shield drugs.
pmc-13649627:
Alexander Muacevic and five colleagues report a man aged 51 with double vision and a palsy of the third eye nerve, whose scans and labs came back clean. The nerve steers most eye moves and the lid. Its palsy can spring from poor blood flow, a squeeze from a growth or artery bulge, or rare hot spots.

No nerve expert was at hand in his small hospital. A small-vessel cause was the top guess, but the blank workup left the list wide. Staff had to weigh watchful waits against more hunts with scant tools. The authors use the case to show how hard such calls are where backup is thin. They map the forks in the road for teams in like spots.
pmc-13649727:
WooYoung Joo and two colleagues tracked what students aim at in university gym classes and how those aims link to life skills over one term. Research has dwelt on why students join in, not what they chase. Their panel held 347 students in 26 class groups, surveyed at the start and end of the term.

Goals rooted in the joy of the task itself, called intrinsic goals, pointed toward better time management at term's end. A hint of a link to leadership faded once strict checks were applied. Goals rooted in looks or status showed no firm links to any of five life skills. Reverse paths, from skills back to goals, also washed out. The authors frame inner goals as the lever worth backing.
pmc-13650127:
Zhipeng Yang and three colleagues, publishing in 2026, review how oxygen levels shape life inside the gut. The gut is often called oxygen-free, yet oxygen actually varies sharply from the intestinal wall to the center and from birth through adult life. That variation decides which microbes can live where.

Newborn guts start oxygen-rich, favoring microbes that tolerate oxygen, and those early settlers consume it and make room for the oxygen-shunning species of the mature gut. In a healthy loop, mature microbes make short-chain fatty acids that feed gut wall cells, whose burning of those fuels keeps oxygen low and the barrier strong. Inflammation, antibiotics, or diet can break the loop, letting oxygen rise and harmful species expand. Oxygen-sensing proteins in host cells tie this balance to immune defense, making oxygen control a core part of gut health.
pmc-13650427:
Hongliang Jin and three colleagues review a signaling pathway that links lung cancer growth to the tumor's ability to hide from the immune system. Drugs that release the immune brakes have improved lung cancer care, yet most patients still respond briefly or not at all, and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway keeps surfacing as part of the reason.

The pathway and the PD-L1 checkpoint protein feed each other: pathway activity raises PD-L1 levels, while PD-L1 signaling inside tumor cells stokes the pathway in return, driving growth, spread, and drug resistance. The pathway also fills the tumor's surroundings with suppressor cells and exhausts killer T cells. The review catalogs attempts to break the circuit, from pathway blockers combined with checkpoint drugs to nano-scale delivery and natural compounds. Toxicity, missing predictive tests, and context-dependent effects still stand between the idea and durable patient benefit.
pmc-13651527:
Christoph Riesinger and one colleague report a two-metal catalyst that swaps fluorine for gallium on aromatic rings, attacking the strongest single bond in organic chemistry. Carbon-fluorine bonds give fluorinated compounds their prized stability in drugs and materials, and that same strength makes them miserable to transform afterward.

Their catalyst pairs nickel with gallium without any supporting ligand holding them together, an unusual freedom that lets the assembly switch between two-metal and three-metal forms as the reaction cycle demands. Spectroscopy, kinetics, and computation, together with isolated intermediates, identified the resting state of the catalyst and the slow step that breaks the carbon-fluorine bond. The payoff is scope: electron-rich fluoroarenes that refused earlier gallylation chemistry now react. The authors credit the dynamic cooperation between the two metals for capabilities no single-metal system had shown.
pmc-13651827:
Ruth Korankye and two colleagues study the only Clubhouse in Wyoming, a member-run community for people living with mental illness, asking how it answers the health inequalities of rural life. Rural residents face provider shortages, long distances, and structural barriers that deepen the disadvantage mental illness already brings.

Interviews with twelve members and four staff, gathered in late summer 2024 for an earlier stigma study, were reanalyzed thematically. Two themes dominated. First came the contributors: scarce mental health services and blocked access to essentials, both corroding mental health. Second came the Clubhouse's response, which touched economic stability, healthcare access and quality, neighborhood conditions, and social connection, the classic social determinants of health. Participants described the model as a supportive environment that rebuilds daily structure and belonging. The authors conclude that such communities deserve a place in rural mental health planning.
pmc-13651927:
Silva and colleagues tested in 2026 whether extra light at flowering improves pitaya fruit quality in Brazil. Pitaya, or dragon fruit, comes from cactus plants in the Selenicereus group and needs long days to flower well. The team gave three cultivars four extra hours of LED light each night during flowering.

Extra light raised fruit mass by about a fifth and made peel colour brighter and stronger. Pulp colour shifted markedly, and fructose, a fruit sugar, rose by nearly a third across the cultivars. Vitamin C also rose, though by a smaller margin. One cultivar, Boreal Red, gained extra sucrose and glucose on top of the shared gains. The authors conclude that night lighting during flowering can lift both eating quality and health-linked compounds.
pmc-13652627:
Mahgol Sadat Hassan Zadeh Tabatabaei led a 2026 review and pooled analysis comparing endoscopic and open carpal tunnel release, the most common nerve operation surgeons perform. Carpal tunnel syndrome progresses from tingling and discomfort to weakness and lost hand skill, and surgery becomes necessary when simpler care fails. The team pooled trial results searched through April 2024, totaling 1,568 open and 1,447 endoscopic procedures.

Endoscopic release returned patients to work about eight days sooner and cut scar-related complications sharply, with an odds ratio of 0.18. No clear differences emerged for revision surgery, permanent or short-term nerve injury, operation time, or overall problems. Surgeons get a balanced verdict from trial evidence. The keyhole approach offers faster recovery and fewer scar problems, but not a proven edge on safety or durability, so choice can rest on surgeon skill and patient priorities.
pmc-6323927:
David Mendez, Anna Gaulton, Patricia Bento, and coauthors described progress in the ChEMBL database in 2019. ChEMBL is a large open store of drug-like molecules and their measured effects on targets. Chemists mine it to find starting points for new drugs.

Recent work moves toward letting researchers deposit their own assay data directly. That would shorten the lag between an experiment and shared knowledge. The team also reports growth in compounds, targets, and curated papers. Open bioactivity data of this scale underpins much of modern computer-aided drug design. Regular releases add newly published assay results, so the store grows with the drug literature.
pmc-6472827:
Remco Bouckaert, Tim Vaughan, Joelle Barido-Sottani, and coauthors described BEAST 2.5 in 2019. BEAST 2 is a platform for Bayesian evolutionary analysis of DNA sequences. Methods in the field had advanced quickly in joint modeling of trees and traits.

The platform lets users combine sequence data with dates, locations, and fossil facts in one analysis. A package system lets specialists add new models without rebuilding the core. The update reports major speed and modeling gains. Evolution and outbreak researchers use it to estimate when lineages arose and how they spread in their own fields.
pmc-6546127:
Christos Kopanos, Vasilis Tsiolkas, Andreas Kouris, and coauthors described VarSome, a human variant search engine, in 2018. Interpreting a DNA variant means gathering evidence from many scattered sources. VarSome pulls those sources into one search page.

Users enter a variant and get its frequency, disease links, predictions, and literature in one view. The project also invites expert users to share judgments, building shared knowledge. Speed matters in clinics facing long variant lists from one genome. VarSome became a daily tool for geneticists triaging what a variant likely means. Links out to major genome browsers and drug databases sit beside each variant report.
pmc-7264227:
Danping Zheng, Timur Liwinski, and Eran Elinav reviewed in 2020 how the microbes living in the human body interact with the immune system. These resident microbes, known together as the microbiota, help train the immune system as it develops. They also keep shaping both the fast, general defenses and the slower, targeted ones throughout life.

The review walks through how this two way conversation works when the body is healthy, and how it breaks down in disease. The authors discuss the signals microbes send, the immune cells that answer, and what happens when the balance tips toward inflammation. Their account helps explain why gut microbes are now studied in conditions far beyond digestion, from allergies to autoimmune illness.
pmc-7503727:
Unai Galicia-Garcia and co-authors explained in 2020 how type 2 diabetes develops and takes hold in the body. This common metabolic disorder rests on two linked failures. The pancreas releases too little insulin from its beta cells, and tissues such as muscle and liver stop answering insulin's signal properly.

The review follows the damage that follows from that double failure, organ by organ and pathway by pathway. It covers the roles of genes, weight, fat tissue, and chronic low grade inflammation in driving the process. It also explains why blood sugar control alone does not capture the whole disease. For students and clinicians, the account ties everyday facts about diabetes to the cell level machinery beneath them.
pmc-7897327:
Xiuling Jiang and co-authors reviewed in 2021 the roles of m6A, the most common internal chemical mark found on RNA in higher organisms. This small modification is added to RNA as it is made, and it is widespread and ancient in evolutionary terms. A set of proteins nicknamed writers places the mark, while other proteins read it and change what happens to the RNA.

The review explains how this marking system affects the life of RNA molecules, from their processing to their breakdown. It then connects the system to health, surveying diseases in which the marking machinery goes wrong. Because the marks can be adjusted, they have become an attractive target for new kinds of medicine.
pmc-8125527:
Carlos Juan and colleagues revisited in 2021 the chemistry of reactive oxygen species, the reactive molecules often shortened to ROS. Living things face these oxidants constantly, both from outside sources and from their own metabolism. A large literature already covers how the molecules form and what they do in the body.

The review organizes that knowledge around the damage and signaling these species cause in the three great classes of biological molecules: DNA, lipids, and proteins. It then connects those molecular effects to the diseases they help bring about. By returning to the basic chemistry, the authors give biologists and doctors a firmer base for judging claims about antioxidants and oxidative stress.
porete-mirror-simple-souls-1927:
Marguerite Porete wrote The Mirror of Simple Souls in old French. Clare Kirchberger gave it English dress in 1927. Porete was a Beguine, a lay nun of the Low Lands. The Church burned her at Paris in 1310 for her book.

The Soul talks with Love and Reason on the path to God. At the top of the path, the soul is lost in God and wills no more. Church men of her day found that claim a grave risk to faith. The book rose from the dead in our age as a jewel of women's soul lore.
procopius-secret-history-atwater-1927:
Procopius wrote the Secret History in rage and hid it: a private blast at Justinian, his wife Theodora, Belisarius, and the whole court. It came out only after his death. Richard Atwater gave it English form in 1927. The book is the most famous character assassination to survive from the ancient world.

Where the Wars praise the emperor, this text calls him a demon in human shape, greedy, cruel, and false. Theodora's stage past and her crimes are told with glee. Half of it is gossip and some of it is plainly wild, yet it matches tax and law records at sharp points. Readers meet the other face of Byzantium here.
proust-cities-plain-moncrieff-1927:
Cities of the Plain is the fourth volume of Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time, published in French in 1921. C. K. Scott Moncrieff translated it into English in 1927. Its title echoes Sodom and Gomorrah, and hidden desire is its great subject.

The narrator watches the Baron de Charlus and begins to grasp his secret life. A whole hidden world of longing and double lives opens across Paris and Balbec. Jealousy toward Albertine starts to poison the narrator's own love. Proust treats these themes with frankness rare for his time and with deep pity. The volume is the darkest comedy in the cycle so far.
questione-sull-alchimia-1827: Questione sull'alchimia is an Italian work on alchemy whose opening pages are illegible in the scan: the text dissolves into broken OCR marks from which no sentence can be recovered. The one legible element is a library stamp of the Glasgow University Library, Ferguson Collection, dated 1921. Nothing of the work's argument, author, or printing can be stated from pages in this state.
radin-primitive-man-as-philosopher-1927:
Paul Radin, a student of Boas, argued in this 1927 book against a common claim of his day. Many writers said so-called primitive peoples did not really think or question. Drawing on his years with the Winnebago, Radin set out to prove the opposite.

Radin profiles native thinkers who debated religion, fate, good and evil, and the nature of things. He shows that every society has its skeptics and philosophers alongside its ritual experts. The book mixes argument with long statements from the men themselves, in their own words. It was a landmark challenge to the idea that deep thought belonged only to civilized nations.
rashridayatantra-1927-1927: Rasahridayatantra is a Sanskrit alchemy tantra shown here by its title page, dated Samvat 1984 and 1927, under a head of garbled scan numbers. The page credits the work to Sri Govinda Bhagavatpada. The commentary is called Mugdhvabodhini. Sri Chaturbhuja Mishra wrote it. Notes are by the Ayurvedacharya Sri Jaydev Vidyalankar. Motilal Banarsidass of the Punjab Sanskrit Pustakalaya published the book. It was printed at their own press.
reynolds-remarks-symmes-theory-1827:
Jeremiah N. Reynolds, a young Ohio editor, wrote this defense of Symmes in 1827. A harsh review of the hollow earth scheme had run in the American Quarterly Review. Reynolds took up his pen to strike back for his friend and his cause.

He meets the review point by point and holds the polar holes to be sound in fact. He goes past defense and calls for a state backed trip to the south seas and pole. That call bore fruit in time, and Reynolds helped spur a great sea voyage of the United States.
russell-outline-philosophy-1927:
An Outline of Philosophy, published in 1927, is Russell's survey of philosophy for general readers. He writes from the standpoint of the new analysis he had helped create. The book moves from perception to physics to man's place in the universe.

Russell treats knowledge as a structure built from sense experience, tested against the findings of modern science. Mind, matter, and value each get his lucid, skeptical handling. The book is generous to opponents and ruthless with fog. For readers who want Russell's whole view in one volume, this remains the standard choice, clear as glass and cool as water.
russell-why-not-christian-1927:
Why I Am Not a Christian began as a lecture delivered in 1927 and became Russell's most famous statement on religion. He examines the traditional arguments for God's existence one by one and finds each of them wanting.

The first cause, natural law, design, and the moral arguments all fail under his calm cross-examination. He then turns to Christ's character and teaching, and to the church's record of cruelty and obstruction. The lecture's serenity is part of its force: no ranting, only questions that will not go away. It has been reprinted ever since as a classic of unbelief.
sacco-vanzetti-frankfurter-1927:
The Trial of Sacco and Vanzetti, Louis Bernheimer's account of the case's key testimony, carries the motto The truth shall make you free. Its foreword notes how few murder cases held world attention for so long. Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, two Italian-born radicals, were seized in the Red Raids of 1920 and found guilty of killings tied to a payroll robbery at Dedham, Massachusetts. On April 9, 1927, they were condemned to the electric chair.

Bernheimer built his summary on Felix Frankfurter's book on the case. Frankfurter, a Harvard Law School professor, had worked from the written trial record itself. Bernheimer offers the shortened version because most readers never saw the testimony behind the verdict. By the foreword's close, protests had spread worldwide, many public figures had proclaimed both men innocent, and only Governor Alvin T. Fuller could halt an execution set for the week of July 10.
santayana-platonism-spiritual-life-1927:
Platonism and the Spiritual Life, published in 1927, collects Santayana's lectures on Plato read as a guide for the spirit. Against scholars who mined Plato for doctrine, Santayana presents him as a teacher of how to live.

The spiritual life, in his reading, is the mind's turn from appetite toward calm regard of lasting forms. He sets this Platonism apart from the church systems that borrowed Plato's name. The lectures are short and luminous, meant for general listeners rather than specialists. They show a thinker of matter honoring the tradition he could not join, with complete understanding and complete detachment.
santayana-realm-essence-1927:
The Realm of Essence, published in 1927, is book first of Realms of Being, the system of Santayana's old age. It sets out his doctrine of essences: the timeless characters of things, what anything is like when it appears to a mind.

An essence, for Santayana, is neither physical nor mental; it simply is the form that experience takes. Smells, colors, numbers, and ideals all live in this realm, contemplated by spirit without existing themselves. The argument is abstract, but the writing keeps his famous grace. This volume lays the foundation for the three realms still to come.
senior-introductory-lecture-pe-1827:
Nassau William Senior opened his Oxford professorship with an Introductory Lecture on Political Economy in 1827. He was the first man to hold a chair of the subject at Oxford, so the lecture had to define the science for a skeptical university. Political economy still smelled of radicals and stockjobbers to many dons.

Senior fixes the scope of the science: it studies wealth, not happiness, and it reasons from a few plain premises about human desire. He promises conclusions that advise governments without dictating to them. The lecture's care about what economics can and cannot prove set the Victorian agenda for the subject's method. Cairnes and Mill later built on the ground Senior marked out. The slim lecture remains the classic first statement of economics as a deductive science, delivered at the moment the subject entered the university.
sinclair-oil-1927:
Upton Sinclair published Oil! in 1927, his epic of the California oil boom and the Teapot Dome scandal years. Sinclair had lived in Southern California for a decade and watched the strikes, booms, and corruption at close range. Boston banned the novel for a brief love scene, which only helped sales.

Bunny Ross, the gentle son of a self-made oil baron, grows up between his father's boardrooms and the radicals who organize the oil fields. His friendship with Paul Watkins, a worker turned communist, pulls him between the two worlds. The novel sweeps through strikes, Hollywood sets, and Washington scandal. Oil! is the fullest fictional account of its era's defining industry, and the source behind the film There Will Be Blood.
spence-history-of-atlantis-1927:
Lewis Spence, a Scottish writer on myth and lore, summed up the Atlantis case in 1927. The History of Atlantis is the most complete early survey of the lost land debate. Spence knew Plato's tale by heart and read widely in dig reports and myth.

He weighs the old sources, the ocean floor, and the myths of many lands for signs of a sunken realm. The book gathers each school of thought, from the sober to the wild, in one clear line. Between the wars it served as the standard guide to the whole question. Every later Atlantis debate starts from ground Spence cleared.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5027:
Rutherford B. Hayes gives four yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from December 3, 1877, to December 6, 1880. Three stars part each address from the next. The first cheers Congress at its first regular session. Health, peace, and plenteous harvests bless the country. Bright hopes point to an early return of thriving. Hard years lie just behind the nation.

To make the country's peace whole stays the chief care. It must stay so till the work is fully done. Good citizens strive as one in that task. Both great parties pledged as much in 1876. Yet a wide fear runs through the land, Hayes notes. The gains of the late changes to the Constitution stand in peril. The good accord that prompted those changes may fail. The truce between the land's two parts may prove barren. Both parts once stood in arms against each other.
summers-geography-witchcraft-1927:
Montague Summers mapped the witch trials in The Geography of Witchcraft in 1927. The book is a mate to his History of the year past. Land by land, he tells where the hunts burned most hot. His own faith colors the tale, as in all his work.

England and Scotland get long tales of their famed trials and witch finders. France, Italy, and Spain add their own grim rolls of names. The New World closes the map with Salem and its kin. The book serves as a gazetteer of fear across three hundred years.
suzuki-essays-zen-buddhism-1-1927:
Daisetz Teitaro Suzuki was a Japanese scholar who spent years in America before publishing Essays in Zen Buddhism, First Series, in 1927. The book introduced Zen to the West in a serious, readable form. Nearly all later Western Zen writing builds on its ground.

Suzuki explains koans, the riddles masters set their students, and satori, the sudden flash of awakening they aim to trigger. He draws on Chinese and Japanese masters, mixing history with direct talk about the Zen view of life. His calm authority made Zen a live option for Western seekers, not just a scholar's topic.
ten-princes-ryder-1927:
Arthur W. Ryder translated Dandin's Ten Princes into English in 1927 for the University of Chicago Press. The Dasha-Kumara-Charita, from seventh-century India, follows ten young princes scattered by chance across the subcontinent. Each prince returns with a tale of disguise, love, theft, and clever escapes to tell the others.

Dandin writes the most ornate prose in Sanskrit, yet Ryder keeps the adventures brisk and funny. The book is the great picaresque of classical India, a rogue's tour of its courts and roads. Its frame of ten storytellers may have fed later tale cycles far beyond India. Ryder's complete version remains the standard English one. Few Sanskrit prose works read with such pace.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated May 13, 1897, No. 27 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a special inducement. The offer is the same atlas offer that stands in the number before this one. A subscriber who pays $2.50 for a new subscription receives Rand, McNally and Company's 1897 Atlas of the World. Countries do not move away, the offer says, but they change. Our knowledge of them increases too.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
John Ormsby translated this stretch of Cervantes' Don Quixote, Volume 2, Part 27. Chapter twenty-six continues the droll adventure of the puppet-showman, with other things in truth right good. The audience sits silent, hanging on the lips of the boy who explains the show, when drums, trumpets, and cannon sound inside the booth.

The noise soon ends, and the boy lifts his voice to present a true story taken, he claims, word for word from French chronicles. A show inside the novel lets Cervantes play with truth claims, as a puppet tale demands belief while the hero watches and judges.
thomas-life-buddha-1927:
Edward Thomas was a scholar of Pali who set out in 1927 to write a critical life of the Buddha, separating legend from history. His Life of Buddha as Legend and History reads the earliest texts with a detective's patience. It became the landmark scholarly biography of its generation.

Thomas weighs birth tales, miracles, and late embellishments against the older discourses that may record real memory. He rebuilds the teacher's career, his order of monks, and his death from that sifted evidence. Readers get both the man the records allow and the legend the centuries built around him.
thomson-new-guide-health-1827:
Samuel Thomson was a New Hampshire farmer who built a new scheme of cure. His New Guide to Health came out in 1827. He held that cold and blocked flow cause most ills. Plant drugs and steam baths, he said, could cure kin at home.

Lobelia, cayenne, and hot baths form the core of his plan. Thomson sold rights to use his scheme to homes all over the States. His revolt struck at high fees and harsh drugs of the trained trade. The book launched the first great wave of alt cure in the young republic.
tibetan-book-of-dead-evans-wentz-1927:
W. Y. Evans-Wentz edited the first Tibetan Book of the Dead in 1927. The source text, the Bardo Thodol, is a Tibetan Buddhist guide for the dead. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup did the English rendering that Evans-Wentz shaped and framed.

The book tells what the soul meets in the forty-nine days after death. Bright lights, calm gods, and fierce forms test the dead person's mind. Priests read the text aloud to guide the soul toward a good rebirth. Its arrival gave Western readers a first full look at Tibetan belief. Carl Jung and other thinkers took its scheme quite seriously.
tob-0127:
COINTELPRO was the FBI's secret program of watching and disrupting groups it judged dangerous. Its White Hate files cover Bureau work against white supremacist organizations in the 1960s. This file, released through the Freedom of Information Act, holds the headquarters record in its second sub-file.

Field reports, memos, and informant material show agents tracking the Klan and kindred groups, sometimes to block violence, sometimes by dirty tricks of their own. The papers are raw history, with the texture of daily bureau work. As a United States government document, the file is public domain by law. It documents both the hate groups and the watchers.
tob-10827:
Volume one of H. P. Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine, published in 1888 under the subtitle Cosmogenesis, unfolds her account of the universe's origin. Blavatsky claimed to comment on an archaic manuscript, the Stanzas of Dzyan. Seven rounds, root races, and cycles spanning millions of years structure her cosmos.

Hindu cosmology and Victorian science are stitched together into a vast evolutionary scheme, spiritual as much as physical. The prose is formidable and strange, full of Sanskrit terms and cosmic diagrams described in words. Whatever its truth, the volume is the founding scripture of modern Theosophy, and later occult movements have mined it ever since.
tob-13527:
A Hebrew text known as 3 Enoch tells how Rabbi Ishmael rose through the palaces of heaven. There he found Enoch himself, no longer a man but Metatron, the highest of angels. The work crowns the Jewish merkabah tradition, the mysticism of the divine throne.

Guides show Ishmael ranks of angels, rivers of fire, and the letters by which the world was made. Metatron explains his own rise from human scribe to prince of the presence. Strange and dense, the book preserves the boldest claims of early Jewish mysticism and shaped later Kabbalah.
tob-4027:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Social Contract, bound here with his Discourses, asks how free people can legitimately be governed. Man is born free, his famous opening declares, and everywhere he is in chains. Rousseau's answer is the general will: citizens obey laws they give themselves as a body, aiming at the common good.

The accompanying Discourses treat inequality's origins and the effects of the arts and sciences, arguments that made his name before the Contract. Together, the volume holds the ideas that electrified the French Revolution and still fuel arguments about democracy, representation, and freedom. Dangerous, brilliant, and endlessly contested, Rousseau writes as if the reader's chains were personal insults.
tob-4127:
Franz Cumont published The Oriental Religions in Roman Paganism in 1911, and the lectures defined a field. Eastern cults, Mithras from Persia, Isis from Egypt, Cybele from Anatolia, and the Syrian gods, spread through the Roman Empire's armies, ports, and slave routes. Cumont argued they conquered pagan Rome from within before Christianity triumphed.

Drawing on inscriptions, temples, and ritual remains, he traces a spiritual marketplace in late antiquity, where salvation religions promising personal immortality displaced civic cults. Later scholars corrected details and softened his grand claim, but the framing remains his. Readers get the classic account of how Rome's religious world changed before Constantine.
twelfth-night-pg1527:
An early Project Gutenberg file of Twelfth Night, or What You Will carries a banner warning that its proofing methods were primitive. An improved edition is named for readers who want cleaner text. The play then opens with its full cast: Orsino, Sebastian, Antonio, Sir Toby Belch, and Feste the clown among them.

Act one begins in an apartment of the Duke's palace, with musicians attending. Orsino speaks the famous request: if music be the food of love, play on. He asks for excess, so the appetite may sicken and die. The scene sits in Illyria, in a city by the sea-coast, as the cast page announces.
un-ga-res-27:
Hunger stalked the world in the first winter after the Second World War. Resolution 27 of the General Assembly was passed on 14 February 1946. It lays out the cause in plain terms. War had cut farm output. Draft animals and farm hands were gone. Drought had shrunk the wheat crop in lands that once grew the most grain. Rice was so short that famine loomed in some areas.

The Assembly urges all governments and peoples to act at once, with drastic steps. Crops must be gathered in full from the farms, and stocks must be saved and shared through the world bodies at work on food. The aim was blunt: head off wide suffering and death, and keep hunger from wrecking the work of rebuilding.
un-ga-res-a-69-27:
New kinds of mass-kill arms, not yet built, are the worry behind Resolution A/69/27, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Assembly recalls a chain of votes on the ban since 1996. Its aim is to head off fresh classes of weapons whose power to destroy could match the arms named in the UN's own 1948 test for weapons of mass destruction.

Talks at the Conference on Disarmament on the point are noted with thanks. The text holds that science will keep opening new paths to harm, and that law must move first. A ban agreed before such arms exist, it argues, is far cheaper in lives than a ban chased after them.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 27, adopted on 14 February 1946, answered the world food emergency that followed the Second World War. War damage, lost farm workers and animals, short fertilizer, and drought had cut wheat output hard. Rice was so scarce that famine threatened in places. The Assembly feared wide suffering if the next harvest also fell short.

Governments were urged to act at once and firmly. They were urged to gather crops well, save food, and cut waste. They were urged to push grain growing to the most for the coming season. States were also asked to publish full figures on their stocks and needs. Food bodies were told to share world supply news openly.

General Assembly resolution 69/27 (2014) renews the Assembly's long-standing call to bar new kinds of weapons of mass destruction. No new type of weapon with destructive effect like those covered by the 1948 definition should emerge. Determined that this should hold, the Assembly reaffirms that sound preventive measures are needed. It asks the Conference on Disarmament to keep the question under close review. When necessary, it should recommend specific talks on named types. States are called on to look with favor on any such recommendations.
un-sc-res-1027:
Macedonia's preventive force gained six more months in November 1995. On 30 November 1995 the Security Council extended UNPREDEP until 30 May 1996. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission a week earlier. The Council restated its support for Macedonia's independence and borders. It recalled its worry about events that could shake the young state. The force's work so far drew praise in the text.

UNPREDEP had to keep cooperating with the European security mission in the country. Member states were asked to look kindly on requests for help. The mission watched the northern border for spillover from nearby wars. It was the United Nations' first attempt at preventive deployment. Its renewals were routine while the region stayed tense.
un-sc-res-127:
A disputed zone around Government House in Jerusalem was placed under truce supervision by the Security Council on 22 January 1958. Jordan had complained in September 1957 about Israeli activities between the armistice lines. The Acting Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization had reported on 23 September 1957. Neither Israel nor Jordan held sovereignty over any part of the zone.

The Council directed the Chief of Staff to regulate activities inside the zone under the Israel-Jordan Armistice Agreement. He was to survey property records and settle who owned what there. As a rule, Israelis could not use Arab-owned property, nor Arabs Israeli-owned property. Civilian activities were to be discussed through the Mixed Armistice Commission, and works begun by Israelis in July 1957 were to pause until the survey ended. The talks had two months to finish, and the Chief of Staff had to report the result.
un-sc-res-1327: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 1327 is catalogued here under 2000. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1427: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 1427, this formal text is catalogued under the year 2001. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1527:
Côte d'Ivoire's small United Nations mission gained a few more weeks from the Security Council on 4 February 2004. The Linas-Marcoussis Agreement of January 2003 was being put into effect, with recent progress noted. The Ivorian president had asked in November 2003 for the mission, MINUCI, to become a full peacekeeping operation. The Secretary-General's January report recommended a stronger United Nations presence.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended MINUCI's mandate to 27 February 2004. It renewed for the same period the authority of the West African ECOWAS forces and the French troops supporting them. The signatories of Linas-Marcoussis were told to carry out their duties quickly. The Secretary-General was asked to prepare for a reinforced presence pending the Council's decision. The short extension held the line while the Council weighed turning a liaison mission into the full operation that followed weeks later.
un-sc-res-1627: Security Council Resolution 1627 dates to 2005, and the collection holds its official text through English Wikisource. The resolution is one link in a chain: it cites earlier texts and is cited by later ones. Preserved in sequence with its neighbors, it lets readers follow the Council's handling of its business number by number.
un-sc-res-1727: Under number 1727, a Security Council decision entered the official record, and this collection holds the record through English Wikisource. Resolutions are the paper trail of world security politics: each one small, the accumulation enormous. This entry preserves its one small piece completely, in the form in which it was issued and circulated.
un-sc-res-1827: Resolution 1827, adopted in 2008, survives here as a Security Council act in its official-record text. The transcription is English Wikisource's copy of the UN record. Inside, opening clauses carry the members' shared account of events; closing clauses carry their instructions. Both are preserved, so the decision can be followed from reasoning to result.
un-sc-res-1927: In 2010 the Security Council recorded Resolution 1927, kept here through a Wikisource copy of the official record. The document's authority is the Charter's, exercised by fifteen states in one vote. What that vote produced, findings and numbered decisions together, is preserved in this entry in the exact form in which it entered UN practice.
un-sc-res-227: Security Council business produced Resolution 227, catalogued in this library as a 1966 record in the DECLASSIFIED group. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-27:
Fighting between Dutch forces and the Republic of Indonesia drew the Council's first word on the conflict on 1 August 1947. Resolution 27 is short and plain. The Council noted with concern the hostilities in progress between the two sides. Indonesia was then fighting for independence from the Netherlands.

The Council called on both parties to cease hostilities at once. The dispute then had to be settled by arbitration or by other peaceful means. The parties had to keep the Security Council informed about the progress of the settlement. The text is a first step only. It did not judge the rights of either side, and it set no force in place. The Council's long involvement in the Indonesian question, which ran until independence, began with this call.
un-sc-res-327:
Zambia paid a heavy price for obeying sanctions on Rhodesia. It had cut its remaining trade ties with the illegal regime. That step closed routes Zambia's own economy depended on. On 2 February 1973 the Security Council praised the decision. It also recognized the special hardships Zambia now faced. A special mission of four Council members was already at work on the problem.

The mission, helped by six United Nations experts, had to assess Zambia's needs. New road, rail, and transport links were the focus. Neighboring states were asked to cooperate with the team. The text is a rare case of the Council counting the cost of its own sanctions. It tried to share a burden it had imposed.
un-sc-res-427:
Lebanon's new United Nations force needed more troops within weeks of landing. On 3 May 1978 the Security Council approved a rise from 4,000 to about 6,000 soldiers. The Secretary-General had asked for the increase by letter the day before. UNIFIL had been created that March to confirm Israel's withdrawal. The Council noted that some Israeli forces had already left. The rest had to go without further delay.

The Council also deplored attacks on the force. It noted attacks by irregular groups inside Lebanon as well. A closing paragraph restated the force's terms of reference. The build-up showed how hard the mission's ground would be. UNIFIL remains in south Lebanon to this day.
un-sc-res-727:
A deadly attack on European monitors sharpened the Council's push for a Yugoslav cease-fire on 8 January 1992. Five members of the European Community Monitoring Mission had died in an incident on 7 January. The parties had agreed an unconditional cease-fire at Geneva on 23 November 1991. An implementing accord on its terms had been signed at Sarajevo on 2 January 1992.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report of 5 January 1992. It endorsed his plan to send up to fifty liaison officers at once to help hold the cease-fire. All parties were urged to honor the Geneva and Sarajevo promises and bring about a full halt to the fighting. They had to take every step to keep United Nations staff and the European monitors safe. The Council restated the arms embargo of resolution 713 (1991). The liaison officers were the advance edge of the force authorized weeks later.
un-sc-res-827:
Reports of mass killings and organized rape in the war in Bosnia horrified the world in 1993. The Council had already decided, in Resolution 808, that a war crimes court should be created. A report from the Secretary-General set out how to build it. Resolution 827, adopted in 1993 and dated to 25 May of that year in later texts, is the founding act.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council approved the Secretary-General's report and set up the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Its one purpose was to prosecute people responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. The crimes covered were those committed there since 1 January 1991. All states had to cooperate fully with the court. They also had to change their own laws where needed, so the court's orders could be carried out. The tribunal's seat depended on arrangements to be made with the Netherlands.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Macedonia's preventive shield gained another six months under Resolution 1027. It was adopted unanimously on 30 November 1995. UNPREDEP troops watched the young republic's northern borders. Their presence aimed to stop the Yugoslav wars spilling over. The Secretary-General's report of 23 November 1995 backed renewal.

The mandate now ended on 30 May 1996. Members praised the force's calming role. They urged continued cooperation with European security observers in the area. States were asked to answer the Secretary-General's requests for support. A fuller review was also commissioned. He would report on every aspect of the mission by 31 January 1996, if possible. The Council would then judge the mission against regional events.

A strip of no-man's-land in Jerusalem is the subject of Resolution 127. It passed by a full vote on 22 January 1958. Jordan had charged Israel with acts in the zone by the old Government House. The zone lay between the truce lines of 1949. A UN truce chief had filed a report on the area in 1957.

The Council noted that no side held sway over any part of the zone. It told the truce chief to run all acts inside it under the 1949 pact. He had to weigh who owned each plot of land. Jews could not use Arab-owned plots, nor Arabs Jewish-owned ones, unless both agreed. He was also told to survey land records to fix who owned what.

How the United Nations runs peacekeeping is itself the subject on 13 November 2000. A major review of peace operations, known as the Brahimi report, had just landed, along with the Secretary-General's plan for carrying it out. An annex to the text spells out the changes the Council backed.

The annex promises missions clear, credible orders they can actually carry out, backed by real strength where deterrence is needed. It asks the United Nations to join peace talks early when a settlement may lead to peacekeepers being sent. Better planning, faster deployment, and closer work with regional groups are also promised, with the Council checking progress over time.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 29 July 2002, and the Abkhazia conflict is taken up again. As in January, the Council recalled the October 2001 shooting down of a UNOMIG helicopter, which killed nine people. Those responsible had still not been found, and talks on the core dispute remained stuck.

The lack of progress is again called unacceptable, and breaches of the 1994 Moscow ceasefire agreement are condemned. Both sides are urged to rebuild trust, restart joint work, and act on earlier confidence measures. Georgia is asked to improve security for joint patrols in the Kodori Valley, and both sides are pressed to improve law and order in the Gali district.

Resolution 1527, adopted unanimously on 4 February 2004, buys a few weeks for the UN political mission in Côte d'Ivoire. The mission, MINUCI, was helping carry out the Linas-Marcoussis peace agreement after civil war divided the country. Côte d'Ivoire's president had asked for MINUCI to become a full peacekeeping operation, and a January report from the Secretary-General supported a bigger deployment.

The Council extended MINUCI's mandate until 27 February 2004 and renewed the authorization for French and West African forces backing the peace process. The short fuse was deliberate: the Council was about to decide on a full operation, which arrived weeks later as UNOCI, with thousands of troops.

Sudan's mission, UNMIS, is extended until 24 March 2006 on 23 September 2005. The north-south peace agreement was being carried out, and a Government of National Unity had been formed, a historic step. The country's First Vice President had died in a crash in July, yet both parties kept working to hold the peace together.

The parties are urged to meet their remaining promises under the peace deal, above all setting up the Assessment and Evaluation Commission. Reports are asked for every three months on the mission's work. Troop-contributing countries are urged to study the Secretary-General's guidance closely. The extension kept international support behind the deal while Darfur remained a separate, unresolved crisis.

Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions are renewed until 31 October 2007 on 15 December 2006. Expert panel reports in October and December described a crisis that persisted and worsened, with heavy humanitarian costs and large-scale displacement. The measures renewed are the arms embargo, travel bans, and asset freezes first set in 2004 and added to the year after.

Acting under Chapter VII, all Ivorian parties, including the transitional government, are demanded to stop blocking the peace process and the work of the United Nations operation and French forces. The Secretary-General and France are asked to report on obstructions. States, above all in the region, must report on their enforcement, and the measures would be reviewed at the end of the period.

UNMEE, the Ethiopia-Eritrea mission, is terminated on 30 July 2008, effective 31 July 2008. Eritrea's restrictions had made the mission's work impossible, forcing its troops out of the border zone that February. The two countries, the Council says, share responsibility for carrying out the Algiers Agreements they signed.

Ethiopia and Eritrea are demanded to meet their duties under those agreements in full, including respect for the Temporary Security Zone and the boundary ruling they accepted as final and binding. The Secretary-General is asked to explore further contacts with both countries and to keep the Council informed. The Council stands ready to help the two sides settle the border dispute and normalize their relations.

Five months after a huge earthquake devastated Haiti, the Security Council adopted Resolution 1927 on 4 June 2010. The quake of 12 January 2010 had wrecked government buildings and killed United Nations staff. Large camps of displaced people had formed, and they brought new risks. The resolution concerns MINUSTAH, the United Nations mission that was already working in Haiti.

The Council authorized 680 extra police as a temporary surge. That raised the mission's limits to 8,940 troops and 4,391 police in total. The extra police were to focus on building up the Haitian National Police. The mission also had to protect people in the camps and fight sexual violence and gang crime. It had to help Haiti prepare and run its coming elections. The surge was a short-term answer to the emergency, not a permanent increase.

Who would lead the United Nations into 1967 was the single question behind Resolution 227, adopted at a private meeting on 18 October 1966. U Thant, the Secretary-General named in the text, had said he was willing to consider serving until the end of the General Assembly's session that year. The Council recommended that the General Assembly extend his appointment to that point. The Council itself would finish considering the appointment question in the meantime. The text records one step in a handover, not a final choice.

One of the young Council's first acts backed Indonesia's break from Dutch rule. On 1 August 1947, it adopted Resolution 27. Dutch forces and the Republic of Indonesia were then at war. The republic had claimed freedom from the Netherlands after the Second World War. The text notes the fighting with concern.

Both parties must stop fighting at once, the Council says. They must then settle their dispute by talks or other calm means. They must keep the Council posted on progress. The vote was taken in parts, not on the whole text. The move was the Council's first step into a colonial war. That role grew as empires fell in the decades after.

Zambia paid a steep price for standing by the Rhodesia bans. Its trade ran south, through the banned land. In 1973 Lusaka chose to cut the last links. That meant new roads, rails, and ports had to be found fast. Resolution 327 passed on 2 February 1973 by fourteen votes to none. The Soviet team held back.

The Council praised Zambia's choice in warm terms. It took full note of the pain the move would cause. A team of four Council men would judge Zambia's needs. Six UN aides would help them weigh the task. New routes by road, rail, air, and sea were the goal. Near states had to help the team work. Its word was due by 1 March 1973. The file shows the bans' cost fell on friends too.

A young peace force in Lebanon needed more troops in 1978. UNIFIL had deployed that March after Israel invaded the south. The Secretary-General wrote on 1 May asking for a bigger force. Resolution 427 passed on 3 May 1978. Twelve members voted yes. Two Soviet bloc states held back.

The Council agreed to raise the force. It grew from four thousand troops to about six thousand. The text notes that some Israeli units had pulled out. It tells Israel to finish the pullout from all of Lebanon at once. Attacks on the UN force drew sharp words. All sides in Lebanon were told to respect the blue helmets in full.

On 8 January 1992 the Council passed Resolution 727 by a full vote. It deals with a weak truce in Yugoslavia and a grim attack. The day before, five men of a European watch team died when their craft was shot down. At the same time, the warring sides had signed a pact at Sarajevo on 2 January. It set out how to keep the truce agreed at Geneva in November.

The Council backed the UN chief's report of 5 January and praised his work. It cheered the Sarajevo pact. It also backed his plan to send up to fifty army liaison men to Yugoslavia at once. Their job was to help hold the truce. A much larger UN force came the next month.

War crimes in Bosnia drove the Council to build a court in 1993. On 25 May, it adopted Resolution 827 under Chapter VII. Reports spoke of mass killings and mass rape of women. Ethnic cleansing was still going on. The Council said it was set on ending such crimes.

The text creates an ad hoc court for the former Yugoslavia. The court will try those charged with grave breaches of the laws of war since 1991. The text also adopts the court's statute, its rule book. All states must help the court in full. They must shape their home laws to fit its demands. The seat was left open, pending a deal with the Netherlands.
undset-the-cross-kristin-lavransdatter-i:
Undset closes her famous trilogy with The Cross, in Archer's 1927 English version. Kristin, now widowed and old, looks back on a life of love, pride, sin, and loss. Norway in her last years faces the terror of the Black Death.

Seeking peace at last, Kristin leaves her estate and ends her days in a convent. There she serves the sick as plague sweeps the land. Faith, long resisted, becomes her final refuge and strength. The long arc from wilful girl to humble penitent ends here, and many readers count the trilogy among the great novels of its century.
vagbhata-rasaratnasamuccaya-1927-1927: Sanskrit title pages, printed in Devanagari type, name the Rasaratnasamuccaya of Vagbhata. The work is a classic on rasa, the art of medicines made from minerals and metals. The edition calls itself the first, printed at Calcutta in 1927. It adds a commentary named Rasaratnasamuccayabodhini, by two pandit editors whose names stand on the title page in Sanskrit. Pages present here are title pages only. The scan renders the script roughly, so the verses of the text itself are not shown.
whitehead-symbolism-1927:
Symbolism: Its Meaning and Effect, published in 1927, prints Whitehead's Barbour-Page Lectures at the University of Virginia. In three lectures he asks how symbolism, in language, ritual, and art, mediates between perception and meaning.

Whitehead argues that we perceive the world in two modes: direct presentational immediacy, and causal efficacy, the heavy pressure of the past. Symbols fuse the two, and error enters when the symbol is mistaken for what it stands for. The lectures are among his most accessible. They form a bridge between his philosophy of nature and the great system of Process and Reality.
whitney-v-california-1927:
Whitney v. California is a 1927 decision of the United States Supreme Court. The text opens with a numbered summary of points on review of state court rulings. A federal question, the court says, must appear on the record and must have been decided below. Later points turn to Anita Whitney and the Communist Labor Party of California.

Whitney had helped form the party, which the state charged broke its Criminal Syndicalism Act. That act barred teaching or aiding crime or sabotage as a path to change. The court treated her knowledge of the party's aims as a matter for the jury's verdict. Free speech claims meet state power in this famed case. The full opinion follows the summary.
woolf-to-lighthouse-1927:
Virginia Woolf published To the Lighthouse in 1927, drawing on her childhood summers in St Ives, Cornwall. Her parents stand behind Mr and Mrs Ramsay, the novel's central pair. Woolf considered it her best book, and many readers agree.

The Ramsays plan a boat trip to the lighthouse that bad weather cancels. Their young son James longs for the trip while guests, including the painter Lily Briscoe, watch the family's tensions. A bare middle section then sweeps ten years past: war, deaths, an emptying house. In the last part the trip finally happens, and Lily finishes her painting. Woolf turns time and memory into the real plot.
wurzburg-hexenverbrennung-1627:
Burnings at Würzburg and Bamberg fill a German pamphlet of 1627, written while the trials still ran. HexenVerbrennung Bistum Würzburg Bamberg reports the work of the two prince-bishops' courts. In those lands the hunt for witches burned as hot as anywhere in Europe.

The pamphlet tells who was seized, what was charged, and how the fires were lit, in the plain style of the day's news. It treats the burnings as just and needful work, and says so openly. That tone is the point for modern readers. The print shows how mass trials were sold to the public as they happened.
xenophon-ephesus-ephesian-tale-rooke-172:
The Ephesian Tale, by Xenophon of Ephesus, is one of the five ancient Greek novels that survive whole. It tells of Abrocomas and Anthia, a beautiful pair who marry at Ephesus and are then torn apart by fate. John Rooke's English version of 1727 was the first ever made of the tale.

Pirates, false deaths, cruel masters, and long sea roads keep the lovers apart across the Mediterranean world. Both stay faithful through every trial, and the gods of Ephesus bring them home at last. The plot of the Greek romance, with its storms and near misses, starts here in near-full form. Rooke's old English keeps its period charm.
